design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial in an inpatient research unit: 20 adults with cocaine dependence, recruited by newspaper advertisement and admitted soon after last use, were randomized 1:1 to modafinil or placebo for the first weeks of abstinence. Nocturnal polysomnography on three nights in each of abstinence weeks 1, 2 and 3 (averaged per week), multiple sleep latency tests on one day each week, morning and evening visual analogue sleep and alertness ratings and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale. Twelve healthy men without drug use, recorded on a single night after an adaptation night, served as an unrandomized reference group for week 3.
can_establish: Whether modafinil, compared with placebo, changed polysomnographic sleep, daytime sleep latency and self-rated sleep and sleepiness during the first three weeks of supervised abstinence; and, as an observational time trend within both arms, how measured and self-rated sleep changed over those weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether modafinil helps sleep outside a supervised inpatient unit with fixed bedtimes, no caffeine and no napping, or whether better sleep reduces relapse (not tested); whether the sleep changes over abstinence are caused by stopping cocaine rather than by the unit routine (no group that kept using, and no group without cocaine dependence followed over the same weeks); effects in people who use cocaine without dependence.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisements for cocaine research: 44 passed phone screening, 29 qualified at interview, 21 entered and 20 completed; most saw the study as their only route to inpatient treatment (Methods › Cocaine Dependent Participants; Patient perspectives).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV current cocaine dependence by psychiatrist interview; urine positive for cocaine and negative for other drugs at admission. Excluded: chronic medical or neurological conditions, dependence on substances other than cocaine and nicotine, other Axis I diagnoses, psychoactive prescription medicines in the past year; no history of a sleep disorder, and light caffeine use only.
sample.demographics: Mean age 44 (SD 7) with placebo and 40 (SD 5) with modafinil; 16 men and 4 women (9 and 1 with placebo, 7 and 3 with modafinil); 13 African American and 7 white; 3.2 and 3.3 days since last cocaine use on the first study day; baseline Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index 4.3 and 3.5; self-reported use in the previous 90 days given in Table 1 (some cells garbled; see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: One of 21 left voluntarily shortly after admission and was not analysed (arm not stated); all 20 others completed.
sample.selection_effects: Mostly treatment-seeking volunteers (18 of 20 in the text, 16 of 20 in Table 1) without other psychiatric or sleep disorders, light caffeine use and limited other substance use; paid $500 for completion.

exposure.measurement: Randomized, double-blind study medicine given on the unit; abstinence confirmed by urine screens three times a week in a supervised unit.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: modafinil 400 mg or placebo by mouth every morning at 07:30 for 16 days (study days 1 to 16), starting within 3 days of admission, that is between the 2nd and 6th day of abstinence; the dose could be lowered to 200 mg for intolerance and was lowered in one participant on days 3 and 4 because of palpitations. Fixed time in bed 23:00 to 07:00; polysomnography on nights 1 to 3, 7 to 9 and 14 to 16 after an adaptation night; multiple sleep latency tests at 11:30, 14:00 and 16:30 on days 2, 8 and 15 (three naps, ended after three epochs of sleep); Stanford Sleepiness Scale at 10:00, 15:30 and 21:00. Caffeine-free unit, no daytime napping, smoking allowed at three 15-minute outdoor breaks a day.
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other substances (except nicotine) excluded; urine negative for other drugs at admission. Past-90-day alcohol use averaged 117 (SD 133) drinks with placebo and 75 (SD 86) with modafinil; no participant showed alcohol withdrawal. Tobacco smoking continued at set breaks.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Supervised inpatient abstinence verified by urine toxicology three times a week; study weeks 1 to 3 correspond roughly to abstinence days 2 to 6 through about day 20.

comparison.controls: Placebo arm (10). For the week-3 comparison, 12 healthy men aged 30 to 50 (mean 39, SD 9) with no drug or psychiatric history, sleeping in the same laboratory for one adaptation and one experimental night but living outside the unit and receiving no capsule.
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1 (method and concealment not described); the arms did not differ significantly in age, sex, race, substance use, days abstinent or baseline sleep quality (Table 1). The healthy men were chosen to match the age range; they drank less alcohol and had non-significantly lower baseline PSQI.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep before cocaine use is unknown; the healthy reference group differs in sex, setting, number of recorded nights and drug history.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Healthy reference men had no substance use history, including nicotine.

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography (two central EEG channels, EOG, chin EMG, ECG; scored to American Academy of Sleep Medicine criteria by one scorer blinded to study day and group): sleep onset latency, total sleep time, N1-2, N3 (slow-wave) and REM time, REM latency. Modified multiple sleep latency test. Visual analogue ratings on waking (sleep quality, depth, feeling rested, alertness) and at bedtime (alertness that day). Stanford Sleepiness Scale three times a day. Adverse events.
outcomes.validity_norms: Polysomnography and the multiple sleep latency test are standard, though the test was shortened here and occipital leads were missing; the visual analogue scales are based on the St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire.
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disturbance as longer sleep latency, shorter total sleep and less slow-wave or REM sleep; 'normalizing' as no significant difference from the healthy reference group at week 3.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six polysomnographic measures, daytime sleep latency, five visual analogue ratings and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale were each tested for drug, week and interaction effects, with post-hoc tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Polysomnograms scored blind to day and group; blinding of the sleep latency tests not stated; self-ratings by participants (blinding integrity not assessed).

analysis.effect_sizes: Linear mixed models (treatment between, week within). Modafinil main effects: sleep onset latency F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027; N3 time F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029. Drug by week interactions: total sleep time F(2,36) = 7.4, p = 0.0021; REM latency F(2,36) = 3.6, p = 0.039; REM time F(2,36) = 3.5, p = 0.04; week-3 post hoc: longer total sleep F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013, shorter REM latency F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013, REM time not different at any week (p > 0.17). Daytime sleep latency, week 1: 15 (SEM 2) minutes with modafinil against 10 (SEM 2) with placebo, F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04. Stanford Sleepiness Scale: drug trend F(1,144) = 3.4, p = 0.069; drug by week by time-of-day interaction F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036. Group means for the polysomnographic measures are shown only in figures, so no standardized effect sizes or intervals can be given.
analysis.covariates: None reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration is mentioned (page searched for registration terms).
analysis.selective_reporting: All planned sleep outcomes appear to be reported, but only as test statistics and figures; no means, SDs or intervals for the polysomnographic outcomes are given in the text.
analysis.power: The authors say the study was powered only to detect the previously observed changes over abstinence within each group, not drug effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over three weeks of supervised abstinence, measured sleep got worse on most measures (longer time to fall asleep, shorter total and REM sleep) while slow-wave sleep rose and self-rated sleep improved. Compared with placebo, modafinil shortened time to fall asleep and increased slow-wave sleep throughout, lengthened total sleep and shortened REM latency in week 3, lengthened daytime sleep latency in week 1 only, and lowered some daytime sleepiness ratings; it did not change self-rated sleep. More people on modafinil had adverse events (6 of 10 against 2 of 10).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that modafinil "promotes nocturnal sleep, normalizes sleep architecture, and decreases daytime sleepiness". Gaps: (1) 'normalizes' rests on post-hoc comparisons at one week with 12 unrandomized healthy men recorded on one night outside the unit, and total sleep with modafinil was still below theirs; (2) the abstract says abstinence worsened all measured outcomes, but slow-wave sleep increased; (3) the discussion says modafinil reduced the REM-sleep deficit, but no week showed a REM-time difference; (4) the daytime-sleepiness benefit on the objective test was confined to week 1; (5) adverse events, more frequent with modafinil, are not weighed in the conclusions. The authors acknowledge the small sample and powering.

timeline.event: Morgan et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend 82:238-249) describe 'occult insomnia': measured sleep worsening over abstinence while self-rated sleep improves, in a separate inpatient sample from the same group.
This trial: first study of modafinil on sleep in people abstinent from cocaine, by the authors' account; it reproduces the 2006 time course in its placebo arm.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial of modafinil on sleep; the abstinence time course has been reported by the same group in earlier samples (not read here), so it is replicated only within one team. Larger outpatient trials of modafinil for cocaine dependence exist but were not read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA011744-06 and KL2RR024138; State of Connecticut Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Yale University and Harvard Medical School sleep researchers; the first author also reported palpitations with modafinil in a letter cited in the paper.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, registered, double-blind trial of modafinil against placebo (and against non-drug sleep support) in people stopping cocaine, with outpatient sleep measured objectively, a healthy and a continuing-use comparison followed over the same weeks, blinding checked, adverse events recorded, and relapse as an outcome.

domains.note: Randomized 1:1; sequence generation and concealment not described; arms similar at baseline on the tabulated variables.
Double-blind with placebo, but modafinil is a wake-promoting drug and adverse events were three times as frequent on it; blinding integrity not checked. Inpatient routine identical across arms.
One of 21 left shortly after admission; all 20 others completed.
Polysomnography scored blind to day and group (low risk); self-rated sleep and sleepiness by participants who may have recognised modafinil.
No registration; 13 outcomes each tested for several effects without correction; values reported mostly as test statistics and figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns rather than high because the main sleep outcomes are objective and blind-scored and attrition is negligible; the concerns are the undescribed randomization, possible functional unblinding for self-ratings, many outcomes without correction and no registration. With 10 people per arm, the estimates are imprecise. May be cited for the direction of modafinil's effects on polysomnographic sleep and sleepiness under inpatient conditions, and, as an observational time trend, for measured sleep worsening while self-rated sleep improves over early cocaine abstinence; not for 'normal' sleep with modafinil, nor for effects outside a supervised unit.

key_findings.finding: Of 44 people with cocaine problems who passed phone screening, 29 qualified, 21 entered and 20 completed (10 modafinil, 10 placebo); the arms were similar in age (44 and 40), sex, race, days since last cocaine use (3.2 and 3.3), substance use and baseline sleep quality.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cocaine Dependent Participants; Results › Demographics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Across both arms, abstinence week affected every polysomnographic measure; from week 1 to week 3 sleep onset latency increased (t(36) = -4.9, p < 0.0001), total sleep time fell (t(36) = 2.8, p = 0.008), REM sleep time fell (t(36) = 3.0, p = 0.005), REM latency increased (t(36) = -4.0, p = 0.0003) and slow-wave (N3) sleep time increased (t(36) = -3.5, p = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Over the same weeks, participants rated their sleep and alertness as improving: main effects of week on overall sleep quality (F(2,36) = 9.0, p = 0.0007), depth of sleep (6.3, p = 0.0044), feeling rested (5.9, p = 0.0063), alertness on waking (8.3, p = 0.0011) and daytime alertness (7.2, p = 0.0023); modafinil had no effect on any of these ratings (all p > 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Modafinil against placebo: shorter sleep onset latency (F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027) and more slow-wave sleep (F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029; more than double the placebo value at all time points, per the Discussion) across weeks; in week 3, longer total sleep time (F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013) and shorter REM latency (F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013); REM sleep time did not differ at any week (all p > 0.17).
key_findings.locator: Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Daytime sleep latency on the multiple sleep latency test: no main effect of modafinil or week; modafinil gave a longer latency only in week 1 (15, SEM 2, against 10, SEM 2, minutes; F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04).

Stanford Sleepiness Scale: a trend for less sleepiness with modafinil (F(1,144) = 3.4, p = 0.069) and a drug by week by time-of-day interaction (F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036); post hoc, modafinil went with less sleepiness at the morning ratings and at the afternoon ratings in weeks 2 and 3, and no change at the evening rating.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Sleep, Alertness and Sleepiness Measures, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: At week 3, against 12 healthy men: significant three-group differences in slow-wave sleep (F(2,29) = 4.9, p = 0.015), REM time (3.5, p = 0.04), total sleep time (12.1, p < 0.0001), sleep onset latency (4.7, p = 0.017), N1-2 time and REM latency; post hoc, slow-wave sleep with modafinil did not differ from the healthy men, REM time was lower and sleep latency longer with placebo (not with modafinil) than in the healthy men, and total sleep with modafinil remained non-significantly below theirs. Self-rated sleep quality did not differ (placebo 77, SE 5; modafinil 81, SE 5; healthy 67, SE 6; p = 0.16).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparisons to Controls; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: 8 participants (6 on modafinil, 2 on placebo) had 9 events; headache in 4 on modafinil and 1 on placebo, nausea without vomiting in 2 on modafinil, palpitations in 1 on modafinil (seen in the emergency department; dose temporarily reduced), conjunctivitis in 1 on placebo; the others were mild.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says progressive abstinence worsened all measured polysomnographic outcomes, but slow-wave (N3) sleep time increased from week 1 to week 3 (t(36) = -3.5, p = 0.001), as the Discussion acknowledges.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence course is not uniformly worse; slow-wave sleep rose while other measures worsened.

reporting_issues.issue: The P values for the effect of abstinence week on REM sleep time (F(2,36) = 8.4, printed p = 0.0002) and REM latency (F(2,36) = 11.1, printed p = 0.001) appear swapped: the editors' calculation gives p of about 0.001 and 0.0002 respectively.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Both effects remain significant; the printed values should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 18 of the 20 participants were seeking treatment; Table 1 gives 8 of 10 in each arm (16 of 20).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Inpatient Facility; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample was mostly treatment-seeking either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 renders some cells with stray spaces (44 2 then 9; 31 1 then 6; 50 3 then 9), so the past-90-day cocaine days and grams cannot be read directly; read as 44 (SD 29) against 31 (SD 16) days and 50 (SD 39) against 40 (SD 25) grams they reproduce the printed P values of 0.25 and 0.47 approximately (editors' check: about 0.23 and 0.50).
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline cocaine use should be quoted from the published version, not from this rendering.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says modafinil reduced the development of REM sleep deficits over abstinence, but post-hoc tests found no difference in REM sleep time between arms at any week (all p > 0.17).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Polysomnographic Sleep Measurement, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, final paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The claimed REM benefit rests on an interaction without a difference at any time point.

reporting_issues.issue: Polysomnographic means and SDs are given only in figures (images); the text reports test statistics only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of modafinil's effects (for example, minutes of extra sleep) cannot be stated from the text.

design_detail: Clinical case series with structured diagnostic interviews: 30 consecutive self-referred outpatients with DSM-III cocaine abuse at a Yale-affiliated clinic in New Haven, assessed for DSM-III axis I disorders only after a cocaine-free period, and seen in individual therapy once to three times a week for 4 to 6 weeks plus weekly groups. The course of symptoms after binges and during abstinence comes from the therapists' semistructured interviews and from the patients' accounts of earlier attempts to stop; from it the authors propose a three-phase model (crash, withdrawal, extinction). They call the findings preliminary.
can_establish: What people seeking treatment for heavy binge cocaine use reported, and were seen to experience, after binges and while trying to stop: a source of hypotheses, including the three-phase model.
cannot_establish: How often a crash or the later phases happen, how long they usually last, whether they are caused by stopping cocaine rather than by sleep loss, other drugs, medication or setting, or whether they occur outside this clinic: there was no comparison group, raters were not blind, much of the course came from recollection, and 20 of the 30 took medication during follow-up.

sample.recruitment: Consecutive self-referred people seeking treatment at the Drug Dependence Unit of the Connecticut Mental Health Center and the APT Foundation, New Haven; all outpatients, none hospitalized (p. 108).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-III cocaine abuse and amphetamine-like (sympathomimetic) dependence; at least weekly use and at least 14 g (or $1,400) in the 3 months before treatment; cocaine the main drug; no regular use (more than twice a week) of other drugs except cannabis and alcohol; dependence on cannabis or alcohol, or signs of withdrawal from other drugs, excluded (p. 108).
sample.demographics: Mean age 28.6 (19 to 37); 73% men; 80% white, 13% Black, 6% Hispanic; mean education 12.8 years; 70% employed; route intravenous 43%, intranasal 37%, smoked 20%; mean 4.8 years since first use (Table 1, p. 108).
sample.attrition: Not reported; the one person with ADD could not stop daily use and was not observed through abstinence (p. 110).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment seekers with heavy binge use at one clinic; the detailed course describes the 14 without other diagnoses, and draws partly on recollections of earlier failed attempts to stop.

exposure.measurement: A 110-item cocaine-use history instrument under development; abstinence corroborated by urinalysis and by significant others who did not use drugs (p. 109).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: binges from under 4 hours to 6 or more days (figure legend, p. 110); an estimated mean of 147.2 g in the previous 6 months (range 20 to 700; Table 1); weekly use by diagnostic group in Table 3.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis and alcohol were allowed below dependence; over 80% had used sedatives (alcohol or opioids) at least once to sleep during a crash (p. 111).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Diagnoses were made only after three consecutive nights of normal sleep following the crash and 10 days without cocaine; the course of symptoms comes from sessions during abstinence and from recollection.

comparison.controls: None.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history by interview only; 16 of 30 met criteria for another axis I disorder, and the authors could not say whether cocaine use or the disorder came first.

outcomes.instruments: DSM-III diagnoses from a structured interview based on the NIMH Diagnostic Interview Schedule (full in the first 17, abbreviated in the last 13), Utah criteria for adult ADD and the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression; abstinence symptoms from semistructured clinical interviews, with no standard rating of crash or later symptoms (p. 109).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed for the symptom observations.
outcomes.operationalization: Phases defined clinically by clusters of symptoms and their timing (figure, p. 110).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Raters were the treating therapist (the first author) and the group therapists, who were not blind to reports of cocaine use (p. 109).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Percentages of the 14 described in detail (p. 111): suicidal ideation 43% and paranoia 36%, limited to the crash; crash episodes met criteria for major depression with melancholic (70%) or delusional (43%) features except for their short duration; anxiety 84% and irritability 63% in phase 2; 86% bought preselected amounts before a binge; over 80% used sedatives to sleep. Diagnoses (p. 109): 54% received an axis I diagnosis besides cocaine abuse (13% major depression, 20% dysthymia, 17% cyclothymia; one person ADD).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable (1986 clinical study).
analysis.selective_reporting: Observations are presented as uniform (all subjects), without individual data or ranges for most phases.
analysis.power: Not applicable; 14 people for the detailed course.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Clinicians' observations and patients' accounts of a crash after binges (low mood within minutes, then exhaustion, long sleep and overeating, with craving high at first and then absent), followed, in those who stayed off cocaine, by a few near-normal days and then weeks of low pleasure, low energy, anxiety and returning craving, and later by cravings set off by reminders.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors present a three-phase sequence (crash 9 hours to 4 days; withdrawal 1 to 10 weeks; extinction indefinite) as the regular course after stopping, while stating in the Comment that the findings are preliminary and limited by small samples and the lack of structured instruments and blind observation (p. 112). Gaps: (1) the figure's durations are presented as general although they rest on 14 people's reports, some of them recollections; (2) the text allows up to 6 days for the crash against 4 days in the figure; (3) 20 of the 30 took medication, so the length of phase 2 was not observed without medication in most; (4) that phase 2 is the main target for treatment is a hypothesis, which a later controlled residential study did not support (Weddington et al., 1990).

timeline.event: This case series proposes the crash, withdrawal and extinction phases.
Brower & Paredes letter arguing that the distinction between crash and withdrawal is arbitrary, and the reply by Kleber & Gawin (as described by Weddington et al., 1990, p. 861).
Weddington et al., controlled residential study of 12 men: steady improvement in mood and craving over 28 days without the phases.

replication.where_it_stands: The origin of the widely cited crash-withdrawal-extinction model. Its account of the crash is a clinical description; the durations of its phases have not been confirmed by a controlled study, and the one controlled residential study read here did not find the phases.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA03467, in part (p. 113).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Yale University School of Medicine; the first author was the treating therapist and a rater; other research on the same sample (open medication trials, neuroendocrine studies) is reported elsewhere (p. 108).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people stopping after binge use, at home and in residential care, with daily ratings of mood, craving, sleep (actigraphy) and appetite on validated scales from the last dose for 10 weeks, a comparison group, blind raters and no medication during observation.

domains.note: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients with heavy binge use at one clinic; the detailed course describes only the 14 without other diagnoses.

domains.domain: Measurement of symptoms and their timing
domains.note: Semistructured interviews by the treating therapists, no standard rating of crash or later symptoms, and timing partly from recollections of earlier attempts to stop.
Raters were the therapists (including the first author) and were not blind to reports of cocaine use (p. 109).
No comparison group; 20 of 30 people took medication during follow-up, so the later phases were not observed without it in most (p. 112).
The Comment calls the findings preliminary, but the figure presents durations as a general model and the text says symptoms followed the sequence in all 14.
Crash duration differs between text and figure, and several percentages cannot be fractions of the 14 people described (reporting issues 1 and 2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a case series (METHODS §5.3); the editors' domains above describe its limits. It is cited for what people seeking treatment described after binges and for the origin of the phase model, never for how often or how long these symptoms occur.

key_findings.finding: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients (mean age 28.6, 73% men; 43% intravenous, 37% intranasal, 20% smoked), with at least weekly use and at least 14 g in the previous 3 months.

Raters were the treating therapist and group therapists and were not blind to reports of cocaine use; abstinence reports were corroborated by urinalysis and significant others; diagnoses were deferred until three nights of normal sleep after the crash and 10 days without cocaine.
The course was described in detail for the 14 people without other diagnoses and followed three phases in all 14; the impressions rest on observation and on accounts of earlier attempts to stop.
key_findings.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Phenomenon, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Crash: when supplies ran out, low mood rose within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose with intense craving that faded if no more cocaine came; then low mood, loss of pleasure, insomnia, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by 8 to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating. Passing suicidal ideation (43% of the subsample) and paranoia (36%) were limited to the crash.

Craving was absent in the late crash and during heavy sleep; over 80% had used alcohol or opioids at least once to sleep; five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it. Eight described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days; the figure gives 9 hours to 4 days.
key_findings.locator: Phase 1: Crash, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 111); Figure and legend (p. 110)

key_findings.finding: Phase 2: one to five days of near-normal mood and sleep with little craving, then weeks of anhedonia, mild low mood, low energy, anxiety (84%) and irritability (63%), with craving returning and following these symptoms, lasting 1 to 10 or more weeks; earlier attempts to stop had all failed within several days after this phase began.

Phase 3: a baseline mood without anhedonia, with episodic craving set off by reminders such as old friends or places of use; ten people described intense craving returning after up to 28 weeks without it.

All 16 people with other diagnoses and 4 of the others were treated with medication, so phase 2 and phase 3 in them could not be observed without medication; people with major depression had the most severe crash and little relief in phase 2.
key_findings.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Symptoms and Diagnosis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors call the findings preliminary, limited by small sample size and the lack of structured instruments or blind observation, and say the study needs replication.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says eight people described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days, while the figure gives the crash as 9 hours to 4 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit of the crash is 4 or 6 days depending on where one reads; the hours given in the text (1 to 40 plus 8 to 50) add up to under 4 days.

reporting_issues.issue: Several percentages given for the 14 people (melancholic features 70%, anxiety 84%, irritability 63%) do not correspond to any whole number of 14, while others (43%, 36%, 86%) do.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of some percentages is unclear (some may refer to the whole sample of 30 or to another subgroup).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says a quarter of the sample smoked cocaine, but Table 1 gives 6 of 30 (20%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the route totals as '2 (6%-33%)', '7 (13%-54%)', '7 (11%-64%)' and '16 (30%-54%)': the first figure in each bracket is the group size with a misplaced % sign, and 16 of 30 is 53.3%, not 54%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting; the brackets give the share of each route group with a diagnosis (33%, 54%, 64%; 53% overall).

design_detail: Controlled longitudinal study on a closed residential research unit (NIDA Addiction Research Center, Baltimore, 1987-88): 12 men with severe DSM-III-R cocaine dependence, admitted within 48 hours of last use, and 10 men without substance use disorder (except nicotine), each living on the unit for 28 days; self-rated mood, craving (cocaine group only) and sleep, vital signs and weight on 11 study days, analysed with mixed-design ANOVA (group, time, interaction).
can_establish: The course of self-rated mood, craving and sleep over the first 4 weeks of supervised abstinence in a setting without cocaine or cues, compared with men without drug dependence living on the same unit.
cannot_establish: The course outside a controlled setting (no cocaine, no reminders), in women, in people who binge or smoke crack (10 of 12 injected daily), during the first hours after last use (first measure on admission day, up to 48 hours after use), within the day (one morning measure every 2 to 4 days), or of sleep measured objectively.

sample.recruitment: Consecutively self-referred men recruited through newspaper and radio advertisements and notices to treatment clinics and emergency departments in Baltimore: 30 people with cocaine dependence made appointments, 16 came, 14 were admitted and 12 completed; 18 controls made appointments and 10 were admitted and completed (p. 862). Participants were paid on completion ($16.50 a day; $50 for those who left early).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cocaine group: severe active DSM-III-R cocaine dependence; one gram or more a week for at least 12 weeks; a positive urine test for cocaine; willing to stay on a closed unit for 4 to 6 weeks. Excluded: other current substance abuse or dependence except nicotine; positive urine for drugs other than THC and cocaine; medical illness; psychosis or cognitive incapacity; infectious disease; illiteracy; treatment required by courts or employers. Controls: the same, with no lifetime substance use disorder except nicotine (p. 862).
sample.demographics: Cocaine group against controls: mean age 28.1 (SEM 1.9) against 32.1 (1.3); 92% against 80% Black; education 11.5 against 11.2 years; employed 50% against 30%; antisocial personality disorder 58% against 0%; current nicotine dependence 83% against 30% (Table 1, p. 863).
sample.attrition: Two of 14 men in the cocaine group left (on days 3 and 5) and were excluded; all 10 controls completed (p. 862).
sample.selection_effects: Self-referred, paid men willing to live on a locked unit for a month; completers only; 10 of the 12 injected daily rather than binging or smoking (p. 867).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine dependence diagnosed by one psychiatrist with the SADS-L supplemented by questionnaires; recent use confirmed by urine benzoylecgonine on admission and, in 8 men, by sputum and urine over the first 12 hours, consistent with last use no earlier than 48 hours before admission (p. 864).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (self-report, Table 1, p. 863): 6.7 g a week (SEM 0.4) in the 4 weeks before evaluation and 5.3 g (0.3) in the week before admission; use on 10.8 of the previous 14 days; dependence for 3.7 years; intravenous 10, smoked 1, intranasal 1.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis was allowed: 4 of 12 in the cocaine group and 2 of 10 controls had THC-positive urine on day 1; 42% of the cocaine group had past cannabis dependence; cigarettes were allowed on the unit (pp. 863-864).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Daily observed urine tests showed no drug use on the unit (p. 864); last use within 48 hours before day 1.

comparison.controls: Ten men without lifetime substance use disorder (except nicotine), living on the same unit under the same procedures.
comparison.matching: Not matched; no significant differences in age, race, education, employment, marital status or other axis I disorders, but antisocial personality disorder and nicotine dependence were more common in the cocaine group (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mood before cocaine use unknown; SCL-90-R scores for the week before intake were higher in the cocaine group on every factor (Table 1).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Thirty per cent of controls had current nicotine dependence; none had another substance use disorder.

outcomes.instruments: Profile of Mood States (65 adjectives), Beck Depression Inventory (13-item), a 100-point visual analogue scale of craving over the past 24 hours (cocaine group only; controls could not rate it), the St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire, resting heart rate, blood pressure and weight, on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28, between 9 AM and noon (p. 863).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments; the authors note that self-reported sleep can differ from sleep measured by EEG (p. 867).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time and differences between groups; phases judged from the shape of the curves, without a statistical test.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-report; participants and staff knew who was in which group.

analysis.effect_sizes: F ratios only (Table 2; df 1,20 for group, 10,200 for time and interaction, 10,110 for craving): Beck depression 13.949, 10.670, 8.526 (all P<.01); total mood distress 5.082 (P<.05), 9.359, 5.537 (P<.01); depression/dejection 8.806, 5.586, 3.744 (P<.01); tension/anxiety 5.681 (P<.05), 6.483, 5.431 (P<.01); vigor not significant; craving time 17.270 (P<.01). Sleep: difficulty falling asleep, group 10.428 (P<.01) with no time effect; clear-headed on arising, interaction 2.001 (P<.05); the other sleep factors showed time effects only. Heart rate group 4.360 and interaction 1.979 (P<.05); weight group 6.806 (P<.05) and time 31.838 (P<.01). Weight gain 4.6 kg (6.5%) against 3.8 kg (4.3%); heart rate up 10.9 beats a minute against down 2.3 from day 1 to day 28. Daily means appear only in Figures 1 to 4 (values not extracted).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable (1990).
analysis.selective_reporting: All measures are tabulated in Table 2; physiological results are reported elsewhere.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 12 and 10 men.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the cocaine group, self-rated mood distress, depression and craving were highest on admission day and lower over the 28 days, mostly within about 2 weeks, with significant group, time and interaction effects; reports of sleep did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep; both groups' sleep improved over time.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says mood distress and craving “decreased gradually and steadily”, and the Comment that the changes were not cyclical or phasic and that short-term abstinence describes them better than withdrawal (pp. 861, 866-867). Gaps: (1) no test of a phasic or non-steady pattern was done, and the plotted means of several mood scales rise again around days 7 to 9 before falling (editors' reading of Figure 1; no values extracted); (2) the setting had no cocaine and no reminders of it, which the authors name as a possible reason for the difference from outpatient reports; (3) the first measure came up to 48 hours after last use, so the earliest part of a crash may have been missed.

timeline.event: Gawin & Kleber, clinical case series proposing crash, withdrawal and extinction phases.
Brower & Paredes letter and the reply by Kleber & Gawin on whether crash and withdrawal are distinct (as described, p. 861).
This controlled residential study: steady improvement without phases.

replication.where_it_stands: The first controlled residential test of the phase model read here; it found steady improvement without phases in a setting free of cocaine and cues. A sleep-laboratory study of inpatient abstinence already in the library (Morgan et al., 2010) adds that measured sleep worsened while self-rated sleep improved.

funding.funder: Not stated; the study was done at the NIDA Addiction Research Center by NIDA staff (affiliations, p. 861).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed; the opinions are stated to be the authors' own, not NIDA's (p. 861).
funding.affiliations_note: NIDA, Rockville, and the Addiction Research Center, Baltimore; the first author was the psychiatrist and case manager who saw all participants 5 days a week.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people stopping cocaine after binge use, in residential and community settings, with momentary ratings of mood and craving several times a day from the last dose for 10 weeks, actigraphy, and a pre-specified test for phases.

domains.note: The groups differed in antisocial personality disorder (58% against 0%), nicotine and past cannabis dependence, and in time with staff (more counselling for the cocaine group); 3 of 12 in the cocaine group and 7 of 10 controls had pituitary challenge tests (levodopa, protirelin); none adjusted for.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Dependence diagnosed by one psychiatrist; time, amount and purity of the last dose not standardized (p. 867).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Paid, self-referred men willing to live on a locked unit; 16 of 30 came to evaluation and only completers were analysed, which can favour people whose distress eased.
Counselling, daily psychiatrist contact, recreation and the challenge tests could change mood; acetaminophen in two men of each group.
Two of 14 in the cocaine group left early and were excluded; craving not rated by controls.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Unblinded self-ratings once every 2 to 4 days in the morning; no objective sleep measure.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All 21 measures are reported in Table 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for a non-randomized two-group comparison. The time course within the cocaine group is the main finding; it is vulnerable to selection (completers in a locked unit) and to the setting, and the comparison with controls is confounded by personality disorder and attention. It is cited for the course of self-rated symptoms in a cue-free residential setting, not for people stopping at home.

key_findings.finding: Twelve men with severe cocaine dependence (10 injecting daily) and 10 men without drug dependence lived on a closed research unit for 28 days; 30 men with cocaine dependence had made appointments, 16 came, 14 were admitted and 2 left on days 3 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Subjects and Methods › Subjects, 8th and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Measures (Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory, craving scale for the past 24 hours, St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire, vital signs, weight) on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18, 21, 25 and 28 between 9 AM and noon; controls did not rate craving.
All men in the cocaine group had used cocaine within 48 hours before admission (urine and sputum findings consistent); daily urine tests showed no drug use on the unit.

Mood distress and depression scores were raised in the cocaine group and changed over time differently from controls: Beck depression F = 13.949 (group), 10.670 (time), 8.526 (interaction); total mood distress 5.082, 9.359, 5.537; vigor did not differ.
Craving was highest on the day of admission and fell significantly over the 28 days (F = 17.270, df 10,110, P<.01).
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Craving for Cocaine (p. 864); Figure 2 and Table 2 (p. 865)

key_findings.finding: Sleep: no group differences except more difficulty falling asleep in the cocaine group throughout (group F = 10.428) and more improvement in clear-headedness on waking (interaction F = 2.001); all sleep measures except difficulty falling asleep improved in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Self-reports of Sleep (p. 864); Figure 3 and Table 2 (p. 865)

key_findings.finding: Weight gain did not differ (4.6 kg or 6.5% against 3.8 kg or 4.3%); heart rate rose 10.9 beats a minute in the cocaine group and fell 2.3 in controls from day 1 to day 28; blood pressure did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Outcome › Weight, Heart Rate, and Blood Pressure (p. 864, continued p. 866)

key_findings.finding: The authors report that mood, craving and night waking improved gradually and were not cyclical or phasic during the first 4 weeks, unlike the earlier phase models, and suggest the cue-free controlled setting as a reason; they were surprised that both groups' sleep improved, possibly from adapting to the unit.

In Figure 1, the cocaine group's mean scores on several Profile of Mood States scales (tension, depression, anger, fatigue, confusion, total distress) fall from day 1 to day 5, rise again around days 7 to 9, then fall and stay low from about day 11 or 14; the Beck depression line falls more evenly.
key_findings.note: Editors' description of the plotted means; no values were extracted, and the error bars are wide.

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: small all-male, mostly Black sample of mostly daily injectors; reliance on self-report; the experimental setting; no standard last dose or uniform starting point; THC-positive participants; no sleep EEG; only the first month; morning measures only.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives height as 2.8 (SEM 0.1) and 2.9 (0.1) metres, which is impossible for adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: A unit or transcription error; heights are not used in any analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives use on 10.8 (SEM 0.02) of the previous 14 days; Table 1 gives 10.8 (0.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is the plausible one.

reporting_issues.issue: The group effect for anger/hostility is marked P<.05 in Table 2, but F = 4.347 on 1 and 20 degrees of freedom gives p = 0.0501 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline; anger/hostility should not be counted as clearly different between groups.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 120, first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Cocaine/Weddington_1990_ShortTermAbstinenceControlled.pdf, pp. 861-868 (scanned with an OCR text layer; pp. 862-867 checked against the rendered page images, including Tables 1-2 and Figures 1-4); final published version

design_detail: Series of operant experiments in rats (PLoS ONE 2007, e698). Male Wistar rats with jugular catheters chose, in a discrete-trials procedure (12 trials a day, 10 minutes apart: 4 forced sampling trials, always in the order cocaine lever, saccharin lever, cocaine lever, saccharin lever, an order chosen to prevent drug-induced taste aversion, then 8 free choices, for 15 days), between a lever that delivered one intravenous cocaine infusion and a lever that gave 20 s of access to 0.2% saccharin water. Three between-group conditions (only cocaine rewarded, only saccharin rewarded, both rewarded) were followed by within-animal tests of cocaine dose, saccharin delay and response cost, tests with water, no fluid and 4% sucrose as the alternative, a reversal test in rats that had first learned to prefer cocaine, and tests after 18 days of extended (6 h a day) cocaine access and during cocaine intoxication. A secondary synthesis read ventral striatal dopamine values off the figures of 18 rat microdialysis papers. Every finding on this card is in rats; nothing was measured in people.
can_establish: That under this discrete-trials procedure, male Wistar rats with no previous experience of refined sugar almost all chose a saccharin (or sucrose) drink over an intravenous cocaine infusion, and kept doing so across the cocaine doses, delays and response costs tested, after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine.
cannot_establish: That sweet taste outweighs cocaine for people, for female rats or under other procedures (longer access, other spacing of trials, other alternatives); that the escalated rats were addicted in any sense beyond escalated intake; or anything about sugar addiction or drug use in human societies, which the authors offer as speculation.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals: naive young adult male Wistar rats from Charles River, France; housed 2 or 3 per cage under a reversed 12-h light cycle with food and water freely available; standard chow without added synthetic or refined sugar; tested in the dark phase (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Rats that completed fewer than 50% of the 8 daily choice trials after 15 days were excluded: 20 of 132, 16 in the cocaine-only condition and 4 in the both-rewarded condition (Materials and Methods › Data analysis).
sample.demographics: Male only; 221–276 g at the start; no previous operant training and no experience of refined sugar or artificial sweetener.
sample.attrition: 20 of 132 rats (15%) excluded, unevenly across conditions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded, none saccharin-only). The paper does not say whether the printed group sizes (30, 9 and 43) count rats before or after exclusion; the degrees of freedom of the main analysis, F(28,1106), fit 82 analysed rats in the three conditions, in which case about a third of the cocaine-only condition (16 of 46) was excluded (editors' calculation).
sample.selection_effects: One strain, one sex, one supplier; rats were not food- or water-restricted. Exclusion removed rats that did not engage with the task, mostly in the cocaine-only condition. How rats were assigned to conditions and chosen for the later subgroup tests is not described, and the named groups cannot all be independent (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Intravenous self-administration through a jugular catheter (patency checked with etomidate when needed), each infusion triggered by a lever press and recorded by the apparatus; cocaine hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier (Materials and Methods › Surgery; Drugs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats, not applicable to people: cocaine hydrochloride IV, 0.25 mg per infusion over 4 s (dose as salt) in the main procedure; 0.25, 0.75 and 1.5 mg per infusion in a dose test, with the inter-trial interval lengthened with dose (10, 16.4 and 23.1 min); extended-access group 6 h a day for 18 days (0.25 mg per infusion in the first hour, 0.75 mg after); intoxication group 1 h of cocaine-only access before each day's choices. In the both-rewarded condition rats took about 3 infusions a day, sampling included (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Alternative reward: 20 s of access to 0.2% sodium saccharin (at most 0.3 ml) or 4% sucrose.
exposure.polysubstance: None: one drug, and rats had no other drug exposure.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: cocaine was available during testing; the intoxication group chose immediately after 1 h of cocaine access.

comparison.controls: Between groups: rats for which only the saccharin lever (N=9) or only the cocaine lever (N=30) was rewarded. Within animals: water and no fluid as the alternative (same 10 rats), and 4% sucrose (a separate 10 rats). The reversal and escalation groups were compared with the initially drug-naive both-rewarded rats.
comparison.matching: Same strain, sex, supplier and weight range; all three conditions were indifferent between the levers on day 1 (Results, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Individual differences that could predict choice (for example sweet preference or sensitivity to cocaine) were not measured before allocation.

outcomes.instruments: Lever choice (share of completed choice trials on each lever, plotted against an indifference level of 0), recorded automatically; latencies to sample and to choose; locomotion by infrared beam crossings for 10 min after the first cocaine infusion of the day (sensitization); daily cocaine intake during extended access; delay to onset of cocaine effects timed by observation (12 rats); ventral striatal dopamine values read off published figures (18 papers).
outcomes.validity_norms: Discrete-trials choice between a drug and an alternative is an established procedure, mostly from monkey studies that the authors discuss. An individual rat was counted as preferring the cocaine lever when it chose it on more than 60% of trials over the last 3 days (Results, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Preference: choosing one lever on more than 50% of completed choices (group means tested against indifference) or, for individual rats, more than 60% over the last 3 stable days. Addiction: inferred from escalation of intake over 18 days of 6-h access; compulsive use despite negative consequences and relapse were not tested in this paper.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across experiments; Fisher's LSD tests after ANOVA within experiments. The count of 18 is the editors' count of distinct tests reported in the Results.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Choice, latencies and locomotion were recorded automatically. The onset delay of cocaine effects was timed by an observer who knew cocaine had been given; blinding is not reported for any procedure.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes; F, t and z tests with significance thresholds, and group means shown only in figures (images, not viewable in this reading). Printed values: Condition×Day F(28,1106)=8.71, P<0.01; both-rewarded vs saccharin-only F(14,700)=0.41, NS; choice latency 14.5±5.0 vs 6.5±2.4 s, t(50)<1; sampling latency cocaine lever 48.5±10.2 vs saccharin lever 5.6±1.7 s, F(1,42)=17.44, P<0.01; sensitization Day×Intervals F(40,1160)=5.06 (cocaine-only) and F(40,1680)=6.57 (both-rewarded), P<0.01; first both-rewarded day in rats trained with saccharin only, Group×Intervals F(20,1000)=1.66, P<0.05; dose: locomotion F(2,20)=18.77, P<0.01, choice F(2,20)=0.07, NS; saccharin delay F(3,30)=6.58, P<0.01; response cost F(2,18)=8.04, P<0.01; escalation from 7.34±2.50 to 26.04±1.21 mg/day, F(16,160)=15.98, P<0.01; rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (initially naive), 8.3% (after reversal), 0.0% (after escalation), z<1.96 for both comparisons; escalated rats' sampling latencies 15.6±8.1 vs 4.0±0.8 s, F(1,10)=2.06, NS. Degrees of freedom match the stated group sizes throughout (editors' check).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: Most results appear only as figure means with significance marks; individual data are shown for 3 representative rats only. The 94% in the abstract does not appear in the results (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 9 to 43 rats, subgroups of 10 or 11.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In male Wistar rats under one discrete-trials procedure (8 choices a day, 10 minutes apart; about 3 cocaine infusions a day when both rewards were available), almost every rat chose the sweet drink over intravenous cocaine, and this held across the doses, delays and costs tested, after reversal, after escalated intake and during intoxication; the same rats preferred cocaine to plain water.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings “clearly demonstrate” that intense sweetness can surpass cocaine reward even in drug-sensitized and -addicted individuals; here addiction rests on escalated intake after 18 days of extended access, without tests of compulsive use or relapse. The extensions to people (that sugar-rich diets could lead to addiction through supranormal stimulation of sweet receptors, and that widespread sugar may shield modern societies against the spread of drug addiction) are labelled as speculation in the abstract and Discussion, 6th paragraph; no human data were collected. The conclusion that the reward value of cocaine is “bounded” is tied to this procedure: the authors note that monkeys in earlier studies preferred high cocaine doses over food, in one study over a sucrose pellet, and that a species difference cannot be ruled out (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

timeline.event: Rhesus monkeys chose intravenous cocaine over food in a choice procedure (Aigner & Balster, 1978, as described in this paper); animal study.
Rhesus monkeys preferred the highest cocaine dose over a 1-g sucrose pellet (Woolverton & Balster, 1979, as described in this paper); animal study, contrary to the rat result.

Rats: concurrently available sweetened water (saccharin plus glucose) prevented acquisition or reduced maintenance of low-dose cocaine self-administration (Carroll et al., 1989; and Carroll & Lac, 1993, as described in this paper).

Human inpatient laboratory study: choice between smoked cocaine and a money or merchandise voucher in six participants (Hart et al., 2000; read in full on its own study card, sc_hart_2000); a study in people, kept apart from the rat findings
Rats: social interaction as the alternative to drugs (Venniro et al., 2018; on the General list, not yet appraised).
Critical history of the Rat Park experiments and how animal environment studies shaped accounts of addiction (Gage & Sumnall, 2019; read in full on its own study card, sc_gage_2019)

replication.where_it_stands: Within this paper the rats' preference held across many manipulations, but in one strain, one sex and one procedure. Earlier monkey choice studies found the opposite preference, as the authors discuss, and the General list notes that later choice studies show the outcome depends on the drug, the procedure and the alternative (Kearns, 2023; Banks & Negus, 2017; not yet appraised). It is evidence about how a non-drug alternative competes with cocaine in rats, not evidence about people.

funding.funder: Université Victor-Segalen Bordeaux 2, the French Research Council (CNRS), the Conseil Régional Aquitaine, the National Research Agency (ANR) and the Fondation pour la Recherche Médicale (FRM) (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist (Footnotes › Competing Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: University Bordeaux 2 and Bordeaux 1, CNRS UMR 5227. The extended-access escalation model and the view that escalated rats show signs of addiction come from the senior author's earlier work (Ahmed & Koob, 1998; Ahmed et al., 2002, as cited). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For rats: choice experiments in females and males of several strains, with randomized allocation and order, blinded handling, a pre-registered protocol and full reporting of excluded animals, varying trial spacing, access duration and the kind of alternative. For people, a different design entirely: laboratory and field studies of how available non-drug rewards change cocaine choice (as in contingency management), which no rat study can answer.

domains.note: No random component is described for allocating rats to the three conditions, and the within-animal tests ran in a fixed ascending order (cocaine 0.25, 0.75, 1.5 mg; saccharin delay 0, 6, 12, 18 s; cost 2, 4, 8 presses; no fluid, water, saccharin), so order and practice effects are confounded with the manipulated variable.
Same strain, sex, supplier and weight range; all conditions indifferent between the levers on day 1. Per-group weights are not reported.
Not reported.
Rats were housed 2 or 3 per cage and tested in 12 chambers; how cages and chambers were assigned is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported; contingencies were programmed, but handling and catheter care by staff who knew each rat's condition cannot be excluded.
Choice was recorded for every rat, but the subgroups tested for dose, delay, cost, water and sucrose were drawn from the trained rats without a stated method of selection.
The main outcomes (lever choice, latencies, beam-break locomotion) were recorded automatically. The one observer-timed measure, the onset delay of cocaine effects, was not blinded but is not central.

20 of 132 rats were excluded for completing fewer than half the choice trials, a reason linked to the outcome, unevenly across conditions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded, none saccharin-only). The main both-rewarded result lost 4 rats and is unlikely to change; comparisons with the cocaine-only condition are more exposed.
No protocol (none would be expected in 2007); every experiment named in the Methods is reported, mostly as figure means; the abstract's 94% cannot be traced in the Results.
Rats were reused across later experiments without saying which, so earlier tests may carry over; the dopamine synthesis read values off figures from 18 papers chosen without stated criteria.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; the overall here is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items that bear on the main result. The core outcome was recorded automatically, and the preference is large and consistent across experiments, which limits detection bias. But no random allocation is described, the dose, delay and cost tests ran in fixed ascending order, 15% of rats (most of them in the cocaine-only condition) were excluded for not engaging with the task, and the use of rats across experiments is not reported. The paper may be cited for what male Wistar rats did in this procedure, labelled as an animal finding; it may not be cited for sweet or cocaine preference in people, for addiction in people, or for a general ranking of rewards.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat; Wistar; male only; young adults of 221–276 g at the start (Charles River, France); N=132, of whom 20 were excluded.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Cocaine hydrochloride, intravenous through a jugular catheter, 0.25 mg per infusion over 4 s in the main procedure (0.75 and 1.5 mg in a dose test; 0.75 mg after the first hour in the extended-access phase); 12 trials a day spaced 10 minutes apart (4 forced, 8 choices) for 15 days; extended access 6 h a day for 18 days in one group; 1 h of cocaine-only access before choices in another. Alternative: 20 s of 0.2% saccharin (or 4% sucrose) drinking.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given: doses are stated per infusion in mg of salt, not per kg, and the authors make no human-equivalent statement. None is calculated here.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Partly. Intravenous self-administration is a standard model of cocaine taking, and the extended-access group models escalating intake. But the main procedure allowed 8 choices a day spaced 10 minutes apart (about 3 infusions a day when saccharin was available, against about 30 when rats take cocaine freely over the same time), offered a small, immediate sweet drink as the only alternative, used rats that were neither food- nor water-restricted and had never tasted refined sugar, and studied males only. People's choices involve delayed, social, economic and legal consequences that the procedure does not model.

key_findings.finding: Rats (male Wistar, drug-naive, no previous refined sugar): offered one intravenous cocaine infusion (0.25 mg) or 20 s of 0.2% saccharin water on each choice trial (both levers rewarded, N=43), the group preferred saccharin from the 2nd day of testing, as quickly as rats for which only saccharin was available (N=9; both-rewarded vs saccharin-only F(14,700)=0.41, NS). Rats with only the cocaine lever rewarded (N=30) came to prefer it from day 9 (significant from day 11). Condition×Day F(28,1106)=8.71, P<0.01.
key_findings.note: The Discussion (5th paragraph) says instead that the both-rewarded rats reached a reliable saccharin preference more rapidly than the saccharin-only rats (day 2 against day 7); the formal comparison found no difference (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Rats: once behaviour was stable, choosing saccharin took as long in the both-rewarded condition (14.5±5.0 s) as in the saccharin-only condition (6.5±2.4 s; t(50)<1). Rats sampled the cocaine lever almost every time from day 7 but pressed it more slowly than the saccharin lever during sampling (48.5±10.2 vs 5.6±1.7 s; F(1,42)=17.44, P<0.01).

Rats preferred cocaine over plain water, so the saccharin preference was not explained by thirst (the same 10 rats were tested with no fluid, water and saccharin, in that order); a separate 10 rats preferred 4% sucrose over cocaine as others preferred saccharin.
key_findings.note: Group values are shown only in Figure 2, an image not viewable in this reading.

key_findings.finding: Rats: the few cocaine infusions taken in the both-rewarded condition produced locomotor sensitization similar to that in the cocaine-only condition (Day×Intervals F(40,1680)=6.57 and F(40,1160)=5.06, P<0.01); rats first trained with saccharin only were less sensitized on their first both-rewarded day (Group×Intervals F(20,1000)=1.66, P<0.05).

Rats (subgroups of the both-rewarded group): raising the cocaine dose to 0.75 and 1.5 mg per infusion increased locomotion (F(2,20)=18.77, P<0.01) but not cocaine choice (F(2,20)=0.07, NS; N=11); delaying the saccharin by up to 18 s slightly reduced saccharin choice without reversing the preference (F(3,30)=6.58, P<0.01; N=11); raising the cost from 2 to 8 presses increased the saccharin preference (F(2,18)=8.04, P<0.01; N=10).

Rats that had first learned to prefer the cocaine lever (cocaine-only condition, N=24) switched to saccharin once both levers were rewarded; 8.3% of them still preferred cocaine (more than 60% cocaine choices over the last 3 days), against 2.3% of initially drug-naive rats (z<1.96).

Rats given 6 h of cocaine access a day for 18 days (N=11) escalated intake from 7.34±2.50 to 26.04±1.21 mg/day (F(16,160)=15.98, P<0.01) and then, within 10 days of choice, preferred saccharin; none preferred cocaine (0.0% vs 2.3% of initially naive rats); the preference held across cocaine doses, with a small decrease at the highest dose.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 5b and insert; Materials and Methods › Induction of cocaine intake escalation

key_findings.finding: Rats that self-administered cocaine for 1 h before each choice session (N=10) still developed a robust saccharin preference, switching abruptly from the cocaine lever to the saccharin lever when the choices began (3 representative rats shown).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 5c–e; Materials and Methods › Choice during cocaine intoxication

key_findings.finding: Rats: the preference was not exclusive. In the both-rewarded condition rats chose cocaine on about 15.6% of choices on average (range across experiments 7–23%), about 3 infusions a day with sampling, against about 30 infusions that rats take freely over the same period; in the saccharin-only condition they pressed the unrewarded cocaine lever on 8.3% of choices.

Rats, secondary synthesis: from the figures of 18 rat microdialysis papers found through Medline, the authors report that intravenous cocaine self-administration raised ventral striatal dopamine much more than sucrose or saccharin drinking, and argue that dopamine release alone does not explain the choice.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Figure 6; Materials and Methods › Meta-analysis
key_findings.note: Values only in Figure 6 (not viewable); papers selected by content and relevance without stated criteria, values estimated from published figures.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that in earlier discrete-trials studies most monkeys preferred high doses of intravenous cocaine over food, in one study over a 1-g sucrose pellet, and give possible reasons (sweet drink vs dry food, effort required, amount of the alternative, a species difference).

No measurement in people. The extension to human diets and drug use (sugar-rich diets as supernormal stimuli that could lead to addiction; widespread sugar as a possible shield against the spread of drug addiction) is offered by the authors as speculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 94% of rats preferred saccharin; no 94% appears in the Results, which give the share of rats preferring cocaine by a more-than-60% criterion (2.3% of initially naive, 8.3% after reversal, 0.0% after escalation) and an average of 15.6% cocaine choices.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Abstract; Results, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline figure cannot be traced: which groups and which criterion it uses are not stated. Editors' arithmetic: the three groups with stated percentages hold 1 of 43, 2 of 24 and 0 of 11 rats preferring cocaine, 3 of 78 in all, so 96% did not; only the two drug-experienced groups together (2 of 35) would round to 94%, and the paper does not say that this is its basis.

reporting_issues.issue: Group sizes named in the text (30, 9 and 43 in the three conditions, 11 escalated, 10 intoxicated, and two groups of 10 in Figure 2) add up to 123 if the Figure 2 groups were separate rats, more than the 112 left after 20 exclusions; if they were drawn from the cocaine-only and both-rewarded conditions, as the Results' 1st paragraph implies (those conditions held more rats because the dose, delay, effort, reversal, calorie and thirst experiments were run in them), the named independent groups (30, 9, 43, 11 and 10) add up to 103, fewer than 112. Subgroups for dose (11), delay (11), cost (10), sucrose and water were drawn from the trained rats, and the text implies rats served in several experiments, but which rats did what is not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 1st, 4th, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Figure 2 legend; Materials and Methods › Subjects and Data analysis
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of independent animals behind each conclusion, and what each had experienced before later tests, cannot be reconstructed; carry-over between experiments is possible.

reporting_issues.issue: It is not stated whether the 20 exclusions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded) come before or after the printed group sizes, but the degrees of freedom of every test that names its groups match the printed sizes (main ANOVA 82 rats; F(14,700), t(50) and F(20,1000) 52; F(40,1160) 30; F(40,1680) 43), so these are the sizes after exclusion: 16 of 46 cocaine-only rats (35%) against 4 of 47 both-rewarded rats (8.5%) were excluded for not completing choice trials (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Materials and Methods › Data analysis; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of how quickly rats came to prefer cocaine or saccharin rests on the rats that engaged with the task; rats that rarely chose were removed mostly from the cocaine-only condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The extended-access phase lasted 18 days in the Methods but "3 weeks" in the Results; the ANOVA of daily intake (F(16,160)) implies 17 analysed sessions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 7th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Induction of cocaine intake escalation
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the length of the escalation phase is uncertain by a few days.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results (3rd paragraph) say the both-rewarded rats acquired the saccharin preference as quickly as the saccharin-only rats, in line with the formal comparison (F(14,700)=0.41, NS; 2nd paragraph), but the Discussion (5th paragraph) says they did so more rapidly (day 2 against day 7) and explains the difference by cocaine's ambivalent effects.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor. The days on which each group's preference first reached significance are not a test of a difference; the formal comparison found none, so the Discussion explains a difference the data do not show.
