The funding sources had no role in design, analysis, interpretation or the decision to submit (pp. 787, 790).
funding.declared_conflicts: Potential financial conflicts of interest: none disclosed (p. 790).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and the Institute for Exercise and Environmental Medicine, Presbyterian Hospital of Dallas (p. 790). The authors' own earlier study is the source for the dose being non-euphoric and for cocaine's central sympathetic action (reference 11). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A registered, adequately powered randomized crossover study in people who already use cocaine, at more than one dose, with an inert placebo as well as lidocaine, measuring heat production (by indirect calorimetry) alongside skin blood flow, sweating and core temperature, during both passive heating and exercise, with the blinding checked and every participant's data reported at each core temperature.

domains.note: Order was randomized, but how the sequence was generated and concealed, and how many people received each order, are not reported. Core temperature and skin blood flow before heating were similar in the two sessions.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Sessions 3 to 6 days apart at the same time of day; treatment order was included in the models and had no effect on any outcome, although with 7 people that test has little power.

Double-blind with an active local-anaesthetic control, but cocaine raised blood pressure and heart rate before heating and blinding was not checked; this matters most for the self-rated thermal sensation.

No withdrawals reported, but the number of participants contributing at 37.86°C and at each sensation rating is not given; the lidocaine mean core temperature ended below 37.86°C, and Figure 3 has no cocaine value at the top rating.

Core temperature, skin blood flow and sweat rate are instrument measures, and thresholds were picked by an investigator blinded to condition. Thermal sensation is self-rated and depends on blinding (see deviations).
No protocol or registration; about 22 comparisons without correction; the 'highest common esophageal temperature' at which conductance and sweat rate were compared is not defined in the methods.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, carefully instrumented within-person experiment whose main measurements are objective and whose thresholds were read blind. Concerns are the unreported randomization details, the unchecked blinding (relevant to the perception result), the unclear number of participants behind the comparisons at the highest temperatures, and the absence of a protocol. The card may be cited for what one low intranasal dose did to heat-loss responses and thermal perception in 7 healthy cocaine-naive people under passive heating; not for the size of the effect in people who use cocaine, for heat production, or for risk in hot weather.

key_findings.finding: Before heating, cocaine did not change esophageal temperature compared with lidocaine (36.79 ± 0.01 against 36.75 ± 0.08°C, mean ± SE) but raised mean arterial pressure (93 ± 3 against 85 ± 3 mm Hg, P=0.001) and heart rate (74 ± 5 against 67 ± 4 beats/min, P=0.01); skin vascular conductance did not differ significantly (9 ± 2 against 7 ± 2% of maximum, P=0.09). n=7, each in both conditions.

During heating, heart rate rose in both conditions (to 107 ± 5 with cocaine and 105 ± 5 beats/min with lidocaine, P>0.2), mean arterial pressure did not rise, and at the end of heating it was still higher with cocaine (92 ± 2 against 87 ± 2 mm Hg, P<0.01). Skin temperature rose similarly in both conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 787, continuing on p. 788); Figure 1, top (p. 788)

key_findings.finding: Esophageal temperature rose more during heating after cocaine than after lidocaine (P<0.001, two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance). The text gives no size for the difference.
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi enlargement of Figure 1 (approximate): from about 36.8°C in both conditions to about 37.8°C with cocaine and about 37.5°C with lidocaine after about 38 minutes of heating; the curves begin to separate around 10 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine raised the esophageal temperature at which skin vasodilation began (37.37 ± 0.09 against 37.06 ± 0.07°C, P=0.01) and at which sweating began (37.38 ± 0.09 against 37.07 ± 0.06°C, P=0.002), with no change in the slopes of either response.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the rounded P values (paired t-test, 6 df): a shift of 0.31°C, 95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51°C (vasodilation) and 0.16 to 0.46°C (sweating).

key_findings.finding: At the 'highest common esophageal temperature' of 37.86°C, skin vascular conductance was 49 ± 9% of maximum with cocaine against 70 ± 5% with lidocaine (P=0.03), and sweat rate 0.8 ± 0.2 against 1.0 ± 0.1 mg/cm² per minute (P=0.04).
key_findings.note: How many participants contributed at 37.86°C is not reported (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine lessened the rise in thermal discomfort although core temperature rose more: the esophageal temperature at each perceived-heating rating from 5.0 to 7.5 (on a scale of 4.0, neutral, to 8.0, unbearably hot) was compared by paired t-tests, and the difference first became significant above 37.0°C and widened as core temperature rose (P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph (p. 786); Statistical Analysis (p. 787); Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 788); Figure 3 (p. 789)
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi enlargement of Figure 3 (approximate): the asterisks mark ratings 5.5 to 7.5; at 'very hot' (7.0), about 37.4°C with lidocaine and 37.7°C with cocaine. Figure 3 shows a lidocaine value at 'unbearably hot' (8.0), about 37.8°C, and no cocaine value at that rating.

key_findings.finding: The authors cite a test–retest variability of 0.09°C for the sweating threshold (from another study) and state that cocaine raised both thresholds by more than three times that.

Study conditions: intranasal cocaine hydrochloride or lidocaine hydrochloride, 2 mg/kg as a 10% solution, given before passive whole-body heating with water at 46°C in a tube-lined suit, supine, in sessions 3 to 6 days apart; the cocaine dose is described as half the standard dose for rhinolaryngological procedures.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Experimental Protocol (p. 786, continuing on p. 787)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the effect was seen at a very low dose that did not produce euphoria (citing their earlier study), that larger doses would be expected to add heat production, and that results from healthy cocaine-naive people may not apply to people with long-term cocaine use.
The authors speculate, without testing it, that hot weather, crowded nightclubs and raves would greatly amplify cocaine's effect on body temperature.

Background stated in the introduction, not data from this study: fatal cocaine overdose is typically associated with blood cocaine of 3 to 6 mg/L, while deaths with hyperthermia can occur at levels 10 to 20 times lower.
key_findings.note: Second-hand (Escobedo et al., 1991; Kosten & Kleber, 1988, the paper's references 1 and 2); a claim about post-mortem levels should cite those sources, not this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the control 'placebo (lidocaine, 2 mg/kg)' and the design placebo-controlled, but lidocaine is an active local anaesthetic, used, as the Methods say, to control for cocaine's local anaesthetic property; no inert placebo was given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison isolates effects of cocaine beyond local anaesthesia; it cannot exclude an effect of lidocaine itself on the outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline result, a greater rise in core temperature with cocaine, is given in the text only as P<0.001 with no magnitude; its size has to be read from Figure 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should use the figure reading with its approximation stated (about 0.2 to 0.3°C at the end of heating), not 'substantially'.

reporting_issues.issue: Conductance and sweat rate were compared at the 'highest common esophageal temperature' of 37.86°C, which the Methods do not define; in Figure 1 the mean lidocaine core temperature ends at about 37.5°C, so not every participant can have reached 37.86°C under lidocaine, and the number contributing is not given. The curve ends in Figure 2 (about 67% and 54% of maximum, read from the figure) also differ somewhat from the values in the text (70% and 49%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The P values of 0.03 and 0.04 may rest on fewer than 7 people; the comparison at that temperature should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 2 marks the cocaine–lidocaine difference at P<0.01, while the text gives P=0.03 (conductance) and P=0.04 (sweat rate) for the same responses; the test behind the legend (presumably the whole-curve analysis of variance) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different P values describe the same panel; cite the text values for the comparison at 37.86°C.

reporting_issues.issue: The standard error of the pre-heating esophageal temperature with cocaine is printed as ±0.01°C, against ±0.08°C with lidocaine; with 7 people this implies a between-person SD of about 0.03°C (editors' calculation), implausibly small beside the 0.21°C implied for the other session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a typographical error; it does not affect the conclusion that cocaine did not change core temperature before heating.

reporting_issues.issue: The duration of heating and the rule for stopping it are not stated; Figure 1 plots about 38 minutes in both conditions, and Figure 3 shows a lidocaine value at 'unbearably hot' with no cocaine value at that rating.
reporting_issues.consequence: If heating was stopped by tolerance or time, the end-of-heating comparisons depend on it; the paper does not allow this to be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The thermal-sensation scale is anchored at 4.0 as 'neutral' in the Methods but labelled 'Comfortable' in Figure 3, whose legend says the ratings were modified from the source scale; the number of men and women among the 7 is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the scale's anchors and the sample's composition cannot be fully checked.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Ann Intern Med 136(11), pp. 785–791 (all pages; Figures 1–3 checked on rendered pages, Figures 1 to 3 also enlarged at 300 dpi and the values marked as read from them are approximate; no table; no supplement; the author contributions said to be online were not available). The published letter with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002, 10.7326/0003-4819-137-10-200211190-00017) was not among the files read.

design_detail: Retrospective review of New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner files, 1990–1995, analysed as an ecological comparison of days (filed as retrospective-cohort, the nearest design the schema has: the units are calendar days, each classed as 'hot' or 'other' by the city's daily maximum temperature, and the outcome is the number of deaths certified on that day). Split sample: the 1990–1992 'index sample' (1096 days, 1382 cocaine overdose deaths) and the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine detected (1990–1995) were used to choose a threshold of 31.1°C (88°F); the threshold was then tested on the 1993–1995 'cross-validation sample' (1095 days; 2008 cocaine overdose deaths). Negative-control outcomes: daily counts of opiate overdose deaths without cocaine (793) and of other overdose deaths (85). Proxy for population cocaine use on each type of day: the share of homicides (4638 tested) and of traffic deaths at ages 15–54 (815 tested) with cocaine in blood.
can_establish: That in New York City in 1993–1995 more deaths per day were certified by the medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose on hot days than on other days, while the counts of opiate and other overdose deaths and the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in blood did not differ significantly by type of day.
cannot_establish: That heat raises the risk of death for a person who uses cocaine (nobody's heat exposure, dose or use on the day was known, and there is no count of the people using cocaine each day); by what mechanism (hyperthermia or cardiovascular strain); that the association is specific to cocaine (the cocaine and opiate estimates were never compared directly); or that it is due to temperature rather than to something else that differs between summer days and the rest of the year (no adjustment for season, month, day of week, holidays or trend).

sample.recruitment: Records (registry): all deaths in New York City handled by the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, which assesses every death believed unnatural, identified by manual review of all its medical files for 1990–1995 (pp. 1795–1796, Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: A death entered the overdose series if the medical examiner certified it as an unintentional overdose caused by one or more drugs; overdoses certified as suicide or homicide were excluded (Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph, pp. 1795–1796). Certification as death from intoxication required toxicology within the range usually found in such deaths, a history and circumstances consistent with fatal intoxication, and an autopsy without a disease or injury inconsistent with continued life (same section, 2nd paragraph, p. 1796). When several drugs were present above trace amounts, all were customarily listed as the cause, unless one was extremely high and the others at concentrations seen in people dying of other unequivocal causes (3rd paragraph, p. 1796). Deaths were then put into three hierarchical, mutually exclusive groups: (1) cocaine causative, judged from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology; (2) opiates causative, with cocaine or its metabolite not detected or detected in clinically insignificant amounts; (3) other substances (4th paragraph, p. 1796). Hyperthermia sample: deaths certified as due to hyperthermia and not classified as unintentional overdoses (n=48), of which those with benzoylecgonine detected at autopsy (n=10) (p. 1796, Methods › Temperature Data, 2nd paragraph). Traffic comparison restricted to ages 15–54 because 95% of cocaine overdoses occur in that range (p. 1796, Comparison Groups).
sample.demographics: Cocaine overdose deaths 1993–1995: mean age 39.0 years (SD 8.8), 94.9% aged 15–54; 1569 men (78.1%) and 439 women (21.9%); 505 non-Hispanic white (25.2%), 884 non-Hispanic Black (44.0%), 605 Hispanic (30.1%), 14 Asian or other (0.6%) (p. 1797). Homicides positive for cocaine: mean age 32.9 (SD 9.0), 97.5% aged 15–54, 83.6% men; traffic deaths positive for cocaine: mean age 34.4 (SD 8.5), 79.5% men (p. 1798). Hyperthermia deaths (n=48): 34 male (70.8%), 14 female (29.2%); 3 infants under 1 year, 29 aged 15–54, 16 over 54 (p. 1797).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). Coverage: complete autopsies in 93% of the 2008 cocaine overdose deaths (p. 1797); cocaine tested in blood in 4638 of 4793 homicides (96.8%) and in 815 of 921 traffic deaths at ages 15–54 (88.5%) (p. 1798); 40 of the 48 hyperthermia deaths (83.3%) screened for benzoylecgonine and cocaine, 41 for ethanol (p. 1797).
sample.selection_effects: Deaths are counted only through medical examiner certification, so the series depends on the examiner's judgment that cocaine caused the death. Deaths certified as hyperthermia were kept out of the overdose series even when benzoylecgonine was found (10 in six years); the authors suggest that some deaths certified as acute cocaine intoxication may have been undetected hyperthermia, because hyperthermia is a clinical diagnosis without pathological findings and people may be found hours after death (p. 1799, Comment, 4th paragraph). The homicide and traffic groups were chosen as proxies for cocaine use in the same population because of similar demographics and neighbourhoods (p. 1796, Comparison Groups); they are not samples of people who use cocaine.

exposure.measurement: Hourly temperatures from the National Weather Service station in Central Park, Manhattan, for every day from 1 January 1990 to 31 December 1995; the exposure is the city-wide daily maximum (p. 1796, Temperature Data). A day was 'hot' if its maximum hourly temperature, or that of the preceding day, was 31.1°C (88°F) or more (a 1-day lag; Methods › Temperature Data, 4th paragraph, pp. 1796–1797; Table 1 footnote, p. 1797). The threshold was chosen from the median maximum temperature on the dates of the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine detected (30.9°C; range 17.2 to 39.4°C; mean 29.6°C, SD 6.1) and from the index-sample plot, flat to 27.8°C and rising more steeply from 31.1°C (pp. 1796–1797; Figure 1). The heat index correlated with the daily maximum at r=0.986, and analyses using it were said to give similar results, which are not shown (pp. 1797, 1800).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known. The authors state that the amount of cocaine used before death, the temperature to which people were exposed when they used it, and whether they used occasionally or heavily are all unknown (p. 1800, Comment, 10th paragraph). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded from autopsy toxicology and compared between types of day, not adjusted for. Among cocaine overdose deaths on hot and other days: ethanol 42.9% and 41.4%; opiates 57.1% and 61.7%; benzodiazepines 10.3% and 11.5%; barbiturates 1.2% and 1.4%; salicylates 0.9% and 1.3% (p. 1798). At least one of five drug classes the authors associate with a risk of hyperthermia (antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiparkinsonian and antihistaminic drugs, psychostimulants and sympathomimetics, phencyclidine) was found in 20.3% and 22.0% (Table 2, p. 1798). The 'cocaine overdose' group therefore means deaths in which cocaine was judged causative, with opiates present in most of them; the opiate group excludes deaths with clinically significant cocaine.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). The timing of the last cocaine use before death is not known.

comparison.controls: Within each overdose group, the 949 'other' days against the 146 hot days of 1993–1995. Negative-control outcomes: daily counts of opiate overdose deaths without cocaine and of other overdose deaths. Proxy for cocaine use in the population: the share of homicides, and of traffic deaths at ages 15–54, with cocaine in blood, on hot against other days.
comparison.matching: None. Cocaine overdose deaths on hot and on other days did not differ significantly by age, race, sex or location of death (p. 1797).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: where people were and what temperature they were exposed to (indoors or outdoors, air conditioning), the amount and pattern of cocaine use, tolerance, heart disease, and the number of people using cocaine on each day. Not modelled: season, month, day of week, holidays, humidity (beyond the unshown heat-index analysis) and trend over the years.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: By definition, the opiate group had no cocaine or only clinically insignificant amounts. The homicide and traffic comparisons concern cocaine in blood only.

outcomes.instruments: Medical examiner certification of cause and manner of death (history, circumstances, autopsy and laboratory data) (p. 1796). Toxicology by the single laboratory of the medical examiner's office on urine and blood taken at autopsy and stored at 4°C: benzoylecgonine screened in urine by enzyme immunoassay (positive at 0.3 mg/L or more) or, without urine, in blood by radioimmunoassay (0.1 mg/L or more), positives substantiated by radioimmunoassay in another tissue; cocaine in blood by gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection (0.1 mg/L or more), positives confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; opiates by urine enzyme immunoassay or blood radioimmunoassay; ethanol by headspace chromatography; other drugs by several methods (p. 1796, Toxicologic Procedures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. The interval between death and autopsy, and between autopsy and assay, is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Outcome: the number of deaths per day certified as unintentional overdose in each of the three hierarchical groups; for the comparison groups, the proportion of deaths with cocaine in blood. Hyperthermia deaths: medical examiner certification of hyperthermia as the cause, which the authors note is a clinical diagnosis rather than one established by pathological findings (p. 1799).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two-tailed alpha of .05 for each of the five tests (three Mann-Whitney comparisons of daily counts, two chi-square tests of proportions) (p. 1797). The differences in Table 2 were not tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the certification, which was made in routine practice before the study. Whether abstraction from the files was blind to the weather is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cross-validation sample 1993–1995 (Table 1, p. 1797): cocaine overdose deaths averaged 2.34 per day on hot days (SD 1.68; 341 deaths on 146 days) and 1.76 on other days (SD 1.37; 1667 deaths on 949 days), Mann-Whitney z=3.98, P<.001, a 33% higher mean. Opiate overdose deaths 0.81 (SD 0.94) and 0.71 (SD 0.86), z=1.08, P=.28. Other overdose deaths 0.08 and 0.08 (SD 0.28 each), z=0.39, P=.69. Share with cocaine in blood: homicides 18.9% (136 of 719) on hot days and 19.5% (766 of 3919) on other days, chi-square 0.11, P=.69; traffic deaths 9.5% (12 of 126) and 10.3% (71 of 689), chi-square 0.01, P=.91 (p. 1798). Editors' calculation from the counts in Table 1 (Poisson rate ratios with 95% intervals; they ignore the overdispersion and the autocorrelation of 0.12 the paper reports, so they are somewhat too narrow): cocaine 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49); opiates 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38); other overdoses 1.07 (0.58 to 1.97); ratio of the cocaine to the opiate rate ratio 1.17 (0.93 to 1.47), P about .18. Difference in mean daily cocaine deaths 0.58 (0.29 to 0.87) (editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs). Editors' calculation of the excess: about 85 more cocaine overdose deaths on the 146 hot days than the other-day rate predicts, about 4% of the 2008 deaths in the three years.
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted Mann-Whitney tests with the day as unit, and chi-square tests with the person as unit (p. 1797). Autocorrelation of daily cocaine overdose deaths 0.12 (P<.001); deaths on the previous day accounted for 1.4% of the variance (pp. 1797–1798).
analysis.selective_reporting: Split-sample design: the threshold was chosen on 1990–1992 data and tested once on 1993–1995 data, which guards against choosing the threshold that fits best. The heat-index analyses are described as similar but not shown (p. 1800). The class-by-class percentages of Table 2 are presented without tests, and the text calls the proportions nearly identical although one class differs by about half (5.0% against 9.7%).
analysis.power: Not reported. The 'other overdose' comparison rests on 85 deaths (0.08 a day) and cannot detect even large relative differences (editors' rate-ratio interval 0.58 to 1.97); the opiate comparison cannot exclude an increase of about a third.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In New York City in 1993–1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's maximum reached 31.1°C had a third more deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). Opiate and other overdose deaths did not differ significantly (0.81 against 0.71; 0.08 against 0.08), and the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in blood was unchanged. Over six years, 10 of the 40 screened deaths certified as hyperthermia had benzoylecgonine detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that high ambient temperature is associated with a significant increase in cocaine overdose mortality, that the increase is not explained by changes in cocaine use in the general population, and that cocaine use "appears to be even more dangerous on hot days" (p. 1795). Gaps: (1) the association is between days and death counts; no person's heat exposure or use was known, which the authors acknowledge (p. 1800). (2) The Comment calls the association specific to cocaine (p. 1798), but this rests on non-significant opiate and other-overdose tests, not on a comparison of the estimates; by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio is 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38) and does not differ significantly from the cocaine ratio of 1.33. (3) Season and other time-varying factors were not adjusted for. (4) The 'not explained by use' argument rests on homicide and traffic victims as proxies for people using cocaine on each day, and on an unshown statement that screening rates do not change with the weather (p. 1799). (5) The Comment's statement that a quarter of hyperthermia decedents under 55 had used cocaine immediately before death (p. 1798) reads the detection of cocaine as the timing of use, and its comparison with a 1.3% survey prevalence of past-month use (p. 1799) sets a toxicology finding in deaths against self-report in households. Against this, the discussion is restrained: it says the temperature effect has no major influence on annual cocaine mortality, because only about 10% of days reach the threshold (pp. 1798–1799), and that a direct effect cannot be proved (p. 1800).

timeline.event: Editorial on this paper in the same JAMA issue (Kilbourne, 1998, 'Cocaine use and death during heat waves'; cited on p. 1795 as the editorial comment on p. 1828; not among the files read for this card).

Auger et al. (2017), 'Association of elevated ambient temperature with death from cocaine overdose' (Drug and Alcohol Dependence), is on the project's reading list for the same question; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication was read for this card. The project's reading list names a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths or emergency visits (Bohnert et al., 2010; Henderson et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2023), none appraised yet; the status should be set when they are. Within this paper the result was reproduced out of sample, from the 1990–1992 data on which the threshold was chosen to the 1993–1995 data on which it was tested.

funding.funder: Grant DA 06534 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) and the Dewitt Wallace Reader's Digest Foundation (p. 1800).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Departments of Psychiatry and of Public Health, Cornell University Medical College; one author (Hirsch) from the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, New York, and the Department of Forensic Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, the office whose certifications are the study's outcome data (p. 1795). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A time-series or case-crossover analysis of cocaine-involved deaths over many years and several cities, with daily temperature and humidity, adjusted for season, day of week, holidays and trend, in which opioid-only deaths are analysed in the same model so that the difference between drugs is tested directly; with scene information (indoors or outdoors, air conditioning) and recorded signs of hyperthermia, to separate a heat effect on people who used cocaine from more use on hot days.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind: hot days are summer days, and season, month, day of week, holidays and trend were not modelled. The negative-control outcomes (opiate and other overdose deaths; cocaine positivity in homicides and traffic deaths) partly address this, but they are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate.

One weather station's daily maximum stands for everyone's exposure; nobody's actual temperature (indoors, air conditioning) is known. The threshold was chosen on earlier data, which avoids fitting it to the test data. Misclassification of this kind would mostly weaken an association.
All deaths certified by one city's medical examiner over three years, whatever the weather.
None relevant to the comparison.
Complete autopsies in 93% of cocaine overdose deaths; cocaine tested in 96.8% of homicides and 88.5% of traffic deaths.

Cause of death is the examiner's judgment from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology, not blind to the circumstances of the death; hyperthermia certification, which removed 10 cocaine-positive deaths from the overdose series, depends on findings that may themselves vary with the weather.
One prespecified threshold tested out of sample; all three overdose groups and both comparison groups reported. The heat-index analyses are mentioned but not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The count data are complete medical examiner series, and the split-sample test of a threshold chosen in advance is a real strength. But the comparison of hot with other days is entirely unadjusted, so seasonal factors that travel with heat cannot be excluded, and the comparisons offered against them are too imprecise to show that the association is specific to cocaine. ROBINS-E overall follows the worst domain (confounding). The card may be cited for the higher number of certified cocaine overdose deaths on hot days in New York City in 1993–1995, for how those deaths were defined and tested, and for the other drugs found in them; not for an individual's risk, for a mechanism, or for an effect shown to be specific to cocaine.

key_findings.finding: In 1993–1995 (1095 days, 146 of them hot), New York City had 2008 deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose: a mean of 2.34 a day (SD 1.68; 341 deaths) on hot days against 1.76 (SD 1.37; 1667 deaths) on other days, Mann-Whitney z=3.98, P<.001, a 33% higher mean.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: A 'hot' day is one on which that day's or the previous day's maximum reached 31.1°C (88°F) (Table 1 footnote); the abstract describes hot days without the lag day.

key_findings.finding: Opiate overdose deaths without cocaine: 0.81 a day (SD 0.94; 118 deaths) on hot days against 0.71 (SD 0.86; 675 deaths) on other days, z=1.08, P=.28. Other overdose deaths: 0.08 against 0.08 (12 and 73 deaths), z=0.39, P=.69. The smoothed plots show no visible change with temperature for either group.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 1797); Results › Fatal Unintentional Overdoses of Opiates and Other Drugs (p. 1798); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 1799)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: opiate rate ratio 1.14 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.38) against 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49) for cocaine; the two do not differ significantly (ratio 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47). A null opiate test is not evidence that the association is confined to cocaine.

key_findings.finding: The share of deaths with cocaine in blood did not change with the weather: homicides 18.9% (136 of 719) on hot days and 19.5% (766 of 3919) on other days, P=.69; traffic deaths at ages 15–54, 9.5% (12 of 126) and 10.3% (71 of 689), P=.91.

Cocaine overdose deaths were mostly deaths with other drugs present as well: opiates were detected in 57.1% (hot days) and 61.7% (other days), ethanol in 42.9% and 41.4%, benzodiazepines in 10.3% and 11.5%; at least one of five drug classes the authors link to a risk of hyperthermia in 20.3% and 22.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: How a death was counted as a cocaine overdose: the medical examiner certified an unintentional overdose by one or more drugs (toxicology in the range usual in such deaths, consistent history and circumstances, no disease or injury inconsistent with life at autopsy); the authors then classed it as cocaine-caused when cocaine was judged causative from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology, ahead of opiates and other drugs in a hierarchy. Complete autopsies were done in 93% of the 2008 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph (pp. 1795–1796) to 4th paragraph (p. 1796); Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 2nd paragraph (p. 1797)

key_findings.finding: Toxicology was done in one laboratory on autopsy urine and blood stored at 4°C: benzoylecgonine by urine immunoassay (positive at 0.3 mg/L or more) or blood radioimmunoassay (0.1 mg/L or more), confirmed in another tissue; cocaine in blood by gas chromatography (0.1 mg/L or more), confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry.

Of 48 deaths certified as hyperthermia in 1990–1995 (not classed as overdoses), 40 were screened: benzoylecgonine was detected in 10 (25% of those screened, 21% of all 48) and cocaine in 7; opiates in 1 of 40 and ethanol in 5 of 41. Restricted to ages 15–54 (n=27), 37.0% had benzoylecgonine and 25.9% cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Deaths Due to Hyperthermia, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The same section gives 29 deaths aged 15–54 (60.4%); the denominator of 27 is not explained (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The threshold of 31.1°C (88°F) was chosen from the median daily maximum on the dates of the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine (30.9°C; range 17.2 to 39.4°C) and from the 1990–1992 index sample (1096 days, 1382 cocaine overdose deaths), in which the cumulative mean of deaths was flat up to 27.8°C and rose more steeply from 31.1°C.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Temperature Data, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (the 4th continuing on p. 1797); Figure 1 (p. 1797)

key_findings.finding: Daily cocaine overdose deaths were autocorrelated at 0.12 (P<.001); deaths on the previous day accounted for 1.4% of the variance. Decedents on hot and on other days did not differ significantly by age, race, sex or location of death. The two days with the most cocaine overdose deaths (printed as n=9) had maxima of 37.2°C and 33.3°C.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 3rd paragraph (p. 1797, continuing on p. 1798)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that only about 10% of days in a year reach 31.1°C in New York City, so the temperature effect does not have a major influence on annual cocaine overdose mortality.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: about 85 deaths above the other-day rate on the 146 hot days, some 4% of the 2008 deaths of 1993–1995.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that some deaths certified as acute cocaine intoxication may have been undetected hyperthermia, because hyperthermia is a clinical diagnosis without pathological findings and people who die after using cocaine may not be found for hours.

Limitations stated by the authors: the dose used before death, the temperature at the time of use, and whether people used occasionally or heavily are unknown; the threshold applies to a group, not to individuals, and may differ in other cities.

reporting_issues.issue: The hyperthermia section reports 29 deaths aged 15–54 (60.4% of 48), but the analysis restricted to that age group uses n=27, with 37.0% (10) positive for benzoylecgonine and 25.9% (7) for cocaine; the difference is not explained (it may be the number screened).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Comment's 'a quarter of all individuals younger than 55' (p. 1798) rests on 7 of 27, a denominator that excludes the three infants under 1 year and possibly two unscreened deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says at least 1 in 4 deaths known to result from hyperthermia had a positive cocaine test (p. 1799), but 1 in 4 is the share of the 40 screened deaths (10); of all 48 the known minimum is 10 (21%), as the Results state (p. 1797).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower bound is about 1 in 5, not 1 in 4; cite 10 of 40 screened (25%) or 10 of 48 (21%).

reporting_issues.issue: For homicides, the printed chi-square of 0.11 with 1 df corresponds to P of about .74, not the printed .69; recomputed from the printed counts, the uncorrected chi-square is about 0.15 (P about .69) and the continuity-corrected value about 0.12 (P about .73). The traffic result (chi-square 0.01, P=.91) matches a continuity-corrected test (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the conclusion (no difference either way), but the statistic and its P value come from different versions of the test.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract defines hot days as days with a maximum of 31.1°C or more, whereas the analysis also counts the day after such a day as hot (1-day lag; p. 1797, Methods and Table 1 footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 33% difference applies to days that were hot or followed a hot day; a claim should use the paper's own definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Comment say cocaine overdose deaths increased steadily above the threshold, but this is read from a cumulative mean curve (Figure 1) and from 5-degree moving averages (Figure 2), whose highest-temperature points rest on few days and which do not rise smoothly; no test of trend is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper supports a higher mean above the threshold, not a demonstrated dose–response above it.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the proportion of cocaine overdose deaths positive for drugs associated with hyperthermia was nearly identical on hot and other days (p. 1798); this holds for 'any drug' (20.3% against 22.0%), but antiparkinsonian and antihistaminic drugs were found in 5.0% against 9.7%. No class was tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the class differences cannot be interpreted without tests.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that drug screening rates are not influenced by hot weather in New York City is given without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument from the comparison groups that cocaine use did not rise on hot days depends on this unshown premise.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 4 gives the period as 1992 through 1995, whereas the cross-validation period, and the legends of Figures 2 and 3, are 1993 through 1995. The opiate cut-off in blood is printed as '0.1 mg' without a volume (p. 1796).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the results.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), JAMA 279(22), pp. 1795–1800 (all pages; Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4 checked on rendered pages; figure values not extracted beyond what the text states; no supplement). The editorial comment named on p. 1795 (Kilbourne, 1998, 10.1001/jama.279.22.1828) was not among the files read.

design_detail: Inpatient human laboratory study (short report), within-person: six people who smoked cocaine almost daily each completed eight sessions. In the first four sessions the alternative to cocaine was a voucher for $5 in money, in the last four a $5 merchandise voucher (fixed order, not randomized or counterbalanced); each session offered one cocaine dose level (0 mg placebo, 12, 25 or 50 mg smoked cocaine base; order of doses within each block not reported). A session began with a sample trial (the session's dose and its voucher type), followed by five choice trials 14 minutes apart, each requiring 200 key presses for the chosen option. The vouchers could be turned into $5 in money, or into a $5 voucher for goods at named stores, only when the participant left the hospital (every voucher could be cashed in only when the study ended), so the non-drug reward was deferred while the dose was immediate. Outcome: number of cocaine choices (0–5 per session, 0–20 per voucher type). Described by the authors as double-blind.
can_establish: That in six people who smoked cocaine almost daily, studied as inpatients, cocaine choices rose with dose, and that about two fewer of 20 cocaine options were taken when a $5 money voucher was the alternative than when a $5 merchandise voucher was, under this fixed-order procedure.
cannot_establish: Whether money itself rather than the order of the conditions (money sessions always came first) produced the difference; how much either voucher reduced cocaine choice (there was no condition without an alternative); whether the difference holds at any single dose (none was significant), in people seeking treatment, outside the laboratory, or for abstinence (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Word-of-mouth referral and newspaper advertisements in New York City; inpatients of the Irving Center for Clinical Research, New York Presbyterian Hospital, for the whole study, with television, radio and films available and visitors not allowed (p. 88, Methods › Participants; Procedure, 1st paragraph). Whether participants were seeking treatment is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Almost daily use of smoked cocaine; passing comprehensive medical and psychological evaluations; serum pregnancy test at screening and urine pregnancy test at the start of sessions for women (p. 88). No diagnostic criteria and no criteria about other drug use are reported.
sample.demographics: Four women (three African-American, one Hispanic) and two men (both Caucasian); age 30–39 years (mean 36); spending $100–$500 (mean $280) a week on cocaine (p. 88).
sample.attrition: None reported; Figure 2 shows all six participants in both voucher conditions (p. 89).
sample.selection_effects: A small self-selected group of people who smoked cocaine frequently and consented to an inpatient study in which cocaine would be given, possibly daily (p. 88); not described as treatment-seeking. The authors report that all participants used substantially larger amounts of cocaine outside the laboratory than in the sessions (p. 90).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine given by research staff in each session; choices recorded by computer (pp. 88–89).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: smoked cocaine base, prepared by the hospital pharmacy from cocaine hydrochloride supplied by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, at 0 (placebo), 12, 25 or 50 mg per dose; one dose level per session, a sample dose plus up to five chosen doses at 14-minute intervals, each given only if heart rate and blood pressure were within the study's preset safety limits (pp. 88–89). The number of sessions per day and the interval between sessions are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco cigarettes were allowed outside sessions (p. 88); alcohol and other drug use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Inpatient throughout; time since last cocaine use before the first session and any urine toxicology are not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant's choices with a $5 money voucher against a $5 merchandise voucher (redeemable at specific stores; both kinds exchangeable only upon discharge), across the same four dose levels; 0 mg served as a placebo dose. No condition without an alternative (p. 90, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person comparison).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a within-person comparison; how much each participant valued money relative to merchandise was not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Number of cocaine choices per session (0–5) and per voucher type (0–20), recorded by computer. Subjective-effects questionnaires, heart rate and blood pressure every 2 minutes, and blood samples were also collected (p. 88, Apparatus), but no results for them are reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: The choice procedure and the merchandise vouchers are the laboratory's own, used in its studies of possible cocaine medications (Haney et al. 1998, 1999; Ward et al. 1998, as cited, pp. 87, 90).
outcomes.operationalization: Reinforcing effect of cocaine = number of times the cocaine option was chosen over the voucher; effectiveness of an alternative = fewer cocaine choices. The 0 mg (placebo) choices are counted as cocaine choices.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: one two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA (dose × voucher type) plus voucher comparisons at each of the four doses (p. 89).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Choices were recorded automatically. The design is called double-blind (p. 87), but each sample trial told participants which voucher was available (p. 88); participants closed their eyes when given a dose to hide dose cues; how staff were blinded is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Dose: F(3, 15)=15.26, P<0.001; voucher type: F(1, 5)=7.48, P<0.05; no significant interaction and no significant voucher difference at any single dose (p. 89, Results). Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi (bar heights fall on whole numbers): total cocaine choices out of 20, money vs merchandise, 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7 and 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8. Editors' calculation: mean paired difference 2.17 choices (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12); the paired t of 2.73 squares to 7.48, reproducing the printed F(1, 5). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (means fall on sixths): money vs merchandise, 0 mg 0.67 vs 1.50, 12 mg 2.50 vs 2.67, 25 mg 3.67 vs 4.17, 50 mg 3.83 vs 4.50 choices of 5; 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) came from the placebo sessions (placebo chosen on 4 vs 9 of 30 trials), and for the active doses the totals were 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: Subjective-effects ratings, heart rate, blood pressure and blood samples were collected (p. 88) but not reported; the order of doses within each voucher block is not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; six participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six inpatients chose cocaine more often as the dose rose, and on average 2.2 fewer of 20 cocaine options (95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation) in the money-voucher sessions, which always came first, than in the merchandise-voucher sessions; no single dose showed a significant difference, one participant chose identically in both, and more than a third of the difference came from placebo sessions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the data demonstrate that money vouchers are a more effective alternative reinforcer than merchandise vouchers, generalizing to people who use cocaine (p. 87). The discussion turns the difference into money being 10% more effective and suggests a $5.50 merchandise voucher would in theory equal $5.00 in cash (p. 90), a proportionality not tested; it concedes that there was no condition without a voucher and no randomization of order, and argues order effects are unlikely from the group's other studies and participants' reports of heavier use outside (p. 90). It then extends the result to outpatient contingency management, suggesting cash or larger vouchers would further enhance abstinence (p. 90), an outcome not measured here.

timeline.event: Higgins, Bickel & Hughes: in a laboratory study, intranasal cocaine choice fell as the value of a money alternative rose (as described, p. 87).
Hatsukami et al.: smoked cocaine self-administration fell as money value rose (as described, p. 90).
Chutuape et al.: methadone patients rewarded for drug-free urine chose cash vouchers over a take-home dose 75% of the time (as described, p. 90).
This study: money vs merchandise vouchers of equal face value, six inpatients, fixed order.

replication.where_it_stands: No replication of the money-versus-merchandise comparison is among the papers read for this round. The earlier laboratory studies the authors cite found that larger money alternatives reduced cocaine choice; the field evidence that non-drug alternatives reduce use comes from contingency management trials, not from this study.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-06234; the Irving Center for Clinical Research of the New York Presbyterian Medical Center, where participants resided, supported by National Institutes of Health grant MOI-RR-00645 (Acknowledgements, p. 91).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute, and Department of Psychiatry, College of Physicians and Surgeons of Columbia University (p. 87). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study with randomized or counterbalanced order of alternatives, a condition without any alternative, several values of each kind of voucher, analyses of active doses separately from placebo, and enough participants (including people seeking treatment); then a field comparison of cash and merchandise incentives in contingency management with abstinence as the outcome.

domains.note: Money-voucher sessions always came first and merchandise sessions last; the order of doses within each block is not reported.

The voucher comparison coincides completely with period (sessions 1–4 against 5–8), so changes over the stay (tolerance, habituation to the unit, accumulating vouchers) cannot be separated from voucher type; the authors' argument against order effects rests on other studies and self-report.

Participants knew the voucher type by design (unavoidable for this question); called double-blind without describing staff blinding; doses could be withheld under the vital-sign limits, and whether any were is not reported.
All six participants completed both voucher conditions (Figure 2).
Choices were recorded by computer.
No protocol; subjective, cardiovascular and blood measures were collected but not reported; the per-dose comparisons are reported as not significant, but without statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applied to the within-person comparison of money and merchandise vouchers (the dose–response finding is less exposed). Because the two voucher conditions ran in a fixed order, the voucher effect cannot be separated from time in the study; with six participants it rests on one F test at P<0.05, and no single dose showed a difference. The outcome was recorded automatically and no one dropped out. Cite the paper as a small laboratory demonstration that the kind of non-drug alternative offered can shift cocaine choices in people who smoke cocaine frequently, with the fixed order and the size of the difference (about 2 of 20 choices, a third of it from placebo sessions) stated; do not cite it for treatment, abstinence, or a general ranking of cash over goods.

key_findings.finding: Six people took part: four women (three African-American, one Hispanic) and two Caucasian men, aged 30–39 (mean 36), recruited by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements in New York City; all reported almost daily smoked cocaine use and spending $100–$500 (mean $280) a week on cocaine, and all passed medical and psychological evaluations. Whether they were seeking treatment is not stated.

Participants lived on an inpatient research unit for the whole study and completed eight sessions: four with a $5 money voucher as the alternative, then four with a $5 merchandise voucher (both exchangeable only upon discharge); each session offered one dose level (0, 12, 25 or 50 mg smoked cocaine) in a sample trial and five choice trials 14 minutes apart, each choice requiring 200 key presses, with doses given only within preset heart-rate and blood-pressure limits; tobacco smoking was allowed between sessions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 88) and 3rd paragraph (p. 88, ending at the top of p. 89)

key_findings.finding: Cocaine choices increased with dose (F(3, 15)=15.26, P<0.001) and were fewer when the money voucher was the alternative (F(1, 5)=7.48, P<0.05); there was no significant interaction, and no significant difference between voucher types at any single dose (0, 12, 25 or 50 mg).
All but one participant chose more cocaine doses in the merchandise sessions than in the money sessions (maximum 20 per condition).
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi (bar heights fall on whole numbers): money vs merchandise 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7 and 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8. Editors' calculation: mean paired difference 2.17 (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12); the paired t (2.73) squares to the printed F(1, 5) of 7.48.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows mean cocaine choices (of 5) by dose and voucher type, rising with dose in both conditions, with the merchandise line above the money line at every dose and the largest gap at 0 mg.
key_findings.note: Editors' reading at 300 dpi (means fall on sixths, consistent with the totals in Figure 2): money vs merchandise 0.67 vs 1.50 at 0 mg, 2.50 vs 2.67 at 12 mg, 3.67 vs 4.17 at 25 mg, 3.83 vs 4.50 at 50 mg. Editors' calculation: 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) came from placebo sessions (placebo chosen on 4 vs 9 of 30 trials); active doses 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.

key_findings.finding: The authors express the result as about two fewer of 20 doses with money vouchers, call money vouchers 10% more effective, and suggest that raising merchandise value by 10% ($5.50 against $5.00 in cash) would in theory make the two equivalent. They acknowledge that without a no-voucher condition the absolute influence of either voucher cannot be quantified, and that the order was not randomized (cash first), but judge order effects unlikely because participants in their studies change little across sessions and reported using substantially larger amounts outside the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: The laboratory had used merchandise vouchers in its medication studies to lower the chance that participants would buy drugs with their earnings after discharge; the authors suggest that money alternatives could make laboratory tests of possible cocaine medications more sensitive.

The authors extend the result to outpatient treatment: cash or merchandise vouchers of greater value would further enhance abstinence; in support they cite a contingency-management study in which methadone patients chose cash vouchers over a methadone take-home dose 75% of the time.

Subjective-effects questionnaires were completed, heart rate and blood pressure were recorded every 2 minutes from 30 minutes before dosing, and a catheter was placed for blood withdrawals, but only choice data are reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The study is called double-blind, but each session's sample trial gave participants a voucher showing which alternative was available, so the voucher comparison was open by design; how staff were blinded is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: At most the dose could have been blinded; expectations about the vouchers could act on choices.

reporting_issues.issue: The counted cocaine choices include choices of the 0 mg (placebo) dose; by the editors' reading of Figure 1, 38% of the voucher difference came from placebo sessions, and for the active doses the totals were 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that significantly less cocaine was self-administered with money vouchers overstates the effect on active cocaine; the difference on active doses was about 1.3 of 15 choices.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend refers to asterisks marking significant differences between voucher conditions, but only the group means carry one; the error bars on the means are not defined, and their length matches the SD of the six totals (editors' calculation: 5.3 and 4.6), whereas Figure 1's bars are SEM.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; individual participants' differences were not tested, and readers could take Figure 2's bars for SEM.

reporting_issues.issue: Subjective-effects ratings, heart rate, blood pressure and blood samples were collected but not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be ruled out, and whether any dose was withheld under the vital-sign limits is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of dose levels within each voucher block, the number of sessions per day and the interval between sessions are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose comparison could also be confounded with order or time, and the schedule cannot be compared with real-world use.

design_detail: Inpatient human laboratory study at a university general clinical research centre. Ten paid volunteers who used cocaine and alcohol completed five sessions in a double-blind, balanced crossover: ethanol 1.0 g/kg with deuterium-labelled cocaine-d5 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg/kg; ethanol 1.0 g/kg with cocaine placebo; and double placebo. In every session 7.5 mg of deuterium-labelled cocaethylene-d3 was infused at the same time as the cocaine or its placebo, as a tracer for working out how much cocaethylene the body formed. Ethanol (or orange juice alone) was drunk in five portions over 30 minutes; the cocaine infusion ran at a constant rate over 15 minutes, starting 1 hour after the first drink. Sessions were at least a week apart and participants stayed on the unit for 36 hours after dosing. Separately, 6 of the 10 returned 1 to 3 months later for a sixth session with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg and ethanol placebo; the authors state this session was neither blinded nor randomized, and its results are analysed as a subset comparison (n = 6). Labelled cocaine, cocaethylene and benzoylecgonine were measured in plasma and urine by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; breath ethanol, heart rate, blood pressure, rate-pressure product and spoken or computer-entered ratings were recorded.
can_establish: In 10 people who used cocaine and alcohol and were not dependent on drugs other than nicotine, what share of an intravenous cocaine dose given 1 hour after a substantial oral ethanol dose appeared as cocaethylene, how cocaethylene, cocaine and benzoylecgonine concentrations in plasma and urine changed across a four-fold range of cocaine study doses, and how heart rate, blood pressure and ratings changed in those same conditions relative to ethanol alone and double placebo.
cannot_establish: Whether cocaethylene itself caused any of the effects measured (it was never given alone at an active dose, and its formation cannot be separated from the presence of ethanol); whether the combination is more harmful than cocaine alone (no toxicity outcome, and the cocaine-alone comparison rests on 6 people in an unblinded session months later); what happens when alcohol is drunk after cocaine, at other ethanol doses, or by other routes; and whether any of this extends to the amounts and patterns people use outside a laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper advertisements and referral from people who had taken part in earlier studies; all were paid (pp. 171, 172). To obtain the 10 who were entered and tested, 53 applicants were screened out, by their own preference or by the investigators, most often for not having enough experience with substantial intravenous cocaine doses (pp. 172–173).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Had used cocaine and ethanol; not dependent by DSM-IV criteria on drugs other than nicotine; physical or mental conditions that might raise risk excluded after history, physical examination, screening blood chemistry and electrocardiogram. Written informed consent; approval by the university's human-research committee and the state research advisory panel (p. 171).
sample.demographics: Eight men and two women; mean age 34 (SD 7) years; mean weight 71 (SD 7) kg; eight Caucasian and two African-American (p. 172).
sample.attrition: No dropouts are reported from the five blinded sessions. Only 6 of the 10 took part in the later cocaine-alone session; how those six were chosen is not stated (p. 171).
sample.selection_effects: A small, experienced group selected for tolerating substantial intravenous doses: 53 of 63 applicants were screened out, mainly for too little experience with intravenous cocaine, the preferred route for all 10. None had ever sought treatment for cocaine-related problems, so this is not a treatment sample. Reported alcohol use was light: on average 13 g of ethanol a week (range 2–23 g), while the study's single ethanol dose of 1.0 g/kg is about 71 g at the mean weight, roughly five times the average reported weekly intake (editors' calculation from pp. 172–173). The results therefore describe a drinking exposure unlike these participants' own reported pattern.

exposure.measurement: Drugs given in the laboratory. Cocaine-d5, cocaethylene-d3, cocaethylene-d5, benzoylecgonine and ecgonine esters measured in plasma and urine by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry with deuterium-labelled internal standards; limits of quantitation 5 ng/ml in plasma and 10 ng/ml in urine for the listed compounds. Breath ethanol by infrared spectrophotometry, reported as blood ethanol in g/dl (p. 172). Participants' own use was self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Cocaine-d5 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg/kg or placebo by constant-rate intravenous infusion over 15 minutes, beginning 1 hour after the first drink; 7.5 mg cocaethylene-d3 infused over the same period from a separate syringe into the same line; ethanol 1.0 g/kg (80-proof vodka as a 15.8% wt/vol solution in orange juice) or orange juice alone, in five portions every 6 minutes over 30 minutes (pp. 171–172). The authors state the 15-minute infusion was chosen so that it could be stopped if adverse effects appeared and was not intended to mimic how people use intravenous cocaine (p. 171). Self-reported own use: typical weekly cocaine about 905 mg (range 94–3500 mg); all had used at least 250 mg on one or more occasions; average 13 g of ethanol weekly (range 2–23 g) (pp. 172–173).
exposure.polysubstance: Extensive and quantified but not controlled: 7 of 10 smoked tobacco (mean 20 cigarettes daily); 8 smoked cannabis (mean 2.3 g per week, range 0.6–5.5 g); 3 used amphetamines (mean 375 mg weekly, range 62–1000 mg); 3 used heroin (56 mg weekly, range 50–62 mg); 1 used diazepam (5 mg weekly) (p. 173). None of these was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked to abstain from psychoactive drugs other than caffeine and nicotine for 24 hours before each session, and from cigarettes and caffeine from 2 hours before to 6 hours after dosing; admitted the day before each session and resident for 36 hours after (pp. 171–172). Verification is not described, and the authors report that on two occasions the amount of unlabelled cocaine metabolites in pre-dose urine exceeded the amount after the laboratory dose, which they take as evidence of use outside the study (p. 180).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant served in all five blinded conditions, which included ethanol with cocaine placebo and a double placebo. The cocaine-alone condition (ethanol placebo with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg) was an open, non-randomized sixth session in 6 of the 10, 1 to 3 months later (p. 171).
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the deuterium labels allowed cocaine-derived cocaethylene-d5 to be told apart from the infused cocaethylene-d3 in the same session, so the drug and its metabolite did not have to be given on separate days (pp. 170–171).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetic questions. For the rated effects, the pre-dose value in each session is the only baseline; tolerance from the participants' own use was not measured, and the authors raise lingering tolerance as a possible reason for small differences between conditions (p. 180).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group). Tobacco, cannabis and other drug use was recorded for all participants and not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma and urine concentrations and derived non-compartmental pharmacokinetic parameters (AUC to infinity by the trapezoidal then log-trapezoidal method, Cmax, Tmax, half-life, plasma and renal clearance, volume of distribution); fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene from the ratio of cocaethylene-d5 to cocaethylene-d3 areas under the curve and the known 7.5 mg cocaethylene-d3 dose, corrected for molecular weights of 308 and 322. Heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure by automated monitor, and rate-pressure product as their product. Spoken 0–100 ratings of ethanol intoxication, cocaine intoxication and total intoxication; computer-entered 100 mm visual analogue ratings of drug combination liking and 'good' drug effect, anchored 0 (none) to 100 (most ever) (pp. 171–172).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assay limits of quantitation are given; assay precision is not reported in this paper. The rating scales are study-specific, have no norms, and the intoxication ratings were spoken aloud rather than entered privately.
outcomes.operationalization: Nothing is operationalized as harm or toxicity. 'Liking' and 'good drug effect' are single ratings; 'total intoxication' is a global rating covering all drugs given. Analyses are of change scores from the pre-dose value, as a time course and as each person's peak.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Each pharmacokinetic parameter in Tables 1–5 and each physiological and subjective measure was tested by repeated-measures ANOVA at P <= 0.05, with least-squares-means pairwise comparisons after a significant F test and the Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; urine molar amounts were compared with Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests (p. 172).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The five crossover sessions were double-blind, with ethanol-scented cotton in a double-walled container to mask the placebo drink. The sixth cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized (pp. 171, 180). Assays are objective; intoxication ratings were spoken to staff.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations and P values; no confidence intervals and no standardized effect sizes; F statistics are not printed. Fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene 17 ± 6% (mean ± SD), from a mean 1.8 mg of cocaethylene-d5 per 10 mg of cocaine-d5 (range 1.0–4.0 mg), with no significant difference between cocaine doses (p. 173). Cocaethylene-d5 Cmax 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/ml and AUC 57.4 (40.7), 109 (33.0) and 217 (62.7) h ng/ml at cocaine 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg, with dose-corrected values not differing (Table 3, p. 175). Cocaine-d5 Cmax 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/ml (Table 1, p. 174). In the n = 6 comparison of cocaine 1.2 mg/kg with and without ethanol (Table 4, p. 176): cocaine half-life 1.91 (0.51) vs 1.29 (0.15) h (P < 0.02), renal clearance 2.53 (1.02) vs 1.53 (1.05) l/h (P < 0.02), amount excreted unchanged 2 630 000 vs 1 490 000 ng (P < 0.02), while AUC (1030 vs 1010) and Cmax (968 vs 823) did not differ; benzoylecgonine Cmax 452 (62.2) vs 652 (111) ng/ml (P < 0.01), urine concentration 7770 vs 14 800 ng/ml (P < 0.02) and amount excreted 18 500 000 vs 31 300 000 ng (P < 0.01).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person repeated-measures ANOVA on change scores.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: For the cocaine-alone comparison (n = 6) no physiological or subjective means, SDs or figure are shown: Fig. 4 plots only the five n = 10 conditions, and the text reports that comparison as P values alone (pp. 177–179). Diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product are described in words without data for that comparison.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 10 participants (6 for the cocaine-alone comparison), non-significant differences cannot be read as showing no difference; the authors attribute several null results to the small sample and large variability in ratings (p. 180).

interpretation_gap.results_show: When a 1.0 g/kg ethanol dose was drunk an hour before intravenous cocaine, about one-sixth of the cocaine dose (17 ± 6%) appeared as cocaethylene, in proportion to the cocaine dose across a four-fold range; cocaethylene peak concentrations (17–53 ng/ml) stayed far below the cocaine peaks (250–891 ng/ml) and peaked 1.3–1.6 hours after dosing. With ethanol present, less benzoylecgonine was formed and excreted and more cocaine was excreted unchanged. In the 6 people tested both ways, ratings of total intoxication and of drug liking were higher over the time course with ethanol than with cocaine alone, while peak ratings, blood pressure and rate-pressure product did not differ.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that participants liked and experienced more total intoxication after the combination than after either drug alone (p. 169). Against ethanol alone this rests on time-course analyses only: peak ratings of liking and good drug effect did not differ between ethanol alone and any cocaine condition (p. 179). Against cocaine alone it rests on 6 of the 10 people in an unblinded, non-randomized session held 1 to 3 months later, where cocaine intoxication across time and peak ratings did not differ (p. 179); the authors themselves note that expectation may have influenced those ratings (p. 180). The Discussion and Conclusions raise greater toxicity of cocaethylene than of benzoylecgonine as something that might increase risk, explicitly conditional on rat findings applying to humans (p. 179), and say the biotransformation may contribute to changes that might alter clinical presentation (p. 180); no toxicity, morbidity or clinical outcome was measured. The suggestion that lower benzoylecgonine could reduce the sensitivity of some urine screens near their cut-off is stated as a possibility requiring further study (pp. 179–180).

timeline.event: Jatlow et al. report cocaethylene in post-mortem and emergency-room blood after combined cocaine and ethanol use and show it is active at the dopamine transporter in rats and self-administered by monkeys
McCance et al. (as cited here, p. 170): intranasal cocaine with ethanol raised cocaine concentrations and produced greater rated effects than cocaine alone

Perez-Reyes (as cited here, p. 170) found no differences between cocaine alone and cocaine plus ethanol when ethanol was given after cocaine, which the authors contrast with their own order of administration
Multiple-dose study of concurrent cocaine and alcohol, used here as the comparison for intranasal dosing
Intravenous cocaethylene compared directly with cocaine in people with cocaine dependence: less potent than cocaine on heart rate and on rated effects
Review of the effects of concurrent alcohol and cocaine use

replication.where_it_stands: By the authors' account the first use of deuterium-labelled compounds and intravenous dosing to quantify how much cocaethylene is formed in people; the 17% figure is the paper's distinctive contribution and has not been re-measured by this method in any paper read for this card. Its finding that ethanol did not raise cocaine AUC or peak concentration differs from earlier intranasal studies, which the authors attribute to the route (pp. 179–180). Whether cocaethylene adds anything to the effects of cocaine plus alcohol in people remains open: the one direct comparison read here found cocaethylene less potent than cocaine (Hart et al., 2000).

funding.funder: United States Public Health Service grants DA01696, DA12393 and DA00053 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; carried out in part in the university's General Clinical Research Center with support of the Division of Research Resources, National Institutes of Health (grant 5 M01 RR-00079) (p. 181).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors were at the Drug Dependence Research Center, Langley Porter Psychiatric Institute, University of California, San Francisco (p. 169). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study in which cocaethylene itself is given at concentrations matching those formed from cocaine plus alcohol, in the same people, in randomized and blinded order, with a clinically meaningful outcome (for example cardiac or hepatic measures) rather than ratings alone; and, for the combination, a design with several ethanol doses, both orders of drinking, and a blinded cocaine-alone condition within the same crossover rather than months later.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the crossover conditions)
domains.note: The five conditions are described as a double-blind balanced crossover, but the method of generating the sequence, concealment of allocation and the balancing scheme are not described, and no period or carry-over analysis is reported. The sixth cocaine-alone session was explicitly not randomized and came 1 to 3 months after the others, so for that comparison this domain is high.

The five crossover sessions were double-blind with an olfactory mask for the placebo drink, but the cocaine-alone session was open to participants and staff (p. 180), and that session carries the paper's comparison with cocaine without alcohol. Use of cocaine outside the study is documented on two occasions from pre-dose urine (p. 180).

All 10 completed the blinded sessions, but only 6 returned for the cocaine-alone session and the basis for that selection is not reported; one urinary cocaethylene value in Table 5 is an outlier that was removed, with no sensitivity analysis.

Concentrations and cardiovascular measures are objective and the stable-isotope method is a strength. The subjective outcomes are single unvalidated ratings, intoxication ratings were spoken aloud to staff, and in the one unblinded session participants knew what they had received.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; many parameters and ratings tested without correction; the cocaine-alone comparison is reported as P values with no means, SDs or figure for the physiological and subjective measures; the abstract, Results and Table 5 give three different numbers for the same fall in urinary benzoylecgonine (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two different questions sit on this card. The conversion and disposition findings rest on a within-person design with labelled compounds and an objective assay, and are the paper's solid contribution; the pharmacodynamic comparison with cocaine alone rests on an open, non-randomized session in 6 people months later. RoB 2 takes the overall judgment from the worst domain, and the unblinded comparator makes that high. Cite this source for the share of an intravenous cocaine dose converted to cocaethylene when a substantial ethanol dose is drunk beforehand (17 ± 6%), for cocaethylene concentrations being far below cocaine concentrations in the same sessions, for the shift of cocaine metabolism away from benzoylecgonine with ethanol present, and for the absence of detectable cocaethylene when cocaine was given without ethanol. Do not cite it for cocaethylene causing any effect, for the combination being more toxic or more harmful than cocaine alone, or for anything about how the combination is used outside a laboratory.

key_findings.finding: With ethanol 1.0 g/kg given an hour before intravenous cocaine, 17 ± 6% (mean ± SD) of the cocaine dose was converted to cocaethylene: a mean of 1.8 mg of cocaethylene-d5 per 10 mg of cocaine-d5 (range 1.0–4.0 mg). The fraction did not differ significantly between the 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg cocaine conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.5 Fractional conversion of cocaine to cocaethylene

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene concentrations stayed far below cocaine concentrations in the same sessions: cocaethylene-d5 Cmax 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/ml against cocaine-d5 Cmax 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/ml at cocaine 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg. Cocaethylene peaked later (Tmax 1.31–1.55 h) than cocaine (0.28–0.36 h) and had a half-life of about 2.5 h against about 1.8 h for cocaine.
No assayable cocaethylene-d5 was found in the cocaine-only condition, and none in the two conditions without active cocaine; cocaethylene appeared only when both cocaine and ethanol were given.

In the 6 people given cocaine 1.2 mg/kg with and without ethanol, ethanol did not raise cocaine AUC (1030 vs 1010 h ng/ml) or Cmax (968 vs 823 ng/ml), but lengthened cocaine half-life (1.91 vs 1.29 h, P < 0.02) and increased renal clearance (2.53 vs 1.53 l/h, P < 0.02) and the amount of unchanged cocaine excreted in 24 hours (2 630 000 vs 1 490 000 ng, P < 0.02).

With ethanol present, less benzoylecgonine was formed and excreted: peak plasma benzoylecgonine 452 vs 652 ng/ml (P < 0.01), urine concentration over 0–24 h 7770 vs 14 800 ng/ml (P < 0.02) and amount excreted in 24 hours 18 500 000 vs 31 300 000 ng (P < 0.01) in the cocaine-plus-ethanol and cocaine-alone conditions (n = 6).
key_findings.note: The same comparison is given as 48% in the abstract, 52% in the Results and 62% in Table 5; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Ethanol shifted the balance of urinary products after cocaine 1.2 mg/kg: compared with cocaine alone, ecgonine ethyl ester-d0 rose about fifteen-fold (0.324 to 4.71 micromoles), unchanged cocaine-d5 rose to 176% (4.87 to 8.58) and benzoylecgonine-d5 fell to 62% (112 to 69.3), each P < 0.05, while ecgonine methyl ester (58%) and ecgonine ethyl ester-d3 (92%) did not differ significantly.

Heart rate, rate-pressure product and ratings of cocaine and total intoxication rose with the cocaine dose; mean peak total intoxication in the highest-dose condition was 74% of 'the most ever', and peak heart rate was higher in the two highest cocaine conditions than in the lowest.

Ratings of drug liking and good drug effect across time were higher after ethanol with cocaine 1.2 mg/kg than after ethanol alone (P < 0.04), but peak ratings of liking and good drug effect did not differ between ethanol alone and any cocaine condition.

In the 6 people tested both ways, the combination produced a higher time-course rating of total intoxication (P < 0.02) and of drug liking (P < 0.04) and a higher heart rate across time (P < 0.05) than cocaine alone, while peak cocaine and total intoxication, peak heart rate, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and rate-pressure product did not differ.
key_findings.note: This session was open and non-randomized, held 1 to 3 months after the blinded sessions; no means or figure are shown for these measures.

key_findings.finding: Breath ethanol peaked 55 minutes after the first drink, 5 minutes before the cocaine infusion began, at a mean of at least 0.12 (SD 0.014) g/dl in every experimental condition; ethanol intoxication ratings did not differ between treatments.

Participants' own reported use: typical weekly cocaine about 905 mg (range 94–3500 mg), intravenous by preference for all 10, and on average 13 g of ethanol weekly (range 2–23 g); none had ever sought treatment for cocaine-related problems, and 7 of 10 smoked tobacco, 8 smoked cannabis, 3 used amphetamines, 3 used heroin and 1 used diazepam.
