design_detail: Invited narrative review in Current Opinion in Hematology (5 pages, 44 references) by two emergency physicians and medical toxicologists at the Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Center, Denver, on the medical consequences of levamisole in illicit cocaine: agranulocytosis, cutaneous vasculopathy, leukoencephalopathy, other effects, and laboratory testing. There is no search strategy, no selection criteria and no appraisal of the cited studies. The human evidence cited is case reports and case series, two urine-prevalence studies, and analyses of seized drugs.
can_establish: What the case literature up to 2011 described for agranulocytosis and skin vasculopathy in people who had used levamisole-contaminated cocaine (clinical picture, timing of neutrophil recovery, autoantibodies, histology), what the authors advised for hospital work-up, and the detection windows they give for levamisole in blood and urine.
cannot_establish: How often people exposed to levamisole through cocaine develop any of these conditions (no incidence among exposed people is given anywhere); that levamisole rather than cocaine itself causes a given case (attribution in the cited reports rests mostly on cocaine use and the known effects of medical levamisole; the review does not say how many cases had levamisole measured); that leukoencephalopathy occurs through cocaine (the review says no such case had been reported); or how well any treatment works (no controlled data).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence cited: case reports and series of agranulocytosis and vasculopathy (refs 13, 14, 18–20, 24–44), two 2011 urine studies from Denver and San Francisco (refs 11, 12), US seizure data and a Luxembourg analysis of seized cocaine (refs 9, 10), and older literature on medical use of levamisole.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria stated; the stated aim is to outline findings from the preceding year (p. 27).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Author-selected literature, mostly case reports, which favour severe, unusual or well-documented cases. Three cited papers (refs 11, 18, 31) and both figures come from the first author's own work. No study with a denominator of exposed people is cited for any complication.

exposure.measurement: As summarized: exposure to levamisole is inferred from cocaine use (history, or benzoylecgonine in urine), with levamisole itself detected in some cases; the first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation appeared in early 2010 (ref. 18, p. 28); the review does not say how many of the cited cases had levamisole measured (laboratory confirmation is mentioned also for the patient in Figure 2, p. 29).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Only the adulterant content of seized cocaine is reported: levamisole first detected by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in 2003; 30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated by 2008; 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA containing levamisole in January 2010; levamisole the most abundant adulterant, at low concentrations (1.5–4.1%), in illicit cocaine samples analysed in Luxembourg (p. 28). Cases followed smoking, injection and nasal use; most agranulocytosis cases followed smoking, but whether smoking carries a greater risk than other routes is unclear (p. 28).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; the review names lidocaine-like local anaesthetics and diltiazem as other cutting agents in cocaine (p. 28).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. The only comparisons offered are the background incidence of agranulocytosis in the general population, about 5 cases per million per year (ref. 6, p. 28), and the 0.4–20% of medically treated patients who formed antineutrophil antibodies (p. 27).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review notes that a genetic predisposition (HLA-B27, HLA class 1) reported for medical levamisole has not been replicated among patients exposed to levamisole through cocaine (p. 29).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (review). Testing described: gas chromatography–mass spectrometry for levamisole in urine and plasma, available at public-health, reference and crime laboratories (p. 30).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Agranulocytosis, neutropenia, cutaneous vasculopathy and leukoencephalopathy as described in the cited cases; no case definitions are given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: background agranulocytosis incidence about 5 per million per year (p. 28); antineutrophil antibodies in 0.4–20% of medically treated patients (p. 27); levamisole in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples positive for cocaine metabolites (p. 28); about half of the patients in the Alberta–British Columbia series had more than one episode of agranulocytosis with renewed cocaine use (p. 28); spontaneous neutrophil recovery 5–10 days after exposure ends, against recovery within 2–3 days of GCSF in most case reports (p. 29); neutropenia in about half of vasculopathy cases (p. 30); levamisole plasma half-life about 5.6 hours, and urine positive for about 2–3 days in most patients, on preliminary evidence (p. 30).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as such; several figures carry no citation (the January 2010 DEA figure, the SAMHSA estimate, the 5.6-hour half-life), and the 2008 figure is cited to a source that cannot contain it (reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review describes case reports and small series of agranulocytosis and skin vasculopathy in people who had used cocaine, frequent detection of levamisole in seized cocaine and in the urine of patients testing positive for cocaine in two cities, spontaneous neutrophil recovery within about 5–10 days of stopping exposure, no treatment trials, and no reported case of leukoencephalopathy acquired through cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says more than three fourths of people who use cocaine in the US are exposed to levamisole and that a "significant minority" will develop neutropenia, vasculopathy and/or leukoencephalopathy (p. 27). Gaps: (1) the three-fourths figure has no stated basis; the body's figures are two local samples of urine screens positive for cocaine metabolites (78% and 88%; only the Denver reference title names a hospital) and seizure data (73.2%, below three fourths) (p. 28); (2) no incidence among exposed people is cited, so the significant minority has no number behind it; (3) the body states that no case of leukoencephalopathy through cocaine had been reported (p. 30), yet the Purpose (levamisole known to cause neurologic complications), the Summary and the Conclusion list it among the consequences (pp. 27, 30); (4) whether levamisole or cocaine causes the cases is not discussed, and the review does not say how many cited cases had levamisole measured (it mentions laboratory confirmation for the first in-depth case report and for the patient in Figure 2, pp. 28–29); (5) from the large number of anecdotal reports since 2009 it judges the skin vasculopathy, rarely reported with medical levamisole, much more common with levamisole in cocaine, without any denominator (p. 29); (6) it relays, from animal data and theory, that levamisole might enhance cocaine's euphoric effects or make it more addicting (p. 28), which claims do not carry. The Key Points and Conclusion (ask patients about cocaine, defer extensive work-up while waiting for spontaneous recovery) are the authors' clinical opinion for hospital care.

timeline.event: First reports of agranulocytosis after levamisole-contaminated cocaine in Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado (refs 13, 14, as cited p. 28)
First in-depth case report of agranulocytosis with laboratory confirmation of levamisole (Buchanan et al., J Med Toxicol; ref. 18)
Urine studies in Denver and San Francisco: levamisole in 78% and 88% of samples positive for cocaine metabolites (refs 11, 12, as cited p. 28)
This review
Pathology review of levamisole-induced vasculitis for pathologists

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative summary of the early case literature. On how often complications occur among exposed people it offers nothing; causal attribution rests on the pattern of cases and on the known effects of medical levamisole. Claims should cite the primary series (and later systematic work, if found) with their case definitions and testing, using this review only for the clinical description and the testing windows.

funding.funder: Not reported (Acknowledgements: none, p. 30).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that there are no conflicts of interest (p. 30).
funding.affiliations_note: Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Center, Denver Health and Hospital Authority, and University of Colorado School of Medicine (p. 27). The first author's own case reports and urine-prevalence study are among the main sources (refs 11, 18, 31).

what_would_settle_it: A population-based case–control or cohort study of people who use cocaine, with levamisole measured in cases and comparison participants alike, to estimate how often agranulocytosis and vasculopathy occur per exposed person and whether levamisole explains them beyond cocaine itself.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria.
Case reports and series are summarized without appraising how cases were identified or whether levamisole was confirmed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of the first author's papers (refs 11, 18, 31) and both figures; otherwise the case literature is cited widely.

The idea that levamisole makes cocaine more reinforcing is labelled as theory (p. 28), but the Summary and Conclusion present leukoencephalopathy through cocaine as an established consequence although no case had been reported (pp. 27, 30).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often and how surely levamisole harms people exposed through cocaine (exposed people without complications, and cocaine itself as an alternative cause, are under-represented)
domains.note: Exposure is described as near-universal and complications as affecting a significant minority without any incidence figure, and the vascular effects of cocaine itself are not weighed as an alternative explanation.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high concern overall, driven by the absence of a systematic search or appraisal and by a one-sided framing of frequency. The review is a fair clinical description of the case literature to 2011 and cites its sources. Claims may cite it for the clinical picture, the timing of neutrophil recovery reported in cases, the testing windows, and the seizure and urine prevalence figures (second-hand, with their sources); never for how often complications occur, and not for leukoencephalopathy acquired through cocaine.

key_findings.finding: Prevalence of levamisole cited: first detected by the DEA in cocaine seized in 2003; 30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated by 2008; 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA in January 2010 contained levamisole; in illicit cocaine samples analysed in Luxembourg levamisole was the most abundant adulterant, though at low concentrations (1.5–4.1%); studies from Denver and San Francisco published in 2011 found levamisole in 78% and 88% of urine samples that screened positive for cocaine metabolites.
key_findings.note: The 2008 figure is cited to ref. 3, a 1999 report on children treated with levamisole, which cannot be its source; the January 2010 figure has no citation.

key_findings.finding: Agranulocytosis after levamisole-contaminated cocaine was first reported in 2009 (Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona, Colorado); the first in-depth case report with laboratory confirmation appeared in early 2010. Most patients developed agranulocytosis after smoking cocaine, but the review says it is unclear whether smoking carries a greater risk than other routes; about half of the patients in one series (ref. 20, Alberta and British Columbia) had more than one episode with renewed cocaine use.

Mechanism as summarized: levamisole is thought to act as a hapten, leading to antibodies against neutrophils; 0.4–20% of patients treated medically formed such antibodies; ANCA are also commonly detected; the bone marrow is typically hypercellular with relative myeloid hypoplasia, with or without megakaryocyte hyperplasia.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph (pp. 27–28); Neutropenia and Agranulocytosis, 1st paragraph (pp. 28–29); Figure 1 (p. 29)

key_findings.finding: Treatment of agranulocytosis: no controlled trials; most case reports describe neutrophil recovery within 2–3 days of GCSF, but spontaneous recovery 5–10 days after exposure ends is also described, so the added benefit of GCSF in patients without active infection is unclear; the authors suggest deferring marrow biopsy in neutropenic patients with a clear history of cocaine exposure unless counts fail to recover in the expected time.

Cutaneous vasculopathy, described from a large number of anecdotal reports since 2009 (refs 24–44): purpuric plaques in a retiform or stellate pattern, bullae, necrosis, ulcers; typical sites ears, cheeks, nose and extremities; women predominate among cases although cocaine use is more common in men; diffuse autoantibodies (antineutrophil, c- and p-ANCA, anticardiolipin, anti-dsDNA, antiphospholipid); small-vessel vasculitis, thrombotic vasculopathy or both on histology; neutropenia in about half of cases.
key_findings.locator: Cutaneous Vasculopathy, 1st paragraph (begins p. 29, ends p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Lesions usually resolve within a few weeks of stopping cocaine; other treatments used (corticosteroids, colchicine, phentolamine, anticoagulation, skin grafting) lack systematically collected data.

Leukoencephalopathy has been associated with medical levamisole; no case acquired through cocaine had been reported at the time, though the authors mention one probable case at their institution without details; no data support or refute any treatment.

Testing: levamisole can be detected by GC-MS in urine and plasma; its plasma half-life is about 5.6 hours (estimated population mean), so serum is likely negative when the last exposure was more than 24 hours earlier; preliminary evidence suggests that urine stays positive about as long as benzoylecgonine, roughly 2–3 days in most patients. The authors write that specific testing may be unnecessary in many cases, and the Conclusion recommends testing in select cases.
key_findings.note: No source is cited for the 5.6-hour figure; refs 11 and 12 are cited for the urine window.

key_findings.finding: Background incidence of agranulocytosis in the general population: about 5 cases per million per year (ref. 6).
No incidence of any complication among people exposed to levamisole through cocaine is given anywhere in the review.

What levamisole is: a veterinary medicine used mainly against worm infestations in cattle, sheep and pigs; because of its immune-modulating properties it was used for autoimmune disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, nephrotic syndrome) and cancers (breast, lung), and the review says it is approved by the US FDA as adjuvant chemotherapy (with 5-fluorouracil) for colon cancer, although no manufacturer markets it for human use in the United States.
key_findings.note: The 2015 review (card sc_roberts_2015, p. 1058) says instead that the FDA banned levamisole in the US in 2000; a claim on its medical status should not rest on either review alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary says a significant minority of exposed people will develop leukoencephalopathy, and the Purpose that levamisole is known to cause neurologic complications (p. 27), but the body states that no case acquired through cocaine had been reported (p. 30).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the body: no case reported at the time.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2008 figure (30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated) is cited to ref. 3, a 1999 report on children treated with levamisole; the January 2010 DEA figure (73.2%), the SAMHSA estimate of 5.9 million people aged 12 and over using cocaine in 2002–2003 (measure not stated) and the 5.6-hour half-life carry no citation, nor does the statement, attributed to SAMHSA, that cocaine use is more prevalent in men (p. 29).
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be traced through the review; cite primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary's more than three fourths of people who use cocaine in the US exposed to levamisole (p. 27) cites no figure; the body's figures are two local samples of urine screens positive for cocaine metabolites, 78% in Denver (whose reference title names an inner-city hospital) and 88% in San Francisco, and seized cocaine, 73.2%, which is below three fourths (p. 28).
reporting_issues.consequence: The three-fourths figure is an extrapolation from two local urine samples, not a national estimate; do not cite it as the share of people who use cocaine who are exposed.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 31 (the first author's report of ear vasculitis) is given as J Med Toxicol 2011;29:299–303, while ref. 18 in the same list gives J Med Toxicol 2010;6:160–164; the project's cocaine reading list records this report as Buchanan et al. 2010.
reporting_issues.consequence: Check the citation details before linking ref. 31 to a project record.

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 4.2.9; relative risks) of double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trials of central nervous system stimulant medication for cocaine dependence. PubMed, the Cochrane Library and IDIS searched from 1966 to November 2006 (last search 1 December 2006), with reference lists and contact with first authors; the list of stimulant drugs was built from ATC and AHFS drug classes. Nine trials (640 patients, 11 drug-placebo comparisons) of mazindol (2), dexamphetamine (3), methylphenidate (2), modafinil (1) and bupropion (1). Outcomes: dropout, cocaine use as the proportion of urine samples positive for benzoylecgonine during the trial, craving (not pooled) and dropout for adverse events. A planned exploratory analysis added three trials whose cocaine use during the trial was imputed as the mean of the baseline and final proportions of positive urines.
can_establish: Whether, in the nine placebo-controlled trials published by 2006 (640 patients, mostly men, about half also opioid-dependent, mostly smoking or injecting cocaine), stimulant medications singly or together reduced dropout or the proportion of cocaine-positive urine samples, and how often they led to dropout for adverse events.
cannot_establish: Efficacy of any single drug with useful precision (one to three small trials each, 30 to 149 patients, 42 to 182 days); effects in women, in people who snort cocaine or in people without opioid dependence; effects beyond six months; the safety of these drugs beyond dropout for adverse events; or whether the exploratory signal for dexamphetamine is real, since it rests on imputed outcomes and on per-protocol data from two trials by one group (one of them also in the main analysis), and in part on a single arm (without it, all stimulants 0.93, 0.84 to 1.03; editors' calculation).

sample.recruitment: Database search: PubMed, the Cochrane Library and the Iowa Drug Information System, each from 1966 to November 2006, run twice (last search 1 December 2006); reference lists of retrieved trials and four reviews hand-searched; first authors contacted for further articles (p. 1872, Search strategy). Fig. 2 also names clinicaltrials.gov among the databases. 584 citations screened (582 in the text), 551 excluded as not assessing a stimulant for cocaine dependence, 33 potentially eligible, 24 excluded (20 open trials, 2 pharmacokinetic trials, 2 crossover trials), 9 included; four trials were supplemented with unpublished data from their authors (p. 1873; Fig. 2, p. 1875).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled parallel-group trials of a stimulant in patients with cocaine dependence reporting retention, cocaine use by urine benzoylecgonine, or craving; no publication restrictions. Excluded: trials of people with cocaine abuse rather than dependence (p. 1872). Stimulants: drugs from selected ATC and AHFS classes with at least one published study showing a stimulant effect (pp. 1872-1873). From a report of two trials, only the dexamphetamine trial was used (p. 1875).
sample.demographics: Pooled baseline characteristics from the trials reporting each (Table 2, p. 1879): 11.9% women; mean age 34.9; 48.3% White, 40.9% Black, 10.8% other; 28.6% employed; mean years of cocaine use 7.7 to 14.0 across trials; 65.3% used crack; route intranasal 12.8%, smoked 51.4%, intravenous 35.8%; 46.9% opioid-dependent, 88.1% of whom were in the three trials requiring dual dependence; ADHD 7.6%. Adult ADHD was an inclusion criterion in one trial (Schubiner 2002), an exclusion criterion in three, and not assessed or not specified in five (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout 167 of 344 on stimulants and 138 of 296 on placebo (48.5% and 46.6%, editors' arithmetic from Fig. 3, p. 1880). Cocaine use was analysed per protocol in the two Grabowski dexamphetamine trials (Table 1: 112 of 128 with at least one positive urine at baseline; an evaluable sample of 62 of 94 who took at least one dose) (pp. 1876-1877).
sample.selection_effects: Few, small trials; eight of nine funded by NIDA; mostly men who smoke or inject cocaine, about half also opioid-dependent and treated with methadone; every trial added psychotherapy of varying intensity (Table 1). One mazindol trial (Margolin 1995 [39], 37 patients) enrolled methadone-maintained patients already abstinent from cocaine for at least 2 weeks, a relapse-prevention design unlike the other eight (Table 1, p. 1876). The authors judge the pooled sample biased towards patients with a poor prognosis (p. 1882; p. 1884).

exposure.measurement: Randomized, double-blind assignment to drug or placebo within each trial.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral daily doses as given in the trials (Table 1, pp. 1876-1878): mazindol 1 mg or 2 mg; sustained-release dexamphetamine 15-30 or 30-60 mg (two trials, one with methadone 1.1 mg/kg/day in all arms) and immediate-release dexamphetamine 20-60 mg; immediate-release methylphenidate 30-90 mg, or 45 mg of immediate plus sustained release; modafinil 200-400 mg; bupropion 200-300 mg. Planned follow-up 42 to 182 days.
exposure.polysubstance: About half the patients were opioid-dependent; three trials required dual cocaine and opioid dependence with methadone maintenance. Some trials excluded dependence on other drugs and one did not (Table 1). Alcohol use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: cocaine use was the outcome, measured by urine benzoylecgonine once every 2 weeks to three times a week depending on the trial (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Placebo with the same psychotherapy as the drug arm in each trial; in the two three-arm trials the placebo group was divided between the two comparisons (p. 1873).
comparison.matching: By randomization within each trial.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparisons; ADHD status unknown in five trials.

outcomes.instruments: Dropout (failure to complete the trial); cocaine use as the proportion of benzoylecgonine-positive urine samples during the trial; craving by a 0-10 Likert scale, visual analogue scales, a 5-point analogue scale, the Tiffany cocaine craving questionnaire, or the CSSA, BSCS and CCQ; dropout for adverse events; trial quality by the Jadad scale (0 to 5, below 3 poor), which rates the reporting of randomization, double-blinding and withdrawals (p. 1873; Table 3, p. 1882).
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine benzoylecgonine is objective; craving instruments differ between trials, so craving was not pooled.
outcomes.operationalization: Cocaine use RR: ratio of the proportions of positive urine samples, entered in Fig. 4 as events out of the number of patients (for example 17/30 vs 25/32 for modafinil), so the proportion of samples is treated as if it were a proportion of patients; the authors say these data were transformed to fit the other pooled studies (p. 1880).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcome families; editors' count of 21 pooled estimates in Figs 3 and 4 (five drugs and two totals for each of dropout, main and exploratory cocaine use), plus two post hoc subgroup estimates and the adverse-event comparison.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: All trials double-blind (an inclusion criterion); blinding integrity was not assessed. In the review, one author selected trials and extracted data, a second checked the extraction, and reviewers were not blinded to authorship or journal (p. 1873).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects relative risks (drug vs placebo). Dropout (Fig. 3, p. 1880): mazindol 0.93 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.47); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12), I-squared 45.2%; methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79); all stimulants without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); all 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10), I-squared 0%. Cocaine-positive urines, main analysis of six trials (Fig. 4A, p. 1881): mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12); all without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); all 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05). Exploratory analysis of nine trials with imputed values (Fig. 4B): dexamphetamine 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94); all 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), p = 0.03. Post hoc, trials requiring dual cocaine and opioid dependence: dropout 0.85 (0.56 to 1.30), cocaine use 0.86 (0.68 to 1.09) (p. 1879). Dropout for adverse events 15/344 (4.4%) vs 4/296 (1.3%), p = 0.03 (p. 1879). No absolute risk differences or prediction intervals. Editors' checks: DerSimonian-Laird pooling of the printed counts reproduces the dropout totals and every Fig. 4 total; from the same counts, retention gives RR 1.03 (0.93 to 1.15), not the abstract's 0.94; without the high-dose arm of Grabowski 2001 the exploratory dexamphetamine RR becomes 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00) and the all-stimulant estimate 0.93 (0.84 to 1.03).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (randomized comparisons). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, a subanalysis by Jadad score (results described in one sentence) and a post hoc subanalysis of dual-dependence trials.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Analyses by drug and for all stimulants, and subanalyses by trial quality and ADHD, are described as planned a priori (pp. 1872-1873), but no registered or published protocol is cited; the analysis without bupropion and the dual-dependence subanalysis were post hoc (pp. 1873, 1879); the ADHD subanalysis could not be done.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's headline RRs for retention and cocaine use appear nowhere in the results; the Jadad-score subanalysis is reported without estimates; Table 3 gives no craving values for two trials; the abstract's statement that no serious adverse event was reported has no counterpart in the Results, and several trials did not specify adverse-event assessment (Table 1).
analysis.power: The authors calculate that 144 to 584 patients per arm (80% power, two-tailed p = 0.05, 50% dropout) would be needed, more than in any included trial (p. 1882).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across nine small trials (640 patients), no stimulant medication, singly or pooled, reduced dropout (all stimulants RR 0.97, 0.85 to 1.10) or cocaine-positive urines in the main analysis (all 0.94, 0.84 to 1.05; without bupropion 0.84, 0.67 to 1.04), which itself includes one dexamphetamine trial's per-protocol sample (62 of 94 randomized). Only an exploratory analysis that imputed cocaine use for three trials and used per-protocol data for two dexamphetamine trials showed fewer positive urines with dexamphetamine (0.73, 0.60 to 0.90) and with stimulants pooled (0.87, 0.77 to 0.99). Dropout for adverse events was 4.4% vs 1.3%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's main conclusion matches the results: the main outcomes do not support stimulants for cocaine dependence (p. 1871). But its two headline RRs (retention 0.94, 0.81 to 1.09; cocaine use 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02) are not in the figures, and it describes the secondary results as hopeful, mainly with dexamphetamine and modafinil. The modafinil estimate was not significant (0.73, 0.50 to 1.04); the dexamphetamine signal depends on means of baseline and final proportions, on per-protocol subsets of two trials by one group, and in part on one arm listed in Fig. 3 with 42 dropouts of 46; the Discussion calls per-protocol bias unlikely without analysis (p. 1884). The abstract's statement that no serious adverse event was reported is not supported by any result in the text, which describes information on adverse reactions as too limited to draw conclusions (p. 1880). The Discussion also reverses the exploratory reductions for all stimulants with and without bupropion (p. 1882).

timeline.event: Margolin et al. (mazindol; bupropion, two trials) and Stine et al. (mazindol): included trials, none showing differences in dropout, cocaine use or craving (Table 1).
Grabowski et al.: sustained-release dexamphetamine, cocaine use lower in the per-protocol sample; included (Table 1); its high-dose arm gives the largest exploratory effect in Fig. 4B.
Grabowski et al.: dexamphetamine with methadone in people with heroin dependence, cocaine use lower in the evaluable sample; included (Table 1).
Dackis et al.: modafinil, cocaine use lower in the trial's own analysis, a trend after the review's transformation; included (Table 1; p. 1880).
This meta-analysis; the authors call for a follow-up meta-analysis including the ongoing trials (p. 1884).
Pérez-Mañá et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of indirect dopamine agonists for psychostimulant dependence; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Sangroula et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of modafinil for cocaine dependence; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Biso et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of methylphenidate for cocaine use disorder; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
Paterson et al.: systematic review of pharmacological interventions for cocaine use disorder; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).

replication.where_it_stands: An early meta-analysis of stimulant (agonist-like) medication for cocaine dependence covering nine trials to 2006. It supports only the statement that this evidence showed no benefit on dropout or on the main cocaine-use outcome; later reviews on the project's list must be appraised before the encyclopedia states where the question stands now.

funding.funder: Two grants to X. Castells, from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (a public research body of the Spanish Ministry of Health) and from Mutual Mèdica de Catalunya i Balears (a mutual insurance company providing health insurance for physicians) (p. 1884, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of competing interests appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Psychiatry Service and Clinical Pharmacology Service (Fundació Institut Català de Farmacologia), Hospital Universitari Vall d'Hebron, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona. Of the included trials, eight of nine were NIDA-funded, three were co-funded by manufacturers (Wyeth for the two mazindol trials, Cephalon for modafinil) and one had pharmaceutical industry help (Table 1).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, registered, double-blind trials of single stimulant medications (particularly sustained-release dexamphetamine and modafinil) in people with cocaine use disorder, analysed by intention to treat with patient-level abstinence outcomes (for example urine-confirmed abstinent weeks), explicit handling of missing urines, checks of blinding, and inclusion of women and of people who neither inject nor use opioids; then an updated meta-analysis, ideally of individual patient data.

domains.note: Patients with cocaine dependence, stimulant medication, placebo, retention, urine-confirmed cocaine use and craving (p. 1872).
Analyses are described as planned a priori, but no protocol is cited; two analyses were added post hoc.
Only double-blind parallel-group randomized trials were included, without stated reasons; open and crossover trials were excluded at the last step without explanation (Fig. 2).

Three databases with the PubMed strategy printed (Fig. 1), no publication restrictions, reference lists, contact with first authors and a search a month before submission; no Embase or PsycINFO and no grey literature; clinicaltrials.gov appears only in Fig. 2.
One author selected the trials (p. 1873).
One author extracted with a standardized form and a second checked, with discrepancies resolved by consensus (p. 1873).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 24 trials excluded after full assessment appear only as category counts in Fig. 2.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives participants, design, randomization, drug and daily dose, psychotherapy, outcome measures, follow-up length, analysis type, funding and Jadad score for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The Jadad scale rates the reporting of randomization, blinding and withdrawals; it does not assess allocation concealment or selective reporting, and the authors themselves call it a reporting-quality scale (p. 1873).

domains.note: Funding of each trial is in Table 1, summarized in the text (p. 1875).

Random-effects relative risks with split control groups are appropriate for dropout, but the cocaine-use outcome treats each group's proportion of positive urine samples as if it were a proportion of patients, the exploratory analysis imputes the outcome from baseline and final values, and per-protocol results are pooled with intention-to-treat results, in the main urine analysis too (Grabowski 2004 enters Fig. 4A as its evaluable sample, 62 of 94 randomized); the authors acknowledge the transformation (p. 1880). A close call for an outcome-level problem, recorded with the reasons.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The only analysis by trial quality used the Jadad score and is reported in one sentence without estimates (p. 1879).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Per-protocol bias in the two dexamphetamine trials is called unlikely without analysis (p. 1884); attrition of about 48%, unblinding by stimulant effects and selective reporting are not discussed, while the exploratory positive results are presented as hopeful.

Chi-square tests and I-squared reported for every pool; differences between the dexamphetamine trials are discussed (formulation, schedule, per-protocol analysis, a highly marginalized sample) (p. 1883).
Not investigated; the authors state it was controlled by searching several sources and contacting authors (p. 1883).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is reported in the Acknowledgements, but there is no declaration of competing interests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: six critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded trials, a reporting-quality scale instead of a risk-of-bias assessment, an outcome transformation that treats urine samples as patients, no discussion of attrition or unblinding as sources of bias, no investigation of publication bias) and the search is only partly comprehensive. The null main results can still be cited because they are reproducible from the printed counts and consistent across drugs: dropout 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10) and positive urines 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05). The positive exploratory results cannot. Cite for: no detectable benefit of stimulant medications, singly or together, on dropout or on the proportion of cocaine-positive urines in the nine trials published by 2006 (640 patients, mostly men, about half opioid-dependent), and slightly more dropout for adverse events (4.4% vs 1.3%). Do not cite for: efficacy of dexamphetamine or modafinil, or the absence of serious harms.

key_findings.finding: Nine randomized trials met the criteria, with 640 patients (344 given a stimulant, 296 placebo) and 11 drug-placebo comparisons: mazindol 2 trials, dexamphetamine 3, methylphenidate 2, modafinil 1, bupropion 1; four trials were supplemented with unpublished author data.
key_findings.locator: Results › Article search, 1st paragraph (p. 1873) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1875); Results › Clinical trial and subject features, 1st paragraph (p. 1875, the 11 comparisons); Fig. 2 (p. 1875)

key_findings.finding: Trials had 30 to 149 patients and 42 to 182 days of planned follow-up; seven were two-armed and two three-armed; eight of nine were funded by NIDA; Jadad scores were 2 (two trials), 3 (six) and 4 (one).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical trial and subject features, 1st paragraph (p. 1875); Table 1 (pp. 1876-1878)

key_findings.finding: Patients (Table 2): 11.9% women, mean age 34.9, 28.6% employed, 65.3% used crack, routes intranasal 12.8%, smoked 51.4% and intravenous 35.8%, 46.9% opioid-dependent (88.1% of them in three trials requiring dual dependence), ADHD 7.6%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Clinical trial and subject features, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text gives 89.1% men and 65.8% crack, against 11.9% women and 65.3% crack in Table 2. Sex, age and opioid dependence come from all nine trials, race from six, length of use and type of cocaine from five, and employment, route and ADHD from four (p. 1879).

key_findings.finding: Dropout did not differ between stimulants and placebo for any drug or overall: all stimulants RR 0.97 (0.85 to 1.10), I-squared 0%; without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12); methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); mazindol 0.93 (0.59 to 1.47); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79). Dropouts were 167 of 344 vs 138 of 296.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 3 (p. 1880)

key_findings.finding: Main analysis of cocaine-positive urines (six trials): all stimulants RR 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05); without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12). Leaving out each comparison in turn changed no conclusion.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy and safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 4A (p. 1881)
key_findings.note: Grabowski 2004 enters Fig. 4A as 11/23 and 6/19 against 6/10 and 5/10 (62 patients), its evaluable sample of those who took at least one dose, not the 94 randomized (Table 1, p. 1877), so the main analysis also pools per-protocol with intention-to-treat data.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory analysis adding three trials with cocaine use imputed as the mean of baseline and final proportions: dexamphetamine RR 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all stimulants 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99), p = 0.03; without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data synthesis and statistical analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 1873); Results › Efficacy and safety, 2nd paragraph (p. 1879); Fig. 4B (p. 1881)
key_findings.note: The largest single contribution is the high-dose arm of Grabowski 2001 (0.60, 0.41 to 0.88; 31 patients analysed), an arm listed in Fig. 3 with 42 dropouts of 46; without it the dexamphetamine RR is 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00), the exploratory estimate for all stimulants 0.93 (0.84 to 1.03) and without bupropion 0.86 (0.74 to 1.00) (editors' calculation: random effects with the Mantel-Haenszel heterogeneity statistic, which reproduces the printed totals 0.87, 0.77 to 0.99, Q 11.85, I-squared 15.6%, and 0.82, 0.71 to 0.94, exactly).

reporting_issues.issue: Citation and wording errors: Table 3 cites Schubiner 2002 as [44] (Shearer's number; Schubiner is [43]); the Table 1 caption cites the Jadad scale as [33] (it is [35]); the two-armed trials are cited as [37-41,43,44], where [37] is a methods reference and Dackis [46] is missing; the text says sample sizes ranged from 30 to 149 days; Table 1 describes the Grabowski 2004 participants as cocaine- and methadone-naive heroin-dependent patients, which taken literally contradicts their inclusion; 582 citations in the text against 584 in Fig. 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor errors that make the review harder to audit.

design_detail: Editorial (JAMA, Editorials section, 1998;279(22):1828–1829) by Edwin M. Kilbourne, MD, of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, commenting on Marzuk et al. (1998), a study of ambient temperature and deaths from unintentional cocaine overdose in New York City published in the same issue (cross-referenced to p. 1795). It contains no new data; it summarizes and appraises the study, sets it against earlier heat-wave mortality research and proposes further studies. 11 references, two of them the author's own.
can_establish: What a physician at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, who had published on heat-wave mortality (references 1 and 3), argued in print, alongside the study, about the strengths and limits of Marzuk et al.: that the design is close to ecological and open to confounding, which alternative explanations the study addressed, that the absolute daily increase was small, and which individual-level studies would be needed.
cannot_establish: Any fact about cocaine, heat or mortality beyond the figures it repeats from Marzuk et al. and older heat-wave studies: it reports no data of its own, its figures for the Marzuk study are second-hand, and its arguments for causation (specificity, a gradient, biological plausibility) are the author's reasoning, not tests.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The study discussed used data from the New York City Medical Examiner's Office, as the editorial describes it (p. 1828, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the 11 references were chosen by the author.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The editorial discusses one study; its background figures come from heat-wave studies from 1934 onward and from two of the author's own publications (references 1 and 3). How the references were chosen is not described.

exposure.measurement: As described for the Marzuk study: temperature was a single daily value from the Central Park weather station for the whole population, and daily data on individual thermal microenvironments were unavailable (p. 1828, 4th and 5th paragraphs). The amount of cocaine each person took is raised only in the last paragraph, as information future studies should gather (p. 1829).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed, except that overdose deaths from opiates and other drugs served in the study as a comparison (as described, p. 1828, 6th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: As described for Marzuk et al.: days of different temperatures; overdose deaths from opiates and other drugs; homicides and motor-vehicle crash deaths, in which cocaine involvement was checked for a rise in hot weather (p. 1828, 6th and 7th paragraphs). The editorial proposes an individual-level comparison with people who use cocaine and survive the heat (p. 1829).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the editorial notes that individual-level confounders could not be evaluated in the study it discusses (p. 1828, 5th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). In the study discussed, the outcome was deaths identified as due to unintentional cocaine overdose from medical examiner records, as summarized by the editorial (p. 1828, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Second-hand figures: in Marzuk et al., days at or above 31.1 °C (88 °F) had a mean increase of 0.58 cocaine-overdose deaths a day; for comparison, all-cause excess deaths averaged 50 to 143 a day in 5 New York City heat waves between 1972 and 1996 (p. 1829, 2nd paragraph on the page). Background: the 1980 heat wave in St Louis and Kansas City caused 308 deaths above the expected number, with daily mortality in St Louis up to 3 times usual; the 1995 Chicago heat wave more than 700 deaths, with daily mortality more than 5 times usual (p. 1828, 1st paragraph). In 7 heat-wave studies since 1934, cardiovascular deaths rose 7%–59% above baseline (13%–42% of excess deaths) and cerebrovascular deaths 25%–104% (6%–52%); in 6 of them respiratory deaths rose 0%–84% (0%–14%) (p. 1829, 1st paragraph on the page).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable; the editorial selects which results of the study to discuss.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results of its own: it is a published comment on one study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Kilbourne writes that Marzuk et al. present substantive evidence that the risk of death from cocaine overdose rises sharply in hot weather (p. 1828, 3rd paragraph), and later that the increase, though statistically significant, is relatively small, 0.58 deaths a day (p. 1829), the two statements describing relative and absolute size respectively. He presents the specificity of the association (no rise in opiate overdose deaths), the absence of more cocaine involvement in homicides and crash deaths, what appears to be a gradual, essentially monotonic rise in risk above a threshold temperature (a possible dose–response gradient) and biological plausibility as indications of cause, while stating that the design resembles ecological studies and that factors associated in time with hot weather cannot be ruled out (p. 1828). His argument that effects during prolonged heat waves may be larger than on single hot days (p. 1829) is reasoning without data. His comparison of 0.58 cocaine-overdose deaths a day with 50 to 143 all-cause excess deaths a day in heat waves sets a cause-specific count against all-cause mortality, so it illustrates absolute scale, not a smaller effect of heat. He also writes that the findings add yet another etiology to the list of known or suspected causes of excess deaths in populations exposed to prolonged heat (p. 1828, 10th paragraph), and on the next page that other putative causes, which arose less regularly and with smaller apparent effects, may represent coincidence (p. 1829, 11th paragraph); he does not relate that caution to the cocaine association. He concludes that causation remains to be established (p. 1829).

timeline.event: Marzuk et al.: New York City medical-examiner study of ambient temperature and deaths from unintentional cocaine overdose, the study this editorial discusses (same issue, p. 1795)

This editorial: judges the association plausible but not established as causal; calls for replication in other cities during heat waves and for individual-level comparisons of people who died with people who use cocaine and survived the heat.
Crandall et al., laboratory study of the mechanism of cocaine-induced hyperthermia in humans (held in the library; not read for this card)

Auger et al., association of elevated ambient temperature with death from cocaine overdose, a later study of the question listed in the project's search log (no reference record yet; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: The comment linked to Marzuk et al. in PubMed (project search log), written in the same issue. Its methodological points (an exposure measured once a day for a whole city, no individual-level data, a small absolute increase) are the questions to put to the primary study and to later studies such as Auger et al. (2017), which are to be appraised from their full texts. Claims about the size of the association should cite Marzuk et al. directly, not this editorial.

funding.funder: None stated (editorial).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta; reprint address in the Data Management Division, National Immunization Program (p. 1828, footnote). The author cites two of his own publications on heat-wave mortality (references 1 and 3); reference 3, his 1997 book chapter, is the only source given for the statements that only a minority of heat-wave excess deaths are due to heatstroke and that, other than heatstroke, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and pulmonary disease are the causes most consistently associated with excess deaths and account for the greatest number of them (p. 1828, 2nd and 10th paragraphs).

what_would_settle_it: As the editorial proposes (p. 1829, last paragraph): replication in other cities during local heat waves, more information on person-level risk factors (for example a home air conditioner and the amount of cocaine taken), and an individual-level comparison of people who died of cocaine overdose in the heat with people who use cocaine and survived it. The editors would add, beyond the editorial, measures of each person's thermal microenvironment such as indoor temperature (the editorial notes that such data were unavailable, p. 1828), and death investigation and certification held constant across seasons.

domains.note: An editorial: no search, no criteria; 11 references chosen by the author.

The study discussed is appraised qualitatively (ecological features, single daily temperature, no individual data, small absolute effect), but its analyses are taken as reported, and the older heat-wave studies are cited without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The study discussed is not the author's; 2 of 11 references are his own background publications, one of them the sole source for the statements on the causes of heat-wave excess deaths.

The causal question is explicitly left open, but the gradient, specificity and plausibility points are offered as indications of cause, and the claim that effects would be larger during heat waves is argued without data.

domains.domain: Balance of the case for and against a causal effect of heat on cocaine-overdose deaths
domains.note: Both the design's limits and the arguments for causation are presented; apart from a rise in the number of people using drugs, other time-varying explanations (for example seasonal changes in what is sold or used with cocaine, or in how deaths are investigated and certified) are not named; he acknowledges only in general terms that factors or events closely associated in time with hot weather cannot be ruled out (p. 1828, 5th paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the unsystematic selection. The editorial is a careful, contemporaneous expert comment. It can be cited as evidence that a CDC physician who had published on heat-wave mortality, writing in the same issue, judged the Marzuk et al. association plausible but not established as causal, and for the specific limitations he named. It adds no data; figures about the Marzuk study must be cited from the primary paper.

key_findings.finding: An editorial in JAMA's Editorials section by Edwin M. Kilbourne, MD, of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlanta, commenting on Marzuk et al. in the same issue (cross-reference to p. 1795); it reports no data of its own and has 11 references.
key_findings.locator: Title, cross-reference box and author footnote (p. 1828); signature and reference list (p. 1829)

key_findings.finding: Kilbourne describes Marzuk et al. as identifying deaths attributable to cocaine overdose from New York City Medical Examiner's Office data and showing them to be more frequent in hot weather, and calls this substantive evidence that the risk of death from cocaine overdose rises sharply during hot weather.

He states that the design shares some features with ecological studies (based on group rather than individual information), which are highly susceptible to confounding: temperature was one daily value for the whole population from the Central Park weather station, daily data on individual thermal microenvironments were unavailable, the data were insufficient to determine even whether the people using cocaine with the hottest individual microenvironments were at highest risk, and factors or events closely associated in time with hot weather cannot be ruled out.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (left column) and 5th paragraph (right column, 1st on the column)

key_findings.finding: He reports the study's evidence against a simple rise in the number of people using drugs in hot weather: overdose deaths from opiates and other drugs did not increase, which he reads as an effect of heat specific to cocaine, and two comparison groups (homicides and motor-vehicle crash deaths) showed no sign of more cocaine use in hot weather.

As further indications of cause and effect he cites an apparently gradual, essentially monotonic rise in risk above a threshold temperature in the 1993–1995 cross-validation sample (a possible dose–response gradient) and biological plausibility: cocaine and heat stress both have metabolic and cardiovascular effects, raised body temperature has been implicated in cocaine overdose deaths, and joint effects could be additive or synergistic.

On magnitude: for days at or above 31.1 °C (88 °F), Marzuk et al. recorded a mean increase of only 0.58 deaths a day, against 50 to 143 all-cause excess deaths a day in 5 New York City heat waves between 1972 and 1996. Kilbourne calls the increase statistically significant but relatively small, and argues against dismissing it, because hot days are not heat waves, heat effects accumulate over several days, and the effect during heat waves may therefore be larger.
key_findings.locator: 12th and 13th paragraphs of the editorial (2nd and 3rd paragraphs on the page, left column)

key_findings.finding: He calls for replication in other cities during local heat waves, collection of person-level risk factors (for example a home air conditioner and the amount of cocaine taken), and individual-level comparison of people who died with people who use cocaine and survived the heat, so that the need for, and targets of, any prevention programme can be judged.

Background given for heat-wave mortality: the 1980 heat wave in St Louis and Kansas City caused 308 deaths above the expected number, with daily mortality in St Louis up to 3 times usual; the 1995 Chicago heat wave caused more than 700 deaths, with daily mortality more than 5 times usual; in most heat waves only a minority of excess deaths are attributed to heatstroke.

In 7 heat-wave studies since 1934, cardiovascular deaths rose 7%–59% above baseline and accounted for 13%–42% of excess deaths; cerebrovascular deaths rose 25%–104% and accounted for 6%–52%; in 6 of the 7, respiratory deaths rose 0%–84% and accounted for 0%–14%.
key_findings.locator: 11th paragraph of the editorial (1st on the page, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The figure of 50 to 143 excess deaths a day in 5 New York City heat waves between 1972 and 1996 is cited to a single 1975 paper (reference 11), whose title covers the heat waves of 1972 and 1973 only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source for the later heat waves in the range is not given, so the comparison figure cannot be checked from the cited reference.

design_detail: Short narrative review in the Resident Short Reviews series of Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine (4 pages, 27 references) by a pathology resident and a senior pathologist at Houston Methodist Hospital, describing vasculitis attributed to levamisole in people who use levamisole-adulterated cocaine: clinical, histological and laboratory features, differential diagnosis, and treatment. Five illustrations (one clinical photograph, four skin-biopsy micrographs) without a stated source patient, and one summary table. No search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal.
can_establish: How pathologists described the skin and laboratory picture of vasculitis attributed to levamisole in cocaine as of 2014 (retiform purpura; microvascular fibrin thrombi with or without leukocytoclastic vasculitis; neutropenia; ANCA and other autoantibodies) and which differential diagnoses they consider.
cannot_establish: How often this vasculitis occurs among people who use cocaine, whether its incidence is rising (no data are given), that levamisole rather than cocaine itself is the cause in a given patient (the review says testing for levamisole is unnecessary for diagnosis), or how well any treatment works.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited evidence: case reports and small series (refs 5–12, 16–18, 26, 27), a CDC report and toxicology studies on prevalence (refs 3, 13–15), and references on pathogenesis and ANCA testing (refs 19–25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Author-selected literature, mostly case reports, which favour dramatic and well-documented cases. The source of the five illustrations (which patient, whether levamisole was tested) is not stated (p. 1059).

exposure.measurement: As summarized: cocaine use by history or by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine, confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; levamisole detected by mass spectrometry in some reports (refs 11, 12, 13), but the review states that testing for levamisole is not required for diagnosis (p. 1060).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported. The review states that about 70% of cocaine in the US contains levamisole (refs 3, 13, 14; p. 1058).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (review). Tests described: skin-biopsy histology; blood counts (leukopenia below 4000/µL, neutropenia below 1500/µL, agranulocytosis below 500/µL); erythrocyte sedimentation rate; coagulation studies; ANCA by indirect immunofluorescence on ethanol-fixed neutrophils, confirmed by proteinase-3 and myeloperoxidase immunoassays; antinuclear antibody; lupus anticoagulant; toxicology (p. 1060).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: No case definition; the entity is described by retiform purpura, the histology, the laboratory findings and a history of cocaine use (Table, p. 1061).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: male-to-female ratio 1:3 and mean age at presentation 44 years (ref. 12, p. 1058); about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole (p. 1058); levamisole half-life 5.6 hours (ref. 26, p. 1060).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinicopathological description, drawn from case reports and small series, of a retiform purpuric rash with microvascular thrombi and/or leukocytoclastic vasculitis, neutropenia and autoantibodies in people who use cocaine, which in nearly all reported cases resolved once cocaine use stopped.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract cites a "rising incidence" (p. 1058) and the Conclusion an "increasing incidence" (p. 1061) of the entity; no incidence or trend data are given, only the statement that detection of levamisole in cocaine has increased (p. 1058). The Introduction says that finding levamisole by urine toxicology and mass spectrometry in patients with suspected vasculitis confirmed it as the cause (p. 1058); but if about 70% of cocaine contains levamisole (the review's own figure, p. 1058), most patients who use cocaine will test positive whatever caused their rash, so detection shows exposure, not cause. The review says testing for levamisole is not required, because levamisole is so common in cocaine and because the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings (p. 1060); in the editors' reading, cases are therefore attributed to levamisole without measuring it. The treatment advice (stop cocaine; it may be prudent to avoid corticosteroids because of neutropenia and wound infection) is the authors' opinion for hospital care, resting on case reports (p. 1060).

timeline.event: Levamisole-induced vasculitis described in a patient treated for rheumatoid arthritis (Macfarlane & Bacon, ref. 2, as cited p. 1058)
CDC report of agranulocytosis associated with cocaine use in four states, March 2008 to November 2009 (ref. 3)
Walsh et al. (ref. 11): retiform purpura in people using cocaine, with evidence the authors took to incriminate levamisole
Narrative review of agranulocytosis and other consequences of levamisole-contaminated cocaine

replication.where_it_stands: A teaching summary for pathologists. The histological description is consistent across the cited cases; the attribution to levamisole, and any statement about frequency or trend, are not quantified in it. Claims should cite primary case series with testing data.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have no relevant financial interest in the products or companies described in the article (p. 1058).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Pathology and Genomic Medicine, Houston Methodist Hospital, and Weill Cornell Medical College (p. 1058); a resident-authored short review. None of the cited studies is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A case–control study of people who use cocaine with and without retiform purpura or neutropenia, with levamisole and cocaine measured in both groups and standard histological and laboratory definitions; for treatment, a comparative study of corticosteroids versus none in confirmed cases.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria.
Case reports are summarized without appraisal, and detection of levamisole in case series is described as confirming the cause.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited studies is by the authors.
Pathogenesis is labelled uncertain and the corticosteroid advice is framed as prudence, but a rising incidence and a confirmed cause are stated as facts.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on cause and frequency (cocaine itself as an alternative cause, and the absence of incidence data, are under-represented)
domains.note: Differential diagnoses of other vasculitides are covered well, but whether cocaine itself contributes, and how rare the condition is among people exposed, are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high concern overall because there is no systematic search and no appraisal of the case literature. As a description of histological and laboratory features for pathologists the review is clear and properly sourced. Claims may cite it for the clinical, histological and laboratory picture and the differential diagnosis; not for frequency, trend, causation, or treatment effects.

key_findings.finding: Clinical picture: a tender, purpuric rash in a retiform or stellate pattern, with or without central necrosis, on the extremities, trunk, nasal tip, digits, cheeks or ears; bullae are not uncommon and skin sloughing allows bacterial superinfection; ear and digit lesions have been reported to self-amputate.
Demography cited: predilection for women (male-to-female ratio 1:3) and mean age at presentation 44 years, both cited to one paper (ref. 12) whose title describes a single patient.
key_findings.note: The number of cases behind the ratio and the mean age is not given.

key_findings.finding: Laboratory findings: leukopenia (<4000/µL), neutropenia (<1500/µL) including agranulocytosis (<500/µL), raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal coagulation, and autoantibodies including p- and c-ANCA, antinuclear antibody and lupus anticoagulant.

Histology: leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small vessels and multiple fibrin thrombi in small vessels of the superficial and deep dermis, classically both but often only one; microvascular fibrin thrombi are the most consistent feature, and some authors consider the combination relatively specific; epidermal changes depend on the biopsy site.
key_findings.locator: Pathologic Features, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1058, continues on p. 1059); Figures 2–5 (p. 1059)

key_findings.finding: Bone marrow in patients with agranulocytosis: myeloid hypoplasia, mild megakaryocyte hyperplasia and increased marrow plasma cells, with circulating plasmacytoid lymphocytes; the review says these marrow and blood features can help distinguish cocaine-related from other causes of agranulocytosis (refs 17, 19).
Pathogenesis is uncertain; an immune complex–mediated process is favoured on skin immunofluorescence, and for agranulocytosis a hapten mechanism has been suggested.

ANCA specificity: antibodies against human neutrophil elastase are cited as strongly associated with cocaine-induced lesions and as possibly helping to distinguish levamisole-induced vasculitis from other ANCA-associated vasculitides.
key_findings.note: Per its title, the cited study (ref. 25, 2004) concerns cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions, not levamisole vasculitis.

key_findings.finding: Testing: levamisole half-life 5.6 hours; detectable by GC-MS but described as not necessary for diagnosis; cocaine use is screened by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine and confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; testing for levamisole is described as not required for two reasons: levamisole is so prevalent in cocaine, and the diagnosis can be made from the other clinical, pathological and laboratory findings.

Differential diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitides (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome), septic vasculitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cryoglobulinaemia, warfarin-induced skin necrosis and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; histological overlap makes clinical correlation essential.

Treatment and prognosis: the ideal treatment is undetermined; nearly all cases resolve once cocaine use stops; corticosteroids have not definitively been shown to improve or speed healing, and the authors suggest it may be prudent to avoid them because of neutropenia and wound infection; plasmapheresis appears only in case reports; some patients needed debridement, skin grafting or amputation.

Context stated: about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole; levamisole has been detected in cocaine since 2003, with detection increasing; medical use has ended (the review says the FDA banned it in 2000), so current cases are attributed exclusively to adulterated cocaine.
key_findings.note: The review also says levamisole is added to increase volume and weight and possibly to potentiate cocaine's psychotropic effects (refs 3, 13, 14); this is a speculation given without data, and claims do not carry it.

key_findings.finding: Attribution as stated by the review: after the first reports of the vasculitis in late 2009 and early 2010, researchers isolated levamisole by urine toxicology and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry in patients with suspected levamisole-induced vasculitis, which the review presents as confirming that levamisole was the cause (refs 11, 12).
key_findings.note: Editors' reading: with about 70% of US cocaine said to contain levamisole (same paragraph), detection in a patient shows exposure; the review gives no count of how many reported cases had levamisole measured and no comparison with people who use cocaine without the condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the FDA banned levamisole in the US in 2000 (p. 1058) is cited to refs 3 and 4, and ref. 4 is a 1999 paper that cannot document a 2000 ban; another review read in this round (Buchanan & Lavonas; card sc_buchanan_2012) says instead that levamisole remained FDA-approved as adjuvant colon-cancer treatment but was no longer marketed for human use in the US.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regulatory history should come from a primary regulatory source, not from either review.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex ratio (1:3) and mean age (44 years) are cited to a single paper whose title describes one patient (ref. 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be traced to a number of cases; do not cite them from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Conclusion describe a rising or increasing incidence (pp. 1058, 1061) without incidence or trend data; the only trend stated concerns detection of levamisole in cocaine (p. 1058).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as evidence of a rising incidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The source of the clinical photograph and the four micrographs (which patient, consent, whether levamisole was detected) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The images illustrate typical features but cannot be taken as confirmed cases.
