design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses of logit-transformed proportions (PROSPERO CRD42020179683) of the prevalence of cocaine-induced psychosis (CIP) in people who use cocaine and have no primary psychotic disorder or mood disorder with psychotic features. CIP combines cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (CIPS: symptom questionnaires such as the Cocaine Experience Questionnaire and the SAPS-CIP, or study-specific questions, in two studies a single symptom) with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder diagnosed on DSM criteria (CIPD/SIPD: PRISM or MINI interviews). Two pooled groups: current CIP in current use (3 studies, n=102, two of them laboratory cocaine-administration studies) and lifetime CIP in lifetime use (17 studies, n=5286, almost all treatment samples). In all, 20 studies and 5388 participants; subgroup analyses by definition, risk of bias, instrument, region, sample size and share with dependence; meta-regression on year of publication.
can_establish: How often people in cocaine treatment samples (and in two small laboratory samples) reported, or were diagnosed with, cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms or disorder in studies published up to 2020, and how strongly the figure depends on the definition: about 68% lifetime for symptoms against about 16% for a DSM disorder.
cannot_establish: The prevalence in people who use cocaine outside treatment (no general-population sample); that cocaine alone produced the symptoms (other drug use was common and could not be analysed); effects of dose or route (not analysable); or a single meaningful prevalence across definitions (I² 97%, and the overall interval printed is narrower than a standard random-effects interval, editors' calculation). The authors' corrigendum corrects only the regional figures.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to 31 August 2020, limited to English-language studies of adult humans, with reference-list snowballing (p. 2); the flow chart also lists ClinicalTrials.gov (70 records) and the EU clinical trials register (45) (p. 3). Participants in the included studies were people seeking or receiving treatment (mostly outpatient addiction services; one inpatient service; one psychiatric emergency unit), and three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies, two of them in the current-use group and one (Reid 2004) in the lifetime group (p. 3; Fig. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cross-sectional, case-control or cohort studies of people with current or past cocaine use (use, abuse, dependence) that excluded people with primary psychotic disorders or mood disorders with psychotic features, or reported them separately, and that reported the prevalence of CIP (p. 2). Excluded: CIP diagnosed only by retrospective chart review; samples limited to people with CIP; samples whose main drug was not cocaine; no prevalence of CIPS, CIPD or SIPD reported; case reports and qualitative studies (p. 2). Three laboratory challenge studies were included although the listed designs do not cover them (p. 3).
sample.demographics: Mean sample size printed as 269.2 (23 to 2192); mean share of men 68% (49–100%), two studies men only; mean age 37.0 years (study means 23–45); mean age at first cocaine use 22.2 (11 studies, n=1888); mean years of cocaine use printed as 22.4 (7 studies, n=916). USA 13 studies, Spain 4, French Caribbean 1, Canada 1, Brazil 1 (p. 3), the review's count, which fits only its uncorrected regional grouping (reporting issue on the corrigendum).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Clinical samples throughout: the authors state the estimates could be inflated by selection and admission-rate (Berkson) bias (p. 7). English only and no grey literature. The current-use estimate rests on two laboratory cocaine-challenge studies (12 of 28; 29 of 44; paranoia, by their titles) and one psychiatric emergency series (12 of 30) (Fig. 2, p. 4). The largest lifetime study (Zaytas 2013, 2192 participants, 41% of the lifetime total) and Floyd 2006 have no entry in the reference list, and Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007, whose reference entries share authors, are entered with identical counts (181 of 243) (Fig. 3, p. 5; pp. 7–8).

exposure.measurement: Each included study assessed cocaine dependence with DSM-III or DSM-IV (p. 3); otherwise exposure is whatever each study reported (history of use, dependence).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable: dose and severity of dependence were reported too rarely, and route could not be analysed (pp. 5–7). Two lifetime studies reported a higher estimated lifetime cocaine dose in people with CIP, and one laboratory study reported that CIP was dose-dependent (pp. 6–7).
exposure.polysubstance: Reported in few studies: current use of alcohol 39.5% (2 studies), opioids 50.1% (2), cannabis 39.7% (3), other stimulants 30.8% (1); lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% (3), opioids 30% (2), cannabis 32% (2) (p. 3). Its contribution to CIP could not be determined (p. 6); the authors argue that cannabis-induced psychosis is an unlikely explanation of the findings (p. 6) and that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible (p. 6).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; lifetime CIP was assessed retrospectively in most studies (p. 6).

comparison.controls: None (prevalence among people who use cocaine).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis and other vulnerability factors were not analysable; individual-level data were not available (p. 6).

outcomes.instruments: CIPS: Cocaine Experience Questionnaire (6 lifetime studies), SAPS-CIP (1), study-specific questions (6), and paranoia during laboratory cocaine administration (2 current-use studies); CIPD: PRISM semi-structured interview (4 studies, 3 lifetime and 1 current) and MINI (1) (pp. 4–5). Risk of bias of included studies: the Hoy et al. (2012) tool for prevalence studies, 10 items plus a summary judgment, applied independently by two authors; items without enough information were rated high risk, and studies defining CIPS by a single symptom were rated high risk on case definition (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The PRISM was designed to separate substance-induced from primary disorders (p. 4); the CEQ and SAPS-CIP quantify symptoms ranging from transient to persistent (p. 6).
outcomes.operationalization: CIP = current CIP in people currently using cocaine, or lifetime CIP in people with lifetime use; CIPS and CIPD were combined after the authors found that most studies measured symptoms rather than disorder (p. 2). For three PRISM studies the prevalence had to be extracted after removing patients with primary psychosis (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 24 are the pooled estimates reported in the text: 2 main pools, 21 subgroup and sensitivity estimates, and 1 meta-regression; subgroup differences were judged by residual heterogeneity, not by formal tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; screening and extraction were done in duplicate (p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects meta-analysis of logit proportions. Current use (3 studies, n=102): 50.2% (95% CI 32.0–68.4), I²=66%; without the Mooney laboratory study 41.4% (29.5–54.4), I²=0%; CIPD 40.0% (14.9–71.7), one study; CIPS 55.2% (32.8–75.7), two laboratory studies, I²=72% (p. 4; Fig. 2). Lifetime use (17 studies, n=5286): 55.6% (50.2–61.0), I²=97%, τ²=0.1597 printed in Fig. 3; CIPS 68.4% (62.8–73.5), 13 studies; CIPD 16% (10.6–23.2), 4 studies; I²=89% in each (pp. 4–5; Fig. 3). Low risk of bias only (14 lifetime studies): 55.6% (50.5–60.6), I²=97%; CIPS 68.3% (63.2–73.1); CIPD 11.7% (7.6–17.4), I²=0% (pp. 4–5). By instrument: CEQ 70.1% (62.6–76.7), 6 studies; SAPS-CIP 84.2% (69.0–92.7), 1 study; study-specific questions 63.4% (55.2–70.9), 6 studies; PRISM 11.7% (7.4–17.9), 3 studies; MINI 35.8% (18.9–57.1), 1 study (p. 5). By region: North America 66.5% (57.6–74.3); South America and the Caribbean 56.1% (34.2–75.5); Europe 25.1% (15.1–38.6). By study size: under 60 participants 69.2% (52.8–81.9); 60–200, 36.2% (22.8–52.3); over 200, 59.8% (46.7–71.7). By dependence: majority dependent (4 studies) 53.5% (33.4–72.5); all dependent (13) 54.3% (44.8–67.2) (p. 5). Year of publication did not explain heterogeneity (p. 6). Editors' calculations from the study counts printed in Figs 2 and 3: the printed lifetime overall estimate, interval and study weights are reproduced exactly only when the between-study variance estimated within the CIPS and CIPD subgroups (τ²=0.1597) is used for the overall model; a standard DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model of all 17 studies gives the same 55.6% with τ²=0.593, a 95% CI of 46.0–64.8% and a 95% prediction interval of 18.7–87.2%. CIPS with its own τ² (0.138): 68.4% (63.1–73.2), prediction interval 47.8–83.6%; CIPD with its own τ² (0.482): 16.0% (8.5–28.3). Without Tang 2007 (identical counts to Cubells 2005): overall 54.2% (44.1–64.0), CIPS 67.7% (62.1–72.9).
analysis.covariates: None at review level; individual-level variables could not be examined (p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42020179683, registered on 14 July 2020 (p. 2), 24 days before the manuscript was received on 7 August 2020 (p. 1); the search is dated to 31 August 2020, after submission (presumably updated in revision, which is not stated). The planned focus on CIPD was changed to CIP, combining CIPS and CIPD, after the search showed that most studies measured symptoms (p. 2). The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Meta-regressions were planned for several moderators, but only year of publication was explored, because individual-level data were unavailable (pp. 3, 6). Per-study characteristics and risk-of-bias judgments are only in supplements (Tables S1–S2) that were not read.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The current-use group has 3 studies and 102 people, and several subgroups rest on one study; all subgroup analyses are study-level comparisons among few studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In studies of people in cocaine treatment, about two thirds reported having had cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms at some time (68.4%, 13 studies, I² 89%), while about one in six met DSM criteria for a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (16%, 4 studies); the two cannot be summarized by one figure (I² 97%). The current-use estimate (50.2%) comes from 102 people in two laboratory cocaine-challenge studies and one psychiatric emergency series.
interpretation_gap.claimed: This PDF has no abstract. The Discussion reports one overall prevalence per group (50.2% and 55.6%) as high and calls the definition of CIP the only moderator accounting for heterogeneity (p. 6), although the definition subgroups left residual I² of 72% and 89% (pp. 4–5) and the overall lifetime interval is narrower than a standard random-effects interval (editors' calculation). The title speaks of people who use cocaine in general; the Conclusions more accurately restrict the finding to people in contact with health services (p. 7). The Discussion states that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible, because other drugs were used in all studies, and that cross-sectional retrospective designs preclude causal conclusions (p. 6), yet the outcome is called cocaine-induced throughout. The clinical-relevance section extrapolates a risk of transition to schizophrenia from amphetamine data (p. 7) and recommends systematic screening, which these data do not test.

timeline.event: Lecomte et al.: meta-analysis giving a lifetime prevalence of substance-induced psychotic disorder of 42.7% in people with methamphetamine use disorders (as cited, p. 6)

Meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced psychoses to schizophrenia: no study of transition after cocaine-induced psychotic disorder; 22% after amphetamine-induced psychotic disorder (as cited, p. 1)
This review, described by its authors as the first meta-analysis of the prevalence of CIP (p. 6)

Corrigendum (10.1016/j.pnpbp.2021.110434): one study (Roncero et al., 2017) moved to the right region and the regional estimates corrected (North America 67.9%, Europe 30.7%); nothing else changed. Read by the adjudicator on 12 November 2026.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of the prevalence of cocaine-induced psychosis identified by its authors. Its definition-specific estimates (symptoms about 68%, DSM disorder about 16%, lifetime, in treatment samples) are the usable results; the single pooled figures and the current-use figure are not. Its corrigendum (2022) corrects only the regional figures.

funding.funder: Internal funding only (p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: Stefan Kaiser has received royalties for cognitive test and training software from Schuhfried; Michel Sabe and Nan Zhao declare no conflict of interest (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Division of Adult Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Geneva University Hospitals (p. 1). Open access under a CC BY licence (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A general-population cohort of people who use cocaine, assessed with structured interviews that separate transient symptoms from DSM substance-induced psychotic disorder and from primary psychosis, with dose, route and other drug use measured prospectively, would give the prevalence outside treatment and how it depends on use; an individual-participant meta-analysis of existing treatment cohorts with a common definition is the achievable near-term step.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with current or lifetime cocaine use without primary psychosis), condition (CIP, as CIPS and CIPD), designs and settings specified; prevalence needs no comparator.

PROSPERO CRD42020179683, registered 14 July 2020, 24 days before submission, so it cannot be confirmed that methods were fixed before the work began; the change from CIPD to combined CIP is stated and justified (p. 2).
Designs are listed without an explanation, and three laboratory challenge studies outside the listed designs were included.

Five databases, search terms and snowballing, with two trial registries in the flow chart; but English-only and adult-only limits without justification and no grey literature (item 4 read as written, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Titles, abstracts and methods inspected independently by two authors (p. 2).
Two authors with a predefined form; disagreements resolved by consensus or a third reviewer (p. 2).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons and counts in the flow chart and three named exclusions (p. 3), but no list of the 206 excluded full texts; the supplements were not read, and none is described as such a list.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: study-level details are only in Supplementary Table S1, which was not read; the article gives pooled characteristics and the counts in the forest plots.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A tool designed for prevalence studies (Hoy et al., 2012), covering selection and measurement, applied independently by two authors (p. 2); per-study ratings are in an unread supplement, and the summary counts in the text are inconsistent (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of logit proportions suits prevalence data, but the headline pools combine laboratory paranoia with clinical diagnoses and single-symptom with DSM definitions (I² 97%); the overall lifetime interval is reproduced only with the within-subgroup τ², which narrows it (editors' calculation); and two reports with identical counts from overlapping author groups are pooled as separate studies.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Re-analysis restricted to low-risk studies (14 lifetime studies) reported (pp. 4–5).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Selection and admission-rate bias, the cross-sectional retrospective designs and the low-risk-only analysis are discussed (pp. 6–7).
Subgroup analyses by definition, instrument, region, size and dependence, a meta-regression on year, and discussion of the residual heterogeneity (pp. 4–7).
Not investigated, on the argument that publication does not depend on the prevalence a study reports (p. 2); a subgroup by study size is the only related analysis.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Table S1, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. Four critical items are not met (4, 7, 11 and 15) and one is met only in part (2), which gives critically low confidence. That rating does not make the review useless: it reports its estimates by definition and by instrument, and its forest plots print every study's counts, so the definition-specific estimates can be used and checked. The card may be cited for the lifetime prevalence of cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (about 68%) and of DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (about 16%) among people in cocaine treatment, with the provisos that these are treatment samples and that other drug use was common (the corrigendum, now read, corrects only the regional figures); the single pooled figures (50.2% and 55.6%) should not be cited as a prevalence among people who use cocaine, and the current-use figure not at all.

key_findings.finding: 20 studies (5388 participants) were included from 1688 unique records and 226 full texts: 3 studies of current CIP in current use (102 participants) and 17 of lifetime CIP in lifetime use (5286); all cross-sectional except three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Search results; 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 (p. 3); 3.5 and 3.6, 1st paragraphs (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Participants were people seeking or receiving treatment (lifetime studies described as recruited through outpatient addiction treatment, except one inpatient service); the current-use group consisted of one psychiatric emergency series and two laboratory cocaine-challenge studies. Means across all 20 studies: 68% men, age 37.0; USA 13 studies, Spain 4, French Caribbean, Canada and Brazil 1 each.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Studies and patient characteristics, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs (6th begins p. 3, ends p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime CIP in lifetime use: 55.6% (95% CI 50.2–61.0), 17 studies, I²=97%. By definition: psychotic symptoms (CIPS) 68.4% (62.8–73.5), 13 studies; DSM psychotic disorder (CIPD) 16% (10.6–23.2), 4 studies; I²=89% in each.
key_findings.locator: 3.6 CIP in lifetime cocaine users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 4); Fig. 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts in Fig. 3: the printed overall interval uses the within-subgroup τ² (0.1597); a standard random-effects model of all 17 studies gives 55.6% (46.0–64.8), τ²=0.593, prediction interval 18.7–87.2%. With its own τ² the CIPD estimate is 16.0% (8.5–28.3). The corrigendum does not change these figures.

key_findings.finding: Current CIP in current use: 50.2% (32.0–68.4), 3 studies, n=102, I²=66%. The studies: psychotic symptoms (CIPS in Fig. 2; paranoia, by the studies' titles) during laboratory cocaine challenges in 12 of 28 (Kalayasiri 2006b) and 29 of 44 (Mooney 2006), and CIPD in 12 of 30 at a psychiatric emergency unit (Elangovan 1993); without Mooney 2006, 41.4% (29.5–54.4).
key_findings.locator: 3.5 CIP in current cocaine users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2

key_findings.finding: By instrument (lifetime): CEQ 70.1% (62.6–76.7), 6 studies, I²=50; SAPS-CIP 84.2% (69.0–92.7), 1 study; study-specific questions 63.4% (55.2–70.9), 6 studies, I²=94%; PRISM 11.7% (7.4–17.9), 3 studies; MINI 35.8% (18.9–57.1), 1 study.
key_findings.note: The SAPS-CIP figure (84.2%) is a single study, Vergara-Moragues 2014 (96 of 114 in Fig. 3), one of the two studies that counted one psychotic symptom as a case (3.4, p. 4) and, by the card's best fit, one of the three left out of the low-risk analysis: the highest instrument figure rests on the loosest case definition.

key_findings.finding: Restricting to studies at low risk of bias (14 lifetime studies) left the overall and symptom estimates almost unchanged, 55.6% (50.5–60.6) and CIPS 68.3% (63.2–73.1), but the disorder estimate fell from 16% (4 studies, I² 89%) to 11.7% (7.6–17.4), I²=0%, consistent with the one MINI study (Willi 2017, 35.8%) being left out.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: these values are reproduced when three lifetime studies are dropped (best fit: Vergara-Moragues 2014, Miguel 2018, Willi 2017), consistent with 14 low-risk studies, not the 15 stated in 3.4.

key_findings.finding: By region, as corrected by the authors' corrigendum (Sabe et al., 2022): North America 67.9% (57.0–77.2), South America and the Caribbean 56.1% (34.2–75.5), Europe 30.7% (18.7–46.1), I² 85%, 78% and 98%; the article printed 66.5% (57.6–74.3), 56.1% (34.2–75.5) and 25.1% (15.1–38.6), with one study (Roncero 2017) wrongly in North America. By study size: under 60 participants 69.2%, 60–200 participants 36.2%, over 200 participants 59.8%; by share with dependence: 53.5% and 54.3%. None reduced the residual heterogeneity (I² 95–97%).
key_findings.locator: 3.9, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 5); corrected text of 3.9 in the corrigendum (its p. 1) and corrected Fig. S4 (its p. 2)

key_findings.finding: Other drug use was reported in few studies: current alcohol 39.5% (2 studies), opioids 50.1% (2), cannabis 39.7% (3), other stimulants 30.8% (1); lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% (3), opioids 30% (2), cannabis 32% (2). Its contribution could not be analysed, and neither could dose, severity of dependence or route.

The authors state that the estimates could be inflated by selection and admission-rate (Berkson) bias in treatment samples, and that, because almost all studies were cross-sectional with retrospective assessment of cocaine use, it is difficult to draw conclusions about cause.
Publication bias was not investigated; the authors argue that whether a study reporting a prevalence is published does not depend on the prevalence it reports.

reporting_issues.issue: This PDF has no abstract or keywords: the article opens with the Introduction (p. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The article's own summary of its results is only in the Discussion and Conclusions; the corrigendum does not supply an abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 3 prints the same τ² (0.1597) for the lifetime overall model, 55.6% (50.2–61.0), as for each subgroup, and the shared τ² widens single-study subgroup intervals: Elangovan 1993 (12 of 30) has its own interval of 24–58% but a printed subgroup interval of 14.9–71.7% (Fig. 2). Editors' calculation from the Fig. 3 counts: the printed overall estimate, interval and weights are reproduced exactly only when the between-study variance estimated within the CIPS and CIPD subgroups is applied to the overall model; a standard random-effects model of the 17 studies gives the same point estimate with a 95% CI of 46.0–64.8% (τ²=0.593).
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall lifetime interval overstates precision by about half; the definition-specific estimates are the citable ones.

reporting_issues.issue: Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007 are entered with identical counts (181 of 243 each), and their reference entries share authors (Cubells, Tang, Farrer); the review discusses sample overlap only for Araos 2015 and Pavon 2013 (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: If the two reports share a sample, 243 people are counted twice; without Tang 2007 the CIPS estimate is 67.7% (62.1–72.9) and the overall 54.2% (44.1–64.0) (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Two studies in Fig. 3, Floyd 2006 (36 of 51) and Zaytas 2013 (1500 of 2192, the largest study), have no entry in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The largest contributor to the lifetime pool (41% of its participants) cannot be identified from the article; Supplementary Table S1 (not read) may name it.

reporting_issues.issue: Risk-of-bias counts do not fit the groups: 2 of the 3 current-use studies are given as 50% and 15 of the 17 lifetime studies as 75% (3.4), while the low-risk re-analysis retains 14 lifetime studies (3.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The low-risk results are reproduced with 14 studies (editors' calculation), so 14 of 17 is the likely count; the printed percentages are wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Values differ between Results and Discussion: CIPS in current use 55.2% (p. 4; Fig. 2) against 55.7% (p. 6); lifetime overall 55.6% (pp. 4, 6) against 54.7% (p. 6); PRISM 11.7% (p. 5) against 11.6% (p. 6). Labelling slips: the lifetime subgroup paragraph is introduced as being about the current-use group (p. 4); three PRISM (CIPD) studies are said to need extraction of CIPS prevalence (p. 4); Europe is labelled Spain and France (p. 5) although no included study is listed from France itself (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the Results and figure values; the slips do not change the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Two printed intervals are not symmetric on the logit scale used for pooling: the all-dependent subgroup, 54.3% (44.8–67.2), and South America and the Caribbean, 56.1% (34.2–75.5) (p. 5); recomputed from the Fig. 3 counts with the region model's common τ² (0.349), the latter is 56.1% (34.2–75.9) (editors' calculation). The other intervals in the text are symmetric (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: One bound in each is probably mistyped; do not cite these two intervals. The corrigendum's text repeats 34.2–75.5 (reporting issue on the corrigendum).

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria list cross-sectional, case-control and cohort designs (p. 2), but three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies were included, two of which make up two thirds of the current-use group (p. 3; Fig. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The current-use prevalence mixes paranoia induced in the laboratory with clinical diagnoses and should not be cited as a prevalence in people who currently use cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Dates and sources: the search is dated to 31 August 2020 (p. 2) but the manuscript was received on 7 August 2020 (p. 1), and the flow chart lists two trial registries (p. 3) that the Methods do not mention.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a search update during revision, but undocumented; the search cannot be reproduced exactly from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Corrigendum (Sabe et al., 2022, Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry 112, 110434; 2 pages): in the subgroup analysis by region (3.9 and Fig. S4) one study, Roncero et al. (2017), had been included in the wrong subgroup. Corrected figures (corrigendum p. 1): North America 67.9% (57.0–77.2), South America and the Caribbean 56.1% (34.2–75.5), Europe 30.7% (18.7–46.1), I² 85%, 78% and 98%, residual I² 95%; the corrected Fig. S4 (corrigendum p. 2) places Roncero 2017 (422 of 767) in Europe with four other studies. Nothing else is corrected, and the authors state that the conclusions are unaffected. Editors' checks: every Fig. S4 subtotal is reproduced from its counts with one common τ² (0.5033), the residual variance after splitting by region, which the figure also applies to all 17 studies (55.6%, 46.6–64.2); the figure's South America interval (30.9–78.6) differs from the corrigendum's text, which repeats the article's 34.2–75.5; three study labels differ from Fig. 3 with the same counts (Araos 2014, Floyd 2005, Willi 2016 against Araos 2015, Floyd 2006, Willi 2017). The article's country count (USA 13, Spain 4; p. 3), not revised, fits only the uncorrected grouping; with Roncero 2017 in Europe it would be 12 and 5 (editors' inference). The article's reference list has no entry for the included Roncero 2017 study: its only Roncero 2017 entry (Curr Neuropharmacol 15:315–323, cited in the Discussion) is not the study the corrigendum names (Eur Psychiatry 42:63–69).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the regional figures from the corrigendum; the rest of the article stands as printed. Because the regions share one τ², each region's own spread is understated (with its own τ², Europe 30.4%, 10.3–62.6; editors' calculation). The country count is probably 12 USA and 5 Spain; Supplementary Table S1 (not read) would settle it.

reporting_issues.issue: Setting: the review describes the lifetime studies as recruited through outpatient addiction treatment except one inpatient study (3.2, p. 3), but the reference-list titles of two lifetime disorder studies name therapeutic communities (Vergara-Moragues 2012; Gonzalez-Saiz 2014; pp. 7–8), and one lifetime study (Reid 2004, 21 of 23, men only) is one of the three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies (3.1, p. 3; Fig. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Treatment samples' is accurate; 'outpatient' is the review's description and does not fit every study.

reporting_issues.issue: The review attributes the PRISM interview to Elangovan 1993 (3.3, p. 4), the one disorder study in the current-use group, while its own reference for the PRISM is dated 1996 (Hasin et al., 1996; p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: The instrument, and with it the disorder label for that study in Fig. 2, cannot be confirmed without the primary study; this does not change the lifetime estimates.

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies reporting mortality among people with problematic or dependent cocaine use, done for the Global Burden of Disease Expert Group on Mental Disorders and Illicit Drug Use. EMBASE, Medline and PsycINFO searched for publications from 1990 to 2008, with grey literature, reference lists of reviews, an expert group and unpublished data requested from cohort investigators. Nine cohorts were found and seven gave mortality estimates (USA 2, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil, Italy). Crude mortality rates (CMR) per 100 person-years were taken or recalculated from deaths and person-years; standardized mortality ratios (SMR) were taken as reported (four cohorts); causes of death are described for four cohorts. Estimates were deliberately not pooled.
can_establish: Which cohort studies of mortality in people with problematic or dependent cocaine use had been reported up to 2008, and the range of their crude mortality rates (about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years) and of the four reported SMRs (about 4.4 to 7.7 against the general population of the same age and sex), with the leading causes of death in four cohorts.
cannot_establish: A pooled or typical mortality rate for people who use cocaine (no pooling, heterogeneous cohorts); mortality among people who use cocaine without injecting, treatment or arrest, since no cohort followed people who only snort cocaine; how much of the excess is due to cocaine itself rather than injecting, HIV, heroin and alcohol use and social disadvantage, since SMRs standardize only for age and sex; or mortality after the cohorts' follow-up periods (1985-2005).

sample.recruitment: Database search (EMBASE, Medline, PsycINFO) for publications from 1990 to 2008 with librarian-designed strings; grey literature through online and library databases; reference lists of review articles; an expert group asked for missed studies; cohort investigators asked for additional data, several of which are cited as personal communications from September to November 2008 (pp. 89-92; Table 1 note, p. 91).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort studies reporting raw data on mortality related to problematic use of or dependence on cocaine. Excluded: not a cohort study, no report of mortality among people using cocaine, no primary data, or case reports of cocaine-related deaths without a denominator (p. 89, 2.2 and 2.3); the flowchart also excludes a wrong time period, before 1990 (Fig. 1, p. 90). Non-English abstracts were screened; one Spanish article contributed data and 14 non-English articles were excluded, none reporting cohort mortality (p. 90, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Cohorts (Table 1, p. 91; pp. 92-93): Brazil 1992-1999, 131 people in treatment for crack dependence; Canada (VIDUS) 1996-2004, 717 people injecting cocaine only; the Netherlands 1985-1993, a subsample of HIV-negative people mainly injecting cocaine within a cohort of 632; USA (RAVEN, Seattle) 1994-1997, 319 injecting cocaine daily and 52 smoking crack daily (overlapping); USA (ALIVE, Baltimore) 1988-2005, 518 injecting cocaine only and 2439 injecting cocaine and heroin, 25% HIV-positive at baseline; France 1992-1999, 2212 people arrested for cocaine or crack use or dealing, mean age 27 at baseline; Italy (Bologna) 1989-2004, 347 people in treatment for cocaine dependence, mostly intranasal, 309 of them men.
sample.attrition: Not reported for most cohorts. Brazil: 70% followed at 12 years, with 4 further deaths not used because no person-years were reported. The excluded Dutch cohort lost 61 of 160 (Table 1, p. 91; p. 92).
sample.selection_effects: All cohorts were recruited through injecting-drug-use research, treatment or arrest, mostly from socially disadvantaged settings and several with high HIV prevalence; none followed people who only snort cocaine (p. 93, 4.1). Five cohorts are from North America or Western Europe, one from Brazil. Several estimates come from personal communications rather than published reports.

exposure.measurement: As defined in each cohort at baseline: primary drug injected, daily injecting or crack smoking, treatment for cocaine dependence, or arrest for cocaine use or dealing; the review calls all of these problematic or dependent cocaine use (p. 90, Results, 4th paragraph). Changes in drug, route or frequency during follow-up were not captured (p. 94).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route differed between cohorts: injection (Canada, the Netherlands, ALIVE, RAVEN), crack smoking (Brazil; RAVEN daily non-injecting group), mostly intranasal (Italy), not stated (France). Frequency: daily injecting in RAVEN and ALIVE.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level. The largest ALIVE group injected heroin as well as cocaine; in Italy concomitant alcohol problems were associated with mortality (p. 92); other drug use is not reported for most cohorts.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The general population of the same age and sex in each country (SMRs, four cohorts); otherwise none. Within cohorts: people injecting cocaine only against cocaine and heroin (ALIVE), and HIV-positive against HIV-negative people (VIDUS, ALIVE).
comparison.matching: SMRs standardize for age and sex only; CMRs are unadjusted by definition (p. 90, 3.1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: None was adjusted for. The authors name general health, route of use, HIV prevalence, access to general and specialist care and possibly social disadvantage as possible reasons for the differences in crude rates between cohorts (p. 93), and social disadvantage, poorer access to health care, violence and other high-risk behaviours and the quality of the cocaine supply as reasons the cohorts may not represent other people who use cocaine (pp. 93-94). Heroin co-injection (the ALIVE cocaine-and-heroin group, p. 92) and alcohol problems (associated with mortality within the Italian cohort, p. 92) are further factors the editors add.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The general-population comparators include people who use drugs; not discussed.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality: CMR per 100 person-years, taken as reported or calculated from deaths and person-years; where only deaths and total years of follow-up were reported, deaths were assumed to occur halfway through follow-up; SMRs as reported; two studies gave only case fatality (p. 90, 2.5, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Causes of death: counts and percentages (Table 2) or cause-specific SMRs.
outcomes.validity_norms: How deaths were identified in each cohort (linkage to death registers, death certificates, contact with families or services) and who assigned the causes are not reported; cause categories differ between cohorts (Table 2 footnotes, p. 92). The authors recommend classifying causes with agreed definitions (p. 94).
outcomes.operationalization: CMR: deaths per 100 person-years of follow-up. SMR: observed deaths divided by those expected for people of the same age and sex in the general population of that country (p. 90, 2.5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive review; the only tests quoted are the cohorts' own HIV comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening by two researchers independently, with shortlists compared and resolved by consensus; extraction by two researchers, compared for consistency (p. 89, 2.1 and 2.4).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate. CMR per 100 person-years (Table 1, p. 91): Canada VIDUS 6.16 (95% CI 5.21 to 7.11; 161 deaths, 2613.2 person-years); ALIVE cocaine only 4.69 (4.03 to 5.45; 175 deaths, 3727 person-years); ALIVE cocaine and heroin 4.37 (4.07 to 4.68; 787 deaths, 18,023 person-years); the Netherlands 4.6 (9 deaths, 194 person-years); Brazil 3.51 (23 deaths); RAVEN daily crack smoking 3.53 (3 deaths, 85 person-years) and daily injecting 0.53 (0.10 to 1.58); France 0.69 (0.55 to 0.87; 80 deaths, 11,496 person-years); Italy 0.54 in men and 0.50 (0.22 to 0.91) in total (7 deaths, all men, 1289 person-years). SMRs: Brazil 7.60; France 4.36 (men) and 7.70 (women); Canada 4.74 (4.19 to 5.29); Italy 4.75 in men (2.26 to 9.96) (p. 92; Table 1). By HIV status: VIDUS 9.83 (7.59 to 12.54) vs 4.91 (3.98 to 5.99), p < .001; ALIVE 7.74 and 7.98 (HIV-positive, cocaine and heroin; cocaine only) vs 3.25 and 3.45 (HIV-negative) (p. 92). Editors' checks of Table 1 against its own deaths and person-years are listed under reporting issues.
analysis.covariates: None at review level.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The abstract says searches and extraction were undertaken using protocols; no registered or published protocol is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: The quality index (adapted from McGrath et al., 2004) is described only in Appendix D (not available); Table 1 prints scores from 1 to 15 without the scale's range, and the Italian cohort has no score. Key figures for the Canadian, US (ALIVE) and French cohorts rest on unpublished personal communications.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Several estimates rest on few deaths: 3 in each RAVEN group, 7 in Italy, 9 in the Netherlands.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Seven cohorts of people injecting cocaine, smoking crack, in treatment for cocaine dependence or arrested for cocaine offences reported crude mortality rates of about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years and, in four of them, SMRs of about 4.4 to 7.7 against the general population of the same age and sex. In the two cohorts of people who inject drugs the commonest causes of death were AIDS and overdose, followed by sepsis or endocarditis in ALIVE and by traumatic deaths in VIDUS; in the Brazilian crack cohort, gunshot wounds and AIDS.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the SMRs suggest mortality four to eight times higher among people who use cocaine than in age and sex peers (p. 88). The Discussion itself calls this an extremely crude summary (p. 93) and the limitations explain why it cannot be generalized to all people with cocaine dependence, still less to all who use cocaine (p. 93); the abstract's conclusion about uncertain generalizability is appropriately cautious. Remaining gaps: the abstract does not say that the SMR cohorts were injecting, treatment or arrestee samples with high HIV prevalence and heavy heroin use, so the 4-8 figure cannot be read as an effect of cocaine; the CMR range differs between abstract (0.53 to 6.16), table (from 0.50) and Discussion (0.48 to 6.16); and the Italian SMR is 4.75 in the Results and 4.6 in the Discussion.

timeline.event: Van Haastrecht et al.: Amsterdam cohort of people who use drugs (included; 4.6 deaths per 100 person-years among HIV-negative people mainly injecting cocaine).
Ribeiro et al.: São Paulo cohort of 131 people treated for crack dependence (included; SMR 7.6 at 5 years); OFDT French national cohort of people arrested for cocaine or crack (included).
Wang et al.: ALIVE cohort, Baltimore, on HIV infection and overdose mortality (included; cause-of-death data supplied by personal communication).
Pavarin: Bologna cohort of 347 people in treatment for cocaine dependence (included; SMR 4.75 in men).
Arendt et al.: Danish nationwide follow-up of people treated for cocaine and other drug use disorders; on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (title only).
This review: the first systematic review of prospective studies of mortality in problematic or dependent cocaine use, by the authors' account (p. 89).

Pavarin: follow-up of 178 people treated for crack problems; van Amsterdam et al.: systematic review of mortality in people who use both opioids and cocaine compared with opioids only; both on the project's cocaine list, not yet read (titles only).

replication.where_it_stands: The review documents how thin the cohort evidence on cocaine mortality was up to 2008: seven heterogeneous cohorts, four SMRs, several figures from personal communications. Its 4-8 SMR range should be cited only for the populations studied. Later cohorts and reviews on the project's list must be appraised before the encyclopedia states a current figure.

funding.funder: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of NSW, Australia; L. Degenhardt holds an Australian NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (p. 94, Role of funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: None (p. 94, Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Completed as part of work for the Global Burden of Disease Expert Group on Mental Disorders and Illicit Drug Use (p. 94, Acknowledgements). Co-author T. Kerr (British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS) supplied the VIDUS estimates by personal communication (p. 92; Table 1 note); co-authors S. Mehta and G. Kirk are at the Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, from where the ALIVE data were supplied by personal communication (pp. 92, 94). No procedure for appraising data from co-authors' own cohorts is described. Recorded as a flag, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Record-linkage cohorts of people whose main drug is cocaine, drawn from treatment services, arrest records, emergency departments and harm-reduction services and including people who snort cocaine, followed through national death registers, reporting person-years, SMRs by age, sex and route, and cause-specific mortality adjusted for injecting, HIV, opioid and alcohol use and socio-economic position; then a pooled analysis of such cohorts.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (problematic or dependent cocaine use), cohort design, comparator for excess mortality (general population via SMR) and outcomes (crude, excess and cause-specific mortality, mortality by HIV status) are stated (p. 89).
The abstract mentions protocols, but no registered or published protocol is cited and its content is not described.
The Introduction explains why prospective cohorts rather than poisoning registers or post-mortem series were chosen (p. 89).

Three databases, grey literature, reference lists, an expert group and contact with investigators, which would otherwise merit at least partial yes; but publications were limited to 1990-2008 and a wrong time period (before 1990) was an exclusion reason, without justification. Applied as written, as for other cards of this project (decision p-amstar2-item4 pending with the senior author).
Two researchers independently compiled shortlists, compared and resolved by consensus (p. 89, 2.1).
Two researchers extracted data and compared results, resolving differences by consensus (p. 89, 2.4).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusions are given as category counts in Fig. 1; only the two cohort studies excluded at the last step are named with reasons (Table 1b).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, years, sample type, N, person-years, deaths, CMR and SMR; age, sex, HIV prevalence, follow-up length and ascertainment of deaths are missing for most cohorts.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A quality index adapted from McGrath et al. (2004) was scored, but its criteria are only in Appendix D, which was not available; the main text gives a total score without range or domains, and none for the Italian cohort.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No pooling, explicitly justified by the few and heterogeneous cohorts (p. 90, 2.5).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations discuss selection of injecting and treatment samples, HIV, geography, social disadvantage and baseline-only exposure definitions as reasons the estimates may not generalize (pp. 93-94).
Differences in CMR are discussed in terms of general health, route, HIV, access to care and disadvantage, with the authors stating they cannot tell which factors contribute (p. 93).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a declaration of no conflicts are given; the involvement of co-authors in included cohorts is not flagged.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 9 can only be judged from Appendix D, which was not read, but the overall rating does not depend on it. Three critical items are not met (no registered protocol, an unexplained limit on publication years, no list of excluded studies), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; even with items 2 and 4 read leniently, item 7 alone would give low confidence. The rating concerns whether the review can be trusted to have found and fairly summarized every cohort; it does not mean its figures are wrong. The review is transparent about its limits and does not pool. Its numbers are second-hand: several come from personal communications, and Table 1 has internal inconsistencies (reporting issues). Cite for: the range of crude mortality rates and the four SMRs reported by cohorts of people who inject cocaine, smoke crack, are in treatment or were arrested (data 1985-2005), and their leading causes of death. Do not cite for: the mortality of people who use cocaine in general, or for an effect of cocaine itself.

key_findings.finding: Flowchart: 1911 database records plus 4 from reference lists; after excluding 1167 not about cocaine and 452 not about mortality associated with cocaine use, 296 remained; after further exclusions and 3 expert-group and 2 grey-literature additions, 64 papers were extracted and 9 papers on 7 cohort studies gave usable mortality data.
key_findings.note: The Results text gives different counts for the same steps (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Nine cohort studies since 1990 included people who use cocaine; seven gave mortality estimates (USA 2, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil, Italy). Two were excluded for insufficient data: a Dutch cohort of 160 with 61 lost to follow-up, and a UK treatment cohort of 1075 (247 with cocaine dependence) that did not report deaths among them.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 90); Table 1b (p. 91); 3.1 All-cause mortality, 9th paragraph (p. 92)

key_findings.finding: Crude mortality rates per 100 person-years: Canada (VIDUS, 717 people injecting cocaine only) 6.16 (5.21 to 7.11), 161 deaths in 2613.2 person-years; ALIVE cocaine only 4.69 (4.03 to 5.45), 175 deaths in 3727 person-years; ALIVE cocaine and heroin 4.37 (4.07 to 4.68), 787 deaths in 18,023 person-years; the Netherlands 4.6 (9 deaths, 194 person-years); Brazil 3.51 (23 deaths among 131); RAVEN daily crack smoking 3.53 (3 deaths, 85 person-years) and daily injecting 0.53 (0.10 to 1.58); France 0.69 (0.55 to 0.87), 80 deaths in 11,496 person-years; Italy 0.54 in men and 0.50 (0.22 to 0.91) overall, 7 deaths, all in men.
key_findings.note: Three rows do not agree with their own deaths and person-years (RAVEN daily injecting, Italy, Brazil); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: SMRs against the general population of the same age and sex were reported by four cohorts: Brazil 7.6 at 5-year follow-up; France 4.36 in men and 7.70 in women; Canada 4.74 (4.19 to 5.29); Italy 4.75 in men (2.26 to 9.96).

Mortality by HIV status: in VIDUS 9.83 per 100 person-years (7.59 to 12.54) among HIV-positive and 4.91 (3.98 to 5.99) among HIV-negative people injecting cocaine (p < .001); in ALIVE, where 25% were HIV-positive at baseline, 7.74 and 7.98 among HIV-positive people (cocaine and heroin; cocaine only) and 3.25 and 3.45 among HIV-negative people.

Causes of death: in the Brazilian crack treatment cohort, gunshot wounds 10 of 23 deaths (44%) and AIDS-related illness 6 (26%); in the Italian cohort's 309 men, cause-specific SMRs of 14.85 (4.79 to 46.04) for vascular diseases, 7.07 (1 to 50.16) for suicide and 9.95 (1.40 to 70.61) for overdose.

ALIVE causes of death (Table 2), in rank order: people injecting cocaine and heroin (787 deaths), AIDS 206 (26.2%), overdose 134 (17.0%), sepsis or endocarditis 81 (10.3%), traumatic deaths 60 (7.6%), cardiac 54 (6.9%), liver or gastrointestinal 50 (6.4%), cancer 47 (6.0%), chronic drug-related 46 (5.8%), pneumonia 24 (3.0%), suicide 3 (0.4%), other 82 (10.4%); people injecting cocaine only (175 deaths), AIDS 62 (35.4%), overdose 20 (11.4%), sepsis or endocarditis 15 (8.6%), cancer 13 (7.4%), traumatic 12 (6.9%), liver or gastrointestinal 10 (5.7%), chronic drug-related 9 (5.1%), pneumonia 8 (4.6%), cardiac 7 (4.0%), suicide 2 (1.1%), other 17 (9.7%).

VIDUS causes of death (Table 2): overdose 53, AIDS 30, traumatic deaths 23, suicide 7, cardiac 6 and sepsis or endocarditis 5 of 158 deaths; the text reports overdose 35%, HIV and AIDS 20% and traumatic deaths 15% as the commonest.
key_findings.note: The printed percentages use a denominator of 150 (with 158 they are 33.5%, 19.0% and 14.6%; editors' arithmetic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The authors summarize the SMRs, extremely crudely in their words, as deaths occurring four to eight times more often than in the general population of the same age and sex, and attribute differences in CMR to general health, route, HIV, access to care and possibly disadvantage, without being able to say which.

Limitations stated by the authors: most cohorts were people injecting cocaine daily or with crack dependence, mostly from socially disadvantaged settings; no study followed people who only snort cocaine; HIV was highly prevalent in several cohorts and the effect of antiretroviral treatment could not be examined; drug use was defined at baseline only.

No pooled estimates were made because of the few studies, the varied populations and the limited statistics reported; where only deaths and total years of follow-up were reported, CMRs were approximated by assuming deaths occurred halfway through follow-up.
key_findings.locator: 2.5 Reporting of mortality estimates, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The study flow cannot be reconciled: the text gives 1917 articles, 1160 excluded as not about cocaine, 71 studies remaining and 10 articles or reports on nine cohorts; Fig. 1 gives 1911 plus 4 records, 1167 excluded as not about cocaine, 64 papers extracted and 9 papers on 7 cohorts; and the text's own exclusions (1160, 452, 151, 32, 23, 17) leave 82, not 71 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of studies screened and excluded at each step is uncertain; this weakens the audit trail behind AMSTAR 2 items 4 and 7.

reporting_issues.issue: The range of crude mortality rates is given as 0.53 to 6.16 in the abstract and 0.48 to 6.16 in the Discussion, while the lowest value in Table 1 is 0.50 (Italy, total).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the range from Table 1 (about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years).

reporting_issues.issue: The Italian SMR in men is 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96) in Table 1 and the Results but 4.6 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The French cohort is 2212 people in Table 1 and 2122 in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transcription error; the CMR (80 deaths in 11,496 person-years) is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: VIDUS deaths are 161 in Table 1 and the text, 158 in Table 2 (whose counts sum to 158) and in Fig. 2, while Table 2's VIDUS percentages correspond to a denominator of 150 and sum to 105.3% (editors' arithmetic); Fig. 2 plots shares out of 158 (AIDS about 19%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The VIDUS cause-of-death percentages should be recalculated from the counts (overdose 33.5%, AIDS 19.0%, traumatic 14.6% of 158) before citation.

reporting_issues.issue: RAVEN daily injecting group: 3 deaths in 319 person-years gives 0.94 per 100 person-years (exact 95% CI 0.19 to 2.75; editors' calculation), not the printed 0.53 (0.10 to 1.58), which would fit about 566 person-years; a footnote says the same 3 deaths are counted in both RAVEN groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lowest CMR in the abstract (0.53) is itself in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: Italian row: 7 deaths in 1289 person-years gives 0.54 per 100 person-years, which the table prints as the men's rate, while the total is printed as 0.50; with all 7 deaths in men, the men's rate must exceed the total, so the 1289 person-years appear to be the men's only (editors' arithmetic). The men's CI (0.00 to 1.07) is also a symmetric approximation that reaches zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Italian person-years and rates cannot be taken from the table without checking the primary report.

reporting_issues.issue: Brazilian row: no person-years are given; the CMR of 3.51 equals 23 deaths over 655 person-years, that is 131 people times 5 years, counting full follow-up for those who died; the review's stated mid-point method would give about 3.85 and the 44.3-month average follow-up in the table about 4.8 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Brazilian CMR may be underestimated; the method used for it is not the one described.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the ALIVE cohort as HIV-seronegative people who inject drugs, but the text says 25% were HIV-positive at baseline and reports CMRs for HIV-positive participants, and AIDS is the leading cause of death in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table label is wrong; the ALIVE estimates include HIV-positive people.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Netherlands row, N = 632 is the whole cohort, while the 9 deaths and 194 person-years refer to the HIV-negative subsample mainly injecting cocaine, whose size is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people behind the Dutch CMR is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The text refers to Table 4 for the ALIVE causes of death; the paper has two tables (Table 2 is meant). The Italian cohort is described as non-injecting people dependent on crack (p. 90) and elsewhere as mostly intranasal (pp. 92-93). Table 1 has no caption, and the method for the 95% CIs of cause-of-death shares in Table 2 is not given (they are wider than binomial intervals: 62 of 175 gives about 28% to 43%, printed 24.4% to 46.4%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor reporting errors that make the tables harder to audit.
