design_detail: Secondary analysis (the authors' 'substudy') of the Acute Cardiac Ischemia–Time-Insensitive Predictive Instrument (ACI-TIPI) Clinical Trial, a prospective multicentre trial of a computerized decision aid run in 1993 in the emergency departments (EDs) of 10 US hospitals (public and private, community and tertiary, urban to semirural). Of 10,689 trial patients evaluated for possible acute cardiac ischaemia (ACI), the 293 with cocaine-associated presentations (reported recent cocaine use or a positive toxicology screen) are described and compared, without adjustment, with all other trial patients (n=10,396) and with those younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use (n=2,165). Outcome: confirmed ACI (acute myocardial infarction, AMI, by WHO criteria; unstable angina by the trial's classification), assigned with data up to 30 days. Appraised with the JBI checklist as a prevalence analysis.
can_establish: That among 293 ED patients with cocaine-associated presentations evaluated for possible ACI at 10 US hospitals in 1993, confirmed ACI was recorded in 6 (2.0%; exact 95% CI 0.76–4.4%) and AMI in 2 (0.7%; 0.08–2.4%), both with a diagnostic ECG at presentation, with none among the 37 whose chief complaint was not chest pain; and that these proportions were lower than among the other trial patients.
cannot_establish: The true frequency of ischaemia in such patients, because serial cardiac markers were missing for most of the 166 discharged from the ED and cocaine use was identified only when clinicians asked or tested; or that cocaine use goes with a lower risk of ACI (unadjusted comparisons with older patients enrolled under different age rules, in a comparison group that includes patients whose cocaine use was unknown).

sample.recruitment: All consenting ED patients enrolled in the 1993 ACI-TIPI Clinical Trial at 10 hospitals: Baystate Medical Center (Springfield, MA); Boston City Hospital, Boston University Medical Center and New England Medical Center (Boston, MA); Medical College of Virginia (Richmond); Medical College of Wisconsin (Milwaukee); Newton-Wellesley Hospital (Newton, MA); Rhode Island Hospital (Providence); University of Cincinnati Medical Center; University of North Carolina Hospitals (Chapel Hill) (p. 470).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Trial entry (p. 470): consenting ED patients aged 30 or older, or 18 or older if suspected or reported to have recently used cocaine, with a chief complaint of chest, left arm, jaw or epigastric pain or discomfort, shortness of breath, dizziness, palpitations or other symptoms suggestive of ACI. Cocaine-associated = reported cocaine use or a positive toxicology screen for cocaine metabolites; all such patients are included. No time window for recent use is given.
sample.demographics: Cocaine group (Table 1, p. 471): mean age 33.5 years (SD 7.5); 25% women; black 77%, white 19%, Hispanic 3% (n=291); any chest pain 94%, chest pain as chief complaint 87% (p. 472); shortness of breath 65% (n=280); diabetes 3% and previous MI 7% (n=267); history of angina 12% (n=268); current smokers 87%, former 2%, never 11% (n=266).
sample.attrition: Follow-up data needed to assign a confirmed diagnosis were obtained for 94% of the cocaine group and 99% of all trial patients (p. 471). Of the 166 patients discharged from the ED, 38 (23%) returned for the scheduled 24-hour re-evaluation; the others were telephoned, or hospital records, computerized logs and death records were checked (pp. 471, 473). 30-day mortality is reported for 245 of 293 (84%) (Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: Cocaine use was identified at clinicians' discretion: uniform screening was not required at any centre, so some patients who had used cocaine, possibly including some with ACI, fell into the comparison group (p. 474). The share of trial patients with cocaine-associated presentations ranged from 0.3% to 8.3% by hospital (p. 472). Consent was required and refusals are not reported. The trial's decision-aid arms are not described for this substudy.

exposure.measurement: Patient report of recent cocaine use or a positive toxicology screen for cocaine metabolites (p. 470); screening was ordered at clinicians' discretion (p. 474). How many were identified by report and how many by toxicology is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported (no time since use, route or amount).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported apart from smoking (87% current smokers, n=266).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (assessed at presentation; time since last use not recorded).

comparison.controls: (1) All other trial patients (n=10,396), classified as not using cocaine, a group that includes patients whose use was unknown (p. 472); (2) the subset younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use (n=2,165), chosen because the different age rules for entry (18 or older with suspected cocaine use, 30 or older otherwise) preclude an age-matched comparison (p. 473); under those rules this subset was mostly aged 30–44 (editors' inference), but patients aged 18–29 enrolled because recent cocaine use was suspected, who neither reported use nor tested positive, would also be counted in it (p. 470); Table 2 gives a mean of 37.5 years (SD 4.4).
comparison.matching: None, and no adjustment. The comparison groups differ in age (59.3 and 37.5 vs 33.5 years), sex (49% and 45% vs 25% women), ethnicity and smoking (Tables 1–2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary anatomy and earlier cardiac testing unknown; histories self-reported; time since cocaine use not recorded.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not recorded; the comparison groups include patients whose cocaine use was not asked about or tested.

outcomes.instruments: Data at ED presentation, during hospitalization and at 30-day follow-up: ECGs; serial total CK and CK-MB in admitted patients by institutional guidelines; follow-up diagnostic studies (echocardiography, nuclear imaging, catheterization, stress testing) from records; discharged patients asked to return for a 24-hour re-evaluation with ECG and CK, and telephone contact, hospital records, computerized logs and local and national death records for those who did not (pp. 470–471). AMI by WHO criteria, at least 2 of: ischaemic-type chest discomfort, changes on serial ECGs, rise and fall of serum cardiac markers. Unstable angina by the trial classification: Canadian Cardiovascular Society class 4, or class 3 with symptoms new or changed within 3 days, supported by confirmatory testing, reversible ECG changes, ACI events during follow-up or anti-anginal treatment started by clinicians (p. 471).
outcomes.validity_norms: WHO criteria were standard for the period; the authors note that CK and CK-MB can be raised in people using cocaine without MI and that WHO criteria may miss minimally raised values (p. 474). Who assigned the diagnoses, and whether they knew cocaine status, is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Confirmed ACI' = AMI or unstable angina as defined above. A rise and fall of markers could be shown only with serial samples, which were available for 109 of 127 admitted but 37 of 166 discharged patients (p. 473).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 13 comparisons in each of Tables 1 and 2 (chi-square or unpaired t-tests, two-sided, p<.05; p. 472).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cocaine group (p. 469; Table 1): confirmed ACI 6/293, 2.0% (95% CI 0.76–4.4%); unstable angina 4, 1.4% (0.37–3.5%); AMI 2, 0.7% (0.08–2.4%); coronary care admission 14%; 30-day mortality 0 of 245. Versus all other trial patients (Table 1): AMI 0.7% vs 8.6% (difference 7.9 percentage points, 95% CI 6.8 to 9.0), unstable angina 1.4% vs 9.3% (7.9, 6.5 to 9.4), admission 14% vs 18% (P=.14), 30-day mortality 0% vs 2.6% (P=.011). Versus trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use (Table 2): AMI 0.7% vs 2.8% (2.1, 0.9 to 3.3; P=.033), unstable angina 1.4% vs 2.4% (P=.27), intensive care admission 14% vs 8% (P=.0018), 30-day mortality 0% vs 0.6% (P=.24). All unadjusted. The abstract's intervals for the cocaine group match exact binomial intervals (editors' check).
analysis.covariates: None; the authors attribute the demographic differences to the age rules for entry and to hospital populations without analysing them (p. 473).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol for the substudy is mentioned; the authors call it hypothesis-generating (p. 475).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: how cocaine use was established (report or toxicology), time since use, the trial arm of the cocaine-group patients, the distribution of presenting ECG findings, and results for the cocaine group by hospital.
analysis.power: Not reported; with 2 AMIs, the comparison with the under-45 group rests on very few events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this ED trial population, 6 of 293 patients with cocaine-associated presentations had confirmed ACI (2.0%) and 2 an AMI (0.7%), both with a diagnostic ECG on arrival; none of the 37 with chief complaints other than chest pain had ACI. Twenty had a raised CK-MB on arrival, of whom 2 met WHO criteria for MI; 8 of these 20 were discharged from the ED and 2 of the 8 had a follow-up CK-MB. In unadjusted comparisons the proportions were lower than in the other, older trial patients and in trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or related symptoms infrequently had ACI, and AMI even less often, and that this suggests selectivity in hospitalization (pp. 469–470). The discussion adds that patients without ECG evidence of ischaemia are at very low risk and at significantly lower risk than all ED patients evaluated for ACI (p. 475), but no analysis by presenting ECG is reported beyond the two MIs, and the comparison with all ED patients is unadjusted and confounded by age, sex and the trial's entry rules. Because serial markers were missing for most discharged patients and WHO criteria require a rise and fall, the 0.7% is a lower bound for MI under these criteria, which the authors partly acknowledge (pp. 474–475). The suggestion that symptom resolution after a benzodiazepine given in the ED and a repeat ECG without ischaemia may support discharge (p. 475) is not tested in these data; the authors label it provisional. The description of the 10,689 trial patients as essentially all patients presenting with such symptoms (p. 473) is not backed by a count of eligible patients who were not enrolled.

timeline.event: Prospective COCHPA series of chest pain after cocaine use: MI by CK-MB criteria in 14 of 246 (5.7%), one of the two prospective series from which this study's AMI proportion differs about sevenfold (pp. 470, 473)
Kontos et al.: 6 AMIs among 241 ED evaluations of cocaine-associated chest pain, 4 with diagnostic ST elevation on the ED ECG, as described in this paper (p. 473; not read in this round)
Single-centre observation-unit cohort citing this study among evidence that serious cardiovascular complications are infrequent in lower-risk patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (p. 516)

replication.where_it_stands: The low AMI proportion in this broad ED sample assessed with WHO criteria (0.7%) and the higher one in a chest-pain series assessed with CK-MB (about 6% in COCHPA) reflect differences in who was included and how MI was defined and ascertained; neither of these two used troponin, and the one later study in the timeline that measured troponin I (Weber et al., 2003) did so in lower-risk patients kept for observation and did not report how many of them had an MI at presentation, so the proportion under current definitions is not settled.

funding.funder: Supported by Agency for Healthcare, Research and Quality grant No. R01 HS07360 and US Public Health Service General Clinical Research Center MO.LRR00533 (as printed, p. 469).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Boston Medical Center (Boston University), the Center for Cardiovascular Health Services Research at New England Medical Center (Tufts) and Rhode Island Hospital (Brown) (p. 469). Selker, Beshansky and Griffith are authors of the ACI-TIPI trial report (ref. 14), Selker is first author of the instrument's development papers (refs. 15, 16), and the discussion recommends evaluating the computerized ACI-TIPI in this population (p. 475); Feldman and Fish were also COCHPA investigators (Hollander et al., 1994, p. 339). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of consecutive ED patients evaluated for possible ACI, with uniform toxicology screening, serial troponin measurement in every patient including those discharged, blinded adjudication of MI and unstable angina by current definitions, and an age- and sex-adjusted comparison with patients without cocaine use, would give the proportion with ischaemia and show whether it differs.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: ED patients evaluated for possible ACI at 10 varied US hospitals (public and private, community and tertiary, urban to semirural): an appropriate frame for cocaine-associated presentations evaluated for ischaemia.

All consenting trial patients were included, but cocaine-associated presentations were identified only when clinicians asked or tested (no uniform screening, p. 474), and refusals of consent are not reported.
293 patients give the ACI proportion with an exact interval of 0.76–4.4%; the AMI estimate rests on 2 events.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Hospitals and patient characteristics are described (Table 1), but not time since cocaine use, how use was established, or the trial arm.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Confirmed-diagnosis data for 94%, but 30-day mortality for 84% (245 of 293) and serial markers for only 37 of 166 discharged patients.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: WHO criteria and the trial's unstable-angina classification are standard, but a rise and fall of markers cannot be shown without serial samples, and 18 of 20 patients with a raised CK-MB on arrival did not meet the WHO criteria.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Admitted patients had serial CK and CK-MB by institutional guidelines; discharged patients usually one sample and a requested return visit (23% returned); the adjudication procedure is not described.

Exact intervals for the cocaine-group proportions (abstract), but unadjusted chi-square comparisons between groups that differ in age by design, and values that differ between abstract, text and tables.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Consent was required for trial entry and refusals are not reported; follow-up for confirmed diagnoses reached 94%.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for prevalence analyses. The frame is broad and the outcome criteria standard, but cocaine-associated presentations were identified at clinicians' discretion and the WHO marker criterion could rarely be met in the 57% discharged from the ED without serial markers, so the 2.0% ACI and 0.7% AMI are best read as lower bounds under these criteria. The editors summarise the risk of bias of the proportions as moderate; the comparisons with other patients are unadjusted and confounded by the entry rules and are not appraised as effects of cocaine. It may be cited for: confirmed ACI in 6 of 293 (2.0%, exact 0.76–4.4%) and AMI in 2 (0.7%, exact 0.08–2.4%) among ED patients with cocaine-associated presentations evaluated for ischaemia in 1993, both MIs with diagnostic presenting ECGs; no ACI among the 37 with non-chest-pain complaints; and the variation by hospital (0.3–8.3% of trial patients). It should not be cited as showing that cocaine use is associated with a lower risk of ACI.

key_findings.finding: Of 10,689 ED patients enrolled in the ACI-TIPI trial at 10 hospitals, 293 (2.7%) reported recent cocaine use or had a positive toxicology screen for cocaine metabolites; the share ranged from 0.3% to 8.3% by hospital.
key_findings.note: The abstract gives the upper end of the range as 8.4% (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine group: mean age 33.5 years (SD 7.5), 75% men, 77% black; current smokers 87% (n=266); history of MI 7% (n=267); chest pain present in 94% and the chief complaint in 87%.
Confirmed ACI in 6 of 293 (2.0%; 95% CI 0.76–4.4%): unstable angina 4 (1.4%; 0.37–3.5%) and AMI 2 (0.7%; 0.08–2.4%). Both patients with AMI had clear ECG evidence of MI on the presenting ECG.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 469); Results, 7th paragraph, and Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 473)
key_findings.note: The Results give the AMI interval as 0 to 1.6% (see reporting issues); the abstract's intervals match exact binomial intervals (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: None of the 37 patients whose chief complaint was dizziness, dyspnoea, syncope or another symptom other than chest pain had confirmed ACI.

Of the 166 patients discharged from the ED, 38 (23%) returned for the scheduled 24-hour re-evaluation; of the 127 hospitalized, 42 (33%) were admitted to the coronary care unit, 14% of the cocaine group vs 18% of the other trial patients (P=.14).

Cardiac enzyme levels were available for 244 patients (printed as 85%) and two or more tests for 145 (50%): serial CK results for 109 of 127 admitted (86%) and more than one CK result for 37 of 166 discharged (22%).

Twenty patients (7%) had a raised CK-MB on ED arrival, of whom 2 (10%) had AMI; 12 of the 20 had follow-up CK-MB results (10 of 12 admitted, 2 of 8 discharged); there were no deaths or cardiovascular readmissions within 30 days among the 15 of these 20 with outcome data.

Versus all 10,396 other trial patients (classified as not using cocaine, including unknown use): AMI 0.7% vs 8.6% (difference 7.9 percentage points, 95% CI 6.8–9.0), unstable angina 1.4% vs 9.3% (7.9, 6.5–9.4), 30-day mortality 0% (n=245) vs 2.6% (n=9,873; P=.011); the other patients were older (mean 59.3 vs 33.5 years) and more often women (49% vs 25%).

Versus 2,165 trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use: AMI 0.7% vs 2.8% (difference 2.1 percentage points, 95% CI 0.9–3.3; P=.033), unstable angina 1.4% vs 2.4% (P=.27), intensive care admission 14% vs 8% (P=.0018), 30-day mortality 0% (n=245) vs 0.6% (n=1,925; P=.24); mean age 37.5 vs 33.5 years.

Entry ages differed: 30 or older for most patients, 18 or older if recent cocaine use was suspected or reported; the authors attribute the age and ethnicity differences to these rules and to hospital populations.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph (p. 470); Results, 3rd paragraph (starting p. 472)

key_findings.finding: Uniform screening for cocaine use was not required at any centre; clinicians decided whom to screen, so some patients who had used cocaine, possibly including some with ACI, may have been classified with the comparison groups.

AMI required at least 2 of 3 WHO criteria (ischaemic chest discomfort, serial ECG changes, rise and fall of cardiac markers); the authors found an important number of patients using cocaine with CK and CK-MB elevations who did not meet them, and note that CK and CK-MB can rise in people using cocaine without MI.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 6th paragraph (p. 471); Discussion, 5th and 7th paragraphs (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Follow-up data needed to assign a confirmed diagnosis were obtained for 94% of the cocaine group (99% of all trial patients); the authors acknowledge that nonfatal MIs may have been missed in patients not rehospitalized within 30 days who did not complete follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 5th paragraph (starting p. 470); Discussion, 12th paragraph (starting p. 474)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that few ED patients with cocaine-associated symptoms had confirmed ACI and that patients without ECG evidence of ischaemia are at very low risk; they suggest, provisionally because the substudy is hypothesis-generating, that symptom resolution after a benzodiazepine given in the ED and a repeat ECG without ischaemia may support discharge with referral for addiction counselling.

reporting_issues.issue: The range of cocaine-associated presentations across hospitals is 0.3% to 8.4% in the abstract (p. 469) but 0.3% to 8.3% in the Results (p. 472) and the Discussion (pp. 473, 474).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 8.3% appears three times in the body of the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CI for AMI (2 of 293, 0.7%) is 0.08% to 2.4% in the abstract (p. 469), consistent with the exact method named in the Methods (p. 472), but 0 to 1.6% in the Results (p. 473), which matches a truncated normal approximation (exact interval 0.08–2.44%, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's exact interval should be used; the Results interval understates the upper limit.

reporting_issues.issue: AMI among trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use is 2.8% in Table 2 and the abstract but 2.4% in the Results text (p. 473), which is that group's unstable-angina figure in Table 2; the printed P=.033 fits 2.8% (chi-square p of about 0.03 with 61 of 2,165, against about 0.06 with 52 of 2,165, editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text value is a slip; 2.8% should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 14% of the cocaine group (42 of 293) is called coronary care unit admission in the abstract and Results (pp. 469, 473) and intensive care unit admission in Tables 1–2, in the abstract's comparison with patients under 45 and in the Results (pp. 469, 471–473).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the comparison groups' 18% and 8% refer to coronary care or to any intensive care.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiac enzyme levels are said to be available for 244 (85%) patients (p. 473), but 244 of 293 is 83%; two or more tests are given for 145 patients, while the admitted (109) and discharged (37) patients with serial results sum to 146 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; marker coverage was about 83%, not 85%.

reporting_issues.issue: 30-day mortality in the cocaine group is reported for 245 of 293 patients (Table 1, p. 471), whereas follow-up 'required to assign a confirmed diagnosis' is reported for 94% (pp. 471, 474).
reporting_issues.consequence: Vital status at 30 days is missing for 48 patients (16%); the 0% mortality rests on 245, and the 94% does not describe mortality follow-up.

reporting_issues.issue: In Tables 1–2 the difference column, headed as cocaine group versus comparison group, gives the comparison group minus the cocaine group (for example AMI 7.9 = 8.6 − 0.7; women 24 = 49 − 25; current smoking −56 = 31 − 87).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read in the heading's direction the signs are reversed; the differences should be restated with their direction when cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The account of Tokarski et al.'s series is internally inconsistent: its AMI incidence is given as 4.7% (p. 470) and as 4.8%, 2 of 42 (p. 474), and 18 patients (19%) are said to have had abnormal CK and CK-MB (p. 474), although 18 of 42 is 43%; Hollander et al. (1994, p. 331) give 8 of 42 (19%) with raised isoenzymes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand figures for the Tokarski series should not be taken from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the AMI difference against patients younger than 45 (2.1 percentage points) has a 95% CI of 0.9 to 3.3, which matches a Wald interval (implied z about 3.5, P about .0005), whereas the printed P=.033 matches an uncorrected chi-square test (about .03); the interval rests on 2 events in the cocaine group (editors' calculation with 60 or 61 of 2,165; a continuity-corrected test gives about .05).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval overstates the precision of the difference and does not agree with its own P value; the comparison rests on 2 infarctions, is unadjusted, and is of borderline significance.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Ann Emerg Med 36(5), pp. 469–476 (all 8 pages, digital text layer, including the funding note and acknowledgements); Tables 1 and 2 checked on 150-dpi renderings; no supplement.
verification.checked_by: AI reader 442 (round-2 check) and AI reader 452 (card adjudication)

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 442 (round-2 check): missed: the Table 2 AMI difference interval of 0.9 to 3.3 is a Wald interval (z about 3.6, P about .0004), which does not fit the printed P=.033 (uncorrected chi-square .030); with 2 events in the cocaine group the interval overstates precision. Worth a reporting issue.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading Table 2 (p. 472; AMI 0.7% of 293 vs 2.8% of 2,165, difference 2.1, 0.9 to 3.3, P=.033) and the Methods (p. 472: chi-square, two-sided): editors' recalculation gives Wald 0.92–3.26 with P about .0005 (60 events) and chi-square P 0.032 (Yates 0.052). Added as a reporting issue.

disagreements.first_pass: The low AMI proportion in this broad ED sample assessed with WHO criteria (0.7%) and the higher one in a chest-pain series assessed with CK-MB (about 6% in COCHPA) reflect differences in who was included and how MI was defined and ascertained; none of these studies used troponin, so the proportion under current definitions is not settled.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 442 (round-2 check): missed: where_it_stands says none of these studies used troponin, but Weber et al. (2003), in the timeline, measured troponin I (pp. 510–511).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading Weber et al. (2003), p. 510 (Abstract › Methods) and p. 512 (troponin I at 0, 3, 6 and 9 hours), and Kontos et al. (1999), which used CK and CK-MB mass (troponin only in its references): sentence now limits 'no troponin' to this study and COCHPA and says what the troponin study did and did not report.

disagreements.first_pass: under those rules this subset was aged 30–44 (editors' inference).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 442 (round-2 check): missed: the inference that the under-45 comparison group was aged 30–44 is not certain; patients aged 18–29 enrolled on suspected cocaine use without a report or positive screen would have been classed as not using cocaine (Table 2: mean 37.5, SD 4.4).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 470 (Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph: entry at 18 or older if cocaine use was suspected or reported; cocaine-associated only if reported or toxicology-positive) and Table 2 (p. 472): 'aged 30–44' softened to 'mostly', with the reason.

design_detail: Critical review with a stated search (PubMed, Google Scholar, Embase; studies published 1999–2016) of human studies comparing people with a history of cocaine use with non-drug-using controls on cognitive tests, either alone (Table 1, 22 studies) or with brain imaging (Table 2, 25 studies: 6 MRI, 14 fMRI, 3 PET, 2 EEG, editors' count of rows), each tabulated with the reviewers' caveats (normative comparison, matching on age and education, control of other drug use, number of measures, sample size). No quantitative synthesis; a short section on animal studies. Read from the accepted manuscript, not the version of record.
can_establish: Which methodological safeguards (comparison with norms, demographic matching, control of other drug use, more than one measure per domain, verified abstinence) were missing from the tabulated studies as the reviewers judged them, and that many imaging studies reported brain differences without a group difference on the cognitive task they used.
cannot_establish: Whether long-term cocaine use does or does not cause cognitive deficits (nothing is pooled, every tabulated human study is cross-sectional, and by the reviewers' own account most are confounded and unnormed); what proportion of measures showed differences (never counted); or that the tabulated studies are the relevant literature (no record of selection, no list of exclusions, and many studies tabulated by Spronk et al., 2013, are absent).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Search of PubMed, Google Scholar and Embase with terms combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive functioning, cognitive deficits and cognitive impairment, limited to human laboratory studies; search dates, numbers retrieved and screened, the selection procedure and reasons for exclusion are not reported (§2 Methods, PDF p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies of long-term effects published 1999–2016 comparing people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug-using controls, using neuropsychological tests, MRI, fMRI, PET or EEG; abstinence defined as at least 72 hours without cocaine; groups of 18 or fewer flagged as small (§2 Methods, PDF p. 5). The tables nonetheless include a study without a control group, a study comparing treatment completers with non-completers, and several studies testing people within 72 hours of use or with cocaine-positive urine (see reporting issues).
sample.demographics: Not summarized. Tables 1–2 give group sizes and diagnoses (DSM-III or DSM-IV dependence or abuse, or recreational use), with age and education differences mentioned only in the caveats.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is undocumented. Editors' cross-check: about 30 long-term studies tabulated by Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3), all within this review's date range, do not appear in Tables 1–2, including van der Plas et al. (2009), which this review's own introduction cites as replicating a WCST impairment; whether they were excluded or missed cannot be told. The tabulated samples are mostly people with cocaine dependence recruited for research or treatment, with some recreational samples (Colzato, Hulka, Preller, Reske, Sellaro, Soar, Vonmoos).

exposure.measurement: Varies across tabulated studies: DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis or self-described recreational use; urine toxicology in some, self-report only in others (flagged, for example, for Cunha, Oliveira, Sellaro, Soar, Morein-Zamir and the social-gaze fMRI study of Preller); hair toxicology in Vonmoos et al. (2013) (Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 26–39).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted by the review: the tables have no columns for amount, frequency, duration or route of use.
exposure.polysubstance: Flagged study by study in the caveats and counted in the text (other drug use not controlled in 8 of 22 neuropsychological studies, 8 of 14 fMRI studies and 5 of 6 MRI studies; PDF pp. 8, 10–11); not analysed. The reviewers note that one MRI sample included people dependent on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and heroin (Ersche et al., 2011; PDF p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Defined as at least 72 hours, but Tables 1–2 include studies with shorter or unknown abstinence or cocaine-positive urine at testing or screening (editors' count: at least 8 of 22 neuropsychological and 7 of 25 imaging studies; unknown for 6 more).

comparison.controls: Non-drug-using controls in most tabulated studies; some controls used alcohol, cannabis or MDMA (Sellaro et al., 2013; drug use in the control group of the Preller social-gaze fMRI study); further comparison groups with pathological gambling (Albein-Urios et al., 2012), alcohol dependence (Goldstein et al., 2004) and methamphetamine use (Simon et al.); one fMRI study had no control group (Goldstein et al., 2007) and one study compared treatment completers with non-completers only (Streeter et al., 2008).
comparison.matching: Per the reviewers: 5 of 22 neuropsychological studies not matched on age and 6 not matched on education; in several imaging studies groups with cocaine use disorder around 40 years old were compared with controls around 30 (PDF pp. 8, 14). The reviewers also report statistical adjustment in some primary studies: education in Fernández-Serrano et al. (PDF p. 8), age as a covariate in the MRI study of Franklin et al. (PDF p. 9), and age and education in the Goldstein et al. (2004) PET analysis relating brain metabolism to test scores (PDF p. 13).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No tabulated human study measured cognition before cocaine use; the reviewers propose demographically adjusted norms as the reference instead (§5 Discussion, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Sometimes present and flagged in the caveats; not systematically reported.

outcomes.instruments: Wide range across studies: Stroop, Go/No-Go, stop-signal task, WCST, Iowa Gambling Task, delay discounting, CVLT, RAVLT, n-back, digit span, CANTAB tests, Trail Making, DSST, social-cognition tasks; structural MRI (voxel-based morphometry), task fMRI, FDG-PET and EEG event-related potentials (Tables 1–2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review's central argument: individual performance should be judged against demographically adjusted norms (for example T scores below 40, or cut-offs of 1, 1.5 or 2 SD below the normative mean), not only against a control group (PDF pp. 3, 15).
outcomes.operationalization: For the reviewers, impairment requires performance below demographically adjusted norms, ideally on more than one measure per domain, with age, education, sex and other drug use matched or controlled; a statistically significant group difference is not by itself impairment (PDF pp. 8, 14–15).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis); the review does not count measures across studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review; not extracted for the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed or pooled. The review reports tallies of study features: of 22 neuropsychological studies, 3 with more than one measure per domain, 5 not age-matched, 6 not education-matched, 8 not controlling for other drug use, 13 without normative interpretation (PDF p. 8); of 14 fMRI studies, 8 with a single measure, 8 not controlling for other drug use, 11 without a cognitive group difference (PDF pp. 11–12); of 6 MRI studies, 3 drawing behavioural conclusions without cognitive testing, 2 not controlling for age, 5 not controlling for other drug use (PDF p. 10); of 3 PET studies, 2 not age-matched and 2 without a cognitive group difference (PDF p. 13). Editors' count from Table 1: 19 of the 21 studies with a non-drug-using control group list poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No record of selection or exclusions; several of the text's tallies disagree with the entries of Table 1; the abstract's statement that differences were found on a minority of measures rests on no count reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.power: The reviewers flag groups of 18 or fewer as small, from a power calculation for d = 0.74 giving 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 for 90% (PDF p. 5). Editors' calculation (two-sided two-sample t-test, α = .05, noncentral t): d = 0.74 needs 30 per group for 80% power and 40 for 90%; 18 per group gives about 58% power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 47 tabulated studies, most neuropsychological studies list poorer performance of a cocaine group than controls in at least one domain (editors' count 19 of 21 with controls), and the reviewers themselves say differences are most consistent in executive function and working or verbal memory; most imaging studies report brain differences, while 11 of 14 fMRI and 2 of 3 PET studies found no group difference on their, often single, cognitive task. Most studies lacked normative comparison, demographic matching or control of other drug use; in the two studies whose caveats mention norms, performance was within the normative range, and the one PET study using age-adjusted scores found mild impairment (less than 1 SD below the control mean).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and highlights state that “differences in cognitive performance were observed on a minority of measures” (PDF pp. 2–3), a proportion the paper never counts, and conclude that the evidence does not support broad deficits and that the view that people who use cocaine have broad deficits is inaccurate and may harm treatment and policy (PDF pp. 3, 16). The tabulated studies can show that impairment has not been demonstrated to the reviewers' standard, but not that deficits are absent: the same confounding and lack of norms that undermine claims of impairment also undermine a claim of no impairment, and the highlights concede that the strongest evidence of harm concerns executive functions (PDF p. 2). The animal section, declared outside the review's scope, ends with a firm statement that preclinical research does not support neurotoxicity or permanent prefrontal change (PDF p. 7).

timeline.event: Quantitative review of studies from 1987–2002 (Jovanovski et al.), cited by this review as covering the earlier period
Review with meta-analyses of 2003–2013 studies (Spronk et al.) concluding that long-term use goes with a general cognitive impairment; this review quotes that conclusion and disputes it

Systematic quantitative review of the effect of abstinence duration on cognition (Potvin et al., 2014), cited in this review's introduction as reference 35 (PDF p. 4); read for the round of 12 November 2026: 46 studies to the end of 2012, grouped by abstinence
This review: 22 neuropsychological and 25 imaging studies tabulated with caveats; no pooling
Systematic review and meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition (López-Martín et al.; appraised separately)

replication.where_it_stands: Spronk et al. (2013) and this review read largely overlapping cross-sectional evidence in opposite directions: the first pools group differences and calls them general impairment, the second stresses missing norms, matching and control of other drugs and calls the impairment view inaccurate. Both readings go beyond the data. Poorer average performance of people with cocaine dependence than controls in executive function and memory is consistently reported; its cause, its persistence with abstinence and its clinical meaning remain unsettled.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the accepted manuscript).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no financial interests and no conflicts of interest (Declarations of interest, PDF p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Columbia University (Frazer, Richards) and Department of Psychiatry, University of Vermont Medical Center (Keith). None of the tabulated studies is by the review's authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review with a documented search and selection, study-level risk-of-bias assessment and a quantitative synthesis that scores each study against demographically adjusted norms (the proportion of each group below a stated cut-off, as well as group differences), with moderator analyses by verified abstinence, alcohol and other drug use, education and recreational versus dependent use; and prospective cohorts that test cognition before regular cocaine use and repeatedly during biologically verified abstinence.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence, abstinent at least 72 hours), exposure, comparator (non-drug-using controls) and outcomes (cognition and neuroimaging) are stated (PDF p. 5).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.

The reviewers explain that ethical limits on giving cocaine to people without prior use leave comparisons of abstinent people with controls as the available design (Introduction, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 4).

Three sources with search terms, and a date range justified by earlier reviews (PDF p. 5); but no search date, no full strategy, Google Scholar as a main source, no reference-list or grey-literature searching and no language statement. About 30 studies tabulated by Spronk et al. (2013) within the date range are absent, which suggests the search or selection was incomplete.
Not reported.
Not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies and no flow of records.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1–2 give domains and tests, group sizes and diagnoses, abstinence, direction of findings and caveats (PDF pp. 26–39), but no amounts or frequency of use, ages, education values or recruitment settings.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The caveats column addresses confounding (age, education, other drug use, psychiatric comorbidity) for most studies and some selection and exposure-measurement problems, but without a stated tool or criteria, unevenly, and with text tallies that disagree with the table. A close call between partial yes and no; the overall rating does not depend on it.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No quantitative synthesis.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No quantitative synthesis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The interpretation is built around the studies' confounding, lack of norms and single measures (PDF pp. 8, 10–15), although this is used to dismiss impairment rather than to grade it.
Conflicting results between studies are discussed and attributed to differences in age, education, other drug use, single measures and inpatient housing (for example PDF pp. 11–14).
No quantitative synthesis; the reviewers note in passing that selecting only significant comparisons overstates estimates (PDF p. 14).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no financial interests or conflicts (PDF p. 16); funding of the review is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (no protocol; no list of excluded studies) and two are met only in part (search; informal risk-of-bias appraisal without a tool), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; the meta-analysis items do not apply. The review's value lies in its study-by-study caveats and its argument that group differences need normative benchmarks and control of confounding; it may be cited for that argument and, with each point checked in the primary paper, for specific methodological weaknesses and for imaging studies that found brain differences without cognitive differences. It may not be cited as evidence that cocaine use leaves cognition unimpaired: its own Table 1 lists poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain in most studies, its tallies disagree with its tables, its selection is undocumented and visibly incomplete, and its tables include studies that breach its own abstinence and control-group criteria.

key_findings.finding: Search and inclusion: PubMed, Google Scholar and Embase searched with terms combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive functioning, cognitive deficits and cognitive impairment, limited to human laboratory studies; studies of long-term effects published 1999–2016 comparing people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug-using controls; abstinence defined as at least 72 hours without cocaine. No search dates, screening numbers, selection procedure or list of exclusions are given.

Groups of 18 or fewer were flagged as small, from an a priori power calculation for an effect of d = 0.74 (a global cognitive index from an earlier study): 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 per group for 90% at a significance level of .05.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (two-sided two-sample t-test, α = .05): d = 0.74 needs 30 per group for 80% power and 40 for 90%; 18 per group gives about 58% power.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 tabulates 22 studies using neuropsychological tests only; Table 2 tabulates imaging studies, which the text counts as six MRI, fourteen fMRI and three PET studies (two EEG studies are also listed); each row gives domains and tests, participants, abstinence, findings and the reviewers' caveats.
key_findings.locator: §4.1, 4th paragraph; §4.2, last paragraph; §4.4, 3rd paragraph; §4.5, 4th paragraph; Tables 1–2

key_findings.finding: Reviewers' tallies for the 22 neuropsychological studies: 3 used more than one measure per domain, 5 did not match groups on age, 6 did not match on education, 8 did not control for other drug use and 13 did not interpret results against norms.
key_findings.note: Only the age tally matches the caveat entries of Table 1; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Reviewers' tallies for the fourteen fMRI studies: eight used one cognitive measure per domain, eight did not control for other drug use, and eleven found no significant group difference on the cognitive measure, so their conclusions rest on the imaging alone.
Reviewers' tallies for the six MRI studies: three drew conclusions about behaviour without any cognitive testing, two did not control for age and five did not control for other drug use.
key_findings.locator: §4.2 MRI studies without cognitive testing, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: PET: of three studies, two did not match groups on age and two found no cognitive group difference while reporting regional activity differences (Bolla et al., 2003, Iowa Gambling Task after about 25 days' abstinence; Bolla et al., 2004, modified Stroop, with an older cocaine group, 36 vs 30 years, housed as inpatients longer than controls, 23 vs 3 days).
key_findings.locator: §4.5 PET studies, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 12–13); Table 2, Bolla et al. (2003) and (2004) (PET) rows (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: The one PET study that used age-adjusted test scores (Goldstein et al., 2004; 42 people with cocaine dependence, 40 with alcohol dependence, 72 controls) found mild impairment in the cocaine group, less than 1 SD below the control mean, with the alcohol group more impaired. The table adds that the groups were not matched on sex, handedness, age or education, and that people in the cocaine group who reported current or past alcohol use did worse on attention and executive function than those who did not.
key_findings.locator: §4.5 PET studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 13); Table 2, Goldstein et al. (2004) (PET) row (p. 38)

key_findings.finding: In the two Table 1 studies whose caveats mention a normative comparison, performance was not outside the normative range: Reske et al. (2010), CVLT, 13 people who used cocaine recreationally vs 48 stimulant-naive controls; Woicik et al. (2011), WCST and CVLT, 107 vs 107, although the cocaine group also had poorer set-shifting and later-trial recall than controls.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Reske et al. (2010) row (p. 29) and Woicik et al. (2011) row (p. 31)
key_findings.note: The table does not say whether the primary authors or the reviewers made the normative comparison.

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table 1: 19 of the 21 studies with a non-drug-using control group list poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one domain (none listed for Cunha et al. and for the Preller sensorimotor-gating study; Streeter et al., 2008, had no control group). The arrows summarize domains, not individual measures.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Cognitive findings column and legend (p. 31)
key_findings.note: The Cunha et al. (2010) decision-making (Iowa Gambling Task) entry carries the no-difference arrow but is annotated that the cocaine group made more disadvantageous choices (PDF p. 27); counted as poorer, the count would be 20 of 21.

key_findings.finding: The highlights state that the strongest evidence for harmful effects concerns executive functions (attention, inhibition, working memory), and the discussion that executive function and working or verbal memory are where differences from controls have been found most consistently; the reviewers argue that a significant difference alone does not show impairment.

Confounding examples given by the reviewers: controls with more education than the cocaine group (17 vs 11.87 years in Fernández-Serrano et al.); cocaine groups older than controls (about 40 vs 30 years in four studies; 37 vs 30 years in Kaufman et al., 2003).
key_findings.locator: §4.1, 3rd paragraph (p. 8); §4.4, 2nd paragraph (p. 11); §5 Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 14); Table 2, Kaufman et al. (2003) row for the year (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Tables 1–2: at least 8 of the 22 neuropsychological and 7 of the 25 imaging studies list some participants tested after less than 72 hours of abstinence or with cocaine-positive urine on the test or screening day (for example Fillmore and Rush, 2002, who required cocaine-positive urine; Vadhan et al., 2009, abstinence entered as the morning of testing; Tomasi et al., 2010, 17 of 20 urine-positive); abstinence is unknown for 6 more.

Animal evidence, kept apart from the human findings and declared outside the review's scope: the reviewers argue that rodent regimens (for example 30 mg/kg cocaine by intraperitoneal injection daily for 2 weeks in drug-naive rats) are about three times larger than the amounts people with heavy long-term use report, scaling by body weight; in rhesus monkeys self-administering cocaine, reversal-learning and working-memory deficits seen 3 days after use had normalized after 3 months of abstinence, although novel and appetitive distractors still disrupted performance in the cocaine group only, and after 20 months without cocaine there was no task difference but higher cerebellar metabolic activity.

The reviewers propose judging impairment against demographically adjusted norms, for example T scores below 40 (more than 1 SD below the normative mean) or cut-offs of 1, 1.5 or 2 SD, with groups matched or adjusted for age, education and sex.

Conclusions: the reviewers state that the evidence does not support broad cognitive deficits from chronic cocaine use, call that view inaccurate and say it may harm treatment programmes and policy; they also reject the suggestion that people with cocaine use disorder cannot benefit from cognitive behavioural therapy.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods define abstinence as at least 72 hours and the section headings describe abstinent samples, but Tables 1–2 include studies with less than 72 hours of abstinence or cocaine-positive urine (editors' count: at least 8 of 22 and 7 of 25), for example Colzato et al. (2007), 2 days; Sellaro et al. (2013), at least 2 days; Simon et al., positive on the test day; Parvaz et al. (2015), use within 72 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Results from people tested during recent use or early withdrawal are mixed with long-term effects, the very confound the reviewers raise for the animal studies (PDF p. 7). Two rows also differ from Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3): Colzato et al. (2007) is listed there with more than 7 days' abstinence, and Woicik et al. (2011), shown here as at least 72 hours, with under 72 hours and mostly positive urine; the caveat in this review's own Woicik row says that 19 completers tested negative for cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Two tabulated studies lack the non-drug-using control group the inclusion criteria require: Goldstein et al. (2007, fMRI) is marked as having no control group, and Streeter et al. (2008) compares treatment completers with non-completers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The criteria were not applied consistently; these rows cannot inform a comparison with people who do not use cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The text's tallies disagree with Table 1's own caveat entries: other drug use not controlled is counted as 8 studies, but the table flags at least 11 (adding Colzato 2009, Sellaro 2013 and Vonmoos 2013); education as 6, but the cited list includes reference 81, an fMRI study from Table 2, and omits two Table 1 studies the table flags (Vonmoos 2013 and the Preller sensorimotor-gating study); no normative interpretation as 13 of 22, while the table flags 11 explicitly and notes a normative comparison for two; more than one measure per domain as 3 of 22, although the same section credits Fernández-Serrano et al. with several measures per domain and Table 1 lists several tests per domain for others (for example Bolla 1999, Colzato 2009). Among the fMRI studies, the eleven counted as showing no cognitive difference include Kübler et al. (2005), which Table 2 lists with poorer visuospatial working memory.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary counts that claims would cite cannot be relied on as printed; counts should be taken from the table rows, with their own uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and highlights state that cognitive differences were observed on a minority of measures, but no count of measures, or of studies with and without differences, appears anywhere in the results; the editors' count from Table 1 finds poorer performance in at least one domain in 19 of 21 studies with controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline result is unverifiable from the paper; at the level of studies it is contradicted by Table 1, though it may hold for the in-scanner tasks of the imaging studies (11 of 14 fMRI, 2 of 3 PET without a difference by the reviewers' count).

reporting_issues.issue: The power calculation behind the small-sample flag gives 18.8 per group for 80% power and 25.3 for 90% at d = 0.74; the editors' calculation for a two-sided two-sample comparison at α = .05 gives 30 and 40 per group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold of 18 per group is lenient: studies with 19 to 29 per group are not flagged as small although they had less than 80% power for d = 0.74 (about 58% at 18 per group).

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of animal and human exposure scales the rat dose to a 70 kg person by body weight alone, with no allometric or pharmacokinetic basis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' note (METHODS §5.4): body-surface-area scaling, the usual allometric method, divides a rat mg/kg dose by about 6, which would reverse the three-fold comparison; the argument that rodent regimens far exceed human use is not established by this calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: Selection is undocumented, and the editors' cross-check shows it is incomplete: about 30 long-term studies listed by Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3), all within this review's 1999–2016 window, are not tabulated (for example Abi-Saab 2005, Kjome 2010, Lane 2007, Li 2006, Moeller 2004 and 2005, Rahman 2005, Tanabe 2009, van der Plas 2009, Verdejo-Garcia 2007, Woicik 2009), and van der Plas et al. (2009) is cited in the introduction (reference 18) as replicating a WCST impairment yet does not appear in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison uses Spronk et al. (2013), Table 3, PDF pp. 6–9 of that review. Without an exclusion list it cannot be told whether these studies failed the criteria or were missed; conclusions about the literature as a whole rest on an unrepresentative subset of unknown selection.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation and labelling errors: five tabulated studies have no entry in the reference list (Reske 2010, Sellaro 2013, Soar 2012 and Vonmoos 2013 in Table 1; Parvaz 2015 in Table 2); table years differ from the reference list (Cuhna 2010 vs Cunha 2011; Simon 2008 vs 2001; the two Preller studies of 2013 and 2014 swapped; Castelluccio 2013 vs 2014); reference 76, cited for the Fernández-Serrano primary study, is a 2011 review (the primary study is reference 9); reference 108, cited for cocaine neurotoxicity in animals, concerns methamphetamine; references 16 and 17, cited as replications of a WCST impairment, are a theoretical perspective article and a study of self-efficacy; the same Hester and Garavan paper appears as references 4 and 102.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several primary studies cannot be traced from this review alone; identify them by DOI before citing. Some errors may have been corrected in the version of record, which was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Internal errors in Table 2 rows: Hanlon et al. (2011) gives a mean abstinence of 1.9 days for the abstinent group and 243.8 for the current-use group, apparently transposed; Hester and Garavan (2004) gives a minimum of 72 hours with a mean of 42 hours, which cannot both be right; Gooding et al. (2008) lists poorer CPT discriminability and more commission errors but says in the caveats that no significant behavioural differences were found; Ersche et al. (2011) marks response inhibition and sustained attention with the arrow the legend reserves for better performance while describing slower responses and more missed targets. Two more rows give contradictory or disputed abstinence: Kaufman et al. (2003), 'Minimum 72h/18-72h', which cannot both be right, and Kübler et al. (2005), 'Minimum 72', where Spronk et al. (2013, Table 3) list under 72 hours (PDF p. 36).
reporting_issues.consequence: These rows should not be cited from the table; the primary papers must be read.
