design_detail: Cross-sectional event-related fMRI case–control study (1.5 T). 15 people actively using cocaine (all urine-positive, tested 12 to 72 hours after last use) and 15 non-using controls performed a GO–NOGO task in which a frequent button press had to be withheld for letters held in working memory (memory lists of 1, 3 or 5 letters; 18 runs of 60 trials, 7 of them NOGO). Outcomes: percentage of correct inhibitions, GO reaction time, and activation during successful inhibitions in 29 clusters. The task measures withholding a prepotent response, not stopping a response already started (as a stop-signal task would).
can_establish: That in this small sample of people who had used cocaine within the previous 72 hours, withholding a frequent response was less accurate than in controls, more so as the memory load rose, without slower GO responses, and that activation in anterior cingulate, pre-SMA and right superior frontal clusters during successful inhibitions was lower than in controls.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the differences (no pre-use data; the groups differed in age, smoking, education and cannabis use); whether they persist with abstinence (everyone was tested within 72 hours of use); whether the errors reflect failed inhibition rather than forgetting the memory list (memory was not tested in the scanner and was checked in only 7 of the cocaine group); or that the cerebellar activation is compensatory (it went with poorer performance).

sample.recruitment: Not reported for either group; the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Medical College of Wisconsin (pp. 11017–11018, Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All right-handed (Edinburgh inventory); by self-report no current or past neurological or psychiatric disorder and no dependence on any substance other than cocaine (cocaine group only), caffeine or nicotine. Urine tests were negative for all drugs in every control and positive for cocaine or its metabolites in everyone in the cocaine group; people in the cocaine group positive for any drug other than cocaine, nicotine or cannabis were excluded (pp. 11017–11018).
sample.demographics: Controls: 8 women, mean age 31 (range 20–40). Cocaine group: 6 women, mean age 40 (range 22–48). Education 13.9 vs 11.5 years, reported as not significantly different without a test statistic. Ethnicity not reported (p. 11017).
sample.attrition: None: no participant showed significant residual head motion, so all 30 were analysed (p. 11018).
sample.selection_effects: Recruitment sources are not reported, and no diagnostic interview for cocaine dependence is described although the title refers to cocaine addiction. The cocaine group was on average 9 years older, more often male, had 2.4 fewer years of education, and 10 of its 15 members smoked tobacco against 1 of 15 controls.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported frequency, duration and spending; recent use confirmed by urine (cocaine or metabolites, indicating use within 72 hours) (p. 11018). No diagnostic assessment of cocaine dependence is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: mean 5 times a week (range 1–7) for a mean of 14 years (range 5–27), mean US$252 a week (range 25–1000). Route not reported (p. 11018).
exposure.polysubstance: 12 of 15 in the cocaine group reported occasional cannabis use (mean 15 days since last use, none in the 24 hours before scanning); 10 of 15 in the cocaine group and 1 control smoked tobacco regularly (mean 12.5 cigarettes a day) and were not asked to abstain from smoking; alcohol use is not reported for either group (p. 11018).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not abstinent: self-reported time since last use mean 41 hours (range 12–72), urine positive for cocaine or metabolites in all; no one showed overt signs of intoxication (p. 11018).

comparison.controls: 15 non-using volunteers whose urine tests were negative for all drugs (p. 11018). The abstract calls them drug-naive; the Methods describe them only as nondrug-using.
comparison.matching: Not matched: mean age 31 vs 40, women 8 vs 6, education 13.9 vs 11.5 years, tobacco smokers 1 vs 10. Age and sex were entered as covariates in one behavioural analysis only; education, smoking and cannabis use were never adjusted for (p. 11019).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measure of inhibitory control and no estimate of premorbid IQ; childhood ADHD or conduct problems are not assessed beyond the self-reported absence of psychiatric disorder.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Urine negative for all drugs; 1 control smoked tobacco regularly; alcohol use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Working-memory-load GO–NOGO task (WM-IT): a memory list of 1, 3 or 5 letters shown for 6 s, an 8 s rehearsal period, then 60 letters each shown for 1 s followed by 0.5 s blank; participants pressed for letters not in the list (53 GO trials) and withheld the press for list letters (7 NOGO trials); 18 runs, 6 per load, in the same order for everyone (p. 11018; Figure 1). Editors' calculation: 42 NOGO trials per load, 126 in all. fMRI: 1.5 T GE Signa; event-related deconvolution of successful inhibitions at each load and of errors pooled across loads; voxelwise threshold t=5.226 (p=0.0001) with an 87 µl minimum cluster from Monte Carlo simulation; cluster means compared in repeated-measures analyses with a modified Bonferroni correction (pp. 11018–11019).
outcomes.validity_norms: No normative data. Memory for the letter lists was not tested in the scanner; a recall version given outside the scanner to 7 of the cocaine group gave mean recall of 93.54% for 5-letter lists, compared with above 95% in more than 80 control participants from the authors' earlier administrations, not with this study's controls (p. 11018).
outcomes.operationalization: Inhibitory control = the percentage of NOGO trials on which the press was withheld; 'executive dysfunction' = a group difference against these 15 controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. Activation in the 29 clusters of Table 1 was tested for load, group and interaction effects with a modified Bonferroni correction; the behavioural analyses (correct inhibitions and GO reaction time) and the brain–behaviour correlations were not corrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to computer-scored task data; not reported for the image analysis.

analysis.effect_sizes: Correct inhibitions: load F(2,56)=53.94, p<0.01; group F(1,28)=15.03, p<0.01; group × load F(2,56)=3.34, p<0.05; with age and sex as covariates, group F(1,28)=11.89, p<0.01 and group × load F(2,56)=3.26, p<0.05. GO reaction time: load F(2,56)=188.31, p<0.0001; group F(1,28)=0.42, p=0.52; group × load F(2,56)=1.33, p=0.27 (p. 11019). Group means appear only in Figure 2 (p. 11020). Editors' calculation from the group effect F(1,28)=15.03: a standardized difference of about 1.4 (95% CI about 0.6 to 2.2) in the mean correct-inhibition rate across loads. Activation: higher in controls in left anterior cingulate (BA 32/24, 1325 µl), right pre-SMA (BA 6, 1298 µl) and right superior frontal gyrus (BA 10/9, 889 µl) (Table 1, p. 11019). ACC activity and correct inhibitions at the 5-letter load: r=0.44, p<0.01 (p. 11019). ACC group × load F(2,56)=3.63, p<0.05, with a rise across loads in controls, F(2,28)=10.51, p<0.001, and none in the cocaine group, F(2,56)=0.64, p>0.05 (p. 11020). Left culmen and left pyramis group × load F(2,56)=4.60 and 4.43 (printed p<0.01); activity in these clusters and inhibition performance r=−0.54 and r=−0.51 (p<0.005) in the whole sample and r=−0.47 (p<0.08) and r=−0.48 (p<0.07) within the cocaine group (n=15) (p. 11020).
analysis.covariates: Age and sex in one behavioural analysis; none in the imaging analyses; education, smoking, cannabis and alcohol never adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: Behavioural means and their dispersion are given only in a figure, without saying what the error bars show. Brain–behaviour correlations are reported only for the ACC at the 5-letter load and for the two cerebellar clusters.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 15 per group, the cerebellar correlations within the cocaine group did not reach significance, which the authors attribute to the smaller sample (p. 11020).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 people tested 12 to 72 hours after cocaine use and 15 non-using controls, the cocaine group withheld the response less often at every memory load, with a larger gap at higher loads, and did not differ in GO reaction time. During successful inhibitions, activation was lower in three frontal and cingulate clusters; ACC activation rose with load in controls but not in the cocaine group; two left cerebellar clusters showed rising activation with load in the cocaine group, and higher activation there went with poorer inhibition.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the study demonstrates that the cocaine group's poorer control goes with reduced anterior cingulate and right prefrontal activity, calls the cerebellar pattern compensatory, links the load effect to working-memory demands said to rise during cue-induced craving, and says the results reveal a neuroanatomical basis for a dysexecutive component of addiction that may prolong use or predispose to relapse (p. 11017). The discussion states that the results show "for the first time" that the difficulty with inhibition "relates directly" to a reduced capacity to modulate ACC and prefrontal activity, and that effects of cocaine on these regions may directly contribute to impulsive drug taking during craving (p. 11021). Gaps: (1) the comparison is cross-sectional, without pre-use data, with groups that differ in age, education, smoking and cannabis use, so neither the brain differences nor the behavioural deficit can be attributed to cocaine; (2) everyone in the cocaine group was tested within 72 hours of use, so acute after-effects or early withdrawal cannot be separated from lasting effects; (3) craving and relapse were not measured; (4) the cerebellar activation correlated with worse performance, which the authors themselves say may mark the people who found the task hardest (p. 11021), so 'compensatory' is an interpretation, not a finding; (5) because recall of the memory list was not measured in the scanner, some NOGO errors may reflect forgetting rather than failed inhibition.

timeline.event: Kaufman et al. GO–NOGO fMRI study reporting anterior cingulate hypoactivity in people who use cocaine, cited by these authors as earlier evidence (p. 11020)
This study: poorer GO–NOGO inhibition under working-memory load in 15 people tested within 72 hours of cocaine use, with lower ACC, pre-SMA and right superior frontal activation.

Lane et al.: Go/No-Go task with easy and hard discriminations in 18 people with current cocaine dependence and 15 controls; lower discrimination (d′) in the cocaine group overall, a conceptual replication of poorer Go/No-Go performance with a different task and interpretation

Potvin et al. meta-analysis: this study is not among its 46 studies (testing during scanning was excluded); the pooled impulse-related domain, which includes Go/No-Go and stop-signal tasks, gave d=0.408 in urine-positive studies and d=0.581 at abstinence under 12 weeks

López-Martín et al. meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition includes this study (15 against 15 people) at Hedges' g = 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 for the 1-, 3- and 5-letter loads and 3.56 (95% CI 2.49 to 4.63) aggregated (its Fig. 2); the review does not say how it obtained these values. Editors' calculation: values close to them (about 3.2, 3.9 and 4.9) follow when the Figure 2 error bars (p. 11020) are read as standard deviations, but the printed group F(1,28)=15.03 implies a between-person SD of about 11 points, so the bars fit standard errors (about 0.8 to 1.3 per load read that way), and the group F gives g of about 1.38.

replication.where_it_stands: Poorer GO–NOGO accuracy in people who use cocaine agrees with Lane et al. (2007) and with the pooled impulse-related domain of Potvin et al. (2014). The findings specific to this study (a deficit that grows with working-memory load, static ACC activation, rising cerebellar activation) rest on 30 people tested within 72 hours of use and were not tested again in the papers read for this card. López-Martín et al. (2026) include this study at several times the effect its own statistics give (see the 2026 timeline entry), entries that raise that review's pooled estimate.

funding.funder: United States Public Health Service grant DA14100 and General Clinical Research Center grant M01 RR00058 (p. 11017, first-page footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Trinity College Dublin (Department of Psychology and Institute of Neuroscience) and the Medical College of Wisconsin (Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Medicine) (p. 11017).

what_would_settle_it: A study testing the same people both during recent use and after urine-verified abstinence of several weeks to months, against controls matched on age, sex, education, smoking and alcohol use, with recall of the memory list measured inside the scanner and with both a GO–NOGO task (withholding a response) and a stop-signal task (stopping a started response); ideally a prospective cohort with inhibition measured before regular cocaine use begins.

domains.note: Groups differ in age (31 vs 40), sex, education (13.9 vs 11.5 years) and tobacco smoking (1 vs 10 of 15); 12 of 15 in the cocaine group used cannabis; alcohol not measured. Only age and sex were adjusted, and only in one behavioural analysis.
Recent use is urine-confirmed, but frequency and duration are self-reported, route is not reported, and no diagnosis of cocaine dependence is documented.
Recruitment sources for both groups are not reported, so selection into the study cannot be judged.
Testing 12 to 72 hours after last use: performance may reflect after-effects of recent use or early withdrawal; smokers were not asked to abstain, so nicotine state was uncontrolled.
All 30 analysed; the memory-recall check, however, was done in only 7 of the cocaine group.
Computer-scored inhibition is objective, but whether NOGO errors reflect failed inhibition or forgotten memory lists was not checked in the scanner or in controls.
Behavioural results only in a figure; brain–behaviour correlations reported for selected clusters and conditions; several p-values misreported (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The behavioural difference is sizeable for a sample of this size, but it cannot be attributed to cocaine because of uncontrolled confounding (age, education, smoking, cannabis) and because everyone in the cocaine group was tested within 72 hours of use. The study can be cited for poorer withholding of a prepotent response, increasing with memory load, in people who had recently used cocaine, and for the activation differences as reported; it should not be cited for lasting deficits, for a causal effect of cocaine, for compensation by the cerebellum or for links with craving or relapse.

key_findings.finding: 15 controls (8 women; mean age 31, range 20–40) and 15 people actively using cocaine (6 women; mean age 40, range 22–48); education 13.9 vs 11.5 years, reported as not significantly different.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Everyone in the cocaine group had a urine test positive for cocaine or its metabolites (use within the past 72 hours); self-reported time since last use averaged 41 hours (range 12–72), with no overt intoxication. Self-reported use averaged 5 times a week (range 1–7) for 14 years (range 5–27), and US$252 a week (range 25–1000). Controls' urine tests were negative for all drugs.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 11017; these figures on p. 11018, left column)

key_findings.finding: 12 of 15 in the cocaine group reported occasional cannabis use (mean 15 days since last use; none within 24 hours of scanning); 11 participants, 10 in the cocaine group and 1 control, smoked tobacco regularly (mean 12.5 cigarettes a day) and were not asked to abstain. Alcohol use is not reported.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (continued on p. 11018, left column)

key_findings.finding: Task: memory lists of 1, 3 or 5 letters (6 s display, 8 s rehearsal) followed by 60 letters at 1.5 s each; press for letters not on the list (53 GO), withhold for list letters (7 NOGO); 18 runs, 6 per load, in the same fixed order for all participants.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Behavioral task, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 42 NOGO trials per load, 126 in all.

key_findings.finding: Recall of the memory lists was not tested during scanning; a recall version given to 7 of the cocaine group outside the scanner gave mean recall of 93.54% for 5-letter lists, set against above 95% in more than 80 controls from the authors' earlier work.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Behavioral task, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Memory load reduced correct inhibitions (F(2,56)=53.94, p<0.01) and slowed GO responses (F(2,56)=188.31, p<0.0001). Controls inhibited more successfully than the cocaine group (group F(1,28)=15.03, p<0.01), with the advantage growing with load (group × load F(2,56)=3.34, p<0.05); GO reaction time did not differ (group F(1,28)=0.42, p=0.52; interaction F(2,56)=1.33, p=0.27). With age and sex as covariates: group F(1,28)=11.89, p<0.01; group × load F(2,56)=3.26, p<0.05.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the group F: standardized difference in mean correct-inhibition rate about 1.4 (95% CI about 0.6 to 2.2).

key_findings.finding: Percentage of correct inhibitions by group and load is shown only in a line graph; the cocaine group is below controls at all three loads and the gap widens at 5 letters.
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi crop (approximate): controls about 91%, 85% and 77%; cocaine group about 80%, 71% and 57% at 1, 3 and 5 letters; error bars of about 3 to 4 points whose type (SD or SEM) is not stated. Editors' calculation: the group F(1,28)=15.03 (p. 11019) implies a between-person SD of about 11 points, so the bars fit SEMs; read as SDs they give g of about 3.2 to 4.9, close to the values a 2026 meta-analysis entered for this study (see the replication timeline).

key_findings.finding: During successful inhibitions, controls showed greater activation than the cocaine group in three clusters: left anterior cingulate (BA 32/24, 1325 µl), right pre-SMA (BA 6, 1298 µl) and right superior frontal gyrus (BA 10/9, 889 µl). ACC activity correlated with correct inhibitions at the 5-letter load (r=0.44, p<0.01).
ACC activation showed a group × load interaction (F(2,56)=3.63, p<0.05): it increased with load in controls (F(2,28)=10.51, p<0.001) and stayed unchanged in the cocaine group (F(2,56)=0.64, p>0.05).

Two left cerebellar clusters (culmen and pyramis) showed group × load interactions (F(2,56)=4.60 and 4.43), with activity rising with load in the cocaine group and falling in controls; activity in them correlated with poorer inhibition across the sample (r=−0.54 and r=−0.51, p<0.005) and, short of significance, within the cocaine group (n=15; r=−0.47, p<0.08; r=−0.48, p<0.07).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 11020); Table 1, Group by load interaction column (p. 11019)

key_findings.finding: The authors concede that the higher cerebellar activity, which went with poorer performance, may not be detrimental but may simply indicate which participants found the task most difficult.

reporting_issues.issue: The cerebellar group × load interactions F(2,56)=4.60 and F(2,56)=4.43 are printed as p<0.01; editors' calculation gives p≈0.014 and p≈0.016.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both are significant at 0.05 but not at the stated 0.01; the cerebellar findings are weaker than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation between ACC activity and correct inhibitions (r=0.44) is printed as p<0.01 without its sample size. Editors' calculation: if all 30 participants were included, the two-tailed p is about 0.015.
reporting_issues.consequence: The p-value holds only one-tailed or with a larger sample than the study had; the correlation is weaker evidence than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis with age and sex as covariates is reported with the same degrees of freedom as the unadjusted analysis (F(1,28), F(2,56)), and the within-group test for the cocaine group's ACC (n=15) is reported as F(2,56), whereas the controls' test is F(2,28). Editors' note: with two covariates the degrees of freedom would be (1,26) and (2,52), and a within-group test on 15 people has (2,28).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; recomputing with the expected degrees of freedom does not change any conclusion, but it leaves unclear how the covariate model was fitted.

reporting_issues.issue: Behavioural results are given only as F tests and a line graph (Figure 2) without numerical means or a statement of what the error bars show; the text speaks of the number of correct inhibitions, the figure of percentage correct.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group means can only be read approximately from the figure, and the effect size can be estimated only from the F statistic.

reporting_issues.issue: Coordinates differ by 1 mm between Table 1 and the Figure 3 legend: pre-SMA y=6 vs 5, ACC y=33 vs 32, culmen z=−26 vs −25.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typographical inconsistency; no effect on the findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract refer to cocaine addiction and to drug-naive controls, but the Methods describe no diagnostic assessment of cocaine dependence and characterize controls only as non-using with negative urine tests; the education difference (13.9 vs 11.5 years) is called non-significant without a test statistic.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the cocaine group met dependence criteria, and whether controls had ever used drugs, is unknown; claims should describe the sample as people using cocaine several times a week, tested within 72 hours of use.

(2026), which enters this study as g = 3.56 (2.49 to 4.63) in Fig. 2B and as 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 per load in Fig. 2A; those values are reproduced only by reading Figure 2's error bars as SDs; the group F gives about 1.38.

design_detail: Prospective multicentre observational series (the authors call it a cohort study) of consecutive patients enrolled in the emergency departments (EDs) of six US inner-city teaching hospitals from April 1991 to May 1992, the Cocaine Associated Chest Pain (COCHPA) study: 246 patients with anterior, precordial or left-sided chest pain who reported cocaine use in the past week. Primary endpoint: myocardial infarction (MI) by CK-MB or ECG criteria within 24 hours of presentation. One group and no comparison group; patients with and without MI are compared within the series, and the initial ECG is assessed as a test for MI. Appraised with the JBI checklist as an incidence (proportion) study.
can_establish: How often MI defined by CK-MB elevation was diagnosed (14 of 246, 5.7%) among patients enrolled with chest pain after cocaine use at six US urban EDs in 1991–1992, what these patients were like, and how poorly the initial ECG and single clinical features separated patients with MI from those without (ECG sensitivity 5 of 14).
cannot_establish: The true proportion with MI (31 patients had no cardiac enzymes, the protocol obtained CK-MB when total CK was raised, and very-low-risk patients may not have been enrolled), the proportion under troponin-based definitions, whether cocaine caused the infarctions (no comparison group), or that no useful predictor of MI exists (14 events were too few for a multivariable model, p. 333).

sample.recruitment: EDs of six US inner-city teaching hospitals (the abstract says municipal hospitals); patients identified prospectively and enrolled by study investigators before admission or release; written informed consent from all (p. 332). Enrolment by site (Appendix A, p. 339): Bronx Municipal Hospital Center 99 (from 30 April 1991), New York City Poison Control Center 13 (from 1 July 1991), Highland General Hospital, Oakland 57 (from 1 January 1992), Boston City Hospital 45 (from 29 January 1992), University of Rochester Medical Center 16 (from 25 October 1991), Queens Hospital Center 16 (from 1 December 1991); all sites stopped enrolling on 29 May 1992 (p. 332).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: anterior, precordial or left-sided chest pain not explained by local trauma or a radiographic abnormality, and cocaine use in the past week (p. 332). Excluded: isolated right-sided chest pain (on anecdotal experience that MI is very unlikely there) and patients whose chest radiograph showed an abnormality believed to explain the pain, such as pneumonia or pneumothorax (pp. 332–333). No age limits are stated.
sample.demographics: Median age 33 years (MI group 36.5, IQR 33–44; no-MI group 33, IQR 26–38); 71.5% men; 83.3% not white (no-MI group 62.5% African-American, 19.4% Hispanic, 17.7% white; MI group 85.7% African-American, 14.3% Hispanic); 83.3% smoked tobacco (median 12 pack-years, IQR 5–20); other cardiac risk factors each under 20%; history of chest pain 51%, of MI 4% (pp. 330–331, 334, 337; Table 1).
sample.attrition: One patient was excluded for not taking part in follow-up (p. 331), yet all analyses use 246 patients. Two patients arrived in cardiac arrest and died within 8 hours; of the other 244, follow-up data were obtained for 223 (91.4%), all alive (pp. 331–332). Released patients who did not return within 24 hours were telephoned within 2 weeks; patients ruled out for MI in hospital or the observation unit were not telephoned (p. 333). One released patient whose second sample showed a raised CK-MB could not be traced (p. 335).
sample.selection_effects: Consecutive enrolment was intended, but no log of eligible patients is reported, and the authors concede that clinicians may not have notified investigators of patients judged at very low risk, which would inflate the MI proportion (p. 336); the journal's reviewers add that patients may have agreed to a study requiring disclosure of cocaine use mainly when quite symptomatic (p. 339). One site contributed 99 of 246 patients (40%). Isolated right-sided pain was excluded. Urban teaching hospitals in four US cities, 1991–1992.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cocaine use in the past week, recorded on a standardized form at the ED visit (length and frequency of use, route, estimated amount in the past 24 hours, time of last use) (p. 332). Urine was tested for cocaine metabolites only when the treating physician ordered it: 91 of 92 patients tested (98.9%) were positive. The authors did not require urine testing, reasoning that patients would be unlikely to claim cocaine use in its absence (p. 333).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported. All but one used cocaine regularly: median 5.0 years of use (IQR 2–7) and median 10 episodes a month (IQR 4–30). Route: smoked 179 (72.8%), insufflated 67 (27.2%), injected 26 (10.6%); 23 (9.3%) used two or more routes. Median 5 hours from last use to presentation (IQR 2–22); chest pain began a median of 60 minutes after use (IQR 3–645) and lasted a median of 120 minutes (IQR 30–367); 81% presented within 24 hours of last use (pp. 332–334). The estimated amount used in the past 24 hours was collected but is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: A history of other substance use was recorded (p. 332) but is not reported. Tobacco: 83.3% smoked cigarettes; smoking in the 12 hours before presentation was not associated with MI (p. 336; no figures given). Alcohol is not mentioned.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: patients were assessed at presentation, a median of 5 hours after last use.

comparison.controls: No comparison group. Patients with MI (n=14) are compared with those without (n=232) on demographics, history, chest-pain features, vital signs, ECG and laboratory values (Tables 1–4). For context the authors cite an MI incidence of 4.2% in chest-pain patients aged 25–39 from an earlier study (Lee et al., 1985, ref. 40), not a concurrent comparison (p. 336).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary anatomy is unknown (no patient was catheterized, p. 335); cardiac history before cocaine use is not known beyond self-reported risk factors and previous diagnoses.

outcomes.instruments: MI: prolonged chest pain plus either CK-MB above the institutional upper limit of normal or standard ECG evolution of MI within 24 hours of presentation, diagnosed independently by the investigators (p. 333). Admitted patients had total CK every 8–12 hours for 24 hours, and an MB fraction was obtained when total CK exceeded the upper limit of normal; for released patients a CK sample was requested in the ED and they were asked to return within 24 hours for a second (p. 333). Initial ECG classified into six categories with a closed-question format (Table 4 reports five, with one 'Ischemic' row; see reporting issues), read independently by two investigators before MI status was known, disagreements resolved by consensus (p. 332). Other final diagnoses (ischaemic, atypical, non-cardiac chest pain) by the attending physician's clinical impression (p. 333). Arrhythmias, heart failure and deaths from the hospital course and follow-up.
outcomes.validity_norms: CK-MB was the standard marker of the time; troponin was not used. Thresholds differed by institution (each based on its own normal volunteers, p. 333). The specificity of CK-MB elevation after recent cocaine use is not discussed in this paper; Feldman et al. (2000, p. 474) note that CK and CK-MB elevations occur in people using cocaine who do not have MI.
outcomes.operationalization: 'MI' = the CK-MB or ECG definition above; all 14 cases rested on a raised CK-MB and none on ECG changes alone (pp. 331–332). Patients with no isoenzyme measurement (31 of 246) count as not having MI.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p<0.05 for all tests (p. 333). About 40 comparisons of patients with and without MI are reported with a significance result or a 'no difference' statement: 13 in Table 1, 9 in Table 2, 5 in Table 3, 1 in Table 4 and about 12 in the text.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: ECG readers were blinded to MI status (p. 332); blinding of the investigators who assigned the MI diagnosis is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: MI 14/246 = 5.7% (95% CI 2.7–8.7%), apparently a normal-approximation interval; the exact binomial interval is 3.1–9.4% (editors' calculation). The authors' sensitivity analyses: 7.3% (3.2–11.4%) among patients with two or more isoenzyme measurements and 8.6% (3.9–13.2%) among admitted patients (p. 336), which match 11 of 151 and 12 of 140 (editors' reconstruction). MI among patients presenting within 24 hours of use 7.8% (3.9–11.8%) and within 12 hours 7.4% (2.3–12.6%), denominators not given (p. 334). Initial ECG consistent with ischaemia or infarction as a test for MI: sensitivity 35.7% (10.6–60.8%), specificity 89.9% (86–93.8%), positive predictive value 17.9% (3.7–32.1%), negative predictive value 95.8% (93.1–98.5%) (p. 334), corresponding to 5/14, 205/228, 5/28 and 205/214 in Table 4 (editors' reconstruction; exact interval for the sensitivity 12.8–64.9%). Patients with vs without MI: median age 36.5 vs 33 years (p=0.025), history of chest pain 21.4% vs 52.6% (p=0.047), shortness of breath 28.6% vs 61.2% (p=0.033), ischaemic or infarction ECG (p=0.014), initial CK raised 86% vs 46% (p=0.009), initial CK 515 vs 177 (units printed as mg/dL; p=0.0002), admitted 86% vs 55% (p=0.027). The printed p-values for history of chest pain, shortness of breath, ECG category and admission are reproduced by a continuity-corrected chi-square or Fisher's exact test (editors' check). Upper 95% limit for late complications among the 14 with MI: 21% (p. 337).
analysis.covariates: None; univariate comparisons only. The authors state that 14 MIs were too few for a multivariable logistic model likely to validate in another data set (p. 333).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Collected but not reported: estimated cocaine amount in the past 24 hours, history of other substance use and HIV status (p. 332). Laboratory values other than CK (haematocrit, creatinine, prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, glucose, cholesterol) are described only as unhelpful, without data (p. 334). MI by site is not reported.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. With 14 events the MI proportion has a relative precision of about plus or minus 50%, and comparisons between patients with and without MI have little power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 246 patients enrolled with chest pain after cocaine use, 14 (5.7%) had MI by CK-MB criteria within 24 hours, an estimate the authors show rising to 7.3% and 8.6% when restricted to patients with fuller enzyme testing or to admitted patients; 2 patients are known to have died, both after arriving in cardiac arrest, neither with pathologic evidence of MI. Patients with MI were somewhat older, less often reported previous chest pain or shortness of breath, and more often had an ischaemic ECG and a raised initial CK, but the initial ECG detected only 5 of the 14 infarctions. No arrhythmia needing intervention, heart failure or infarct extension developed in hospital; the 4 patients with heart failure had it on arrival.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says there was no clinical difference between patients who had MI and those who did not (p. 330), whereas Tables 1, 2 and 4 and the text report several significant differences; the authors' underlying point, that no feature identified very-low-risk patients, is reasonable for the ECG (sensitivity 5 of 14) but cannot be extended to all clinical features from 14 events without a multivariable model. The discussion calls the cohort large and unselected (p. 336) while conceding, two paragraphs later, that very-low-risk patients may not have been enrolled. The abstract's statement that all cases requiring intervention were evident on presentation rests on 14 MIs, for which the authors give an upper 95% limit of 21% for late complications (p. 337). The comparison with a 4.2% incidence in chest-pain patients aged 25–39 (p. 336) is with another study and era. The recommendation to rule out MI in every patient with chest pain within 24 hours of cocaine use (p. 337) is a clinical judgment drawn from the 5.7% figure, not a tested strategy.

timeline.event: Retrospective series of 136 cocaine-associated MIs from the same group: uses this study's roughly 6% MI incidence as one assumption in estimating that fewer than 1.6 per 1000 young patients with cocaine-associated chest pain would have complications missed by 12-hour observation, and describes COCHPA as covering an average of 8 months per site (p. 1085)

One-year follow-up of 203 COCHPA patients (Hollander et al., 1995, Acad Emerg Med 2:179–184; not among the files): actuarial survival 98%, with death or nonfatal MI only in patients who continued to use cocaine, as described by Weber et al. (2003, p. 516)
Weber et al. (2000) is cited with this study by Weber et al. (2003, p. 516) as finding a 6% MI rate in cocaine-associated chest pain (not read in this round)

Substudy of the ACI-TIPI trial (293 patients with cocaine-associated complaints, broader symptoms, WHO criteria): acute MI in 2 (0.7%), which the authors call a sevenfold difference from this study and the Tokarski series and attribute to broader inclusion and different MI criteria (pp. 470, 473)

Single-centre observation-unit cohort of 302 lower-risk patients with cocaine-associated chest pain: no cardiovascular deaths and 4 of 256 nonfatal MIs within 30 days; describes this study's complication findings (p. 515)

replication.where_it_stands: The roughly 6% figure (exact interval about 3–9%) applies to patients who reached urban US EDs with chest pain after cocaine use in the early 1990s, with MI defined by CK-MB and incompletely ascertained. A broader ED sample assessed with WHO criteria found a much lower acute MI proportion (0.7%; Feldman et al., 2000), and later practice uses troponin-based definitions, so the proportion under current definitions is not settled by this study.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the article).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the emergency departments of the participating hospitals and the New York City Poison Control Center, writing for the COCHPA Study Group; the study was presented at the 1992 AAPCC/AACT/ABMT/CAPCC meeting (p. 330). The first two authors also wrote the later series that uses this study's MI incidence (Hollander et al., 1995b), and the first author is senior author of the observation-unit study (Weber et al., 2003). Recorded as context for reading the later papers, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre study of all consecutive ED patients with chest pain after cocaine use, with a screening log of eligible patients, toxicology confirmation, serial troponin testing at fixed times in every patient whether admitted or released, blinded adjudication of MI by a current universal definition, and 30-day follow-up by record linkage across hospitals and death registers, reporting the proportion with MI and its exact confidence interval.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: ED patients with chest pain after cocaine use in the past week at six urban US teaching hospitals; isolated right-sided pain was excluded on anecdotal grounds, and one site supplied 40% of patients.

Consecutive enrolment by investigators was intended, but no screening log or count of eligible patients is given, and the authors concede that clinicians may not have referred patients they judged at very low risk (p. 336).
246 patients and 14 events give the MI proportion to within about 3 percentage points either way (relative precision about 50%); too few events for subgroup estimates or predictors.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sites, dates and enrolment per site, demographics, cocaine use, presentation, ECG and disposition are described (Tables 1–4, Appendix A).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: MI could be diagnosed only where CK-MB was measured: 31 patients had no isoenzymes and only 151 of 246 had two or more; patients without measurements count as not having MI; 21 survivors had no follow-up data.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: A stated MI definition (CK-MB above the institutional limit or ECG evolution, with prolonged chest pain), standard for 1991–1992; but the protocol obtained CK-MB when total CK was raised (measurement with a normal total CK is not described), thresholds differed between institutions, and troponin was not used.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Admitted patients had CK every 8–12 hours for 24 hours; for released patients a CK sample was requested in the ED, with a requested return visit; telephone follow-up only for released patients who did not return (p. 333).

Proportions with 95% intervals, but normal-approximation intervals at small counts (exact interval for 14/246 is 3.1–9.4%), no denominators for the time-window estimates, and about 40 unadjusted comparisons without correction.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Only one exclusion for non-participation is reported and follow-up reached 223 of 244 survivors (91.4%), but refusals among eligible patients are not counted and the 21 without follow-up are not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. The study is prospective, uses a stated MI definition, blinded ECG reading and denominators for most figures, but complete enrolment was not shown, MI ascertainment was incomplete and unequal between admitted and released patients (with CK-MB obtained when total CK was raised), and the printed intervals are normal approximations; the authors' own sensitivity analyses move the estimate from 5.7% to 8.6%. The editors summarise the risk of bias as moderate. It may be cited for: the proportion of enrolled patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who had MI by CK-MB criteria (14 of 246; 5.7%, exact interval 3.1–9.4%) with its ascertainment caveats; the clinical profile of the series; the low sensitivity of the initial ECG (5 of 14); and the absence of in-hospital arrhythmias needing intervention, heart failure or infarct extension in this series. It should not be cited for MI proportions under troponin definitions, for the claim that no clinical feature predicts MI, or for causation.

key_findings.finding: 246 patients with chest pain after cocaine use were enrolled at six EDs; 14 (5.7%; 95% CI 2.7–8.7%) met the MI criteria, all because of a raised CK-MB and none on ECG changes alone. Other final diagnoses: ischaemic heart disease 35, atypical chest pain 101, non-cardiac chest pain 96.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph (p. 331); Results › Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 332)
key_findings.note: The printed interval behaves like a normal-approximation interval; the exact binomial interval for 14/246 is 3.1–9.4% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: 140 patients (56.9%) were admitted or kept in the ED observation unit (up to 24 hours) and 106 (43.1%) were released from the ED. Two patients are known to have died, both after arriving in cardiac arrest, within 8 hours of arrival; neither had pathologic evidence of MI. Of the other 244, follow-up data were obtained for 223 (91.4%), all alive.

Cardiac isoenzymes were measured in 215 patients (87%), and two or more times in 151 of them (70%). Restricted to patients with two or more measurements, MI incidence was 7.3% (95% CI 3.2–11.4%); restricted to admitted patients, 8.6% (3.9–13.2%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Laboratory Evaluation, 1st paragraph (p. 334); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 336)
key_findings.note: The two restricted estimates match 11 of 151 and 12 of 140 (editors' reconstruction; 12 of the 14 patients with MI were admitted, p. 335).

key_findings.finding: An MB fraction was obtained when total CK exceeded the institutional upper limit of normal (whether CK-MB was ever measured with a normal total CK is not stated). Admitted patients had CK every 8–12 hours for 24 hours; for released patients a CK sample was requested in the ED and they were asked to return within 24 hours for a second. Released patients who did not return within 24 hours were assessed by telephone within the next 2 weeks; patients ruled out in hospital or the observation unit were not telephoned.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Laboratory Values and Cardiac Isoenzymes, 1st paragraph; Methods › Follow-up, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cocaine use in the past week was self-reported (the entry criterion); urine was tested only at the treating physician's discretion, and 91 of 92 patients tested (98.9%) had cocaine metabolites.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants (p. 332); Methods › Laboratory Values and Cardiac Isoenzymes, 2nd paragraph (p. 333); Results › Cocaine Use, 1st paragraph (starting p. 332)

key_findings.finding: Profile: median age 33 years, 71.5% men, 83.3% not white, 83.3% cigarette smokers; all but one used cocaine regularly (median 5.0 years; median 10 episodes a month); 179 (72.8%) smoked cocaine, 67 (27.2%) insufflated and 26 (10.6%) injected it; median 5 hours from last use to presentation; chest pain began a median of 60 minutes after use and lasted a median of 120 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 330); Results › Cocaine Use, 1st paragraph (pp. 332–333); Results › Presentation, 1st paragraph (p. 334); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 335)

key_findings.finding: All 14 patients with MI had chest-pain onset and presented within 24 hours of cocaine use. MI incidence was 7.8% (95% CI 3.9–11.8%) among patients presenting within 24 hours and 7.4% (2.3–12.6%) within 12 hours; 81% of patients presented within 24 hours of last use.
key_findings.note: Denominators are not given. With all 14 MIs within 24 hours, 7.8% implies about 179 patients (the printed interval also fits 14/179; editors' calculation), 73% of 246 rather than the 81% stated; the number with a known time of last use is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Patients with MI differed from those without in median age (36.5 vs 33 years, p=0.025), history of chest pain (21.4% vs 52.6%, p=0.047) and shortness of breath (28.6% vs 61.2%, p=0.033). Sex, race, cardiac risk factors, chest-pain location and quality, other symptoms, vital signs, and the route, length and frequency of cocaine use and time since use did not differ significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 331); Results › Cocaine Use, 1st paragraph, end (p. 333); Table 2 and Table 3 (p. 334)

key_findings.finding: Initial ECGs (n=242): normal in 68 (28.1%); of 104 nonspecific ECGs, 76 showed ST elevation over 1 mm from early repolarization. Among the 14 with MI the initial ECG was normal in 3, nonspecific in 2, abnormal but not diagnostic in 4, ischaemic in 1 and suggestive of acute infarction in 4; among 228 without MI, 65, 102, 38, 20 and 3. An ECG showing ischaemia or infarction had sensitivity 35.7% (95% CI 10.6–60.8%), specificity 89.9% (86–93.8%), positive predictive value 17.9% (3.7–32.1%) and negative predictive value 95.8% (93.1–98.5%) for MI.
key_findings.note: The four values correspond to 5/14, 205/228, 5/28 and 205/214 (editors' reconstruction from Table 4); the exact interval for the sensitivity is 12.8–64.9%.

key_findings.finding: Initial CK was raised more often in patients with MI (86% vs 46%, p=0.009) and was higher (515 vs 177, units printed as mg/dL; p=0.0002); 10 of the 14 had a raised CK-MB in the first sample, and all 14 had a raised CK-MB within 24 hours of arrival; in 4 only the initial CK-MB was raised.
key_findings.locator: Results › Laboratory Evaluation, 1st paragraph (starting p. 334, continuing p. 335)

key_findings.finding: Patients later found to have MI were more often admitted (86% vs 55%, p=0.027) but not more often to a monitored bed (58% vs 56%). Two patients with MI were released from the ED: one, whose isoenzymes were measured only as part of the study protocol, had total CK 2,150 and MB fraction 150 (7%) and returned a week later with recurrent chest pain; the other, with an initial CK of 258, walked out after his second sample was drawn, a sample that later showed CK 567 and MB 69 (12%), and could not be traced.

Of the 14 MIs, 5 were Q-wave and 9 non-Q-wave; 7 involved the inferior wall. No patient developed an arrhythmia needing intervention, heart failure or infarct extension in hospital. Twelve patients had arrhythmias: 4 supraventricular (3 with atrial fibrillation on arrival), 4 ventricular (2 arrived in cardiac arrest) and 4 bradyarrhythmias; the 4 patients with heart failure had it on arrival. No patient received thrombolytic therapy or cardiac catheterization; all 16 treadmill tests (6 in patients with MI) were negative.

The authors note their estimate may be too low (complete isoenzyme sets were not obtained for all patients; telephone follow-up probably would not detect every missed MI) or too high (clinicians may not have notified investigators of patients considered at very low risk; if clinicians identified low-risk patients accurately, the reported frequency would be an overestimate).

For the 14 patients with MI the authors give an upper 95% limit of 21% for late complications. They conclude that MI is not uncommon in cocaine-associated chest pain (abstract) and that it is reasonable to rule out MI in every patient with chest pain within 24 hours of cocaine use (Conclusions).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Conclusions (p. 330); Future Questions, item 1, and Conclusions (p. 337)

key_findings.finding: In a comment printed with the article, the journal's reviewers think it likely that the sample over-represents patients whom clinicians thought most likely to have significant chest discomfort, think it unlikely that most patients would admit cocaine use and agree to such a study unless quite symptomatic, and note that a number of patients did not return for follow-up, so the authors used telephone or mail for their follow-up information.
key_findings.locator: Further Thoughts from the Reviewers, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Patients are said to have been enrolled over 46 months (p. 331), but the first site started on 30 April 1991 and all sites stopped on 29 May 1992 (p. 332; Appendix A, p. 339), about 13 calendar months. The site-by-site enrolment periods sum to about 46 site-months (editors' calculation), and the same group later describes COCHPA as covering an average of 8 months per site (Hollander et al., 1995b, p. 1085).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 46-month figure is enrolment time summed over sites, not the study's calendar length; any rate per month or per year needs the site-months.

reporting_issues.issue: One patient was excluded for not taking part in follow-up (p. 331), yet every analysis uses 246 patients (14 + 232; 140 + 106), and the reviewers read this as a single refusal to participate (p. 339).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether 247 patients were enrolled or whether the excluded patient remains in the denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The incidences of MI within 24 hours (7.8%) and within 12 hours (7.4%) of last cocaine use are given without denominators; with all 14 MIs presenting within 24 hours, 7.8% implies about 179 patients, 73% of 246, whereas the same paragraph says 81% presented within 24 hours (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The time-window estimates cannot be checked; the time of last use was probably unknown for some patients, but how many is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 percentages for patients without MI do not match their counts (systolic pressure 91–139 mm Hg: 150 printed as 64.5%, computed 64.7%; below 90 mm Hg: 3 printed as 0.4%, computed 1.3%; pulse 60–100: 151 printed as 65.0%, computed 65.1%), and Table 4 shows normal ECG 65 as 29.0% (computed 28.5% of 228) and nonspecific 102 as 45.0% (computed 44.7%), a column summing to 100.8% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the counts add up to the group totals (232 and 228), so the counts rather than the printed percentages should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Total CK and CK-MB values are printed in mg/dL (initial CK 515 vs 177; a released patient's CK 2,150 with MB 150), a mass-concentration unit not used for an enzyme activity such as CK (the companion series reports CK in U/L; Hollander et al., 1995b, p. 1083). The statement that initial CK levels were 'less likely to be the peak' (85% vs 36%) does not say which proportion the percentages describe.
reporting_issues.consequence: The CK values cannot be compared with reference ranges, and the direction of the peak-CK comparison is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that there was no clinical difference between patients with and without MI (p. 330), whereas Table 1, Table 2, Table 4 and the text report significant differences in age, history of chest pain, shortness of breath, ECG category and initial CK.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract understates the differences found; what the data support is that none of them separated patients with MI well enough to identify a very-low-risk group.

reporting_issues.issue: The results say that all 223 patients with follow-up data were alive at follow-up (p. 332), but the follow-up interval is not defined: released patients were telephoned within 2 weeks if they did not return, while patients ruled out in hospital were not telephoned (p. 333).
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of deaths among survivors covers different, unstated time windows (hospital stay or up to about 2 weeks) and should not be cited as a 30-day mortality.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% intervals are normal-approximation intervals at small counts: for 14/246 the printed 2.7–8.7% compares with an exact interval of 3.1–9.4%, and for the ECG sensitivity (5/14) the printed 10.6–60.8% with an exact 12.8–64.9% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed intervals sit slightly too low; claims should use the exact intervals or say that the printed ones are approximations.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods classify initial ECGs into six categories, separating ischaemia known to be old (an unchanged comparison ECG) from ischaemia not known to be old (p. 332), but Table 4 has five rows with a single 'Ischemic' row (p. 335), and the paper does not say where ECGs with ischaemia known to be old were placed. The sensitivity and specificity count 'Ischemic' and 'Suggestive of acute infarction' as positive (5/14 and 205/228; editors' reconstruction).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether ECGs with old, unchanged ischaemia counted as positive is unknown; if they did, the 89.9% specificity and 17.9% positive predictive value describe any ischaemic-looking initial ECG, not new ischaemia.

design_detail: Retrospective multicentre chart review by the Cocaine Associated Myocardial Infarction (CAMI) Study Group at 29 acute-care hospitals in the United States, covering 1987–1993; the authors call it a retrospective cross-sectional survey (p. 1237). Hospital patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction whose initial ECG met TIMI criteria for thrombolysis were split into those who received thrombolytic therapy (n=25) and those who did not (n=41), and in-hospital deaths, complications, cardiac enzyme peaks and clinical signs of reperfusion were compared. The treating clinicians decided who was thrombolysed; the study did not. Filed as a retrospective cohort appraised with ROBINS-I because a hospital treatment is compared between non-randomized groups.
can_establish: That among 25 hospital patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction who were thrombolysed in 1987–1993, none had an intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding needing transfusion and none died in hospital, and that treated and untreated ECG-eligible patients did not differ significantly in enzyme peaks or in-hospital complications.
cannot_establish: That thrombolysis carries a low risk in this population (0 of 25 is compatible with a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14%); its safety in patients thrombolysed for ST elevation who turned out not to have an infarction (excluded by design); or whether it works (treatment was not randomized, co-treatments differed, and efficacy was judged from chart notes and from enzyme peaks sampled every 8–12 hours).

sample.recruitment: Records (clinic): at 29 acute-care institutions (named in the Acknowledgment, p. 1240), patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction from 1987 to 1993 were found by cross-referencing ICD-9 codes for myocardial infarction with the codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse (the coding categories searched), and by reviewing the records of all patients with infarction aged 40 or younger for evidence of cocaine use (p. 1237, Methods › Patients).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All three criteria were required: (1) cocaine use in the 24 hours before presentation by history, or cocaine metabolites on a urine screen; (2) infarction by both the international diagnostic criteria (ref. 24) and the attending physician's clinical impression; (3) an initial ECG meeting TIMI criteria for thrombolysis (p. 1237). Patients not meeting the ECG criteria were excluded before the comparison (p. 1238).
sample.demographics: Not thrombolysed (n=41) vs thrombolysed (n=25): mean age 38.1 (SD 9.8) vs 39.8 (SD 10.3); men 73% vs 88%; nonwhite 83% vs 64%; hypertension 34% vs 20%; diabetes 7% vs 4%; hypercholesterolaemia 20% vs 20%; family history 34% vs 48%; tobacco 85% vs 96%; previous infarction 10% vs 16% (Table 1, p. 1238).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). Reperfusion information was charted for 21 of the 25 thrombolysed patients (p. 1238).
sample.selection_effects: The number excluded for not meeting the ECG criteria is not given, and whether the 25 and 41 count patients or infarctions is not stated (136 infarctions occurred in 130 patients) (p. 1238). Case-finding relied on coding of cocaine or drug abuse and on chart review limited to patients aged 40 or younger, so older patients and those whose cocaine use was not recorded were less likely to enter. Requiring a confirmed infarction removes patients who were thrombolysed for ST elevation without an infarction, a group the authors say may be large (in one series 43% met TIMI criteria without infarction, p. 1239). Who received thrombolysis was decided by clinicians at 29 hospitals over 7 years, for reasons not recorded. In-hospital outcomes are reported only for the 66 ECG-eligible patients (pp. 1238–1239); the course of the other patients of the 130, and complication rates and timing for the whole series, are in the companion report of the same series (Hollander et al., 1995b).

exposure.measurement: Intervention: thrombolytic therapy as recorded in the chart. The agent and dosing regimen were abstracted (p. 1238) but are not reported; one patient is said to have received streptokinase. Cocaine use: chart history of use within 24 hours or a positive urine screen.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Thrombolytic agents and doses not reported. Time since last cocaine use, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: under 4 hours 39% vs 40%, under 24 hours 81% vs 64%. Duration of chest pain at presentation: under 1 hour 20% vs 28%, 1–3 hours 34% vs 48%, 3–6 hours 12% vs 12%, 6–24 hours 20% vs 8%, over 24 hours 5% vs 4%, unknown 2% vs 0%; three untreated patients had no chest pain (Table 1, p. 1238). Route of cocaine use was abstracted but not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or reported, apart from tobacco (85% vs 96%).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (acute presentation).

comparison.controls: 41 hospital patients with cocaine-associated infarction whose initial ECG met TIMI criteria but who were not thrombolysed; the reasons are not recorded.
comparison.matching: None. Measured baseline variables did not differ significantly, but co-treatment did: aspirin 49% vs 76% and beta-adrenergic blockade 5% vs 32% in the untreated and treated groups, with no p-values printed; nitroglycerin 85% vs 96% (NS); calcium-channel blockers 17% vs 24% (Table 1, p. 1238). Editors' calculation (Fisher's exact test on counts reconstructed from the percentages and group sizes): aspirin p=0.04, beta-blockade p=0.005.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Contraindications to thrombolysis, certainty of the ECG diagnosis, coronary anatomy, delay from arrival to treatment, hospital and year were not compared; these drive both the treatment decision and outcomes.

outcomes.instruments: Chart review. Serial cardiac isoenzymes every 8 to 12 hours, giving peak CK and CK-MB and time to peak. Complications recorded: heart failure, ventricular tachycardia, supraventricular tachydysrhythmias, bradydysrhythmias, ventricular rupture, septal perforation and death; for thrombolysed patients, clinical evidence of reperfusion and complications attributable to thrombolysis. Major complications were defined as intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding requiring transfusion (p. 1238).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical reperfusion signs (resolution of ECG changes, resolution of chest pain, reperfusion dysrhythmias) were taken from chart notes, and reperfusion was counted when two or more were present, a rule stated only in the Discussion (p. 1239). No angiographic patency or ventricular-function data.
outcomes.operationalization: Safety: major complications attributed to thrombolysis (intracerebral haemorrhage, bleeding requiring transfusion), with minor complications described one by one. Efficacy proxies: peak CK and CK-MB, time to peak, and clinical reperfusion.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p<0.05 for every test (p. 1238). The 10 are the nine comparisons in Table 2 plus lactate dehydrogenase, reported only in the text.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; chart abstraction by site investigators, with treatment known.

analysis.effect_sizes: Major complications attributed to thrombolysis: 0 of 25 (printed 95% CI 0 to 12%); no in-hospital deaths in either group; minor complications in 2 of 25 (a self-limited febrile reaction after streptokinase, not treated; vaginal bleeding without transfusion) (p. 1238). Editors' calculation: 12% equals 3/25, the rule-of-three approximation to a one-sided 95% limit; the exact two-sided 95% interval for 0 of 25 is 0 to 13.7%. Reperfusion signs in 14 of 21 thrombolysed patients with information (67%): resolution of ECG changes 62%, resolution of chest pain 86%, reperfusion dysrhythmias 29% (p. 1238). Not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed (Table 2, p. 1239): median peak CK 1,115 U/L (562–2,669) vs 1,911 (763–3,580); median peak CK-MB 154 (29–283) vs 180 (67–409), unit not given in the table and printed as mg/dL in the abstract; time to peak CK 14.4 vs 13.7 hours (p=0.8); time to peak CK-MB 13.6 vs 11.3 hours (p=0.57); heart failure 7% vs 4%; sustained ventricular tachycardia 2% vs 0%; supraventricular tachycardia 2% vs 8%; bradydysrhythmias 10% vs 12%; deaths 0% vs 0%; all reported as not significant.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted Mann-Whitney U or t tests and chi-square or Fisher's exact tests (p. 1238).
analysis.selective_reporting: Thrombolytic agents and dosing regimens were abstracted but not reported. Lactate dehydrogenase peaks are said not to differ (p. 1238) but appear in no table. Table 1 prints no p-values for the aspirin, calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker rows, and the Results text names only nitroglycerin among co-treatments that did not differ (p. 1238), although the Discussion acknowledges more beta-blockade in the treated group (p. 1239).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 25 treated patients, a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14% cannot be excluded (editors' calculation), against the under-2% the authors cite for patients without cocaine use (p. 1239). The authors state the sample is too small to compare complication rates with patients who do not use cocaine (p. 1239).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No intracerebral haemorrhage, transfusion-requiring bleeding or in-hospital death among 25 patients thrombolysed for cocaine-associated infarction at 29 hospitals over 7 years, with two minor complications; no significant differences from 41 untreated ECG-eligible patients in enzyme peaks, time to peak or complications, in groups that differed in co-treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that thrombolysis "appears to be safe" (p. 1237), and the Discussion that on this series it would appear safe (p. 1239). Zero events in 25 patients is compatible with a major-complication rate of up to about 12–14% (the paper prints 0 to 12%), so the data exclude only a very high rate; the Limitations put it more accurately, saying the risk does not appear so high as to prohibit use (p. 1239). The series also leaves out the patients most exposed to inappropriate thrombolysis (ST elevation without infarction), whom the authors themselves identify as a problem (p. 1239). On efficacy the abstract is appropriately uncertain, and the Discussion names beta-blocker co-treatment as a possible confounder (p. 1239). The closing management sequence for hospital care (oxygen, intravenous access, benzodiazepines, aspirin and nitroglycerin; then primary angioplasty or thrombolysis for persisting infarction) is the authors' clinical opinion with cited support, not a result of this study (p. 1240).

timeline.event: Bush (ref. 23): report of a patient with cocaine-associated infarction who died of an intracerebral haemorrhage after thrombolysis, the report behind the safety concern (as cited, p. 1239)
Lange et al.: beta-adrenergic blockade potentiated cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction (ref. 5), cited here for the beta-blocker imbalance between groups
This series: 0 of 25 thrombolysed patients had a major complication; combined by the authors with 11 earlier case reports, 1 intracerebral haemorrhage in 36 thrombolysed patients (2.8%)

Companion report of the same CAMI series (Hollander et al., Arch Intern Med 1995): 136 infarctions in 130 patients at 29 hospitals, no in-hospital deaths, complications recorded 64 times in 49 patients (36%), about half present on arrival, first complication more than 12 hours after arrival in 5 of 49
Single-hospital series with this paper's first author as last author: 6% of 250 patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain met WHO criteria for infarction

replication.where_it_stands: No randomized or adequately sized comparative study of thrombolysis in cocaine-associated infarction is cited; the authors themselves call for prospective studies of ventricular function and arterial patency with standardized co-treatment before widespread use (p. 1240). The safety evidence in this paper is 25 patients plus 11 case reports.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency medicine and toxicology departments at SUNY Stony Brook, Bellevue Hospital Center and the New York City Poison Control Center (NYU), and Mount Sinai Medical Center, Cleveland (p. 1237); 29 participating centres listed (p. 1240). An editorial comment appeared in the same issue (p. 1189, per the note on p. 1237); it was not among the files read.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective registry or trial of patients with cocaine-associated ST-elevation infarction comparing reperfusion strategies with standardized co-treatment, with angiographic patency and ventricular function as outcomes, recording every patient thrombolysed for ST elevation whether or not an infarction is confirmed, and large enough (several hundred treated patients) to estimate major bleeding at rates near 1–2%.

domains.note: Clinicians chose whom to thrombolyse, reasons and contraindications were not recorded, and nothing was adjusted. Measured baseline variables did not differ significantly in small groups, though race came close (83% vs 64% nonwhite; editors' p 0.08–0.15).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Entry required an infarction confirmed after treatment, which excludes patients thrombolysed for ST elevation without infarction; case-finding relied on coding and on chart review limited to patients aged 40 or younger; the number excluded and the unit of analysis are unclear.
Receipt of thrombolysis is recorded in the chart; agents and regimens are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-treatment differed: beta-blockade 32% vs 5% and aspirin 76% vs 49% (editors' p 0.005 and 0.04); the authors note that beta-blockade may have confounded the assessment of efficacy (p. 1239).
Reperfusion information for 21 of 25; completeness of enzyme series and complication records not reported.
Intracerebral haemorrhage and transfusion are hard outcomes; reperfusion was judged from chart notes by unblinded abstractors, and sampling every 8–12 hours limits comparisons of time to peak.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Agents, doses and lactate dehydrogenase data were abstracted but not reported; p-values omitted for co-treatments that differed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I overall follows the worst domains (confounding, selection and co-intervention). For the safety count in the treated group (no major complication in 25) the main problems are selection (patients thrombolysed without infarction are excluded) and imprecision rather than confounding; for the comparison of treated with untreated patients on enzyme peaks and complications, confounding by indication and unequal co-treatment leave the comparison close to uninformative. The card may be cited for what happened to 25 hospital patients thrombolysed for cocaine-associated infarction in 1987–1993 (no major bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage, no deaths, two minor complications) and for how little that observation can exclude; not as evidence that thrombolysis is as safe here as in other patients, or that it does or does not work.

key_findings.finding: Case-finding at 29 US hospitals, 1987–1993: 136 cocaine-associated myocardial infarctions in 130 patients; after excluding those whose initial ECG did not meet TIMI criteria, 25 had received thrombolytic therapy and 41 met the ECG criteria but had not.
key_findings.note: The number excluded, and whether 25 and 41 count patients or infarctions, is not stated.

key_findings.finding: No in-hospital deaths in either group; no intracerebral haemorrhage or bleeding requiring transfusion attributed to thrombolysis (0%, printed 95% CI 0 to 12%); two minor complications: a self-limited febrile reaction after streptokinase, and vaginal bleeding that did not need transfusion.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 0 of 25 has an exact two-sided 95% interval of 0 to 13.7%; 12% is the rule-of-three value (3/25).

key_findings.finding: Clinical evidence of reperfusion (two or more signs) in 14 of 21 thrombolysed patients with charted information (67%): resolution of ECG changes 62%, resolution of chest pain 86%, reperfusion dysrhythmias 29%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy of Thrombolytic Therapy (p. 1238); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1239)

key_findings.finding: Not thrombolysed (n=41) vs thrombolysed (n=25): median peak CK 1,115 U/L (562–2,669) vs 1,911 (763–3,580); median peak CK-MB 154 (29–283) vs 180 (67–409); time to peak CK 14.4 vs 13.7 hours (p=0.8); time to peak CK-MB 13.6 vs 11.3 hours (p=0.57); none significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy of Thrombolytic Therapy (p. 1238); Table 2 (p. 1239)
key_findings.note: No unit is given for CK-MB in Table 2; the abstract prints mg/dL (p. 1237).

key_findings.finding: In-hospital complications, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: heart failure 7% vs 4%, sustained ventricular tachycardia 2% vs 0%, supraventricular tachycardia 2% vs 8%, bradydysrhythmias 10% vs 12%, death 0% vs 0%; none significant.

Co-treatment, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: nitroglycerin 85% vs 96% (NS), aspirin 49% vs 76%, calcium-channel blockers 17% vs 24%, beta-adrenergic blockade 5% vs 32%; no p-values printed for the last three.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Fisher's exact test on counts reconstructed from the percentages: 20/41 vs 19/25 and 2/41 vs 8/25): aspirin p=0.04, beta-blockade p=0.005.

key_findings.finding: Baseline, not thrombolysed vs thrombolysed: mean age 38.1 vs 39.8; men 73% vs 88%; nonwhite 83% vs 64%; last cocaine use under 4 hours 39% vs 40% and under 24 hours 81% vs 64%; anterior infarction 49% vs 48%; Q-wave 46% vs 56%; all reported as not significant.
key_findings.note: The abstract describes the groups as similar at p>0.20 (p. 1237); editors' tests on reconstructed counts give p=0.08–0.15 for race depending on the test, and 81% is not a possible share of 41 (33/41 = 80.5%).

key_findings.finding: Adding this series to 11 earlier case reports of thrombolysis for cocaine-associated infarction, the authors count 1 intracerebral haemorrhage (fatal, from a case report) among 36 thrombolysed patients (2.8%).

Limitations stated by the authors: too few patients to compare complication rates with patients who do not use cocaine; difficulty of identifying infarction on the ECG after cocaine (in one cited series 43% met TIMI criteria without infarction); no demonstrated benefit; unstandardized co-treatment, with more beta-blockade in the treated group possibly confounding efficacy.

The authors recommend a cautious policy on thrombolysis in cocaine-associated chest pain with ST elevation and prospective studies with standardized co-treatment before widespread use; their hospital management sequence is opinion supported by other references, not a result of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives median peak CK-MB as 180 vs 154 mg/dL (p. 1237); Table 2 gives no unit (p. 1239), and mg/dL is not a plausible unit for CK-MB; the abbreviation box also defines CK-MB simply as creatine kinase (p. 1237).
reporting_issues.consequence: The CK-MB values cannot be compared with other studies; cite them only as similar between groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed 95% CI for 0 of 25 (0 to 12%) is the rule-of-three value; the exact two-sided interval is 0 to 13.7% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either way the data cannot exclude a major-complication rate several times the under-2% the authors cite for patients without cocaine use.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups were similar in age, sex, race, risk factors, time since cocaine use and duration of pain at p>0.20 (p. 1237), and Table 1 gives 81% of the untreated group with use in the previous 24 hours (p. 1238). Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 (counts from percentages and group sizes): race (34/41 vs 16/25 nonwhite) gives p=0.08 (chi-square), 0.15 (Yates) or 0.14 (Fisher); sex gives 0.15–0.26 and use within 24 hours 0.14–0.23; and 81% of 41 is not attainable (33/41 = 80.5%, 34/41 = 82.9%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The groups were less similar than the abstract says; with groups of 41 and 25, non-significance says little about comparability.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints no p-values for aspirin (49% vs 76%), calcium-channel blockers or beta-blockade (5% vs 32%), and the Results text lists only nitroglycerin among co-treatments that did not differ (p. 1238).
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' Fisher tests give p=0.04 (aspirin) and p=0.005 (beta-blockade): the groups differed in co-treatment, which the Discussion acknowledges only for beta-blockade (p. 1239).

reporting_issues.issue: 136 infarctions occurred in 130 patients, but the comparison is described in patients without saying how repeat infarctions were handled, and the number excluded for not meeting TIMI criteria is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator and the unit of analysis are unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Lactate dehydrogenase peaks are said not to differ (p. 1238) but appear in no table; the thrombolytic agents and dosing regimens were abstracted (p. 1238) but are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcomes and treatment details that were collected cannot be checked.

verification.source_read: PDF of the scanned print pages (version of record), Chest 107(5), pp. 1237–1241 (5 page images; the OCR text layer has errors, so every number was read on 150-dpi renderings; Tables 1–2 checked; p. 1241 holds the last references and an advertisement; no supplement). The editorial comment named on p. 1237 (Chest 107(5), p. 1189) was not among the files read.

disagreements.first_pass: The number excluded for not meeting the ECG criteria is not given, and whether the 25 and 41 count patients or infarctions is not stated (136 infarctions occurred in 130 patients) (p. 1238). Case-finding relied on coding of cocaine or drug abuse and on chart review limited to patients aged 40 or younger, so older patients and those whose cocaine use was not recorded were less likely to enter. Requiring a confirmed infarction removes patients who were thrombolysed for ST elevation without an infarction, a group the authors say may be large (in one series 43% met TIMI criteria without infarction, p. 1239). Who received thrombolysis was decided by clinicians at 29 hospitals over 7 years, for reasons not recorded.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 359 (missed): outcomes are reported only for the 66 ECG-eligible patients; the paper gives no in-hospital course for the other patients of the 130 and no overall complication rate (for example 38%) or timing (90% within 12 hours).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on pp. 1238–1239 (Results and Table 2 cover 25 + 41 patients); sentence added naming the companion report, read in this round (Hollander et al., 1995b, Arch Intern Med 155:1081–1086: complications 64 times in 49 patients, 36%; first complication after 12 hours in 5 of 49; no in-hospital deaths among 136) (AI reader 388).

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 359 (missed): the 38% and 90% figures linked to this series must come from another report of it.
disagreements.resolution: Entry added for the companion report, read in this round (pp. 1081, 1083–1084) (AI reader 388).

disagreements.resolution: True as printed (also in Hollander et al., 1995b, p. 1086) but bears on no finding; not added (AI reader 388).
