design_detail: Single-centre clinical series of consecutive emergency department (ED) visits for symptoms suggestive of myocardial ischaemia after cocaine use at the Medical College of Virginia Hospitals (Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond), January 1994 to June 1996. Data were collected prospectively on a standardized form, with retrospective review of records to fill gaps and retrospective ascertainment of 30-day cardiac events; the analysis unit is the visit (241 visits by 218 patients). All patients were triaged by the hospital's existing chest-pain strategy: high-risk patients to the coronary care unit (CCU) without imaging, the rest injected with technetium-99m sestamibi in the ED and imaged by gated single-photon emission computed tomography 60 to 90 minutes later. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist because every figure the site would use is a proportion in a defined consecutive sample (how often myocardial infarction was diagnosed, how often scans were positive, what 30-day follow-up found); the paper also reports a diagnostic-accuracy sub-analysis of the scan against a cardiac-marker definition of infarction, which would call for QUADAS-2 and is described but not separately appraised here (flagged for the senior author).
can_establish: How often myocardial infarction was diagnosed among the patients who were admitted and had serial cardiac markers, how often rest sestamibi scans were read as positive, and what retrospective 30-day follow-up found in the patients discharged after a negative scan, in one US emergency department in 1994 to 1996.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the symptoms, the scans or the events (every patient had used cocaine; there is no comparison group with chest pain who had not); the true frequency of infarction in the whole cohort (serial markers were obtained only in the 69 admitted visits of 241); whether early imaging is safer or more effective than routine CCU admission (no comparison group and no randomization); the accuracy of the scan with useful precision (only 2 infarctions occurred among the patients imaged); or anything about the amount, route, timing or chronicity of cocaine use, which the authors state were not documented.

sample.recruitment: Consecutive ED presentations at one urban academic hospital over 2.5 years; no advertising or sampling. 218 patients underwent 245 ED evaluations; 11 had more than one evaluation and 4 left against medical advice before the evaluation was complete and were excluded, leaving 241 visits (p. 641, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: symptoms consistent with myocardial ischaemia associated with recent cocaine use, with cocaine use established by the patient acknowledging recent use or by a positive urine drug screen. Urine screening was routine only for admitted patients who had a history of cocaine use or were younger than 50 without known coronary disease. Excluded: 4 patients who left against medical advice. One patient with uninterpretable images was counted in the group that did not undergo imaging (pp. 640, 641).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 641), denominator not stated: mean age 36±8 years; 67% male; hypertension 25%; diabetes mellitus 6%; tobacco use 63%; family history of coronary disease 23%; hyperlipidaemia 3%; mean 1.2±1.0 risk factors; prior myocardial infarction 8%. Race, employment and the interval between cocaine use and presentation are not reported.
sample.attrition: 30-day follow-up was unknown for 18 patients (8% of 241), who were checked only against Virginia Division of Health Statistics death registry data; of the 172 not admitted, 39 returned for outpatient stress imaging and 115 of the remaining 133 were known to be alive and event-free at 30 days (p. 642).
sample.selection_effects: A single urban academic ED whose standing triage protocol already used rest perfusion imaging, in the years when cocaine-associated infarction was newly recognized, so admission thresholds and imaging access are specific to that service. Identification depended on the patient disclosing recent use or on a urine screen that was not applied to everyone, and the authors note that it is unlikely all patients with cocaine-associated chest pain were captured, citing evidence that up to 25% of patients with a positive drug test deny recent use (p. 644). The analysis counts visits, not patients, so the 11 patients with more than one visit are counted more than once.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported recent cocaine use, or a positive urine drug screen; screening was routine only among admitted patients meeting the two stated criteria, so for the 172 visits that were not admitted, cocaine use probably rests largely on self-report (editors' inference; the paper does not say whether screens were ordered in the ED). The paper does not report how many patients were identified each way, nor the assay used or its cut-off (p. 640).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not documented. The authors state they were unable to record the timing, amount, route of ingestion or the presence of long-term use, and add that the amount used has not been shown to predict cocaine-associated infarction, citing an earlier multicentre study (p. 644).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Tobacco use is recorded as a cardiac risk factor in 63% (Table 1, p. 641); alcohol and other drugs are not reported, and no co-detected substances from the urine screens are given.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the interval between cocaine use and presentation was not recorded. Half of the patients imaged were injected with the tracer during ongoing symptoms, so the other half were not (p. 642).

comparison.controls: None. Every patient had used cocaine; there is no group with chest pain who had not used cocaine, no untested or unimaged comparison group, and no comparison of the imaging strategy against routine CCU admission. Published rates from other cohorts are discussed in the Discussion but were not analysed alongside these data (p. 643).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use cardiac imaging or marker levels. Prior cardiac status is captured only as self-reported history (prior infarction 8%, known coronary disease used in triage); left ventricular hypertrophy was recorded only on the ECG, and duration of cocaine use was unknown, so the 'chronic cocaine use' explanation offered for the symptoms (p. 643) cannot be tested in these data.

outcomes.instruments: Total serum creatine kinase (CK) by Vitros without pretreatment and CK-MB by mass assay (Behring Diagnostics), with a CK relative index calculated as CK-MB×100/total CK; serial sampling in admitted patients only. Gated single-photon emission computed tomography after 20 to 30 mCi of technetium-99m sestamibi injected in the ED, triple-headed camera, 180 degrees at 3-degree increments, 2 seconds per stop, gating at 8 frames per cardiac cycle, mean acquisition 18 minutes, read by one experienced nuclear medicine attending physician. ECGs read by a cardiologist blinded to clinical findings and outcomes. Thirty-day events ascertained from chart review, scripted telephone interviews, record review and state death-registry data (pp. 640, 641).
outcomes.validity_norms: CK-MB mass with a relative index was the standard definition of infarction in 1999 (troponin was not used). The scan's reference standard is therefore the marker definition, which was applied only to admitted patients. No reproducibility, second reader or inter-observer agreement is reported for the scans, and whether the reader knew the clinical details is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Myocardial infarction: CK-MB of 8.0 ng/mL or more with a relative index of 4.0 or more, together with a characteristic rise and fall of markers. A positive scan: a perfusion defect with associated wall-motion and thickening abnormality; everything else was read as negative for ischaemia and infarction. Cardiac event within 30 days: infarction, significant coronary disease (70% stenosis or more) or cardiac death. ECG: acute infarction if ST elevation of 1 mm or more in 2 contiguous leads; ischaemia if ST depression of 1 mm or more or symmetric ischaemic T-wave inversion of 3 mm or more (pp. 640, 641).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; P below .05 was treated as significant (p. 641). The comparisons reported are six chest-pain characteristics and mean age between the 12 patients with infarction or significant coronary disease and all others; no P value, numerator or denominator is printed for any of them.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: ECG interpretation was blinded to clinical findings and outcomes. Blinding is not reported for the nuclear medicine physician reading the scans, for the cardiac-marker interpretation or for the retrospective ascertainment of 30-day events (pp. 640, 641).

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions only; the paper prints no confidence intervals except for the two accuracy estimates. Infarction: 6 of 69 admitted visits (8.7%) and 6 of 241 visits overall (2.5%); editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals 3.3% to 18.0% and 0.9% to 5.3%. Positive rest scans 5 of 216 (2.3%; editors' calculation 0.8% to 5.3%). Significant coronary disease among the 211 negative scans: 2 (0.9%; editors' calculation 0.1% to 3.4%). Inducible ischaemia at stress imaging 5 of 67 (7.5%; editors' calculation 2.5% to 16.6%). Printed accuracy, admitted patients who were imaged: sensitivity 100% (95% CI 50% to 100%), specificity 99% (86% to 100%); all patients imaged: sensitivity 100% (50% to 100%), specificity 99% (96% to 100%). Only the last reproduces from the printed counts (211 of 214 patients without infarction, 98.6%, editors' exact interval 96.0% to 99.7%); see reporting issues.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment, no regression, no account of repeated visits by the same patient.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is cited (1999). The authors state that the triage strategy is standard care at the institution and that monitoring and data collection formed part of a continuous quality improvement process, which was not considered to need approval of the Committee on the Conduct of Human Research (p. 640).
analysis.selective_reporting: No protocol exists to check against. Within the paper, the chest-pain comparisons are reported only as percentages with a statement of no significant difference, and the denominators of Table 1 and of the CK percentages are not printed.
analysis.power: Not reported and not relevant to the descriptive proportions, but decisive for the accuracy estimates: with 2 infarctions among the patients imaged, sensitivity has an exact 95% interval of 15.8% to 100% (editors' calculation). The authors acknowledge that the low number of events gave wide intervals for sensitivity (p. 644).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 241 consecutive ED visits for chest pain or related symptoms after cocaine use at one hospital, infarction was diagnosed in 6 (2.5% of visits; 8.7% of the 69 admitted visits, which were the only ones with serial cardiac markers); 5 of 216 rest sestamibi scans (2%) were positive; of the 211 patients with a negative scan, 2 had significant coronary disease at angiography; among the 172 not admitted, 39 had normal outpatient stress imaging and 115 of the remaining 133 were known to be alive and event-free at 30 days, with 18 (8%) not traced beyond a death-registry query.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that acute infarction is infrequent in patients presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain, that positive rest scans are uncommon and suggest ischaemia is infrequently the cause of the symptoms, and that early perfusion imaging may offer an effective alternative to routine CCU admission (pp. 639, 644). Three gaps. (1) The denominator: infarction could be diagnosed only where serial markers were taken, which was in 69 of 241 visits; the authors name this as a limitation (p. 644), but the headline rate of 2.5% is nevertheless calculated over all 241. (2) The follow-up: the statement that there were no cardiac events at 30 days after a negative scan rests on 115 traced patients of the 172 not admitted, plus 39 with normal outpatient stress imaging, with 18 untraced except in a death registry that can show deaths but not non-fatal events. (3) The strategy claim is uncontrolled: no patient was managed any other way in this study, so 'an effective alternative to routine CCU admission' is an inference from a single-arm series, as is the supporting observation-unit argument drawn from a separate 113-patient report (p. 644); the Discussion also says, without hedging, that a low clinical suspicion, a nonischaemic ECG and a negative scan together identify patients whom it is safe to discharge from the ED (p. 644, 9th paragraph), which rests on 154 of the 172 not admitted being traced (39 normal stress scans, 115 event-free) and on no serial markers in them. The accuracy figures are the weakest numbers in the paper and are the ones most likely to be cited; the authors' own caution about wide intervals (p. 644) understates the problem that the printed sensitivity interval does not match the 2 infarctions among imaged patients.

timeline.event: Prospective multicentre evaluation of cocaine-associated chest pain (COCHPA; Hollander, Hoffman, Gennis et al., Acad Emerg Med), cited by this paper as finding infarction in 6% of 246 patients evaluated, including patients discharged from the ED

Series of patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction, cited here for the finding that significant coronary disease was present in about two thirds of 52 patients who had angiography after infarction
This study: infarction in 6 of 241 visits (2.5%), positive rest perfusion scans in 5 of 216 (2%), no cardiac events at 30 days among those discharged after a negative scan who could be traced

ACI-TIPI substudy (Feldman et al., Ann Emerg Med): acute MI by WHO criteria in 2 of 293 ED patients with cocaine-associated complaints at 10 US hospitals in 1993 (0.7%), both with diagnostic ECGs on arrival; it cites this study's 6 infarctions among 241 evaluations, 4 with diagnostic ST elevation, as consistent with its own results (p. 473)
How common is myocardial infarction in cocaine-associated chest pain (Weber et al., Acad Emerg Med); on the project's reading list and appraised separately in this round
American Heart Association scientific statement on the management of cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction; on the project's reading list and appraised separately in this round

replication.where_it_stands: That infarction is diagnosed in only a small minority of people presenting to an emergency department with chest pain after cocaine use is reported consistently across the cohorts cited here and in Feldman et al. (2000), with estimates from under 1% (0.7% by WHO criteria in a broader ten-hospital sample) to about 6%, depending on whom each study included and how many patients were admitted and tested. What this study adds is the rarity of positive rest perfusion scans; whether an imaging-based discharge strategy is as safe as admission has not been tested against a comparison group in this or, so far as this reader can tell from the papers cited here, any other study on the project's list.

funding.funder: Not reported. The article carries no funding or grant statement; the imaging strategy is described as standard care at the institution (p. 640).
funding.declared_conflicts: A footnote on the title page states that two of the six authors (Dr Jesse and Dr Tatum) are associated with a speakers' bureau sponsored by Dupont and give lectures on cardiovascular topics at various institutions (p. 639). The paper names Dupont Pharma as the maker of the sestamibi tracer studied (Cardiolite) (p. 640).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Internal Medicine (Cardiology), Emergency Medicine and Radiology, Medical College of Virginia / Virginia Commonwealth University. The triage strategy being described is the authors' own, previously published by the same group, and two of the three supporting references for the strategy and the assay are their own papers (pp. 640, 645). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A multicentre prospective cohort of emergency department patients with chest pain after cocaine use in which the same reference testing (serial high-sensitivity troponin) and the same structured follow-up (record linkage to admissions and deaths at 30 days and 1 year) are applied to every patient, admitted or discharged, with a concurrent comparison group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine; and, for the management question, a randomized comparison of early perfusion imaging with standard observation, reporting absolute event rates in both arms.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Consecutive presentations to one urban academic ED over 2.5 years fit the target of people seeking emergency care for chest pain after cocaine use, but a single centre whose standing protocol already used rest perfusion imaging, in 1994 to 1996, limits the frame.

Consecutive and unselected within the ED, with only 4 of 245 evaluations excluded; but entry depended on the patient disclosing recent use or on a urine screen that was routine only for some admitted patients, and the authors accept that not all eligible patients were captured (p. 644).

241 visits give the main proportions reasonable precision (infarction 2.5%, editors' exact 95% interval 0.9% to 5.3%), but the accuracy sub-analysis rests on 2 infarctions among patients imaged and cannot support a sensitivity estimate.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The setting and triage protocol are described fully; Table 1 gives age, sex and cardiac risk factors but prints no denominator, and nothing is reported about the amount, route, timing or chronicity of cocaine use, or about other substances.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The infarction proportion is calculated over 241 visits although serial markers were obtained only in the 69 admitted visits; the ECG table covers 238; 30-day follow-up was unknown for 18 (8%) and for the discharged patients rested on charts, telephone calls and a death registry.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Serial CK-MB mass with a relative index and a characteristic rise and fall was a valid definition of infarction in 1999 for those tested, and ECGs were read blind; but the exposure that defines the cohort, cocaine use, was identified by self-report or an unspecified urine screen that cannot date use.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The reference test was applied only to admitted patients, imaging to 216 of 241, and stress imaging to 67; scans were read by a single physician with no stated blinding, no second reader and no agreement measure.

Proportions are reported without intervals; visits rather than patients are the unit, with no account of the 11 patients who attended more than once; denominators for Table 1 and the CK percentages are not printed; the chest-pain comparisons carry no test statistics; and the printed accuracy intervals do not reproduce from the printed counts (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Follow-up was missing for 18 of 241 (8%), handled by a state death-registry query, which can exclude death but not non-fatal infarction or revascularization in those patients.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist because the figures the site would use are proportions in a defined consecutive sample; a QUADAS-2 reading of the embedded accuracy analysis would flag the same two central problems, a reference standard applied only to the admitted minority (partial verification) and an index test read by one unblinded observer. Editors' summary: high risk of bias for any rate taken from this paper. The direction is known: because serial markers were obtained in 69 of 241 visits, the 2.5% infarction rate is a floor whose distance from the truth is bounded only by 30-day follow-up that was itself incomplete for 8%. Citable for: what was done to these patients and what was found in them, with the denominators stated, namely 6 infarctions among 69 admitted visits, 5 positive rest scans among 216, 2 patients with significant coronary disease among 211 negative scans, 5 of 67 stress studies showing inducible ischaemia, and no cardiac events at 30 days among the traced patients discharged after a negative scan; also for the definitions used (cardiac markers, scan positivity, cardiac event) and for the authors' disclosed ties to the tracer's manufacturer. Not citable for: the frequency of infarction after cocaine use in general, the sensitivity or specificity of sestamibi imaging, any causal statement about cocaine and the heart, or any comparison between early imaging and admission.

key_findings.finding: 218 consecutive patients underwent 245 ED evaluations for symptoms suggestive of myocardial ischaemia related to cocaine use between January 1994 and June 1996; eleven had more than one evaluation, 4 left against medical advice and were excluded, leaving 241 visits analysed. One patient with uninterpretable images was counted with those not imaged.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 640, study period); Results, 1st paragraph and Figure (p. 641)
key_findings.note: The Results spell out the number of patients with repeated visits as a word, not a numeral.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine use was established by the patient acknowledging recent use or by a positive urine drug screen; screens were routine only for admitted patients with a history of cocaine use or aged under 50 without known coronary disease. The timing, amount, route and chronicity of use were not documented.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 640); Discussion, 11th paragraph (p. 644)
key_findings.note: The paper does not say how many patients were identified by self-report and how many by a positive screen; because screening was routine only for some admitted patients, for the 172 visits that were not admitted the exposure probably rests largely on self-report (editors' inference; the paper does not say whether screens were ordered in the ED).

key_findings.finding: Myocardial infarction was defined as CK-MB of 8.0 ng/mL or more with a CK relative index (CK-MB×100/total CK) of 4.0 or more together with a characteristic rise and fall of markers; serial CK and CK-MB sampling was done in admitted patients only.

Infarction was documented in 6 of the 69 admitted visits, which the paper gives as a rate of 8.7% among admitted patients and 2.5% among all patients (the 241 analysed visits). Four of the 6 had diagnostic ST elevation and were given thrombolytic agents without complications; the other 2 had positive perfusion scans. All 6 underwent coronary angiography, which showed significant coronary disease in 4.
key_findings.locator: Figure (p. 641, for the denominator of 241); Results, 4th paragraph (p. 642)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: 3.3% to 18.0% for 6 of 69 and 0.9% to 5.3% for 6 of 241.

key_findings.finding: A total of 216 patients underwent acute rest perfusion imaging, out of the 241 analysed visits; half of them were injected while symptoms were ongoing. Five (2%) scans were positive: 2 of these patients had infarction and a third had a history of infarction. Of the 211 patients with a negative scan, 2 (one of whom was injected while free of symptoms) had significant coronary disease at angiography.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 5 of 216 is 2.3% (0.8% to 5.3%); 2 of 211 is 0.9% (0.1% to 3.4%).

key_findings.finding: Printed accuracy against the cardiac-marker definition of infarction: among admitted patients who were imaged, sensitivity 100% (95% CI 50% to 100%) and specificity 99% (95% CI 86% to 100%); including all patients imaged, sensitivity 100% (50% to 100%) and specificity 99% (96% to 100%). Only 2 infarctions occurred among the patients who were imaged.
key_findings.note: The all-imaged specificity reproduces as 211 of 214 patients without infarction (98.6%, editors' exact interval 96.0% to 99.7%); the sensitivity interval and the admitted-only specificity do not reproduce from the printed counts (see reporting issues). Partial verification: the reference standard was applied only to admitted patients.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up stress perfusion imaging was done in 67 patients: 60 (90%) normal, 4 (6%) with reversible defects, 2 (3%) with a fixed defect only and 1 (1%) with both. Three of the 4 with reversible defects had angiography, which showed significant coronary disease in 2 and a 50% lesion in the third. Mean peak heart rate on exercise was 88%±8% of the predicted maximum (median 89%), with 70% reaching 85% and 84% reaching 80%.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: patients with any reversible component are 5 of 67 (7.5%, 2.5% to 16.6%), which matches the Discussion's 7% but not the abstract's 6 of 67.

key_findings.finding: Of the 172 visits not admitted, 39 patients returned for outpatient stress perfusion imaging and all had normal results; of the remaining 133, 115 were known to be alive and without cardiac events 30 days after the ED visit, and follow-up was unknown for 18 (8%), none of whom appeared in Virginia Division of Health Statistics death-registry data. Cardiac events were defined as infarction, significant coronary disease (70% stenosis or more) or cardiac death within 30 days, ascertained retrospectively from charts, scripted telephone interviews, records and the death registry.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 2nd paragraph (p. 640); Results, last paragraph before Discussion (p. 642)

key_findings.finding: ECG findings in 238 patients (not available in 3 who were not admitted): normal 79 (33%), nonspecific changes 54 (23%), left ventricular hypertrophy with or without strain 30 (13%), early repolarization 30 (13%), early repolarization with hypertrophy 13 (6%), ischaemia 14 (6%), old infarction 7 (3%), acute infarction 5 (2%), nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay 5 (2%), other 1 (0.4%).
key_findings.note: The rows sum to 238 (editors' arithmetic). Early repolarization with and without hypertrophy together is 43 of 238 (18%), which is the text's 'almost 20%' on p. 641.

key_findings.finding: Chest-pain characteristics did not distinguish the 12 patients with infarction or significant coronary disease from all others: sharp 33% versus 33%, dull 8% versus 7%, tightness 33% versus 23%, pressure 17% versus 13%, typical 45% versus 55% and atypical 55% versus 45%. The mean age of patients with infarction (40±8 years) did not differ significantly from the rest (36±8 years).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (pp. 641–642), for the chest-pain characteristics; Results, 4th paragraph (p. 642), for the mean ages
key_findings.note: No numerators, denominators, test statistics or P values are printed for any of these comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Among patients without infarction, mean peak CK was 300±320 U/L (median 200 U/L); 12 (20%) had a peak CK above 400 U/L and 20 (34%) above 300 U/L. Five patients had a peak CK-MB above 8 ng/mL (17, 16, 11, 8.8 and 8.2 ng/mL) without an elevated relative index, with the peak on the initial sample in all 5 and lower values later; 3 of these had angiography, with significant disease in 2, and a fourth had a fixed defect on stress testing.
key_findings.note: The denominator is not printed; the percentages imply about 59 to 60 patients, which is fewer than the 63 admitted patients without infarction (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the low admission rate, with serial marker results in only a minority of patients; missing follow-up for 8%; the absence of any record of timing, amount, route or long-term use; the likelihood that not all eligible patients were included, since up to 25% of patients with a positive drug test deny recent use; and the wide confidence intervals for sensitivity caused by the low number of events.

Study context: the imaging-based triage strategy was already standard care at the institution, and monitoring and data collection were part of a continuous quality improvement process that the authors state was not considered to need approval of the institution's human research committee.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed sensitivity of 100% with a 95% interval of 50% to 100% cannot come from the 2 infarctions among the patients who were imaged: the exact interval for 2 of 2 is 15.8% to 100% (Wilson 34.2% to 100%; editors' calculation). The printed lower limit is nearer to what all 6 infarctions in the cohort would give, 4 of which were in patients who were never imaged (6 of 6: exact 54.1% to 100%; 1 − 3/6 = 50% by the rule of three), though it is not the exact interval for 6 of 6 either. The specificity of 99% (96% to 100%) for all patients imaged does reproduce, as 211 of 214 patients without infarction (98.6%, 96.0% to 99.7%), but the admitted-only specificity of 99% (86% to 100%) does not: 40 of 42 is 95.2% (83.8% to 99.4%) and 41 of 42 is 97.6% (87.4% to 99.9%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The accuracy estimates should not be cited. If they are described at all, say that both rest on 2 infarctions among imaged patients and that the published sensitivity interval is narrower than those 2 events allow.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure's branch for the 44 admitted patients who were imaged accounts for only 42 of them (4 positive and 38 negative). The Results give 211 of the 216 scans as negative, which with the Figure's 171 negatives among those not admitted requires 40 negatives among the admitted (40 plus 4 positive is 44); the same Results paragraph says none of the 44 admitted patients with negative scans had an infarction, and the abstract repeats the Figure's 38.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator for the statement that no admitted patient with a negative scan had an infarction is printed as 38 (abstract, Figure) or 44 (Results); only 40 (44 imaged admitted minus 4 positive) agrees with the Figure's 44 and the Results' 211 negatives, so 44 is not internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure's legend describes 239 patients while the Figure itself begins at 241 and the Results give 241 visits from 245 evaluations; the abstract says 218 patients had 241 ED visits, which omits the 4 excluded evaluations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three different totals circulate for the same cohort; use 241 analysed visits from 218 patients, which is the number the Figure and the Results both carry.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Figure, the outcomes listed under the 171 patients with negative scans who were not admitted (39 with negative stress imaging, 115 with no events, 18 with no follow-up) sum to 172, that is to the whole not-admitted imaged group including the 1 patient with a positive scan, who is shown separately with no follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up counts cannot be attributed solely to patients with negative scans, which is exactly the group the abstract's 30-day claim is about.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 6 of the 67 patients undergoing stress perfusion imaging had reversible perfusion defects, while the Results give 4 with reversible defects and 1 with both a fixed and a reversible defect, and the Discussion says 7% had inducible ischaemia (5 of 67 is 7.5%, editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 5 of 67 with the composition stated; the abstract's 6 is not supported by the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages are printed without their denominators in two places: Table 1 gives patient characteristics with no N, and the CK percentages among patients without infarction (12 at 20% and 20 at 34%) imply about 59 to 60 patients, which is not stated and is fewer than the 63 admitted patients without infarction.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any characteristic or CK proportion taken from this paper must be quoted without a denominator, or with the denominator described as unstated.

reporting_issues.issue: The unit of analysis is the ED visit (241), although 11 of the 218 patients attended more than once; no analysis accounts for repeated visits by the same patient.
reporting_issues.consequence: All proportions are per visit, not per patient, and their intervals are narrower than a patient-level analysis would give.

reporting_issues.issue: The ECG methods state that maximal ST deviation was measured .08 msec from the J point; the conventional measurement, and what the Q-wave criterion in the next sentence (.04 sec) implies, is 80 msec (0.08 second).
reporting_issues.consequence: A unit misprint; it does not affect the counts in Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of chest-pain characteristics between the 12 patients with infarction or significant coronary disease and all others is reported only as percentages with a statement that there was no significant difference; no numerators, denominators, test statistics or P values are given, and with 12 patients in one group a difference of 10 percentage points (tightness 33% versus 23%) could not have been detected. The typical and atypical figures for the 12 (45% and 55%) cannot be proportions of 12 (5 of 12 is 42%, 6 of 12 is 50%, 7 of 12 is 58%) but fit 5 and 6 of 11, so one value is missing or another denominator was used (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's conclusion that chest-pain characteristics do not discriminate is an absence of evidence in a very small group, not evidence of absence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure shows 1 positive rest scan among the 172 visits that were not admitted, with no follow-up (p. 641), although the Methods say that patients with positive rest imaging were admitted to the CCU (p. 640); the text does not mention or explain this patient.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either one patient with a positive scan left without admission or follow-up, a deviation from the stated protocol, or the Figure is in error; whether this patient had an infarction is unknown, and the patient is one of the 5 positive scans.

design_detail: Cross-sectional laboratory comparison of 18 adults with current DSM-IV cocaine dependence (83% with a cocaine-positive urine test) and 15 controls, all recruited by newspaper advertisement, on a computerized Go/No-Go task with easy and hard No-Go discriminations (240 trials: 180 Go, 30 easy No-Go, 30 hard No-Go), scored with signal-detection indices (d′ for discrimination, Beta for response bias), plus reaction time and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11). The task measures withholding a prepotent response, not stopping a response already started (as a stop-signal task would).
can_establish: That in this small advertisement-recruited sample, people with current cocaine dependence discriminated Go from No-Go displays less accurately than controls across trial types (d′ group effect, p=.042) and reported higher BIS-11 total and non-planning impulsiveness scores.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the difference (no pre-use data; the groups differed by 3.4 years of education and in age, sex and ethnicity, and the reported models are unadjusted); that the deficit is specific to hard trials (the group × difficulty interaction was not significant); that it reflects visual processing rather than motor inhibition (the bias and reaction-time differences were not significant and visual processing was not measured); or whether it persists with abstinence (most of the cocaine group were urine-positive).

sample.recruitment: Local newspaper advertisements for both groups; screening at intake with the SCID-I and SCID-II for DSM-IV and the Addiction Severity Index (pp. 719–720, Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cocaine group: current DSM-IV cocaine dependence (age 23–55). Controls: no history of substance dependence (age 21–55). Both: excluded for DSM-IV Axis I disorders including ADHD, dependence on any other drug, and medical conditions such as neurological or cardiovascular disease (p. 719).
sample.demographics: Mean ± SEM. Age 34.07 ± 2.63 (controls) vs 39.22 ± 2.46 (cocaine group); 8 men and 7 women vs 13 men and 5 women; ethnicity 4 Hispanic, 5 African American, 2 Asian, 4 Caucasian vs 1 Hispanic, 12 African American, 5 Caucasian; education 16.0 ± .40 vs 12.6 ± .46 years (Table 1, p. 719).
sample.attrition: All 33 completed the task; one person in the cocaine group did not complete the BIS-11 (p. 721).
sample.selection_effects: Paid volunteers answering advertisements, not a treatment sample. Despite the shared recruitment route, the groups look drawn from different populations: controls had on average 3.4 more years of education (editors' calculation: standardized difference about 1.9), were younger and more often women, and differed in ethnic composition; the authors state that the groups were not well matched (p. 722).

exposure.measurement: SCID-I diagnosis of current DSM-IV cocaine dependence and the Addiction Severity Index at intake; urine positive for cocaine in 83.33% of the cocaine group (editors' calculation: 15 of 18) and in no control. The day of the urine test relative to the testing session is not stated (pp. 719–720; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Total years of cocaine use 14.61 ± 1.70 (mean ± SEM); past-month use 21.11 ± 4.89 with no unit stated; route, amount and time since last use are not reported (Table 1, p. 719).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on any drug other than cocaine was an exclusion criterion (whether this covered nicotine is not stated); alcohol, tobacco and cannabis use are not reported for either group.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not required and not reported: participants had current dependence and 83% had a cocaine-positive urine test; time since last use is not given.

comparison.controls: 15 adults with no history of substance dependence, recruited by the same newspaper advertisements and screened with the same interviews (pp. 719–720).
comparison.matching: Not matched, as the authors state (p. 722). Age, sex and education were entered as covariates in preliminary models and then dropped because they did not interact with group or trial type; all reported results are unadjusted (p. 722). Ethnicity was not considered.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measure of inhibition or discrimination and no estimate of premorbid IQ; ADHD excluded only as a current Axis I diagnosis.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: No history of substance dependence; current use of alcohol, tobacco or other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Go/No-Go task: two patterned boxes about 3 cm apart shown for 500 ms, then a blank screen for 1900, 2100 or 2300 ms; a mouse click within 600 ms counted as a response; on No-Go trials one box differed from the Go pattern either clearly (easy) or slightly (hard), on a randomly chosen side; 240 trials (180 Go, 30 easy No-Go, 30 hard No-Go) in about 11 minutes; instructions and a payoff scheme based on the optimal-criterion formula to discourage always or never responding; earnings US$11.21 (cocaine group) and US$12.28 (controls), each ± 0.44, plus US$10 an hour (pp. 720–721; Figure 1). BIS-11 total and its non-planning, motor and attention subscales, given after the task (p. 721).
outcomes.validity_norms: Signal-detection indices separate discrimination (d′) from response bias (Beta); no normative data. BIS-11 scores compared between groups only.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Response inhibition deficit' = lower d′ (natural-log transformed because d′ and Beta were not normally distributed) in the cocaine group; Beta indexes bias toward responding (pp. 721–722).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc t-tests at .025 for the two trial types and at .0125 for the four BIS-11 scores; ANOVA effects and reaction time uncorrected (p. 722).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (computer-scored).

analysis.effect_sizes: d′ (log-transformed, mean ± SEM; Table 2, p. 722): easy 1.26 ± .06 (controls) vs 1.15 ± .04 (cocaine group); hard 0.89 ± .06 vs 0.66 ± .08. ANOVA: group F(1, 31)=4.52, p=.042; trial type F(1, 31)=133.24, p=.0001; group × trial type F(1, 31)=1.89, ns; post-hoc hard t(31)=−2.16, p=.019; easy t(31)=−1.50, ns. Beta: easy 2.33 ± .01 vs 2.38 ± .03; hard 2.20 ± .03 vs 2.25 ± .02; group F(1, 31)=2.25, ns; trial type F(1, 31)=51.42, p=.0001; interaction F(1, 31)=.10, ns; post-hoc t(31)=−1.38 (hard) and −1.19 (easy). Reaction time (Go and hard No-Go trials) 395.28 ± 9.70 vs 416.95 ± 9.76 ms, t(31)=1.58, ns. BIS-11 total 54.22 ± 2.06 vs 65.59 ± 2.68, t(30)=3.27, p=.002; non-planning 20.87 ± .88 vs 27.53 ± 1.12, t(30)=4.58, p=.0001; motor 20.33 ± .64 vs 23.18 ± 1.34 and attention 13.33 ± 1.16 vs 14.94 ± .86, not significant (pp. 722–723). Editors' calculation from the t values: standardized differences of about 0.76 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.46) for hard d′, 0.52 (−0.17 to 1.22) for easy d′, 0.55 (−0.15 to 1.25) for reaction time, 1.16 (0.41 to 1.91) for BIS-11 total and 1.62 (0.82 to 2.42) for non-planning; two-tailed p for t(31)=2.16 is about 0.039, and for the interaction F(1, 31)=1.89 about 0.18.
analysis.covariates: None in the reported models (age, sex and education removed after preliminary models; p. 722).
analysis.selective_reporting: Covariate-adjusted results, percentages of correct Go responses and No-Go errors, and untransformed d′ and Beta are not reported. The post-hoc p-value for hard trials matches a one-tailed test, which is not declared.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 18 and 15 participants only large differences could be detected reliably; the non-significant interaction cannot show either that the group difference was the same on easy and hard trials.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lower d′ in the cocaine-dependence group across trial types (group main effect, p=.042), without a significant group × difficulty interaction; a hard-trial difference that is significant only under a one-tailed test; no significant group difference in Beta or in reaction time; higher BIS-11 total and non-planning scores.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the cocaine group performed significantly worse on difficult but not easy trials and that differences in d′ but not Beta, together with slower reaction times, suggest that the deficit lay in visual information processing rather than in inhibiting motor activity (p. 717); the discussion repeats this (pp. 723–724). Gaps: (1) the difficulty-specific pattern is not supported by a significant interaction (F(1, 31)=1.89), and the hard-trial result depends on an undeclared one-tailed test (two-tailed p about 0.039 against the stated threshold of .025); (2) the 'slower reaction times' were a non-significant 21 ms difference (t(31)=1.58); (3) a non-significant Beta difference in 33 people does not show that response bias was equal; (4) visual processing was not measured separately; (5) the comparison is unadjusted for a 3.4-year education gap and other demographic differences, and most of the cocaine group had recently used cocaine, so neither a lasting nor a causal effect of cocaine can be inferred. The discussion is more cautious than the abstract, allowing that the results may reflect both reduced inhibitory control and weaker conflict monitoring (p. 724).

timeline.event: Fillmore and Rush, impaired inhibitory control in people who use cocaine chronically; cited here with Kaufman et al. (2003) and Li et al. (2006) as earlier reports of impaired response inhibition (p. 718)
Hester and Garavan: GO–NOGO task with working-memory load in 15 people tested within 72 hours of cocaine use and 15 controls; poorer inhibition in the cocaine group, increasing with load
This study: lower d′ on a Go/No-Go task with easy and hard discriminations in 18 people with current cocaine dependence.

Potvin et al. meta-analysis includes this study among its 46; the pooled impulse-related domain (Go/No-Go, stop-signal and decision tasks) gave d=0.408 in urine-positive studies (8 studies) and d=0.581 at abstinence under 12 weeks (10 studies)

López-Martín et al. meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition includes this study (18 against 15 people) at Hedges' g = 3.13 (95% CI 2.11 to 4.15) (its Fig. 2). Editors' calculation: that value is reproduced exactly when the hard-trial d′ SEMs of Table 2 (p. 722) are read as standard deviations; the study's own t(31) = −2.16 gives g of about 0.74 (d about 0.76).

replication.where_it_stands: Poorer Go/No-Go performance in people with cocaine dependence agrees with Hester and Garavan (2004) and with the pooled impulse-related domain of Potvin et al. (2014); because Potvin et al. include this study, the two are not independent support. The findings specific to this study (dependence on task difficulty; a visual-processing rather than motor-inhibition account) were not tested again in the papers read for this card. López-Martín et al. (2026) also include it, at about four times the effect its own statistics give (see the 2026 timeline entry), an entry that raises that review's pooled estimate; neither review is independent support for this study.

funding.affiliations_note: University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences; Graduate School of Biomedical Science) and Baylor College of Medicine, Houston (p. 717).

what_would_settle_it: A larger study with groups matched on education, age, sex and ethnicity, with smoking and alcohol use measured, abstinence status verified on the day of testing, and both a Go/No-Go task with graded discrimination difficulty and a stop-signal task (stopping a started response), with two-tailed tests and the group × difficulty interaction as the declared primary test; a prospective design would be needed to show cause.

domains.note: Education 16.0 vs 12.6 years, age, sex and ethnicity differ; covariates were dropped from the reported models; alcohol, tobacco and cannabis not measured; no premorbid IQ.

Current DSM-IV cocaine dependence by structured interview (SCID-I), with urine testing; but 83% were urine-positive and neither time since last use nor the day of the urine test is reported (Table 1, p. 719; p. 720), so effects of recent use or withdrawal cannot be separated from lasting ones. Amount and route not reported, and the past-month measure has no unit.
Same advertisement route for both groups, but the large education gap suggests the controls were drawn from a different population; response rates not reported.

No intervention after the start of exposure is described: people with current dependence were recruited by newspaper advertisement and tested on a later day (pp. 719–720). Recent use is judged under Measurement of the exposure.
All 33 in the task analyses; one BIS-11 missing.
Computer-scored task with signal-detection indices; BIS-11 is a self-report questionnaire.
Adjusted models not reported; an undeclared one-tailed post-hoc test; the abstract emphasizes the hard-versus-easy contrast despite a non-significant interaction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The group difference in d′ is modest (p=.042 overall) and unadjusted for a large education gap and other demographic differences, so it cannot be attributed to cocaine. The study can be cited for lower Go/No-Go discrimination and higher self-reported impulsiveness in people with current cocaine dependence compared with these controls; it should not be cited for a deficit specific to difficult trials, for a visual-processing explanation, or for deficits persisting after abstinence.

key_findings.finding: 33 adults: 18 with current DSM-IV cocaine dependence (age 23–55) and 15 controls without any history of substance dependence (age 21–55), both recruited through local newspaper advertisements and screened with the SCID-I, SCID-II and Addiction Severity Index; Axis I disorders including ADHD, dependence on any other drug and medical conditions were exclusions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph (begins p. 719, continues on p. 720)

key_findings.finding: Sample characteristics (mean ± SEM), controls vs cocaine group: age 34.07 ± 2.63 vs 39.22 ± 2.46; 8 men and 7 women vs 13 men and 5 women; education 16.0 ± .40 vs 12.6 ± .46 years; cocaine group total years of use 14.61 ± 1.70, past month 21.11 ± 4.89 (unit not stated); cocaine-positive urine 0 vs 83.33%.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 83.33% of 18 = 15 people.

key_findings.finding: Each trial showed two patterned boxes for 500 ms followed by a blank screen of 1900, 2100 or 2300 ms; a click within 600 ms counted as a response. The session had 240 trials, 180 Go (75%), 30 easy No-Go and 30 hard No-Go (12.5% each), and lasted about 11 minutes; payoffs were set to discourage always or never responding, and earnings averaged US$11.21 in the cocaine group and US$12.28 in controls.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures and Procedure, 1st paragraph (begins p. 720), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 721); Figure 1 (p. 720)

key_findings.finding: d′ and Beta were log-transformed because they were not normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk p<.05) and analysed by mixed ANOVA (group × trial type) with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc t-tests at .025. Age, sex and education were entered in preliminary models, then removed because they showed no significant interactions with group or trial type; all reported results are without covariates.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph (begins p. 721, continues on p. 722)

key_findings.finding: d′: significant main effects of group (F(1, 31)=4.52, p=.042) and trial type (F(1, 31)=133.24, p=.0001); group × trial type not significant (F(1, 31)=1.89). Post-hoc: cocaine group worse on hard No-Go trials (t(31)=−2.16, p=.019) but not on easy No-Go trials (t(31)=−1.50, ns).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (begins p. 722; statistics on p. 723)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the two-tailed p for t(31)=2.16 is about 0.039, above the stated .025 threshold; the printed .019 is the one-tailed value. The interaction p is about 0.18.

key_findings.finding: Log-transformed d′ (mean ± SEM), controls vs cocaine group: easy trials 1.26 ± .06 vs 1.15 ± .04; hard trials 0.89 ± .06 vs 0.66 ± .08.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the t values: standardized differences about 0.76 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.46) for hard and 0.52 (−0.17 to 1.22) for easy trials; the intervals overlap almost entirely. Table 2 gives SEMs, not SDs: read as SDs, the hard-trial values give g of about 3.13, the value a 2026 meta-analysis entered for this study (see the replication timeline).

key_findings.finding: Beta (response bias): no group effect (F(1, 31)=2.25, ns), a trial-type effect (F(1, 31)=51.42, p=.0001), no interaction (F(1, 31)=.10); post-hoc t(31)=−1.38 (hard) and −1.19 (easy). Table 2 values (log, mean ± SEM): easy 2.33 ± .01 vs 2.38 ± .03; hard 2.20 ± .03 vs 2.25 ± .02.
Reaction time on Go and hard No-Go trials was about 21 ms slower in the cocaine group (395.28 ± 9.70 vs 416.95 ± 9.76 ms), not significant (t(31)=1.58).

BIS-11: the cocaine group scored higher on total score (65.59 ± 2.68 vs 54.22 ± 2.06; t(30)=3.27, p=.002) and non-planning (27.53 ± 1.12 vs 20.87 ± .88; t(30)=4.58, p=.0001), not on motor impulsivity (23.18 ± 1.34 vs 20.33 ± .64) or attention (14.94 ± .86 vs 13.33 ± 1.16).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: standardized differences about 1.16 (95% CI 0.41 to 1.91) for total and 1.62 (0.82 to 2.42) for non-planning.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the d′ difference without a Beta difference, with slower reaction times, points to difficulty discriminating the displays within 500 ms rather than to a failure to withhold the motor response, and that this task places higher visual-processing demands than typical Go/No-Go tasks; they allow that the results may reflect both reduced inhibitory control and weaker conflict monitoring.

reporting_issues.issue: The hard-trial post-hoc result t(31)=−2.16 is printed with p=.019, and the stated Bonferroni threshold is .025; one-tailed testing is not declared. Editors' calculation: .019 is the one-tailed value, and the two-tailed p is about 0.039.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under two-tailed testing the hard-trial difference would not meet the paper's own threshold; the only robust d′ result is the group main effect (p=.042).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion contrast significant hard-trial with non-significant easy-trial differences, but the group × trial type interaction was not significant (F(1, 31)=1.89).
reporting_issues.consequence: The data do not show that the group difference depended on task difficulty; claims should report a general d′ difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion cite slower reaction times in the cocaine group as part of the evidence for a visual-processing explanation, although the 21 ms difference was not significant (t(31)=1.58).
reporting_issues.consequence: The visual-processing interpretation rests partly on a null result.

reporting_issues.issue: Covariates were dropped because they did not interact with group or trial type, which does not address their confounding of the group effect itself; adjusted results are not reported although education differed markedly (16.0 vs 12.6 years; editors' arithmetic: 3.4 years).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reported group differences are unadjusted for large demographic differences.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives past-month cocaine use as 21.11 ± 4.89 (mean ± SEM, cocaine group of 18) without a unit, and the timing of the urine test is not stated. Editors' calculation: if this were days of use in the past 30 days, the SEM would imply an SD of about 20.7, more than the maximum possible (about 13.7) for that range and mean.
reporting_issues.consequence: The recent intensity of use, and how recently participants had used cocaine before testing, cannot be determined.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation numbers do not match the reference list: the SCID is cited as (23), which is the BIS-11 paper; the BIS-11 as (25) and (22), which are a psychophysics textbook and the SCID; Patton et al. as (25); and reference (30) is cited although the list ends at 29. The optimal-criterion formula prints loss(incorrect No-Go) in both numerator and denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; some sources are hard to trace and the payoff formula appears to contain a typographical error; the data are unaffected.

Post-exposure interventions: some-concerns (83% urine-positive and time since last use unknown: performance may reflect recent use or withdrawal rather than lasting effects.)

Overall high unchanged.
