Recorded in the timeline, where_it_stands and the Table 2 note, because a reader may meet the 2026 value for this study.

design_detail: Systematic review (24 studies) and multilevel random-effects meta-analysis (20 studies, 23 effect sizes) of cross-sectional comparisons between adults with a cocaine use disorder (DSM, ICD or equivalent criteria; by the inclusion criteria, current use or at most two months of abstinence) and control participants without cocaine use, on behavioural tasks of inhibition: stop-signal, go/no-go, Stroop, Five Digit Test, Immediate Memory Task, probabilistic reversal learning and the Attention Network Task. Hedges' g, positive for poorer inhibition in the cocaine group; dependence between effect sizes from the same study handled with an assumed correlation of 0.7 (0.0 to 0.8 in sensitivity analyses); metafor in R (estimator not stated); moderators by Q test and meta-regression; four publication-bias indicators on one effect per study; study quality by the JBI case-control checklist. PROSPERO CRD42024592030; PRISMA 2020; databases searched to January 2024.
can_establish: The average standardized difference on laboratory inhibition tasks between adults with cocaine use disorder and control participants across 20 small cross-sectional studies published up to January 2024, how widely it varies between studies, and how much it depends on a few studies.
cannot_establish: That cocaine use caused poorer inhibition (cross-sectional comparisons, unadjusted for the age and education differences the review itself documents, with a relation the authors call likely bidirectional), how large the difference is in any particular group (prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26), whether it changes with abstinence (study-level meta-regression across samples ranging from current use to about 11 months of abstinence), or whether inhibitory-control training helps (no training study was reviewed).

sample.recruitment: Search of Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed without date limits up to January 2024, English-language peer-reviewed articles (PDF p. 3). Primary samples were clinical (people seeking treatment from clinical services, detoxification programmes or rehabilitation centres) in 14 of the 24 studies and 12 of the 20 meta-analysed, and community (recruited through advertisements, flyers, newspapers or electronic media) in 10 and 8; 15 of the 24 studies were from the USA, the others from Spain, the UK, Belgium, Switzerland and Australia (PDF pp. 3, 11).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English articles on cocaine use and cognitive inhibition in people aged 18 or older with a cocaine use disorder diagnosed by DSM, ICD (CIE) or equivalent criteria, with current use or at most two months of abstinence; a control group with no history of cocaine use; cross-sectional design; behavioural tasks of inhibition. Excluded: animal-only studies and imaging-only studies without behavioural tasks; other mental or neurodevelopmental disorders in both groups; another drug use disorder as first diagnosis; any drug use in controls except tobacco when both groups smoked (PDF p. 3). Of 38 full texts excluded, 19 had no healthy control group, 6 did not meet DSM criteria, 3 had an unknown main substance, 3 had drug use in controls and 2 did not assess inhibition; five were excluded for single other reasons, including methamphetamine use, heroin use and current psychiatric diagnoses in the cocaine group (Fig. 1, PDF p. 7).
sample.demographics: Meta-analysed samples (Table 2, PDF p. 8): 542 people with cocaine use disorder in groups of 11 to 55 and 656 controls in groups of 15 to 107; 78.97% men (two studies did not report sex); mean age 38.41 in the cocaine groups and 35.21 in controls (study means 28.18 to 52.6 and 28.6 to 42.66). By the editors' count, the cocaine group was 5 or more years older than its controls in 7 of the 19 studies reporting both ages. Years of regular use: study means 5.12 to 17.3 in 14 of the 20 meta-analysed studies (Table 1). Education, IQ and ethnicity are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Four of the 24 reviewed studies did not enter the meta-analysis because their authors did not answer requests for data (PDF p. 3); by elimination from Tables 1 and 2 they are Kaufman et al. (2003), Torres et al. (2013), Van Der Plas et al. (2009) and Zilverstand et al. (2023), two reporting significant and two non-significant differences.
sample.selection_effects: English only, a full-text filter in PubMed, no grey-literature or reference-list search reported, and a printed PubMed string that omits one of the stated search terms (executive function) (PDF p. 3). Very small samples (median group sizes 22.5 with cocaine use disorder and 26.5 controls, editors' calculation from Table 2), mostly men, and frequent age and education differences between groups. The criterion of at most two months of abstinence was not applied as stated: five included studies report mean abstinence of 152 to 335 days (Table 1). Seven of the 24 included studies are missing from the reference list, so they cannot be identified unambiguously from the article.

exposure.measurement: Cocaine use disorder by DSM, ICD or equivalent criteria (inclusion criterion). Table 1 lists structured diagnostic interviews (mostly SCID) for most studies, but no clinical or diagnostic assessment (NA) for Hester & Garavan (2004), Kaufman et al. (2003) and Wang et al. (2018). Years of regular use and days of abstinence as reported by the primary studies; amount and route were not extracted. Two studies included people using cocaine and/or crack (Ceceli et al., 2023; Ersche et al., 2008).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Years of regular use: study means 5.12 to 17.3 (14 of the 20 meta-analysed studies; Table 1, PDF pp. 4–6). Amount, frequency and route: not extracted.
exposure.polysubstance: Table 1 lists current use of other drugs in the cocaine groups: alcohol 6.67% to 100%, cannabis 12.5% to 80%, heroin 3.7% to 33.34%, and amphetamines, opioids, hallucinogens, MDMA, benzodiazepines or polysubstance use (62% in Stevens et al., 2015) in some samples; only cocaine in 7 of the 24 studies; not determined in several. The two Verdejo-García studies are of cocaine and heroin polysubstance samples (reference titles). Co-occurring substance use could not be analysed as a moderator because most studies did not report it in detail (PDF p. 15). Controls: no drug use except tobacco where both groups smoked.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: By the inclusion criteria, current use or at most two months. Table 1 (means; PDF pp. 4–6): current use in four studies (Bjork et al., 2022; Ersche et al., 2008; Lane et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2011); 3 days in two (Hester et al., 2007; Hester & Garavan, 2004); 12.62, 13.5 and 21 days in three (Stevens et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Vonmoos et al., 2013); 152 to 335 days in five (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a; Ceceli et al., 2023; Bell et al., 2014b; Hester et al., 2013); not given for the rest. Zilverstand et al. (2023), in the review only, compared early (2 to 5 days) and longer-term abstinence. How abstinence was verified was not extracted.

comparison.controls: Control participants without a history of cocaine use and without other drug use except tobacco where both groups smoked; recruitment as in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not required by the criteria. The review's own quality narrative reports group differences in education, age, sex or ethnicity, or inadequate matching, in 11 of the 24 studies (9 of the 20 meta-analysed), and Table 2 shows the cocaine groups 3.2 years older on average (38.41 vs 35.21); no pooled estimate is adjusted for these (PDF pp. 8, 14). The review's JBI item 7 (strategies to deal with confounding stated) is rated yes for 18 of the 24 studies (no for Bell et al., 2014a and 2014b, Kaufman et al., 2003, Vonmoos et al., 2013, and Wang et al., 2018; unclear for Albein-Urios et al., 2012; Table 3, PDF pp. 9–10), so some primary studies addressed confounding, though the pooled estimate uses unadjusted differences.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study measured inhibition before cocaine use (all cross-sectional). Pre-existing impulsivity, ADHD, education and IQ are not synthesized; the authors themselves state that inhibition may also influence cocaine use (PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded except tobacco; the alcohol use of controls is not described.

outcomes.instruments: Stop-signal task (stop-signal reaction time; 10 of the 24 studies), go/no-go tasks (commission errors or no-go accuracy, including an error-awareness and a working-memory-load version; 8), Stroop (2), Five Digit Test (2), Immediate Memory Task (1), Probabilistic Reversal Learning (perseverative responses; 1) and the Attention Network Task (conflict effect; 1) (PDF pp. 11–12; Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Experimental tasks without normative data; the authors state that clinical relevance therefore cannot be established (PDF p. 15). Study quality: JBI case-control checklist rated by the first author and an external collaborator, item kappas 0 to 0.5 (two not computable), converted to percentages (mean 89.06%) and labelled very low, low or moderate risk without stated thresholds (PDF pp. 9–11).
outcomes.operationalization: Poorer inhibition means a positive Hedges' g (the cocaine group's worse task score relative to controls). Different tasks and outcome variables are pooled as one construct, cognitive inhibition, which here also includes reversal learning, attentional conflict and impulsive responding; the variable taken from each study is shown only through Table 1's result column.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One pooled outcome. Five moderator tests and four publication-bias indicators in three models were run without correction; all moderator tests were non-significant, so multiplicity does not change the conclusions.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the external quality rater is described as blind to the review's objectives (PDF p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: Multilevel random-effects model, 23 effect sizes from 20 samples, within-study correlation assumed 0.7: g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03), p < .001; Q = 134.26, I² = 83.61%; 95% prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26; aggregated model (one effect per study) g = 0.64 in the text, 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) in Fig. 2B; leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72 (PDF p. 12). Study-level g (Fig. 2, PDF p. 13): 18 studies between −0.55 and 1.20; Hester & Garavan (2004) 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 (aggregated 3.56) and Lane et al. (2007) 3.13. Moderators: percentage of men Q(1) = 0.71, p = .401; years of use 0.21, p = .648; age 0.48, p = .488; days of abstinence 1.96, p = .162; clinical vs community 1.50, p = .220. Publication bias (one effect per study): fail-safe N 35; Begg 0.36, p = .028; Egger 3.00, p = .008; trim and fill one study; adjusted estimate not reported (Table 4). Editors' calculations (REML random effects on the 20 values printed in Fig. 2B, standard errors from the printed 95% CIs): this reproduces g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) and the leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72, with τ about 0.80; without Hester & Garavan (2004) and Lane et al. (2007), g = 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), I² about 65%, τ about 0.36, prediction interval about −0.39 to 1.21, and the classic Egger test is no longer significant (t = 1.05, p = 0.31; with all 20 studies t = 3.01, p = 0.007); clinical samples 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), community samples 1.03 (0.07 to 1.99), community samples without the two outlying studies 0.32 (−0.04 to 0.68). With Lane et al. (2007) and Hester & Garavan (2004) replaced by the values their own test statistics give (g about 0.74, SE 0.36, and 1.38, SE 0.41; see reporting issues): g = 0.46 (0.25 to 0.67), I² about 66%, prediction interval about −0.37 to 1.28 (t-based), classic Egger t = 1.63, p = 0.12; with Hester & Garavan taken instead as the mean of its three loads read from its Figure 2 as standard errors (about 1.04), 0.45 (0.25 to 0.65) (AI reader 392's recalculation).
analysis.covariates: None at review level: the pooled effects are unadjusted group differences. Study-level meta-regressions on percentage of men, mean age, years of regular use and days of abstinence, and a Q test for clinical vs community samples; the number of studies in each meta-regression is not reported (at most 14 for years of use and for abstinence, by the editors' count of Table 1).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42024592030; PRISMA 2020 (PDF p. 2). The registration date and any deviations from the protocol are not stated in the article, and the PROSPERO record was not read. The article's own abstinence criterion was not applied as stated (see reporting issues).
analysis.selective_reporting: τ is said to be computed but is not reported; the clinical and community subgroup estimates, the trim-and-fill-adjusted estimate and the number of studies in each meta-regression are not reported in the article (they may be in Supplementary Material 1, not read). The outlying effect sizes in Fig. 2 are not mentioned in the text.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed; the authors call the number of studies small and the samples low and ask for larger samples, especially in community studies (PDF pp. 14–15). Study-level meta-regressions on 20 or fewer studies have little power to detect moderation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 20 small cross-sectional studies (542 people with cocaine use disorder, 656 controls), the cocaine groups performed worse on average on laboratory inhibition tasks (g = 0.65, 0.28 to 1.03), with high heterogeneity (I² 83.6%) and a prediction interval from −0.95 to 2.26. Two small studies entered with effects of 3.1 to 4.9 raise the average; both values are misentered (their own reports give about 0.74 and 1.4), and with them corrected the editors' recalculation gives 0.46 (0.25 to 0.67), or 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62) without them. Individually, 16 of 27 comparisons were significant (stop-signal reaction time: 4 of 10 studies). Funnel asymmetry was significant (Egger p = .008) and is no longer significant without the two outlying studies in the editors' reconstruction. No study-level moderator (sex, age, years of use, abstinence, sample type) was detected. The cocaine groups were older on average and, in about half the studies, differed from controls in age, education, sex or ethnicity without adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the findings highlight the link between impaired inhibition and cocaine use disorder and suggest that inhibitory-control training would be promising, without the prediction interval or the publication-bias results (PDF p. 1). The third aim (PDF p. 2) and the conclusion frame the difference as an effect of cocaine ("cocaine use affecting inhibition as we observed in this study", PDF p. 15), although the same paragraph calls the relation likely bidirectional and the design is cross-sectional. The Discussion calls the studies of good quality with relatively low risk of bias (PDF p. 14) while the review's own appraisal lists unadjusted group differences in 11 of 24 studies; the funnel asymmetry is described as a small publication bias with no adjusted estimate (PDF pp. 13–15); a non-significant clinical-versus-community test is read as showing that training would suit both outpatient and in-treatment settings (PDF p. 14); null study-level meta-regressions are reported as showing that abstinence and years of use do not affect the estimate (PDF p. 14); the two outlying studies are not mentioned. Training itself was not studied, and the authors note that evidence on it is limited (PDF p. 15).

timeline.event: Jovanovski, Erb & Zakzanis quantitative review of neuropsychological tests in 15 studies: the most-studied inhibition-type measure there, Stroop Color-Word interference, had a mean d of −0.11 across 7 effect sizes; not cited by this review.
Spronk et al. comprehensive review of the cognitive effects of cocaine (to be appraised from its full text); not cited by this review.

Smith, Mattick, Jamadar & Iredale meta-analysis of behavioural inhibition (stop-signal and go/no-go tasks) across substances; as summarized by this review (PDF p. 15), it found inhibitory deficits with heavy use of or dependence on cocaine, MDMA, methamphetamine, tobacco and alcohol, and in pathological gambling.
Frazer et al. systematic critical review of long-term cognitive effects of cocaine (to be appraised from its full text); not cited by this review.

Rush et al. randomized pilot study of inhibitory-control training, with contingency management for clinic attendance, in cocaine use disorder; cited by this review as the limited evidence on training (PDF p. 15).
This review (published online 10 November 2025): g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) across 20 studies to January 2024.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent meta-analysis of behavioural inhibition in people with cocaine use disorder held by the project. It supports a cross-sectional difference in average task performance in the direction of poorer inhibition, of uncertain size (0.65 as published; about 0.46 with its two misentered studies corrected from their own reports, or 0.41 without them, by the editors' recalculation; prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26 as published, about −0.37 to 1.28 after correction), and cannot show cause or reversibility. An earlier cross-substance meta-analysis (Smith et al., 2014) reached the same direction according to this review; the project's earlier neuropsychological reviews (Jovanovski et al., 2005; Spronk et al., 2013; Frazer et al., 2018) are not cited. The primary studies in Table 1 are inside the pooled estimate and must not be cited as independent support alongside it.

funding.funder: A García-Palmer grant from IdISBa granted to the first author (external internship agreement, annex number 2637; 08/01/2023–09/30/2023), as printed in the acknowledgements (PDF p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no conflict of interest (PDF p. 15).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of the Balearic Islands and the Health Research Institute of the Balearic Islands (IdISBa), the University of Oviedo and McMaster University's Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research. None of the five authors is an author of the 17 included studies listed in the reference list; the other 7 included studies are not listed and cannot be checked. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, task-specific meta-analysis (stop-signal reaction time, go/no-go commission errors and Stroop interference analysed separately) with every effect size re-extracted and checked against the primary papers, restricted to samples matched on age and education or using adjusted estimates, and with abstinence measured and verified at testing; and, for the direction of effect, prospective cohorts that measure inhibition before regular cocaine use begins, or co-twin and sibling designs, with repeated testing during abstinence.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: PECO stated: adults with cocaine use disorder from clinical and community samples, cocaine or crack use, a control group, and inhibitory processing at the cognitive-behavioural level (PDF pp. 2–3).

PROSPERO CRD42024592030 and PRISMA 2020 are stated, but the registration date relative to the January 2024 search, the registered analysis plan and any deviations are not reported, and the record was not read. The article's own abstinence criterion was not applied as stated.
Cross-sectional designs were required without saying why; studies following people through abstinence, for example, are not discussed.

Three databases, no date limit, search terms and an example PubMed string (full strategies in Supplementary Material 1, not read); but English-only and full-text filters without justification, no grey literature, registries, reference lists or experts, a printed PubMed string that omits one stated term, and a search run 22 months before online publication. Judged no under AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written (unjustified language restriction), as for batch 3 cards; the senior author decides the project's reading (decision p-amstar2-item4).

Full texts were assessed independently by two reviewers (agreement 57 of 62, kappa 0.84), with a third author for uncertain cases; title and abstract screening is described as done by the same two reviewers, without saying whether independently (PDF p. 3).
No statement that data were extracted in duplicate or checked by a second person; the author contributions credit the first author with the review table and two other authors with the meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article states that the 38 excluded full texts and the reasons for exclusion are listed in Supplementary Material 1 (Table 2), which was not read; Fig. 1 gives the reasons in aggregate. If the list is there, this item is met.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 (country, sample type, concurrent drug use, years of use, days of abstinence, task, assessments, result) and Table 2 (group sizes, ages, sex); missing are the diagnostic method for three studies, education, the exact outcome variable used, and which group was used in studies with more than one cocaine group.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI case-control checklist covering comparability, matching, confounding and the measurement of exposure and outcome, rated by two people; but not selective reporting, low inter-rater agreement (item kappas 0 to 0.5), matching rated not applicable for the 10 studies classed as cross-sectional, and summary labels without stated thresholds that call studies low risk despite unadjusted group differences.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Multilevel random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with an assumed within-study correlation, sensitivity to that correlation, a prediction interval and leave-one-out analyses are appropriate techniques. But unadjusted group differences were pooled without justification although the review's own appraisal documents unadjusted age and education differences, conceptually different tasks were pooled without a task-level analysis, and effect sizes of 3.1 to 4.9 from two small studies were neither checked nor examined; the primary papers show both are misentered (standard errors read as standard deviations), and with them corrected the editors' recalculation gives about 0.46 instead of 0.65. The overall rating does not depend on this item.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No subgroup or sensitivity analysis by quality score or risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion calls the studies of good quality and relatively low risk of bias and concludes that cocaine use affects inhibition, without considering the confounding by age and education that the review's own appraisal documents (PDF pp. 14–15).

Q, I² and a prediction interval are reported; heterogeneity was investigated with five moderators (none significant) and discussed as a limitation. Task type, named as a source of heterogeneity, was not tested and the two outlying studies were not discussed; judged met on balance.

Four indicators (fail-safe N, Begg, Egger, trim and fill), overall and by sample type, discussed as some or small publication bias (PDF pp. 13–15); but no adjusted estimate is reported and significant asymmetry (Egger p = .008) is called small. Judged met on balance.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (IdISBa García-Palmer grant) and the absence of conflicts are declared (PDF p. 15).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items fail (4: restricted search; 11: unadjusted, mixed-task pooling without checking outlying effects; 13: a low-risk label and a causal conclusion despite documented confounding), so confidence is critically low by the AMSTAR 2 rule; item 7 is provisional (supplement not read) but cannot change the rating, which would stay critically low even if item 11 were judged met. The review has real strengths: registration, a PRISMA flow, duplicate full-text selection with agreement statistics, multilevel modelling, a prediction interval, publication-bias tests, and shared data and code. It may be cited for: a cross-sectional difference in average performance on laboratory inhibition tasks between adults with cocaine use disorder and controls (g = 0.65, 0.28 to 1.03), always with the prediction interval (−0.95 to 2.26) and the editors' corrected result (about 0.46 with its two misentered studies corrected from their own reports; 0.41 without them); and for the absence of detected moderation by study-level sex, age, years of use, abstinence or sample type, as an absence of evidence. It may not be cited for: cocaine causing poorer inhibition, recovery or its absence with abstinence, the included studies being at low risk of bias, or inhibitory-control training being effective.

key_findings.finding: Search of Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed without date limits to January 2024 (English; PubMed with full-text and human filters): 1725 records (922 Scopus, 715 PubMed, 88 Web of Science); 499 duplicates removed; 1226 titles and abstracts screened and 1164 excluded; 62 full texts assessed independently by two reviewers (agreement on 57, 91.9%, kappa 0.84); 38 excluded; 24 studies in the systematic review and 20 (23 effect sizes) in the meta-analysis. The authors of four studies were asked for data and did not respond.
key_findings.locator: Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Selection and Data Collection Process, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; also Fig. 1 (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Inclusion: peer-reviewed English articles; people aged 18 or older with a cocaine use disorder by DSM, ICD (CIE) or equivalent criteria, with current use or at most two months of abstinence; a control group with no history of cocaine use; cross-sectional design; behavioural tasks of inhibition. Exclusion: other mental or neurodevelopmental disorders in both groups, another drug use disorder as first diagnosis, and drug use in controls other than tobacco when both groups smoked.

The meta-analysis pooled 542 people with cocaine use disorder (groups of 11 to 55) and 656 control participants (15 to 107); 78.97% men overall; mean age 38.41 in the cocaine groups and 35.21 in controls. Of the 20 meta-analysed studies, 12 used clinical and 8 community samples (14 and 10 of the 24 reviewed); 15 of the 24 were from the USA.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (PDF p. 8); Results › Study Characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 11)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 2: the cocaine group was 5 or more years older than its controls in 7 of the 19 studies reporting both ages (largest gap 52.6 vs 36.4 years, Bjork et al., 2022).

key_findings.finding: Tasks across the 24 studies: stop-signal task 10, go/no-go 8, Stroop 2, Five Digit Test 2, Immediate Memory Task 1, Probabilistic Reversal Learning 1, Attention Network Task 1 (one study used two tasks).
key_findings.locator: Results › Inhibition Tasks Used in the Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Multilevel random-effects meta-analysis (23 effect sizes from 20 samples, within-study correlation assumed 0.7): g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03), p < .001, poorer inhibition in the cocaine groups; heterogeneity Q = 134.26, I² = 83.61%, p < .001; 95% prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26. The aggregated model with one effect per study gave g = 0.64 in the text (0.65, 0.28 to 1.03, in Fig. 2B), and leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.51 to 0.72; other assumed correlations (0.0 to 0.8) gave similar results according to the authors (Supplementary Material 1, not read).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Cocaine Use and its Impact on Inhibitory Control › Meta-analysis on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 12)
key_findings.note: τ is said to be computed (PDF p. 8) but is not reported. Editors' calculation: REML random effects on the 20 study values printed in Fig. 2B, with standard errors from the printed confidence intervals, reproduces g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) and the leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72, with τ about 0.80.

key_findings.finding: Study-level effects (Fig. 2): 21 of 23 positive; 18 studies lie between −0.55 (Vonmoos et al., 2013; 30 vs 68; 95% CI −0.99 to −0.12) and 1.20 (Stevens et al., 2015); two small community-sample studies lie far outside: Hester & Garavan (2004), three conditions of the same 15 vs 15 participants, g = 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 (aggregated 3.56, 2.49 to 4.63), and Lane et al. (2007), 18 vs 15, g = 3.13 (2.11 to 4.15).
key_findings.note: Values read from the Fig. 2 image (no text layer) on a 300-dpi crop. Editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values): without these two studies g = 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), I² about 65%, τ about 0.36, prediction interval about −0.39 to 1.21. For group differences of g = 3.1 to 4.9, about 94% to 99% of each group would lie on its own side of the midpoint under normal distributions. Both values are misentered (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: No moderator was significant: percentage of men Q(1) = 0.71, p = .401; years of regular use Q(1) = 0.21, p = .648; mean age Q(1) = 0.48, p = .488; days of abstinence Q(1) = 1.96, p = .162; clinical vs community sample Q(1) = 1.50, p = .220 (printed as p < .220). Subgroup estimates and the number of studies in each meta-regression are not given in the article.
key_findings.locator: Meta-analysis on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values): clinical samples g = 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), community samples 1.03 (0.07 to 1.99), the latter 0.32 (−0.04 to 0.68) without the two outlying studies, both of which are community samples. Years of use and abstinence are available for at most 14 of the 20 studies in Table 1 (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Publication bias, on one effect per study (k = 20): fail-safe N 35, Begg rank correlation 0.36 (p = .028), Egger test 3.00 (p = .008), trim and fill one missing study; clinical samples (k = 12): 17, 0.12 (p = .638), 1.11 (p = .294), none; community samples (k = 8): 2, 0.58 (p = .061), 2.45 (p = .050), one. The authors describe this as a small publication bias; no adjusted estimate is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (PDF p. 13); Results › Publication Bias, 1st paragraph (PDF pp. 13–14)
key_findings.note: Editors' reconstruction (classic Egger regression on the Fig. 2B values): t = 3.01, p = 0.007 with all 20 studies, matching the printed result; without Hester & Garavan (2004) and Lane et al. (2007), t = 1.05, p = 0.31.

key_findings.finding: In the narrative synthesis, 16 of 27 comparisons across the 24 studies were significant: stop-signal reaction time was significantly longer in the cocaine group in 4 of 10 studies; go/no-go commission errors or accuracy differed in 5 of 8; the Attention Network Task, reversal-learning and Immediate Memory Task studies were significant; one of two Stroop and one of two Five Digit Test studies were significant. Of the 23 meta-analysed effects, 21 pointed to poorer performance in the cocaine group.
key_findings.locator: Systematic Review on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 1st to 5th paragraphs (PDF pp. 12–13); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Days of abstinence in Table 1 (study means): current use in four studies; 3 days in two; 12.62, 13.5 and 21 days in three; 152, 226.1, 293.23, 314.3 and 335 days in five (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a; Ceceli et al., 2023; Bell et al., 2014b; Hester et al., 2013); not given for the others. The early-abstinence group of Zilverstand et al. (2023; review only) had 2 to 5 days.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column Years of consumption (y) & days of abstinence (d)

key_findings.finding: Concurrent drug use in the cocaine groups (Table 1): alcohol 6.67% to 100%, cannabis 12.5% to 80%, heroin 3.7% to 33.34% (29.62% in Bell et al., 2014a, 25% in Bell et al., 2014b, 33.34% in Hester et al., 2013), with amphetamines, opioids, hallucinogens, MDMA and benzodiazepines in some samples; only cocaine in 7 of the 24 studies. The authors could not analyse co-occurring substance use or mental disorders because most studies did not report them in detail.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column Comorbidity of current drug consumption (PDF pp. 4–6); Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Study quality (JBI case-control checklist; first author and an external collaborator; item kappas 0.47, 0.38, 0.45, 0.48, 0, 0.33 and 0.18 for items 1 to 7, not computable for items 8 and 9, and 0.5 for item 10): mean score 89.06%; 10 studies rated very low risk of bias, 13 low and 1 moderate. The review's own narrative reports group differences in education, age, sex or ethnicity, or inadequate matching, in 11 of the 24 studies, most of them rated low risk.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (PDF pp. 9–10); Methods › Quality Assessment, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 11); Results › Methodological Quality of Included Studies, 2nd to 5th paragraphs (PDF p. 14)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from the narrative (PDF p. 14): Hester & Garavan (2004), Van Der Plas et al. (2009), Vonmoos et al. (2013), Bell et al. (2014a, 2014b), Elton et al. (2014), Liu et al. (2011), Wang et al. (2018), Albein-Urios et al. (2012), Lane et al. (2007) and Kaufman et al. (2003); 9 of them are in the meta-analysis.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: co-occurring substance use and mental disorders could not be analysed; some publication bias; few studies with small samples; high heterogeneity; experimental tasks without norms, so clinical relevance cannot be judged. Conclusion: people with cocaine use disorder have decreased inhibition compared with controls; the relation is likely bidirectional; inhibitory-control training is proposed as a target, with limited evidence so far (one pilot trial cited).

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria require current use or at most two months of abstinence (PDF p. 3), but Table 1 reports mean abstinence of 152 to 335 days in five included studies, all in the meta-analysis (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a, 2014b; Ceceli et al., 2023; Hester et al., 2013).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimate mixes current use with abstinence of up to 335 days, and the null abstinence meta-regression rests on study means across this mixed range. In an exploratory editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values), these five studies pool to g = 0.20 (−0.17 to 0.58) and the other 13, without the two outlying studies, to 0.48 (0.23 to 0.73); the comparison is post hoc and underpowered and cannot show recovery.

reporting_issues.issue: Two small studies have effect sizes far outside the rest that the text never mentions, and the primary papers show that both values are misentered. Lane et al. (2007), 3.13 (2.11 to 4.15): entering the standard errors of Lane et al.'s Table 2 (hard No-Go d′, 0.66 ± 0.08 against 0.89 ± 0.06, mean ± SEM, 18 and 15 people) as if they were standard deviations reproduces g = 3.13 exactly, whereas Lane et al.'s own t(31) = −2.16 gives about 0.74 (the p = .019 that this review's Table 1 records is the one-tailed value; two-tailed about .039). Hester & Garavan (2004), 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 for the three memory loads: reading that study's Figure 2 error bars (about 3 to 4 points, type not stated) as standard deviations gives about 3.3, 3.9 and 5.0, whereas its group effect F(1,28) = 15.03 gives about 1.4 and implies a between-person standard deviation of about 11 points, so the bars are standard errors. This review's Table 1 also gives that study's tobacco use as 73.33%, which is 11 of 15 (10 people in the cocaine group plus 1 control; 10 of 15 is 66.67%), and 3 days of abstinence where the study reports a mean of 41 hours (range 12 to 72).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled g of 0.65, the high heterogeneity and the funnel asymmetry depend substantially on these two misentered values. Editors' recalculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values): with the two replaced by the values their own test statistics give, g = 0.46 (0.25 to 0.67), I² about 66%, classic Egger p = 0.12; without them, 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), Egger p = 0.31. Other entries may carry similar errors; only these two primary papers have been read.

reporting_issues.issue: For two studies, Table 1's record of the primary result does not match the review's own effect size: Hester et al. (2013) is recorded as significantly worse no-go accuracy (p < .05) but has g = 0.60 (−0.13 to 1.33) in Fig. 2; Vonmoos et al. (2013) is recorded as non-significant but has g = −0.55 (−0.99 to −0.12), a significant difference favouring the cocaine group. Vonmoos et al. studied recreational and dependent groups (Table 1), and which group was used is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a different outcome, contrast or group was extracted, or there are extraction or sign errors; together with the outlying values, the effect-size extraction needs checking against the primary papers before the pooled value is relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: Seven of the 24 included studies are not in the reference list: Albein-Urios et al. (2012), Bell et al. (2014a, 2014b), Hester et al. (2013), Li et al. (2008), Torres et al. (2013) and Vonmoos et al. (2013); in Tables 1 to 3 their names carry no link to a reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Six of the 20 meta-analysed studies cannot be identified unambiguously from the article (they may be identified in the supplement or OSF files, not read), which prevents checking their effect sizes, including the mismatches above.

reporting_issues.issue: The quality summary does not match the review's own observations: studies with unadjusted differences in education, age or sex are rated low risk (for example Elton et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2007); the matching item is rated not applicable for the 10 studies classed as cross-sectional, which lifts their scores to 100%; the thresholds for very low, low and moderate risk are not defined; item 4 (valid measurement of exposure) is rated yes for Hester & Garavan (2004), Kaufman et al. (2003) and Wang et al. (2018) although Table 1 lists no diagnostic assessment for them; and the text omits the kappa of 0 for item 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that the studies were of good quality and relatively low risk of bias (PDF p. 14) should not be repeated; confounding by age and education is unaddressed in about half of the studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says clinical and community samples had similar years of regular use, both averaging 14.5 years, but by the editors' calculation from Table 1 the study means average 10.6 years for the 8 clinical and 13.2 years for the 6 community meta-analysed studies that report it (10.5 and 14.2 across all reviewed studies).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the argument that the two sample types were alike in duration of use is not supported as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated search terms include executive function, but the printed PubMed string searches only inhibition, inhibitory control and impulsivity in titles and abstracts, with filters for full text, English and humans.
reporting_issues.consequence: Studies indexed under executive function without these words, and PubMed records without full-text links, may have been missed; the full strategies (Supplementary Material 1) were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: For studies with more than one cocaine group the group used is not stated (Vonmoos et al., 2013, recreational and dependent; Stevens et al., 2015, with and without ADHD), although use without a disorder and other mental disorders are excluded by the criteria; and studies with 25% to 33% concurrent heroin use and two cocaine and heroin polysubstance samples were included while one full text was excluded for heroin consumption (Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the pooled sample meets the stated criteria; if the ADHD subgroup was included, ADHD would confound the inhibition comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement of the review's third aim and the sentence after it (PDF p. 2) follow, almost word for word by the editors' comparison, the statement of aims in Jovanovski et al. (2005, p. 191), which is not cited; nor are later reviews of cocaine and cognition held by the project (Spronk et al., 2013; Frazer et al., 2018).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the results; the review does not compare its findings with the earlier quantitative review of the same literature.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 labels Egger's value as an intercept ('Egger's test Intercept (p value)': 3.00, p = .008), but the printed 3.00 matches the t statistic of the classic Egger regression on the Fig. 2B values (t = 3.01), not its intercept (about 4.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 3.00 as the test statistic, not as the size of the asymmetry.

design_detail: Scientific statement of the American Heart Association, written by the Acute Cardiac Care Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology: a consensus document, not a systematic review. Eleven named cardiologists and emergency physicians reviewed the literature on cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction and issued diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations graded in the ACC/AHA format (Class I, IIa, IIb, III; Level of Evidence A, B, C). The writing committee describes a comprehensive search of English-language publications on humans and animals from 1960 to 2007, with broad searching on cocaine plus targeted searches on named topics, citations generally limited to articles listed in Index Medicus; no databases, search strings, selection criteria or study flow are given. Approved by the AHA Science Advisory and Coordinating Committee on 20 December 2007 and reviewed by outside reviewers nominated by the AHA. This is the document that carries the Class III recommendation against beta blockers in the acute setting, and the single table on p. 1902 states the kind and the size of the evidence behind each recommendation.
can_establish: What the American Heart Association recommended in 2008 for cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction, how it graded each recommendation, and, uniquely among such documents, how many patients and what kinds of study lay behind each therapy, including the 30 and 15 patients behind the Class III recommendations against beta blockers and labetalol.
cannot_establish: Whether any of the recommended or discouraged treatments changes patient outcomes. The statement generates no data, appraises no study formally, and says itself that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated myocardial infarction exists. Its Class III judgments are Level of Evidence C, which in its own definitions means consensus opinion, case studies or standard of care.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a consensus statement. The literature cited was gathered by the writing committee from a search of English-language human and animal publications from 1960 to 2007, with citations generally limited to articles listed in Index Medicus (p. 1897).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No inclusion or exclusion criteria for studies are stated and no study flow is reported. Targeted searches are listed for myocardial infarction, chest pain, emergency department, aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blocker, benzodiazepine, thrombolytics, phentolamine, heparin, primary angioplasty, electrocardiography and stress testing; beta blockers and labetalol, the two therapies given Class III recommendations, do not appear among the named targeted searches (p. 1897).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The populations described are those of the cited studies, chiefly young urban patients: in the Cocaine-Associated Myocardial Infarction series of 130 patients, mean age 38 years, 72% non-white, 91% smokers, 88% with cocaine use in the preceding 24 hours (p. 1899).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence was selected by the committee without stated criteria, from English-language sources, and the search closed in 2007; of the hospital cohorts that later examined beta-blocker outcomes, the first (Dattilo et al.) was published online in June 2007, within the search period, but is not cited, and the others appeared from 2008 on. Several of the central citations on incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit management are studies co-authored by one member of the writing group. The disclosure table shows extensive industry relationships across the writing group, chiefly with diagnostic and cardiovascular-drug companies; this is recorded as a flag, and the therapies at issue here are generic.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no primary data). The statement reviews how cocaine use is ascertained in practice: self-report, or qualitative immunoassay for urinary benzoylecgonine above a usual cut-off of 300 ng/mL, detectable for about 24 to 48 hours after use, with a mean time to first negative specimen of 43.6 +/- 17.1 hours (range 16 to 66) in 18 people who had used cocaine intranasally, and detection as late as 22 days in people using large amounts long-term (p. 1899).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as the conditions of cited studies: the catheterization-laboratory studies gave intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (p. 1903).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed qualitatively: alcohol intensifies the chronotropic effects of cocaine, and cocaine combined with cigarette smoking produces greater increases in heart rate and vasoconstriction than either alone (p. 1898).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable: a consensus statement with no comparison group. The implicit comparator throughout is the management of acute coronary syndrome unrelated to cocaine, from which the statement departs in naming the exceptions (pp. 1901-1902).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: The ACC/AHA classification of recommendations and levels of evidence, defined on p. 1897: Class I beneficial and effective, Class II conflicting evidence or divergent opinion (IIa weight of evidence in favour, IIb usefulness less well established), Class III evidence or general agreement that the treatment is not useful and in some cases may be harmful; Level A from multiple randomized trials, Level B from a single randomized trial or non-randomized studies, Level C from consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care.
outcomes.validity_norms: No formal risk-of-bias appraisal of any cited study. The statement's substitute, and its most useful feature for a reader weighing the recommendations, is the table on p. 1902, which marks for each therapy which kinds of evidence exist (controlled clinical trials, cardiac catheterization laboratory studies, case series or observational studies, case reports, controlled in vivo animal experiments) and gives the total number of patients in the studies and reports behind it.
outcomes.operationalization: Recommendations are about acute hospital management; 'harm' for the Class III judgments is operationalized as worsening coronary vasoconstriction and, in animal models, decreased coronary blood flow, increased seizure frequency and increased mortality (p. 1902).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis or pooling. The statement reports figures from individual sources: myocardial infarction in 6% of patients presenting with chest pain after cocaine use in the COCHPA study (246 patients) and in a retrospective urban series, against 0.7% in the ACI-TIPI study (293 patients) and 2.8% in a series of 218, an overall range of 0.7% to 6% (p. 1898). Of 130 patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction, 38% had cardiac complications, with heart failure in 7% and arrhythmias in up to 43% (ventricular tachycardia 18%, supraventricular tachycardia 5%, bradyarrhythmia 20%), 90% of complications within the first 12 hours and in-hospital mortality of 0% (p. 1899; the arrhythmia figure alone exceeds the 38% with any complication, so the denominators are unclear). In a chest-pain-unit study of 344 patients, 42 high-risk patients were admitted directly, of whom 10 (24%) had myocardial infarction and 10 (24%) unstable angina; of 302 intermediate- to low-risk patients observed, 4 of 256 (2%) sustained a non-fatal infarction and no cardiovascular deaths occurred, and of 158 who had a stress test before discharge 4 (3%) were positive (p. 1901). The electrocardiogram in COCHPA had a sensitivity of 36% and a specificity of 89.9% for true myocardial infarction, with positive predictive value 17.9% and negative predictive value 95.8% (p. 1900). Intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg narrowed coronary arterial diameter by 13% and phentolamine returned it to baseline (p. 1903). No confidence intervals accompany any of these figures except the sensitivity and specificity of rest perfusion imaging (100%, 95% CI 50% to 100%, and 99%, 95% CI 96% to 100%; p. 1900).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a scientific statement; no protocol or registration, and the ACC/AHA grading is applied by committee judgment.
analysis.selective_reporting: The table on p. 1902 is unusually candid about what the recommendations rest on, and the therapeutics section opens by stating that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated myocardial infarction has been reported. Against that, the beta-blocker section describes the catheterization evidence without saying that its participants had never used cocaine, that the propranolol was given directly into the coronary artery, or that only 10 and 9 people respectively received the drugs after cocaine (editors' observation from the cited studies, read in the same session).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The statement's own table shows that of the seven therapies considered for initial management, only benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin have any controlled clinical trial evidence, and that the recommendations against beta blockers and against labetalol rest on cardiac catheterization studies, case reports and animal experiments covering 30 and 15 patients respectively, with no controlled clinical trial and no observational study. Both are graded Level of Evidence C, which the statement defines as consensus opinion, case studies or standard of care.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The statement recommends that beta-adrenergic antagonists be avoided in the acute setting (Class III) and that labetalol offers no advantage (Class III), reinforcing these with quotations from two earlier guidelines, one stating that beta blockers should not be given in cocaine-precipitated ST-elevation infarction because of the risk of exacerbating coronary spasm, the other that propranolol is contraindicated in cocaine overdose. The gap is not between the data and the recommendation, which the committee grades honestly as Level C, but in what travels afterwards: a Class III recommendation in an American Heart Association statement is read as settled, while the document itself shows it rests on two small catheterization studies in patients who had never used cocaine, one of which gave the drug directly into a coronary artery. The statement also argues the risk-benefit balance explicitly and well, noting that beta blockers lower mortality after ordinary infarction but that deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, so the balance differs. The discharge recommendation is appropriately conditional, reserving long-term beta blockers for documented infarction, left ventricular systolic dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmias, individualized and with counselling about recurrent cocaine use.

timeline.event: Intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in 10 of 30 cocaine-naive catheterization patients: the human evidence behind the Class III recommendation
Intravenous labetalol in 9 of 15 similar patients lowered arterial pressure without relieving coronary vasoconstriction: the human evidence behind the labetalol recommendation
This statement, approved December 2007, grades both beta blockers and labetalol Class III, Level of Evidence C
Retrospective cohort of 376 patients finds no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes with or without a beta blocker, and notes that 44% received one despite the recommendation
Meta-analysis of five retrospective cohorts finds no significant pooled difference in infarction or death and suggests the guidelines be reconsidered
Second meta-analysis (eight cohorts, including the five pooled by Pham et al. 2018): no significant pooled difference in in-hospital or long-term death or infarction; no randomized trial by June 2018

replication.where_it_stands: The statement's literature search closed in 2007; the first hospital cohort that examined outcomes (Dattilo et al., online June 2007) fell inside it but is not cited, and the others came later. Those cohorts have not shown the harm the mechanism predicts, but they are non-randomized, treated patients were systematically sicker, and no randomized trial has been done. As of the present reading the Class III recommendation stands in the guidelines while the observational literature pulls against it, and both sides rest on evidence the editors of this encyclopedia rate as weak.

funding.funder: No external funding is reported for the statement; it is a product of the American Heart Association, which states it makes every effort to avoid actual or potential conflicts of interest among writing-panel members (p. 1897).
funding.declared_conflicts: A full disclosure table for the writing group is printed on p. 1904. Seven of the eleven members declare relationships; those marked significant (10,000 US dollars or more in any 12-month period, or 5% or more of gross income, or 5% or more ownership) include research grants from diagnostic and pharmaceutical companies to several members, speakers' bureau or honoraria relationships, and ownership interests for one member (Ohman); a second member's ownership interests (Gibler) are marked modest. Four members (Cercek, Drew, Hsue, Philippides) declare none. The reviewer disclosure table on p. 1905 lists three reviewers, all declaring none (p. 1904-1905).
funding.affiliations_note: The writing group are academic cardiologists and emergency physicians at US centres. One member, Judd E. Hollander, is an author of several of the studies the statement relies on for incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit management (among them its references 19, 32, 36, 39, 40, 47 and 49: the COCHPA study, the 130-patient infarction series, Weber et al. 2000 and the observation-unit study). Another member, Hani Jneid, is an author of the 2018 meta-analysis that calls for the beta-blocker recommendation to be reconsidered (Pham et al., 2018). The declared industry relationships concern diagnostic and cardiovascular products rather than the generic drugs at issue in the recommendations; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the document.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of an intravenous beta blocker against the recommended alternatives in people presenting with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, with infarction, arrhythmia and death as outcomes, which would move both the beta-blocker and the labetalol recommendations off Level of Evidence C. Failing that, a guideline update that states, beside the Class III, how many people have actually received a beta blocker after cocaine in a controlled human study and under what conditions.

domains.note: A search is described, with a date range (1960 to 2007) and a list of targeted topics, which is more than most consensus documents offer, but no database is named, no search string or limits are given, no inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated and no study flow is reported. The search was English-language only. Beta blockers and labetalol, the subjects of the two Class III recommendations, are not among the named targeted searches.

No formal risk-of-bias assessment of any study, but the ACC/AHA class and level system is applied consistently, and the table on p. 1902 states for each therapy which kinds of evidence exist and how many patients they cover, which is a real and unusually transparent form of appraisal. What is missing is any comment on the internal limits of the key studies: that the catheterization participants had never used cocaine, and that in one of them the drug went directly into the coronary artery.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit sections lean on the COCHPA study, a review of cocaine-induced infarction and the randomized observation-unit study, all of which involve one member of the writing group (Hollander) as an author. In a literature this small that is hard to avoid, and the statement does not conceal it, but the reader should know that several of its central numbers come from one group.

The therapeutics section opens by stating that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated infarction exists and that the recommendations rest on animal studies, catheterization studies, observational studies, case series and case reports. Mechanistic reasoning is labelled as such, uncertainty is stated where it exists (the role of calcium channel blockers is called uncertain, the appropriate diagnostic evaluation unclear), and the grading system attaches a level of evidence to every recommendation.

domains.domain: Balance of the evidence on beta-blockade, harm against safety
domains.note: The case for harm is set out in full (catheterization studies, case reports, animal models of seizure and death, esmolol raising blood pressure in up to 25% of patients) while nothing is offered on the other side, and the statement does not note that no human study had then examined clinical outcomes with or without a beta blocker. Much of this imbalance was a property of the 2007 literature rather than of the committee, and the statement partly corrects for it by printing the patient numbers; but a reader cannot tell from the text that only about 19 people had ever been given a beta blocker after cocaine under controlled conditions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a professional body's consensus statement (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain, which is the unsystematic search. This is a better consensus document than most: it grades every recommendation, says plainly that no randomized trial of treatment exists, and prints the size and type of the evidence behind each therapy. It should be cited as the American Heart Association's 2008 judgment and for its statement of what that judgment rests on, including the Class III and Level C grades and the 30 and 15 patients in the table on p. 1902, never as independent evidence that beta blockers harm people who use cocaine. The numbers it reports from individual studies (incidence of infarction, complication rates, electrocardiogram performance) should be cited to those studies, which this encyclopedia appraises separately.

key_findings.finding: The statement grades beta blockers and labetalol Class III (evidence or general agreement that the treatment is not useful and in some cases may be harmful) at Level of Evidence C (consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care), against Class I Level B for benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin, Class I Level C for aspirin, and Class IIb Level C for calcium channel blockers and phentolamine.
key_findings.locator: Table, Classification of Recommendation / Level of Evidence column; definitions on p. 1897

key_findings.finding: The same table records the number of patients in the studies and reports behind each therapy: benzodiazepines 67, nitroglycerin 67, phentolamine 45, calcium channel blocker 15, beta blockers without alpha-blocking properties 30, labetalol 15, fibrinolytics 66.
key_findings.note: The 30 and the 15 are the enrolments of the two catheterization studies (Lange et al. 1990 and Boehrer et al. 1993). Editors' observation from those two papers, read in the same session: only 10 of the 30 and 9 of the 15 actually received a beta blocker after cocaine, so about 19 people in total; and in the 1990 study the propranolol was infused directly into the coronary artery rather than given systemically.

key_findings.finding: In the same table, beta blockers and labetalol are each marked as supported by cardiac catheterization laboratory studies, case reports and controlled in vivo animal experiments, with no mark under controlled clinical trials and none under case series or observational studies; only benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin carry a mark under controlled clinical trials.

The therapeutics section states that no randomized placebo-controlled trials of therapies to improve outcomes in cocaine-associated myocardial infarction have been reported, and that the recommendations are based on animal studies, cardiac catheterization studies, observational studies, case series and case reports.

The beta-blocker section states that coronary vasoconstriction is exacerbated by propranolol, that experimental models show beta-adrenergic antagonists decreasing coronary blood flow and increasing seizure frequency and mortality, that metoprolol has not been studied in cocaine-associated chest pain, that esmolol produced significant increases in blood pressure in up to 25% of patients, and that carvedilol has not been studied in this setting; it concludes that beta-adrenergic antagonists should be avoided in the acute setting.

The statement reasons that although beta blockers lower mortality after myocardial infarction unrelated to cocaine, deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, which alters the balance of risk and benefit.
key_findings.note: The supporting figure is the 0% in-hospital mortality in the 130-patient Cocaine-Associated Myocardial Infarction series cited on p. 1899.

key_findings.finding: On labetalol, the statement says that, although theoretically more attractive than propranolol, it does not appear to offer any advantages (citing Boehrer et al., 1993), and gives as reasons that it has substantially more beta- than alpha-adrenergic antagonist effect, increases the risk of seizure and death in animal models of cocaine toxicity, and does not reverse coronary artery vasoconstriction in humans.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic Strategies > beta-Blockers, final paragraph (p. 1902) continuing at the top of p. 1903
key_findings.note: The human citation is Boehrer et al. 1993, in which 9 patients received labetalol.

key_findings.finding: At discharge, the statement advises that long-term beta-blocker use be reserved for those with the strongest indications (documented myocardial infarction, left ventricular systolic dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmias), individualized on a careful risk-benefit assessment and after counselling the patient about the potential negative interactions between recurrent cocaine use and beta-blockade, because recidivism is high.
key_findings.locator: Discharge Management and Secondary Prevention, final paragraph

key_findings.finding: Myocardial infarction occurred in 0.7% to 6% of patients presenting with chest pain after cocaine use across the cited studies: 6% in the COCHPA multicentre study of 246 patients (its reference 19) and in a retrospective series at an urban university-affiliated hospital by Weber and colleagues (reference 36, Weber et al., 2000), 2.8% in a series of 218 (reference 38, Kontos et al., 1999), and 0.7% among 293 patients in the ACI-TIPI study (reference 37, Feldman et al., 2000); the statement attributes part of the variation to differences in diagnostic criteria and in the populations studied.

Among 130 patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction, 38% had cardiac complications, with heart failure in 7% and arrhythmias in up to 43% (ventricular tachycardia 18%, supraventricular tachycardia 5%, bradyarrhythmia 20%); 90% of complications occurred within the first 12 hours after presentation and in-hospital mortality was 0% (as printed; the percentages cannot all have the 130 patients as denominator, see reporting issues).

The electrocardiogram performed poorly for detecting infarction in this population: in COCHPA, sensitivity 36%, specificity 89.9%, positive predictive value 17.9% and negative predictive value 95.8%; 56% to 84% of patients had an abnormal electrocardiogram, with early repolarization in 32% and left ventricular hypertrophy in 16% in one cohort of 101, and 42% of that cohort had ST-segment elevation although all had infarction excluded by cardiac markers.

In a prospective randomized study of 344 patients evaluated for cocaine-associated chest pain, 42 (12%) high-risk patients were admitted directly, of whom 10 (24%) had an infarction and 10 (24%) unstable angina; 302 intermediate- to low-risk patients were observed for 6 to 12 hours, among whom there were no cardiovascular deaths and 4 of 256 (2%) sustained a non-fatal infarction, and of the 158 (52%) who had a stress test before discharge only 4 (3%) were positive.
key_findings.locator: Evaluation in a Chest Pain Unit
key_findings.note: The statement draws from this its recommendation that intermediate- and low-risk patients can be managed in an observation unit for 9 to 12 hours and that stress testing be optional.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine use was reported as detectable in urine for about 24 to 48 hours after use, with a mean time to the first negative specimen of 43.6 +/- 17.1 hours (range 16 to 66) in 18 people who had used it intranasally, and as late as 22 days in people using large amounts long-term.
key_findings.note: This is the basis for the later observational studies' acknowledged inability to date cocaine use from a urine screen.

key_findings.finding: In the cardiac catheterization studies the statement relies on, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised heart rate, blood pressure and coronary vascular resistance and narrowed coronary arterial diameter by 13%, and phentolamine returned the diameter to baseline.
key_findings.note: Reported as study conditions. The 13% figure is attributed to the 1989 study of the same Dallas group, not to Lange et al. 1990, whose Table 1 gives segment-by-segment falls of about 6% to 10%. The same paragraph calls these catheterization studies randomized controlled trials and reports a rise in heart rate after cocaine; in the two same-dose studies read here, heart rate did not change after cocaine (Lange et al., 1990, Table 1; Boehrer et al., 1993, Table I), and the 1989 study cited for it has not been read.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state that the article was reviewed by 4 outside reviewers nominated by the American Heart Association, while the reviewer disclosure table lists 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extent of external review cannot be verified from the document. It bears on the evidence-report question of how independently the recommendations were checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The table of scientific strength has seven therapy rows (benzodiazepines, aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blocker, phentolamine, beta blockers, labetalol) but its footnote gives patient numbers for eight therapies, adding fibrinolytics, which has no row and no class or level of evidence in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 66 patients behind the fibrinolytic evidence cannot be matched to a graded recommendation; fibrinolysis is discussed in the text, where it is advised only for patients with ST-elevation infarction who cannot have percutaneous intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The named targeted literature searches cover aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blockers, benzodiazepines, thrombolytics, phentolamine and heparin, but not beta blockers or labetalol, which are the two therapies the statement places in Class III.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot tell how the evidence behind the strongest negative recommendations was identified. Combined with the absence of named databases and search strings, this makes the search unreproducible.

reporting_issues.issue: The table counts 30 patients as the evidence base for beta blockers without alpha-blocking properties and 15 for labetalol. These are the full enrolments of the two cited catheterization studies; in those studies only 10 and 9 patients respectively received the beta blocker after cocaine, and in the 1990 study it was infused directly into the coronary artery rather than given systemically.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base for the Class III recommendations is smaller and narrower than the table's own figures suggest. Editors' observation from the two cited papers read in the same session; the statement itself does not mention the route or the number actually dosed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement attributes a 13% narrowing of coronary arterial diameter after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg to the 1989 study of the same group, while the 1990 study using the same dose reports segment-by-segment falls corresponding to about 6% to 10% and the 1993 study reports, in its abstract only, a 13% +/- 10% decrease in the 32 of 40 analysed segments that narrowed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The single figure most often quoted for cocaine-induced coronary narrowing circulates without the sample, the segment or the spread behind it. A claim about the size of this effect should cite the primary table, not the statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The epidemiology paragraph gives the 2004 national survey estimate that 14% of people aged 12 or over (34 million) had ever tried cocaine (reference 3), and then states that more than 1.5 million Americans aged 12 or over (0.6%) used cocaine in the past year in 2002 to 2003 without any citation: the numbering jumps from reference 4 to reference 6, and reference 5 is marked deleted in proof.
reporting_issues.consequence: The past-year figures cannot be traced to a source from this document; prevalence figures should be taken from the surveys themselves.

reporting_issues.issue: In the 130 patients of the Cocaine-Associated Myocardial Infarction study, 38% are said to have had cardiac complications, and arrhythmias are said to have occurred 'in up to 43%' (ventricular tachycardia 18%, supraventricular tachycardia 5%, bradyarrhythmia 20%, which sum to 43%), with heart failure in 7%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Arrhythmias alone cannot exceed the share with any cardiac complication if both are per patient of the 130, so the denominators of these percentages are unclear; they should be taken from the primary report of that study, not from this statement.

reporting_issues.issue: Evaluation in a Chest Pain Unit is internally inconsistent: 10 of 42 high-risk patients with infarction are given as 24% in one column and 23% in the next (10/42 is 23.8%); 4 of 256 non-fatal infarctions as 2% here and 1.6% on p. 1899 (4/256 is 1.56%); and the cited study's observation period is given as 6 to 12 hours, while the statement's recommendation drawn from it is 9 to 12 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Figures and the observation period should be quoted with their exact source sentence; the 9 to 12 hours is the statement's recommendation, not the study's observation period.

reporting_issues.issue: In a retrospective review of 197 patients evaluated in a chest pain unit, 1 patient is said to have developed an infarction, printed as 4.5%; 1 of 197 is 0.5%, and 4.5% fits 1 of about 22, so the denominator is unstated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rate cannot be interpreted as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Citations around the 130-patient infarction series do not match: the mean age of 38 is cited to reference 39 (a one-year follow-up of patients with chest pain) on p. 1898 but to reference 47 on p. 1899, and the distribution of 130 infarctions (anterior 45%, inferior 44%, non-Q 61%) is cited to reference 40, a study of electrocardiographic normal variants in chest pain.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be traced to their source from the citations; they should be checked in the primary report of the series.
