design_detail: Literature search with random-effects meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis V2, Cohen's d) of 46 case–control studies that compared the cognitive test performance of people with a DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence (cocaine use disorder, CUD) with healthy controls, published before 1 January 2013. Tests were grouped into 11 cognitive domains (IQ could not be pooled), and studies were split by abstinence at testing: short-term (urine positive for cocaine, under 72 hours), intermediate (under 12 weeks) and long-term (over 20 weeks; only one composite estimate from 5 studies, fixed-effect). No protocol, no appraisal of the primary studies, no table of included studies.
can_establish: The average standardized difference in test performance between people with a diagnosed cocaine use disorder and healthy controls in published case–control studies up to 2012, by cognitive domain, separately for studies whose participants were urine-positive and studies with abstinence under 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the differences (every pooled study is a cross-sectional comparison without pre-use data, and smoking, depressive symptoms and alcohol were not analysed); that cognition recovers with abstinence (the abstinence groups are different studies, not the same people followed, and the long-term estimate is one composite from 5 studies whose interval includes zero); or how many individuals score in an impaired range (no normative data were pooled).

sample.recruitment: Search of PubMed, Embase and Ovid with the key words printed in the paper, plus the reference lists of included studies; two authors reached consensus on which studies to include (p. 369, Methods › Literature Search and Study Selection). 52 studies met the criteria and 46 were analysed (p. 370, Results › Study Characteristics). How the primary studies recruited their participants (treatment, inpatient, community) is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: participants described as people who use cocaine without a DSM-III, III-R, IV or IV-TR diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence; samples with comorbid Axis I disorders (for example schizophrenia, ADHD, PTSD); studies in which all participants used several substances (for example cocaine with alcohol or heroin); studies without a healthy control group; challenge studies of the short-term effects of cocaine; adults exposed to cocaine in utero; studies reporting test performance during EEG, MRI or PET scanning; studies published after 1 January 2013 (p. 369). One study was also dropped for lacking abstinence information (Lane et al., 2010; p. 370), so abstinence data were in practice required.
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex, education, route, duration of use or abstinence is given for any included study, and there is no table of study characteristics.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Of 52 eligible studies, six named studies were not analysed: one used nonparametric statistics, four used data overlapping with included studies, one gave no abstinence information (p. 370).
sample.selection_effects: Restricting to DSM-diagnosed CUD without Axis I comorbidity, and excluding samples in which everyone used several substances, gives a narrower population than people who use cocaine in general. Samples in which only some participants also had an alcohol use disorder were eligible, and several included titles describe such mixed samples (Robinson et al., 1999; Di Sclafani et al., 2002; Abi-Saab et al., 2005; reference list, pp. 374–376). No grey-literature or registry searching; search dates and language limits are not stated. Hester and Garavan (2004), which tested performance during fMRI, is not among the 46 studies; testing in a scanner was an exclusion criterion.

exposure.measurement: As in each primary study. A DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence was required; how use was measured, and whether abstinence was verified by urine tests in the intermediate and long-term groups, is not reported. Short-term abstinence was defined by a urine test positive for cocaine (p. 370).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted or analysed. The authors list length of use, route (smoked, sniffed or injected), age, amount used and sex as possible sources of variability without testing them (p. 374, Discussion, 8th paragraph, continued from p. 373).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only by excluding studies in which all participants used several substances (p. 369). Alcohol and other drug use were not extracted or tested as moderators. Depressive symptoms and cigarette smoking could not be examined because more than 60% of included studies did not report them (p. 373, Discussion, 8th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Studies were grouped by the average, minimum or maximum abstinence each reported: short-term = urine positive for cocaine (under 72 hours); intermediate = under 12 weeks (12 weeks or less in the abstract and Table 2); long-term = over 20 weeks (20 weeks or more in the abstract and Table 3); no study fell between 13 and 19 weeks (p. 370). Meta-regression on abstinence was rejected because abstinence durations across studies were skewed (Kolmogorov–Smirnov P=0.0001) (p. 370). Which studies fell into which group is not reported.

comparison.controls: The healthy control groups of the primary studies, 1411 people in all; a healthy control group was required (p. 369, exclusion criterion iv; p. 370).
comparison.matching: Not reported: the review does not say how controls were matched in the primary studies or whether groups differed in age, education or premorbid IQ.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use data in any pooled study. The authors note that impulse-related deficits may partly have preceded the onset of CUD (p. 372, Discussion, 3rd paragraph) and that better verbal fluency in some CUD samples may reflect premorbid characteristics (p. 372, 5th paragraph). IQ could not be pooled (2 studies; p. 371).

outcomes.instruments: Standard neuropsychological tests assigned to domains following Lezak et al. (2012) and earlier meta-analyses, for example: WAIS Vocabulary and Similarities, COWAT (verbal fluency/language); Digit Symbol, Trail Making A and B, Stroop reaction time, Grooved Pegboard (speed of processing); Digit Span, Letter–Number Sequencing (working memory); CPT omission errors (attention); Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Stroop interference (executive functions); Go/No-Go, stop-signal reaction time, CPT commission errors, probabilistic reversal learning, Iowa Gambling Task (reward- or impulse-related functions, reported as 'impulsivity'); WMS Logical Memory and Verbal Paired Associates, CVLT, story recall (verbal learning and memory); WMS Visual Reproduction, Benton, Rey–Osterrieth figure (visual learning and memory); Block Design, Rey–Osterrieth copy (visuospatial). Less common tests were assigned by consensus of three authors (p. 369, Methods › Cognitive Domains).
outcomes.validity_norms: Differences against controls only; no normative comparison and no proportion of individuals in an impaired range.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impairment' = a positive standardized mean difference (Cohen's d) favouring controls, called small, medium and large at 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 (p. 370). Within each study, the effect sizes of tests in one domain were averaged into one domain estimate; for the long-term group, all test scores of a study were averaged into a global index (pp. 370–371).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 23 pooled estimates (11 domains for short-term abstinence, 11 for intermediate, 1 long-term composite), each with a Q test of heterogeneity at P<0.1 (p. 370; Tables 1–3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Inclusion was by consensus of two authors; who extracted the data, and whether extraction was done in duplicate, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohen's d (positive = worse in the CUD group), random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) for the domain analyses and fixed-effect for the long-term composite; heterogeneity by Q only (no I², τ² or prediction interval). Short-term abstinence (Table 1, p. 371): attention 0.206 (95% CI −0.041 to 0.454), 4 studies; executive functions 0.388 (−0.024 to 0.801), 7, Q=33.7 (P=0.0001); impulsivity 0.408 (0.209 to 0.606), 8; language/verbal 0.042 (−0.168 to 0.252), 5; speed of processing 0.211 (0.012 to 0.410), 7; verbal learning 0.345 (0.070 to 0.620), 6; verbal memory 0.324 (0.080 to 0.569), 4; visual learning 0.534 (−0.033 to 1.101), 1; visual memory 0.521 (0.128 to 0.914), 4; visuospatial abilities 0.304 (−1.159 to 1.767), 2, Q=10.7 (P=0.001); working memory 0.437 (0.169 to 0.706), 3 after excluding an outlier study. Intermediate abstinence (Table 2, p. 371): attention 0.592 (0.315 to 0.869), 4; executive functions 0.320 (0.158 to 0.481), 13; impulsivity 0.581 (0.406 to 0.756), 10; language/verbal 0.219 (0.061 to 0.376), 12; speed of processing 0.447 (0.293 to 0.600), 21; verbal learning 0.551 (0.362 to 0.740), 15; verbal memory 0.556 (0.341 to 0.770), 12; visual learning 0.452 (0.276 to 0.629), 9; visual memory 0.433 (0.271 to 0.594), 11; visuospatial abilities 0.330 (0.077 to 0.583), 9; working memory 0.521 (0.298 to 0.745), 14, Q=26.8 (P=0.013). Long-term abstinence (Table 3, p. 372): global composite d=0.193 (−0.006 to 0.391), P=0.057, 5 studies, n=443, Q=1.3 (P=0.860), fixed-effect, after excluding an outlier study (Hanlon et al., 2011). Editors' calculation, assuming normal distributions with equal variances: d of 0.43 to 0.59 places the average person in the CUD group at about the 28th to 33rd percentile of the control distribution, and d=0.193 at about the 42nd, so most individuals in both groups score within the same range.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted group differences were pooled. No moderator other than the abstinence category was analysed.
analysis.selective_reporting: No table of included studies or of their characteristics; the abstinence category of each study is not given; the number of participants behind each domain estimate in Tables 1 and 2 is not given; the per-study composite used to group studies by abstinence (p. 370) is reported only for the long-term group, so the long-term composite cannot be compared with a composite for the shorter-abstinence groups. The direction and size of the two excluded outliers are not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Several short-term estimates rest on 1 to 3 studies (visual learning 1, visuospatial 2, working memory 3), and the long-term conclusion on 5 studies, which the authors acknowledge (p. 373). A Q test with so few studies has little power, so 'homogeneous' results do not show an absence of heterogeneity.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 46 case–control studies, people with a diagnosed cocaine use disorder scored lower than healthy controls in most domains. In studies with abstinence under 12 weeks, all 11 domain differences were significant: five with d of 0.5 or more (attention 0.59, impulsivity 0.58, verbal memory 0.56, verbal learning 0.55, working memory 0.52), three between 0.43 and 0.45, and executive functions, visuospatial abilities and language/verbal between 0.22 and 0.33. In studies of urine-positive participants, estimates were smaller for attention, speed of processing and verbal learning and memory, but the difference between the two groups of studies was not tested. In 5 studies with abstinence over 20 weeks, a global composite was d=0.193 (−0.006 to 0.391), P=0.057.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports moderate impairment across 8 domains at intermediate abstinence (the results text names 7 as moderate, and only 5 estimates reach 0.5) and says that cognitive dysfunctions "remain stable during the first months of abstinence and may abate after 5 months" (p. 368); the results and discussion call the long-term composite significant (p. 371), and the conclusion describes near normalization once the 5-month mark is reached (p. 374). Gaps: (1) by Table 3 the long-term estimate is not significant at 0.05 (P=0.057; the interval includes zero), comes from 5 studies with a fixed-effect model after excluding an outlier, and is a composite of all tests that is not comparable with the domain estimates; (2) stability during the first months was not analysed (the intermediate group was not subdivided), and the Discussion's statement that dysfunction persists beyond 3 months of abstinence and may last to nearly the 5-month mark (p. 373, 7th paragraph) has no pooled data behind it, because the intermediate group ends at 12 weeks and no study had 13 to 19 weeks of abstinence (p. 370); (3) recovery, and masking of deficits by residual cocaine effects, are inferred from comparisons between different sets of studies, without a test of the difference and without following the same people; (4) the authors' practical statement that clinical testing should be done only when urine tests are negative (p. 373) rests on these untested differences between studies; (5) Tables 1–3 are titled as effects of cocaine on cognition, although they pool cross-sectional differences that the authors themselves say may partly predate the disorder (p. 372). The discussion does acknowledge the small number of long-term studies and a possible survivorship effect, since people who relapse early are missing from long-term samples (p. 373).

timeline.event: Hester and Garavan fMRI GO–NOGO study of people who had used cocaine within 72 hours: not among the 46 included studies (testing during scanning was an exclusion criterion)

Jovanovski et al. meta-analysis of neurocognitive deficits in people who use cocaine, analysed by test subscore; this review was designed to address its limits (grouping by domain, abstinence duration, impulse-related tasks) (pp. 368–369)
Lane et al. Go/No-Go study of people with current cocaine dependence: one of the 46 included studies (its abstinence category is not reported)
Spronk et al. comprehensive review of the cognitive effects of cocaine (held in the library; not cited by this review and not read for this card)
This review: 46 studies to the end of 2012, 1452 people with CUD and 1411 controls.
Frazer et al. systematic critical review of the long-term effects of cocaine use on cognition (held in the library; not read for this card)
López-Martín et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition (held in the library; its overlap with this review was not assessed here)

replication.where_it_stands: A pooled summary of the case–control literature to 2012. Its domain estimates for abstinence under 12 weeks are the most robust part (9 to 21 studies per domain for most domains); its conclusions about recovery after about 5 months rest on one non-significant composite from 5 studies and on comparisons between different studies. Lane et al. (2007) is inside the pooled estimates and must not be cited beside this review as independent support. Overlap with Jovanovski et al. (2005) and with later reviews cannot be computed from this paper, which does not tabulate its included studies.

funding.funder: No funding statement for the review itself. The first author holds a Young Investigator Salary Award (Junior 1) from the Fonds de Recherche du Québec en Santé and is a supported member of the Centre de recherche de l'Institut Universitaire en Santé Mentale de Montréal (p. 368, first-page footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflicts of interest" (p. 368).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, University of Montreal, and the Centre de recherche de l'Institut Universitaire en Santé Mentale de Montréal; two authors are also affiliated with the Clinique du Nouveau-Départ, Montreal (p. 368). None of the 46 included studies is by these authors; the review cites the group's earlier meta-analyses on alcohol and on schizophrenia as models for its method.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal cohorts that test the same people with a diagnosed cocaine use disorder repeatedly through urine-verified abstinence beyond 6 to 12 months, alongside matched controls retested at the same intervals (to remove practice effects), with smoking, alcohol, depression and premorbid IQ measured and the proportion of individuals below normative cut-offs reported; or an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of existing case–control studies with these covariates.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM-diagnosed CUD without Axis I comorbidity), comparator (healthy controls), outcomes (cognitive domains) and abstinence groups are specified (pp. 369–370).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; abstinence cut-offs were set from the 'natural distribution' of the studies found (p. 370).

Reasons are given for excluding challenge studies, in-utero exposure and in-scanner testing, and a healthy control group was required (p. 369); the choice of cross-sectional case–control designs itself is implicit.

Two named databases (PubMed, Embase) plus 'Ovid', a search platform whose databases are not named; key words printed; reference lists of included studies searched. No search dates beyond the publication cut-off, no stated language policy, no grey literature, registries or expert contact.
Two authors reached consensus on inclusion and exclusion (p. 369); whether they screened independently is not stated, so this is a generous reading.
Not described; only the assignment of less common tests to domains is said to have been agreed by three authors (p. 369).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only the six eligible studies dropped at the last step are named with reasons (p. 370); studies excluded under criteria (i) to (viii) are not listed, and no flow of records is given.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Included studies are given only as citations; no table of populations, abstinence, controls, tests or designs.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of the primary studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of domain estimates, with tests averaged within each study (avoiding double counting), is reasonable; but unadjusted differences from non-randomized comparisons were pooled without justification, the long-term estimate switched to a fixed-effect model on the strength of a non-significant Q from 5 studies after excluding an outlier, and the differences between abstinence groups that the conclusions rest on were never tested.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, hence no sensitivity analysis by study quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Limitations are named (5 long-term studies, survivorship, smoking and depression unreported in more than 60% of studies; p. 373), but no study-level risk of bias was assessed, and the conclusions on near normalization by 5 months and on testing only urine-negative patients do not take these limits into account.

Q reported for every analysis; studies were partitioned by abstinence to reduce heterogeneity, and remaining heterogeneity is discussed with possible sources (definition of domains, length of use, route, age, amount, sex, tests; pp. 373–374). Weakened by reliance on Q alone and by the statement that homogeneity shows the method was valid (p. 374).
Not investigated or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No conflicts declared; the first author's salary award is stated (p. 368).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six critical items are not met (2, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) and one is met in part (4), which gives critically low confidence. The review is transparent about its domain grouping and gives every pooled estimate with an interval, so its domain estimates for intermediate abstinence can be cited as a summary of the published case–control differences, labelled as unadjusted cross-sectional associations of unknown quality. It should not be cited for recovery of cognition after about 5 months of abstinence (one non-significant composite from 5 studies), for masking of deficits by recent use (an untested comparison between different studies) or for any causal effect of cocaine.

key_findings.finding: 46 studies with 1452 people with a cocaine use disorder and 1411 healthy controls were analysed. 52 studies met the inclusion criteria; six named studies were not analysed (one used nonparametric statistics, four used overlapping samples, one gave no abstinence information).
key_findings.note: The text says 5 studies could not be included but names six; 52 − 6 = 46 matches the number analysed (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Eligibility required a DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence and a healthy control group; samples with comorbid Axis I disorders, samples in which all participants used several substances, challenge studies, in-utero exposure, testing during EEG, MRI or PET, and studies published after 1 January 2013 were excluded. PubMed, Embase and Ovid were searched with the printed key words, plus reference lists; two authors agreed on inclusion by consensus.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Literature Search and Study Selection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Abstinence groups were defined from each study's average, minimum or maximum abstinence: short-term = urine positive for cocaine (under 72 hours), intermediate = under 12 weeks, long-term = over 20 weeks; no study had 13 to 19 weeks. Meta-regression on abstinence was not used because the distribution across studies was skewed (Kolmogorov–Smirnov P=0.0001).
key_findings.note: The abstract and the titles of Tables 2 and 3 give the boundaries as 12 weeks or less and 20 weeks or more.

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes were Cohen's d (positive = worse performance in the CUD group; 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 = small, medium, large), averaged within each study across the tests of a domain, then pooled with a random-effects model; heterogeneity was tested with Q at P<0.1, and studies or single tests more than 2 SD from the overall composite effect size were excluded as outliers.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Quantitative Data Synthesis, 1st paragraph (continued from p. 369) and 2nd paragraph; Methods › Homogeneity of Effect-Size Estimates, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Short-term abstinence (urine positive), pooled d (95% CI), number of studies: attention 0.206 (−0.041 to 0.454), 4; executive functions 0.388 (−0.024 to 0.801), 7; impulsivity 0.408 (0.209 to 0.606), 8; language/verbal 0.042 (−0.168 to 0.252), 5; speed of processing 0.211 (0.012 to 0.410), 7; verbal learning 0.345 (0.070 to 0.620), 6; verbal memory 0.324 (0.080 to 0.569), 4; visual learning 0.534 (−0.033 to 1.101), 1; visual memory 0.521 (0.128 to 0.914), 4; visuospatial 0.304 (−1.159 to 1.767), 2; working memory 0.437 (0.169 to 0.706), 3 after excluding one outlier study (Madoz-Gurpide et al., 2011). Q was significant at P<0.1 for executive functions (33.7, P=0.0001), verbal learning (10.0, P=0.076), visual memory (6.3, P=0.097) and visuospatial abilities (10.7, P=0.001).

Intermediate abstinence (under 12 weeks), pooled d (95% CI), number of studies: attention 0.592 (0.315 to 0.869), 4; executive functions 0.320 (0.158 to 0.481), 13; impulsivity 0.581 (0.406 to 0.756), 10; language/verbal 0.219 (0.061 to 0.376), 12; speed of processing 0.447 (0.293 to 0.600), 21; verbal learning 0.551 (0.362 to 0.740), 15; verbal memory 0.556 (0.341 to 0.770), 12; visual learning 0.452 (0.276 to 0.629), 9; visual memory 0.433 (0.271 to 0.594), 11; visuospatial 0.330 (0.077 to 0.583), 9; working memory 0.521 (0.298 to 0.745), 14. All P≤0.011. Q was significant at P<0.1 for speed of processing (29.0, P=0.087), verbal learning (22.8, P=0.064), verbal memory (19.0, P=0.062), visuospatial (13.7, P=0.09) and working memory (26.8, P=0.013).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (normal distributions, equal variances): d of 0.43 to 0.59 corresponds to the average person in the CUD group scoring at about the 28th to 33rd percentile of controls. Participant numbers per domain are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Long-term abstinence (over 20 weeks): only a global composite of all test scores could be computed; d=0.193 (95% CI −0.006 to 0.391), P=0.057, 5 studies, n=443, Q=1.3 (P=0.860), fixed-effect model, after excluding an outlier study (Hanlon et al., 2011). The text calls this estimate small and barely significant.
key_findings.note: Whether n=443 counts both groups or the CUD group only is not stated. Editors' calculation: d=0.193 places the average person in the CUD group at about the 42nd percentile of controls.

key_findings.finding: Full-scale IQ could not be pooled because only 2 studies reported it.

Estimates were smaller in urine-positive studies than at intermediate abstinence for attention (0.206 vs 0.592), speed of processing (0.211 vs 0.447), verbal learning (0.345 vs 0.551) and verbal memory (0.324 vs 0.556); the authors argue that residual effects of recent cocaine use may have improved performance and partly masked deficits (the abstract names residual or acute withdrawal effects). No statistical test of the difference between the two groups of studies is reported.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Discussion (p. 368); Tables 1–2 (p. 371); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 371) and 5th paragraph (p. 372, continuing on p. 373)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the recovery conclusion rests on 5 studies, that a survivorship effect may overestimate improvement because people who relapse early are absent from long-term samples, and that confounding by depressive symptoms or cigarette smoking could not be examined because more than 60% of studies did not report them.

The 'impulsivity' domain (reward- or impulse-related functions) combined response inhibition tasks (Go/No-Go, stop-signal reaction time, CPT commission errors) with decision-making tasks (probabilistic reversal learning, Iowa Gambling Task); the included studies also comprise three delay-discounting studies (Kirby and Petry, 2004; Heil et al., 2006; Johnson, 2012, by their titles), and the authors read the domain as covering both a preference for small immediate over large delayed rewards and impaired suppression of prepotent motor responses. The pooled impulsivity estimates (0.408 in urine-positive studies, 0.581 at intermediate abstinence) are therefore not estimates of inhibitory control alone.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cognitive Domains, 1st paragraph, and Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 369); Tables 1–2 (p. 371); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 372); starred studies in the reference list (pp. 374–375)
key_findings.note: Which studies entered the domain is not reported; the three delay-discounting studies are identified from the starred titles (editors' reading).

reporting_issues.issue: The long-term composite is called 'small and barely significant' (Results) and 'of significant but small magnitude' (Discussion), but Table 3 gives P=0.057 with a 95% CI of −0.006 to 0.391.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimate is not significant at the conventional 0.05 level; the abstract's 'small effect-size estimates' and the conclusion of near normalization by 5 months rest on a non-significant composite from 5 studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports moderate impairment across 8 domains at intermediate abstinence; the Results and Discussion name 7 domains as moderate (visual memory, d=0.433, is called small-to-moderate), and by the authors' own thresholds only 5 estimates reach 0.5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should quote the domain estimates, not the count of 'moderately impaired' domains.

reporting_issues.issue: For short-term abstinence the text describes deficits in executive functions, visuospatial abilities and visual learning and memory, and flags only attention as non-significant, but the intervals for executive functions (−0.024 to 0.801), visuospatial abilities (−1.159 to 1.767) and visual learning (one study, −0.033 to 1.101) also include zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three short-term 'deficits' in the text are not statistically distinguishable from no difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 5 eligible studies could not be included but names six (52 − 6 = 46). One of them, Goldstein and Volkow (2011), is listed in the references as a review article in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, yet is said to have used data overlapping with Hoff et al. (1996).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the count of 46 is consistent with the six names, but the exclusion list contains at least one apparent citation error.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that 13 of 22 analyses were homogeneous and that heterogeneity was rather small (P between 0.05 and 0.1) in 7 of the remaining 9; by Tables 1 and 2, only 6 of the 9 have P between 0.05 and 0.1 (the other three: executive functions and visuospatial at short-term, working memory at intermediate abstinence). The Discussion then takes homogeneity as showing that the method was valid.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor miscount; more importantly, a non-significant Q with 4 to 21 studies does not establish homogeneity, and no I² or τ² is given.

reporting_issues.issue: Abstinence boundaries are stated differently: under 12 weeks and over 20 weeks (Methods, p. 370) against 12 weeks or less and 20 weeks or more (abstract, Tables 2 and 3); short-term is urine positive for cocaine in the Methods and positive for drugs in the abstract and Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; with no study between 13 and 19 weeks, the boundary wording does not change the groups, but the short-term definition is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say which studies entered which abstinence group, although several included studies, by their titles, compared current and abstinent subgroups or retested the same people (Di Sclafani et al., 2002, at 6 weeks and 6 months; Heil et al., 2006; Woicik et al., 2009; Hanlon et al., 2011).
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be checked whether some participants contributed to more than one abstinence group, and the between-group comparisons that the recovery conclusions rest on cannot be audited.

design_detail: Review of human studies of cocaine and cognition with a stated PubMed search, in two parts: 14 placebo-controlled laboratory studies of acute cocaine administration (narrative synthesis only, Table 2) and 61 case–control studies published from 2003 onwards comparing people with a history of cocaine use with non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls (narrative synthesis by cognitive domain, Table 3, plus eight random-effects meta-analyses of standardized mean differences on subsets of three to nine studies). Domains: attention, response inhibition, memory and learning, cognitive flexibility, performance monitoring, reward-based decision making, psychomotor performance. Read from the uncorrected proof, not the version of record.
can_establish: How large the reported test-score differences were, domain by domain, between people with a history of cocaine use (mostly people with cocaine dependence) and control groups in the cross-sectional studies the authors pooled up to about 2013, and which cognitive domains had any placebo-controlled data on acute effects.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the differences (every long-term study is cross-sectional, with no pre-use measurement and no adjustment for education, other drugs or premorbid ability); that the differences amount to impairment (no comparison with norms); how results change with abstinence or with recreational versus dependent use (no moderator analyses); that the pooled estimates are unbiased (one database, no risk-of-bias or publication-bias assessment, studies removed for heterogeneity); or what acute cocaine does to cognition in people without prior use.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Studies were found by a PubMed search combining cocaine with cognition, cognitive or neuropsychology, and with each domain term, limited to humans and adults, plus a check of reference lists; English only; no search dates and no flow of records are given (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Acute studies: placebo-controlled laboratory administration of cocaine. Long-term studies: people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence compared with a non-drug or non-cocaine-using control group free of medical and psychiatric disorders, published from 2003 onwards because studies from 1987–2002 had been reviewed by Jovanovski et al. (2005). Meta-analyses: at least three studies reporting N, means and SDs on an outcome judged representative of the domain; behavioural results from fMRI studies left out (§2.1–2.2, PDF pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Not summarized. Tables 2 and 3 give group sizes, a description of each sample's use (dependence, abuse, recreational use, crack use), frequency and years of use, and abstinence where reported; age, sex and education are not tabulated (PDF pp. 5–9).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Single-database, English-only search without stated dates or a record of screening. Long-term samples are mostly people with cocaine dependence; the authors note that only a minority of studies examined people who use cocaine recreationally (§4.5, PDF p. 16). Every acute study tested people with previous cocaine experience, most with dependence or crack use and several within 72 hours of last use (Table 2, PDF p. 5), so the acute results do not describe people without prior use, as the authors acknowledge (§4.3, PDF p. 15). Table 3 also lists two long-term studies published before the 2003 cut-off (Fillmore, 2002; Kirby et al., 1999).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies. The review tabulates diagnostic category, frequency and total years of use and abstinence, with many entries marked unknown (Table 3, PDF pp. 6–9). In the acute studies cocaine or placebo was given in the laboratory (Table 2, PDF p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Acute studies: intravenous, oral, intranasal and smoked administration, several doses per study; doses appear in Table 2 as study conditions and are not reproduced here. Long-term studies: frequency entries range from under about 3 occasions a month (recreational samples) to several days a week, and duration up to about 21 years of use; many entries are unknown (Table 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled in the analyses. The authors state that most if not all participants in the reviewed studies used several drugs and suggest controls with similar use of other drugs but no cocaine (§4.3, PDF p. 15). Examples in Table 3: a cocaine-dependent sample with and without alcohol use (Abi-Saab et al., 2005) and a sample dependent on two or more substances (Tanabe et al., 2009, footnote f).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Acute studies: from under 72 hours to weeks before the sessions, or a negative urine test (Table 2). Long-term studies: from under 72 hours, or cocaine-positive urine at screening, to months or years, and often unknown; by the editors' count about 23 of the 55 distinct study labels in Table 3 included at least some participants tested within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine. No analysis by abstinence was possible (§4.4, PDF p. 16).

comparison.controls: Acute studies: placebo sessions in the same participants. Long-term studies: non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls free of medical and psychiatric disorders; in some studies the controls used other drugs but not cocaine (for example the polydrug controls of Colzato, 2009a, Table 3).
comparison.matching: Not extracted or assessed by the review.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No study measured cognition before cocaine use. The authors state that group differences can never be read as caused solely by cocaine, that people who use cocaine may differ beforehand in cognition and personality, and that education and lifestyle are major potential confounders (§4.3, PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Varied and not tabulated; non-cocaine-using controls could use other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Paradigms by domain (Table 1, PDF p. 4): attention (P300, CPT, IMT, RVIP, Stroop, Cocaine Stroop, Global–Local task and others); response inhibition (stop-signal task, Go/NoGo, IMT); memory (CVLT, RAVLT, LMT, HVLT, n-back, digit span, spatial working memory); stimulus–response learning; cognitive flexibility (WCST, IED, reversal learning); performance monitoring (ERN, Pe, post-error slowing); reward-based decision making (delay discounting, IGT, BART); psychomotor performance (DSST, Trail Making, finger tapping, grooved pegboard).
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with normative data; every result is a difference from a control group.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means poorer performance than the control group, either a statistically significant difference in a primary study or a pooled standardized mean difference graded small (0.2 or less), moderate (about 0.5) or large (about 0.8 or more) (§2.2, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the eight pooled outcomes or for the many narrative comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review; not extracted for the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects standardized mean differences with 95% CIs (RevMan 5.2.2), long-term studies only; I² is said to have been computed but is not reported for any pool; no prediction intervals, per-study estimates or forest plots. Sustained attention (CPT hits with P300 amplitude) −1.22 (−1.58 to −0.85), number of studies not stated; stop-signal reaction time 0.50 (0.11 to 0.90), 3 studies; failed inhibitions (commission errors) 0.64 (0.44 to 0.84), 9 studies stated, 8 named; immediate recall −0.46 (−0.70 to −0.23), 8 studies; perseverative errors 0.37 (0.17 to 0.57), 5 studies; reward-based decision making (delay-discounting k and IGT net score) 0.53 (0.32 to 0.75), 7 studies; psychomotor motor responses 0.75 (0.46 to 1.04), 3 studies; psychomotor response time −0.24 (−0.47 to −0.02), 6 studies. All are in the direction of poorer performance in the cocaine groups; the sign convention differs between outcomes. Studies were removed for their contribution to heterogeneity in the attention, stop-signal, perseveration and motor-response pools. No acute pooling (too few comparable studies).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted group means and SDs were pooled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Studies were dropped post hoc from four of the eight pools because they contributed to heterogeneity, including studies with null results (Liu et al., 2011, attention; Woicik et al., 2009, finger tapping); the studies in the attention pool are not identified, nor which three stop-signal and which five perseveration studies were kept; participant totals per pool are not given. Several counts in the text disagree with the studies named or with Tables 2 and 3 (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The acute studies had 8 to 48 participants each (editors' count: 13 of 14 had 14 or fewer); the long-term pools rest on three to nine small cross-sectional studies, and the authors call the number of studies per analysis very small (§4.4, PDF p. 16).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Eight pooled standardized differences between cocaine groups and controls, 0.24 to 1.22 in absolute size, each from three to nine cross-sectional studies, with studies dropped for heterogeneity in four pools and no information on heterogeneity, study-level bias or publication bias; narratively, poorer performance of cocaine groups in most domains alongside several null studies. The 14 acute studies (8 to 48 people with previous cocaine use each) found better inhibition in three of four studies and faster DSST responding in two of six, and mostly no effect elsewhere.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes long-term use as “characterized by a general cognitive impairment across functions” (PDF p. 1), and the domain summaries use causal wording (cocaine worsening immediate recall, long-term use having an impairing effect on perseveration, chronic cocaine having a relatively large impact on psychomotor performance; PDF pp. 11, 12, 14) without norms, adjustment for confounding or a pre-use baseline. The response-inhibition summary says every reviewed study points to impairment, although the same section reports two non-significant stop-signal studies and a null study with a composite measure (PDF pp. 10–11). The abstract presents acute enhancement of response inhibition and psychomotor speed, while §4.3 warns that this may only offset pre-existing deficits in people who regularly use cocaine (PDF p. 15), and it offers atherosclerosis as a possible mechanism that the review does not examine (PDF pp. 1, 14–15). The causal caveats of §4.3 are sound but are not carried into the abstract or the domain summaries.

timeline.event: Quantitative review of studies from 1987–2002 (Jovanovski et al.); Spronk et al. start their long-term inclusion in 2003 to follow on from it and describe their long-term results as broadly in agreement with it
This review: 14 acute and 61 long-term studies, eight pooled long-term outcomes

Systematic quantitative review of cocaine and cognition grouped by abstinence duration (Potvin et al., 2014; 46 studies to the end of 2012), read for the round of 12 November 2026; it does not cite this review

Systematic critical review (Frazer et al.) quotes this review's abstract conclusion of general impairment and argues that its own tabulated studies do not support it, mainly because most studies lacked normative comparison, demographic matching and control of other drug use
Systematic review and meta-analysis of cocaine use and cognitive inhibition (López-Martín et al.; appraised separately)

replication.where_it_stands: Poorer average performance of people with (mostly dependent) cocaine use than controls on tests of inhibition, memory, decision making and psychomotor speed recurs across reviews (Jovanovski et al., 2005; this review). Whether the differences come from cocaine, from pre-existing differences, other drugs and alcohol, recent use or withdrawal, and whether they amount to impairment against norms, remains unsettled; Frazer et al. (2018) dispute the general-impairment reading. Acute placebo-controlled evidence is limited to small studies of people who already use cocaine.

funding.funder: ZonMW grant 31160205 to J.G. Ramaekers and R.J. Verkes; the funder had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Role of funding source, PDF p. 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no financial interests and no conflicts of interest (Conflicts of interest, PDF p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Centre, and Donders Institute (Nijmegen); Department of Neuropsychology and Psychopharmacology, Maastricht University. None of the included cocaine studies is by the review's authors; their own work is cited only for comparisons with cannabis and MDMA. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review searching several databases with duplicate screening, study-level risk-of-bias assessment, all eligible studies pooled with heterogeneity reported and explored rather than removed, and moderator analyses by verified abstinence, recreational versus dependent use, alcohol and other drug use and education; for causation, prospective cohorts that test cognition before regular cocaine use and repeatedly during biologically verified abstinence, scored against demographically adjusted norms. For acute effects, placebo-controlled studies that also test a matched group without cocaine use under placebo, to see whether acute improvement is a return toward the control level.

domains.note: Population (adults with a history of cocaine use; acute: participants in placebo-controlled sessions), exposure, comparators (placebo; non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls) and cognitive outcomes are stated (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Placebo-controlled acute studies and case–control long-term studies are required without a stated rationale; only the 2003 cut-off is explained.
PubMed only (with reference lists), English only without justification, no search dates, no grey literature (§2.1, PDF pp. 2–3); AMSTAR 2 requires at least two databases even for a partial yes.
Not reported.
Not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies and no flow of records.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2 and 3 give group sizes, type of use, frequency and years of use, abstinence, tasks and direction of results (PDF pp. 5–9), but no age, sex, education, recruitment setting or other drug use.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the primary studies; confounding is discussed only in general terms (§4.3, PDF p. 15).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects weighting is appropriate, but unadjusted means from observational studies were pooled without justification, different constructs were combined in one pool (CPT hits with P300 amplitude; delay-discounting k with IGT net score; PDF p. 3), and studies were removed post hoc because they raised heterogeneity, in four of eight pools (PDF pp. 4, 10, 12, 14).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk of bias was assessed, so its impact was not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: §4.3 lists general sources of bias (pre-existing differences, polydrug use, education, abstinence; PDF p. 15), but study-level bias was never assessed and the domain conclusions and abstract are written causally.
I² values are never reported; heterogeneity was handled by removing studies, with only scattered task-level explanations (e.g., task difficulty in reversal learning, PDF p. 11).
Not investigated.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funder, its role and the absence of conflicts are stated (PDF p. 16).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Under AMSTAR 2 the review fails all seven critical items (no protocol, single-database search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment, pooling with post hoc heterogeneity-based exclusions and unreported I², conclusions not tempered by study-level bias, no publication-bias assessment), which gives critically low confidence. It remains a useful map of paradigms and of the acute placebo-controlled studies up to about 2013 (Tables 1–3). Its pooled standardized differences may be cited only as summaries of selected cross-sectional group differences with these caveats, not as estimates of cocaine's effect or of clinical impairment. Its acute enhancement findings rest on small studies of people who regularly use cocaine, which the authors themselves say may reflect the offsetting of pre-existing deficits.

key_findings.finding: Search and inclusion: PubMed only, cocaine combined with cognition terms and with each domain term, limited to humans and adults, English only, plus reference lists. Acute studies had to be placebo-controlled laboratory administrations; long-term studies had to compare people with a history of recreational use, abuse or dependence with non-drug or non-cocaine-using controls free of medical and psychiatric disorders and to be published from 2003 (studies from 1987–2002 having been reviewed by Jovanovski et al., 2005). 14 acute and 61 long-term studies were included.
key_findings.locator: §2.1 Literature search and inclusion criteria (single paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis methods: long-term studies only, run in RevMan 5.2.2 with random-effects models; a domain was pooled when at least three studies reported N, means and SDs on an outcome judged representative; behavioural data from fMRI studies were excluded; standardized mean differences with 95% CIs; I² over 75% taken as high, and a study contributing largely to I² was left out of the pool.
key_findings.locator: §2.2 Outline of the review and analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The 14 acute studies had 8 to 48 participants each (editors' count: 13 of the 14 had 14 or fewer; 183 in total). All participants had previous cocaine experience, described as experienced or recreational use, cocaine dependence or crack use; abstinence before sessions ranged from under 72 hours to weeks; routes were intravenous, oral, intranasal and smoked.
key_findings.note: Doses per study are listed in Table 2 as study conditions and are not reproduced on this card.

key_findings.finding: Acute attention: five studies; the text counts two with no effect, two with impairment and one with improvement and reaches no conclusion.
key_findings.note: Table 2 codes the same studies as one decrease, three no effect and one improvement (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Acute response inhibition: three of four studies (Fillmore et al., 2005, 2006; Garavan et al., 2008; 12 to 14 participants each, people who used crack tested within 72 hours of last use or people with recent use) found better inhibitory performance after cocaine than after placebo; the fourth (Fillmore et al., 2002, 8 participants) is described in the text as a dose-related fall in the probability of inhibiting a response. Three of the four studies share a first author (Fillmore).
Acute memory: three studies found no effect on immediate recall, delayed recall or recognition, and one found no effect on repeated acquisition learning.

Acute psychomotor performance: six DSST studies; four found no effect (smoked, intravenous and oral cocaine in people with cocaine dependence or crack use) and two (Higgins et al., 1990, 1993; 8 participants each) found faster responding after intranasal cocaine; too few reported comparable means and SDs for pooling. The authors attribute the difference to the route.
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from Table 2: the two positive studies are also the only ones in recreational samples, so route and type of use cannot be separated.

key_findings.finding: No placebo-controlled acute study existed for cognitive flexibility, performance monitoring or reward processing.

Long-term sustained attention (CPT hits combined with P300 amplitude): pooled SMD −1.22 (95% CI −1.58 to −0.85), lower in the cocaine groups. The number of pooled studies is not stated; other studies, including the one CPT study without a group difference (Liu et al., 2011), were left out because they contributed too much to heterogeneity.

Long-term attention, narrative: four of eight sustained-attention studies found poorer performance and four did not (three of the null studies used the Trail Making Test, which the authors consider a poor attention measure); four Stroop or five-digit studies found no difference in selective attention; all Cocaine Stroop studies found a stronger attentional bias toward cocaine-related words.
key_findings.locator: §3.1.2 Long-term effects, 1st, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (pp. 4–5) and last paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Long-term stop-signal reaction time: of five stop-signal studies (all with longer SSRT in the cocaine group, two not significantly), four reported means and SDs; after leaving out Fillmore and Rush (2002) for heterogeneity, three pooled to SMD 0.50 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.90), longer (poorer) in the cocaine groups.

Long-term failed inhibitions (commission errors on Go/NoGo, IMT and CPT): pooled SMD 0.64 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.84), more errors in the cocaine groups; one study using a composite measure found no difference (Moeller et al., 2010a).
key_findings.note: The text says nine studies were pooled but names eight.

key_findings.finding: Long-term immediate recall (correct recalls on CVLT, LMT or RAVLT): eight studies pooled to SMD −0.46 (95% CI −0.70 to −0.23), fewer items recalled in the cocaine groups; narratively seven studies found poorer and two no different recall.
key_findings.note: One of the seven studies counted as showing poorer recall (Reske, 2010) is coded no effect in Table 3 (p. 7). The two studies the text names as showing no difference (Woicik et al., 2011; Rahman et al., 2005) are both among the eight pooled.

key_findings.finding: Long-term working memory (not pooled): five of eight studies found poorer performance, more consistently on visuospatial than on verbal tasks; stimulus–response learning results were mixed and too few to generalize.

Long-term perseverative errors (WCST, reversal learning, IED): three of eight studies were left out for heterogeneity (Colzato et al., 2009a,b; Ersche et al., 2008; Fernandez-Serrano et al., 2012); the remaining five pooled to SMD 0.37 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.57), more perseverative errors in the cocaine groups, called a small effect by the authors.

Long-term performance monitoring (not pooled): two ERP studies found a smaller error-related negativity (one also a smaller Pe), and three behavioural measures showed less adjustment after errors or stop signals; the authors call the domain little studied.

Long-term reward-based decision making: delay-discounting k and IGT net scores from seven studies pooled to SMD 0.53 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.75), poorer in the cocaine groups. Narratively, three studies found steeper delay discounting; among IGT-type studies seven found poorer and four no different performance; three studies by Moeller et al. (2009, 2010b, 2012) found a stronger choice of cocaine-related pictures.
key_findings.note: The text introduces the IGT studies as ten, then lists seven plus four. Two of the seven pooled studies (Adinoff et al., 2003; Woicik et al., 2009) are among the four IGT studies the text reports as null (PDF p. 13).

key_findings.finding: Long-term psychomotor performance: motor responses (DSST substitutions, finger tapping) from three studies, after leaving out Woicik et al. (2009) for heterogeneity, SMD 0.75 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.04); response latency or completion time from six studies (Hanlon et al., 2010, left out because tested during fMRI), SMD −0.24 (95% CI −0.47 to −0.02); both in the direction of slower performance in the cocaine groups.

Abstinence at testing in the long-term studies ranges from under 72 hours, or cocaine-positive urine at screening, to months or years (the longest: averages of 4.5 years in Goldstein et al., 2007a,b, and 4.7 years in Tanabe et al., 2009, and a range of 0 to 1825 days in Moeller et al., 2009), and is unknown for several studies; by the editors' count about 23 of the 55 distinct study labels include at least some participants tested within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, abstinence column and footnotes c, d, e and g
key_findings.note: Editors' count: labels such as Moeller 2010a,b and Goldstein 2007a,b counted once; entries of at least 2 or 3 days not counted.

key_findings.finding: The authors' own caveats: acute studies tested people who regularly use cocaine, so acute improvement may only offset pre-existing deficits and could be misleading; long-term group differences can never be interpreted as caused solely by cocaine; abstinence varied; most if not all participants used several drugs; lifestyle and education are major potential confounders.
key_findings.locator: §4.3 Considerations in the interpretation of results, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: very few studies per pool, no pooling possible for any acute domain, combining different outcome measures is acknowledged to introduce bias, and no subgroup or moderator analysis by abstinence, history of use or type of use was feasible.
key_findings.locator: §4.4 Limitations of the review, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors propose cocaine-related atherosclerosis as possibly the primary mechanism of a general impairment; the review analyses no vascular measure.

Recreational use: the authors report preliminary evidence of poorer cognitive flexibility in recreational samples (Colzato et al., 2009a,b) but state that few studies examined recreational use and that it is not yet known whether recreational use affects cognition.
key_findings.locator: §3.4.2 Long-term effects, last paragraph (p. 12); §4.5 Directions for future research, 2nd paragraph (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Samples that Table 3 describes as recreational are among the pooled studies: Rahman et al. (2005; 40 vs 39) and Reske (2010; 13 vs 48) among the eight immediate-recall studies, Rahman et al. (2005) and Soar et al. (2012; 17 vs 24) among the response-time studies, and Soar et al. (2012) among the CPT studies with fewer hits from which the sustained-attention pool was drawn. The pooled estimates therefore do not describe people with dependence only.
key_findings.locator: §3.1.2 Long-term effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 4); Table 3, type-of-use column (pp. 6–9); §3.3.2 Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (p. 11); §3.7.2 Chronic effects, 1st paragraph (p. 14)

reporting_issues.issue: Fillmore et al. (2002), acute stop-signal study: the text describes a dose-related fall in the probability of inhibiting a response (poorer inhibition), but Table 2 codes the study as improved performance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of one of only four acute response-inhibition studies is uncertain from the review; the primary paper must be read before it is cited either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Stillman et al. (1993), acute attention: the text reports a slight decline in attention over 4 hours after cocaine and counts it among two studies showing impairment, while Table 2 codes it as no effect with faster orienting.
reporting_issues.consequence: The acute attention tally (two null, two impaired, one improved) does not match Table 2 (one decrease, three null, one improved).

reporting_issues.issue: Reske (2010) is counted in the text among seven studies showing poorer immediate recall, but Table 3 codes it as no effect on the CVLT; it is also among the eight studies in the recall pool.
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrative count of positive studies is overstated by at least one; how this study entered the pooled estimate cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Abi-Saab et al. (2005) is listed in the text among four studies showing psychomotor impairment and enters the motor-response pool, but Table 3 codes its psychomotor tests (DSST, finger tapping, grooved pegboard and others) as no effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The motor-response pool of only three studies, SMD 0.75, includes a study the table describes as null, after a null study (Woicik et al., 2009) was removed for heterogeneity.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts in the text disagree with the studies named: nine commission-error studies with eight named (p. 10); ten IGT studies, then seven impaired plus four null (p. 13); six response-time studies with seven named (p. 14); working memory introduced as seven studies and summarized as five of eight (p. 11); three of five set-shifting studies supported by four citations (p. 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor individually, but the pooled study sets cannot be reconstructed with certainty from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: No I² is reported for any pool although the methods say it was computed, and studies were removed post hoc for their contribution to heterogeneity in four of eight pools (attention, stop-signal, perseveration, motor responses), including null studies; the attention pool's studies are not identified, nor which three stop-signal and five perseveration studies remained; no forest plots, per-study effects or participant totals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled SMDs describe selected subsets with confidence intervals that understate between-study spread; they cannot be checked or reproduced from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The signs of the pooled SMDs are not oriented consistently: poorer performance appears as negative for attention, immediate recall and response time, and as positive for stop-signal reaction time, commission errors, perseveration, decision making and motor responses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Direction must be taken from the text; a claim quoting a sign alone could invert the finding. Refinement: under one cocaine-minus-control convention most pools' printed signs fit their outcome definitions (§2.2, PDF p. 3); the two psychomotor pools run the other way (motor responses, where higher is better, positive; response time, where higher is worse, negative), so their direction rests on the authors' text alone.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 includes two long-term studies published before the 2003 cut-off (Fillmore, 2002; Kirby et al., 1999), and the abstract says all available case-controlled studies were reviewed although long-term studies before 2003 were excluded by design.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the inclusion rule was not applied strictly, and the abstract overstates completeness.

reporting_issues.issue: Study labels in Table 3 carry different sample sizes in different domains: Colzato (2009b) 13 vs 16 and 20 vs 20; Woicik et al. (2011) 107 vs 107 and, under psychomotor performance, 64 vs 64 (the size given for Woicik et al., 2009); van der Plas et al. (2009) 27 vs 36 and 22 vs 21. reporting_issues.consequence: Which primary paper supports a given row is uncertain in several places; primary studies should be identified by DOI before citation.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is the uncorrected proof: author queries Q1–Q16 remain, an editing bracket is left in §4.5, an Uncited references list is printed, and Table 2 labels its last section 3.7 instead of 3.8.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some of the errors listed here may have been corrected in the version of record (Neurosci Biobehav Rev 37(8):1838–1859), which was not read.
