design_detail: Retrospective single-centre case series of all adults admitted from the emergency department (ED) of one urban university-affiliated trauma centre (Hurley Medical Center, Flint, Michigan; annual ED census 55,000) with chest pain after recent cocaine use, 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998. The Methods call it a retrospective cohort study (p. 873) and the Discussion a retrospective case series (p. 876); there is no comparison group. A departmental policy required admission of every patient with cocaine-associated chest pain for at least 23 hours, with cardiac enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours. Charts were abstracted with a closed-question instrument. Outcome: the proportion of admitted patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) by WHO criteria, plus in-hospital complications.
can_establish: How often adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at this one hospital in 1996–1998 met WHO enzyme criteria for myocardial infarction during a 24-hour rule-out (15 of 250), and how often in-hospital complications occurred and when.
cannot_establish: Whether cocaine caused the infarctions or the chest pain (no comparison group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, and use at any time in the previous week was enough to enter); the risk of infarction for a person who uses cocaine (the denominator is admitted patients, not people who use cocaine); what predicts infarction (patients with and without infarction are never compared); or how many small infarctions CK-MB testing missed (the authors cannot exclude a few missed non-Q-wave infarctions, p. 877).

sample.recruitment: Records (clinic): computer-assisted search of medical records for all ED presentations from 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998, cross-referencing ICD-9 codes for chest pain and myocardial infarction with the ICD-9 codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse (the coding categories searched), then checked against an ED log of all admitted patients (p. 874, Methods › Study Setting and Population).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included if aged 18 or older, with a chief complaint of anterior, precordial or left-sided chest discomfort lasting less than 12 hours, and either documented cocaine use in the week before presentation or a urine screen positive for cocaine or its metabolites (p. 874). Excluded: 9 patients discharged from the ED against the admission policy (pp. 874–875).
sample.demographics: Mean age 33.5 years (SD 8.5); 192 men (77%) and 58 women (23%); 208 African American (84%), 24 White (10%), 3 Hispanic (1%), 15 other or unknown (6%). Hypertension 26%, hypercholesterolaemia 8%, family history of coronary disease 34%, diabetes 6%, tobacco use 77%; previous chest pain 40%, previous myocardial infarction 6% (16), heart failure 2%, arrhythmia 1%; mean 1.5 (SD 1.1) traditional cardiac risk factors (Table 1, p. 874; Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 875).
sample.attrition: 9 of 259 identified patients (3.5%) were excluded because they had been discharged from the ED; they did not differ significantly in age, sex, ethnicity or cardiac risk factors, their complications are unknown, and all nine were alive at the end of the study period (pp. 874–875). None of the 250 admitted patients was lost; all survived to discharge (p. 875).
sample.selection_effects: One urban hospital whose patients were mostly young, male, African American and smoking crack; other settings are untested. Patients could enter only if their cocaine use was recorded in a way that produced the cocaine or drug-abuse codes, and urine toxicology was part of the cardiac work-up by policy only for patients aged 50 or under without traditional risk factors (p. 876), so cocaine use in older patients or patients with risk factors was less likely to be found; the authors concede some patients over 50 may have been missed (pp. 876–877). Case-finding was more thorough for the numerator than for the denominator: every chart coded for AMI, with or without cocaine, was reviewed (p. 876), whereas patients without AMI whose cocaine use was not coded could not be found. That asymmetry, like the exclusion of the 9 ED discharges, would tend to raise the proportion with AMI (editors' reading). Patients with ischaemic symptoms other than chest pain were not included (p. 876).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine use in the week before presentation as documented in the chart, or a positive urine screen. Urine toxicology was performed in 196 of 250 patients (78%); 185 were positive (94% of those tested) (p. 875, Results, 3rd paragraph). The authors assume the 6% who reported use but tested negative (11 of the 196 tested, 5.6%; editors' arithmetic, 196 minus 185) bought a mislabelled or heavily adulterated substance or presented after the assay's detection window (p. 877).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amount not recorded. Timing (a precise history was available for all but 3 patients): last use within 24 hours in 193 (printed 78%) and within 4 hours in 57 (printed 22%) (p. 875); the abstract gives 77% within 24 hours (p. 873). Route: crack inhalation 91% in the Results (p. 875), but crack 85%, intravenous 2% and nasal 6% in the abstract (p. 873).
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or reported, apart from tobacco use (77%). Alcohol and other drugs are not mentioned.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (acute presentation).

comparison.controls: None. There is no group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, and patients with and without AMI are not compared with each other.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary anatomy, earlier cardiac testing, and the pattern and amount of cocaine use are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Chart abstraction with a previously described closed-question instrument (interrater reliability reported in an earlier study, ref. 12; the abstract says it had 119 items) (p. 874; abstract, p. 873). Cardiac isoenzymes on presentation and every 8 hours for 24 hours in every patient. AMI by WHO criteria: CK-MB at least twice the institutional normal value with a typical rise and fall; infarcts classed as Q-wave or non-Q-wave and by location on the ECG. The initial ECG was classed in a closed-question format as normal, nonspecific (including early repolarization), abnormal but not diagnostic of ischaemia, ischaemic (old, or not known to be old), or suggestive of AMI (p. 874).
outcomes.validity_norms: WHO criteria with serial CK-MB, the standard of the time. Every diagnosed AMI had CK-MB above 20 IU/L although the threshold was twice normal (10 IU/L); the authors therefore cannot exclude that a very small number of non-Q-wave infarctions were missed (p. 877).
outcomes.operationalization: AMI as above. Complications recorded with their timing during the stay: congestive heart failure, ventricular tachycardia, supraventricular tachydysrhythmias and bradydysrhythmias (p. 874).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions without hypothesis tests; a 95% CI is given for the main outcome (AMI) only (p. 874).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to routine enzyme testing; whether chart abstractors knew the study question is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: AMI in 15 of 250 (6%); 95% CI printed as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results (p. 875) and 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract (p. 873). Editors' calculation: the Results interval is the normal-approximation (Wald) interval (3.06–8.94%); the exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% interval is 3.4% to 9.7%. Of the 15: initial ECG consistent with AMI in 9, ischaemic changes in 4, normal or nondiagnostic in 2; 8 anterior, 6 inferior, 1 indeterminate; 9 Q-wave (60%) (p. 875). Initial ECG in all 250: normal 67 (27%), nonspecific 125 (50%; 41 of them early repolarization), abnormal but nondiagnostic 33 (13%), ischaemia known to be old 6 (2%), ischaemia not known to be old 10 (4%), suggestive of AMI 9 (4%) (p. 875). Complications: bradydysrhythmia 1 (0.4%), heart failure 1 (0.4%), supraventricular tachycardia 3 (1.2%), sustained ventricular tachycardia 2 (0.8%); none more than 12 hours after ED arrival; no deaths before discharge (pp. 875–876). Coronary care unit: 24 patients, mean stay 2.7 days (SD 1.9); mean hospital stay for all 2.2 days (SD 2.0) (p. 875). Editors' calculation: no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (exact two-sided 95% interval 0 to 1.5%).
analysis.covariates: None (descriptive study).
analysis.selective_reporting: Patients with and without AMI are not compared on age, risk factors, ECG, time since use or toxicology, although all were abstracted. Treatments given in hospital (for example nitrates, aspirin, beta-blockers, catheterization) are not reported. The abstract's description of the data instrument (119 items, high interrater reliability) refers to an instrument validated in an earlier study; no reliability was measured in this sample (pp. 873–874).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 15 events the exact 95% interval for the proportion runs from 3.4% to 9.7% (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 250 adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at one Michigan hospital in 1996–1998, 15 (6%) met WHO CK-MB criteria for myocardial infarction; complications were few (7 events), none occurred more than 12 hours after arrival, and no one died in hospital.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion call the 6% an incidence identical to that of prior prospective studies and say the study validates the COCHPA study (abstract, p. 873; Conclusions, p. 877); the last author also led COCHPA (ref. 11). Gaps: (1) 6% is the share of admitted patients, identified through cocaine or drug-abuse coding, whose enzymes met WHO criteria, not an incidence in people who use cocaine, and case-finding was more complete for infarctions than for non-infarctions (p. 876); (2) the uniform admission policy, which the authors say removes the selection bias of earlier studies (pp. 873, 876), addresses ED disposition but not the ascertainment of cocaine use, which depended on coding and on toxicology given mainly to patients aged 50 or under without risk factors; (3) the Discussion says the study confirms a previously suggested risk of 1.6 per 1,000 for adverse events after a 12-hour observation (p. 877), but zero events among 250 patients is compatible with a risk of up to about 15 per 1,000 (editors' calculation), so it cannot confirm a figure that small; (4) the abstract's interval (4.1–8.9%) differs from the Results (3.1–8.9%). The Discussion itself notes, about an earlier series, that an apparent cocaine–infarction association may reflect how common cocaine use is in the community rather than cause and effect (p. 876).

timeline.event: COCHPA, a prospective multicentre study of cocaine-associated chest pain at six municipal hospitals (Hollander et al., Acad Emerg Med 1994; ref. 11): AMI in 6%, criticized for low enrolment at some sites (as summarized on p. 876); the primary report, read in this round, gives 14 of 246 (5.7%)
Same network's multicentre series of cocaine-associated myocardial infarction treated with or without thrombolysis (CAMI Study Group; last author of this paper is its first author)

Kontos et al. (ref. 5): AMI in 2.5% of a cohort of 241 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and in 6 of 69 admitted to the coronary care unit (as summarized on p. 876); the primary report, read in this round, gives 6 infarctions at 241 visits by 218 patients, and 6 of 69 is 8.7% (printed here as 8.5%)
This series: AMI in 15 of 250 admitted patients (6%) under a uniform admission policy

replication.where_it_stands: The 6% matches the authors' own earlier prospective multicentre estimate (COCHPA, 6%), with which it shares the last author, and the 5–6% of two prospective studies the authors cite; the retrospective series they cite ranged from 0% to 31% depending on whom they enrolled (p. 876). All of these come from CK-MB-era testing of patients who reached hospital with chest pain: the figure describes that presenting population and that test, not a risk per occasion of cocaine use. COCHPA (Hollander et al., 1994) and Kontos et al. (1999) were read in this round and carry ids; the retrospective series cited here are not read.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Emergency Medicine at Hurley Medical Center (Flint, MI), the University of Michigan and the University of Pennsylvania (p. 873). The last author, Judd E. Hollander, led the COCHPA study (ref. 11) whose result this paper says it validates, and wrote the 12-hour observation work it says it confirms (refs 12, 18). The study was presented at the North American Congress of Clinical Toxicology in September 1997 (p. 873), before the stated study period ended (February 1998), so that presentation used part of the data.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre cohort of all ED patients with chest pain who report cocaine use or test positive, with toxicology for everyone whatever their age, high-sensitivity troponin, and a comparison group of patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine, reporting the proportion with myocardial infarction and 30-day events by age, risk factors and time since use.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All admitted patients with cocaine-associated chest pain at one hospital, found through ICD-9 coding checked against the ED admission log; one urban centre, and capture of cocaine use depended on coding and on toxicology given mainly to patients aged 50 or under without risk factors.
Every eligible admission over 20 months under a uniform admission policy.
250 patients and 15 events; exact 95% interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Setting, demographics, risk factors, presentation, vital signs and ECG categories reported (Tables 1–3, pp. 874–875).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 250 of 259 analysed; the 9 excluded ED discharges were probably at lower risk; infarctions were searched for through all AMI charts, while patients without AMI could be found only through cocaine coding.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: WHO criteria with serial CK-MB over 24 hours, the standard of the time; small non-Q-wave infarctions may have been missed (p. 877).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours in every patient (p. 874).
A proportion with a normal-approximation interval; the abstract's lower limit (4.1%) differs from the Results (3.1%); exact interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Record review; no participation was required.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI checklist has no overall algorithm; the editors summarize the risk as moderate. The outcome (WHO CK-MB criteria on serial testing in every patient) was measured uniformly, and the admission policy made the admitted population close to the whole ED population with this complaint. The main risk lies in case-finding: patients entered through coding of their cocaine use, toxicology was routine only for younger patients without risk factors, and infarctions were searched for more thoroughly than non-infarctions, which would tend to raise the proportion. The card may be cited for the share of admitted patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who met WHO infarction criteria at this hospital in 1996–1998 (15 of 250, 6%, exact 95% interval 3.4–9.7%), for the low complication rate with no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients, and for who these patients were; not for a risk of infarction per occasion of cocaine use, for causation, or for predictors of infarction.

key_findings.finding: Of 250 adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use, 15 (6%) met WHO criteria for acute myocardial infarction on serial CK-MB testing over 24 hours; 95% CI printed as 3.1% to 8.9%.
key_findings.note: The abstract prints 4.1% to 8.9% (p. 873). Editors' calculation: 3.1–8.9% is the normal-approximation interval; the exact 95% interval is 3.4% to 9.7%.

key_findings.finding: Case-finding: 259 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain were identified by searching ICD-9 codes for chest pain or myocardial infarction crossed with codes for cocaine and/or drug abuse, checked against the ED log of admitted patients; 9 discharged from the ED against the admission policy were excluded, leaving 250.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Setting and Population (p. 874); Results, 1st paragraph (pp. 874–875)

key_findings.finding: Who the patients were: mean age 33.5 years (SD 8.5); 77% men; 84% African American; tobacco use 77%; hypertension 26%; previous myocardial infarction 6%; previous chest pain 40%.

Cocaine exposure: all patients reported use within 7 days or had cocaine metabolites in urine; urine toxicology was done in 196, of whom 185 (94%) were positive; last use within 24 hours in 193 (78%) and within 4 hours in 57 (22%); crack inhalation was the commonest route (91%).
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 77% within 24 hours and crack 85%, intravenous 2%, nasal 6% (p. 873). The two timing counts add up to the whole sample (193 + 57 = 250), which leaves no room for the 3 patients without a precise history or for use 1–7 days earlier, and 193 of 250 is 77.2%; the timing figures are approximate at best.

key_findings.finding: Initial ECG: normal in 67 (27%), nonspecific in 125 (50%; 41 with early repolarization), abnormal but nondiagnostic in 33 (13%), ischaemia known to be old in 6 (2%), ischaemia not known to be old in 10 (4%), suggestive of AMI in 9 (4%). Among the 15 infarctions, the initial ECG was consistent with AMI in 9, ischaemic in 4, and normal or nondiagnostic in 2.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 13 of the 15 infarctions (87%; exact 95% CI 59.5% to 98.3%) had a first ECG consistent with infarction (9) or showing ischaemia (4).

key_findings.finding: Infarct characteristics: 8 anterior (53%), 6 inferior, 1 of indeterminate location; 9 Q-wave (60%); every patient diagnosed with AMI had at least one CK-MB value above twice the upper limit of normal.

In-hospital course: 24 patients were admitted first to the coronary care unit (mean stay 2.7 days, SD 1.9); mean hospital stay 2.2 days (SD 2.0); all 250 survived to discharge. Complications: bradydysrhythmia in 1 (0.4%), heart failure in 1 (0.4%), supraventricular tachycardia in 3 (1.2%), sustained ventricular tachycardia in 2 (0.8%); none occurred more than 12 hours after ED arrival.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (exact 95% upper limit, 1.46%). The paper gives the number of patients with each type of complication and does not say whether any patient had more than one, so the 7 complications are not a count of patients.

key_findings.finding: By departmental policy, urine toxicology was part of the cardiac work-up only for patients aged 50 or under without traditional risk factors; the authors say some patients over 50 who had used cocaine may not have been captured, and that all charts coded for AMI, with or without cocaine, were reviewed to limit coding errors.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and Future Questions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors cannot exclude that a very small number of non-Q-wave infarctions were missed: every diagnosed infarction had CK-MB above 20 IU/L, while the criterion was twice normal (10 IU/L).

Earlier estimates as summarized by the authors: retrospective series 0% to 31% (3 of 48 coronary care patients; 0 of 101 in monitored beds; 22 of 70 admitted patients); prospective studies 5–6% (COCHPA 6%); one imaging cohort 2.5% of 241.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures. COCHPA (Hollander et al., 1994: 14 of 246, 5.7%) and Kontos et al. (1999: 6 infarctions at 241 visits by 218 patients) have been read in this round; the retrospective series have not.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CI for the main outcome is printed as 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract (p. 873) and as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results (p. 875).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Results interval is the normal-approximation interval for 15 of 250; the abstract's lower limit matches no standard method. Cite 15 of 250 with the exact interval 3.4–9.7% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Route and timing differ between abstract and Results: crack 85% (abstract) against crack inhalation 91% (Results); 77% against 78% with use in the preceding 24 hours. The timing counts (193 within 24 hours, 57 within 4 hours) add up to 250 and their percentages to 100%, which cannot be right if 3 patients had no precise history and use up to 7 days earlier allowed entry.
reporting_issues.consequence: Time since last use and route can be cited only approximately: most patients had used within 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 22 patients (11%) with other or unknown pain location, and the Results give 41 (34%) of the nonspecific ECGs (one hundred twenty-five, written in words) as showing early repolarization. Editors' arithmetic: 22 of 250 is 8.8%, the location percentages add to 102%, and 41 of 125 is 32.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Arithmetic slips with no effect on the main outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion required anterior, precordial or left-sided chest discomfort (p. 874), but Table 2 lists 4 patients (2%) with right-sided pain only (p. 875).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the criterion was applied loosely or right-sided anterior pain was counted as anterior; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is called a retrospective cohort study in the Methods (p. 873) and a retrospective case series in the Discussion (p. 876); the study period is called 19 months (p. 876), but 1 July 1996 to 28 February 1998 is 20 months; men are 77% in the abstract and Table 1 (192 of 250) but 76% in the Discussion (p. 877).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling and arithmetic slips; no effect on the main outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract credits the data instrument with 119 items and high interrater reliability (p. 873); the Methods cite the reliability from an earlier study (ref. 12) and no reliability was measured in this sample (p. 874).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reliability of chart abstraction in this study is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives Kontos et al.'s coronary-care-unit figure as six of 69 (8.5%) (p. 876); 6 of 69 is 8.7%, as Kontos et al. print it (Kontos et al., 1999, p. 642).
reporting_issues.consequence: A slip in a second-hand figure; no effect on this study's results.

design_detail: Prospective single-group cohort (the authors call it a longitudinal cohort study) in an emergency department (ED) chest-pain observation unit, 1 January 1998 to 1 January 2000; apparently one hospital, Hurley Medical Center, Flint, Michigan, whose institutional review board approved the study (no other enrolling site is named). Of 344 consecutive patients with chest pain who reported cocaine use or had cocaine metabolites in urine, 42 judged at high risk were admitted directly and excluded; the other 302, at low-to-intermediate risk, entered a 9-to-12-hour observation protocol (troponin I at 0, 3, 6 and 9 hours, continuous ST-segment monitoring, stress testing at first routine and later optional) and were followed for 30 days. Main outcome: death from cardiovascular causes at 30 days. No comparison group. Appraised with the JBI checklist as an incidence study.
can_establish: That among 302 patients at low-to-intermediate risk with cocaine-associated chest pain managed in one hospital's observation unit in 1998–1999, none died of cardiovascular causes within 30 days (exact upper 95% limit 1.2%), two died of other causes, and 4 of the 256 with detailed follow-up had a nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI; exact 95% CI 0.4–4.0%), all four having continued to use cocaine.
cannot_establish: That discharge after 9–12 hours is as safe as admission or longer observation (no comparison group, and the number actually discharged after observation is not reported); outcomes in high-risk patients (admitted directly and excluded) or at other hospitals; the nonfatal MI rate among the 46 patients without detailed follow-up; or that continued cocaine use caused the infarctions (4 events; use was asked only of patients contacted directly).

sample.recruitment: Consecutive patients evaluated in the ED chest-pain observation unit; a daily log of all patients evaluated was compared with enrolment data to ensure that all eligible patients were enrolled (p. 511). Written informed consent was obtained for follow-up; the review board did not require consent for data collected in routine care (p. 512).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included (p. 511): age 18 or older; self-reported cocaine use in the week before presentation or cocaine metabolites on urine screening; chest discomfort as the chief symptom; symptoms consistent with a low-to-intermediate likelihood of unstable angina (Braunwald classification). Excluded: chest pain explained by local trauma, radiographic abnormalities or other clearly non-cardiac causes; and high-risk patients, admitted directly: initial ECG suggesting ischaemia or acute MI, ST-segment elevation or depression of 1 mm or more persisting at least one minute, raised cardiac markers, recurrent ischaemic chest pain, or haemodynamic instability.
sample.demographics: Mean age 37.6 years (SD 9.3); 198 men (66%); black 211 (70%), white 75 (25%), Hispanic 7 (2%), other or unknown 9 (3%); current tobacco use 255 (84%); hypertension 51 (17%); family history of coronary disease 93 (31%); diabetes 10 (3%); previous MI 6 (2%); 112 (37%) had two or more cardiac risk factors (editors' sum of the Table 2 footnote: 85 + 23 + 4). Risk factors and medical history were self-reported (Table 2, p. 514).
sample.attrition: 30-day survival data for 300 of 302 (99%); the other two did not appear in the National Death Index and are counted as alive in the 0/302 (p. 514). Detailed follow-up for 256 (85%), so 46 patients lack data on nonfatal MI and the other secondary outcomes; patients with and without detailed follow-up are not compared (pp. 514–515). Sources: the patient in 249 cases (82%), a household relative 22 (7%), another relative or friend 24 (8%), a primary care provider 5 (2%), the National Death Index 2 (1%) (p. 513).
sample.selection_effects: Apparently one urban hospital and only patients judged at low-to-intermediate risk: the 42 high-risk patients admitted directly included 10 MIs and 10 cases of unstable angina (Table 1, p. 513) and are outside the cohort. Six cohort patients had an initial ECG diagnostic of ischaemia not known to be old (Table 2, p. 514), despite the exclusion rule. 70% of the cohort were black.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at presentation (time of most recent use, route) on a closed-question instrument, or cocaine metabolites on urine screening (Synchron LX), done as the institutional standard in patients aged 50 or younger with presumed ischaemic chest pain and in all observation-unit patients (pp. 511–512). Urine was positive in 282 of 301 patients tested (94%); 247 of 302 (82%) reported use; all who did not report use had cocaine metabolites in urine (p. 513).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported timing among the 247 reporting use: within the preceding week 237 (96%), within 24 hours 169 (68%). Route: inhaled crack cocaine 203, nasal insufflation 51, injection 10; some used more than one route and route is not given for every patient. Chest-pain duration known for 290 (96%): under 6 hours in 171 (59%), under 3 hours in 118 (41%), under 1 hour in 45 (16%) (p. 513). Amounts were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported apart from current tobacco use (84%); one of the two non-cardiovascular deaths was from a heroin overdose (p. 514).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (assessed at presentation). After discharge, 64 of 254 (25.2%) reported recurrent cocaine use within 30 days (Table 3, p. 515).

comparison.controls: None. The 42 directly admitted high-risk patients are described separately (Table 1, p. 513) but not followed up or compared. The discussion compares the outcomes narratively with published 9-to-12-hour protocols in patients who do not use cocaine (p. 516).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary anatomy unknown for most patients (catheterization only after a positive stress test or a later MI); cardiac risk factors self-reported.

outcomes.instruments: Index visit (p. 512): cardiac troponin I (Access AccuTnI, Beckman Coulter) at presentation and 3, 6 and 9 hours, raised if any value exceeded the institutional threshold; continuous 12-lead ST-segment monitoring (Vectra XA) by physician assistants; heart failure and arrhythmias recorded with time of onset; cardiology consultation after 9 hours; graded exercise testing (modified Bruce protocol), with dipyridamole testing if indeterminate; positive test = ST elevation or depression over 1 mm. Initial ECG classified into six categories (Cohen's kappa 0.69, weighted kappa 0.95, in 321 patients) (pp. 511–512). Follow-up at least 30 days after discharge by telephone with the patient or a proxy, telegrams when neither could be reached, medical-record review and the National Death Index; all follow-up data and all reported events confirmed by a hospital-based record search one year after the visit (p. 512).
outcomes.validity_norms: Troponin I was chosen over CK-MB as the marker most specific for myocardial injury after recent cocaine use (citing ref. 16, p. 512). The criteria for an MI during follow-up and for classifying a death as cardiovascular are not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Main outcome: death from cardiovascular causes within 30 days. Secondary: nonfatal MI, ventricular dysrhythmias, recurrent chest pain, recurrent cocaine use and cocaine counselling after discharge (Table 3). Continued cocaine use was asked only when the patient was contacted directly; relatives and colleagues were not asked about it (p. 512).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions with confidence intervals and no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (single group); who classified follow-up events is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (p. 515): cardiovascular death 0/302, printed 0 (0–0.99); ventricular dysrhythmias 0/256, printed 0 (0–1.2); nonfatal MI 4/256, 1.6% (0.1–3.1); recurrent chest pain 63/255, 24.7% (19.4–30.0); recurrent cocaine use 64/254, 25.2% (19.9–30.5); cocaine counselling after discharge 21/251, 8.4% (4.9–11.8). Non-cardiovascular deaths 2/302 (gunshot wound, heroin overdose). Positive stress tests 4/158 (printed as 3%). The zero-event upper limits equal the rule of three (3/n), a one-sided approximation; exact two-sided limits are 1.2% for 0/302 and 1.4% for 0/256, and the exact interval for 4/256 is 0.4–4.0% (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. The sample size was set in advance: 300 patients, to bring the upper confidence limit for a fatal cardiovascular event below 1% on the expectation of no events (pp. 512–513).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: how many of the 302 were discharged after 9–12 hours and how many were admitted from the unit (at least the 4 with positive stress tests were admitted, p. 513), how many had a raised troponin during observation, when the 4 nonfatal MIs occurred (one 3 days after discharge, Table 4), and the definition of a follow-up MI. Exercise testing and cardiac medication use after discharge were not collected (p. 517).
analysis.power: Planned for the upper confidence limit of cardiovascular death to fall below 1%; met only with the rule-of-three approximation (exact upper limit 1.2%, editors' calculation). Not powered for nonfatal MI or for comparisons.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No cardiovascular deaths within 30 days among 302 patients at low-to-intermediate risk observed for 9–12 hours (upper limit about 1%), 2 non-cardiovascular deaths, and 4 nonfatal MIs among the 256 with detailed follow-up (1.6%; exact upper limit about 4%). All four patients with MI had continued to use cocaine and had two or more cardiac risk factors; two had significant two-vessel coronary disease. A quarter reported recurrent chest pain and a quarter recurrent cocaine use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that such patients have a very low risk of death or MI in the 30 days after discharge (p. 510); the discussion says the results demonstrate the safety of a 9-to-12-hour observation period and that patients without recurrent symptoms, raised necrosis markers or dysrhythmias can be safely released (pp. 516–517). Without a comparison group, safety is judged against an implicit threshold, and outcomes are reported for all 302 who entered the unit, not for those actually discharged after 9–12 hours, whose number is not given. The abstract reports the 4 MIs as among the 256 patients with detailed follow-up data, but does not give the number (46, 15%) who lacked them. The recommendation of substance-use treatment strategies because of an increased likelihood of MI with continued cocaine use (p. 517) rests on the observation that all 4 MIs occurred among the 64 patients who reported continued use (none among the other 190 with data; editors' calculation), not on a tested comparison, and use was asked only of patients contacted directly. The discussion's statement that two of the four MI patients had abnormal stress tests is not borne out by Table 4, and its comparison of 20 acute coronary syndromes among 42 high-risk patients with earlier studies' 6% MI rate sets unstable angina and MI together against MI alone.

timeline.event: COCHPA multicentre series cited as the basis (ref. 8): MI in 14 of 246 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and no in-hospital arrhythmia needing intervention, heart failure or infarct extension

Retrospective series of 136 cocaine-associated MIs (ref. 13): first complications more than 12 hours after arrival in 5 of 49 patients with complications; the authors call for a prospective assessment of a 12-hour observation period (p. 1085)

ACI-TIPI substudy (ref. 19): confirmed acute cardiac ischaemia in 6 of 293 ED patients with cocaine-associated complaints; suggests comparing a 12-hour observation period with shorter observation (p. 475)
This study: first prospective test of a 9-to-12-hour observation protocol for cocaine-associated chest pain among the papers read in this round

replication.where_it_stands: Among the papers read in this round, this is the only prospective test of a short observation protocol; it was single-centre, had no comparison arm and used the troponin I assay of its time. Whether it has been reproduced elsewhere was not established in this reading.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the article).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from departments of emergency medicine (University of Michigan and Hurley Medical Center, Flint; University of Texas Southwestern, Dallas; Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania; Northwestern University) (p. 510). The senior author is first author of the COCHPA study (ref. 8), its one-year follow-up (ref. 12), the retrospective MI series (ref. 13) and the ECG classification work (ref. 15) on which the study builds. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A multicentre trial randomizing low-to-intermediate-risk patients with cocaine-associated chest pain to discharge after a short observation protocol with serial high-sensitivity troponin or to admission or longer observation, with complete 30-day outcomes from record linkage across hospitals and death registers and continued cocaine use measured in every patient, would show whether early discharge is as safe as the alternative.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Consecutive patients at one hospital's chest-pain observation unit over two years: suitable for outcomes after an observation protocol in lower-risk patients, but a single urban centre.
Consecutive patients, with a daily log checked against enrolment to capture all eligible patients (p. 511).
300 planned so that the upper limit for cardiovascular death would fall below 1%; 302 enrolled, but the exact upper limit is 1.2%, and nonfatal MI (4 events) is imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Patients (Table 2) and the protocol are described, but not the number discharged after observation, troponin results during observation, or the enrolling hospital by name.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Survival known for 300 of 302 (2 more inferred from absence in the National Death Index); detailed follow-up for 256 (85%); patients without detailed follow-up are not described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Deaths ascertained through several sources and the National Death Index; nonfatal MI from patient or proxy report confirmed by hospital records a year later, but no definition of a follow-up MI or of a cardiovascular death is given, and events treated elsewhere depend on report.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One follow-up procedure for all, but 51 outcomes came from proxies, who were not asked about cocaine use (pp. 512–513).

Proportions with intervals, but the zero-event limits are rule-of-three bounds labelled as 95% CIs, the nonfatal MI interval is a normal approximation (exact 0.4–4.0%), and 'intention to treat' is not defined for a single group.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Survival follow-up 99% and detailed follow-up 85%; refusals of consent for follow-up are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. Consecutive enrolment checked against a log, a stated protocol and near-complete survival data make the 30-day cardiovascular mortality reliable for this kind of patient at this hospital; nonfatal MI is less certain (15% without detailed follow-up, no stated definition), the intervals are approximations, and the number discharged after observation is not reported. The editors summarise the risk of bias as moderate. It may be cited for: no cardiovascular deaths among 302 (exact upper limit 1.2%), 2 non-cardiovascular deaths, 4 nonfatal MIs among 256 (exact 0.4–4.0%), recurrent cocaine use in a quarter of patients with data, and the characteristics of the four patients with MI. It cannot be cited as showing that early discharge is as safe as admission, or that continued cocaine use caused the infarctions.

key_findings.finding: Of 344 patients with chest pain who reported cocaine use or tested positive for it, 42 (12%) were admitted directly as high risk; the other 302 entered the observation unit and formed the study cohort.

Among the 42 directly admitted high-risk patients: MI 10, unstable angina 10, heart failure 3 (present on arrival in all three), sustained ventricular dysrhythmias 2 (both within 9 hours of arrival); cardiac catheterization 21 (coronary disease with over 70% stenosis in 16), percutaneous intervention 12, coronary bypass surgery 1.

Cocaine use was self-reported by 247 of the 302 (82%); urine screening was positive in 282 of 301 tested (94%), and every patient who did not report use had cocaine metabolites in urine. Of those reporting use, 237 (96%) had used within the preceding week and 169 (68%) within 24 hours. Routes: inhaled crack 203, nasal insufflation 51, injection 10.

Cohort: mean age 37.6 years (SD 9.3), 198 men (66%), 211 black (70%), 255 with current tobacco use (84%). Initial ECG: normal 122 (40%), nonspecific ST-T changes 121 (40%), abnormal but not diagnostic of ischaemia 42 (14%), ischaemia known to be old 11 (4%), ischaemia not known to be old 6 (2%).

Protocol: troponin I at presentation and 3, 6 and 9 hours, raised if any value exceeded the institutional threshold; continuous 12-lead ST-segment monitoring; cardiology consultation after 9 hours; stress testing at first for all patients without necrosis or ischaemia at rest, later made optional because positive tests were rare; written information on the risks of cocaine use at discharge.

In the observation unit, 93% of patients were given aspirin, 90% nitrates and 30% benzodiazepines; none received fibrinolytic agents and 4 (1%) a beta-blocker. No patient developed heart failure or dysrhythmias in the unit. 158 of the 302 had stress testing before discharge; 4 were positive and all 4 were catheterized (2 multivessel disease, 1 nonocclusive disease, 1 normal coronary arteries).
key_findings.locator: Results › Course in the Chest-Pain Observation Unit, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 30-day survival data were available for 300 of 302 (99%); the other two did not appear in the National Death Index. Information came from the patient in 249 cases (82%), a household relative in 22 (7%), another relative or friend in 24 (8%), a primary care provider in 5 (2%) and the National Death Index in 2 (1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 2nd paragraph (p. 513); Results › Main Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 514)

key_findings.finding: No patient died of cardiovascular causes within 30 days (0/302; 95% CI printed as 0–0.99%); two died of other causes, one from a gunshot wound and one from a heroin overdose.
key_findings.note: The printed upper limit equals 3/302 (rule of three); the exact two-sided 95% upper limit is 1.2% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Detailed follow-up was available for 256 patients: nonfatal MI 4/256 (1.6%; 95% CI 0.1–3.1), sustained ventricular dysrhythmias 0/256 (0–1.2), recurrent chest pain 63/255 (24.7%), recurrent cocaine use 64/254 (25.2%), cocaine counselling after discharge 21/251 (8.4%).
key_findings.note: Exact intervals: nonfatal MI 0.4–4.0%, ventricular dysrhythmias 0–1.4% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: All four patients with nonfatal MI had continued to use cocaine and had at least two cardiac risk factors (true of 37% of the cohort). All four had MI ruled out at the index visit and were discharged with a diagnosis of non-cardiac chest pain. Two were found to have nonocclusive coronary disease; one presented with MI 3 days after discharge, before a planned outpatient catheterization, and had two-vessel disease treated by bypass surgery; one had severe two-vessel disease treated by angioplasty. Two were taking a beta-blocker (metoprolol, atenolol) at presentation.

Stress testing among the four patients with MI (Table 4): one had an abnormal dipyridamole test and was admitted, with nonocclusive disease at catheterization; one had an indeterminate exercise test followed by a normal dipyridamole sestamibi scan; no stress test is listed for the other two.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, column Findings on Initial Evaluation

key_findings.finding: The sample size of 300 was chosen to bring the upper confidence limit for a fatal cardiovascular event below 1%, on the expectation that there would be none.

All follow-up data were confirmed by a hospital-based record search one year after the visit, which found no deaths or cardiovascular complications beyond those reported by patients or proxies; continued cocaine use was asked only of patients contacted directly.

The authors conclude that the results demonstrate the safety of a 9-to-12-hour observation period and that patients without recurrent symptoms, raised necrosis markers or dysrhythmias can be safely released after it; they advocate evaluation for coronary disease within one to two weeks for patients with traditional cardiac risk factors, and substance-use treatment strategies in such protocols.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists 6 cohort patients (2%) whose initial ECG was diagnostic of ischaemia not known to be old, although patients whose initial ECG suggested ischaemia were to be admitted directly and excluded (Methods, p. 511).
reporting_issues.consequence: The high-risk exclusion was not applied strictly (or the two ECG classifications differ); the cohort includes some patients the protocol defines as high risk, which, if anything, makes the low event rate conservative.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of the 302 discharged after the 9-to-12-hour observation, as opposed to admitted from the unit, is not reported; at least the 4 patients with positive stress tests were admitted (p. 513), and the analysis is said to be by intention to treat (p. 512) without a definition.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 30-day outcomes describe everyone who entered the unit, not only those released early, although the conclusion is about outcomes after discharge.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that two of the four patients with nonfatal MI did not undergo stress testing and the other two had abnormal results (p. 516), but Table 4 (p. 515) shows one abnormal dipyridamole test, one indeterminate exercise test followed by a normal dipyridamole sestamibi scan, and no test for the other two.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only one of the four had an abnormal stress test on the table's evidence; claims about stress testing before these infarctions should rest on Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Zero-event intervals are rule-of-three bounds printed as 95% CIs (0/302: 0–0.99%; 0/256: 0–1.2%), whereas exact two-sided upper limits are 1.2% and 1.4%. The other Table 3 intervals are normal approximations: those for 63/255, 64/254 and 21/251 match exactly, and the nonfatal MI interval (0.1–3.1% for 4/256) matches one computed from the rounded 1.6% (unrounded, 0.04–3.08%); the exact interval for 4/256 is 0.4–4.0% (Table 3, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The planned target of an upper limit below 1% for cardiovascular death is met only with the approximation; the nonfatal MI estimate is less precise than printed, with an upper limit near 4%.

reporting_issues.issue: Recurrent cocaine use has a denominator of 254 (Table 3, p. 515), but the methods say continued use was asked only when the patient was contacted directly, which happened for 249 patients (pp. 512–513).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either use was also learned from other sources, which are not described, or the denominators are inconsistent; the 25.2% figure is uncertain in its basis.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion compares the 20 acute coronary syndromes (10 MI, 10 unstable angina) among the 42 high-risk patients with previous studies' 6% rate of MI (p. 516); among all 344 patients evaluated, index-visit MI was at least 10 (2.9%) and acute coronary syndrome at least 20 (5.8%); whether any of the 302 had an MI during observation is not reported (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated similarity sets acute coronary syndromes against a rate of MI; the index MI proportion in this hospital's patients was at least about 3%.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion describes the COCHPA study as finding that congestive heart failure developed in only 2% (p. 515), whereas that study reports heart failure in 4 of 246 patients, all present on arrival, with none developing in hospital (Hollander et al., 1994, p. 335).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the earlier study's own wording should be used for its complications.

design_detail: Prospective, non-randomized drug-challenge study in the cardiac catheterization laboratory of Parkland Memorial Hospital / University of Texas Southwestern. 15 patients undergoing catheterization to evaluate chest pain were measured at three time points: at baseline, 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, and 5 minutes after an intravenous infusion of either saline (group I, n = 6) or labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes (group II, n = 9). Measures at each point: heart rate, mean arterial pressure and coronary arterial area by computer-assisted quantitative angiography of a proximal, a middle and a distal segment of the left anterior descending artery chosen as free of atherosclerotic narrowing. Allocation to saline or labetalol is not described as randomized and no blinding of patients, operators or image analysts is reported, so the parallel arms are a non-randomized comparison of an intervention and the within-person before-after change is the study's main evidence. Same group and same laboratory as the propranolol study (Lange et al., 1990), with the same intranasal cocaine dose; none of the patients admitted to previous cocaine use (self-report).
can_establish: That in 9 catheterization patients who reported no previous cocaine use, intravenous labetalol 0.25 mg/kg given 5 minutes earlier left the coronary arterial narrowing produced by intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg essentially unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm2, still below the pre-cocaine 3.80 mm2) while mean arterial pressure fell from 117 to 110 mm Hg; and that in 6 patients given saline instead, nothing changed after the infusion.
cannot_establish: Whether labetalol helps or harms people who present to hospital after using cocaine: no clinical outcome was measured, the patients reported no previous cocaine use, and only one dose was given. It also cannot establish that labetalol is worse or better than propranolol (the two drugs were studied in separate papers with different control arms and no head-to-head comparison), that the degree of alpha- or beta-blockade achieved was adequate (none was measured, and heart rate did not fall), or that the labetalol and saline arms were comparable, since allocation was not randomized and the two arms differed at baseline.

sample.recruitment: Patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for the evaluation of chest pain at the same centre as the 1990 propranolol study; how they were approached or how many were eligible or declined is not reported (p. 608).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Undergoing catheterization for chest pain; none admitted to previous cocaine use; the paper states that no patient received beta-adrenergic blockers for more than 6 months before the study (the wording is ambiguous, see reporting issues), that all anti-anginal agents were stopped more than 12 hours before, and that patients were studied fasting after 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam (p. 608). No exclusion criteria such as hypertension or recent infarction are stated, unlike the 1990 study.
sample.demographics: 7 men and 8 women, aged 40 to 79 years. 6 had angiographically normal coronary arteries and 9 had atherosclerotic disease (70% or greater luminal diameter narrowing of a major epicardial vessel: one-vessel in 5, two-vessel in 2, three-vessel in 2). Age, sex and disease distribution by arm are not reported (pp. 608-609).
sample.attrition: No patient is reported lost. 40 coronary arterial segments were analysed where the stated method (a proximal, a middle and a distal segment in each of 15 patients) implies 45; the 5 unanalysed segments are not accounted for (Patients and Methods > Data Analysis, p. 609, against the abstract, p. 608).
sample.selection_effects: Middle-aged and older cardiac patients under investigation for chest pain, none of whom admitted to previous cocaine use, given one controlled intranasal dose. 9 of the 15 (60%) had obstructive coronary disease. The 6:9 split between saline and labetalol is unexplained and the arms differ at baseline (heart rate 83 against 71 beats/min, mean arterial pressure 96 against 107 mm Hg, coronary arterial area 4.59 against 3.80 mm2), so arm membership is not independent of the measured variables.

exposure.measurement: Both drugs given in the laboratory. Serum cocaine concentration measured from a blood sample drawn 15 minutes after the intranasal dose: 0.14 +/- 0.05 mg/L in the saline arm and 0.19 +/- 0.11 mg/L in the labetalol arm (Table I, p. 609). Labetalol concentrations were not measured and no index of achieved alpha- or beta-blockade is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Single intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, described by the authors as one half to two thirds the amount used for intranasal anesthesia and chosen for its established safety; then a single intravenous infusion of labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes, which the authors identify as the recommended dose and route for severe hypertension, or an equivalent saline infusion (pp. 608-610).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients received 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam as premedication and iodinated contrast for angiography; anti-anginal drugs were withdrawn more than 12 hours earlier. No other drug or alcohol use is reported and no toxicology screening is described (p. 608).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: no patient admitted to previous cocaine use (p. 608).

comparison.controls: Two comparisons. Within-person: each patient's values after the infusion against the same patient's values after cocaine and at baseline (the comparison the conclusion rests on). Between-arm: the 6 patients given saline after cocaine against the 9 given labetalol, allocated without stated randomization.
comparison.matching: None. No matching, no adjustment, and no test of baseline comparability between arms is reported, although Table I shows the arms differed in heart rate, mean arterial pressure, coronary arterial area and achieved cocaine concentration.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (no prior cocaine exposure). Unmeasured are the degree of adrenergic blockade achieved by labetalol, each patient's coronary reactivity before cocaine, and how coronary disease severity and sex were distributed between the arms.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The saline arm received the same cocaine dose, premedication and contrast, differing only in the infusion given afterwards.

outcomes.instruments: Systemic arterial pressure through the side-port of a 9F femoral arterial sheath; heart rate by electrocardiographic monitoring; cineangiography of the left coronary artery with computer-assisted quantitative coronary analysis (Cardiovascular Angiography Analysis System, Rotterdam), measuring coronary arterial area in mm2 in a proximal, a middle and a distal left anterior descending segment chosen as free of atherosclerotic narrowing (pp. 608-609).
outcomes.validity_norms: Quantitative angiography of disease-free segments is the standard method of the period and was used identically in the companion propranolol study, which makes the two comparable in technique. The outcome is lumen geometry, not perfusion: unlike the 1990 study, no coronary blood flow, coronary vascular resistance or transcardiac oxygen content difference was measured here, so nothing can be said about the resistance vessels, which is where propranolol's effect was largest.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Alleviation' of vasoconstriction is operationalized as a change in mean coronary arterial area 5 minutes after the infusion relative to the post-cocaine value; no ischemic or clinical endpoint was defined, and no adverse events are reported either way.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three variables (heart rate, mean arterial pressure, coronary arterial area) at three time points in two arms, by repeated-measures analysis of variance at an uncorrected threshold of p < 0.05 (p. 609).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The 1990 companion study states that analyses were done without knowledge of the agent given; this paper makes no such statement, and no blinding of patients or operators is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means +/- 1 standard deviation, compared within each arm across the three time points by repeated-measures analysis of variance; p < 0.05 significant (p. 609). Table I (p. 609), labetalol arm (n = 9): heart rate 71 +/- 12, 73 +/- 12 and 69 +/- 12 beats/min at baseline, after cocaine and after labetalol, with no value significantly different from baseline; mean arterial pressure 107 +/- 13, 117 +/- 14 (p < 0.05 against baseline) and 110 +/- 11 (not marked as different from baseline); coronary arterial area 3.80 +/- 1.42, 3.47 +/- 1.37 and 3.37 +/- 1.32 mm2, both post-cocaine values significantly below baseline. Saline arm (n = 6): heart rate 83 +/- 14, 83 +/- 15, 84 +/- 15; mean arterial pressure 96 +/- 14, 106 +/- 14 and 102 +/- 10, both raised against baseline; coronary arterial area 4.59 +/- 3.86, 3.82 +/- 3.14 and 3.70 +/- 3.10 mm2, both below baseline. Editors' calculation from these means: coronary area fell 8.7% after cocaine and 11.3% after labetalol relative to baseline in the labetalol arm, and 16.8% and 19.4% in the saline arm; the mean arterial pressure fall after labetalol is 7 mm Hg, 70% of the 10 mm Hg rise cocaine had produced. No confidence intervals, no effect sizes and no between-arm test are reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for the baseline differences between arms, for coronary disease severity, for sex or for the different cocaine concentrations achieved.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or prespecified primary outcome is mentioned. Approved by the Human Subjects Review Committee of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center with written informed consent (p. 608). Manuscript submitted 15 September 1992 and accepted 16 November 1992 (p. 608).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Results section reports no measured values: apart from the coronary-anatomy counts in its first paragraph, the two group paragraphs state only directions of change and refer the reader to Table I and Figure 1. The abstract's quantitative headline (13% +/- 10% decrease in coronary arterial area in 32 of 40 segments) appears nowhere in the body, the table or the figure, and the segment-level analysis behind it is never described. Table I marks only comparisons with baseline, while the abstract's p < 0.05 concerns the post-cocaine to post-labetalol fall in pressure, a comparison whose test is not shown.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 9 patients in the labetalol arm and 6 in the saline arm, the finding of interest is a null result for coronary area (3.47 to 3.37 mm2); no equivalence margin or confidence interval is given, so the study cannot distinguish 'labetalol does not relieve vasoconstriction' from 'this study was too small to detect relief'.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 catheterization patients who reported no previous cocaine use, intranasal cocaine narrowed disease-free left anterior descending segments by about 9% and raised mean arterial pressure by 10 mm Hg; intravenous labetalol 0.25 mg/kg then lowered mean arterial pressure by 7 mm Hg while mean coronary arterial area moved from 3.47 to 3.37 mm2, remaining significantly below the pre-cocaine value. In the 6 patients given saline instead, the post-cocaine state persisted unchanged. Heart rate did not change at any point in either arm.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the closing paragraph conclude that labetalol reverses the cocaine-induced rise in arterial pressure but does not alleviate cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction, and the discussion adds that nitroglycerin, shown elsewhere to reverse both, may be preferable in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (pp. 608, 610). Three gaps. First, a null result in 9 patients with no confidence interval or equivalence margin is reported as an established absence of effect. Second, the explanation offered, that labetalol's beta-blocking activity predominates over its alpha-blocking activity at usual doses (p. 610), is an interpretation rather than a measurement: no index of alpha- or beta-blockade was obtained, and heart rate did not fall, which is the usual sign that beta-blockade took effect. Third, the preference for nitroglycerin rests on a different study in other patients, not on any comparison made here. The authors do state the two main limitations themselves, naming the single dose and the single route of cocaine, and the single labetalol dose (p. 610).

timeline.event: Same laboratory: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow and raised coronary vascular resistance in 10 patients
This study: intravenous labetalol after the same cocaine dose lowered arterial pressure without changing coronary arterial area in 9 patients
American Heart Association scientific statement discusses labetalol for cocaine-associated chest pain and cites this study

replication.where_it_stands: No one has repeated this challenge, in cocaine-naive patients or in people who use cocaine, and no trial has compared labetalol with another agent in cocaine-associated chest pain with clinical outcomes. The evidence on labetalol's coronary effect after cocaine in humans is this single non-randomized study of 15 patients, with no blinding reported.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no grant-support statement, unlike the 1990 companion paper from the same group (p. 608).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (the journal did not require one in 1993).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors were in the Department of Internal Medicine (Cardiovascular Division), University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, and the Cardiac Catheterization Laboratory, Parkland Memorial Hospital, Dallas. Two of them (Hillis, Lange) are authors of the 1990 propranolol study, so the human evidence on beta-blockade after cocaine in the coronary circulation comes from a single group.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, blinded comparison in people presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain of labetalol against a benzodiazepine, a nitrate or placebo, with ischemic and clinical outcomes and an objective measure of the adrenergic blockade achieved. Within the laboratory paradigm, a study with enough patients to set a confidence interval around the coronary-area change, and a measure of alpha- and beta-blockade, would at least show whether the null result reflects the drug or the sample size.

domains.note: Allocation to saline or labetalol is not described as randomized and the arms differ at baseline in heart rate (83 against 71 beats/min), mean arterial pressure (96 against 107 mm Hg), coronary arterial area (4.59 against 3.80 mm2) and achieved cocaine concentration (0.14 against 0.19 mg/L); nothing is adjusted and no between-arm test is reported. The within-person comparison is less exposed to this, but confounding by time after cocaine remains, and the saline arm is the only control for it.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: All patients were under catheterization for chest pain and all contributed from baseline, so there is no selection on the outcome; but how they were identified, how many were eligible or declined, and how the 6:9 split arose are not reported.
Both the cocaine dose and the infusion given were determined and recorded at the time; serum cocaine concentration confirms the exposure in each arm.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: No blinding of patients, operators or analysts is described, and the 1990 companion study's explicit statement that analyses were done blind to the agent is absent here. Deviations are not reported, but nothing would have concealed which infusion was running.
40 segments are analysed where the stated method implies 45; the missing 5 are unexplained and not attributed to any patient or arm.

Quantitative angiography and intra-arterial pressure are objective measures, but blinding of the image analysis is not stated and the outcome is lumen area in disease-free epicardial segments only, which cannot detect the resistance-vessel effect that was the larger finding in the propranolol study.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The Results report no measured values (only the coronary-anatomy counts); the abstract's only quantitative statement about the cocaine effect (13% +/- 10% in 32 of 40 segments) has no counterpart anywhere in the paper, and the test behind the abstract's p < 0.05 for the fall in pressure after labetalol is not shown in Table I, which marks only comparisons with baseline.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The measurements are objective and the design has the right shape for its question, with a parallel saline arm, but the comparison is unrandomized between groups that differ at baseline, no blinding is reported, and the quantitative results live almost entirely in a single table whose numbers the abstract does not match. The source can be cited for what happened to mean arterial pressure, heart rate and quantitative coronary arterial area in 9 cocaine-naive patients given labetalol 0.25 mg/kg 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, and in 6 given saline, as a single small study with no blinding reported. It cannot be cited for the clinical effect of labetalol in people who use cocaine, for a comparison between labetalol and propranolol, or as evidence that labetalol definitely does not relieve coronary vasoconstriction, since the study has no confidence interval around its null result and no measure of the blockade achieved.

key_findings.finding: 15 patients (7 men, 8 women, aged 40 to 79 years) undergoing catheterization for chest pain received intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, then intravenous saline (n = 6) or labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes (n = 9); none admitted to previous cocaine use.
key_findings.locator: Patients and Methods > Patients, 1st paragraph; Experimental Protocol (continuing p. 609)
key_findings.note: Allocation to the two infusions is not described as randomized and no blinding is mentioned anywhere in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Serum cocaine concentration 15 minutes after dosing was 0.14 +/- 0.05 mg/L in the saline arm and 0.19 +/- 0.11 mg/L in the labetalol arm.

In the labetalol arm (n = 9), coronary arterial area was 3.80 +/- 1.42 mm2 at baseline, 3.47 +/- 1.37 after cocaine and 3.37 +/- 1.32 five minutes after labetalol; both post-cocaine values were significantly below baseline (p < 0.05) and the drug did not restore the lumen.
key_findings.locator: Table I, coronary arterial area rows; Figure 1 (solid triangles)
key_findings.note: Values are mean +/- 1 SD. Editors' calculation: 8.7% below baseline after cocaine and 11.3% after labetalol.

key_findings.finding: Mean arterial pressure in the labetalol arm rose from 107 +/- 13 to 117 +/- 14 mm Hg after cocaine (p < 0.05 against baseline) and fell to 110 +/- 11 after labetalol, a value Table I does not mark as differing from baseline.
key_findings.locator: Table I, mean arterial pressure rows
key_findings.note: The abstract reports the 117 to 110 fall at p < 0.05; that comparison is between two post-drug time points and its test is not shown in the table, whose daggers mark only comparisons with baseline.

key_findings.finding: Heart rate did not change at any time point in either arm (labetalol arm 71 +/- 12, 73 +/- 12, 69 +/- 12 beats/min; saline arm 83 +/- 14, 83 +/- 15, 84 +/- 15), with no value marked as different from baseline.
key_findings.note: Relevant to the authors' explanation that labetalol's beta-blocking activity predominates at usual doses: the usual sign of beta-blockade, a fall in heart rate, did not appear, and no measure of blockade was taken.

key_findings.finding: In the saline arm (n = 6), coronary arterial area fell from 4.59 +/- 3.86 mm2 at baseline to 3.82 +/- 3.14 after cocaine and stayed at 3.70 +/- 3.10 after saline, and mean arterial pressure rose from 96 +/- 14 to 106 +/- 14 and stayed at 102 +/- 10; no variable changed after the saline infusion itself.
key_findings.locator: Table I, saline column; Results > Group I (Saline, n = 6)
key_findings.note: This arm shows the post-cocaine state persists for at least a further 5 minutes without intervention, which is what makes the labetalol arm interpretable.

key_findings.finding: Of the 15 patients, 6 had angiographically normal coronary arteries and 9 had atherosclerotic disease (70% or greater narrowing of a major epicardial vessel): one-vessel in 5, two-vessel in 2 and three-vessel in 2.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (continuing from p. 609 left column)

key_findings.finding: The Results text gives no measured values: the group paragraphs state only directions of change and refer to Table I and Figure 1 (the first paragraph gives only the coronary-anatomy counts).
key_findings.locator: Results > Group I and Group II paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors name two limitations: only one cocaine dose and route (intranasal 2 mg/kg, chosen as one half to two thirds the amount used for intranasal anesthesia, for its established safety) and only one intravenous labetalol dose (0.25 mg/kg, which they identify as the recommended dose and route for severe hypertension), so they cannot comment on larger doses.
key_findings.locator: Comments, limitations paragraph (left column, continuing right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that an agent with both alpha- and beta-blocking activity relieves the rise in systemic arterial pressure caused by cocaine but does not influence cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction, and suggest nitroglycerin may be preferable in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain, citing a separate study.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation and recommendation about hospital care; the study measured pressure, heart rate and lumen area, not clinical outcomes, and made no comparison with nitroglycerin.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's only quantitative statement about the cocaine effect, that of 40 coronary arterial segments analysed cocaine produced a 13% +/- 10% decrease in area in 32, appears nowhere in the Results, Table I or Figure 1, and no segment-level analysis is described in the methods. The 13% is the mean decrease of the 32 segments that narrowed, so the 8 that did not are left out.
reporting_issues.consequence: The most often quoted number in the paper cannot be checked against anything in the body. A claim about how much cocaine narrows coronary arteries should use the per-arm means in Table I, where the fall is 8.7% in one arm and 16.8% in the other (editors' calculation), not the abstract's segment-level figure, which, averaging only the segments that narrowed, overstates the mean narrowing across all segments.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods (Data Analysis, p. 609) state that a proximal, a middle and a distal left anterior descending segment were chosen in each patient, which for 15 patients implies 45 segments; the abstract reports 40 analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Five segments are missing without explanation, and it is not stated from which patients or arms, so the completeness of the angiographic outcome cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I marks significance only against baseline, but the abstract's headline comparison (mean arterial pressure 117 after cocaine against 110 after labetalol, p < 0.05) is between two post-drug time points, and the corresponding comparison for coronary arterial area (3.47 against 3.37, reported as not significant) is likewise not shown in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two comparisons the conclusion rests on are asserted in the abstract and absent from the table, so neither the test nor its precision can be checked. The null result for coronary area has no confidence interval, which is what a claim of 'no alleviation' would need.

reporting_issues.issue: The arms differ at baseline on every measured variable (heart rate 83 against 71 beats/min, mean arterial pressure 96 against 107 mm Hg, coronary arterial area 4.59 against 3.80 mm2) and in the cocaine concentration achieved (0.14 against 0.19 mg/L), yet no between-arm test, adjustment or comment appears.
reporting_issues.consequence: The saline arm cannot serve as a quantitative control for the labetalol arm, only as a demonstration that the post-cocaine state persists; any between-arm reading of the data is confounded.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility sentence states that no patient received beta-adrenergic blockers for more than 6 months before the study, which can be read either as 'none had taken a beta-blocker within the previous 6 months' or as 'none had taken one for longer than 6 months'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Prior beta-blocker exposure matters for a study of adrenergic blockade, and the criterion as printed does not settle what was excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears, although the companion study from the same group three years earlier declared NIH and American Heart Association grant support.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be recorded as absent, only as not reported.
