design_detail: Single-centre retrospective cohort from hospital records (Jacobi Medical Center, Bronx, NY, a municipal hospital), 1 July 2000 to 30 June 2005: 348 admissions of 296 patients to the telemetry, medical and coronary intensive care units of the medicine service, all arriving through the emergency department, with a urine test positive for cocaine metabolite. Admissions in which a β-blocker was given (60) were compared with admissions without one (288). For the myocardial infarction analysis (310 admissions with troponin measured) the β-blocker group was restricted to the 33 admissions in which the drug was given before any troponin rise; by the text, admissions given a β-blocker after a positive troponin were counted with the comparison group (277). Outcomes in hospital only: myocardial infarction (primary) and death from any cause (secondary). Generalized estimating equations with propensity scores; first-admission and chest-pain-admission sensitivity analyses.
can_establish: How often, to whom and for what recorded reasons physicians at one New York municipal hospital gave β-blockers during admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test in 2000–2005, and the crude counts of in-hospital myocardial infarction and death by group.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers lower or raise the risk of myocardial infarction or death after cocaine use: infarctions were counted in the β-blocker group only after the drug was given but in the comparison group from admission, treatment followed clinical indication, and the β-blocker group had 2 infarctions and 1 death.

sample.recruitment: Clinic (hospital records): all admissions to the telemetry, medical and coronary intensive care units of the Medicine Service with a cocaine-positive urine test, 1 July 2000 to 30 June 2005, found by an electronic search of all urine toxicology tests and confirmed by manual review of each paper record (ED course, ECGs, telemetry strips, notes) (p. 118).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: admissions to monitored medicine units with a urine test positive for cocaine metabolite. Excluded: 15 admissions of patients prescribed a β-blocker as outpatients within the past year who did not receive one in hospital, because the authors could not tell whether the drug was present on admission (pp. 118–119). Admissions without a troponin measurement (38) were left out of the infarction analysis only (Figure, p. 120).
sample.demographics: Full cohort (348 admissions): mean age 44 (SD 10), 61% men. β-blocker vs no β-blocker: age 49 vs 43; history of hypertension 68% vs 36%, heart failure 15% vs 6%, coronary disease 22% vs 15%, asthma 17% vs 32%; admission systolic pressure 150 vs 137 mm Hg; albumin 3.8 vs 4.1 g/dL; glucose 173 vs 140 mg/dL; ejection fraction 55% vs 61% among those with echocardiograms (Table 1, p. 121). Race or ethnicity, smoking, HIV and hepatitis C status are not tabulated. Admission diagnoses: chest pain 165, overdose 15, seizure 12, stroke 11, heart failure 8, others (p. 119).
sample.attrition: Not applicable for in-hospital outcomes. 38 of 348 admissions (11%) had no troponin and were left out of the infarction analysis (Figure, p. 120). 36 patients had more than one admission; generalized estimating equations were used, with first-admission sensitivity analyses (pp. 119, 123). The number with echocardiograms is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Patients admitted to monitored units after a positive urine test at one Bronx municipal hospital; about half (165 of 348) were admitted for chest pain. Excluding admissions whose outpatient β-blocker was stopped removes a group selected by the treating physicians' decision. The infarction comparison is selected on timing: only infarctions after the β-blocker counted in the β-blocker group, while infarctions present on arrival or occurring before any β-blocker counted in the comparison group.

exposure.measurement: Cocaine: urine benzoylecgonine by EMIT II Plus enzyme immunoassay, positive above 300 ng/mL; each positive test confirmed in the record (pp. 118–119). The authors state benzoylecgonine is detectable within 4 h of use and above 100 ng/mL for up to 48 h; time of cocaine use and serum cocaine levels were not known (pp. 119, 123–124). β-blocker: orders and laboratory results time-stamped in the electronic record, so the authors could tell whether the drug was given in the emergency department or later and before or after troponin results (p. 118).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cocaine amount, route and timing not recorded. β-blockers given in 60 admissions (17%), first in the emergency department in 18; agents: 40 (66%) described as β-selective (metoprolol, atenolol or propranolol), 13 (21%) combined α/β (labetalol, carvedilol), 8 (13%) both; recorded reasons (one or more): rule out or after myocardial infarction 56, already taking a β-blocker as an outpatient 21, cirrhosis or variceal prophylaxis with propranolol 5, arrhythmia 3 (p. 121). Doses, routes and duration of β-blockade not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or adjusted for. The authors name HIV, hepatitis C and their treatments as possible interacting conditions and included all patients regardless (p. 123).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; recency of cocaine use unknown beyond a positive urine test (pp. 123–124).

comparison.controls: Admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test without a β-blocker (288, full cohort, used for mortality). For infarction: 277 admissions without a β-blocker before the infarction, which by the text includes admissions given a β-blocker only after a positive troponin (pp. 119, 122).
comparison.matching: None. Parsimonious generalized-estimating-equation models kept variables at P<.05 or if they changed the β-blocker coefficient by 10% or more; candidates were those with P<.25 among age, sex, systolic pressure, history of heart disease, heart failure and diabetes, smoking, and admission albumin, potassium, urea, creatinine and glucose; a propensity score for receiving a β-blocker was added (p. 119). Final infarction model: β-blocker, systolic pressure, sex, history of heart failure; mortality model: β-blocker, systolic pressure, sex, diabetes, albumin, age (Table 4, p. 123).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Presenting troponin and ECG, haemodynamic instability and sepsis, recency and amount of cocaine, other drugs, HIV and hepatitis C, and the reasons physicians withheld β-blockers were not modelled; the propensity score's variables and the resulting balance are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Myocardial infarction: troponin I above 0.10 (units not given in the definition; ADVIA Centaur assay with a 99th percentile below 0.07) or significant ST elevation in 2 contiguous leads, with chest pain or an anginal equivalent; an infarction was attributed to β-blocker use only if it occurred after the drug and before a documented troponin rise or ECG change. Death from any cause at any time in hospital after a β-blocker (pp. 118–119).
outcomes.validity_norms: The infarction definition is described as consistent with the joint European Society of Cardiology/American College of Cardiology definition (p. 118).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm or benefit as in-hospital infarction and death. Secondary analyses: troponin above 1.0, ST-elevation infarction, troponin above 0.10 regardless of symptoms (possible silent infarction), and a second troponin rise (p. 122).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six adjusted models in Table 4 (full cohort and first admission, for infarction, infarction in chest-pain admissions, and death), each with its own covariates and propensity score.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Records were abstracted by study physicians (author contributions, p. 124); who judged symptoms and ECG criteria is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Infarction cohort: 2 of 33 (6.1%) with a β-blocker before any troponin rise vs 72 of 277 (26.0%) without one before the infarction; difference 19.9% (95% CI 10.3% to 30.0%); unadjusted OR 0.17 (0.04 to 0.80) (pp. 117, 121). Adjusted ORs (generalized estimating equations with propensity scores, Table 4, p. 123): infarction 0.06 (0.01 to 0.61; 74 events in 310 admissions), first admission 0.08 (0.01 to 0.65; 62 in 269); chest-pain admissions 0.05 (0.00 to 2.08; 51 in 165), first admission 0.09 (0.01 to 0.70; 44 in 140); death 0.22 (0.02 to 2.41; 14 in 348), first admission 0.01 (0.00 to 0.33; 12 in 296). Deaths: 1 of 60 (1.7%) vs 13 of 288 (4.5%), difference 2.8% (−1.2% to 6.7%) (p. 122). Editors' calculation: crude risk ratio for infarction 0.23 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.91; log-scale Wald interval), resting on 2 events in the β-blocker group.
analysis.covariates: Parsimonious models with propensity scores (see comparison.matching). Presenting troponin, ECG findings, timing of the β-blocker relative to arrival, and severity of illness were not adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the adjusted infarction OR and the crude death difference but not the non-significant adjusted death OR (0.22, 0.02 to 2.41). The discussion's first paragraph says β-blockers were associated with lower risk of death and infarction, and the next says deaths were too few for conclusions (p. 124). The covariates of the chest-pain model differ between the Table 4 footnote and the text (p. 123). The propensity-score model is not reported.
analysis.power: The authors state the study was too small to explore mortality (p. 124). The infarction estimates rest on 2 events in the β-blocker group; the first-admission mortality model (OR 0.01) rests on 12 deaths, and how many occurred in β-blocker admissions is not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 2 of 33 admissions given a β-blocker before any troponin rise had an infarction, against 72 of 277 admissions without a β-blocker before their infarction, in a comparison where infarctions present on arrival or occurring before a β-blocker all fall in the comparison group and only 18 of 60 β-blocker courses began in the emergency department. Deaths: 1 of 60 vs 13 of 288; the one death after a β-blocker followed thrombolysis for ST-elevation infarction, with the drug given after the ST elevation. Adjusted odds ratios are very low but rest on 2 infarctions and 1 death in the β-blocker group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Title: β-blockers are associated with reduced risk. The abstract says multivariate analysis showed β-blockers "significantly reduced the risk of myocardial infarction" (p. 117), and the limitations section says the study suggests that it is safe to give β-blockers to patients with positive urine tests (p. 124). The authors call the results preliminary, concede deaths were too few for conclusions, that urine tests may not reflect acute toxicity and that propensity scores adjust only for observed confounders (pp. 123–124), and argue that confounding would bias against β-blockers because recipients were at higher risk (p. 123); the timing asymmetry in how infarctions were counted is not discussed. An OR of 0.05 with interval 0.00 to 2.08 is called of borderline significance, and a difference of 15.1% with interval 0.8% to 31% a trend (pp. 122–123).

timeline.event: Lange et al.: cited by Dattilo et al. as evidence that β-blockade after cocaine increases coronary vasoconstriction (lower coronary blood flow, higher coronary vascular resistance) (p. 117)
Boehrer et al.: cited by Dattilo et al. as showing that labetalol does not reduce cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction (p. 117)

Two editorials accompany this article in the same issue (pp. 127 and 130); the one on p. 130 is Freeman & Feldman, 'Cocaine, myocardial infarction, and beta-blockers: time to rethink the equation?' (identified from Shin et al., 2019, reference 11). Neither was among the files; not read.
Mohamad et al. (Detroit): unadjusted, more troponin elevation with home β-blockers (14% vs 4.4%) and with β-blockers continued or started in hospital (23.3% vs 10.7%), the opposite direction

Rangel et al. (San Francisco, 331 admitted with chest pain): no difference in troponin in the infarction range (15 of 151 vs 18 of 177) or in-hospital death by emergency-department β-blocker; they describe this study as having only a small proportion of patients admitted with chest pain, whereas Dattilo et al. report 165 of 348
Ibrahim et al. (Houston, 378 patients): troponin rise 22 of 162 with vs 20 of 216 without β-blockers, unadjusted

Shin et al. meta-analysis pooled this study's infarction counts (2 of 33 vs 72 of 277; RR 0.23, 0.06 to 0.91) and death counts entered as 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277 (the full-cohort deaths over the troponin-subgroup denominators)

Pham et al. meta-analysis pooled this study's infarction counts (2 of 33 vs 72 of 277; odds ratio 0.18, 0.04 to 0.79) and deaths as 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277; its Results text attributes to this study the one significant increase in infarction, which belongs to Mohamad et al.

replication.where_it_stands: The first clinical study of the question by the authors' account (p. 118), and the only study in the pooled in-hospital infarction analysis of Shin et al. (2019) whose interval lies wholly below 1; the other record studies found no difference (Rangel et al., 2010; Ibrahim et al., 2013) or more troponin elevation with β-blockers (Mohamad et al., 2008). It is also one of the five cohorts pooled by Pham et al. (2018), so neither meta-analysis is independent of it. All are non-randomized studies from one or two hospitals; no randomized trial existed as of 2018 (Shin et al., 2019, p. 45).

funding.funder: Not reported. The 'Funding and support' paragraph contains only the conflict-of-interest disclosure (p. 124).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors stated that no commercial, financial or other relationships that might create a potential conflict of interest exist (p. 124).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Medicine, Jacobi Medical Center, and Department of Epidemiology and Population Health, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx (p. 117). Presented as posters at the Society for General Internal Medicine meeting (April 2006) and the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions (November 2006) (p. 124).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain comparing β-blockade (selective and combined α/β agents separately) with no β-blockade from a common time zero at randomization, with infarction adjudicated blind to treatment by a fixed troponin definition and time since cocaine use recorded; failing that, a target-trial emulation in multicentre records that starts follow-up at the same moment for treated and untreated patients.

domains.note: Physicians chose who received β-blockers, mostly to rule out or after a myocardial infarction (56 of 60) or to continue outpatient treatment (21); recipients were older, more hypertensive, more often had heart failure and lower ejection fraction (Table 1). Adjustment used a few P-value-selected covariates plus an unreported propensity score; presenting troponin and ECG, haemodynamic instability and sepsis were not modelled (the authors concede sepsis may have led physicians to avoid β-blockers, p. 124).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: For infarction, follow-up started at β-blocker administration in the treated group but at admission in the comparison group: infarctions present on arrival or occurring before any β-blocker were counted only against the comparison group, and admissions given a β-blocker after their infarction were moved into it (pp. 119, 122). Only 18 of 60 β-blocker courses began in the emergency department. This immortal-time structure favours β-blockers whatever their effect. Also excluded: 15 admissions whose outpatient β-blocker was stopped, and 38 without troponin.

Classification depended on the timing of the outcome (β-blocker before vs after the troponin rise). The flow figure labels the 31 β-blocker admissions without infarction as given β-blockers after an infarction and the 277 as not given β-blockers, contradicting the text (p. 120). Agent classes sum to 61 for 60 admissions and propranolol is listed as β-selective (p. 121).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Doses, duration of β-blockade and co-interventions (nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, benzodiazepines, thrombolysis) are not reported by group.
38 of 348 admissions (11%) without troponin were left out of the infarction analysis; ejection fraction only for those with echocardiograms (number not given); missing covariate data not reported.

Troponin is objective, but the infarction definition also required chest pain or an anginal equivalent judged from charts by unblinded study physicians; 25 patients with a positive troponin did not meet the criteria (p. 122).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; covariates selected by P values separately for each of six models with separate propensity scores; covariate lists differ between Table 4 and the text; the abstract reports the most favourable adjusted infarction estimate and omits the non-significant adjusted death estimate; first-admission mortality OR 0.01 vs full-cohort 0.22.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because β-blockers are an intervention compared without randomization (METHODS §5.3). The infarction comparison is at critical risk of bias: follow-up for infarction began at β-blocker administration in the treated group but at admission in the comparison group, which also received every admission given a β-blocker after its infarction, so the design favours β-blockers regardless of their true effect; treatment followed clinical indication and the propensity model is unreported. The mortality comparison (1 of 60 vs 13 of 288) is less affected by timing but has a single death in the treated group, in a patient given the drug after an ST-elevation infarction. Citable for: who received β-blockers at one hospital in 2000–2005 and the recorded reasons and agents (60 of 348 admissions), the crude in-hospital infarction and death counts as reported with their definitions, the absence of any death the authors attributed to β-blocker-induced coronary spasm, and the authors' conclusions as claims. Not citable for: β-blockers reducing infarction or death after cocaine use, or for their safety.

key_findings.finding: 363 admissions of 307 patients with a cocaine-positive urine test; after excluding 15 admissions with an outpatient β-blocker not continued in hospital, 348 admissions of 296 patients were analysed. The commonest admission diagnosis was chest pain (165); others included overdose 15, seizure 12, stroke 11 and heart failure 8.

β-blockers were given in 60 of 348 admissions (17%), first in the emergency department in 18: 40 (66%) β-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol or propranolol), 13 (21%) α-β blockade (labetalol, carvedilol), 8 (13%) both. Recorded reasons: rule out or after myocardial infarction 56, outpatient β-blocker 21, cirrhosis or variceal prophylaxis with propranolol 5, arrhythmia 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Study Subjects, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The three agent groups sum to 61, not 60; propranolol, a non-selective β-blocker, is listed among the β-selective agents.

key_findings.finding: Admissions with a β-blocker vs without: mean age 49 vs 43 years; history of hypertension 41 (68%) vs 104 (36%), OR 4.28 (2.17 to 8.44); heart failure 9 (15%) vs 17 (6%), OR 2.55 (1.05 to 6.15); asthma 10 (17%) vs 92 (32%); admission systolic pressure 150 vs 137 mm Hg; albumin 3.8 vs 4.1 g/dL; glucose 173 vs 140 mg/dL; ejection fraction 55% vs 61%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of Study Subjects, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Infarction cohort (310 admissions with troponin measured, 269 patients): 2 of 33 admissions given a β-blocker before any troponin rise had an infarction (6.1%) vs 72 of 277 without a β-blocker before the infarction (26.0%); difference 19.9% (95% CI 10.3% to 30.0%); unadjusted OR 0.17 (0.04 to 0.80). In one of the 2, the β-blocker was ordered 3.5 h before the positive troponin result.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 117); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 119); Table 2 and Results › Main Results, 1st paragraph (p. 121)
key_findings.note: The text gives the difference as 19% and, in the continuation of the same sentence on p. 122, the unadjusted OR interval as 0.04 to 0.08, below the estimate; Table 2 gives 0.04–0.80.

key_findings.finding: How the groups were formed: admissions given a β-blocker after a positive troponin were removed from the β-blocker group because the drug could not have caused their infarction, and the comparison is described as patients "who did not receive β-blockers or received them after" the infarction. Only 18 of the 60 β-blocker courses began in the emergency department.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 119); Results › Characteristics of Study Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 121); Results › Main Results, 1st paragraph, continuation (p. 122)

key_findings.finding: No patient given a β-blocker before a positive troponin had a troponin above 1.0, against 33 patients who received none or received it after the infarction (difference in proportion 57.9%, 95% CI 45.1% to 70.1%); no ST-elevation infarction in the β-blocker group vs 9 in the comparison group; no second troponin rise after a β-blocker vs 4 second infarctions in patients not given one.
key_findings.locator: Results › Main Results, 1st paragraph (starting p. 121, these results on p. 122) and 3rd paragraph (p. 122)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 57.9% equals 33 of 57; neither 33 of 72 (45.8%) nor 33 of 277 (11.9%) gives it, and the denominator is not stated.

key_findings.finding: 25 patients had a positive troponin without meeting the infarction criteria. Using troponin above 0.10 alone, and adding to the β-blocker group one patient given a single dose of metoprolol 24 h before measurement, the difference was 15.1% (95% CI 0.8% to 31%), which the authors call a trend.

14 in-hospital deaths: 1 of 60 admissions with a β-blocker (1.7%) vs 13 of 288 without (4.5%); difference 2.8% (95% CI −1.2% to 6.7%). The death after a β-blocker was from pericardial tamponade after thrombolysis for ST-elevation infarction, the β-blocker given after the ST elevation. Causes: cardiac arrest 6, probable sepsis 7, upper gastrointestinal bleeding 1; troponin measured in 11 of 14 and positive in 7 (0.2 to 69.8 ng/mL); 3 deaths more than 20 days after the positive urine test.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 117); Figure, panel A (p. 120) and Table 1 (p. 121) for the denominators; Table 3 and Results › Main Results, 5th to 8th paragraphs (p. 122)

key_findings.finding: Patients who died were more often women and more often had HIV disease and heart failure, lower systolic pressure and albumin, and higher urea, potassium and creatinine on admission.

Adjusted ORs for β-blocker administration (generalized estimating equations with propensity scores): infarction 0.06 (0.01 to 0.61; 74 events in 310 admissions), first admission 0.08 (0.01 to 0.65; 62 in 269); infarction in chest-pain admissions 0.05 (0.00 to 2.08; 51 in 165), first admission 0.09 (0.01 to 0.70; 44 in 140); in-hospital death 0.22 (0.02 to 2.41; 14 in 348), first admission 0.01 (0.00 to 0.33; 12 in 296).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Sensitivity Analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text on p. 122 gives the full-cohort infarction interval as 0.00 to 0.61. How many of the 12 first-admission deaths occurred after a β-blocker is not reported.

key_findings.finding: The authors state there were no guidelines on β-blocker use at the time, that recipients were at greater risk (coronary disease, poor ventricular function, higher glucose and pressure), and that the β-blocker effect may therefore be underestimated in the unadjusted analysis; they also state that propensity scores cannot adjust for unknown confounders and that conditions such as sepsis may have led physicians to avoid β-blockers.
The authors state that no death in the 5-year period could be directly attributed to coronary spasm induced by β-blockers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 363 consecutive telemetry and ICU patients and 15 excluded patients; the Results and Figure give 363 admissions of 307 patients and, after exclusion, 348 admissions of 296 patients, so the 15 exclusions were admissions of 11 patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the unit of analysis is the admission, with generalized estimating equations for repeated admissions.

reporting_issues.issue: The flow figure labels the 31 β-blocker admissions without infarction as given β-blockers after the development of an infarction, and the 277 as not given β-blockers; the text (Results, 2nd paragraph; Main Results, 1st paragraph) says admissions given a β-blocker after a positive troponin were removed from the β-blocker group and counted with those not given one. The total of 74 infarctions (Tables 2 and 4) shows the 31 were not counted as infarctions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the comparison group cannot be reconstructed: how many of the 277 received a β-blocker after their infarction is not reported (60 β-blocker admissions in the full cohort against 33 in the infarction cohort, with 38 admissions lacking troponin).

reporting_issues.issue: The unadjusted infarction OR is printed in the text as 0.17 with 95% CI 0.04 to 0.08, the upper limit below the estimate; Table 2 gives 0.17 (0.04–0.80).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the table value should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the OR for a history of heart failure as 1.70 (1.23–9.07), an estimate near the lower end of its own interval. Editors' calculation: the counts (6 of 33 vs 18 of 277) give a crude OR of 3.20, and the geometric centre of the printed interval is 3.34.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed estimate is probably a typographical error; the counts and interval agree with an OR of about 3.2 to 3.3.

reporting_issues.issue: The ORs for male sex point the opposite way to the percentages: Table 1, 67% vs 60% men with OR 0.80 (0.43–1.47); Table 2, 73% vs 63% with OR 0.67 (0.30–1.52). The coding (probably female sex) is not stated. Editors' calculation: crude ORs for male sex are 1.33 and 1.55.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but sex is a covariate in the final infarction and mortality models and its coding is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: β-blocker classes are given as 40 (66%) β-selective, 13 (21%) α-β and 8 (13%) both, which sum to 61 for 60 admissions; propranolol is listed among the β-selective agents and also as the drug for variceal prophylaxis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Agent-specific statements (selective vs non-selective vs combined α/β) cannot be drawn reliably from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The covariates of the chest-pain infarction model differ: the Table 4 footnote assigns it systolic pressure, sex and heart failure; the text says systolic pressure and urea. The Limitations section cites Table 3 for the chest-pain subgroup result, which is in Table 4. The text gives the full-cohort infarction interval as 0.00 to 0.61 (p. 122) where the abstract and Table 4 give 0.01 to 0.61.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjustment set for the chest-pain model is uncertain; the lower limits are minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The propensity score is described as the single summarized confounding covariate in the models (p. 119), yet the Table 4 models list covariates in addition to it; the variables in the propensity model and the balance it achieved are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjustment cannot be evaluated or reproduced, and the authors' description of propensity scores as the most rigorous method (p. 124) cannot be checked against what was done.

The two editorials in the same issue (pp. 127 and 130) were not among the files and were not read; no supplement.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 389 (adjudicator), on reading Pham et al. 2018 (Figures 3 and 4, PDF p. 4) against this PDF (same point); and Ibrahim et al. drew on two hospitals (p. 613), so not all are single-centre.

disagreements.first_pass: Title: β-blockers are associated with reduced risk. The abstract says multivariate analysis showed β-blockers "significantly reduced the risk of myocardial infarction" (p. 117), and the limitations section concludes that it is safe to give β-blockers to patients with positive urine tests (p. 124). The authors call the results preliminary, concede deaths were too few for conclusions, that urine tests may not reflect acute toxicity and that propensity scores adjust only for observed confounders (pp. 123–124), and argue that confounding would bias against β-blockers because recipients were at higher risk (p. 123); the timing asymmetry in how infarctions were counted is not discussed. design_detail: Retrospective chart-review cohort of 376 consecutive patients admitted with chest pain and a urine toxicology screen positive for cocaine at the two major hospitals affiliated with an academic teaching university (not named in the paper; the authors' affiliation is Saint Louis University, St Louis, Missouri), January 2000 to December 2007. Patients were identified by a positive immunoassay urine drug screen plus reported cocaine use within the previous 24 hours, then by ICD-9 codes for chest pain, angina or chest discomfort, with every chart reviewed manually by physician members of the research team to exclude chest pain diagnosed as pulmonary in the emergency department. The exposure is whether a beta blocker was given in the first 24 hours of presentation (164 patients, 44%) against not (212). The outcome is a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or all-cause death during the index hospitalization. Because the two groups differed substantially at baseline, the authors built a propensity score for receiving a beta blocker from the pre-treatment characteristics they list (no count is given; 13 or 14 depending on how 'initial ECG findings and cardiac biomarkers' is counted), stratified the cohort by propensity-score quintile and fitted a logistic regression adjusted for that quintile.
can_establish: How often beta blockers were actually given to patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at two urban hospitals over eight years despite guidance against it, which drugs were used, and whether in-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death were more common in those who received one, with the imprecision that about 52 events across 376 patients allows.
cannot_establish: Whether beta blockers are safe in this setting: the adjusted interval runs from a 36% reduction to a near-tripling of the composite outcome, so the study excludes neither substantial harm nor substantial benefit. It also cannot establish that the patients had pharmacologically active cocaine on board when the drug was given (a urine screen stays positive for days), that the two groups were comparable after adjustment (the treated group received far more of every other anti-ischemic therapy, none of it in the propensity model), or that the timing of the beta blocker relative to the outcome was accounted for.

sample.recruitment: Consecutive patients presenting to two academic hospitals from January 2000 to December 2007 with a urine screen positive for cocaine and reported use within the previous 24 hours, with an ICD-9 code for chest pain, angina or chest discomfort; charts reviewed by hand to exclude pulmonary causes of chest pain diagnosed in the emergency department (p. 1802).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: positive immunoassay urine drug test for cocaine, reported cocaine use within 24 hours, ICD-9 chest-pain code. Excluded: chest pain diagnosed as pulmonary in the emergency department (for example pneumonia or pulmonary embolus) (p. 1802). No exclusion for critical illness, and no restriction by age.
sample.demographics: Beta-blocker group against no beta blocker: mean age 46 +/- 9 against 42 +/- 11 years (p < 0.001); 32% against 26% women; 10% against 13% recorded as White and 81% against 76% as Black; chest pain typical for angina 17% against 8% (p = 0.012); history of hypertension 80% against 38%, hyperlipidemia 23% against 11%, diabetes 25% against 14%, known coronary artery disease 33% against 13% (all p <= 0.005); TIMI risk score 0 in 44% against 69% (p < 0.001); systolic pressure 152 +/- 36 against 138 +/- 32 mm Hg and diastolic 89 +/- 26 against 80 +/- 22 mm Hg (both p < 0.001); heart rate 91 +/- 22 against 94 +/- 25 beats/min (p = 0.29) (Table 1, p. 1803).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: a complete-admission chart review with in-hospital outcomes. No patient is reported excluded for missing data, and how missing chart items were handled is not described.
sample.selection_effects: Two urban academic hospitals with a predominantly Black patient population, over a period when guidelines already advised against beta blockers here, so the 44% who received one were selected by their clinicians precisely on grounds related to the outcome: they were older, had more coronary risk factors and known coronary disease, higher TIMI scores, higher presenting blood pressure and worse left ventricular function, and they were far more often admitted to a cardiac intensive care unit (22% against 8%). Treatment is therefore confounded by indication in both directions at once, since the sicker patients also received more of every protective therapy.

exposure.measurement: Beta-blocker administration within the first 24 hours of presentation, taken from the hospital chart along with all other cardiac medications given in that window (p. 1802). Cocaine exposure established by immunoassay urine drug test (Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics) plus reported use within the previous 24 hours; no quantitative cocaine or metabolite measurement, no route and no amount (p. 1802).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses, routes and timing of the beta blockers are not reported, only the agent: metoprolol in 74 patients, labetalol in 44, carvedilol in 43 and atenolol in 3 (p. 1803). Of the 164, 77 received a beta-1 selective drug and 87 received carvedilol or labetalol, which the paper groups as nonselective although both also block alpha receptors (editors' arithmetic from the same sentence).
exposure.polysubstance: Not characterized. No alcohol or other drug use is reported, although cocaine and alcohol are commonly used together and cocaethylene affects the heart. Co-prescribed cardiac drugs differed sharply between groups and are reported: aspirin 84% against 57%, clopidogrel 23% against 8%, systemic anticoagulation 23% against 9%, nitrates 50% against 36%, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24% (all p <= 0.007; Table 1, p. 1803). None of these co-treatments was included in the propensity score.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Unknown and acknowledged as a limitation: a urine screen can stay positive for 48 to 72 hours after use, so how recently cocaine had been taken, and whether it was still pharmacologically active when the beta blocker was given, cannot be established (p. 1805).

comparison.controls: The 212 patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at the same two hospitals in the same period who were not given a beta blocker in the first 24 hours.
comparison.matching: No matching despite the table heading. The analysis stratified patients into propensity-score quintiles and fitted a logistic regression adjusted for quintile; the propensity score was built from age, gender, race, character of chest pain, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, known HIV infection, previous lung disease, previous coronary artery disease, TIMI risk score, blood pressures, and initial electrocardiographic findings and cardiac biomarkers, with a C statistic of 0.82 (pp. 1802, 1804).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The amount, route and timing of cocaine use; alcohol and other drug use; the co-prescribed cardiac drugs that differed greatly between groups; the clinical reasoning that led a physician to give or withhold the drug in each case; and the timing of the beta blocker relative to the event counted as the outcome.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All patients in both groups were cocaine-positive by urine screen; the comparison is between treatment decisions, not between cocaine exposure and none.

outcomes.instruments: Hospital records: death, myocardial infarction, stroke and ventricular arrhythmia during the chest-pain admission, with electrocardiograms, telemetry strips, troponin T and creatine kinase-MB, echocardiography and stress tests as clinically obtained (p. 1802).
outcomes.validity_norms: Myocardial infarction was defined as a troponin-T level above the local upper limit of normal or significant ST-segment elevation in two contiguous leads with chest pain or an anginal equivalent; stroke and ventricular arrhythmias were identified clinically by the treating physicians, not by an independent or blinded adjudicator (p. 1803). Clinical identification by treating physicians who knew what had been given is the main outcome-measurement weakness.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Adverse outcome' is the composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or all-cause death during the index hospitalization, with the four components also reported separately (p. 1803, Table 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 10 counts the composite and its four components, each tested unadjusted and after propensity-score adjustment; the paper also reports two further adjusted comparisons for drug subtypes and about 40 baseline comparisons in Tables 1 and 2, all at p <= 0.05 uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Charts were reviewed by physician members of the research team, and outcomes were those recorded by treating physicians; no blinding of reviewers to beta-blocker status is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted rates (Table 3, p. 1804), beta blocker against none: composite end point 16% against 12%, p = 0.32 (the abstract gives 15.9% against 12.3%); death 3% against 6%, p = 0.13; stroke 3% against 3%, p = 1.00; myocardial infarction 5% against 2%, p = 0.18; arrhythmia 7% against 5%, p = 0.52. Editors' calculation from these percentages and the group sizes: roughly 26 composite events in each arm, about 52 in all. Adjusted for propensity-score quintile (Table 3): composite odds ratio 1.37 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.93), p = 0.42; death 0.66 (0.14 to 3.04); stroke 1.20 (0.27 to 5.36); myocardial infarction 1.67 (0.44 to 6.35); arrhythmia 1.24 (0.38 to 3.98). Secondary analysis by drug type (p. 1804): beta-1 selective 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) and the drugs labelled nonselective 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42), each against no beta blocker; no test of interaction between the two is reported. Cardiac biomarkers were lower in the beta-blocker group (creatine kinase-MB at presentation 3.2 ng/ml, interquartile range 1.8 to 5.5, against 4.5, 2.5 to 10.5, p = 0.006; peak 3.2, 1.7 to 7.1, against 4.9, 2.7 to 12.2, p < 0.001) while troponin T did not differ (peak 0.04 ng/ml, 0.01 to 0.12, against 0.04, 0.01 to 0.21, p = 0.14), and left ventricular ejection fraction was lower in the beta-blocker group (0.41 +/- 0.17 against 0.49 +/- 0.17, p = 0.006) (Table 2, p. 1804).
analysis.covariates: The listed pre-treatment characteristics (no count given) entered the propensity score (listed under comparison > matching); the outcome model adjusted only for propensity-score quintile. Co-prescribed aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, which differed by 14 to 48 percentage points between the groups, were not adjusted for at any stage, nor was the timing of the beta blocker relative to the outcome.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the study protocol was reviewed and approved by the university's institutional review board (p. 1803).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four components of the composite are reported with both unadjusted rates and adjusted odds ratios, which is complete. The weakness is that the subgroup result pointing in opposite directions for the two drug classes is reported as uniformly null, with no interaction test and no comment on the fact that more than half the beta-blocker group received a drug with alpha-blocking activity, which is the pharmacological crux of the question.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With about 26 events per arm the adjusted confidence interval for the composite spans 0.64 to 2.93, so the data are equally compatible with a one-third reduction and with a near-tripling of risk; the individual components, with 3% to 7% event rates, have intervals up to 0.14 to 3.04. The authors call for a prospective trial (p. 1805).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 376 patients admitted with cocaine-positive chest pain, 44% were given a beta blocker in the first 24 hours even though guidelines advised against it. Those given one were older and sicker on every measured axis and also received far more aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. In-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death were statistically indistinguishable between the groups, before and after adjustment for a propensity-score quintile, with confidence intervals wide enough to contain both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that no differences in outcomes were observed between patients treated and not treated with beta-blocker therapy, and the discussion goes further: beta-blocker use in these at-risk patients 'may be safe', the therapy was 'at least neutral' and 'could even potentially have had a protective effect', and treatment 'may be safer than previously suggested' (pp. 1802, 1805). The gap is the standard one between a non-significant result and evidence of safety. The adjusted point estimate for the composite is 1.37, that is in the direction of harm, with an upper limit near 3; the point estimate for myocardial infarction is 1.67. A study with about 52 events cannot support a safety claim from these numbers. The authors' argument that the treated group was sicker and did no worse is reasonable as far as it goes, but it is weakened by their having also received much more of every other anti-ischemic therapy, which is never adjusted for. The authors also write that they used propensity-score analysis to help minimize unmeasured confounding (p. 1805), whereas a propensity score can balance only the measured characteristics entered into it. They do state the key limitations themselves (retrospective design, chart-documentation quality, residual confounding, inability to date the cocaine use) and they explicitly call for a prospective trial.

timeline.event: Mechanistic origin of the concern: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in cocaine-naive catheterization patients
American Heart Association scientific statement advises against beta blockers in the acute setting of cocaine-associated chest pain
This study: no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes in 376 patients, with wide intervals
Meta-analysis pooling observational studies of this question, including this cohort, whose Table 3 percentages it enters as event counts (5 and 2 for infarction, 3 and 6 for death)
Second meta-analysis (eight cohorts) pools this cohort again, with the same percentages entered as event counts

replication.where_it_stands: Several retrospective hospital cohorts, this one among them, have failed to detect the harm the mechanistic studies predict, and the authors of each note the same limits: non-random treatment, uncertain timing of cocaine use and too few events. No randomized trial has been done, so the question remains one where mechanism and observational practice data point in different directions without either being decisive.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no funding statement (p. 1806).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no conflicts of interest to disclose (p. 1806).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Division of Cardiology, Christiana Care Health System (Newark, Delaware); Saint Luke's Mid America Heart and Vascular Institute (Kansas City, Missouri); and the Center for Comprehensive Cardiovascular Care, Saint Louis University.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people presenting with chest pain after recent cocaine use, allocating an intravenous beta blocker against the currently recommended alternatives, with a confirmed recent-use measure rather than a urine screen, blinded outcome adjudication, and enough events to exclude a clinically meaningful difference in infarction and arrhythmia. Short of that, a cohort analysis that handles the timing of treatment relative to the event and adjusts for co-prescribed anti-ischemic drugs would at least remove the two largest sources of bias in the existing observational evidence.

domains.note: Treatment was chosen by clinicians on grounds strongly related to the outcome, and the two groups differ on almost every measured characteristic. The propensity score covers the listed baseline variables but none of the co-treatments, which differ by up to 48 percentage points (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24%, aspirin 84% against 57%), nor the amount, route or timing of cocaine use. Confounding here runs in both directions, so its net size and sign are unknown.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Exposure is defined over the first 24 hours while the outcome is counted over the whole admission, so a patient who dies or has an event early is less likely to have been given a beta blocker. No landmark or time-varying analysis addresses this, and the direction of the resulting bias favours the treated group.

Whether a beta blocker was given is recorded in the chart and is unlikely to be misclassified, but dose, route and timing within the 24 hours are not reported, and 87 of the 164 received carvedilol or labetalol, drugs with alpha-blocking activity that the paper classifies simply as nonselective, which blurs the exposure the mechanistic concern is about.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: This is routine care, so the question is co-intervention rather than protocol deviation; the large differences in aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are co-interventions that could offset any harm from the beta blocker and are not adjusted for.

Charts were reviewed by hand, which the authors offer as mitigation, but no account is given of missing values in the covariates or outcomes, and echocardiography and stress tests were obtained in only some patients and more often in the treated group.

Death and troponin are hard measures, but stroke and ventricular arrhythmia were identified clinically by treating physicians who knew what had been given, with no blinded adjudication, and one of the paper's own definitions ties myocardial infarction 'associated with beta-blocker use' to changes after administration while the composite counts any in-hospital infarction.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The composite and all four components are reported both ways, which is good practice, but the adjusted odds ratio appears as 1.34 in the Results text and 1.37 in the abstract and Table 3, and the drug-subtype analysis is summarised as uniformly null although its two estimates point in opposite directions and no interaction was tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is routine-care data on a question no one has randomized, and it is reported more fully than most such studies, with every component of the composite shown. But treatment was chosen on exactly the grounds that predict the outcome, the exposure window and the outcome window overlap in a way that favours the treated group, the co-treatments that differ most are never adjusted for, and about 52 events cannot support a conclusion of safety. The source can be cited for how often beta blockers were given to patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at two US hospitals in 2000 to 2007, which agents were used, and that in-hospital events were not detectably more common in the treated group, with the adjusted interval 0.64 to 2.93 stated alongside. It cannot be cited for the safety of beta blockers after cocaine use, nor as a refutation of the mechanistic studies, which concern a drug given while cocaine is pharmacologically active, a condition this cohort could not verify.

key_findings.finding: Of 376 consecutive patients admitted with chest pain and a urine screen positive for cocaine at two academic hospitals between January 2000 and December 2007, 164 (44%) received a beta blocker within the first 24 hours, despite guidelines advising against it: metoprolol in 74, labetalol in 44, carvedilol in 43 and atenolol in 3.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic from the same sentence: 77 received a beta-1 selective drug and 87 received carvedilol or labetalol, both of which also block alpha receptors, so more than half the treated group did not receive unopposed beta-blockade (pharmacological background: the paper itself classes carvedilol and labetalol as nonselective and does not mention alpha-blockade). Inclusion also required reported cocaine use within the previous 24 hours, and not all were admitted: 1% of the treated and 4% of the others went home from the emergency department (Table 1).

key_findings.finding: The patients given a beta blocker were older (46 +/- 9 against 42 +/- 11 years) and had more hypertension (80% against 38%), hyperlipidemia (23% against 11%), diabetes (25% against 14%), known coronary artery disease (33% against 13%), typical anginal pain (17% against 8%) and higher TIMI risk scores (all p <= 0.012).

The beta-blocker group also received far more of every other cardiac therapy: aspirin 84% against 57%, clopidogrel 23% against 8%, systemic anticoagulation 23% against 9%, nitrates 50% against 36%, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24% (all p <= 0.007), and were more often admitted to a cardiac intensive care unit (22% against 8%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, other medications ordered and disposition
key_findings.note: None of these co-treatments entered the propensity score, which was built from baseline characteristics only.

key_findings.finding: The composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or death occurred in 16% of the beta-blocker group and 12% of the others (p = 0.32); adjusted for propensity-score quintile the odds ratio was 1.37 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.93), p = 0.42.
key_findings.note: The Results text reports this adjusted odds ratio as 1.34 with the same interval and p value; the abstract and Table 3 give 1.37. Editors' calculation from the percentages: roughly 26 events in each arm.

key_findings.finding: No individual component differed: death 3% against 6% (adjusted odds ratio 0.66, 0.14 to 3.04), stroke 3% against 3% (1.20, 0.27 to 5.36), myocardial infarction 5% against 2% (1.67, 0.44 to 6.35), ventricular arrhythmia 7% against 5% (1.24, 0.38 to 3.98).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, death, stroke, MI and arrhythmia rows
key_findings.note: Every interval is wide enough to include both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit.

key_findings.finding: In the secondary analysis by drug class, the adjusted odds ratio against no beta blocker was 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) for beta-1 selective drugs and 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42) for the drugs labelled nonselective (carvedilol and labetalol, both of which also block alpha receptors).
key_findings.note: The two point estimates lie on opposite sides of 1, in the direction the unopposed-alpha hypothesis would predict, but both intervals include 1 and no test of interaction between the classes is reported; the paper describes the analysis as showing no relation for either subgroup.

key_findings.finding: Creatine kinase-MB was lower in the beta-blocker group at presentation (median 3.2 ng/ml, IQR 1.8 to 5.5, against 4.5, 2.5 to 10.5, p = 0.006) and at peak (3.2, 1.7 to 7.1, against 4.9, 2.7 to 12.2, p < 0.001), while troponin T did not differ at presentation (p = 0.12) or peak (p = 0.14).

Left ventricular ejection fraction was lower in the beta-blocker group (0.41 +/- 0.17 against 0.49 +/- 0.17, p = 0.006), and T-wave inversion was more common (56% against 26%, p < 0.001), while ST-segment depression and elevation did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, ECG changes and echocardiographic data rows

key_findings.finding: The propensity score was built from age, gender, race, character of chest pain, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, known HIV infection, previous lung disease, previous coronary artery disease, TIMI risk score, blood pressures and initial electrocardiographic findings and cardiac biomarkers, with a C statistic of 0.82; patients were stratified by propensity-score quintile and a logistic regression adjusted for quintile was fitted.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 1804, continuing into the right column); quintile stratification in Methods, 3rd paragraph (p. 1803) and Results, 4th paragraph (p. 1804)
key_findings.note: This is stratified adjustment, not matching, although Table 3 is titled and labelled as propensity-score matching.

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the retrospective design and chart-documentation quality, residual confounding beyond the variables collected, and the inability to date the cocaine use, since a urine screen can remain positive for 48 to 72 hours; they call for a prospective trial.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (limitations; begins p. 1805, ends p. 1806)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that beta-blocker use in these higher-risk patients may be safe, that the therapy was at least neutral and could potentially have been protective, and that beta-blocker treatment in cocaine-induced chest pain may be safer than previously suggested.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation; the adjusted point estimate for the composite outcome is 1.37 with an upper confidence limit near 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The propensity-adjusted odds ratio for the composite end point is given as 1.34 in the Results text and as 1.37 in both the abstract and Table 3, with the same confidence interval (0.64 to 2.93) and p value (0.42) in each place.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two numbers is a typographical error. The difference is immaterial to the conclusion, but a claim citing this study should quote Table 3, which agrees with the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 is titled 'In-hospital outcomes before and after propensity score matching' and its column reads 'OR (95% CI) After Propensity Score Matching', while the methods and results describe stratification by propensity-score quintile with a logistic regression adjusted for that quintile, and both groups keep their full size (164 and 212) in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: No matched cohort exists. Readers who take the table at its word will overstate the balance achieved: quintile stratification leaves residual imbalance within quintiles, which matching on individuals would reduce further.

reporting_issues.issue: The myocardial infarction definition gives the local upper limit of normal for troponin T as greater than 0.1 ng/dl, while Table 2 reports troponin T in ng/ml, a thousand-fold difference in unit.
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold that defined the main component of the composite outcome cannot be read unambiguously from the paper. The Table 2 values (medians of 0.04 with upper quartiles of 0.12 to 0.21) are consistent with ng/ml, so the methods statement appears to be the error.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-subtype analysis is summarised as showing no independent relation for either class, although the two adjusted odds ratios lie on opposite sides of 1 (1.83 for beta-1 selective, 0.90 for carvedilol and labetalol), no interaction test is reported, and the paper does not note that both drugs in its 'nonselective' group also block alpha receptors.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one analysis in the paper that bears directly on the unopposed-alpha mechanism is reported in a way that hides it. A claim about beta blockers after cocaine should state which drugs were actually given: more than half of this treated group received an agent with alpha-blocking activity.

reporting_issues.issue: Beta-blocker exposure is defined over the first 24 hours while outcomes are counted across the whole admission, and no analysis accounts for events occurring before the drug could be given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Patients who deteriorated or died early are preferentially counted as untreated, which biases the comparison towards apparent safety of the beta blocker. The size of this effect cannot be judged from the data reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the composite rates to one decimal (15.9% against 12.3%) while Table 3 gives whole numbers (16 against 12), and no event counts are printed anywhere in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of events, the quantity that governs the precision of every estimate in Table 3, has to be reconstructed from percentages (about 26 per arm, editors' calculation) rather than read.

reporting_issues.issue: In-hospital myocardial infarction is defined as troponin T above the laboratory's upper limit (printed as >0.1 ng/dl) or ST-segment elevation with chest pain, and for the treated group infarction associated with the beta-blocker as an increase in angina, troponin or ECG changes after it; yet Table 2 gives peak troponin T with interquartile ranges of 0.01 to 0.12 and 0.01 to 0.21 ng/ml, so more than a quarter of each group was above 0.1, while Table 3 gives infarction in 5% and 2%.
reporting_issues.consequence: How the infarction outcome was restricted (new events, events after admission, events after the beta-blocker) is not stated, and the treated group had a definition of its own, so the infarction component may have been ascertained differently in the two groups; the 5% against 2% and its odds ratio of 1.67 are of uncertain meaning.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives an unadjusted p of 0.13 for death (3% against 6%); no counts consistent with these rounded percentages reproduce it (5 of 164 against 12 or 13 of 212 give 0.23 or 0.17 by chi-square), while the composite (26 against 26, p = 0.32) and infarction (8 against 4, p = 0.18 with continuity correction) can be reproduced (editors' calculations).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the death comparison's exact counts cannot be recovered.
