design_detail: Retrospective chart review at two Houston hospitals (Lyndon B. Johnson and Memorial Hermann), 1998–2011: 378 adults presenting to the emergency department with chest pain, cocaine use in the preceding 24 h and a cocaine-positive urine test. Patients treated with any β-blocker during admission (162 in Table 1) were compared with those who were not (216), and within the β-blocker group patients on β1-selective agents (71) with those on combined α1/β agents (91), for troponin rise, peak troponin and hypertensive urgency. Unadjusted t and χ2 tests. Published in the journal's Research Seminar section.
can_establish: The recorded characteristics of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain at two Houston hospitals over 1998–2011, and the crude frequency of troponin rise (about 11%) and of in-hospital death (18 of 378).
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers changed the risk of troponin rise or hypertensive urgency: the comparison is unadjusted although β-blocker recipients had far more hypertension, coronary disease and low ejection fraction, the timing of β-blockers relative to the troponin rise was not determined, and the main counts are printed in three different versions.

sample.recruitment: Clinic (hospital records): retrospective chart review of emergency-department presentations with chest pain as chief complaint at Lyndon B. Johnson and Memorial Hermann Hospitals, Houston, 1998–2011 (pp. 613–614). How the records were searched is not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age over 18; chest pain on admission; cocaine use in the preceding 24 h; positive urine drug screen for cocaine metabolites (p. 614). No exclusion criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: Mean age 44.9 (SD 10.1); men 71.7%; Black 78.3%, White 11.6%, other 10.1%; typical chest pain 12.2%; hypertension 56.3%, coronary disease 22.2%, diabetes 20.9%, HIV 10.8%. β-blocker vs none: age 46.2 vs 42.3; hypertension 79.0% vs 39.4%; coronary disease 33.3% vs 13.9%; diabetes 27.8% vs 15.7%; hyperlipidaemia 24.1% vs 11.6%; ejection fraction below 50% 37.7% vs 11.6% (Table 1, p. 614).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (in-hospital outcomes). Disposition: 107 (28%) intensive care, 251 (66.4%) telemetry, 12 (3%) discharged from the emergency department, 370 of 378 in all (p. 615). The number of patients with each troponin assay or with an echocardiogram is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Patients presenting with chest pain at two inner-city hospitals over 13 years, almost all admitted to intensive care or telemetry; how cases were found, and whether all eligible presentations were found, is not described.

exposure.measurement: Cocaine: urine benzoylecgonine by EMIT II Plus immunoassay on admission (cut-off not stated) plus documented use in the preceding 24 h (p. 614). β-blocker: any β-blocker during admission, from chart review; the authors state that the timing of β-blockers relative to the troponin rise was not determined (p. 615), and the Results describe the 22 vs 20 troponin rises by β-blocker treatment in the first 12 hours, a window the Methods do not define (p. 614).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cocaine amount, route and exact recency not reported. β-blockers in 162 patients (43%): metoprolol 88 (53%), labetalol 45 (27.2%), carvedilol 44 (26.6%), atenolol 4 (2%) (p. 614). Doses, routes and timing (emergency department or later) not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Patients with cocaine-associated chest pain not treated with a β-blocker during admission: 216 in Table 1, 213 in the abstract and text.
comparison.matching: None; no adjustment of any kind (Student t test and χ2 with Yates correction, p. 614).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The large differences in hypertension, coronary disease, diabetes and ventricular function were measured but not adjusted for; the indication for β-blockers, haemodynamics, amount and recency of cocaine and other drugs were not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: Troponin I (Abbott AxSYM, cut-off 0.02 ng/mL, range 0.02–22.78) and troponin T (Boehringer Mannheim ES300, second generation, upper reference 0.1 ng/mL). Troponin elevation: troponin I above 0.6 ng/mL and troponin T above 0.1 ng/mL if creatinine below 2 mg/dL (abstract and methods), or troponin I above 0.6 or troponin T above 0.1 (table footnotes). Peak troponin taken as a measure of infarct size. Hypertensive urgency: systolic 180 mm Hg or more or diastolic 110 mm Hg or more after a β-blocker (pp. 613–615).
outcomes.validity_norms: The troponin I threshold (0.6 ng/mL) is 30 times the stated assay cut-off; mean peak troponin pools results from two different assays.
outcomes.operationalization: Safety was operationalized as the proportion with a troponin rise, the mean peak troponin among those with a rise, and hypertensive urgency after a β-blocker; deaths, arrhythmias and strokes were reported for the whole cohort only.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Troponin rise: 22 of 162 (13.6%) with a β-blocker vs 20 of 216 (9.3%) without, P=.191 (Table 1); the abstract gives 22 of 162 vs 20 of 213 and the text 20 of 165 vs 22 of 213 (P=.2 in both). Mean peak troponin among those with a rise: 6.7 vs 5.7 ng/mL (P=.6); β1-selective (n=5) vs α1/β (n=16): 7.5 vs 4.1 ng/mL (P=0.4); no SDs or ranges. No hypertensive urgency after any β-blocker. Editors' calculation from Table 1: risk ratio 1.47 (95% CI 0.83 to 2.59), risk difference 4.3 percentage points, Yates χ2 1.34 (P=0.25).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: In-hospital deaths (18), arrhythmias (24) and strokes (13) are given for the whole cohort but not by β-blocker group, although the stated objective was safety (p. 615). The main comparison appears in three versions, and the subgroup sizes in the text conflict with Table 2.
analysis.power: The authors say a type II error cannot be ruled out and that the margin of error was below 5%, without a calculation (p. 615). Editors' calculation: with 42 events the risk ratio's interval runs from 0.83 to 2.59.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Troponin rise was numerically more frequent with β-blockers (13.6% vs 9.3%) in an unadjusted comparison in which β-blocker recipients had twice the prevalence of hypertension and coronary disease and three times the prevalence of low ejection fraction, and in which troponin rises before the β-blocker cannot be separated from those after it. No hypertensive urgency was recorded after a β-blocker; blood pressures before treatment are not reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says β-blocker use "did not increase the incidence of MI nor made the existing one worse" (p. 615); the Conclusion says β-blockers did not appear to change the incidence of troponin rise and that β1-selective agents did not appear to worsen troponin levels compared with α1/β agents (p. 616); the limitations say the findings consolidate emerging data on safety (p. 615). The authors acknowledge that timing was not determined and that power was lacking (p. 615). A non-significant unadjusted difference whose interval allows a 2.6-fold higher risk, with timing unknown, does not support a safety conclusion, and the β1 vs α1/β comparison rests on 5 and 16 patients (or 12 and 10 in Table 2).

timeline.event: Lange et al.: one of the 2 studies, totalling only 19 patients, on which (by the account Ibrahim et al. cite) the recommendation against β-blockers was based (p. 615)
Boehrer et al.: the second of those two studies (p. 615)

McCord et al., American Heart Association scientific statement: described by Ibrahim et al. as contraindicating β-blockers in the acute setting while allowing them in the discharge regimen after careful risk–benefit assessment, graded IIIC (p. 615)
Dattilo et al.: fewer infarctions after β-blockers (cited by Ibrahim et al., p. 615)

Mohamad et al. (Detroit; the same troponin I assay description, but myocardial injury defined as any troponin I above 0.02 ng/mL rather than 0.6): more troponin elevation with home or in-hospital β-blockers, unadjusted. Not cited by Ibrahim et al., whose methods, discussion and limitations reproduce passages of it word for word (reporting issue 8)
Rangel et al. (San Francisco): no difference in troponin or in-hospital events by emergency-department β-blocker, unadjusted (not cited by Ibrahim et al.)
Shin et al. meta-analysis pooled this study's Table 1 counts (22 of 162 vs 20 of 216; RR 1.47, 0.83 to 2.59) for in-hospital infarction
Pham et al. meta-analysis pooled this study's Table 1 counts (22 of 162 vs 20 of 216; odds ratio 1.54, 0.81 to 2.93), dating it 2012

replication.where_it_stands: One of four record studies on in-hospital outcomes read in this round (this one from two hospitals); like Rangel et al. (2010) it finds no clear difference, against fewer infarctions in Dattilo et al. (2008) and more troponin elevation in Mohamad et al. (2008). Its counts are inside the pooled estimates of Shin et al. (2019) and Pham et al. (2018) and should not be cited beside either as independent support.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Cardiology and pulmonary/critical-care divisions at the University of Florida (Jacksonville), the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, the University of South Alabama and the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (p. 613); study approved by the Houston institutional review board (p. 614).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain comparing β-blockade (selective and combined α1/β agents separately) with none from randomization, with serial troponin measured at fixed times after randomization by one assay and adjudicated blind to treatment; at minimum, a cohort that records the time of each β-blocker dose relative to troponin measurements and adjusts for the reasons for treatment.

domains.note: No adjustment at all; β-blocker recipients had much more hypertension (79.0% vs 39.4%), coronary disease (33.3% vs 13.9%), diabetes, left ventricular hypertrophy and ejection fraction below 50% (37.7% vs 11.6%) (Table 1). Treatment was given for indications that are themselves linked to troponin rise.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Case identification not described; 13 years at two hospitals; follow-up begins at presentation, but β-blockers were given at unreported times during admission, so patients had to remain in hospital to be classified as treated.

Any β-blocker during admission, with timing relative to the troponin rise not determined (p. 615), so troponin rises before treatment (and treatment given because of them) are counted against β-blockers. Drug counts (181 exposures) and their percentages (denominator 165) do not match the 162 treated, and labetalol plus carvedilol (89 exposures) cannot fill the 91-patient α1/β group of Table 2.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Doses, durations and co-interventions are not reported.
How many patients had troponin I, troponin T or echocardiography, and how missing values were handled, is not reported; disposition accounts for 370 of 378.

The troponin-elevation rule is stated two ways ('and' with a creatinine condition; 'or' without one), yet the troponin-positive group's mean creatinine was 2.17 mg/dL; peak troponin averages two different assays; hypertensive urgency was taken from charts without pre-treatment pressures; assessors not blinded.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Three versions of the main comparison; subgroup sizes in the text (5 and 16) conflict with Table 2 (12 and 10); deaths, arrhythmias and strokes not reported by group despite a safety objective; no protocol.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because β-blockers are an intervention compared without randomization (METHODS §5.3). The comparison is at critical risk of bias: wholly unadjusted despite large differences in cardiac disease between groups, with the timing of β-blockers relative to the troponin rise unknown and group counts that cannot be reconciled across abstract, text and tables. Citable for: a description of 378 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain at two Houston hospitals in 1998–2011 (43% given a β-blocker during admission, mostly metoprolol, labetalol or carvedilol; troponin rise in 11%; 18 in-hospital deaths overall) and for the authors' conclusions as claims. Not citable for: β-blockers being safe, or β1-selective agents being no worse than combined α1/β agents.

key_findings.finding: 378 patients: Black 78% (296), White 12% (44), other 10% (38); typical chest pain 12% (46); coronary disease 22% (84), hypertension 56% (213), diabetes 21% (79); admission ECG changes (ST elevation or depression, T-wave inversion) in 43% (163).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 613); Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph and Table 1 (p. 614)
key_findings.note: The ECG figure appears only in the abstract.

key_findings.finding: 162 patients (43%) received at least one β-blocker during admission: metoprolol 88 (53%), labetalol 45 (27.2%), carvedilol 44 (26.6%), atenolol 4 (2%).
key_findings.note: The drug counts sum to 181, so some patients received more than one; the percentages correspond to a denominator of 165 (88 of 165 is 53.3%), not 162; labetalol plus carvedilol give 89 exposures, fewer than the 91 patients of the α1/β group in Table 2 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: β-blocker vs no β-blocker: age 46.2 vs 42.3 years (P<.001); hypertension 79.0% vs 39.4%, coronary disease 33.3% vs 13.9%, diabetes 27.8% vs 15.7%, hyperlipidaemia 24.1% vs 11.6%; ejection fraction below 50% 37.7% vs 11.6%, left ventricular hypertrophy 22.8% vs 11.6%, wall-motion abnormality 20.4% vs 8.8%; HIV 9.3% vs 12.0%.

Troponin rise in 42 patients (11.1%): 22 of 162 (13.6%) with a β-blocker vs 20 of 216 (9.3%) without, P=.191 (Table 1); the abstract gives 22 of 162 vs 20 of 213 and the text 20 of 165 vs 22 of 213, with P=.2 in both. Editors' calculation from Table 1: risk ratio 1.47 (95% CI 0.83 to 2.59).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 613); Table 1 and Results › 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 614)

key_findings.finding: Mean peak troponin among patients with a rise: 6.7 ng/mL with vs 5.7 ng/mL without a β-blocker (P=.6); β1-selective (n=5) vs α1/β (n=16): 7.5 vs 4.1 ng/mL (P=0.4); no SDs or ranges given.
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives 12 troponin rises among 71 patients on β1-selective agents and 10 among 91 on α1/β agents, not 5 and 16.

key_findings.finding: No hypertensive urgency (systolic 180 mm Hg or more, or diastolic 110 mm Hg or more) was identified after any β-blocker; blood pressures before treatment are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2, 1st paragraph (starting p. 614; this sentence at its end on p. 615)

key_findings.finding: β1-selective (71) vs α1/β agents (91): similar age, sex and comorbidities; ejection fraction below 50% in 22.5% vs 49.4% (P<.001).

Patients with a troponin rise had higher creatinine (2.17 vs 1.32 mg/dL, P<.001), more diabetes (33.3% vs 19.6%, P=.046) and more ejection fraction below 50% (45.2% vs 19.3%, P<.001) than those without.

Disposition and outcomes for the whole cohort: one hundred seven (28%) admitted to intensive care, 251 (66.4%) to telemetry, 12 (3%) discharged from the emergency department; arrhythmias in 24 (6%), stroke in 13 (3%), 18 (5%) died in hospital. None of these is reported by β-blocker group.

The authors state that the timing of β-blocker administration relative to the troponin elevation was not determined, that historical data on the timing of cocaine exposure and on adherence to prescribed β-blockers are of uncertain accuracy, and that the hypertension prevalence of 56% could confound responses to β-blockers.

The authors describe the American Heart Association statement as contraindicating β-blockers in the acute setting while allowing them in the discharge regimen after careful risk–benefit assessment (graded IIIC), and cite criticism that the recommendations rested on 2 studies totalling 19 patients.

reporting_issues.issue: The main comparison is printed three ways: abstract 22 of 162 vs 20 of 213; text 20 of 165 vs 22 of 213; Table 1 22 of 162 (13.6%) vs 20 of 216 (9.3%). The abstract's groups sum to 375, the text's and Table 1's to 378; group sizes differ (162 or 165 treated; 213 or 216 untreated), and in the text the larger count is assigned to the untreated group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction and denominators of the primary comparison are uncertain; Table 1's version is the one pooled by Shin et al. (2019).

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the β1-selective vs α1/β comparison of peak troponin as n=5 vs n=16 (21 patients), while Table 2 gives 12 and 10 troponin rises (22, matching the 22 in Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The agent comparison cannot be relied on; with either set of numbers it rests on about 20 patients.

reporting_issues.issue: Drug exposures (metoprolol 88, labetalol 45, carvedilol 44, atenolol 4) and their percentages do not fit the 162 treated patients or the Table 2 split of 71 β1-selective and 91 α1/β patients. Editors' arithmetic: the exposures sum to 181, the percentages use a denominator of 165, and labetalol plus carvedilol give only 89 exposures for 91 α1/β patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: How patients receiving both kinds of agent were classified is unknown; the agent groups cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: Troponin elevation is defined as troponin I above 0.6 ng/mL and troponin T above 0.1 ng/mL if creatinine was below 2 mg/dL (abstract, methods) but as troponin I above 0.6 or troponin T above 0.1 in the table footnotes; the troponin-positive group's mean creatinine was 2.17 mg/dL, so patients with creatinine of 2 or more were included, and how their troponin was classified is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The outcome definition actually applied is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the age SD of the troponin-negative group (n=336) as 24.2, while Table 1 gives an SD of 10.1 for all 378. Editors' calculation: a subgroup of 336 with SD 24.2 would make the overall SD at least 22.8.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in Table 3; minor for the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Subgroup counts do not add up across tables: typical chest pain 25 in the β-blocker column of Table 1 but 15 + 11 in Table 2; asthma 13 vs 1 + 8; COPD 8 vs 3 + 6; Table 3 rows sum to 48 for typical pain (Table 1: 46), 80 for diabetes (79), 40 for HIV (41), 64 for left ventricular hypertrophy (62) and 84 for ejection fraction below 50% (86).
reporting_issues.consequence: The tables were not built from one consistent dataset or contain transcription errors; individual percentages should be quoted with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: Disposition counts (one hundred seven to intensive care, 251 to telemetry, 12 discharged) do not account for all 378 patients. Editors' arithmetic: they total 370.
reporting_issues.consequence: Eight patients' disposition is unaccounted for.

reporting_issues.issue: Passages of this paper match passages of Mohamad et al. (American Journal of Therapeutics, Detroit) word for word: the description of the urine assay and of the troponin I assay with the same range of 0.02–22.78 ng/mL, the inclusion-criteria wording, the chart-review sentence, the opening of the Discussion and most of the limitations paragraph. Mohamad et al. are not cited, and the author lists do not overlap. Editors' comparison of the two PDFs' text: 15 shared runs of 8 to 37 identical words, about 235 words outside the reference lists.
reporting_issues.consequence: There is no sign that the data overlap (different city, period and sample size), so the two studies are not double counts; but methods text reproduced from another study cannot be taken as a study-specific description of the Houston laboratories, and uncited text reuse is a publication-integrity question for the senior author, not a judgment of misconduct.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods compare patients treated with any β-blocker during admission with those not treated (p. 614), but Results 3.2 splits the 42 patients with a troponin rise into 22 treated with β-blockers and 20 not treated in the first 12 hours (p. 614), a window the Methods do not define.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure window behind the main comparison (22 vs 20 troponin rises; Table 1's 22 of 162 vs 20 of 216, pooled by Shin et al. and Pham et al. as β-blockers during admission) is unclear.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled physiological challenge study in a cardiac catheterization laboratory of an urban teaching hospital (University of Texas Southwestern / Parkland Memorial Hospital). 30 clinically stable patients undergoing catheterization to evaluate chest pain were randomized to intranasal saline (group 1, n = 15) or intranasal cocaine hydrochloride 2 mg/kg as a 10% solution (group 2, n = 15). Fifteen minutes later, 5 of the group 1 patients and all 15 group 2 patients received a 5-minute intracoronary infusion: propranolol 0.4 mg/min (total 2 mg) after saline (group 1A, n = 5) or after cocaine (group 2B, n = 10), or intracoronary saline after cocaine (group 2A, n = 5). The coronary sinus catheter paced the heart to hold heart rate constant so that neither investigator nor patient could tell which agent was infused. Outcomes at each step: heart rate, systolic and mean arterial pressure, rate-pressure product, coronary sinus blood flow by thermodilution, arterial-coronary sinus oxygen content difference, and quantitative arteriographic diameters of the proximal, mid and distal left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries. No patient had previously used cocaine; the comparison is therefore a drug challenge in cocaine-naive cardiac patients, not a trial of treatment in people presenting after cocaine use.
can_establish: That in 10 cocaine-naive patients under catheterization, 2 mg of intracoronary propranolol given 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg was followed by a further fall in coronary sinus blood flow and a further rise in coronary vascular resistance, while a matched intracoronary saline infusion after cocaine (n = 5) and propranolol after intranasal saline (n = 5) were not; and that intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised arterial pressure and reduced coronary flow and epicardial diameters in 15 such patients.
cannot_establish: Whether systemically administered beta-blockers (intravenous or oral, the forms used in hospitals) harm people who present with cocaine-associated chest pain: the drug here went directly into the coronary artery at 2 mg in patients with stable symptoms under investigation for chest pain, without acute ischemia and with no history of cocaine use. Nor can it establish any clinical outcome (infarction, arrhythmia, death), the effect of cocaine doses or routes other than 2 mg/kg intranasally, the effect in people who use cocaine regularly (none had used it before), or that the potentiation is statistically reliable against the post-cocaine state, since the randomized between-arm comparison (group 2A versus 2B) was never tested and the within-person resistance change from the post-cocaine value had P = 0.074.

sample.recruitment: Clinically stable patients referred for cardiac catheterization to evaluate chest pain at an urban teaching hospital. 34 consecutive patients with stable symptoms and no exclusion criterion were eligible; 3 declined and 1 was excluded when initial angiography showed severe left main coronary artery disease, leaving 30 (p. 898).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: stable symptoms, undergoing catheterization for chest pain. Excluded: hypertension, recent myocardial infarction, history of pseudocholinesterase deficiency, and (after angiography) severe left main disease. Anti-anginal drugs, including beta-blocking agents, calcium antagonists and long-acting nitrates, were stopped more than 12 hours before the study; patients were studied fasting after 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam (p. 898).
sample.demographics: 30 patients, 25 men and 5 women, aged 38 to 68 years. Group 1: 11 men and 4 women, 43 to 65 years. Group 2: 14 men and 1 woman, 38 to 68 years. Coronary anatomy of the whole sample: 7 angiographically normal, 11 one-vessel, 9 two-vessel and 3 three-vessel disease (70% or greater luminal narrowing of a large epicardial artery). No patient had a history of previous cocaine use (pp. 898-899).
sample.attrition: None reported after randomization; all 30 appear in the tables. Four of the 34 eligible patients did not enter the study (3 declined, 1 excluded on angiography) (p. 898).
sample.selection_effects: Older cardiac patients (mostly men) with chest pain under investigation, 23 of the 30 with one- to three-vessel obstructive coronary disease and none with any cocaine experience, given a single controlled intranasal dose in a catheterization laboratory. This is the opposite of the population the finding is used about: people who use cocaine, often repeatedly and at much larger amounts, who arrive at an emergency department with chest pain. The authors themselves note that reported cocaine-associated infarctions follow amounts often above 1000 mg, far more than the 110 to 210 mg given here (p. 902). Patients were also pretreated with diazepam and had their own anti-anginal drugs withdrawn, and the 5:10 split of group 2 between intracoronary saline and propranolol is not explained.

exposure.measurement: Both drugs were given in the laboratory. Serum cocaine was measured by gas chromatography 15 minutes after dosing. Propranolol was infused into the left coronary artery, so no systemic concentration applies (p. 898).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Single intranasal dose of 10% cocaine hydrochloride solution, 2 mg/kg body weight (110 to 210 mg across patients), described by the authors as one half to two thirds the amount routinely used for topical rhinolaryngologic anesthesia and chosen because of its proven safety; the resulting serum concentration was 0.097 +/- 0.051 mg/L (range 0.02 to 0.22 mg/L). Intracoronary propranolol 0.4 mg/min over 5 minutes (total 2 mg) or an equal-duration intracoronary saline infusion, begun 15 minutes after the intranasal dose (pp. 898-899).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients received 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam as premedication before the study, and iodinated contrast for angiography; anti-anginal medication (beta-blockers, calcium antagonists, long-acting nitrates) was withdrawn more than 12 hours earlier. Other drug or alcohol use by the patients is not reported, and no toxicology screening is described (p. 898).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: no patient had used cocaine before the study (p. 898).

comparison.controls: Three comparisons are available. (1) Randomized, between-person: intranasal saline (n = 15) against intranasal cocaine (n = 15), for the effect of cocaine. (2) Randomized, between-person within group 2: intracoronary saline (n = 5) against intracoronary propranolol (n = 10) after cocaine. (3) Non-randomized, within-person: each group 2B patient's values after propranolol against the same patient's values after cocaine and at baseline, which is the comparison the paper's conclusion rests on.
comparison.matching: Randomization only; no matching, and no baseline comparison between groups 2A and 2B is reported or tested. Their printed baselines differ (coronary sinus blood flow 126 +/- 25 mL/min in group 2A against 139 +/- 28 in group 2B; Tables 3A and 3B, pp. 900-901). Heart rate was held constant by coronary sinus pacing during the infusions, which removes rate as a confounder of the flow change but also removes the main visible sign of beta-blockade.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (no prior cocaine exposure). Unmeasured are each patient's coronary reactivity before the drug, their endothelial function, and whether the angiographic disease pattern was balanced between groups 2A and 2B; the sample's own disease counts are internally inconsistent (see reporting issues).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Control patients received the same premedication and contrast, and intranasal saline in place of cocaine; 5 of them also received intracoronary propranolol, which is the arm that shows propranolol alone did not reduce coronary flow (Table 2, p. 899).

outcomes.instruments: Coronary sinus blood flow by continuous thermodilution through a pacing thermodilution catheter placed via a basilic vein; systemic arterial pressure through the femoral arterial sheath side-port; heart rate by electrocardiographic monitoring; arterial and coronary sinus blood sampled for oxygen content; cineangiography of the left coronary artery in two orthogonal right anterior oblique projections, measured by computer-assisted quantitative coronary analysis (Cardiovascular Angiography Analysis System) at an image resolution of 3.8 line pairs/mm; coronary vascular resistance derived as mean arterial pressure divided by coronary sinus blood flow (pp. 898-899).
outcomes.validity_norms: Thermodilution gives total left coronary flow, not regional myocardial perfusion, as the authors state among their limitations (p. 901). Quantitative arteriography of six named segments is the standard method of the period; the authors report that all analyses were done without knowledge of which agent had been given (p. 898).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Potentiation' is operationalized as a further fall in coronary sinus blood flow and a further rise in coronary vascular resistance after intracoronary propranolol relative to the post-cocaine measurement, plus constriction greater than 10% in one or more epicardial segments. No ischemic clinical endpoint was prespecified; the one ischemic event is reported descriptively.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 counts the variables in each table (7 hemodynamic and metabolic measures and 6 arterial segments); each is tested at two or three time points in four groups, so well over a hundred paired tests are printed across Tables 1, 2, 3A and 3B, all at an uncorrected threshold of P < 0.05 (p. 898).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Stated: all hemodynamic and arteriographic analyses were done without knowledge of which agent (intranasal saline or cocaine, intracoronary saline or propranolol) had been given; patients and investigators were also blinded during administration, with pacing used to conceal the heart-rate effect of propranolol (pp. 898-899).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means +/- SE with 95% confidence intervals for mean change, paired t-tests, P < 0.05 as significant; no adjustment, no model, no effect sizes in standardized units (p. 898). Cocaine against saline (Table 1, p. 898): with intranasal cocaine, systolic pressure +11 mm Hg (5 to 16), mean pressure +9 (4 to 13), rate-pressure product +0.9 x 10^3 (0.4 to 1.4), coronary sinus blood flow -17 mL/min (-29 to -5), coronary vascular resistance +0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24), transcardiac oxygen content difference +0.6 mL/dL (0.1 to 1.0); with saline, every change was within 1 unit of zero and no P value was below 0.27. Epicardial diameters after cocaine fell by 0.10 to 0.25 mm across the six segments, significant in four (P from 0.001 to 0.026) and not in the mid (P = 0.13) and distal (P = 0.087) circumflex. Editors' calculation from the Table 1 group 2 baselines and mean changes: the falls are 5.6% (proximal left anterior descending), 8.9% (mid), 10.2% (distal), 9.0% (proximal circumflex), 7.1% (mid) and 6.5% (distal). Propranolol after cocaine (group 2B, n = 10; Table 3B, p. 901, and text p. 899): coronary sinus blood flow 139 +/- 28 mL/min at baseline, 120 +/- 20 after cocaine and 100 +/- 14 after propranolol, a further fall of 15% +/- 18% (22% +/- 20% from baseline), mean change from the post-cocaine value -20 mL/min (-42 to -1), P = 0.050, and from baseline -40 (-77 to -2), P = 0.040; coronary vascular resistance 0.87 +/- 0.10, 1.05 +/- 0.10 and 1.20 +/- 0.12 mm Hg/mL per min, a further rise of 19% +/- 28% (46% +/- 44% from baseline), mean change from the post-cocaine value +0.16 (-0.02 to 0.33), P = 0.074, and from baseline +0.33 (0.12 to 0.53), P = 0.005. Saline after cocaine (group 2A, n = 5; Table 3A, p. 900): flow 0 mL/min (-8 to 8), P = 0.95, and resistance -0.08 (-0.18 to 0.03), P = 0.11, against the post-cocaine value. Propranolol after intranasal saline (group 1A, n = 5; Table 2, p. 899): flow -2 mL/min (-6 to 2), P = 0.19, and resistance +0.01 (-0.07 to 0.09), P = 0.66.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for coronary disease severity, sex, age or baseline flow, and no test of whether groups 2A and 2B were comparable at baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or prespecified primary outcome is mentioned; the study predates trial registration. Approved by the Human Subjects Review Committee of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, with written informed consent after disclosure of possible adverse effects (p. 898).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four groups and all measured variables appear in the tables, which is unusually complete. The selectivity is in the summary rather than the data: the abstract gives the group 2B subgroup's values as the cocaine effect, states P < 0.05 for variables that Table 1 shows above 0.05, and states P < 0.05 for both propranolol effects when Table 3B gives P = 0.074 for the resistance change from the post-cocaine value (see reporting issues). The randomized comparison between groups 2A and 2B, the one comparison protected by randomization, is never tested.
analysis.power: The authors name low statistical power among their limitations, attributing it to the small number of patients (p. 902). The decisive comparison rests on 10 patients, with 5 as the saline control; the standard deviations around the percentage changes (18% and 28%) are larger than the changes themselves (15% and 19%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In cocaine-naive patients undergoing catheterization, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised blood pressure and rate-pressure product, reduced coronary sinus blood flow and narrowed epicardial segments, while intranasal saline changed nothing. In the 10 patients who then received 2 mg of propranolol into the coronary artery, flow fell further and resistance rose further relative to both the post-cocaine value and baseline, though the resistance change from the post-cocaine value had P = 0.074; in 5 patients given intracoronary saline instead, nothing changed further, and in 5 patients given propranolol after intranasal saline, nothing changed at all. Five of the 10 propranolol patients had an epicardial segment constrict by more than 10%, and one had a complete coronary occlusion with ischemic symptoms and ST elevation that resolved with sublingual nitroglycerin and left no rise in creatine kinase.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction is potentiated by beta-adrenergic blockade and that beta-adrenergic blocking agents probably should be avoided in patients with cocaine-associated myocardial ischemia or infarction (p. 897); the closing paragraph repeats this for the patient with cocaine-induced chest pain and adds that nitrates or calcium antagonists may help, while noting they are not proved beneficial (p. 902). The distance between result and recommendation is large in three steps. First, route and setting: 2 mg of propranolol delivered directly into the left coronary artery of a cocaine-naive patient under catheterization is not the intravenous or oral beta-blocker a hospital gives, and the authors acknowledge they did not test other routes (p. 902). Second, outcome: the measured endpoints are flow, resistance and lumen diameter, not infarction, arrhythmia or death; the discussion's step from these to the magnitude of ischemia is reasoning, not measurement. Third, statistical support: the abstract's 'P < 0.05 for both' is not what Table 3B prints for the change from the post-cocaine state. The authors are otherwise careful, listing four limitations, reporting the one serious adverse event in full, and marking their statements about larger amounts of cocaine as unproven.

timeline.event: This study: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary flow in 10 cocaine-naive catheterization patients

The same group gave intravenous labetalol (a combined alpha- and beta-blocker) after the same intranasal cocaine dose to 15 catheterization patients (7 men and 8 women): labetalol lowered mean arterial pressure but left the cocaine-induced coronary narrowing unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm2), neither relieving nor worsening it
American Heart Association scientific statement cites this study in recommending against beta-blockers in the acute setting of cocaine-associated chest pain
Registry comparison of hospitalized patients with cocaine-associated chest pain given or not given a beta-blocker: no difference in in-hospital outcomes
Meta-analysis of observational studies of beta-blocker use in cocaine-associated chest pain finds no increase in the pooled outcomes

Second meta-analysis of the hospital cohorts (eight, including the five pooled by Pham et al. 2018): no significant pooled difference in in-hospital or long-term death or infarction; no randomized trial by June 2018

replication.where_it_stands: The physiological finding has never been repeated in people who use cocaine, and no randomized trial of a systemic beta-blocker in cocaine-associated chest pain had been reported by June 2018 (Shin et al., 2019). What has accumulated since is observational hospital data that have not shown the harm this mechanism predicts but cannot exclude it (five cohorts, pooled in two overlapping meta-analyses: Pham et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019), and the same group's labetalol study, in which a combined blocker neither relieved nor worsened the cocaine-induced narrowing. The mechanism stands; its clinical translation is contested.

funding.funder: Ischemic SCOR grant HL 17669 from the National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, Maryland, and a grant from the Texas Affiliate of the American Heart Association, Austin, Texas (p. 902).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (the journal did not require one in 1990).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were in the Cardiology Division, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas. The same group produced the earlier study of cocaine-induced vasoconstriction and the later labetalol study, so the main line of human evidence on this question comes from one laboratory.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people presenting to hospital with cocaine-associated chest pain, comparing an intravenous beta-blocker with placebo or with an alternative such as a benzodiazepine or a nitrate, with infarction, arrhythmia, length of stay and death as outcomes and coronary flow or imaging in a subgroup. Short of that, a study giving an intravenous rather than intracoronary beta-blocker to people who actually use cocaine, at amounts they use, would close the route-and-population gap that separates this laboratory result from the bedside question.

domains.note: Patients were randomized twice (saline against cocaine, then intracoronary saline against propranolol within group 2) and the assignment was concealed from patient and investigator, with pacing used to hide propranolol's heart-rate effect. But the method of sequence generation and allocation concealment is not described, the unequal 5:10 split of group 2 is not explained, and no baseline comparison between groups 2A and 2B is reported, although their printed baseline flows differ by 13 mL/min.

Blinding appears to have held and no protocol deviations are reported. The concern is analytic rather than procedural: the conclusion is drawn from within-person before-after changes in group 2B rather than from the randomized contrast with group 2A, so the effect of time, of the preceding cocaine dose and of repeated instrumentation is not separated from the effect of propranolol by the randomization that was available.
All 30 randomized patients appear in the tables with no missing values reported; the one patient with coronary occlusion remained in the analysis.

Flow, pressure, oxygen content and lumen diameter are objective, and the analyses were done blind to the agent given. Thermodilution measures total rather than regional flow, which the authors state, but this does not bias the comparison between infusions.

No protocol or prespecified outcome; more than a hundred uncorrected paired tests across four groups. The abstract reports the 10-patient subgroup's values as the cocaine effect, attaches P < 0.05 to variables Table 1 shows at P = 0.13 and 0.087, and attaches P < 0.05 to both propranolol effects when Table 3B gives P = 0.074 for the resistance change from the post-cocaine value. The randomized between-arm comparison is never tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The physiology is carefully done and blinded, and the three-way control structure (saline then propranolol, cocaine then saline, cocaine then propranolol) is a genuine strength: it shows that neither propranolol alone nor the passage of time after cocaine reproduces the further fall in flow. The high rating comes from the selection of the reported result, which RoB 2 does not let the overall judgment fall below: the headline claim is stated with a certainty the tables do not carry, and the one randomized comparison that could have supported it was not analysed. The source can be cited for what intracoronary propranolol did to coronary flow, resistance and epicardial diameter in 10 cocaine-naive catheterization patients 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, for the absence of that change under intracoronary saline and under propranolol without cocaine, and for the single occlusion event. It cannot be cited for the effect of systemic beta-blockers on people who use cocaine, for any clinical outcome, or as evidence that beta-blockade is harmful at the bedside.

key_findings.finding: 30 patients undergoing catheterization for chest pain were randomized to intranasal saline (n = 15) or cocaine 2 mg/kg (n = 15); 25 were men, ages ran from 38 to 68 years, and no patient had a history of previous cocaine use.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Patients (p. 897); Materials and Methods > Experimental Protocol, 2nd paragraph, and Results, 1st paragraph (p. 898)

key_findings.finding: The intranasal dose was 110 to 210 mg of cocaine hydrochloride as a 10% solution, giving a serum concentration of 0.097 +/- 0.051 mg/L (range 0.02 to 0.22 mg/L) at 15 minutes; the authors describe it as one half to two thirds the amount routinely used for topical rhinolaryngologic anesthesia and chose it because of its proven safety.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Experimental Protocol, 2nd paragraph; Results > Propranolol-Treated Group (Group 2), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: After intranasal cocaine (n = 15), systolic pressure rose 11 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 16), mean pressure 9 (4 to 13), rate-pressure product 0.9 x 10^3 (0.4 to 1.4), coronary sinus blood flow fell 17 mL/min (-29 to -5) and coronary vascular resistance rose 0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24); after intranasal saline (n = 15) no variable changed (all P >= 0.27).
Epicardial diameters fell after cocaine in all six measured segments, by 0.10 to 0.25 mm, significantly in four (P 0.001 to 0.026) but not in the mid (P = 0.13) or distal (P = 0.087) left circumflex.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the same rows: the falls correspond to 5.6%, 8.9% and 10.2% in the proximal, mid and distal left anterior descending and 9.0%, 7.1% and 6.5% in the circumflex, a wider range than the 6% to 9% the abstract gives.

key_findings.finding: No patient developed chest pain or electrocardiographic signs of ischemia after cocaine alone.

In the 10 patients given intracoronary propranolol 2 mg after cocaine, coronary sinus blood flow was 139 +/- 28 mL/min at baseline, 120 +/- 20 after cocaine and 100 +/- 14 after propranolol, a further fall of 15% +/- 18% (22% +/- 20% from baseline), and coronary vascular resistance was 0.87 +/- 0.10, 1.05 +/- 0.10 and 1.20 +/- 0.12 mm Hg/mL per min, a further rise of 19% +/- 28% (46% +/- 44% from baseline), with no change in rate-pressure product or transcardiac oxygen content difference.
key_findings.locator: Results > Propranolol-Treated Group (Group 2), 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing into the right column)
key_findings.note: Values are mean +/- SE. The percentage changes have standard errors larger than the changes themselves.

key_findings.finding: In Table 3B the propranolol change from the post-cocaine value was -20 mL/min (-42 to -1) for flow, P = 0.050, and +0.16 mm Hg/mL per min (-0.02 to 0.33) for resistance, P = 0.074; the changes from baseline were -40 mL/min (-77 to -2), P = 0.040, and +0.33 (0.12 to 0.53), P = 0.005.
key_findings.locator: Table 3B, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows (first row of each pair is the change from the post-cocaine value, second from baseline)
key_findings.note: This is the comparison the paper's conclusion rests on; for resistance it does not reach the paper's own threshold of P < 0.05, and the flow change, printed as P = 0.050, does not meet it either (Data Analysis, p. 898: P less than 0.05 significant).

key_findings.finding: In the 5 patients given intracoronary saline after cocaine, nothing changed further: flow 0 mL/min (-8 to 8), P = 0.95, and resistance -0.08 (-0.18 to 0.03), P = 0.11, against the post-cocaine value, while resistance remained raised against baseline (+0.13, 0.03 to 0.23, P = 0.021).
key_findings.locator: Table 3A, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows

key_findings.finding: In the 5 patients given intracoronary propranolol after intranasal saline, no hemodynamic or arteriographic variable changed: flow -2 mL/min (-6 to 2), P = 0.19, and resistance +0.01 (-0.07 to 0.09), P = 0.66.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows
key_findings.note: This arm is what separates an effect of propranolol on the cocaine-exposed coronary circulation from an effect of propranolol in general.

key_findings.finding: In 5 of the 10 patients given propranolol after cocaine (4 with and 1 without coronary artery disease), one or more epicardial segments constricted by more than 10%; in one patient a coronary artery occluded completely, with ischemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation, resolving after sublingual nitroglycerin with no rise in serum creatine kinase.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 902) shows the arteriograms of this patient; its legend states the lumen was reduced diffusely by 12% after cocaine, with the circumflex occluded after propranolol.

key_findings.finding: The authors list four limitations: thermodilution measures total rather than regional myocardial flow; only one cocaine dose and route was tested; only the intracoronary route of propranolol was tested; and the small number of patients gives low statistical power.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, limitations paragraph (begins p. 901, right column; continues p. 902, left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that beta-adrenergic blockade potentiates the fall in coronary blood flow caused by cocaine and that beta-blockade probably should be avoided in the patient with cocaine-induced chest pain, adding that nitrates or calcium antagonists may help although this is not yet proved.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, summary paragraph (continuing into the right column)
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' recommendation about hospital care, not as a finding of the study; the study measured coronary flow, resistance and lumen diameter, not clinical outcomes.

key_findings.finding: After intracoronary propranolol (n = 10), none of the six measured segment diameters changed significantly from the post-cocaine value (Table 3B, first row of each segment: P 0.19 to 1.00).
key_findings.note: The arteriographic potentiation rests on individual patients (5 of 10 with a segment narrowing more than 10%, one occlusion), not on a change in the group means.

key_findings.finding: The authors report that coronary sinus flow fell and coronary vascular resistance rose after propranolol in all 10 patients given it after cocaine, while the large epicardial arteries responded very differently between patients: constriction profoundly worsened in 1, augmented in 4 and little affected in 5.

The authors state that they cannot exclude that the small intracoronary dose (2 mg, given during coronary sinus pacing) lowered coronary sinus flow by reducing myocardial contractility; they argue against it from the absence of a flow fall with propranolol after intranasal saline (group 1A, Table 2) and from the epicardial constriction seen in some patients.
key_findings.note: Coronary vascular resistance is computed as mean arterial pressure divided by coronary sinus flow, so a fall in flow from lower demand would also appear as a rise in resistance.

reporting_issues.issue: The coronary anatomy counts for group 2 do not sum to its size: of the 30 patients, 3 of the 7 with normal arteries, 6 of the 11 with one-vessel disease, 5 of the 9 with two-vessel disease and all 3 with three-vessel disease are said to be in group 2, which totals 17 in a group of 15.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least two of the four subtotals are wrong, so the disease burden of the cocaine group, and its comparability with the saline group, cannot be established from the paper. This matters for reading the arteriographic results, since segment responses differed between patients with and without coronary disease.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cocaine effect as coronary sinus blood flow falling from 139 +/- 28 to 120 +/- 20 mL/min and resistance rising from 0.87 +/- 0.10 to 1.05 +/- 0.10; these are the values of the 10-patient subgroup that later received propranolol, not of the 15 patients who received cocaine, whose values in the Results and Table 1 are 135 +/- 20 to 118 +/- 15 mL/min and 0.87 +/- 0.07 to 1.06 +/- 0.08.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract's numbers as the cocaine effect is quoting a subgroup of 10. The direction and approximate size are the same, so no conclusion changes, but the n behind the figures does.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states P < 0.05 for all the variables it lists as changed by cocaine, including coronary arterial diameters; Table 1 gives P = 0.13 for the mid and P = 0.087 for the distal circumflex. The abstract also gives the diameter fall as between 6% and 9%, while the Table 1 values correspond to 5.6% to 10.2% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract presents the epicardial constriction as uniform and uniformly significant when two of six segments were neither. Claims about cocaine narrowing epicardial arteries should cite Table 1 segment by segment, not the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that propranolol further decreased coronary sinus blood flow and increased coronary vascular resistance with P < 0.05 for both; Table 3B gives P = 0.050 for the flow change and P = 0.074 for the resistance change measured from the post-cocaine value. Only the comparisons with baseline, which also contain the cocaine effect itself, reach P < 0.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's central claim of potentiation is weaker in the table than in the abstract. Any claim that beta-blockade worsened cocaine-induced vasoconstriction should state which comparison it uses, and that the resistance change against the post-cocaine state did not reach the paper's own threshold in 10 patients.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the distal left anterior descending row after intranasal saline reads -0.07 (0.41 to 0.28): the lower limit has lost its minus sign, so the printed interval runs backwards and does not contain its own point estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error in a control-arm row; the intended interval is almost certainly -0.41 to 0.28. It does not affect any conclusion but shows the tables were not fully proofed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3B the first propranolol row for the rate-pressure product reads -0.5 (-1.2 to 2.7). Every other interval in that table is centred on its point estimate; this one is centred on 0.75.
reporting_issues.consequence: One limit is likely mistyped. The variable is one the authors use to argue that myocardial oxygen demand did not change, so the imprecision falls on a supporting rather than a primary claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The group that received intracoronary propranolol after intranasal saline is called group 1A in the Methods and Results and group 1B in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the argument that propranolol alone does not reduce coronary flow has to infer that group 1B means the group 1A of Table 2; no group 1B is defined anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: The randomized comparison between the patients given intracoronary saline after cocaine (n = 5) and those given propranolol after cocaine (n = 10) is never tested; every printed P value for the propranolol effect comes from within-person paired t-tests.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one contrast whose comparability randomization guaranteed is not reported, so the estimate of potentiation carries the risk of a before-after design (time after cocaine, repeated instrumentation) that the design had the means to avoid.

design_detail: Single-centre retrospective chart review (Detroit Receiving Hospital emergency department), January 2004 to June 2005: 364 adults with chest pain, cocaine use in the preceding 24 h and a cocaine-positive urine test; troponin I measured in the emergency department in 245. Two unadjusted comparisons: patients recorded as taking a β-blocker at home at presentation (100) vs not, for troponin elevation; and patients whose β-blocker was continued in hospital (39; the comparison is reported as continued or started, without group sizes) vs other admitted patients, for a later troponin rise. χ2 and t tests.
can_establish: The crude proportion of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and a detectable troponin at one Detroit emergency department in 2004–2005, their characteristics, and crude troponin rates by recorded home β-blocker use.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers taken before or during admission raise the risk of myocardial injury after cocaine use: the comparisons are unadjusted although home β-blocker use goes with coronary disease (history of coronary disease in 52% of troponin-positive vs 5% of troponin-negative patients), the agents and timing are not reported, and the printed statistics are internally inconsistent.

sample.recruitment: Clinic (hospital records): patients presenting with chest pain to the Detroit Receiving Hospital emergency department, January 2004 to June 2005, by comprehensive chart review (pp. 531–532). How the records were identified is not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age over 18; cocaine use in the preceding 24 h; positive urine drug screen for cocaine metabolites (p. 532). No exclusions stated.
sample.demographics: Mean age 46.8 (SD 8.2); African American 90.6%; men 73.4% (text) or 73.3% (Table 1); tobacco 90.3%, alcohol 77.7%, injecting drug use 26.4%; history of coronary disease 8.24%, hypertension 54.1% (Table 1, p. 533). Cocaine route: smoking 78%, intranasal 10%, intravenous 12% (p. 532).
sample.attrition: Troponin measured in 245 of 364 (67%); the β-blocker comparisons appear to use all patients, tested or not, as denominators (14 of 100 on home β-blockers). 114 (31%) admitted; 40 catheterized.
sample.selection_effects: One inner-city emergency department; troponin testing and admission were decided by the emergency physicians, and the authors state that symptoms such as nausea, vomiting and dyspnoea probably prompted admission (pp. 532, 534).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine: urine benzoylecgonine by EMIT II Plus immunoassay on admission (cut-off not stated) plus reported use within 24 h (p. 532). Home β-blocker: from self-report or medical records (p. 532); the authors say adherence to home β-blockers is difficult to ascertain (p. 534). In-hospital β-blocker: described both as continued (39 patients) and as continued or started, from chart review (p. 532).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cocaine route as above; amount and frequency not reported. β-blocker agents, doses and timing are not reported for either comparison.
exposure.polysubstance: Urine also positive for opiates in 26.4% and for cannabis in 38.2%; tobacco 90.3%, alcohol 77.7% (pp. 532–533); not adjusted for and not reported by β-blocker group.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Patients not taking a β-blocker at home (number not stated; 264 by subtraction); for the in-hospital comparison, admitted patients in whom a β-blocker was not continued or started (number not stated).
comparison.matching: None; χ2 and t tests only (p. 532).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Coronary disease and hypertension, the usual reasons for a home β-blocker, were recorded but not used to adjust the β-blocker comparisons; the indication and timing of in-hospital β-blockers were not recorded.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Recorded for the whole cohort only (urine opiates and cannabis), not by β-blocker group.

outcomes.instruments: Troponin I (Abbott AxSYM, cut-off 0.02 ng/mL, range 0.02–22.78); acute infarction or myonecrosis defined as troponin I above 0.02 ng/mL with chest pain; in-hospital progression defined as a subsequent cardiac enzyme rise (threshold and timing not stated); ECGs with Minnesota coding; catheterization findings (p. 532).
outcomes.validity_norms: The threshold is the manufacturer's cut-off, so any detectable troponin counted; no ECG criterion.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm: any detectable troponin at presentation (home β-blocker comparison) or a later enzyme rise in hospital (in-hospital comparison).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Troponin positive in 27 patients, reported as 7.3% of the 364. Home β-blocker: 14% of 100 vs 4.4% of patients not on β-blockers, χ2 6.9, P<0.01; the 14 were 51% of all troponin-positive patients. β-blocker continued in hospital: 9 of 39 progressed to infarction; continuation or start of a β-blocker on admission 23.3% vs 10.7%, χ2 5.6, P<0.01 (p. 532). Editors' calculations: 27 of the 245 tested is 11.0%; 13 troponin-positive patients among the 264 not on home β-blockers is 4.9%, crude risk ratio 2.84 (95% CI 1.39 to 5.83); a χ2 of 5.6 with 1 df corresponds to P≈0.018; 9 of 39 is 23.1%.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: Neither comparison group's size is given; the in-hospital group is described as continued (39) and as continued or started; P values in Table 1 are shown for some rows only (none for coronary disease, 15.8% vs 4.8%); the statement that infarction was unrelated to the amount, route or frequency of cocaine use is made without data (p. 534).
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors say the number of infarctions was small and lacked power for firm recommendations (p. 534).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Unadjusted, troponin was detectable more often in patients recorded as taking a β-blocker at home (14 of 100) than in those not (about 5%), and a later troponin rise was reported in 9 of 39 patients whose β-blocker was continued in hospital and in 23.3% vs 10.7% of patients with a β-blocker continued or started vs not (denominators not given). A history of coronary disease, the usual indication for a home β-blocker, was present in 52% of troponin-positive and 5% of troponin-negative patients.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The stated aim was to study the "causal and detrimental effects" of β-blockers (p. 531). The abstract says the findings seem to suggest that initiating or continuing β-blockers after admission increased the likelihood of myonecrosis, that pre-existing use "seems to render a higher risk" of myocardial injury, and that initiation or continuation during hospitalization should be discouraged (p. 531); the conclusion repeats this (p. 535). The limitations acknowledge unquantified baseline and treatment differences and lack of power for firm recommendations (p. 534). Causal language and a treatment recommendation rest on two unadjusted comparisons confounded by coronary disease, with unreported denominators and inconsistent statistics.

timeline.event: Lange et al.: described by Mohamad et al. as the single study behind most data on β-blockers in cocaine-related chest pain, in 30 volunteers undergoing catheterization given intranasal cocaine or saline (randomized, blinded) followed by intracoronary propranolol, which further increased coronary vascular resistance (pp. 533–534)
Boehrer et al.: cited by Mohamad et al. for labetalol reversing the cocaine-induced rise in arterial pressure without relieving coronary vasoconstriction (p. 534)
Dattilo et al. (Bronx): fewer infarctions after in-hospital β-blockers, the opposite direction, in a comparison biased towards β-blockers by how infarctions were timed
Rangel et al. (San Francisco): no difference in in-hospital troponin or events by emergency-department β-blocker, unadjusted

Ibrahim et al. (Houston): no clear difference in troponin rise (22 of 162 vs 20 of 216), unadjusted; their paper reproduces passages of this paper's methods, discussion and limitations word for word without citing it

Shin et al. meta-analysis entered this study's home β-blocker comparison as 14 of 100 vs 13 of 254 (RR 2.74, 1.33 to 5.61), with timing 'on presentation', in a pool defined as β-blockers during admission or at discharge

Pham et al. meta-analysis entered this study's home beta-blocker comparison as 14 of 100 vs 13 of 264 (odds ratio 3.14, 1.42 to 6.95), the only significant increase in its infarction analysis, which its text attributes to Dattilo et al.

replication.where_it_stands: The only study in the pooled in-hospital infarction analyses of Shin et al. (2019) and Pham et al. (2018) with a result significantly against β-blockers; its comparison concerns β-blockers taken before admission, which that review's own inclusion criterion (β-blockers during admission or at discharge) does not cover, and it supplies much of the pool's heterogeneity (editors' re-analysis on the Shin card). The other record studies found fewer infarctions (Dattilo et al., 2008) or no clear difference (Rangel et al., 2010; Ibrahim et al., 2013). No randomized trial existed as of 2018 (Shin et al., 2019, p. 45).

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflicts of interest: None (p. 531).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Cardiology, Wayne State University, Detroit; correspondence via the Division of Cardiology, Harper University Hospital (p. 531); study approved by the Wayne State institutional review board (p. 532).

what_would_settle_it: For pre-existing β-blocker use: a cohort that records indication, agent and adherence and compares troponin outcomes after adjustment for coronary disease and hypertension; for β-blockers started or continued in hospital: a randomized comparison with time zero at randomization and serial troponin measured at fixed times by one assay, adjudicated blind to treatment.

domains.note: No adjustment. Home β-blocker use marks established cardiovascular disease; history of coronary disease was 51.9% among troponin-positive vs 5.1% among troponin-negative patients (Table 2), and in-hospital β-blockers were presumably given for clinical reasons that are not recorded.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Troponin was measured in only 245 of 364, selected by clinical suspicion; the in-hospital comparison is restricted to admitted patients, whose admission depended on symptoms; case identification not described.

Home β-blocker use from self-report or records, with adherence unknown (p. 534); the in-hospital group is described as continued (39) and as continued or started; agents, doses and timing not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions and β-blocker regimens not reported.
119 of 364 (33%) had no troponin in the emergency department, yet the home β-blocker comparison appears to use all patients as denominators, counting untested patients as without injury.

Any troponin above the assay's 0.02 ng/mL cut-off counted as infarction or myonecrosis; for in-hospital progression the threshold and timing of the subsequent enzyme rise are not stated; chart review not blinded.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; two unadjusted comparisons with unreported comparison groups and inconsistent statistics (9 of 39 continued, then 23.3% vs 10.7% for continued or started with no denominators; χ2 5.6 reported as P<0.01); P values shown selectively in Table 1.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because β-blockers are an intervention compared without randomization (METHODS §5.3). Both comparisons are at critical risk of bias: they are unadjusted, the exposure (home β-blockers) is a marker of the coronary disease that also predicts troponin elevation, a third of patients had no troponin measured, and the printed statistics cannot be reproduced. Citable for: a description of 364 patients with cocaine-associated chest pain at one Detroit emergency department in 2004–2005 (smoked cocaine in 78%, urine opiates in 26.4%, admission in 31%, troponin above 0.02 ng/mL in 27 of 245 tested, no cardiac deaths) and for the authors' conclusions as claims. Not citable for: β-blockers, taken before or during admission, raising the risk of myocardial injury, or for any treatment recommendation.

key_findings.finding: 364 patients with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine test: mean age 46.8 (SD 8.2), African American 90.6%, men 73.4%; urine also positive for opiates in 26.4% and cannabis in 38.2%; cocaine smoked by 78%, taken intranasally by 10% and intravenously by 12%; 114 (31%) admitted.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographic and clinical characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Troponin I was measured in the emergency department in 245 patients; 27 had troponin above 0.02 ng/mL with chest pain, reported as 7.3% of the whole sample; they were older than those with normal troponin (50.3 vs 47.1 years, P<0.05).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results › Demographic and clinical characteristics, 1st paragraph; Results › AMI/MN and CAD, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 27 of 364 is 7.4%, and 27 of the 245 tested is 11.0%.

key_findings.finding: Troponin-positive (27) vs troponin-negative (218) patients: history of coronary disease 51.9% vs 5.1%, injecting drug use 48.1% vs 31.7%, insulin-treated diabetes 15% vs 5.0%, creatinine 2.0 vs 1.3 (P=0.02) and blood urea nitrogen 29 vs 15 (P<0.01), units not stated. The authors state that chest-pain type and details did not differ, without tests, although Table 2 shows sharp pain in 11.1% vs 41.1%.

100 patients were taking a β-blocker at home at presentation (from self-report or records); 14% of them had troponin elevation, forming 51% of all troponin-positive cases, vs 4.4% of patients not on β-blockers (χ2 6.9, P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods and Results (p. 531); Results › Influence of β-blockade, 1st paragraph (p. 532)
key_findings.note: The comparison group's size is not given; 13 troponin-positive patients among the 264 not on home β-blockers would be 4.9% (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: 9 of the 39 patients whose β-blocker was continued in hospital progressed to infarction by a subsequent enzyme rise; continuation or start of a β-blocker on admission was reported as 23.3% vs 10.7% (χ2 5.6, P<0.01). Agents, doses, timing and the comparison group's size are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods and Results (p. 531); Results › Influence of β-blockade, 1st paragraph (p. 532)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 9 of 39 is 23.1%, and a χ2 of 5.6 with 1 df corresponds to P≈0.018, not P<0.01.

key_findings.finding: Of the 364 initial ECGs, 84 (23%) were normal and 27 (7%) showed early repolarization; 9 showed ST elevation or hyperacute T waves; left ventricular hypertrophy 16.2%, ST depression of 1 mm or more 4.1%, T-wave inversion 10.7%; QTc prolonged in nearly 50%.
40 patients were catheterized during the admission; one-, two- and three-vessel disease (stenosis over 50%) were reported in 18.5%, 16% and 4%, and normal coronary arteries in 62%.
key_findings.note: These percentages cannot be whole numbers of 40 patients (18.5% of 40 is 7.4) and sum to 100.5% (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: No patient died from acute infarction or cardiac complications.

The authors describe most data on β-blockers in cocaine-related chest pain as coming from a single catheterization study of 30 volunteers given intranasal cocaine or saline followed by intracoronary propranolol, and cite ACC/AHA guidelines as supporting β-blockers (class IIa) for cocaine-associated chest pain with hypertension or sinus tachycardia.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (starting p. 533, the 30 volunteers on p. 534) and 5th paragraph (p. 534)

reporting_issues.issue: The proportion with myocardial injury (7.3%) is given over all 364 patients although troponin was measured in only 245. Editors' arithmetic: 27 of 364 is 7.4%, and 27 of 245 is 11.0%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rate among patients actually tested is understated by about a third, and untested patients appear in the β-blocker denominators as uninjured.

reporting_issues.issue: Neither β-blocker comparison gives the comparison group's size or count: 4.4% in patients not on home β-blockers and 10.7% in admitted patients without continued or started β-blockers. Editors' arithmetic: 13 of 264 is 4.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparisons cannot be reconstructed; meta-analysts have had to infer the denominators (Shin et al., 2019, used 254).

reporting_issues.issue: The in-hospital comparison gives 9 of 39 patients with a continued β-blocker progressing to infarction, then 23.3% vs 10.7% for continuation or starting of β-blockers with neither denominator given, and reports χ2 5.6 as P<0.01. Editors' calculation: 9 of 39 is 23.1%, so 23.3% may rest on a different group, and χ2 5.6 with 1 df gives P≈0.018.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that in-hospital β-blockers increased the likelihood of myonecrosis at P<0.01 is not supported by its own figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 entire-cohort values do not match the admitted (114) and discharged (250) subgroups: non-insulin-treated diabetes 15% against subgroup values of 22.8% and 16.8%; men 73.3% against 66.7% and 78.4%; blood urea SD 1.5 for the whole cohort against 15.0 and 4.0 in the subgroups. Editors' arithmetic: the weighted averages are 18.7% and 74.7%, and an overall SD cannot be smaller than the subgroup SDs in this way.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 contains transcription errors; individual entire-cohort figures should be quoted with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The share of troponin-positive patients with a history of coronary disease is 51.7% in the text but 51.9% in Table 2; 51.7% is not a possible proportion of 27 patients.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2's 51.9% (14 of 27) is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The catheterization results (18.5%, 16%, 4% and 62% of 40 patients) are not whole numbers of patients. Editors' arithmetic: they sum to 100.5%, and 18.5% of 40 is 7.4.
reporting_issues.consequence: The angiographic findings cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that infarction was unrelated to the amount ingested, route or frequency of cocaine use, but no analysis or data on amount or frequency are presented.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot be cited as a finding of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors state that chest-pain characteristics did not differ between admitted and discharged patients (Results › Demographic and clinical characteristics, 1st paragraph, p. 532) or between patients with and without myonecrosis (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 534), without tests, but the tables show large differences in pain character: sharp pain in 21.1% of admitted vs 42.4% of discharged patients (Table 1, p. 533) and in 11.1% of troponin-positive vs 41.1% of troponin-negative patients (Table 2, p. 534). Editors' calculation from the counts the percentages imply (24 of 114 vs 106 of 250; 3 of 27 vs about 90 of 218): uncorrected χ2 15.5 (P<0.001) and 9.3 (P=0.002).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statements that chest-pain features did not differ cannot be cited as findings; the tables show sharp pain less often, and pressure-type pain more often, in admitted and in troponin-positive patients.
