design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of beta-blocker use against no beta-blocker use in patients presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain. MEDLINE and EMBASE searched to 1 September 2016 with the terms 'beta blocker', 'cocaine' and six named beta blockers, plus hand-searching of reference lists of extracted studies and reviews, journal supplements, online highlights and direct discussion with experts; no language restriction. Eligible: retrospective or prospective studies in adults aged 18 or over with chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome and cocaine use confirmed by a positive urine screen or self-report, comparing beta-blocker with no beta-blocker therapy and reporting non-fatal myocardial infarction or in-hospital all-cause mortality. 580 citations screened, five studies included, all retrospective and none randomized (the review names a setting only for Mohamad et al., a Detroit emergency department; the primary papers, read in this round, place the others in the Bronx, San Francisco and Houston and, by the authors' affiliation, St Louis). Raw unadjusted event counts were pooled with Mantel-Haenszel random-effects odds ratios in Review Manager 5.1; heterogeneity by Cochran's Q and I-squared, with I-squared of 25% or more taken as significant; individual study quality rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a funnel plot of the five studies was inspected for publication bias.
can_establish: What the five retrospective hospital cohorts published to September 2016 reported when their raw event counts are pooled: whether non-fatal myocardial infarction and death were more common among patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were given a beta blocker, and how widely those cohorts disagree with one another.
cannot_establish: Whether beta blockers are safe in cocaine-associated chest pain. Every included study is a non-randomized comparison in which sicker patients were preferentially treated; the review pools unadjusted counts rather than the studies' own adjusted estimates, the myocardial-infarction analysis has I-squared of 71% with individual odds ratios running from 0.18 to 3.30, and the pooled confidence intervals (0.68 to 2.75 for infarction, 0.26 to 1.79 for death) exclude neither appreciable harm nor appreciable benefit. It also cannot establish anything about beta-blocker type, dose or route, which the authors state were not extractable, or about patients in whom cocaine was pharmacologically active, since exposure rests on urine screens that stay positive for days.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE and EMBASE to 1 September 2016 plus hand-searching and expert consultation; 580 citations screened to 5 included studies (PDF pp. 2-3, Figure 1). All five are single- or two-centre retrospective hospital studies (the review names a setting only for Mohamad et al., a Detroit emergency department; the primary papers, read in this round, place the others in the Bronx, San Francisco and Houston and, by the authors' affiliation, St Louis), published between 2008 and 2014, with inclusion periods from 1998 to 2011 (Table 1, PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: retrospective or prospective studies, adults aged 18 or over, chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome as defined by each study, cocaine use by positive urine screen or self-report, and non-fatal myocardial infarction or in-hospital all-cause mortality reported, with a beta-blocker against no-beta-blocker comparison. Excluded: animal studies, case reports, observational studies, reviews, studies not focused on acute non-traumatic chest pain, studies without the outcomes of interest and studies without the comparison. No restriction by follow-up length or sample size (PDF p. 2).
sample.demographics: Pooled across studies (Table 2, PDF p. 3), no beta blocker against beta blocker: mean age 44.6 +/- 3.2 against 48.0 +/- 2.5 years (p < 0.001); male 67% against 71%; African-American 75% against 80% (p = 0.041); hypertension 40% against 97%; diabetes 15% against 26%; coronary artery disease 17% against 30%; hyperlipidaemia 10% against 20%; prior congestive heart failure 10% against 26% (all p < 0.001); lung disease 17% against 12% (p = 0.007); HIV 11% against 7% (p = 0.119); serum creatinine 1.5 +/- 0.2 against 1.8 +/- 0.4 mg/dl (p < 0.001). The denominators in this table are internally impossible in two rows (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition within the primary studies is not reported; three of the five studies contributed mortality data and all five contributed infarction data.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases with no registry or grey-literature search, no list of excluded studies, and a search closing 1 September 2016 for a paper published in June 2018, so about 21 months of literature is missing. All five included studies are retrospective hospital cohorts, each from a single centre or two, from populations in which treatment was chosen by clinicians precisely on grounds that predict the outcome. The literature is small enough that a single study's extraction error or a single unpublished cohort could move the pooled estimate, and the funnel plot of five studies cannot detect that.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study recorded: administration of a beta blocker, in most of the included studies within the first 24 hours of presentation. Cocaine exposure by positive urine drug screen or reported use, as each study defined it. The review states that dose and route of the beta blocker were generally not delineated across studies and that outcomes by beta-blocker type (selective against non-selective) were not available, so neither could be analysed (PDF p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable; not reported by the included studies in extractable form. Table 1 records the percentage of beta-1 selective agents in four of the five studies: 66%, not available, 87%, 61% and 47% (PDF p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level. The primary studies' handling of alcohol and other drug use is not extracted, and no study-level covariate for it appears.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Unknown and named as a limitation: urine toxicology can stay positive for 48 to 72 hours after use, so the timing and amount of cocaine cannot be established, although the authors argue urine testing reflects real-world practice and note that most included studies counted in-hospital events during a window in which cocaine might still interact with the drug given (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: Within each primary study, patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were not given a beta blocker.
comparison.matching: None at review level: raw 2 x 2 counts were pooled unadjusted, although several of the primary studies reported propensity-adjusted estimates of their own. The review does not say why unadjusted rather than adjusted estimates were combined.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Confounding by indication in every included study (the treated patients were older and had far more cardiovascular disease), co-prescribed anti-ischemic drugs, the timing of treatment relative to the outcome, and the amount, route and timing of cocaine use. None of these is adjusted for or explored at review level.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All patients in both arms of every study were cocaine-positive; the contrast is between treatment decisions.

outcomes.instruments: As each primary study defined them. The infarction forest plot labels the outcome 'Myocardial Infarction (trop, EKG, symptoms)', that is troponin, electrocardiogram and symptoms, without a common threshold across studies (Figure 3, PDF p. 4). Mortality is all-cause, stated in the eligibility criteria as in-hospital, although one included study contributed events over two years from presentation (PDF pp. 2, 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with up to 4 stars for selection, 2 for comparability and 3 for ascertainment of exposure and outcomes; 6 or more taken as high quality. All five studies scored 7 or 8 and were therefore all rated high quality (Table 1, PDF p. 3), a result that does not separate them despite their estimates ranging from a fivefold apparent benefit to a threefold apparent harm.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Safety' is operationalized as the absence of a statistically significant pooled increase in non-fatal myocardial infarction or all-cause mortality.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: two pooled outcomes, no subgroup analyses and no meta-regression were performed, the authors stating that type-specific outcome data were unavailable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Study selection was done by two investigators reviewing abstracts, titles and full texts, and quality assessment and data extraction independently by three investigators (PDF p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mantel-Haenszel random-effects odds ratios. Non-fatal myocardial infarction, five studies, 94/610 (15.4%) with a beta blocker against 162/1146 (14.1%) without: pooled odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 0.68 to 2.74 in Figure 3; the abstract and text give 0.68 to 2.75), Z = 0.87, p = 0.39, tau-squared 0.40, Q = 13.76 on 4 degrees of freedom (p = 0.008), I-squared 71%. The individual estimates run in both directions: Datillo 2008, 2/33 against 72/277, odds ratio 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79); Mohamad 2008, 14/100 against 13/264, 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95); Rangel 2010, 51/151 against 55/177, 1.13 (0.71 to 1.80); Ibrahim 2012, 22/162 against 20/216, 1.54 (0.81 to 2.93); Fanari 2014, 5/164 against 2/212, 3.30 (0.63 to 17.24). All-cause mortality, three studies, 6/348 (1.7%) against 22/666 (3.3%): pooled odds ratio 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), Z = 0.79, p = 0.43, tau-squared 0.00, Q = 0.03 on 2 degrees of freedom (p = 0.98), I-squared 0%, from Datillo 1/33 against 13/277, 0.63 (0.08 to 5.01); Fanari 3/164 against 6/212, 0.64 (0.16 to 2.60); Rangel 2/151 against 3/177, 0.78 (0.13 to 4.72). No prediction interval, no absolute risk difference and no number needed to treat or harm is given. Mantel-Haenszel random effects with the DerSimonian-Laird variance (heterogeneity from the Mantel-Haenszel estimate) reproduces every printed single-study odds ratio, weight, tau-squared, chi-squared, I-squared, Z and pooled odds ratio in both figures exactly (editors' recomputation), so the analyses are internally sound apart from the inputs: the row for Rangel et al. is a double count, and the rows for Fanari et al., for deaths in Dattilo et al. and for Mohamad et al. do not match the comparisons described (see reporting issues). The Fanari counts in both analyses are percentages mistaken for counts (see reporting issues); recomputing them from the percentages Fanari prints gives odds ratios of about 2.67 for infarction and about 0.48 for death (editors' calculation from 8/164 against 4/212 and 5/164 against 13/212, the counts implied by Fanari's Table 3 percentages of 5%, 2%, 3% and 6%).
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Unadjusted counts were pooled; the adjusted estimates several primary studies report were not used, and no meta-regression or subgroup analysis was attempted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, no registration number and no PROSPERO record are mentioned. The methods state the study was performed in compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses for Protocols statement, which is the guideline for writing protocols, while no protocol is reported (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Both prespecified outcomes are reported with forest plots and full counts, which is good practice. The narrative is where selection enters: the one study with a significant increase in infarction is described in the Results with the wrong citation and attributed to the study that in fact found a significant decrease, and the Discussion's statement that beta-blocker use has not been associated with worsening infarction cites the four studies including that one. Arrhythmia and stroke are mentioned as reported by three and two studies respectively, with the comment that no differences were noted, but no data for them are shown.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 256 infarction events and 28 deaths across the five studies leave intervals compatible with both substantial harm and substantial benefit; with I-squared of 71% in the infarction analysis the pooled interval understates the true dispersion, and no prediction interval is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling the raw counts of five retrospective hospital cohorts, neither non-fatal myocardial infarction (odds ratio 1.36, 0.68 to 2.74) nor all-cause mortality (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79) differed significantly between patients given and not given a beta blocker. The infarction studies disagree sharply (I-squared 71%, tau-squared 0.40): one found a fivefold lower risk with a beta blocker and another a threefold higher risk, both statistically significant, with the remaining three in between. The mortality estimate is consistent across its three studies but rests on 28 deaths in total.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that beta-blocker use does not appear to be associated with an increased risk of infarction or mortality, and the discussion goes further: the results 'support contemporary clinical practice', suggest 'we reconsider the guidelines', and indicate that beta-blocker therapy 'may be a safe option' (PDF pp. 1, 3). Four gaps. First, absence of evidence is read as evidence of absence: the infarction point estimate is 1.36, in the direction of harm, with an upper limit of 2.74. Second, a pooled estimate is presented as a summary of studies whose individual results point in opposite directions and are statistically incompatible; with I-squared of 71% the average is not a quantity that describes any of them. Third, the recommendation to reconsider guidelines rests entirely on non-randomized data in which the treated patients were systematically sicker, pooled without using the primary studies' own adjustment. Fourth, the review's narrative misstates its own forest plot about which study found harm. The limitations section is otherwise candid, naming the retrospective designs, the inability to date cocaine use, the absence of dose, route and drug-type data, the heterogeneity and the possibility of publication bias, and the conclusion calls for further study.

timeline.event: Intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in cocaine-naive catheterization patients: the mechanistic basis of the guideline against beta blockers
Intravenous labetalol after intranasal cocaine lowered arterial pressure without relieving coronary vasoconstriction in the same laboratory
American Heart Association scientific statement advises against beta blockers in the acute setting, citing the catheterization studies
One of the five pooled cohorts: no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes in 376 patients, with wide intervals
This meta-analysis pools the five retrospective cohorts and reports no significant difference in infarction or death
Shin et al. meta-analysis pools the same five cohorts and three others (eight): no significant difference; Fanari et al.'s percentages again entered as counts

replication.where_it_stands: The review identifies the central fact of this literature: no randomized trial exists, and the guideline rests on two small catheterization studies (described here as 45 people given intravenous beta-blockers; in fact 19 received a blocker after cocaine). A second meta-analysis, read in this round (Shin et al., 2019), pooled the same five cohorts and three others and also found no significant difference; the two reviews share their core data and repeat the same Fanari extraction error, so they are not independent confirmations. The four primary cohorts other than Fanari et al., also read in this round, show that the two significant single-study results come from the comparisons most open to bias. Pooling these retrospective records has not resolved the question.

funding.funder: One author (Dr Addison) is supported by a K12-CA133250 grant; the remaining authors declare no specific grant for this research from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (PDF p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: Competing interests: none declared. Patient consent not required. Provenance: not commissioned, externally peer reviewed (PDF p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Johns Hopkins, Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard, Ohio State University, Baylor College of Medicine and the Michael E. DeBakey Veterans Affairs Medical Center. One author, Hani Jneid, is also an author of the 2008 American Heart Association statement whose Class III recommendation the review asks to reconsider (McCord et al., 2008). An interim analysis was presented at the American College of Cardiology Scientific Sessions in 2015, three years before publication (PDF p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of an intravenous beta blocker against the currently recommended alternatives in people presenting with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, powered for infarction and arrhythmia and with blinded outcome adjudication. Short of that, an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of the existing cohorts, using each study's adjusted estimate, handling the timing of treatment relative to the event, and separating beta-1 selective agents from the combined alpha-beta blockers, would extract far more from this literature than pooling unadjusted counts does.

domains.domain: 1. Research questions and inclusion criteria include the components of PICO
domains.note: Population (adults with chest pain suspicious for acute coronary syndrome and cocaine use), intervention (beta blocker), comparator (no beta blocker) and outcomes (non-fatal myocardial infarction, in-hospital all-cause mortality) are all stated.

domains.domain: 2. Explicit statement that review methods were established before the review, and justification of deviations
domains.note: No protocol, registration or a priori statement. The methods cite compliance with the PRISMA statement for Protocols, which is the guideline for writing a protocol, while no protocol is reported anywhere.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of the selection of study designs for inclusion
domains.note: The authors state they included retrospective or prospective studies because no randomized trials have been conducted. The same paragraph nevertheless lists 'observational studies' among the exclusions, which contradicts the five retrospective observational studies actually included.

Two databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE), keywords given, reference lists of included studies and reviews hand-searched, journal supplements and online highlights searched, experts consulted, no language restriction, search within 24 months of submission. Missing for a full yes: trial or study registries, an explicit grey-literature search and the full search strategy with limits.
Abstracts, titles and full-text articles were reviewed by two investigators.
Quality assessment and data extraction were independently performed by three investigators. The duplication did not catch the extraction error in the Fanari rows of both forest plots.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification for exclusions
domains.note: A flow diagram is given, but no list of the studies read in full and excluded, and no reasons for individual exclusions.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, setting, inclusion period, group sizes, percentage of beta-1 selective agents and quality score for each study. Missing: per-study populations, outcome definitions, follow-up windows and any dose or route detail, which the authors state was not available.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory technique for assessing risk of bias in individual studies
domains.note: The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale covers selection, comparability (that is, confounding) and ascertainment of exposure and outcome, which meets the partial criterion for non-randomized studies, but not selection of the reported result. All five studies scored 7 or 8 of 9 and were classed as high quality despite confounding by indication being the dominant problem in each, so the instrument did not discriminate.

domains.domain: 10. Sources of funding of the included studies reported
domains.note: No funding information for any included study is reported.

Raw unadjusted counts from non-randomized studies were pooled with Mantel-Haenszel random effects, although several primary studies report propensity-adjusted estimates; no justification for combining unadjusted estimates is given, which is the specific requirement for non-randomized studies. Pooling proceeded despite I-squared of 71% on the primary outcome, above the review's own stated threshold of 25%.

domains.domain: 12. Assessment of the potential impact of risk of bias on the results of the meta-analysis
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis by study quality, by Newcastle-Ottawa score or by any design feature.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for when interpreting and discussing the results
domains.note: The limitations name the retrospective, non-randomized nature of the data and the resulting information and selection bias as the most prominent problem, though the conclusion that the therapy may be safe does not reflect it.

domains.domain: 14. Satisfactory explanation for, and discussion of, heterogeneity
domains.note: Heterogeneity is acknowledged and attributed in general terms to the non-randomized data, variable populations and few studies, but no subgroup analysis, meta-regression or outlier examination was performed, and the two studies with significant effects in opposite directions are not discussed as such.

domains.domain: 15. Adequate investigation of publication bias and discussion of its likely impact
domains.note: A funnel plot of five studies is presented and publication bias is named as a possible influence; a funnel plot with five studies cannot detect asymmetry and no statistical test was performed.

domains.domain: 16. Potential sources of conflict of interest, including funding for the review, reported
domains.note: Funding of one author stated and competing interests declared as none.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four of the seven critical items fail: no protocol (item 2), no list of excluded studies (item 7), inappropriate statistical combination (item 11) and no adequate assessment of publication bias (item 15), with item 9 only partially met. More than one critical weakness gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The review's own data, fully reported in the two forest plots, are its most useful product, and the limitations section is honest. The source can be cited for the fact that no randomized trial of beta blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain existed as of September 2016, for the identity and size of the five retrospective cohorts, and for their individual event counts and odds ratios as printed in Figures 3 and 4, with the caution that the Fanari rows are misextracted. It should not be cited for the pooled estimates as evidence that beta blockers are safe in this setting, and a claim resting on it must state the heterogeneity (I-squared 71%) and that one included study found a threefold increase in infarction.

key_findings.finding: Five retrospective single- or two-centre hospital studies published between 2008 and 2014, with inclusion periods from 1998 to 2011, met the criteria; no randomized trial of beta blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain was found. Newcastle-Ottawa scores were 7, 7, 8, 8 and 8 of 9. The review names a setting only for Mohamad et al. (a Detroit emergency department).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2, continuing PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Pooling all five studies, non-fatal myocardial infarction occurred in 94 of 610 patients (15.4%) given a beta blocker and 162 of 1146 (14.1%) not given one: random-effects odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 0.68 to 2.74), Z = 0.87, p = 0.39, with tau-squared 0.40, Q = 13.76 on 4 degrees of freedom (p = 0.008) and I-squared 71%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3, forest plot totals and heterogeneity line
key_findings.note: The abstract and the Results text give the upper confidence limit as 2.75 where the forest plot prints 2.74.

key_findings.finding: The five infarction estimates point in opposite directions: Datillo 2008 odds ratio 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79) from 2/33 against 72/277, Mohamad 2008 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95) from 14/100 against 13/264, Rangel 2010 1.13 (0.71 to 1.80), Ibrahim 2012 1.54 (0.81 to 2.93) and Fanari 2014 3.30 (0.63 to 17.24).
key_findings.note: Two of the five are individually significant and they disagree in direction: one shows roughly a fivefold lower risk with a beta blocker, the other a threefold higher risk. This is what the I-squared of 71% reflects. Read in their own papers this round, the two are the comparisons most open to bias: Dattilo et al. counted infarctions against the beta-blocker only after the drug while the comparison group counted every infarction and took in patients treated after their infarction (Dattilo et al., 2008, pp. 118-122), and Mohamad et al.'s row compares beta-blockers already taken at home before arrival (Mohamad et al., 2008, p. 532).

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality, reported by three studies, occurred in 6 of 348 patients (1.7%) given a beta blocker and 22 of 666 (3.3%) not given one: odds ratio 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), p = 0.43, tau-squared 0.00, Q = 0.03 on 2 degrees of freedom (p = 0.98), I-squared 0%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4, forest plot totals and heterogeneity line
key_findings.note: 28 deaths in total across the three cohorts.

key_findings.finding: Patients given a beta blocker in the pooled baseline table were older (48.0 against 44.6 years) and had far more hypertension (97% against 40%), diabetes (26% against 15%), coronary artery disease (30% against 17%), hyperlipidaemia (20% against 10%) and prior heart failure (26% against 10%), while lung disease was more common in those not given one (17% against 12%).
key_findings.note: Two rows of this table are internally impossible (see reporting issues), so the pooled percentages should be treated as indicative only.

key_findings.finding: The review states that beta-blocker dose and route were generally not delineated across the included studies, that overlap or switching of agents could not be excluded, and that outcomes by beta-blocker type (selective against non-selective) were not available, so no analysis by drug class was possible.
key_findings.note: This is the specific gap that keeps the review from testing the mechanism it is about, since the concern applies to unopposed beta-blockade rather than to agents that also block alpha receptors.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the guideline recommendations against beta blockers here derive from animal studies, expert opinion and two haemodynamic studies of 45 human participants in total, given intravenous beta blockers in a catheterization laboratory nearly three decades earlier.
key_findings.note: The two studies cited are Lange et al. 1990 and Boehrer et al. 1993, which together enrolled 45 patients (30 and 15); but 15 of Lange's 30 received propranolol into the coronary artery (10 of them after cocaine) and 9 of Boehrer's 15 received intravenous labetalol after cocaine, so 19 received a blocker after cocaine and only 9 by vein (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the retrospective non-randomized data with information and selection bias, urine screens staying positive for 48 to 72 hours so that timing and amount of cocaine cannot be established, the inability to exclude that some patients were given beta blockers for haemodynamic reasons rather than chest pain, the significant heterogeneity, and possible publication bias and lack of access to primary patient data.

The authors conclude that beta-blocker therapy may be a safe option in patients presenting with chest pain and suspected cocaine use, that the results support contemporary clinical practice, and that the guidelines on beta blockers in this setting should be reconsidered.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation; the pooled infarction point estimate is 1.36 with an upper confidence limit of 2.74 (2.75 in the text), and the analysis is of unadjusted counts from non-randomized studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fanari rows of both forest plots appear to be the percentages printed in that study's Table 3 entered as event counts. Figure 3 gives Fanari 5/164 against 2/212 and Figure 4 gives 3/164 against 6/212, which are exactly the numbers 5, 2, 3 and 6 that Fanari prints as percentages under a column headed 'BB (%)'. The counts those percentages imply are about 8 and 4 for infarction and about 5 and 13 for death.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both of Fanari's contributions are wrong, in opposite directions. Recomputed from the percentages, its infarction odds ratio is about 2.67 rather than 3.30 and its mortality odds ratio about 0.48 rather than 0.64 (editors' calculation). Fanari carried 11.4% of the infarction analysis but 48.5% of the mortality analysis, so the pooled mortality estimate is the one materially affected. Exact counts cannot be recovered, because the source prints only rounded percentages; a claim citing the pooled mortality estimate should say so.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that one early study showed a statistically significant increase in myocardial infarction with beta-blocker use and cite reference 15 (Datillo et al.), whose entry in Figure 3 is an odds ratio of 0.18 (0.04 to 0.79), a significant decrease, and whose own title reports beta blockers as associated with reduced risk. The study that showed a significant increase is Mohamad et al. (reference 16), odds ratio 3.14 (1.42 to 6.95).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence that acknowledges harm in the included literature points at the wrong study. Compounding this, the Discussion states that beta-blocker use has not been associated with worsening non-fatal infarction and cites references 16 to 19, a list that includes the very study with the significant threefold increase. A reader relying on the narrative rather than the forest plot would conclude that no included study found harm.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 reports 365 patients with hypertension among 348 assessed in the beta-blocker group (97%), a count larger than its own denominator, and gives the number assessed for mean age as 1157 in the no-beta-blocker group and 637 in the beta-blocker group, both larger than the group totals of 1146 and 610 stated in the same table heading. Three percentages also do not match their counts: male sex 454 of 666 is 68% (printed 67), lung disease 130 of 705 is 18% (printed 17) and 46 of 346 is 13% (printed 12) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least three numbers in the baseline table are impossible, so the pooled baseline comparison cannot be verified. Since the imbalance in this table is the review's evidence that the treated patients were sicker, the direction of the argument survives but its magnitudes should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants is given as 1794 in the abstract and in the first line of the discussion, and as 1756 in the Results (1st and 3rd paragraphs) and in the column headings of Table 2 and the totals of Figure 3 (Figure 4 pools 1014 patients from three studies); the study-level totals in Table 1 sum to 1756 (1146 plus 610).
reporting_issues.consequence: A 38-patient discrepancy with no explanation; 1794 equals the numbers assessed for mean age in Table 2 (1157 + 637), larger than the group totals, which may be where it comes from. Claims should use 1756, which matches the analysed data.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility paragraph lists 'observational studies' among the exclusions while the inclusion criterion admits retrospective or prospective studies, and all five included studies are retrospective observational cohorts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated design criterion is self-contradictory, so the reader cannot tell what was eligible; in practice the review included exactly the design its exclusion list rules out.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility criteria specify all-cause mortality in hospital, but the review states that one included study (Rangel et al.) contributed events over two years from presentation, and the paper does not say whether the in-hospital or the two-year mortality figure was pooled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which estimate entered Figure 4 cannot be determined from this paper; Rangel et al., read in this round, settles it: the Figure 4 row (2 of 151 against 3 of 177) is its in-hospital deaths (Rangel et al., 2010, Table 3, p. 877), so the pooled mortality is in-hospital.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state compliance with the PRISMA statement for Protocols, a guideline for writing review protocols, while no protocol, registration number or a priori analysis plan is reported; the relevant reporting guideline for a completed review is PRISMA itself.
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation gives an impression of prospective planning that the paper does not support. The review should be read as unregistered.

reporting_issues.issue: The review defines I-squared of 25% or more as significant heterogeneity, finds 71% in the primary analysis, and proceeds to pool and to recommend reconsidering guidelines, with the explanation that guidance was needed; no prediction interval, subgroup analysis or meta-regression accompanies the pooled estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled odds ratio of 1.36 summarises studies that are statistically incompatible with one another. Any claim citing it must carry the heterogeneity, and the individual study estimates are more informative than the average.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 dates Ibrahim et al. to 2012 while the reference list gives 2013, and the same study's name is spelled Datillo in Table 1 and the figures but Dattilo in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor bibliographic inconsistency; it matters only for matching the included studies to their records.

reporting_issues.issue: Rangel et al.'s row in the infarction plot (51 of 151 against 55 of 177) is not an infarction count in that study: it equals the sum of its positive-troponin row (36 against 37, troponin in the indeterminate or infarction range) and its infarction row (15 against 18), so the 15 and 18 patients in the infarction range are counted twice (Rangel et al., 2010, Table 3, p. 877).
reporting_issues.consequence: Rangel et al. carry 27.8% of the weight in the infarction analysis and their infarction proportion appears as 31% to 34% instead of 10%; this also explains much of the spread in infarction proportions across the plot. Editors' calculation with Rangel et al.'s infarction-range counts: odds ratio 0.97 for that study, and a pooled odds ratio of 1.31 (0.60 to 2.87), or 1.32 (0.62 to 2.80) with Fanari et al.'s implied counts as well; neither is significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Two further rows do not match the comparison the review describes: Mohamad et al.'s row (14 of 100 against 13 of 264) is its comparison of beta-blockers already taken at home before arrival (Mohamad et al., 2008, p. 532), not of beta-blockers given in hospital; and Dattilo et al.'s death row (1 of 33 against 13 of 277) places the full cohort's deaths (1 of 60 against 13 of 288) over the denominators of its infarction analysis (Dattilo et al., 2008, pp. 120-122).
reporting_issues.consequence: The only significant increase in the infarction analysis concerns patients already on a beta-blocker at home. Editors' calculation with Dattilo et al.'s full-cohort deaths and Fanari et al.'s implied deaths: pooled death odds ratio 0.51 (0.22 to 1.17), not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's beta-1-selective percentages do not match their counts for two studies: Ibrahim et al. 92 of 162 is 57% (printed 61%) and Dattilo et al. 22 of 33 is 67% (printed 66%); Rangel 131 of 151 (87%) and Fanari 77 of 164 (47%) match.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the shares of selective agents are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the clinical basis of the guidelines as two haemodynamic studies with a total of 45 human subjects given intravenous beta-blockers; in those studies 15 of 30 received propranolol, infused into the coronary artery (10 of them after cocaine), and 9 of 15 received intravenous labetalol after cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence behind the guideline is smaller and less like clinical use than the review says: 19 people received a blocker after cocaine, and only 9 by vein (Lange et al., 1990, pp. 898-899; Boehrer et al., 1993, p. 609).

design_detail: Single-centre retrospective cohort from hospital records (San Francisco General Hospital), 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2006: 331 consecutive patients admitted with chest pain (ICD-9 codes for chest pain, angina or chest discomfort) and a cocaine-positive urine test taken in the emergency department. Of the 328 who came through the emergency department, 151 received a β-blocker there and 177 did not. Primary predictor: β-blocker in the emergency department; primary outcome: death, from the National Death Index. Secondary predictors: any β-blocker during the stay, discharge on a β-blocker; secondary outcomes: troponin in the first 24 h, ECG and blood-pressure changes, ventricular arrhythmia, intubation, vasopressors, length of stay, and cardiovascular death from death certificates. Median follow-up 972 days. Unadjusted tests for in-hospital outcomes; linear regression for blood pressure and Cox models for death.
can_establish: What was recorded in hospital, and in the National Death Index over a median of 2.7 years, for patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain at San Francisco General Hospital who did or did not receive a β-blocker in the emergency department, mostly as unadjusted comparisons.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers are safe or protective after cocaine use: physicians chose who was treated (patients needing vasopressors rarely received β-blockers), in-hospital comparisons were unadjusted, the cardiovascular-death result rests on 19 deaths with seven or more covariates, and a discharge prescription says nothing about later use.

sample.recruitment: Clinic (hospital records): consecutive admissions identified in the hospital's electronic database (THREDS, maintained by the Division of Internal Medicine) by ICD-9 chest-pain codes and positive urine toxicology; two reviewers abstracted data from paper charts and the electronic record; deaths found by searching the National Death Index with names, social security numbers and birth dates (p. 875).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: admission with chest pain and a urine sample collected in the emergency department positive for benzoylecgonine (EMIT II Plus until October 2003, CEDIA after December 2003; cut-off 300 ng/mL). Excluded: chest pain diagnosed in the emergency department as pulmonary in origin, such as pneumonia or pulmonary embolism (p. 875).
sample.demographics: β-blocker in the emergency department vs not: mean age 51 vs 48 years; men 74% vs 71%; Black 77% vs 73%, White 13% vs 19%; homeless 40% vs 42%; current smokers 80% vs 86%; hypertension 70% vs 58%; prior coronary disease 28% vs 24%; prior myocardial infarction 25% vs 21%; heart failure 15% vs 16%; HIV positive 5% vs 10%; outpatient β-blocker 37% vs 28% (Table 1, p. 876).
sample.attrition: National Death Index information for 317 of 331 (14 without; reasons not given) (p. 877). ECG-change outcomes only for patients with an ECG after the β-blocker; the comparison group for them is restricted to 52 patients whose first β-blocker was given on the ward (Table 3 footnote, p. 877). Echocardiograms were available for 162 and an angiogram or stress test for 83 (Table 4 footnotes, p. 877).
sample.selection_effects: Admitted patients only (patients discharged from the emergency department are absent), coded as chest pain, at one public teaching hospital; mostly Black men around 50, 40% homeless. β-blocker use was left to the treating physicians, with no protocol (p. 875).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine: urine benzoylecgonine in the emergency department (cut-off 300 ng/mL). A patient-reported history of cocaine use within 48 h was documented in 94 patients (30%), last use a median 24 h (IQR 12–48) before the visit (p. 875). β-blockers: drug, route and time from the records; time from triage to the first emergency-department dose median 100 min (IQR 49–279) vs 1070 min (IQR 691–1878) for a first dose on the ward (p. 876).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cocaine amount and route not recorded. First emergency-department dose: intravenous metoprolol 113 (74%), oral metoprolol 17 (11%), intravenous labetalol 18 (12%), oral labetalol 3 (2%), oral atenolol 1 (1%), oral propranolol 1 (1%) (p. 875). Discharge regimens (124 patients): metoprolol 68 (55%), atenolol 31 (25%), labetalol 19 (15%), carvedilol 4 (3%), propranolol 2 (2%) (p. 877). Doses not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded apart from tobacco (current smokers 80% vs 86%, Table 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Patients admitted through the emergency department with cocaine-associated chest pain who did not receive a β-blocker there (177), a group that includes patients first given a β-blocker later on the ward. For blood-pressure and ECG changes, the comparison is with patients whose first β-blocker was given on the ward (p. 875; Table 3 footnote).
comparison.matching: None. Mortality models adjusted for potential confounders described as including age, race, sex, end-stage renal disease, outpatient ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker and discharge on a calcium-channel blocker, and for cardiovascular death also a positive troponin; covariates chosen by convention or if associated with predictor and outcome at P<.20 (pp. 875, 877). The blood-pressure model adjusted for other antihypertensives given with the first β-blocker (p. 876). In-hospital outcomes were compared without adjustment (Table 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Haemodynamic instability and the clinical reasons for withholding β-blockers, amount and recency of cocaine (time of use known for 94), other drug and alcohol use, and treatment and adherence after discharge (the authors could not assess these, p. 879).

outcomes.instruments: Death and date of death from the National Death Index; cardiovascular death from death certificates; troponin I (Bayer Immuno 1 before June 2003, Bayer ADVIA Centaur June 2003 to January 2005, Siemens Centaur February 2005 to December 2006), any detectable level positive, below 1.5 ng/mL indeterminate, above 1.5 ng/mL taken to represent acute infarction; blood pressure and ECG just before and after the first β-blocker; intubation and vasopressors in the first 24 h; ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia needing cardioversion or defibrillation; length of stay (p. 875).
outcomes.validity_norms: Three troponin assays over the period with the same thresholds; infarction defined by troponin level alone.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm: death (primary), and troponin elevation, worsening ECG, intubation, vasopressors and malignant ventricular arrhythmia in hospital; 'unopposed' α-stimulation was examined as a rise in systolic pressure after the β-blocker.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; three predictors (emergency department, any time in hospital, discharge) and 13 outcomes, covariates selected by P<.20.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for chart abstraction or ECG reading; death came from an external register.

analysis.effect_sizes: In hospital, β-blocker in the emergency department vs not, unadjusted (Table 3, p. 877): positive troponin 36 (24%) vs 37 (21%), P=.52; troponin in the infarction range 15 (10%) vs 18 (10%), P=.94; intubation 4 (3%) vs 10 (6%), P=.18; vasopressors 1 (1%) vs 12 (7%), P=.005; ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia 1 (1%) vs 1 (1%); death 2 (2%) vs 3 (2%), P=.76; median stay 2 days in both. Systolic pressure: median change −8 mm Hg (IQR −21 to 3) after an emergency-department β-blocker vs +5 mm Hg after a first β-blocker on the ward, P=.003; adjusted mean difference 8.6 mm Hg greater fall (95% CI 2.5 to 14.7), P=.006 (p. 876). Long term (median 972 days): 45 of 317 died (14%); unadjusted HR for death 0.97 (0.53 to 1.79) for a β-blocker in the emergency department, 0.81 (0.44 to 1.48) during the stay, 0.90 (0.47 to 1.71) at discharge (Table 4); adjusted HR for death with discharge on a β-blocker 0.53 (0.26 to 1.08), P=.08; cardiovascular death (19 deaths) unadjusted HR 0.64 (0.2 to 2.0), adjusted 0.29 (0.09 to 0.98), P=.047 (p. 877). Editors' calculation: crude risk ratio for troponin in the infarction range 0.98 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.87).
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching. Adjusted analyses were done for blood pressure and for long-term death only.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives no number for the primary outcome (death by emergency-department β-blocker, HR 0.97) and headlines a secondary predictor with a secondary outcome (discharge on a β-blocker and cardiovascular death, HR 0.29). The abstract and the Results list vasopressor use among outcomes without meaningful or significant differences, although Table 3 shows 1% vs 7% (P=.005). Results restricted to β-blockers within 6 hours of presentation are reported only as similar, without numbers.
analysis.power: The authors report 80% power to detect 5% vs 11% with a two-sided α of .05 (p. 878); editors' calculation: with 151 and 177 patients that power is about 50% (53% by the arcsine method), and 80% would need about 310 per group. Editors' arithmetic: the cardiovascular-death model has 19 events for at least seven covariates, under 3 events per variable; the authors themselves say the estimate is likely overinflated (p. 878).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Unadjusted in-hospital outcomes were similar with and without an emergency-department β-blocker (troponin in the infarction range 10% in both; deaths 2 vs 3), but patients given β-blockers rarely needed vasopressors (1% vs 7%), consistent with physicians withholding β-blockers from unstable patients. Systolic pressure fell more after an emergency-department β-blocker than after a first dose on the ward. Death over a median 972 days was not associated with any β-blocker exposure (HRs 0.81 to 0.97, intervals including 1); a 71% lower adjusted hazard of cardiovascular death with discharge on a β-blocker rests on 19 deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that β-blockers do not appear to be associated with adverse events (p. 874). The Comment says discharge on a β-blocker shows these drugs may have beneficial properties, and that even if confounding by indication was present "the drugs were clearly safe in a large proportion of these patients" (p. 878); the conclusion says administration appears safe and may even be beneficial and that outpatient β-blockers may protect against cardiovascular death (p. 879). The authors acknowledge that the cardiovascular-death estimate is likely overinflated (p. 878) and that only a randomized trial can address the limitations (p. 879). No difference detected among patients whom physicians chose to treat does not show safety for patients they chose not to treat, and the abstract's statement on vasopressors contradicts Table 3.

timeline.event: Lange et al.: described by Rangel et al. as the only catheter-based study to show worsening of cocaine-induced vasospasm, with intracoronary propranolol (pp. 874, 878)
Boehrer et al.: described by Rangel et al. as showing neither worsening nor improvement of vasoconstriction with intravenous labetalol (p. 878)

Dattilo et al.: fewer infarctions after β-blockers among admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test; Rangel et al. say only a small proportion of that cohort was admitted with chest pain (p. 875), whereas Dattilo et al. report 165 of 348 admissions
Mohamad et al. (Detroit): unadjusted, more troponin elevation with home β-blockers and with β-blockers continued or started in hospital

An item in the same issue is signalled on p. 874 ('See also page 880'), and a letter titled 'Beta-blockers and cocaine: still a bad idea' (Gupta, Greller & Hoffman, Arch Intern Med 2010;170(20):1859–1860, with an author reply) is cited by Shin et al. (2019, reference 12); by journal, year and the author reply it is probably correspondence on this paper. Neither was among the files; not read.
Ibrahim et al. (Houston): troponin rise 22 of 162 with vs 20 of 216 without β-blockers, unadjusted

Shin et al. meta-analysis pooled this study's in-hospital counts (infarction 15 of 151 vs 18 of 177; death 2 of 151 vs 3 of 177) and, for long-term death, the emergency-department contrast (18 of 149 vs 27 of 168), not the discharge contrast

Pham et al. meta-analysis entered as this study's infarctions 51 of 151 vs 55 of 177, the sum of its positive-troponin and infarction-range rows (36 + 15; 37 + 18), and its in-hospital deaths as 2 of 151 vs 3 of 177

replication.where_it_stands: One of the four record studies read in this round with Dattilo et al. (2008), Mohamad et al. (2008) and Ibrahim et al. (2013), and the only one with long-term mortality; its in-hospital results agree with Ibrahim et al. (2013) in showing no clear difference, while Dattilo et al. (2008) report fewer and Mohamad et al. (2008) more myocardial injury with β-blockers. Its counts are inside the pooled estimates of Shin et al. (2019) and of Pham et al. (2018), whose infarction row for this study double-counts its troponin rows, and should not be cited beside either meta-analysis as independent support. No randomized trial existed as of 2018 (Shin et al., 2019, p. 45).

funding.funder: An American Heart Association Western States Affiliate Medical Student Award (to the first author) and grant UL1 RR024131 from the National Center for Research Resources (NCRR), a component of the National Institutes of Health (p. 879).
funding.declared_conflicts: Financial Disclosure: None reported (p. 879).
funding.affiliations_note: First author at Harvard Medical School (a medical student award funded the work); other authors at the University of California, San Francisco (cardiology), Cleveland Clinic, and San Francisco General Hospital (epidemiology and biostatistics; cardiology) (pp. 874, 879).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain comparing a β-blocker (selective and combined α/β agents separately) with none from randomization, with blinded adjudication of in-hospital events, and a separate randomized comparison of discharge β-blocker vs none with adherence and continued cocaine use measured during follow-up; failing that, a multicentre target-trial emulation with a common time zero and adjustment for the reasons β-blockers were withheld.

domains.note: No protocol; physicians decided (p. 875). β-blocker recipients were older, more hypertensive, had higher triage pressure and more outpatient cardiovascular drugs, and received more nitroglycerin, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, aspirin and statins in the emergency department (Tables 1–2). Vasopressors in 1% vs 7% suggest unstable patients were not given β-blockers. In-hospital comparisons were unadjusted; mortality models used P-value-selected covariates.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: For the primary emergency-department comparison, follow-up and treatment start close together (median 100 min after triage): moderate. For the discharge comparison behind the abstract's cardiovascular-death result, only survivors to discharge could be discharged on a β-blocker and the prescription was a post-admission decision; how in-hospital deaths were classified is not stated: serious. Admitted patients only.

Emergency-department β-blocker timing and agent came from time-stamped records; but the no-β-blocker group includes patients treated later on the ward, and discharge on a β-blocker is a prescription with unknown later adherence (p. 879).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions differed (sublingual nitroglycerin 73% vs 51%, nitroglycerin paste 43% vs 23%, ACE inhibitor or ARB 22% vs 7%; Table 2) and were adjusted for only in the blood-pressure analysis; treatment after discharge unknown.

14 of 331 without death-register information; Table 1 percentages in the comparison group imply unreported missing values (for example 143 smokers printed as 86% of 177); time of cocaine use known for 94; ECG-change comparisons restricted to patients with post-β-blocker ECGs (52 controls).

All-cause death from the National Death Index is objective; cardiovascular death depends on death-certificate coding; three troponin assays over the period; ECG reading and chart abstraction not reported as blinded.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; three predictors and 13 outcomes; covariates chosen by P<.20; the abstract headlines the secondary discharge × cardiovascular-death result (HR 0.29, P=.047, 19 events) and gives no number for the null primary result; results within 6 hours reported without numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because β-blockers are an intervention compared without randomization (METHODS §5.3). The in-hospital comparisons are at serious risk of bias from confounding by indication (unadjusted, with signs that unstable patients were not treated); the long-term cardiovascular-death result adds selection on survival to discharge, unknown adherence and an overfitted model. Citable for: in-hospital event counts by emergency-department β-blocker status as unadjusted descriptions; the absence of a rise in systolic pressure after an emergency-department β-blocker (adjusted 8.6 mm Hg greater fall than after a first dose on the ward); the β-blockers used and their timing at this hospital; mortality of 14% over a median 972 days after admission with cocaine-associated chest pain; and the absence of an association between any β-blocker exposure and all-cause death (primary predictor HR 0.97, 0.53 to 1.79). Not citable for: β-blockers being safe in general after cocaine use, protection against cardiovascular death, or effects in patients physicians judged unsuitable for β-blockers.

key_findings.finding: 331 patients were admitted with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine test; all but 3 came through the emergency department, where 151 (46%) received a β-blocker. First dose: intravenous metoprolol 113 (74%), oral metoprolol 17 (11%), intravenous labetalol 18 (12%), oral labetalol 3 (2%), oral atenolol 1 (1%), oral propranolol 1 (1%).
key_findings.note: The six first-dose counts sum to 153, not 151 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: A patient-reported history of cocaine use within 48 h was documented in 94 patients (30%), last use a median 24 h (IQR 12–48) before the visit; mean 29 h (SD 21) vs 22 h (SD 18) before triage in the β-blocker and comparison groups, P=.13.

Patients given an emergency-department β-blocker were older (51 vs 48 years), had higher triage systolic pressure (159 vs 141 mm Hg) and more hypertension (70% vs 58%), more outpatient ACE inhibitor or ARB (42% vs 29%), statin (17% vs 8%) and recent aspirin (34% vs 24%); in the emergency department they also received more sublingual nitroglycerin (73% vs 51%), nitroglycerin infusion (11% vs 3%) and paste (43% vs 23%), ACE inhibitor or ARB (22% vs 7%), aspirin (72% vs 60%) and statin (9% vs 3%).
key_findings.locator: Tables 1 and 2; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 214 patients (65%) received a β-blocker at some point in hospital; compared with the others they more often had prior coronary disease (30% vs 19%), prior bypass grafting (6% vs 1%) and outpatient β-blocker therapy (43% vs 12%). Time from triage to the β-blocker: median 100 min (IQR 49–279) in the emergency department vs 1070 min (IQR 691–1878) for a first dose on the ward.

Systolic pressure fell after an emergency-department β-blocker (median change −8 mm Hg, IQR −21 to 3), a significantly larger decrease than after a first β-blocker on the ward, P=.003; the ward group's median change is printed as +5 mm Hg with an IQR of −17 to 4, figures that cannot both be right. Adjusted for antihypertensives given at the same time, the emergency-department group had an 8.6 mm Hg greater fall (95% CI 2.5 to 14.7), P=.006.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 874); Results › Outcomes During the Hospitalization, 1st paragraph (p. 876)
key_findings.note: The ward group's median (+5) lies outside its printed interquartile range (−17 to 4).

key_findings.finding: In hospital, emergency-department β-blocker vs none, unadjusted: positive troponin 36 (24%) vs 37 (21%), P=.52; troponin in the infarction range 15 (10%) vs 18 (10%), P=.94; intubation in the first 24 h 4 (3%) vs 10 (6%), P=.18; vasopressors in the first 24 h 1 (1%) vs 12 (7%), P=.005; ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia needing cardioversion or defibrillation 1 (1%) vs 1 (1%); death 2 (2%) vs 3 (2%), P=.76; median stay 2 days in both.
key_findings.note: Percentages in some rows imply denominators other than 151 and 177 (for example ST elevation on the first ECG, 18 printed as 14%); the footnote restricts the comparison group to 52 patients for ECG changes.

key_findings.finding: Among patients with an elevated troponin, peak levels were similar in those given β-blockers (n=36; median 1.4 ng/mL, IQR 0.3 to 6.4) and in others (median 1.0 ng/mL, IQR 0.2 to 12.4), P=.78; results were reported as similar when restricted to β-blockers given within 6 hours of presentation, without numbers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes During the Hospitalization, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 124 patients were discharged on a β-blocker: metoprolol 68 (55%), atenolol 31 (25%), labetalol 19 (15%), carvedilol 4 (3%), propranolol 2 (2%); they were older, more often had hypertension and coronary disease, and were more often discharged on aspirin, statins and nitroglycerin.

Of 317 patients with National Death Index information, 45 (14%) died over a median 972 days (IQR 555–1490): 18 (12%) with and 27 (16%) without an emergency-department β-blocker (P=.38); 14 (12%) of those discharged on a β-blocker vs 29 (15%) of those not (P=.44); 19 of the 45 (42%) from cardiovascular causes by death certificate.
key_findings.note: 14 + 29 = 43, not 45, and the group denominators are not given (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Hazard ratios for death (Table 4, apparently unadjusted): β-blocker in the emergency department 0.97 (0.53–1.79), during the stay 0.81 (0.44–1.48), at discharge 0.90 (0.47–1.71). Other predictors: end-stage renal disease 7.36 (3.21–16.8), abnormal systolic function 3.66 (1.69–7.89; echocardiograms in 162), heart failure 3.14 (1.68–5.85), positive troponin 2.29 (1.30–4.04).
key_findings.note: Table 4 does not say whether its estimates are adjusted; the text implies they are not.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for potential confounders including age, race, sex, end-stage renal disease, outpatient ACE inhibitor or ARB and discharge on a calcium-channel blocker, discharge on a β-blocker had HR 0.53 (0.26–1.08, P=.08) for death. For cardiovascular death the unadjusted HR was 0.64 (0.2–2.0, P=.44) and, adjusted for covariates that also included a positive troponin, 0.29 (0.09–0.98, P=.047); removing patients discharged on labetalol or carvedilol did not change the results.

The authors call the cardiovascular-death estimate likely overinflated and partly due to small numbers, report 80% power to detect 5% vs 11%, and state they could not assess behaviour or treatment after discharge.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with 151 and 177 patients and a two-sided α of .05, power to detect 5% vs 11% is about 50% (53% by the arcsine method), not 80%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give a study period of 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2006 (six years); the Results speak of a 5-year period.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the period is stated twice in the Methods and abstract as 2001–2006.

reporting_issues.issue: The six first emergency-department doses are printed as 113, 17, 18, 3, 1 and 1 patients (74%, 11%, 12%, 2%, 1%, 1%) for the 151 treated. Editors' arithmetic: they sum to 153, and 113 of 151 is 74.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: One count is probably mistyped; agent shares are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The median systolic change after a first β-blocker on the ward is printed as +5 mm Hg with an interquartile range of −17 to 4, so the median lies outside its own interquartile range.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the three numbers is wrong; the comparison of blood-pressure change rests on the adjusted mean difference instead.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 percentages in the comparison group do not match n=177: current smokers 143 printed as 86%, heart failure 27 as 16%, outpatient β-blocker 47 as 28%; missing values are not reported. Editors' arithmetic: 143 of 177 is 80.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline comparisons rest on unreported denominators; differences in smoking between groups may be smaller than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists vasopressor use, and the Results list vasopressor agents, among outcomes with no meaningful or significant difference, but Table 3 shows vasopressors in 1 (1%) vs 12 (7%), P=.005.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one significant in-hospital difference favours the β-blocker group and points to confounding by indication (unstable patients not given β-blockers); the abstract hides it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3's column headers give n=151 and n=177, but its footnote restricts the comparison group to the 52 patients whose first β-blocker was given on the ward and who had a post-β-blocker ECG, without saying which rows the restriction applies to.
reporting_issues.consequence: Row denominators for the ECG outcomes are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Deaths by discharge status (14 + 29 = 43) do not add up to the 45 deaths, and group denominators for the mortality comparisons are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The discharge comparison cannot be reconstructed, including whether the 5 in-hospital deaths are counted in the group not discharged on a β-blocker.

reporting_issues.issue: The urine assays are dated June 1993 to October 2003 (EMIT) and after December 2003 (CEDIA), leaving October to December 2003 unaccounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment argues that a clinically significant difference in cocaine dose between the groups was unlikely given the "lack of baseline differences in BP" (6th paragraph, p. 878), but Table 1 gives triage systolic pressure of 159 vs 141 mm Hg (P<.001, p. 876), and the Comment's 4th paragraph says starting pressure was higher in patients given a β-blocker in the emergency department (p. 878).
reporting_issues.consequence: The authors' argument against confounding by cocaine dose rests on a premise their own data contradict; it cannot be cited as evidence that the groups were comparable.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment reports 80% power to detect a difference of 5% vs 11% with a two-sided α of .05 (6th paragraph, p. 878). Editors' calculation: with 151 and 177 patients, power for that difference is about 50% (normal approximation; 53% by the arcsine method), and 80% would need about 310 patients per group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The authors' statement that the sample was likely sufficient to exclude large effects is not supported: a difference of 5% vs 11% would be missed about half the time.

The item signalled on p. 880 of the same issue and later correspondence were not among the files and were not read; no supplement.

disagreements.resolution: Added after comparing Pham et al.'s Figure 3 row with Table 3 here (p. 877; 300 dpi).

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian–Laird; relative risks pooled from crude event counts) of observational studies comparing patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or recent cocaine use who did or did not receive a β-blocker during admission or at discharge. MEDLINE, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library searched to 11 June 2018. Eight cohort studies (seven retrospective, one prospective; one a conference abstract), 2,048 patients. Four pooled outcomes: in-hospital death (5 studies, 4 estimable), in-hospital myocardial infarction or necrosis (6), long-term death (3) and long-term infarction (2).
can_establish: What the crude event counts of eight non-randomized studies, as extracted, give when pooled: no clear difference in in-hospital or long-term death or infarction between patients who did and did not receive β-blockers, with intervals wide enough to include sizeable benefit or harm.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers are safe or effective after cocaine use: the pooled studies compare patients whom clinicians selected for treatment, the pooling uses unadjusted counts, the comparisons pooled are of different exposures (home β-blockers at presentation, β-blockers before an infarction, in the emergency department, at any time in hospital, at discharge), and some counts were mis-extracted.

sample.recruitment: Database search (MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library) from inception to 11 June 2018 with the terms beta-blocker(s) or beta blocker(s) and cocaine, plus bibliographies of relevant articles; 273 records (PubMed 100, EMBASE 144, Cochrane 29), 218 after removing 55 duplicates, 50 full texts, 8 studies included (p. 41, Figure 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Observational studies of patients presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain or recent cocaine use that compared outcomes between patients who did and did not receive a β-blocker during admission or at discharge and reported in-hospital or long-term infarction (or myocardial necrosis) or death; journal articles and conference abstracts eligible (p. 41). Full-text exclusions (42): review articles 18, letters 3, design not meeting criteria 16, no outcome data 3, abstract of a published study 2 (Figure 1, p. 41).
sample.demographics: Studies from 1998 to 2014 (period not available for one); mean or median ages 42 to 57; women 6% to 37% where reported; all eight used urine toxicology to establish recent cocaine use; one study enrolled patients with acute coronary syndrome (Cediel et al.) and one included admissions without chest pain (Dattilo et al.: 47% chest pain) (pp. 42–43, Tables 1 and 2). Countries and settings are not described.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases and reference lists; no trial-registry or grey-literature search beyond conference abstracts; the language statement reads 'with any restriction', apparently meaning without; search terms limited to beta-blocker(s) and cocaine, without individual drug names (p. 41). The included studies are single-centre record studies in which clinicians chose who received β-blockers.

exposure.measurement: As defined in each study: positive urine drug screen, with reported use within 24 h in two studies by the review's Table 2 (Ibrahim, Fanari) and also in Mohamad et al., whose own inclusion criteria required it (Mohamad et al., p. 532), and a positive screen within 48–72 h of admission in one (Table 2, p. 43). β-blocker timing as classified by the review: on presentation (Mohamad), during admission (Dattilo, Ibrahim; Fanari within the first 24 h; Cediel during admission or at discharge), in the emergency department (Rangel), during admission while having chest pain or at discharge (Schmidt), at discharge (Finks) (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable. Agents (Table 2): metoprolol predominated; labetalol, carvedilol, atenolol and propranolol in smaller shares; carvedilol only in one study (Finks); not specified in two (Mohamad, Cediel). No subgroup analysis by agent or timing was possible (p. 45).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Patients in the same studies who did not receive a β-blocker as each study defined the exposure.
comparison.matching: None at review level; crude event counts were pooled (p. 41).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Confounding by indication within each study (coronary disease, hypertension, haemodynamic instability) is not addressed by the pooling; adjusted estimates reported by some included studies were not used.

outcomes.instruments: In-hospital and long-term all-cause death; infarction or myocardial necrosis as defined by each study: troponin I above 0.02 ng/mL with chest pain (Mohamad), troponin I above 0.10 ng/mL or ECG changes (Dattilo), troponin above 1.5 ng/mL (Rangel), troponin I above 0.6 and troponin T above 0.1 ng/mL (Ibrahim), troponin T above 0.1 'ng/dL' or ST elevation (Fanari), positive troponin (Schmidt), not available (Finks, Cediel) (Table 2, p. 43).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality assessed with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale; mean score 7; individual scores only in Supplementary Table 2, not read (pp. 41–42).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm: a higher pooled risk of death or infarction with β-blockers; long-term follow-up 1 to 4 years (Table 1).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; eligibility was assessed by two independent investigators (p. 41).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) pooled relative risks, β-blocker vs none (pp. 40, 42; Figures 2–3, p. 44): in-hospital death 0.59 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.47), I2 0%, 6 of 407 vs 24 of 722 (Schmidt et al. excluded, no deaths); in-hospital infarction or necrosis 1.24 (0.74 to 2.06), I2 63%, 72 of 636 vs 142 of 1168; long-term death 0.79 (0.44 to 1.41), I2 26.6%, 26 of 229 vs 46 of 332; long-term infarction 0.96 (0.40 to 2.33), I2 0%, 8 of 80 vs 10 of 164. Study estimates for in-hospital infarction ranged from 0.23 (0.06 to 0.91; Dattilo) to 2.74 (1.33 to 5.61; Mohamad) and 3.23 (0.64 to 16.45; Fanari). No τ2 or prediction intervals. Egger's test P=0.201 (in-hospital death), 0.580 (in-hospital infarction), 0.737 (long-term death). Editors' re-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird on log relative risks with the heterogeneity statistic taken around the Mantel-Haenszel estimate, the method that reproduces every printed pooled estimate, interval, weight, I2 and heterogeneity P exactly from the counts in Figures 2 and 3): in-hospital infarction without Mohamad et al. 1.05 (0.64 to 1.71), I2 51%; without Mohamad and Dattilo et al. 1.17 (0.86 to 1.61), I2 0%; with Fanari et al.'s implied counts (8 of 164 vs 4 of 212) 1.26 (0.76 to 2.06), and with 264 for Mohamad et al. as well 1.26 (0.76 to 2.09); in-hospital death with Dattilo et al.'s full-cohort counts (1 of 60 vs 13 of 288) 0.53 (0.21 to 1.31), with its infarction-cohort counts as its text classifies the groups (0 of 33 vs 11 of 277) 0.55 (0.21 to 1.43) or as its Figure B draws them (1 of 33 vs 10 of 277) 0.62 (0.25 to 1.55), with Fanari et al.'s implied deaths (5 of 164 vs 13 of 212) 0.52 (0.24 to 1.13), and with the implied Fanari deaths together with Dattilo's full-cohort counts 0.48 (0.22 to 1.04), its text-classified counts 0.49 (0.22 to 1.09) or its Figure B counts 0.54 (0.25 to 1.18); none is significant.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported; a PRISMA checklist is given as Supplementary Table 1 (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four planned outcomes are reported. Individual Newcastle–Ottawa scores are only in a supplement. The long-term mortality pool uses Rangel et al.'s emergency-department contrast although the review describes its long-term analyses as based on β-blockers at discharge.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally; the authors note that few studies were available and that Egger's test could not assess publication bias appropriately (pp. 42, 45).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooled crude counts from eight single-centre non-randomized studies show no statistically significant difference in in-hospital death (RR 0.59, 0.24 to 1.47), in-hospital infarction (1.24, 0.74 to 2.06), long-term death (0.79, 0.44 to 1.41) or long-term infarction (0.96, 0.40 to 2.33), with intervals compatible with substantial benefit or harm; the heterogeneity for in-hospital infarction comes from two studies whose comparisons are biased in opposite directions (Mohamad et al., pre-admission β-blockers; Dattilo et al., where no infarction that preceded a β-blocker was counted against it).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that β-blocker treatment "in patients presenting with cocaine intoxication may not be as harmful as originally believed" (p. 40), and the conclusion that it was not associated with in-hospital and long-term death or infarction (p. 45); the discussion adds that β-blockers may be an effective option for hypertension and tachycardia caused by cocaine intoxication when other options fail (p. 45). The included studies identified recent use by urine tests and mostly did not record when β-blockers were given relative to cocaine use or to the infarction, so intoxication was not what was studied; no included study measured effectiveness against hypertension or tachycardia; and a non-significant pooled estimate from confounded crude counts is not evidence of no association. The authors list the observational design, few studies, possible small-study effects, the lack of agent and timing subgroups and varying infarction definitions as limitations (p. 45).

Rangel et al. (San Francisco), included: in-hospital infarction 15 of 151 vs 18 of 177, death 2 of 151 vs 3 of 177 (both as in Rangel et al.'s Table 3, p. 877); long-term death 18 of 149 vs 27 of 168

Espana Schmidt et al. (Int J Cardiol Heart Vasc) and Finks et al. (conference abstract, Pharmacotherapy, carvedilol at discharge), included (as extracted by Shin et al.)
