Lo et al. (Am J Med), systematic review and meta-analysis of the same question; Shin et al. say their results agree with it and that they included more studies than both earlier reviews

replication.where_it_stands: One of three meta-analyses published in 2018–2019 on the question (Pham et al., 2018; Lo et al., 2018; this review). Shin et al. say their results agree with the earlier two and that they included more studies, but do not list which studies the earlier reviews pooled, so the overlap cannot be judged from this paper. The five primary studies read for this encyclopedia (Dattilo, Mohamad, Rangel, Ibrahim, Fanari) are all inside its pooled estimates and must not be cited beside it as independent support.

funding.funder: The authors state they received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of the article (p. 45).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest (p. 45).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Internal Medicine, University of South Florida Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, and Weiss Memorial Hospital, Chicago (p. 40). Open-access article (Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial 4.0).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain (see the primary-study cards); short of that, an individual-patient re-analysis of the existing cohorts with a common time zero, one troponin definition and adjustment for the reasons for treatment, keeping apart β-blockers taken before admission, given acutely, and prescribed at discharge.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (cocaine-associated chest pain or recent cocaine use), intervention (β-blocker during admission or at discharge), comparator (none) and outcomes (infarction or necrosis, death) are stated (p. 41).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Only observational studies, explained by the absence of randomized trials on the topic (p. 45).

Three databases with search terms given, bibliographies of relevant articles, conference abstracts eligible, search within 24 months of submission; but no trial registries, content experts or grey literature, terms without individual drug names, and a language statement ('with any restriction') that is ambiguous.
Eligibility assessed by two independent investigators (p. 41).

The extraction sentence is in the passive and does not name who extracted the counts; the next sentence, on disagreements between the two investigators resolved with the co-authors, follows it under the data extraction and quality assessment heading and may cover extraction as well as eligibility, but duplicate extraction is not stated (p. 41). Judged no on that stricter reading; a yes would be arguable and would not change the overall rating. Several extraction errors are recorded on this card.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives categories and counts for the 42 full-text exclusions but no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1 and 2 give design, period, age, sex, follow-up, event counts, presentation, definition of cocaine use and infarction, agents and timing; settings, countries and doses are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, which covers selection, comparability and outcome; only the mean score (7) is in the article, with individual scores in a supplement not read; confounding by indication and the timing of treatment relative to outcome are not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects pooling of crude event counts from non-randomized studies, without using the adjusted estimates some studies reported and without justifying the use of raw data; comparisons of different exposures (home β-blockers at presentation, β-blockers before an infarction, in the emergency department, during admission, at discharge) were combined.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how study quality or risk of bias affects the pooled estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The risk of bias of the included studies is not used in interpreting the results; the discussion moves from non-significant pooled estimates to β-blockers as a possible treatment option in cocaine intoxication (p. 45).
I2 of 63% for in-hospital infarction is reported but its sources are not investigated or discussed beyond listing variable infarction definitions as a limitation (p. 45).

Egger's test reported for three outcomes (4 to 6 studies each), with the authors' caveat that the studies were too few to assess publication bias appropriately, and small-study effects listed as a limitation (pp. 42, 45). A generous yes: no funnel plot is shown and the likely size of any bias is not discussed, so a no would also be defensible; either way the overall rating is unchanged.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 45).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: four critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, pooling of crude counts across different exposure definitions, risk of bias not considered in interpretation) and two are met only in part (search, risk-of-bias tool). Beyond the instrument, the extraction has errors that bear on what the pooled numbers mean (Dattilo et al.'s death counts, Mohamad et al.'s denominator and pre-admission exposure, Rangel et al.'s long-term contrast), although the editors' re-analysis shows the pooled estimates change little when they are corrected. Citable for: the list of eight studies and their crude counts as extracted (with the corrections on this card), the pooled crude relative risks with their wide intervals, and the absence of randomized trials as of June 2018. Not citable for: β-blockers being safe or effective after cocaine use, or for anything about acute cocaine intoxication.

key_findings.finding: MEDLINE, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library were searched to 11 June 2018: 273 records (PubMed 100, EMBASE 144, Cochrane 29), 218 screened after removing 55 duplicates, 50 full texts, 8 cohort studies included (7 retrospective, 1 prospective; 7 journal articles, 1 conference abstract) with 2,048 patients.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 40); Figure 1 and Search strategy, 1st paragraph (p. 41); Results › Identification of relevant studies, 1st paragraph (pp. 41–42)
key_findings.note: The counts by database (100, 144, 29) and the 55 duplicates are read from the Figure 1 image; they are not in the PDF's text layer.

key_findings.finding: Included: Mohamad et al., Dattilo et al., Rangel et al., Ibrahim et al., Fanari et al., Schmidt et al., Finks et al. (conference abstract) and Cediel et al. (prospective). Five reported in-hospital outcomes only and three in-hospital and/or long-term outcomes (follow-up 2.7, 1 and 4 years); mean or median ages 42 to 57; mean Newcastle–Ottawa score 7.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of studies and patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure timing as classified by the review: on presentation (Mohamad), during admission (Dattilo, Ibrahim, Fanari within the first 24 h, Cediel during admission or at discharge), in the emergency department (Rangel), during admission while having chest pain or at discharge (Schmidt), at discharge (Finks, carvedilol only). Infarction definitions ranged from troponin I above 0.02 ng/mL to troponin above 1.5 ng/mL; metoprolol predominated.

In-hospital death, 5 studies (4 estimable; Schmidt et al. had no deaths): RR 0.59 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.47), I2 0%; 6 of 407 vs 24 of 722; study RRs Dattilo 0.65 (0.09 to 4.78), Rangel 0.78 (0.13 to 4.62), Fanari 0.65 (0.16 to 2.55), Cediel 0.15 (0.01 to 2.93).
key_findings.note: Study-level estimates and totals were read from the forest-plot image (rendered at 300 dpi); they are not in the PDF's text layer.

key_findings.finding: In-hospital infarction or necrosis, 6 studies: RR 1.24 (0.74 to 2.06), I2 63% (P=0.019); 72 of 636 vs 142 of 1168; study RRs Mohamad 2.74 (1.33 to 5.61), Dattilo 0.23 (0.06 to 0.91), Rangel 0.98 (0.51 to 1.87), Ibrahim 1.47 (0.83 to 2.59), Fanari 3.23 (0.64 to 16.45), Schmidt 1.01 (0.63 to 1.64).
key_findings.note: Study-level estimates, totals and the heterogeneity P value were read from the forest-plot image (300 dpi); they are not in the PDF's text layer.

key_findings.finding: Long-term death, 3 studies: RR 0.79 (0.44 to 1.41), I2 26.6%; 26 of 229 vs 46 of 332 (Rangel 0.75, 0.43 to 1.31; Finks 1.28, 0.52 to 3.13; Cediel 0.29, 0.06 to 1.38). Long-term infarction, 2 studies: RR 0.96 (0.40 to 2.33), I2 0%; 8 of 80 vs 10 of 164. Follow-up is given as a mean of 2.6 years.
key_findings.note: The 2.6 years is the mean of the three studies' follow-up times (2.7, 1 and 4 years, Table 1), not a patient-level mean. Study-level values were read from the forest-plot image (300 dpi).

key_findings.finding: Egger's test P=0.201 for in-hospital death, 0.580 for in-hospital infarction and 0.737 for long-term death; not done for long-term infarction (2 studies). The authors say the studies were too few to assess publication bias appropriately.

The authors list as limitations: only observational studies (no randomized trial on the topic), few studies, small-study effects not excluded, no subgroup analysis by agent or timing for lack of information in the studies, and variable infarction definitions.

The authors write that their results agree with two earlier meta-analyses (their references 26 and 27, Pham et al. and Lo et al.) and that theirs included more studies and separated in-hospital from long-term outcomes for the first time; which studies the earlier reviews included is not reported.

The authors describe the 2014 AHA/ACC guideline as recommending against β-blockers in acute coronary syndrome with signs of acute cocaine intoxication unless a coronary vasodilator is being given (class III: Harm), and the 2011 focused update as giving combined α/β agents a class IIb recommendation provided a vasodilator was given close in time, a recommendation absent from the 2014 guideline.

reporting_issues.issue: Dattilo et al.'s in-hospital deaths are entered as 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277 (Table 1; Figure 2A), with the denominators of Dattilo's troponin subgroup. Editors' cross-check with Dattilo et al. (read in full in this round): these are the death counts of Dattilo's full cohort, whose own mortality comparison is 1 of 60 vs 13 of 288 (p. 122). Dattilo et al. give no deaths for the troponin subgroup, and the paper is inconsistent about where admissions given a β-blocker after their infarction belong: the text says they were taken out of the β-blocker group (pp. 119, 121–122), while Figure B draws 31 of them inside the 33 (p. 120). The one death after a β-blocker was in a patient given the drug after the infarction, and 3 other deaths had no troponin measured (Table 3, p. 122), so the subgroup counts would be 0 of 33 vs 11 of 277 as the text describes the groups, or 1 of 33 vs 10 of 277 as Figure B draws them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' re-analysis: pooled in-hospital death RR 0.53 (0.21 to 1.31) with 1 of 60 vs 13 of 288, 0.55 (0.21 to 1.43) with 0 of 33 vs 11 of 277, and 0.62 (0.25 to 1.55) with 1 of 33 vs 10 of 277; the conclusion is unchanged, but the Dattilo row is not a valid extraction.

reporting_issues.issue: Mohamad et al.'s comparison is of β-blockers taken at home before presentation (timing 'on presentation' in Table 2), which the review's inclusion criterion (β-blockers during admission or at discharge, p. 41) does not cover; the denominator for patients not on β-blockers is entered as 254 (Table 1). Editors' cross-check with Mohamad et al. (read in full in this round): 364 patients, of whom 100 were on β-blockers, leave 264. Mohamad et al. measured troponin in the emergency department in only 245 of the 364 (p. 532), so both denominators include patients who were never tested; they also report an in-hospital comparison that fits the review's criterion (a β-blocker continued or started on admission, later infarction 23.3% vs 10.7%, group sizes not given; 9 of 39 continued, p. 532), which cannot be pooled from the printed figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: This study supplies the only significantly adverse estimate (RR 2.74). Editors' re-analysis: without it, pooled in-hospital infarction 1.05 (0.64 to 1.71), I2 51%; with 264 instead of 254 the pooled estimate is 1.25 (0.74 to 2.10). Leaving the study out also leaves out its in-hospital comparison, which also points towards harm (unadjusted).

reporting_issues.issue: The infarction counts of Dattilo et al. (2 of 33 vs 72 of 277) are pooled without comment on how they were formed. Editors' cross-check with Dattilo et al. (read in full in this round): only infarctions after a β-blocker count against the β-blocker group (p. 118). As the text describes the comparison, infarctions before any β-blocker, including those of admissions given a β-blocker after their infarction, were counted in the comparison group (pp. 119, 121–122; Table 2's total of 74 infarctions, p. 121, is consistent with this); Figure B (p. 120) instead draws 31 admissions given a β-blocker after their infarction inside the 33-admission β-blocker group. Either way, no infarction that preceded a β-blocker is counted against it.
reporting_issues.consequence: This estimate (RR 0.23) is biased towards benefit by design; together with Mohamad et al. it produces the I2 of 63%. Editors' re-analysis without both: 1.17 (0.86 to 1.61), I2 0%.

reporting_issues.issue: For long-term outcomes the review says studies identified patients discharged with a β-blocker (p. 42), and enters Rangel et al.'s long-term deaths as 18 of 149 vs 27 of 168. Editors' cross-check with Rangel et al. (read in full in this round): these are Rangel's deaths by emergency-department β-blocker; its discharge contrast is 14 vs 29 deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The long-term mortality pool mixes an emergency-department exposure (Rangel, 56% of the weight) with discharge exposures (Finks, Cediel).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 23% women in Ibrahim et al.'s β-blocker group. Editors' cross-check with Ibrahim et al. (read in full in this round): its Table 1 gives 67.3% men in that group, so 32.7% women.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transcription error.

reporting_issues.issue: The text lists propranolol among the β-selective agents (p. 42), repeating Dattilo et al.'s grouping, and Table 2 gives Fanari et al.'s troponin T threshold in ng/dL where every other threshold is in ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements about the predominance of selective agents are approximate. The ng/dL is Fanari et al.'s own Methods wording (p. 1803), while Fanari's Table 2 reports troponin T in ng/mL (p. 1804): the review copied a typographical error from the source.

reporting_issues.issue: The search is described as run 'with any restriction on language or publication status' (p. 41), which reads as the opposite of what was probably meant (without restriction).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether language or publication-status restrictions were applied is uncertain.

design_detail: Editorial (Annals of Emergency Medicine, Toxicology/Editorial section, 2008;51(2):130–134) by Kalev Freeman, MD, PhD (University of Vermont College of Medicine, Department of Surgery) and James A. Feldman, MD, MPH (Boston University School of Medicine, Department of Emergency Medicine), commenting on Dattilo et al. (2008), the hospital-records study of β-blockers in admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test, in the same issue (cross-reference to p. 117). Eight headed sections: the history of β-blockade for cocaine toxicity; how it became contraindicated; two myths (that chest pain after cocaine is coronary spasm, and that β-blockers after cocaine cause an unopposed α effect); practical problems with avoiding β-blockers; the potential benefit suggested by Dattilo et al.; whether a trial is warranted; and a conclusion. 56 references; no data of its own. It follows, in the same issue, Hoffman's editorial on the same article, which reaches the opposite conclusion (pp. 127–129; sc_hoffman_2008).
can_establish: What two physicians argued in print, in the issue that published Dattilo et al.: that both premises behind withholding β-blockers after cocaine use (spasm as the cause of chest pain; unopposed α-stimulation) rest on uncontrolled observations, which evidence they offered for coronary thrombosis and for β-blockade in other states of high catecholamine levels, which limitations they saw in the study, and why they judged a trial warranted.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers are safe or beneficial in hospital patients after cocaine use: the editorial reports no data, argues largely from pathophysiology and from other conditions, and two of its statements about Dattilo et al. (that patients prescribed β-blockers as outpatients were excluded; that in-hospital mortality was significantly reduced) do not match the study as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The study discussed is described as a nonconcurrent record review of patients admitted to telemetry, intensive care or critical care over 5 years with a positive urine test for benzoylecgonine (p. 132, Potential Benefit of β-Blockade?, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the 56 references were chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is the authors' selection: case reports and a review of case reports, catheterization and perfusion-imaging studies, laboratory studies of catecholamines and heart cells, trials, reviews and guidelines on β-blockers in heart failure, subarachnoid haemorrhage, surgery and myocardial infarction, and retrospective trauma studies. Two references are Feldman's (refs 30, 47). How the references were chosen is not described.

exposure.measurement: As described for the cited studies: a positive urine test for benzoylecgonine in Dattilo et al., which the editorial says does not show clinical intoxication at presentation (p. 132); nasal cocaine during cardiac catheterization in the Lange study (p. 130). No doses are given in the editorial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The editorial states that urine metabolites can be detected for days after acute use and up to 3 weeks after extremely high doses (ref 49, p. 132), and distinguishes patients acutely intoxicated with cocaine from patients with previous, possibly remote, exposure (pp. 132–133).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data). The editorial sets the evidence behind withholding β-blockers after cocaine against the evidence for β-blockers in other conditions with high catecholamine levels (p. 131).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The editorial lists unmeasured confounders in Dattilo et al.: duration of symptoms, which patients had urine tests, and time from exposure to treatment (p. 132).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcomes in the evidence cited: coronary appearance and constriction at catheterization, reversible perfusion defects on imaging, thrombus at early catheterization, blood pressure and pulse in case reports, reinfarction, ventricular fibrillation and cardiogenic shock in the COMMIT trial, survival after trauma, and myocardial infarction and death in Dattilo et al.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable. The editorial argues that systolic blood pressure and coronary constriction are end points that may lack clinical relevance for judging β-blockade (p. 131).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Second-hand figures: Rappolt et al.'s more than 50 successfully treated overdoses (refs 1–3; p. 130); the 1985 case report of one patient whose blood pressure rose from 170/118 to 180/140 mm Hg while pulse fell from 112 to 104 beats/min after propranolol (ref 5; p. 131); esmolol in 7 patients with worse hypertension in 1 and hypotension in another (ref 34; p. 131); thrombus in 9 of 12 patients catheterized within 12 hours of presentation, in a review of 114 published case reports of cocaine-induced infarction (ref 21; p. 131); in Dattilo et al., β-blockers in 60 admissions (17%), 18 of them in the emergency department, 56 given to rule out or after infarction, crude infarction 6.1% vs 26% and in-hospital mortality 1.7% vs 4.5% (p. 132); a 1975 Swedish report of β-blockers in 7 patients with advanced dilated cardiomyopathy (ref 53; p. 132).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a study. The editorial gives Dattilo et al.'s crude percentages without denominators and does not say that the β-blocker group was limited to admissions given the drug before any troponin rise; it describes the animal evidence of harm as rodent or porcine, leaving out the primate study among its own references (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results of its own: a comment arguing that the contraindication of β-blockers after cocaine rests on a single case report, surrogate end points, small series and animal models, with counter-arguments from pathophysiology, a review of case reports, perfusion imaging and other conditions with high catecholamine levels.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors write that Dattilo et al.'s results should be viewed with caution and considered hypothesis-generating (p. 132), but their conclusion goes further: for patients with acute coronary syndrome and a positive urine test who are not acutely intoxicated, clinicians should pursue the apparent beneficial effect of β-blockade, and those who withhold it only because of the urine test may be doing their patients a disservice (pp. 132–133). That recommendation rests on general acute-coronary-syndrome trials and guideline status (p. 132), not on any study of patients after cocaine use, and the line between acute intoxication and previous exposure is not defined beyond physical evidence of cocaine toxicity. Their objections to the evidence behind the contraindication (a single case, surrogate end points, small numbers, animal models) apply equally to their own counter-evidence (a review of 114 case reports, perfusion imaging, analogies with heart failure, subarachnoid haemorrhage, surgery and trauma, two retrospective trauma reviews). Their account of Dattilo et al. overstates the mortality result and misdescribes its exclusions, and, like the other editorial, it does not name the asymmetric start of follow-up rated critical on sc_dattilo_2008, though its point that time to a positive troponin depends on symptom duration touches it. Their history (the move away from propranolol began with a 1985 single-patient case report) is their account; the other editorial in the issue traces the caution to animal and catheterization studies (sc_hoffman_2008).

replication.where_it_stands: Printed beside Hoffman's editorial, this one reads the same history and the same study the other way: the contraindication is called a belief accepted as fact for more than two decades on uncontrolled observations, and a trial is called warranted. Later non-randomized record studies found no clear in-hospital difference with β-blockers (Rangel et al., 2010; Ibrahim et al., 2013) or more troponin elevation with them (Mohamad et al., 2008), and meta-analyses pooled these studies; as of 2018 no randomized trial had tested either editorial's position. Claims about effects must cite the primary studies, and the editorial's two misstatements about Dattilo et al. must not be repeated.

funding.funder: None stated (editorial).
funding.declared_conflicts: By the journal's policy all authors must disclose any commercial, financial and other relationships related to the subject that might create a potential conflict of interest; the authors stated that no such relationships exist (Funding and support, p. 133).
funding.affiliations_note: Freeman: University of Vermont College of Medicine, Department of Surgery; Feldman: Boston University School of Medicine, Department of Emergency Medicine (p. 130). 2 of the 56 references are Feldman's (perfusion imaging, ref 30; physicians' history-taking, ref 47). Supervising editor Richard C. Dart (p. 133), whose 1996 editorial on medical mythology (ref 56) the conclusion quotes; he is also named as supervising editor of the Hoffman editorial in the same issue. Available online 15 October 2007; reprints not available from the authors (p. 133). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the editorial.

what_would_settle_it: As the editorial asks, research rather than opinion for patients acutely intoxicated with cocaine: a randomized trial in hospital patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or acute coronary syndrome comparing a β-blocker (selective and combined α/β agents separately) with none from a common time zero, with blinded adjudication of infarction, reinfarction, ventricular fibrillation, cardiogenic shock and death, and blood pressure recorded after the first dose. The editors would add a predefined, measured distinction between acute intoxication and previous exposure, which the editorial draws but does not operationalize.

domains.note: An editorial: no search or criteria; 56 references chosen by the authors.

The evidence behind the contraindication is appraised (one case, surrogate end points, small numbers, delayed catheterization, animal models), and Dattilo et al. is criticized on blinding of record abstraction, urine testing and unmeasured confounding; but the authors' own supporting evidence (a review of case reports, perfusion imaging, retrospective trauma reviews, benefit in other conditions) is taken at face value, two statements about Dattilo et al. do not match the study, and two citations are wrong (the Lange study; a primate study described as rodent or porcine).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 2 of 56 references are Feldman's (perfusion imaging, ref 30; history-taking, ref 47), neither central to the argument.

Alternative explanations (Starling's law for the 1985 case; the argument that harm would appear in every state of high catecholamine levels) are offered as reasoning, and the study's results are called hypothesis-generating; but the conclusion turns them into a recommendation for patients not acutely intoxicated, and routine β-blocker use in these patients is asserted without support.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against β-blockers in hospital patients after cocaine use
domains.note: The history of the contraindication and the counter-arguments are both set out, and the question for acute intoxication is left open; but the animal evidence of harm is described as rodent or porcine (leaving out the primate study the other editorial treats as central), the propranolol catheterization result is weighed only as a surrogate, and the limits of the analogies with other conditions are not discussed. Under-represented side: evidence and arguments for harm.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the unsystematic selection and the asymmetric, partly inaccurate appraisal. Citable for: what two physicians argued in the issue that published Dattilo et al. (that the contraindication rested on uncontrolled observations, surrogate end points and animal models; that a trial was warranted; and that patients with a positive urine test but no acute intoxication should not be denied standard care for acute coronary syndrome), for their account of the history (the 1985 single-patient report), and for the specific criticisms of Dattilo et al. they raised (blinding of record abstraction, the meaning of a positive urine test, unmeasured confounding). Not citable for: β-blockers being safe or beneficial after cocaine use, a significant mortality reduction in Dattilo et al., how often β-blockers are given to these patients, or the mechanism of cocaine-associated infarction.

key_findings.finding: An editorial in the Toxicology/Editorial section by Kalev Freeman, MD, PhD (University of Vermont College of Medicine, Department of Surgery) and James A. Feldman, MD, MPH (Boston University School of Medicine, Department of Emergency Medicine), on Dattilo et al. in the same issue (cross-reference to p. 117). It reports no data of its own and has 56 references, 2 of them Feldman's (refs 30 and 47).
key_findings.locator: Section label, title, author lines and cross-reference (p. 130); supervising editor and funding statement (p. 133); reference list (pp. 133–134)

key_findings.finding: History as they tell it: in 1976 and 1977 Rappolt and colleagues (refs 1–3) advocated intravenous propranolol for cocaine toxicity after what they reported as a strikingly specific antagonism in more than 50 successfully treated overdoses in San Francisco, at a time when the first report of cocaine-related myocardial ischaemia and infarction was still to come (1982, ref 4). Propranolol was widely used for hypertension in acute cocaine intoxication until 1985, when Ramoska and Sacchetti (ref 5) urged caution because of possible unopposed α-stimulation causing paradoxical hypertension; this began the practice of withholding β-blockers in cocaine-induced acute coronary syndrome, a departure from standard care for myocardial infarction (refs 6–12). In the light of Dattilo et al., they write, the Rappolt solution may actually be correct.
key_findings.locator: Historic Use of β-Blockade in Cocaine Toxicity, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: How β-blockade became contraindicated, in their account: angiographic reports of normal coronary arteries in some patients with infarction after cocaine (refs 21–23) and clinical experiments (refs 24–26) supported coronary spasm as the dominant mechanism; an influential catheterization study by Lange and colleagues reported that in patients given nasal cocaine and then intracoronary propranolol, coronary constriction was potentiated by β-blockade, with an image of abrupt occlusion of the left circumflex artery in one participant reversed by nitroglycerin, and concluded that β-blockade probably should be avoided in cocaine-induced chest pain. Repeated in clinical reviews and successive American Heart Association advanced cardiac life support guidelines, this advice has, they say, been accepted as fact for more than 2 decades, although some authors disagree (ref 28).
key_findings.locator: β-Blockade Becomes Contraindicated, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (right column)
key_findings.note: The Lange study is cited as ref 27, which the reference list gives as a 2001 review by Lange and Hillis; the 1990 study is ref 26 (p. 134). See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Their central claim: both premises of the contraindication, that chest pain after cocaine is mainly coronary spasm and that β-blockers worsen spasm and cocaine's haemodynamic effects through unopposed α-stimulation, lack rigorous investigation and rest mainly on uncontrolled observations and clinical experience.

Against spasm as the main mechanism: early catheterizations showing normal coronary arteries were done late, before acute percutaneous intervention, so a clot that had dissolved on its own could not be excluded (in one case report cited for spasm, catheterization was done a week after admission, ref 22); acute perfusion imaging rarely shows reversible perfusion defects consistent with spasm in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (refs 30, 31); in a review of 114 published case reports of cocaine-induced infarction, a clot (thrombus) was present in 9 of 12 patients catheterized within 12 hours of presentation (ref 21); and cocaine has been reported to raise plasminogen-activator inhibitor, platelet activation and aggregability, and endothelial permeability (refs 6, 27, 32).
key_findings.locator: Myth 1: Cocaine Chest Pain=Spasm, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: The unopposed-α idea began with one patient: Ramoska and Sacchetti (ref 5) saw blood pressure rise from 170/118 to 180/140 mm Hg while the pulse fell from 112 to 104 beats/min after propranolol. Its other support, as they list it: catheterization studies in which propranolol worsened cocaine-induced constriction while labetalol, a combined α- and β-blocker, had no significant effect (ref 33); an esmolol series of 7 patients with worse hypertension in 1 and hypotension in another (ref 34); and animal models they describe as rodent or porcine (refs 35–37). They call these data limited by small numbers and model systems and argue that systolic pressure or coronary constriction may not be clinically relevant end points, since the main benefit of β-blockers in myocardial infarction is preventing reinfarction and ventricular fibrillation (ref 7). For the case itself they offer an alternative explanation through Starling's law: the slower pulse raised end-diastolic pressure and fibre length, and with them contraction and blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: Myth 2: Cocaine+β-Blocker→Unopposed α Effect, 1st paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column) and 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Their argument from other conditions: catecholamines released in a general alarm reaction stimulate both α- and β-receptors, the β-receptor mediating the harmful effects on the heart muscle (faster rate, stronger contraction, calcium overload and necrosis), yet β-blockade is described as of well-established benefit in heart failure, subarachnoid haemorrhage and the perioperative period (refs 17, 18, 40–44), and 2 large retrospective reviews associated it with better survival after severe trauma (refs 45, 46); if β-blockade caused a harmful unopposed-α response under sympathetic stimulation, they argue, it would do so in all these conditions.
key_findings.locator: Myth 2: Cocaine+β-Blocker→Unopposed α Effect, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: They state, without a figure or reference, that despite the advice patients with cocaine-triggered acute coronary syndrome are routinely given β-blockers, because illicit drug use is stigmatized and self-report is unreliable (ref 6), emergency physicians' history-taking about chest pain varies (ref 47), and urine toxicology results are not available in real time when treating an unstable patient, such as one with ST-elevation infarction triggered by cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Practical Problems With Avoiding the Potential Risk of β-Blockade, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Their summary of Dattilo et al.: a nonconcurrent record review of patients admitted to telemetry, intensive or critical care over 5 years with a positive urine test for benzoylecgonine; β-blockers in 60 admissions (17%), 18 of them in the emergency department; the commonest recorded reason was to rule out or after a myocardial infarction (n=56), which they call a very interesting result in itself; crude infarction 6.1% with vs 26% without a β-blocker, and in-hospital mortality 1.7% vs 4.5%. They report the adjusted analyses as showing a significant reduction in infarction and in in-hospital mortality, with a non-significant trend in the chest-pain subgroup, and write that the authors excluded patients prescribed β-blockers as outpatients.
key_findings.locator: Potential Benefit of β-Blockade?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' comparison with sc_dattilo_2008 (the article was not re-read here): the infarction figures are 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277, the β-blocker group limited to admissions given the drug before any troponin rise; the full-cohort adjusted odds ratio for death was 0.22 (0.02 to 2.41), not significant, with only the first-admission model significant (0.01, 0.00 to 0.33); only 15 admissions whose outpatient β-blocker was not given in hospital were excluded, and an outpatient β-blocker was a recorded reason in 21 of the 60 β-blocker admissions. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Their criticisms of the study: it is not clear that the record abstractors were blind to the hypothesis or that recommended chart-review methods were followed (ref 48), so bias in abstracting records or assigning end points is possible; a positive urine test does not show clinical intoxication at presentation, since metabolites can be detected for days after acute use and up to 3 weeks after extremely high doses (ref 49), whereas the authors infer exposure within 48 to 72 hours; whether propensity scores outperform ordinary regression is questioned (refs 50, 51), and neither can control unmeasured confounding (ref 52), such as how long symptoms had lasted (time to a positive troponin is affected by how long the chest pain has lasted), which patients had urine tests, and time from exposure to treatment. The results, they conclude, should be viewed with caution and considered hypothesis-generating.
key_findings.locator: Potential Benefit of β-Blockade?, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' note: sc_dattilo_2008 records the article as stating that benzoylecgonine is detectable above 100 ng/mL for up to 48 h; the 48 to 72 hours is the editorial's wording, not checked against the article. The other editorial in the issue gives 2 to 3 days after intermittent use and up to 2 weeks in chronic use (sc_hoffman_2008, p. 128).

key_findings.finding: On a trial, the opposite of the other editorial in the issue: some may reject one as dangerous and lacking equipoise, but they recall that in 1975 four Swedish investigators reported benefit from β-blockers in 7 patients with advanced dilated cardiomyopathy and a fast resting heart rate, a therapy physicians were reluctant to embrace until prospective trials confirmed it (refs 53, 54). They read the COMMIT trial (ref 7) as showing that β-blockers reduced reinfarction and ventricular fibrillation overall, with cardiogenic shock most frequent in elderly or haemodynamically unstable patients, and note that β-blockade remains a class I recommendation in ST-elevation and non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndromes and a core performance measure for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Neither the hypothesis of benefit after cocaine nor the belief that patients with a positive urine test must be treated differently has been tested; Hollander (ref 6) noted that there had been no controlled trials of any initial management of cocaine-associated ischaemia or infarction.
key_findings.locator: Is a Clinical Trial Warranted?, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Their conclusion, opened with a quotation from the supervising editor's earlier editorial on entrenched but inaccurate beliefs (Dart, ref 56): emergency physicians face two populations, patients acutely intoxicated with cocaine and patients with acute coronary syndrome after previous, possibly remote, cocaine exposure. For acute intoxication the case for withholding β-blockers has significant limitations and the answer should come from research and evidence, not opinion; for patients not acutely intoxicated they see no support for withholding them, write that clinicians who hesitate to give the recommended therapy only because of a positive urine test, without physical evidence of cocaine toxicity, may be doing their patients a disservice, and that for these patients clinicians should pursue the apparent beneficial effect of β-blockade.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion (p. 132, right column, continuing on p. 133, left column); supervising editor (p. 133)

reporting_issues.issue: The catheterization study described as an influential study by Lange et al. (nasal cocaine, intracoronary propranolol, the circumflex occlusion image and its authors' conclusion) is cited as ref 27, which the reference list gives as Lange and Hillis (2001), a review of cardiovascular complications of cocaine; the 1990 study of β-adrenergic blockade is ref 26, cited only within the range 24–26.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the citation reaches a review; the study is lange_1990 in this library.

reporting_issues.issue: Refs 35–37 are described as rodent or porcine models, but ref 37 (Guinn et al., 1980) is titled as a study of intravenous cocaine lethality in nonhuman primates; the other editorial in the issue counts this study among the two seminal animal experiments in which propranolol worsened seizures and death (sc_hoffman_2008, p. 127, its ref 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial's description understates the animal evidence it sets aside: the study it leaves out of its description is the one the opposing editorial treats as central.

reporting_issues.issue: The editorial says Dattilo et al. excluded patients prescribed β-blockers as outpatients in order to examine in-hospital exposure; as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008, only 15 admissions whose outpatient β-blocker was not given in hospital were excluded, and an outpatient β-blocker was a recorded reason for treatment in 21 of the 60 β-blocker admissions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial presents the analysis as isolating in-hospital exposure, which it did not; the description should not be repeated.

reporting_issues.issue: The editorial states that the adjusted analyses showed a significant reduction in in-hospital mortality; as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008, the full-cohort adjusted odds ratio for death was 0.22 (0.02 to 2.41) and the crude difference 2.8% (−1.2% to 6.7%), neither significant, only the first-admission model (0.01, 0.00 to 0.33; 12 deaths) was significant, and Dattilo et al. themselves wrote that deaths were too few for conclusions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial overstates the mortality evidence; mortality claims must cite the study's own estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The crude infarction figures (6.1% vs 26%) are given without denominators, in the same paragraph as the 60 β-blocker admissions, and without saying that the β-blocker group was limited to admissions given the drug before any troponin rise while admissions given it after an infarction were counted in the comparison group (2 of 33 vs 72 of 277 on sc_dattilo_2008).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take 6.1% as a share of all 60 β-blocker admissions; the asymmetric start of follow-up rated critical on sc_dattilo_2008 is not named.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that patients with cocaine-triggered acute coronary syndrome are routinely treated with β-blockers (the word italicized in the source) carries no reference or figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: An empirical claim the editorial does not support; it cannot be cited as evidence of practice.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion credits the study to Nordin et al. (its last author), while the rest of the editorial and its ref 13 name it Dattilo et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; risk of mis-citation.

Page 134 also carries a journal notice (Did you know?), which is not part of this source. Dattilo et al. (2008) was not re-read: statements about it are compared with its card (sc_dattilo_2008). No supplement.
verification.checked_by: AI reader 506 (round-2 check) and AI reader 511 (card adjudication)

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 506 (round-2 check): Minor: they report Dattilo et al.'s suggestion that the protective effect of β-blockade on heart muscle may matter more than its effect on the coronary arteries (Historic Use, 2nd paragraph, p. 130; refs 14–20), part of their mechanistic case, not on the card.
disagreements.resolution: Rejected (p. 130, Historic Use of β-Blockade in Cocaine Toxicity, 2nd paragraph; p. 131, Myth 2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs): the sentence reports Dattilo et al.'s suggestion accurately (Dattilo et al., 2008, Discussion, p. 124), and the editorial's case that β-blockade protects heart muscle from catecholamine injury is already key finding 6; adding it would not change what a reader of the card concludes, so it is not entered.

design_detail: Letter to the editor (Annals of Emergency Medicine, Correspondence, 2008;52(1):88–89; the letter on p. 88, right column, its one reference at the top of p. 89) by three emergency physicians of the Hong Kong Poison Information Centre, United Christian Hospital (Sze Chun Albert Fung, Yiu Cheung Chan, Fei Lung Lau), under the same title as the article it answers, Dattilo et al. (2008). Two paragraphs; no patients of its own: it recalculates the article's published counts as read from the article's flow figure. On p. 89 of the same file, the original authors' reply (headed In reply; Philip B. Dattilo and Charles Nordin, five paragraphs), which answers this letter and Mariani's, concedes that the flow figure was wrong, announces an erratum with a corrected figure and gives counts not printed in the article; its answer to this letter (1st to 4th paragraphs) is recorded here. Neither the letter nor the reply has data of its own design: the reply's counts come from the article's records. Page 88 also carries the end of an unrelated letter (Isbister et al., on citalopram) and p. 89 Mariani's letter (sc_mariani_2008); neither is part of this card.
can_establish: What three emergency physicians argued in print about how Dattilo et al. formed their infarction groups and denominators, and, from the reply printed with it, how the original authors explained those groups (55 of 60 patients given β-blockers in the infarction cohort; the denominator of 33 made up of patients given the drug before any infarction, 2 of whom then had one; patients given it after an infarction counted in the comparison group) and their concession that the flow figure was wrong.
cannot_establish: Anything about the effects of β-blockers after cocaine use: the letter reports no patients of its own, both of its calculations (troponin measured in 55% vs 96%; infarction risk 100%, 2 of 2) rest on the flow figure the original authors corrected, and the reply's counts describe how the groups were formed, not what β-blockers do.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The counts discussed are those of Dattilo et al.'s cohort of admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test (60 given β-blockers, 288 not), as the letter reads them (p. 88).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the letter's only reference is the article it answers.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The letter's first point concerns how many patients in each group had troponin measured, which decided who entered the infarction analysis (p. 88); the reply gives 55 of 60 in the β-blocker group (p. 89).
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable as a sample. The letter examines one study's arithmetic; the reply is written by two of that study's five authors in its defence.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (letter). In the study discussed, β-blocker exposure was classified by whether the drug was given before or after a raised troponin, which is the point at issue (pp. 88–89).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data). The letter and the reply concern the study's comparison group of 277, which by the reply's account included patients given a β-blocker after their infarction (p. 89).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The letter suggests, without data, that the group without β-blockers had more cardiac features prompting troponin testing; the reply points instead to the article's Table 1, in which the β-blocker group had more major cardiac problems (pp. 88–89).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcome discussed: in-hospital myocardial infarction as defined in the study (troponin-based), and which patients had troponin measured.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. The letter's recalculations from the article's flow figure: troponin measured in 33 of 60 patients given β-blockers (55%) vs 277 of 288 not given them (96%); infarction 2 of 33 (6%) vs 72 of 277 (26%); 2 of 2 (100%) if the other 31 in the β-blocker group are excluded (p. 88). The reply's counts: 55 of 60 β-blocker patients (92%) in the infarction cohort, against 96% of patients without β-blockers; the β-blocker denominator of 33 is the patients who had an infarction after the drug or in whom infarction was ruled out; patients given β-blockers after their infarction were counted in the comparison group; percentages stay 6% and 26% (p. 89). Editors' calculation from the reply with the counts on sc_dattilo_2008 (310 admissions with troponin, 38 without, 74 infarctions): 55 − 33 = 22 patients given a β-blocker after their infarction are among the 277 comparison admissions and their 72 infarctions; 5 β-blocker and 33 other admissions had no troponin, so 255 of the 288 admissions never given a β-blocker had troponin (88.5%), whereas 55 + 277 = 332 would exceed the 310 in the cohort; infarction occurred in 50 of those 255 (19.6%). Crude risk ratios (editors' calculation, log-scale Wald intervals): 0.23 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.91) for the published split, 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277; 0.31 (0.08 to 1.21) with the comparison limited to admissions never given a β-blocker, 2 of 33 vs 50 of 255. Neither split starts follow-up at the same moment in both groups.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a study. The reply answers both of the letter's points but does not say how the patients given β-blockers after their infarction (22 by editors' calculation) affect the comparison, and calls its denominator the most conservative without testing an alternative.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data of its own: two calculations from the article's flow figure (troponin measured in 33 of 60 vs 277 of 288; infarction risk 2 of 2 if 31 patients are excluded). The reply printed with it says the figure was wrong, that 55 of 60 patients given β-blockers were in the infarction cohort, and that the 33 were patients given the drug before any infarction, 2 of whom then had one, while those given it after an infarction were counted in the comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter says the limitations it found may affect the study's interpretation and conclusion (p. 88), a hedged claim; its specific calculations do not survive the reply, because they follow the mislabelled figure. The reply states that the paper's data and statistical analysis are not affected by the correction and that it used the most conservative denominator (p. 89); its own account shows that the 26% in the comparison group includes patients given a β-blocker after their infarction (22 by editors' calculation), which raises that group's rate, and that follow-up in effect starts at the β-blocker in one group and at admission in the other, the structure sc_dattilo_2008 rates at critical risk of bias. The exchange corrects the record on how the groups were formed; it adds nothing on whether β-blockers prevent infarction.

timeline.event: Dattilo et al. (February issue): infarction in 2 of 33 admissions given a β-blocker before any troponin rise vs 72 of 277 without one before the infarction; the article's flow figure labelled the groups in a way its text contradicted (reporting issue on sc_dattilo_2008)
Hoffman's editorial in the February issue criticized the study's population and exposure definition, not how its infarction groups were counted
Freeman and Feldman's editorial in the February issue noted that time to a positive troponin depends on symptom duration, but did not question how the groups were counted
Mariani's letter in the July issue, answered in the same reply

Erratum to Dattilo et al. with a corrected flow figure (Figure 1B), published with this correspondence according to the reply; not among the files and not read; its DOI is not in the project's records.

Pham et al. meta-analysis pooled the study's infarction counts as 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277, as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008, that is, with the comparison group that includes patients given a β-blocker after their infarction
Shin et al. meta-analysis pooled the same counts (risk ratio 0.23, 0.06 to 0.91), as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008

replication.where_it_stands: The exchange settles how Dattilo et al.'s infarction groups were formed, which the article's flow figure had left unclear: 55 of the 60 admissions with β-blockers had troponin measured; 33 received the drug before any infarction (2 then had one); the others, 22 by editors' calculation, received it after their infarction and were counted as infarctions without β-blockers. The meta-analyses that pooled the study used the published split (2 of 33 vs 72 of 277, as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008), so they carry this classification. The erratum with the corrected figure was not among the files.

funding.funder: None stated (letter).
funding.declared_conflicts: By the journal's policy all authors must disclose any commercial, financial and other relationships related to the subject that might create a potential conflict of interest; the letter's authors stated that no such relationships exist (Funding and support, p. 88). The reply carries no disclosure statement on p. 89; its own DOI and statement, if printed, would be on the following page, which is not in the file.
funding.affiliations_note: Letter: Hong Kong Poison Information Centre, United Christian Hospital, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China (p. 88). Reply: Philip B. Dattilo and Charles Nordin, Department of Medicine, Jacobi Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY (p. 89), two of the article's five authors answering criticism of their own study. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount either.

what_would_settle_it: On the counting question: the corrected flow figure (the erratum) with counts at each step, and a re-analysis of the same records that starts follow-up at the same moment for treated and untreated admissions (for example at arrival or at the first troponin result), excludes infarctions already present at that moment from both groups and treats β-blocker exposure as time-varying. On the clinical question: a randomized trial in hospital patients with cocaine-associated chest pain, with blinded adjudication of infarction.

domains.note: A letter about one study, its only reference; no search. It cannot be cited as an overview of the evidence.

It checks the study's arithmetic against its published flow figure and finds a real problem, which the original authors concede; but it reads the mislabelled figure literally, without checking that reading against the article's text (as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008, the text and the total of 74 infarctions show the 31 were not counted as infarctions), so both of its calculations are wrong.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None cited.

The inference of baseline differences from troponin testing is hedged (may imply; might have) but offered without data; the 100% figure is presented as a calculation rather than as conditional on the letter's reading of the figure.

domains.domain: Balance of the critique (points against and for the study's handling of its groups)
domains.note: The letter confines itself to the study's counts and states its concern conditionally; it makes no claim about the effects of β-blockers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used (METHODS §5.3), and the overall judgment follows the absence of any search, as for other letters in the library. The letter has no data of its own, and its calculations rest on a figure the original authors corrected. The reply's counts (55 of 60; the make-up of the 33; patients treated after infarction counted in the comparison group) come from the same records as Dattilo et al. and inherit that study's appraisal (ROBINS-I, overall critical, sc_dattilo_2008); they describe how the groups were formed and need no separate rating. Citable for: the original authors' account of how the infarction groups were formed and their concession that the flow figure was wrong. Not citable for: the letter's 55% vs 96% or its 100% (2 of 2), or for any effect of β-blockers.

key_findings.finding: A letter to the editor (Correspondence) by three emergency physicians of the Hong Kong Poison Information Centre, United Christian Hospital, under the same title as the article it answers (Dattilo et al., its only reference). It reports no patients of its own: it recalculates the article's published counts.
key_findings.locator: Letter (p. 88, right column); its reference (p. 89, top of the left column)

key_findings.finding: Its first point, read from the article's flow figure: troponin was measured in 33 of the 60 patients given β-blockers (55%) but in 277 of the 288 not given them (96%). The letter infers that the groups may have differed at baseline (more cardiac features prompting troponin tests in the group without β-blockers) and that such a high drop-off in the β-blocker group affects interpretation.

Its second point: the article gives infarction risk as 6% (2 of 33) with β-blockers vs 26% (72 of 277) without. Reading the other 31 patients in the β-blocker group as infarctions with a raised troponin before the β-blocker, the letter says they were excluded from the numerator but kept in the denominator; excluding them, it calculates, would make the infarction risk in the β-blocker group 100% (2 of 2).

The original authors' reply on the next page (Dattilo and Nordin, two of the article's five authors) says the letter made them realize that the article's Figure 1B did not correctly show how patients with troponin measurements were distributed in the infarction cohort; a corrected Figure 1B is published as an erratum with the letter, and they state that the paper's data and statistical analysis are not affected by the correction.
key_findings.locator: Reply, 1st paragraph (foot of the left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: Answer to the first point: 55 of the 60 patients given β-blockers (92%) were in the infarction cohort, which the authors call close to the share of patients without β-blockers in the same cohort (96%); on baseline differences, they point to the article's Table 1, in which the β-blocker group had more major cardiac problems in several respects.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with the counts on sc_dattilo_2008 (310 admissions with troponin, 38 without): 55 + 277 = 332 would exceed the 310 in the infarction cohort. With 5 β-blocker admissions lacking troponin, 33 admissions never given a β-blocker lacked it, so 255 of those 288 (88.5%) had troponin; the 96% equals 277 of 288 and counts patients given a β-blocker after their infarction (next finding).

key_findings.finding: Answer to the second point: the denominator of 33 is the patients given a β-blocker who either went on to have an infarction or had infarction ruled out (revised figure, n=33). Patients given β-blockers after their infarction were left out of it, because they were defined as infarctions without prior β-blockers, and so became part of the comparison group's denominator. The authors call this the most conservative denominator, because no patient given a β-blocker after an infarction had a second one, and keep 6% and 26%. Editors' reading: with 2 infarctions among the 33, the other 31 are patients in whom infarction was ruled out, so the letter's 100% (2 of 2) rests on the figure the authors corrected.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 55 − 33 = 22 patients given a β-blocker after their infarction are among the 277 comparison admissions and, as the reply's definition implies, among their 72 infarctions (sc_dattilo_2008). Without them, infarction occurred in 50 of 255 admissions never given a β-blocker (19.6%) against 2 of 33 (6.1%): crude risk ratio 0.31 (95% CI 0.08 to 1.21), against 0.23 (0.06 to 0.91) for the published split (log-scale Wald intervals). Counted as treated patients without a later infarction, the 22 would lower the β-blocker group's rate to 2 of 55 (3.6%), the sense in which the authors call 33 conservative. Neither split starts follow-up at the same moment in both groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter's two calculations (troponin measured in 33 of 60 vs 277 of 288; infarction risk 2 of 2 after excluding 31) follow the article's original flow figure, which the original authors say did not present the data correctly; by the reply, 55 of 60 β-blocker patients had troponin measured, and the 31 were patients in whom infarction was ruled out.
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter's 55% vs 96% and its 100% should not be cited as facts about the study; its value is that it prompted the correction and the reply's account of how the groups were formed.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply compares its 92% with 96% for patients without β-blockers, but 96% is 277 of 288, and by the reply's own account the 277 include patients given a β-blocker after their infarction; with 55 of 60 β-blocker patients in the cohort of 310 (sc_dattilo_2008), only 255 of the 288 others can be in it (88.5%; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the testing question (92% vs 88.5%, still similar, so the letter's imbalance argument fails), but the reply's figure mixes the groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply calls its denominator the most conservative, but the patients it leaves out of the β-blocker denominator are counted as infarctions in the comparison group, which raises that group's rate (72 of 277, 26.0%, against 50 of 255, 19.6%, among admissions never given a β-blocker; editors' calculation, assuming as the reply's definition implies that all 22 are among the 72).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 6% vs 26% contrast depends on where infarctions that preceded any β-blocker are counted (crude risk ratio 0.23 with the published split, 0.31 with 95% CI 0.08 to 1.21 against never-treated admissions; editors' calculation); the reply asserts, rather than shows, that the analysis is unaffected. This is the outcome-dependent classification rated critical on sc_dattilo_2008.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter carries the same title as the article it answers (Beta-blockers are associated with reduced risk of myocardial infarction after cocaine use), and so does its reference record.
reporting_issues.consequence: Risk of citing the letter for the article's conclusion, or the reverse; cite by reference id or DOI.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply speaks of patients throughout, while the article's unit of analysis is the admission (348 admissions of 296 patients, as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the reply's counts (60, 55, 33) match the article's admission counts.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Ann Emerg Med 2008;52(1):88–89, 2 pages: the letter (p. 88, right column, with its one reference at the top of p. 89) and the original authors' reply on p. 89 (answering this letter and Mariani's), read in full; both pages checked as rendered at 150 dpi. The end of an unrelated letter (Isbister et al., on citalopram) on p. 88 and Mariani's letter on p. 89 are not part of this card (Mariani's is sc_mariani_2008). The erratum with the corrected figure that the reply announces was not among the files and was not read. Dattilo et al. (2008) was not re-read: its counts are taken from sc_dattilo_2008.

design_detail: Editorial (Annals of Emergency Medicine, Toxicology/Editorial section, 2008;51(2):127–129) by one author, Robert S. Hoffman, MD (Department of Emergency Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, and New York City Poison Center), commenting on Dattilo et al. (2008), the hospital-records study of β-blockers in admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test, published in the same issue (cross-reference to p. 117). Eight running-text paragraphs without headings and 31 references; no data of its own. It traces the history of β-blockers for acute cocaine toxicity, summarizes animal, catheterization, case-series and prognosis evidence, criticizes the study's population and its definition of exposure, and argues against β-blockers in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and against a trial of them. A second editorial on the same article, by Freeman and Feldman, which reaches the opposite conclusion, follows it in the same issue (pp. 130–134; sc_freeman_2008).
can_establish: What an emergency physician of the New York City Poison Center, co-author of the prospective chest-pain studies he cites for prognosis, argued in print in the same issue against the conclusions of Dattilo et al. and against a trial of β-blockers after cocaine use, and which evidence he relied on.
cannot_establish: Whether β-blockers harm or help hospital patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or myocardial infarction: the editorial reports no data; its human evidence of harm is one catheterization study with a surrogate outcome, an esmolol series of 7 patients and one case report; the lethal interaction it invokes comes from animal studies; and its case for lack of benefit rests on low event rates in chest-pain cohorts, not on any comparison of treated and untreated patients.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (editorial). The study discussed is described as a retrospective view of patients with cocaine use admitted to telemetry or intensive care (p. 128, 7th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the 31 references were chosen by the author.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is the author's selection, and its prognosis half comes largely from his own group: 6 of the 31 references name Hoffman among their authors (refs 6, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 31), including the sources of the infarction rate, the one-year follow-up, the in-hospital mortality statement, the share of infarctions presenting within 24 hours and the only human case of harm cited. How the references were chosen is not described.

exposure.measurement: As described for the cited studies: Dattilo et al. defined cocaine exposure by a positive urine test, earlier prospective studies by a history of recent use often confirmed by urine screening (p. 128, 7th paragraph); in the catheterization studies, patients undergoing elective diagnostic cardiac catheterization were given intranasal cocaine (p. 128, 6th paragraph). No doses are given in the editorial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed, apart from tobacco smoking, named as the one common atherosclerotic risk factor of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (p. 127, 5th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The editorial states that urine is generally accepted to stay positive 2 to 3 days after intermittent use and up to 2 weeks in chronic use at the cut-off Dattilo et al. used, and that nearly 90% of documented cocaine-associated infarctions present within 24 hours of last use (p. 128, 7th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data). The editorial contrasts the admissions studied by Dattilo et al. with the prospective cohorts of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (refs 19–21) (p. 128, 7th paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcomes in the evidence cited: seizures and death (animal studies), blood pressure and pulse (esmolol series), coronary artery constriction (catheterization studies), myocardial infarction and death (chest-pain cohorts and Dattilo et al.).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Second-hand figures: esmolol in 7 patients with cocaine toxicity, with significant hypotension in 1 and an acute rise of 60 mm Hg in diastolic pressure in another (ref 7; p. 127, 3rd paragraph); myocardial infarction near 5% of patients with cocaine-related chest pain in prospective studies (refs 19, 21; p. 127, 5th paragraph), given as 5% to 6% later (p. 128, 8th paragraph); 203 patients followed a mean of 408 days after an emergency-department visit for cocaine-related chest pain: 6 deaths, all from non-cardiovascular causes as he states it (the cited paper counts 5 non-cardiovascular deaths and 1 cardiovascular; hollander_1995c, pp. 182–183), 2 non-fatal infarctions, and neither death nor infarction among patients who reported abstinence (ref 22; p. 127, 5th paragraph); nearly 90% of documented cocaine-associated infarctions present within 24 hours of last use (ref 20; p. 128, 7th paragraph); the COMMIT trial of early intravenous then oral metoprolol in 45,852 patients with acute myocardial infarction is cited for a higher risk of cardiogenic shock with early β-blockade (ref 17; pp. 127, 129). The in-hospital mortality of patients with cocaine-associated infarction is given without a figure (ref 20; p. 127, 5th paragraph).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a study. The editorial does not discuss Dattilo et al.'s results (counts or odds ratios) or how its comparison groups were formed; evidence that could favour β-blockers (randomized trials in myocardial infarction not related to cocaine, animal studies favouring β-antagonism, refs 11 and 12, and the labetalol catheterization study, ref 25) is mentioned only in passing.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results of its own: a published comment on one study, with second-hand figures from prospective chest-pain cohorts (largely co-authored by the author), one catheterization study of propranolol, an esmolol case series of 7 patients, one case report and animal lethality studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Hoffman concludes that the preponderance of evidence continues to speak against β-blockers in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain and says the authors' call for a prospective trial "seems not only premature but frankly quite dangerous" (p. 128, 8th paragraph). (1) The human evidence of harm is narrower than his wording: of the three controlled human investigations he calls compelling (refs 23–25), only the propranolol study showed a worse result with a β-blocker, by a surrogate outcome (coronary constriction during catheterization); the phentolamine study is not of a β-blocker, and labetalol was essentially without effect, as his own 6th paragraph describes them (p. 128); actual cases of harm are, he acknowledges, rarely reported, and the one cited is from his own group (ref 31); the lethal interaction he invokes was described in animals (refs 4, 5). (2) Lack of benefit is inferred from low event rates in chest-pain cohorts (infarction in 5% to 6%, in-hospital mortality approaching zero), which limits the absolute benefit available but is not a comparison of treated with untreated patients, and does not address patients with an established infarction, the commonest recorded reason for β-blockers in Dattilo et al. (56 of 60 admissions, sc_dattilo_2008), for whom he describes the randomized-trial evidence as well accepted though questioned on cardiogenic shock (p. 127, 4th paragraph). (3) He does not engage with the study's numbers or with how its groups were formed (the asymmetric start of follow-up that sc_dattilo_2008 rates at critical risk of bias); his criticisms concern the population (fewer than half with chest pain) and the exposure definition (a positive urine test). (4) His argument against a trial treats the harm suggested by surrogate and animal data as settled, which is the question a trial would answer.
