replication.where_it_stands: Hoffman's editorial and Freeman and Feldman's, printed together, read the same history and the same study in opposite ways. Hoffman's position rests on surrogate catheterization data, a 7-patient esmolol series, a case report and animal lethality studies for harm, and on low event rates in prospective chest-pain cohorts, largely from his own group, for lack of benefit; a 2010 letter he co-authored is titled Beta-blockers and cocaine: still a bad idea (identified on sc_rangel_2010; not read). Later record studies, including one restricted to chest pain (Rangel et al., 2010), found no clear in-hospital difference, and meta-analyses pooled these non-randomized studies; as of 2018 the randomized trial that Hoffman said seemed dangerous and Freeman and Feldman called warranted had not been done. Claims about effects or prognosis must cite the primary studies, not this editorial.

funding.funder: None stated (editorial).
funding.declared_conflicts: By the journal's policy all authors must disclose any commercial, financial and other relationships related to the subject that might create a potential conflict of interest; the author stated that no such relationships exist (Funding and support, p. 128).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Emergency Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, and New York City Poison Center (p. 127). Six of the 31 references name Hoffman among their authors (refs 6, 18, 19, 20, 22, 31), among them the prospective chest-pain studies behind the prognosis figures and the only human case report of harm cited. Supervising editor Richard C. Dart, who is also named as supervising editor of the Freeman and Feldman editorial in the same issue; available online 26 October 2007 (p. 128). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the editorial.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in hospital patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or acute coronary syndrome comparing a β-blocker (selective and combined α/β agents separately) with none from a common time zero, with blinded adjudication of infarction, death, malignant arrhythmia and haemodynamic deterioration, blood pressure monitored after the first dose, and time since last cocaine use recorded so that recent intoxication and remote exposure can be analysed separately. Hoffman argues that such a trial seems dangerous, which makes its safety monitoring the central design question; failing a trial, a multicentre target-trial emulation in hospital records with the same common time zero.

domains.note: An editorial: no search or criteria; 31 references chosen by the author.

The animal, catheterization and case-series evidence of harm is accepted without discussion of species, surrogate outcomes, sample size or doses, and the phentolamine and labetalol studies are counted among the compelling evidence of risk; the prognosis cohorts (largely his own) are not appraised; Dattilo et al. is criticized for its population and exposure definition, not for how its groups were formed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 6 of 31 references name Hoffman; they supply the infarction rate (ref 19, with ref 21), the one-year follow-up (ref 22), the in-hospital mortality statement and the share presenting within 24 hours (ref 20), and the only human case of harm (ref 31), that is, the prognosis half of his benefit–risk argument.

Extrapolations are stated as facts: the lethal interaction described in animals is presented as what β-blockers would do to an unpredictable subset of patients, and the danger of a trial is presented as following from the analysis, hedged only by a seems; nothing is labelled as opinion.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against β-blockers in hospital patients after cocaine use
domains.note: Evidence and arguments for possible benefit (randomized trials in myocardial infarction, animal studies favouring β-antagonism, the null labetalol catheterization result) are mentioned briefly or not weighed, and the study under discussion is criticized for its population and exposure without its results being weighed. Under-represented side: possible benefit.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The editorial is a forceful, contemporaneous comment by a toxicologist whose own prospective studies supply much of its prognosis evidence. Citable for: what Hoffman argued in the issue that published Dattilo et al. (that the study's population and its urine-test definition of exposure limit comparison with prospective chest-pain cohorts, that β-blockers offer little room for benefit where infarction occurs in 5% to 6% of patients, and that a trial seemed to him premature and dangerous), and for his account of the history and evidence behind the caution against β-blockers. Not citable for: β-blockers causing harm in patients (its human evidence of harm is one catheterization study with a surrogate outcome, a case series and a case report), or for prognosis figures, which must be cited from the primary studies (hollander_1994, hollander_1995b, hollander_1995c, weber_2000).

key_findings.finding: An editorial in the Toxicology/Editorial section by one author, Robert S. Hoffman, MD (Department of Emergency Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, and New York City Poison Center), on Dattilo et al. in the same issue (cross-reference to p. 117). It reports no data of its own and has 31 references; 6 of them name Hoffman among their authors (refs 6, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 31).
key_findings.locator: Section label, title, author line and cross-reference (p. 127); reference list (pp. 128–129)

key_findings.finding: History as Hoffman tells it: when cocaine use spread in the United States in the late 1970s, clinicians faced young, critically ill patients with an adrenergic storm (severe hypertension and fast heart rate, with agitation and hyperthermia, often going on to seizures and cardiovascular collapse). Propranolol was rapidly accepted as standard treatment, largely through the work of Rappolt and colleagues (refs 1–3), without ever being rigorously evaluated, though many patients appeared to respond; the same clinicians later added clonidine, reporting that propranolol sometimes caused hyperpyrexia, breathlessness, headache and diastolic hypertension (ref 3).

Two animal experiments, in nonhuman primates and in conscious dogs (refs 4 and 5), are described as showing that propranolol clearly made cocaine-induced seizures and death worse; management then turned to sedation and cooling, which he says often sufficed to correct all vital-sign abnormalities (ref 6, co-authored by Hoffman).

The human case evidence on β-blockers in acute cocaine toxicity is small: an esmolol series of 7 patients (Sand et al., ref 7) in which several appeared to benefit, one developed significant hypotension without a change in pulse rate, and another developed severe diastolic hypertension (an acute rise in diastolic pressure of 60 mm Hg), which Hoffman attributes, as presumed, to unopposed α-adrenergic tone. Labetalol had support from several case reports (refs 8–10), and animal results were mixed (refs 11–14).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: He sets these limited data against randomized trials of β-blockers in acute myocardial infarction involving tens of thousands of patients, adopted into national quality-of-care measures (refs 15, 16), while noting recent data raising concern that early β-blockade in myocardial infarction increases the risk of cardiogenic shock (ref 17, the COMMIT trial of early intravenous then oral metoprolol in 45,852 patients).

Prognosis figures he gives, all second-hand: myocardial infarction occurs in about 5% of patients with cocaine-related chest pain in several prospective studies (refs 19 and 21); in a follow-up of 203 patients for a mean of 408 days after an emergency-department visit for cocaine-related chest pain, 6 died, all of non-cardiovascular causes, 2 had non-fatal infarctions, and no patient who reported abstinence from cocaine died or had an infarction (ref 22); and for those who reach hospital, in-hospital mortality is described, without a figure, as within the confidence interval around zero (ref 20). Refs 19, 20 and 22 are co-authored by Hoffman.
key_findings.note: Hoffman's account of ref 22 misstates the causes of death: the cited paper, which he co-authored, counts 5 non-cardiovascular deaths and 1 cardiovascular, a cardiac arrest during a later admission for heart failure from a dilated cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol (Hollander et al., 1995c, Results › Main Outcome Parameters, p. 182; Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 183); its abstract says that none of the 6 died of myocardial infarction (p. 179). His preceding statement that mortality is attributed to noncardiac causes overstates the paper in the same way. Cite these figures from hollander_1995c, not from the editorial.

key_findings.finding: He describes patients with cocaine-associated chest pain as typically much younger than other patients with acute coronary syndromes and, apart from tobacco smoking, without other risk factors for atherosclerotic heart disease (ref 18), and says many arrive with unremarkable vital signs because several hours have passed since they last used cocaine (refs 18–20).

Catheterization evidence: in patients undergoing elective diagnostic cardiac catheterization who were given intranasal cocaine, the resulting coronary artery constriction was made worse by propranolol (ref 23), relieved by phentolamine (ref 24) and essentially unaffected by labetalol (ref 25), a model he says reinforces α-adrenergically mediated constriction as the mechanism and highlights the risks of β-blockade. With the animal studies, he says, this was enough for the American Heart Association International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation to caution against routine β-blockers in patients with cocaine use and chest pain (ref 26). He states, without a reference, that the few randomized trials enrolling patients who use cocaine do not address β-blockade.

His criticisms of Dattilo et al.: earlier prospective studies (refs 19–21) enrolled patients with cocaine use and chest pain, whereas fewer than half of this study's patients had chest pain; its mortality table reflects intensive-care and telemetry admissions for various illnesses; and exposure was a positive urine test rather than a history of recent use. Urine, he states, is generally accepted to stay positive for 2 to 3 days after intermittent use but up to 2 weeks in chronic use at the cut-off the study chose (ref 30), while nearly 90% of patients with documented cocaine-associated infarction present within 24 hours of last use (ref 20); so it is unclear how these patients compare with those in the prospective studies.
key_findings.note: Editors' comparison with sc_dattilo_2008 (the article was not re-read here): chest pain was the admission diagnosis in 165 of 348 admissions (47%), consistent with fewer than half; the urine cut-off was 300 ng/mL for benzoylecgonine. The editorial does not mention how the study formed its infarction groups (the β-blocker group limited to admissions given the drug before any troponin rise), which that card rates at critical risk of bias.

key_findings.finding: His benefit–risk argument: it is hard to suggest a cardiovascular benefit in a condition in which only 5% to 6% of patients presenting with the complaint have a myocardial infarction, those who do have an in-hospital mortality approaching zero, and those in whom infarction is ruled out survive well even if they keep using cocaine. On the risk side he calls the controlled human investigations compelling (refs 23–25) and says one case series (ref 7) shows how variable and unpredictable the interaction is, while acknowledging that actual cases of harm are rarely reported (ref 31, a case report from his own group); he concludes that the preponderance of evidence continues to speak against β-blockers in this setting.
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: On a trial: he says the authors' call for a prospective trial of β-blockers in people who use cocaine "seems not only premature but frankly quite dangerous". He argues their rationale is flawed because much of the benefit of β-blockers in acute coronary syndromes not related to cocaine comes from continued long-term use, while most patients with cocaine-associated chest pain keep using cocaine after discharge (ref 22); giving them β-blockers would, he argues, repeat a practice its pioneers abandoned nearly 30 years earlier (ref 9) and expose an unpredictable subset to the lethal interaction described in controlled animal studies (refs 4, 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The 8th paragraph calls the controlled human investigations (refs 23–25) compelling evidence of risk, but the 6th paragraph's own description shows that only one of the three tested a β-blocker with a worse result (propranolol, ref 23); ref 24 concerned phentolamine, which relieved the constriction, and ref 25 found labetalol essentially without effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editorial's human evidence of harm rests on one catheterization study with a surrogate outcome (coronary constriction), an esmolol series of 7 patients and one case report; its plural, unqualified wording overstates it.

reporting_issues.issue: The in-hospital mortality of patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction is given only as "within the confidence interval surrounding zero" (ref 20), with no deaths, denominator or interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be checked or cited from the editorial; cite hollander_1995b directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the practice was abandoned by its pioneers nearly 30 years earlier (8th paragraph) is cited to a 1988 report on labetalol (ref 9, Gay and Loper; Gay is a co-author of the 1976–1978 propranolol reports, refs 1–3), while the editorial's 1st paragraph says those pioneers added clonidine to their propranolol regimen (ref 3, 1978) and does not say they stopped propranolol.
reporting_issues.consequence: The history is not clearly supported by the sources given; the other editorial in the issue (sc_freeman_2008, p. 130) dates the move away from propranolol to a 1985 case report and argues the pioneers' approach may have been right. Cite the history, if at all, as each editorial's account.

reporting_issues.issue: The editorial says that in the one-year follow-up of 203 patients (ref 22) all 6 deaths were from non-cardiovascular causes, and that mortality after cocaine-related chest pain is attributed to noncardiac causes (p. 127, 5th paragraph); the cited paper, of which Hoffman is the second author, counts 5 non-cardiovascular deaths and 1 cardiovascular, a cardiac arrest during a later admission for heart failure from a dilated cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol, and says that one patient died of cardiovascular disease (Hollander et al., 1995c, Results › Main Outcome Parameters, p. 182; Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 183).
reporting_issues.consequence: The misstatement makes the year after cocaine-associated chest pain look more benign for the heart than the cited paper reports; the causes of death must be cited from hollander_1995c (none from myocardial infarction; 1 of the 6 cardiovascular), not from the editorial.

design_detail: Prospective observational follow-up (the authors' 'inception cohort') of patients enrolled in the emergency departments (EDs) of four of the six centres of the multicentre COCHPA chest-pain study (sc_hollander_1994) between 30 April 1991 and 29 May 1992: 214 ED visits by 205 patients with chest pain after cocaine use in the preceding week. Two died in cardiac arrest at the index visit, leaving 203 for follow-up. Contact by telephone (patient, home, workplace, two relatives, and methadone clinics, pagers or homeless shelters where known), then letters, then hospital charts, at 3, 6 and 12 months after the index visit and again one year after enrolment ended; National Death Index search for everyone lost to follow-up. Main outcomes: one-year Kaplan–Meier survival and nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI) after hospital discharge or ED release; secondary outcomes: recurrent chest pain and continued cocaine use, mostly self-reported (relatives or colleagues were also a source on chest pain, and drug use they volunteered was recorded). Outcomes are compared, unadjusted, by self-reported continued cocaine use (78 vs 52 patients) and by the diagnosis given at the index visit (ischaemic chest pain or MI vs atypical or non-ischaemic chest pain). Risk of bias is rated with ROBINS-E for the comparison by continued use; the one-year counts themselves are descriptive.
can_establish: How many deaths (6, none attributed to MI) and nonfatal MIs (2) were recorded in about a year after an ED visit for cocaine-associated chest pain among 203 patients at four inner-city US centres in 1991–1993, what the deaths were from, and how often the patients who could be asked said they kept using cocaine (78 of 130) and had chest pain again (74 of 136).
cannot_establish: That continuing cocaine use causes later death or MI, or that stopping prevents them: the comparison is unadjusted, rests on 4 deaths and 2 MIs against none, uses unverified self-report from 130 of 203 patients, and its odds ratios have intervals of 0.3–120.3 and 0.2–72.9. Nor can it give the true rate of later MI (counted only from reported or charted hospital discharges, without repeat ECGs or enzymes), outcomes beyond about a year, or rates under current troponin definitions.

sample.recruitment: ED patients identified and enrolled by study investigators before hospital admission or release from the ED, with written informed consent (p. 180). Four of the six COCHPA institutions continued with this protocol: Bronx Municipal Hospital Center, New York (from 30 April 1991), the New York City Poison Control Center (from 1 July 1991), Highland General Hospital, Oakland (from 1 January 1992) and Boston City Hospital (from 29 January 1992); all stopped enrolling on 29 May 1992 (p. 180). The abstract calls them four municipal hospital EDs (p. 179).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Anterior, precordial or left-sided chest pain not explained by local trauma or radiographic abnormalities, in patients who said they had used cocaine in the preceding week (p. 180). No other criteria are stated in this paper; the parent study's exclusions are recorded on sc_hollander_1994.
sample.demographics: The 203 patients (Table 1, p. 181): mean age 34 years (SD 9); 73% men; 83% not white (printed 'non-Caucasian'); tobacco use 86%, hypertension 19%, family history 16%, high cholesterol 5%, diabetes 4%, previous MI 5%, taking cardiac medicines 10%. Cocaine use (Table 2, p. 181; no denominator printed): smoked as crack 71%, insufflated 29%, injected 10% (23 patients, 11%, used two or more routes; one had swallowed cocaine); median 8 times a month (IQR 4–30) for a median of 5 years (IQR 2–8); median 360 minutes from last use to arrival (IQR 173–1,440); all but one used cocaine repeatedly. Index chest pain began a median of 120 minutes after use (IQR 3–720) and lasted a median of 120 minutes (IQR 30–375); substernal in 65%, described as pressure or tightness in 42%; 10 patients (5%) had MI at the index visit (p. 181).
sample.attrition: Vital status known for all 203 at a mean (SD) of 408 (117) days; clinical information from the patient or an acquaintance for 185 (91%), so 18 (9%) have vital status only (editors' arithmetic). Recurrent chest pain was known for 136 (67%) and continued cocaine use for 130 (64%) (p. 182). How many patients were traced only through the National Death Index, and whether those not reached differed from those reached, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Four of the six parent-study centres, inner-city public hospitals and a poison control centre in New York, Oakland and Boston, 1991–1992; patients willing to disclose cocaine use and to consent to a study. Enrolment is called consecutive (pp. 179, 182), but no count of eligible patients or screening log is given in this paper. The comparison by continued use includes only the 130 patients who answered the question, and leaves out the 2 deaths among patients whose later use was unknown.

exposure.measurement: Index cocaine use: self-report of use in the preceding week (the entry criterion); urine tested for cocaine metabolites only when the treating physician ordered it, positive in 99% of the 82 tested (pp. 180–181). Continued use during follow-up: the patient's own answer when reached directly; relatives and colleagues were not asked about drug use, though information they volunteered was recorded; no urine testing at follow-up (pp. 180–181, 183). How continued use was established for the 4 patients who died in the continued-use group is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Index use as in the demographics (Table 2, p. 181). Amount, frequency and route of continued use during follow-up were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Not recorded or analysed. Tobacco use 86% (Table 1); alcohol appears only as the attributed cause of one patient's dilated cardiomyopathy (p. 182); 10% injected cocaine at the index visit, and HIV complications caused 3 of the 6 deaths.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as a test condition. The 52 patients in the 'cocaine use denied' group are classified by their own report at follow-up contacts, without toxicology and without a stated time window.

comparison.controls: No external comparison group. Internal comparisons: patients who reported continued cocaine use (78) against those who said they had stopped (52) (Table 4, p. 182); index diagnosis of ischaemic chest pain or MI (39 patients, 45 visits) against atypical or non-ischaemic chest pain (164 patients, 169 visits) (Table 3, p. 182). For context the Discussion cites a retrospective study (Watson et al., 1991, published as an abstract) of 244 ED patients with cocaine-related complaints and 240 age-, race- and sex-matched patients, with no difference in survival at a median of 478 days (p. 182).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The baseline health of patients who kept using cocaine and of those who stopped was not compared: HIV infection, kidney disease, alcohol use, injection and cardiac history are not reported by group, and most deaths came from conditions the authors say were known at the index visit (p. 183). Coronary anatomy is unknown.

outcomes.instruments: Death: vital status from contact with the patient or acquaintances, hospital charts, and a National Death Index search for every patient lost to follow-up (p. 180); causes of death are given without saying whether they came from death certificates, charts or autopsy (p. 182). Nonfatal MI during follow-up: a hospitalization with a discharge diagnosis of MI, self-reported or found in charts; charts were reviewed at the end of the study for patients reporting admission to a participating hospital, and final diagnoses were confirmed for patients reporting admission elsewhere for possible cardiac symptoms (p. 181); both MIs were confirmed by CK-MB (p. 183). Recurrent chest pain and continued cocaine use: mostly the patient's own report at contact; relatives or colleagues were not asked about drug use, but what they volunteered was recorded (p. 181), and they were a source on chest pain, though not always aware of it (p. 183). Index-visit MI (10 patients): prolonged chest pain with CK-MB above the upper limit of normal; admitted patients had total CK every 8–12 hours for 24 hours, with an MB fraction when CK was raised; released patients had a CK requested and were asked to return within 24 hours (p. 180).
outcomes.validity_norms: Later MI was ascertained from discharge diagnoses and self-report; patients refused repeat ECGs, so unrecognized infarctions could not be detected, and the authors say MI, recurrent chest pain and cocaine use may all be underestimated (p. 183). CK-MB definitions, before troponin.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Late MI' is a hospital discharge diagnosis of MI after the index visit, self-reported or found in charts; 'death' is any death known from contact, charts or the National Death Index; 'recurrent chest pain' and 'continued cocaine use' are mostly the patients' own reports, with some information from relatives or colleagues (pp. 181, 183).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p<0.05 for all tests (p. 181). Seven odds ratios are reported, four in Table 3 and three in Table 4.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The same contact asked about continued cocaine use (the exposure) and about chest pain and MI (the outcomes).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive: 6 deaths among 203 patients (crude 3.0%, exact 95% CI 1.1–6.3%, editors' calculation) over a mean of 408 days; one-year Kaplan–Meier survival 98% (95% CI 95–100%); nonfatal MI in 2 (1%; printed 95% CI 0–2%; the exact interval for 2 of 203 is 0.1–3.5%, editors' calculation). Recurrent chest pain 74 of 136 (54%; 46–63%); continued cocaine use 78 of 130 (60%; 52–68%) (p. 182). Continued use against stopped (Table 4, p. 182): death 4 of 78 (5%) vs 0 of 52, odds ratio 6.3 (0.3–120.3); MI 2 of 78 (3%) vs 0 of 52, 3.4 (0.2–72.9); recurrent chest pain 51 of 68 (75%) vs 16 of 52 (31%), 6.5 (2.9–14.4), p<0.0001 (abstract, p. 179). All three odds ratios and intervals are reproduced exactly by adding 0.5 to every cell (editors' check; the uncorrected chest-pain odds ratio is 6.75). Fisher's exact test gives p=0.15 for death and p=0.52 for MI (editors' calculation). Index diagnosis ischaemic or MI against atypical or non-ischaemic (Table 3, p. 182): deaths 3 (6%) vs 3 (2%), odds ratio 3.9 (0.9–17.9); MIs 1 (3%) vs 1 (1%), 3.8 (0.4–37.3); recurrent chest pain 19 of 30 (63%) vs 55 of 106 (52%), 1.6 (0.7–3.6); continued cocaine use 19 of 26 (73%) vs 59 of 104 (57%), 2.0 (0.8–5.0); no difference significant.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted comparisons and an unadjusted Kaplan–Meier analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: when the deaths and MIs occurred (no Kaplan–Meier curve), the cause of each death by group, and how follow-up time was measured. The abstract gives the p-value for chest pain and says that no MI or death was reported in patients who claimed to have stopped, but not the non-significant odds ratios for death and MI, nor the 2 deaths in patients whose later use was unknown (p. 179).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. The authors state that the sample size prohibits firm conclusions about the effect of continued use on morbidity and mortality (p. 183); with 6 deaths and 2 MIs the comparisons have almost no power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 203 patients who survived an ED visit for chest pain after cocaine use, 6 died over a mean of 408 days, none from MI: 3 from HIV complications, 1 from end-stage renal disease with multiorgan failure, 1 from sepsis, and 1 from cardiac arrest during a hospitalization for heart failure from a dilated cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol. Two had a nonfatal MI. Of those who could be asked, 60% said they kept using cocaine, and they reported chest pain again far more often (75% vs 31%). Both MIs and 4 of the 6 deaths were in patients who reported continued use, the other 2 deaths in patients whose use was unknown, and the differences in death and MI were not statistically significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion say that later risk of MI and death appears low and that urgent evaluation of coronary anatomy or stress testing may not be necessary once MI is ruled out (pp. 179, 183). The MI count rests on reported or charted admissions without repeat testing, so it is a minimum, and the statement about testing is a judgment, not a tested strategy. A 'low' risk of death has no comparison: no expected rate for people with a mean age of 34 is given, and 5 of the 6 deaths were not cardiovascular, so what the data suggest is a low rate of cardiac death, not of death. The abstract's statement that no MI or death was reported in patients who claimed to stop (p. 179) is literally true but invites a causal reading that the limitations section disclaims (p. 183), while that section still says that patients who continue appear to be at increased risk. Most deaths came from illnesses the authors say were known at the index visit (p. 183), so their link with continued use cannot be separated from baseline health.

timeline.event: Parent study (COCHPA): 246 enrolments with cocaine-associated chest pain at six EDs, MI in 14 by CK-MB criteria (5.7%); this follow-up continues at four of its six centres
This one-year follow-up of 203 patients: 6 deaths, none from MI; 2 nonfatal MIs; both MIs and 4 of the deaths in patients who reported continued cocaine use, 2 deaths with unknown use

The same group's series on mortality and complications of cocaine-associated MI; this paper cites the group's earlier abstract on the subject (ref. 37) for the statement that deaths are very rare and complications occur soon after presentation (p. 183)

Hoffman's editorial on β-blockers after cocaine, by a co-author of this study, summarizes it as 203 patients with 6 deaths, all from non-cardiovascular causes (Hoffman, 2008, p. 127, 5th paragraph); this paper counts 5 non-cardiovascular deaths and 1 cardiovascular (pp. 182–183)

Single-centre observation-unit cohort of lower-risk patients with 30-day follow-up; it summarizes this paper as finding death or nonfatal MI only in patients who continued to use cocaine (Weber et al., 2003, p. 516, as recorded on sc_hollander_1994), which leaves out the 2 deaths with unknown cocaine use

San Francisco hospital cohort of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain followed for a median of 972 days: 45 deaths among 328 patients (18 of 151 given a beta-blocker, 27 of 177 not), as entered by Lo et al. (2019, Figure 2) and described there (PDF p. 8)

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no direct replication of a one-year follow-up after cocaine-associated chest pain was read for this card. This paper is the source of the statement that death and MI are uncommon in the year after an ED visit for cocaine-associated chest pain once MI has been ruled out; its counts are small (6 deaths, 2 nonfatal MIs among 203), from 1991–1993, with later MI ascertained only through reported or charted admissions. Its finding that every recorded MI and most deaths occurred in people who kept using cocaine is a crude count of 6 events, and summaries saying that all deaths were in people who continued are not exact (2 of 6 had unknown use); nor are summaries saying that all 6 deaths were non-cardiovascular (Hoffman, 2008, p. 127), since the authors count one cardiovascular death (pp. 182–183). A later San Francisco cohort recorded many more deaths over a longer follow-up (45 of 328 over a median of 972 days, as pooled by Lo et al., 2019), so the low mortality here should not be generalized beyond its period, setting and follow-up length.

funding.funder: Funded in part by a grant from Genentech (Acknowledgments, p. 179).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the emergency departments of SUNY Stony Brook, New York University and the New York City Poison Control Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine and Bronx Municipal Hospital Center, Highland General Hospital (Oakland), and Boston University and Boston City Hospital; a statistical consultant is acknowledged; presented at the 1993 joint annual meeting of the North American poison-control and clinical-toxicology bodies in New York (p. 179). The funder's interest in the question is not stated; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multicentre cohort of consecutive ED patients with cocaine-associated chest pain, with a screening log, followed for at least a year by linkage to hospital and death records (causes of death from certificates and records), with troponin-based MI definitions, repeated measurement of cocaine use by self-report and toxicology, baseline HIV status, kidney disease, alcohol and other drug use and cardiac risk recorded, and adjusted comparisons of death and MI between people who continue and people who stop using cocaine, reported as absolute risks.

domains.note: Crude comparison with no adjustment and no baseline comparison of the patients who kept using and those who stopped. The deaths came mostly from HIV complications (3), renal failure (1) and sepsis (1), conditions the authors say were known at the index visit, and one from an alcohol-attributed cardiomyopathy; with 4 deaths against none, any imbalance in baseline illness, injection or alcohol use could produce the difference.

Continued use is mostly the patient's unverified report at follow-up contacts, with no time window and no toxicology; relatives were not asked, though drug use they volunteered was recorded (p. 181); how the 4 patients who died were classified is not stated.

Only the 130 of 203 patients (64%) with a known answer enter the comparison; being reachable and answering is plausibly related to both continued use and outcome, and the 2 deaths with unknown use are left out.
No information on care after the index visit (cardiac medicines, HIV care, drug treatment), which may have differed between those who kept using and those who stopped.
Exposure missing for 36% and recurrent chest pain for 33% of the cohort; no analysis of whether patients with missing data differed.

Death ascertainment is fairly complete (contact, charts, National Death Index); MI only through reported or charted admissions without repeat testing; recurrent chest pain, the only significant result, is reported mostly by the same patients in the same contacts as their cocaine use (sometimes by relatives or colleagues), with no blinding.

No protocol; the outcomes named in the Methods are reported, but not the timing of deaths; Table 3 uses visits as denominators for patient outcomes; the abstract reports the significant chest-pain result and the zero events in those who stopped, without the non-significant odds ratios.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E was applied to the study's exposure comparison, outcomes by self-reported continued cocaine use (Table 4). That comparison is crude, rests on 6 events, includes 64% of the cohort, classifies exposure by unverified self-report and cannot separate continued use from the illnesses (HIV, renal failure, sepsis) that caused most deaths, so it is at very high risk of bias. The descriptive one-year counts are a separate matter: vital status was traced for all 203 patients (contact, charts and a National Death Index search), so the count of 6 deaths is reasonably complete for its time, while the 2 nonfatal MIs are a minimum. It may be cited for: the number and causes of deaths (6 of 203, none from MI) and the number of nonfatal MIs (2 of 203) in about a year after an ED visit for cocaine-associated chest pain in 1991–1993, with their ascertainment limits; and for how often patients reported continued cocaine use (78 of 130) and recurrent chest pain (74 of 136). It should not be cited for an effect of continued use or of stopping on death or MI, for the safety of any discharge or testing strategy, or for MI rates under current definitions.

key_findings.finding: 205 patients made 214 ED visits with chest pain after cocaine use at the four centres; 2 arrived in cardiac arrest and died within 8 hours of their first visit, so 203 were followed after leaving hospital or the ED.

Who was followed: mean age 34 years (SD 9), 73% men, 83% not white, 86% smoked tobacco, 19% had hypertension and 5% a previous MI. Cocaine was smoked as crack by 71%, insufflated by 29% and injected by 10%, a median of 8 times a month for a median of 5 years; of the 82 patients whose urine was tested, 99% had cocaine metabolites. At the first visit chest pain began a median of 120 minutes after use (IQR 3–720) and lasted a median of 120 minutes (IQR 30–375); patients arrived a median of 360 minutes after last use (IQR 173–1,440); 10 patients (5%) had an MI then.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Table 2; Results › Index Presentation, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 2 and the count of index MIs give no denominator; the Statistical Analysis section says cocaine-use patterns were analysed per visit (214), so these percentages may count repeat visitors more than once. The upper quartile of 1,440 minutes reads as 't .440' in the OCR text layer; it was read on the rendered page and a 300-dpi crop of Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up ran through telephone calls to the patient, home, workplace and two relatives (and methadone clinics, pagers or homeless shelters where known), then letters, then hospital charts for repeat visits, at 3, 6 and 12 months after the first visit and again one year after enrolment ended on 29 May 1992; the National Death Index was searched for everyone lost to follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Population and Setting, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Follow-up, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Whether each patient was alive was known for all 203, at a mean of 408 days (SD 117); fuller clinical information, from the patient or an acquaintance, was available for 185 (91%).
key_findings.note: If every patient was followed to one year after the end of enrolment, no one would have less than 365 days; a mean of 408 days with an SD of 117 is hard to reconcile with that, and the range is not reported (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Six of the 203 died during follow-up and none of the deaths was from a heart attack: 3 died of complications of HIV disease, 1 of end-stage kidney disease with multiorgan failure, 1 of sepsis, and 1 of cardiac arrest while in hospital for heart failure caused by a dilated cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol use. One-year Kaplan–Meier survival was 98% (95% CI 95–100%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 179); Results › Main Outcome Parameters, 1st paragraph (p. 182)
key_findings.note: Crude, 6 of 203 is 3.0% (exact 95% CI 1.1–6.3%, editors' calculation) over a mean of 408 days. When the deaths occurred is not reported, and the paper does not say whether the causes came from death certificates, charts or autopsy. The authors count 5 of the deaths as non-cardiovascular and the cardiac arrest as the one cardiovascular death (p. 182; Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 183); an editorial by a co-author later called all 6 non-cardiovascular (Hoffman, 2008, p. 127).

key_findings.finding: Two patients (1%) had a nonfatal heart attack during follow-up, both confirmed by CK-MB; the printed 95% CI is 0–2%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Main Outcome Parameters, 1st paragraph (p. 182); Limitations and Future Questions, 3rd paragraph (p. 183)
key_findings.note: For 2 of 203 the exact 95% interval is 0.1–3.5% (editors' calculation); the printed interval is a normal approximation cut at zero. Later MI counted only if a hospital discharge diagnosis of MI was reported by the patient or found in charts, and patients refused repeat ECGs, so the authors say further MIs may have gone undiagnosed (p. 183).

key_findings.finding: Most patients who could be asked kept using cocaine: 78 of 130 (60%; 95% CI 52–68%). Chest pain came back in 74 of the 136 asked (54%; 46–63%).

Patients who said they kept using cocaine reported chest pain again much more often than those who said they had stopped: 51 of 68 (75%) vs 16 of 52 (31%), odds ratio 6.5 (95% CI 2.9–14.4); p<0.0001 in the abstract. Ten patients known to be still using could not be asked about chest pain.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 179); Table 4 and its footnote (p. 182); Results › Secondary Outcome Parameters, 3rd paragraph (p. 182)
key_findings.note: Odds ratio reproduced by adding 0.5 to every cell (editors' check; uncorrected 6.75). Exposure and outcome are mostly the patients' own reports at the same follow-up contacts, without toxicology or blinding; relatives or colleagues were also a source on chest pain, though not always aware of it (p. 183), and drug use they volunteered was recorded (p. 181).

key_findings.finding: Both heart attacks and 4 of the 6 deaths were among the 78 patients who said they kept using cocaine; no MI or death was recorded among the 52 who said they had stopped; the other 2 deaths were in patients whose later cocaine use could not be assessed. The differences were not statistically significant: death 4 of 78 (5%) vs 0 of 52, odds ratio 6.3 (95% CI 0.3–120.3); MI 2 of 78 (3%) vs 0 of 52, odds ratio 3.4 (0.2–72.9).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Secondary Outcome Parameters, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Fisher's exact p=0.15 for death and p=0.52 for MI (editors' calculation); with an empty cell the printed odds ratios are products of the 0.5 correction. Which causes of death fell in which group is not reported.

key_findings.finding: The diagnosis given at the first visit was not significantly associated with later events (the authors write that the one-year outcome does not appear related to it): ischaemic chest pain or MI (39 patients, 45 visits) vs atypical or non-ischaemic chest pain (164 patients, 169 visits): deaths 3 (6%) vs 3 (2%), odds ratio 3.9 (0.9–17.9); MIs 1 (3%) vs 1 (1%), 3.8 (0.4–37.3); recurrent chest pain 19 of 30 (63%) vs 55 of 106 (52%), 1.6 (0.7–3.6); continued cocaine use 19 of 26 (73%) vs 59 of 104 (57%), 2.0 (0.8–5.0). The authors report no statistically significant difference, and 3 of the 6 deaths in each group.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and Results › Secondary Outcome Parameters, 2nd paragraph (p. 182); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 183)
key_findings.note: The death and MI odds ratios are reproduced only with visits (45 and 169) as denominators; per patient the deaths were 3 of 39 (7.7%) vs 3 of 164 (1.8%), Fisher's exact p=0.09 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that after a standard rule-out of MI an aggressive search for coronary disease (urgent coronary imaging or stress testing) may not be necessary, that these patients do not appear to be at high risk of MI or death over the following year, and that more emphasis should go on stopping cocaine use.

The authors' own limits: the sample is too small for firm conclusions about continued use; further nonfatal MIs may have gone undiagnosed because patients refused repeat ECGs; relatives did not always know about chest pain; no repeat urine tests were done; so recurrent chest pain, MI and cocaine use may all be underestimated. They call for larger cohort or case-control studies over several years.

As earlier evidence the authors cite their own summary of 24 published cases of cocaine-induced MI (median follow-up 4.5 months: 12 with recurrent ischaemic chest pain, 8 with a second MI) and a retrospective study (Watson et al., 1991, an abstract) of 244 ED patients with cocaine-related complaints and 240 matched patients, with no difference in survival at a median of 478 days.

reporting_issues.issue: Patients were to be followed until one year after enrolment ended on 29 May 1992 (pp. 179–180), which would give everyone at least 365 days and, since the Bronx centre enrolled from April 1991, a mean well above a year (editors' inference); yet follow-up is reported as a mean of 408 days with an SD of 117 (p. 182), which implies that a sizeable share had less than a year unless the distribution was extremely skewed. The range, the definition of follow-up time and the follow-up date for patients traced only through the National Death Index are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the cohort may have had less than a year of follow-up, so the 'one-year' counts may cover a shorter period for some patients; the 98% Kaplan–Meier survival cannot be checked without the timing of the deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 reports patient-level outcomes (deaths, MIs) with odds ratios that are reproduced only with the numbers of visits (45 and 169) as denominators, not the numbers of patients (39 and 164) (editors' recomputation); the death percentage in the ischaemic group (6%) matches neither 3 of 39 (7.7%) nor 3 of 45 (6.7%); and the visit total (45 + 169 = 214) includes the index visits of the 2 patients who died in the ED, who are not among the 203 patients in the same table (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The index-diagnosis comparison mixes units. Per patient the death difference is 3 of 39 vs 3 of 164 (Fisher's exact p=0.09, editors' calculation): still not significant, but larger than the printed odds ratio suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% interval for nonfatal MI is printed as 0–2% (pp. 179, 182); for 2 events among 203 patients the exact binomial interval is 0.1–3.5% (editors' calculation), so the printed upper limit is too low.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite 2 of 203 with the exact interval, which allows a later-MI rate up to about 3.5%, more if MIs were missed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 places 4 of the 6 deaths in the 'cocaine use admitted' group (n=78), but continued use was established by asking the patient directly, relatives were not asked, and no urine was tested at follow-up (pp. 180–181, 183); how continued use was established for patients who died is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure classification of the deaths that drive the comparison is unexplained; it may rest on an earlier contact or on information that relatives volunteered.

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratios in Tables 3 and 4 are all reproduced by adding 0.5 to every cell (editors' check), which the Statistical Analysis section does not mention, and the text prints the chest-pain interval as 2.9–14.4% with a percent sign (p. 182).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor where no cell is empty; where a cell is zero (death and MI in Table 4) the printed odds ratios of 6.3 and 3.4 are products of the correction rather than estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes four municipal hospital EDs (p. 179), but one of the four participating centres is the New York City Poison Control Center (p. 180), and where its patients were seen is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the setting of part of the cohort is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Cross-paper check: the parent study gives enrolments at these four centres of 99, 13, 57 and 45 (Hollander et al., 1994, Appendix A, as recorded on sc_hollander_1994), which sum to 214, the number of ED visits reported here, made by 205 patients (p. 181) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The parent study's denominator of 246 'patients' appears to count visits, so some people may be counted more than once in its MI proportion (14 of 246); claims citing it should say enrolments or visits.

The OCR text contains errors (for example the plus-minus sign read as '?', '29%' as '29 70', '55/106' as '551106', '1,440' as 't .440'), so every number was read on 150-dpi renderings of each page, and Tables 1–4 again on 300-dpi crops.

The authors report no statistically significant difference, and 3 of the 6 deaths in each group.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 506 (round-2 check): Several fields call recurrent chest pain and continued use the patients' own reports (design_detail; outcomes.operationalization; key finding 7 note), but drug-use information volunteered by secondary contacts was recorded (p. 181), secondary contacts were a source on chest pain though not always aware of it (p. 183), and clinical information came from the patient or an acquaintance (185; p. 182).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading pp. 180–181 (Methods › Follow-up, 4th paragraph), p. 182 (Results › Long-term Follow-up: clinical information from the patient or an acquaintance for 185) and p. 183 (Limitations, 3rd paragraph): these fields now say mostly the patients' own reports, with some information from relatives or colleagues; both risk-of-bias judgments stay high.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 506 (round-2 check): Timeline: Hoffman (2008, p. 127), a co-author of this study, summarizes it as 6 deaths all from non-cardiovascular causes; this paper counts one cardiovascular death (pp. 182–183).
