design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Mantel–Haenszel risk ratios, random effects, as labelled on the forest plots) of retrospective hospital cohorts comparing patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were or were not given a beta-blocker. Ovid MEDLINE In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase and the Ovid Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to July 2018 (the text says five databases and names four), with controlled vocabulary and keywords such as cocaine, chest pain and beta blocker, no language restriction, human studies only. 508 records; 12 studies examined further; 2 excluded because they were abstracts and 5 for not meeting the outcome criteria. Five cohorts pooled: Dattilo et al. 2008, Rangel et al. 2010, Ibrahim et al. 2013, Fanari et al. 2014 and Schmidt et al. 2015; 1,447 patients (536 given a beta-blocker, 911 not). Two outcomes, both described as in-hospital: myocardial infarction (MI; 5 studies) and all-cause mortality (4 studies plotted, 3 estimable; Ibrahim 2013 has no row). Read from the version of record (Am J Med 2019;132(4):505–509) and compared word by word with the accepted manuscript from which the card was first written; no number, table or figure value, conclusion or limitation differs between the two.
can_establish: That pooling the crude event counts of five retrospective hospital cohorts published 2008–2015 gives no statistically significant difference in recorded MI (risk ratio 1.08, 0.61–1.91) or death (0.75, 0.46–1.24) between patients with cocaine-associated chest pain who were and were not given a beta-blocker, with intervals that include both appreciable benefit and appreciable harm.
cannot_establish: That beta-blockers are safe, or harmful, after cocaine use: the pooled data are unadjusted counts from non-randomized records in which clinicians chose whom to treat; the in-hospital mortality pool takes 80.6% of its weight from one study's long-term deaths; the included studies were not appraised; no analysis by agent was done, so the statements about labetalol and metoprolol rest on no pooled data; and the one cohort that reported harm was not pooled.

sample.recruitment: Search of four Ovid databases (MEDLINE In-Process and Other Non-Indexed Citations, MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) from inception to July 2018, with controlled vocabulary and keywords such as cocaine, chest pain and beta blocker; no language restriction; human studies only (p. 506, Methods). No reference-list, trial-registry or grey-literature searching is reported. All pooled studies are retrospective hospital-record cohorts (Table, p. 508); their countries and settings are not given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No eligibility criteria are stated beyond the topic (patients with cocaine-associated chest pain treated with or without beta-blockers) and the two end-points (pp. 505–506). Excluded among the 12 articles screened further: 2 abstracts and 5 studies that did not meet the outcome criteria, not listed by name (Figure 1, p. 506). The Discussion names three prospective or randomized studies that could not be pooled for lack of MI and mortality data (Lange et al., 1990; Boehrer et al., 1993; Hoskins et al., 2010) and one retrospective cohort whose data were judged insufficient to derive odds ratios (Mohamad et al., 2008) (pp. 506–507).
sample.demographics: The Table (p. 508; Table 1 in the accepted manuscript): Dattilo et al. 2008, retrospective, n=348, mean age 44, 61% men; Rangel et al. 2010, retrospective, n=331, mean age 50, 70% men, 75% African American; Ibrahim et al. 2013, retrospective, n=378, mean age 45, 72% men, 78% African American; Fanari et al. 2014, retrospective propensity-matched, n=376, mean age 44, 72% men, 78% African American; Schmidt et al. 2015, retrospective with paired or matched controls, n=378, mean age 49, 91% men, 50.35% African American, 44% Hispanic. Agents among treated patients: metoprolol 45% to 85%, labetalol 8% to 27%, carvedilol 8% to 27%, atenolol 1% to 8%, propranolol 1% to 8% (Dattilo et al.: metoprolol, atenolol or propranolol 66%, labetalol or carvedilol 21%, both 13%). The authors note that most participants were African American men (Limitations, p. 508).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the cohorts is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A keyword search of four Ovid databases (five stated), with no reference-list, trial-registry or grey-literature search; abstracts excluded; how screening and selection were done is not described. The one retrospective cohort that reported more MI with beta-blockers (Mohamad et al., 2008) was not pooled because its data were judged insufficient to derive odds ratios (p. 507), although both other meta-analyses on the question pooled it (sc_pham_2018, sc_shin_2019). All pooled cohorts are records in which clinicians chose whom to treat.

exposure.measurement: As each cohort recorded it: a beta-blocker started in the emergency department (ED) or within the first 24 hours of admission in all included studies (p. 506). One study excluded patients already taking a beta-blocker and the other four gave no information on prior use (p. 506), yet the Discussion says that 44% of Fanari's patients were on a beta-blocker when they arrived (p. 507), most likely a misdescription: Fanari et al. describe these 164 patients (44%) as given a beta-blocker in the first 24 hours (Fanari et al., 2014, p. 1803). How each study established recent cocaine use is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted beyond the share of each agent per study (Table, p. 508); no dose, route or timing, and no analysis by agent.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the timing of cocaine use relative to presentation was not extracted.

comparison.controls: Patients in the same cohorts with cocaine-associated chest pain who were not given a beta-blocker.
comparison.matching: None at review level: raw counts were pooled, although two of the pooled studies are described as propensity-score analyses (Dattilo et al., propensity-matched odds ratio for MI 0.08, 0.01–0.65; Fanari et al., a propensity-matched cohort of 376) (p. 507; Table, p. 508).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Confounding by indication: the review notes that treated patients in Ibrahim et al. and Fanari et al. had more diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, higher TIMI scores and more severe coronary disease (pp. 507–508); nothing is adjusted at review level. Prior beta-blocker use, the timing and amount of cocaine, and other treatments are unknown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed; all patients had cocaine-associated chest pain, so the contrast is a treatment decision.

outcomes.instruments: As each study defined them; the review gives no definitions. MI (the Table describes troponin outcomes for Ibrahim et al. and Schmidt et al.); all-cause mortality, described as in-hospital (pp. 505, 506).
outcomes.validity_norms: The risk of bias or quality of the included studies was not assessed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Not associated with adverse clinical outcomes' means no statistically significant pooled risk ratio for MI or all-cause mortality.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: two pooled outcomes; no subgroup, sensitivity or publication-bias analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Whether screening and data extraction were done in duplicate is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mantel–Haenszel random-effects risk ratios (Figure 2, p. 507). MI, 5 studies: 51 of 536 (9.5%) with a beta-blocker vs 119 of 911 (13%) without; risk ratio 1.08 (95% CI 0.61–1.91), tau² 0.20, Chi² 8.12 on 4 df (P=0.09), I² 51%, Z=0.26 (P=0.79). Study rows: Dattilo 2008, 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277, 0.23 (0.06–0.91), weight 12.5%; Rangel 2010, 15 of 151 vs 18 of 177, 0.98 (0.51–1.87), 27.5%; Ibrahim 2013, 22 of 162 vs 20 of 213, 1.45 (0.82–2.56), 29.9%; Fanari 2014, 5 of 164 vs 2 of 212, 3.23 (0.64–16.45), 9.6%; Schmidt 2015, 7 of 26 vs 7 of 32, 1.23 (0.49–3.06), 20.5%. All-cause mortality, 3 estimable studies (Schmidt 2015, 0 of 26 vs 0 of 32, not estimable): 22 of 374 (5.9%) vs 46 of 698 (6.6%); risk ratio 0.75 (0.46–1.24), tau² 0.00, Chi² 0.09 on 2 df (P=0.96), I² 0%, Z=1.11 (P=0.27). Study rows: Dattilo, 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277, 0.65 (0.09–4.78), 6.2%; Rangel, 18 of 151 vs 27 of 177, 0.78 (0.45–1.36), 80.6%; Fanari, 3 of 164 vs 6 of 212, 0.65 (0.16–2.55), 13.2%. Editors' recomputation (Mantel–Haenszel random effects with the DerSimonian–Laird variance) reproduces every printed estimate, interval, weight and heterogeneity statistic. Editors' re-analyses: MI without Dattilo 1.29 (0.88–1.88), I² 0%; MI with Fanari's implied counts (8 of 164 vs 4 of 212) 1.11 (0.64–1.93); mortality with Rangel's in-hospital deaths (2 of 151 vs 3 of 177, as recorded on sc_shin_2019 and sc_pham_2018), 6 of 374 vs 22 of 698 deaths, 0.68 (0.26–1.77); adding Fanari's implied deaths (5 of 164 vs 13 of 212), 0.57 (0.25–1.27). None is statistically significant. No prediction interval, absolute risk difference or number needed to treat is given.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or reporting checklist is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The two stated outcomes are reported with full forest plots. The Clinical Significance box (headed Bullet points in the accepted manuscript) and the Discussion add conclusions about labetalol and metoprolol that no pooled analysis supports (pp. 506, 508). The excluded studies are not listed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 170 MIs and 68 deaths in the pools (28 deaths if Rangel's in-hospital counts are used; editors' arithmetic); the intervals include both appreciable benefit and appreciable harm.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Crude counts from five retrospective cohorts show no statistically significant difference in recorded MI (risk ratio 1.08, 0.61–1.91; study estimates from 0.23 to 3.23, I² 51%) or death (0.75, 0.46–1.24) between patients given and not given a beta-blocker. Most of the deaths, and 80.6% of the mortality weight, come from one cohort's long-term follow-up rather than from hospital stays.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the review "suggests that beta-blocker use is not associated with adverse clinical outcomes" (p. 505), and the Discussion that the suggested ill effects of beta-blockers after cocaine use are not borne out by existing evidence (p. 508): a null result from unadjusted non-randomized counts, with an upper MI limit of 1.91, cannot show the absence of harm. The Clinical Significance box and the Discussion say labetalol seems, or appears, to have the strongest safety evidence, the Discussion because it was tested prospectively among the included studies (pp. 506, 508), but none of the pooled studies is prospective, and the two prospective labetalol studies (15 and 90 patients, with haemodynamic outcomes) were excluded for lacking MI and mortality data (pp. 506–507); metoprolol is said to appear safe with a pointer to the Table, which only lists how often each agent was used, and to the five pooled studies, which the review did not analyse by agent. The review calls itself the first meta-analysis on the question (p. 506) and does not cite Pham et al. (2018). Its suggestion that beta-blockers may have been protective because treated patients had higher baseline risk (p. 508) is untested and reads confounding by indication as benefit. The mortality called in-hospital is mostly long-term mortality.

timeline.event: Catheterization-laboratory study of 30 patients: intracoronary propranolol given after intranasal cocaine further potentiated cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction (as described by Lo et al., pp. 506–507); not pooled, no MI or mortality data

Catheterization-laboratory study of 15 patients: labetalol given after intranasal cocaine lowered blood pressure without further reducing coronary artery area (as described by Lo et al., p. 507); not pooled
Dattilo et al., pooled in all three meta-analyses (Pham et al., this review, Shin et al.) with the same rows: MI 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277; deaths 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277

Mohamad et al., the one cohort reporting more MI with beta-blockers (14% vs 4.4% with beta-blockers taken before arrival): not pooled here (data judged insufficient), pooled by Pham et al. (2018) and Shin et al. (2019)

Rangel et al., pooled in all three; its long-term deaths (18 vs 27) enter this review's in-hospital mortality pool with 80.6% of the weight, whereas Pham et al. and Shin et al. pooled its in-hospital deaths (2 vs 3, per sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019)

Hoskins et al., prospective cohort of 90 patients with cocaine-related acute coronary syndrome given labetalol or diltiazem: similar falls in blood pressure and heart rate, no adverse cardiopulmonary effects (as described by Lo et al., p. 507); not pooled
Ibrahim et al., pooled in all three (this review enters 213 patients without a beta-blocker where Pham et al. and Shin et al. enter 216)

Fanari et al., pooled in all three with the same rows (MI 5 of 164 vs 2 of 212; deaths 3 of 164 vs 6 of 212), which sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019 identify as Fanari's Table 3 percentages entered as counts
Schmidt et al. (IJC Heart & Vasculature), pooled here (MI 7 of 26 vs 7 of 32) and by Shin et al. (MI risk ratio 1.01, 0.63–1.64, per sc_shin_2019), not by Pham et al.
Pham et al., meta-analysis of 5 cohorts (Dattilo, Mohamad, Rangel, Ibrahim, Fanari): MI odds ratio 1.36 (0.68–2.74), death 0.68 (0.26–1.79); not cited by this review

Shin et al., meta-analysis of 8 cohorts that include all 5 pooled here plus Mohamad 2008, a conference abstract (Finks 2015) and Cediel 2018: in-hospital MI risk ratio 1.24 (0.74–2.06), in-hospital death 0.59 (0.24–1.47); cites this review and Pham et al. as agreeing

replication.where_it_stands: Three meta-analyses published in 2018–2019 (Pham et al., 2018; this review; Shin et al., 2019) pool largely the same few retrospective cohorts and all find no significant difference. Overlap: Dattilo 2008, Rangel 2010, Ibrahim 2013 and Fanari 2014 are in all three; Schmidt 2015 is in this review and in Shin et al.; Mohamad 2008 is in Pham et al. and Shin et al. but not here; Finks 2015 (an abstract) and Cediel 2018 are only in Shin et al. All five studies pooled here are among the eight of Shin et al. and four are among Pham's five, and all three reviews carry the same Fanari rows (percentages entered as counts, per sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019) and the same Dattilo death row. The three are therefore not independent confirmations and cannot be cited beside each other, or beside the primary cohorts, as separate support. None of them found a randomized trial with clinical outcomes.

funding.funder: No study-specific funding; the authors state they are solely responsible for design, conduct, analyses and writing (p. 505, footnotes to the left column).
funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors has any disclosures relevant to the content of the manuscript (p. 505, footnote).
funding.affiliations_note: Albert Einstein Medical Center, Philadelphia (Department of Medicine; Department of Cardiology), Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston (Division of Cardiology) and Mount Sinai St. Luke's West Hospital, New York (Cardiology) (p. 505). No author of the review appears among the authors of the pooled studies in its reference list.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in patients in hospital with chest pain after recent, toxicology-confirmed cocaine use, comparing a beta-blocker (selective, or combined alpha and beta blockade such as labetalol) with care without one, with troponin-defined MI and in-hospital and 30-day death as prespecified outcomes. Short of that, an individual-patient-data analysis of the existing cohorts with common outcome definitions, in-hospital and long-term outcomes kept apart, adjustment for the indication for treatment, and analysis by agent.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (cocaine-associated chest pain), intervention (beta-blocker), comparator (none) and outcomes (in-hospital mortality and MI) are stated (pp. 505–506), although eligibility criteria are otherwise not spelled out.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Eligible designs are not stated; the Discussion explains only that the randomized and prospective studies lacked MI and mortality data (p. 506).

Four named Ovid databases (five stated) with keywords and no language restriction meet two partial-yes criteria; but no full strategy, no reference-list, registry or grey-literature searching, and two studies were excluded because they were abstracts (p. 506; Figure 1), a publication-type restriction for which no justification is given. Judged no with item 4 read as written (decision p-amstar2-item4); partial yes if the exclusion of abstracts is not treated as a publication restriction.
Not reported.
Not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives counts and reasons (2 abstracts, 5 outcome criteria) but no list; the Discussion names four unpooled studies (Lange, Boehrer, Hoskins, Mohamad) with reasons, which does not account for all seven exclusions or identify the two abstracts.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The Table gives design, size, age, sex, race, a summary of each study's conclusion and the agents used; comparators, settings, countries, outcome definitions and follow-up times are missing, and the sizes do not match the numbers pooled.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool used; confounding and selection in the non-randomized cohorts were not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects Mantel–Haenszel pooling is a reasonable weighted method, but crude counts were combined without justification although propensity-adjusted estimates exist for at least two of the studies (p. 507), and the mortality pool combines in-hospital deaths with one study's long-term deaths.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment and no sensitivity analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations name the retrospective designs, mixed agents, the population and unknown prior beta-blocker use (pp. 508–509), but the conclusions read the null result as showing safety and the higher baseline risk of treated patients as a possible protective effect (p. 508).
An I² of 51% for MI is called low to moderate (p. 506) without any investigation, although the study estimates run from 0.23 to 3.23.
Neither tested nor discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No study-specific funding and no relevant disclosures (p. 505).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Seven critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2 whatever the reading of item 4. The arithmetic of the pooling is correct (the editors reproduced every printed value), but several inputs are not: the in-hospital mortality pool takes 80.6% of its weight from Rangel's long-term deaths; Fanari's rows match the percentages that the cards of the other two reviews identify as entered in place of counts; Dattilo's death row mixes the full cohort's deaths with a subgroup's denominators; Schmidt et al. contribute 58 patients of a stated 378; and the one cohort reporting harm was not pooled. None of the editors' corrections makes either pooled estimate significant. It may be cited for: the fact that a third meta-analysis of largely the same retrospective cohorts found no significant difference in MI (risk ratio 1.08, 0.61–1.91), and for its list of pooled studies. It should not be cited for in-hospital mortality, for the safety of beta-blockers in general or of labetalol or metoprolol in particular, or as confirmation independent of Pham et al. (2018) and Shin et al. (2019).

key_findings.finding: The search (four Ovid databases named, five stated; inception to July 2018; no language restriction) found 508 records; 12 studies were examined further; 2 were dropped because they were abstracts and 5 because they did not meet the outcome criteria, leaving 5 studies with 1,447 patients, 536 given a beta-blocker and 911 not.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (left column); Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column); Figure 1 (right column)

key_findings.finding: All five pooled studies are retrospective hospital cohorts: Dattilo et al. 2008, Rangel et al. 2010, Ibrahim et al. 2013, Fanari et al. 2014 (propensity-matched) and Schmidt et al. 2015 (paired or matched controls). The Table gives their sizes as 348, 331, 378, 376 and 378 patients.
key_findings.note: The forest plots use 310, 328, 375, 376 and 58 patients from these studies (editors' arithmetic from the group totals in Figure 2); the Table's sizes sum to 1,811, not 1,447. Overlap with the other two meta-analyses (editors' comparison with sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019): Dattilo, Rangel, Ibrahim and Fanari are in all three; Schmidt is also in Shin et al.; all five are among the eight of Shin et al.; Mohamad 2008, pooled by both others, is not here.

key_findings.finding: Heart attack (MI): 51 of 536 patients given a beta-blocker (9.5%) vs 119 of 911 not given one (13%); pooled risk ratio 1.08 (95% CI 0.61–1.91), no significant difference (Z=0.26, P=0.79); heterogeneity tau² 0.20, Chi² 8.12 on 4 df (P=0.09), I² 51%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 505); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 506, right column); Figure 2, Myocardial Infarction, totals (p. 507)
key_findings.note: The crude totals (9.5% vs 13%) point the other way from the pooled risk ratio because 72 of the 119 MIs without a beta-blocker come from one study, Dattilo et al., whose untreated group had a much higher MI rate (editors' arithmetic); the pooled ratio, not the crude percentages, is the comparable figure.

key_findings.finding: The five MI estimates point in different directions: Dattilo 2008, 2 of 33 vs 72 of 277, risk ratio 0.23 (0.06–0.91), weight 12.5%; Rangel 2010, 15 of 151 vs 18 of 177, 0.98 (0.51–1.87), 27.5%; Ibrahim 2013, 22 of 162 vs 20 of 213, 1.45 (0.82–2.56), 29.9%; Fanari 2014, 5 of 164 vs 2 of 212, 3.23 (0.64–16.45), 9.6%; Schmidt 2015, 7 of 26 vs 7 of 32, 1.23 (0.49–3.06), 20.5%.
key_findings.note: Read from the journal's Figure 2 image (1955 × 1031 pixels at 300 ppi, a sharper copy of the accepted manuscript's figure); every value legible and identical to the manuscript's; they are not in the PDF's text layer. Only Dattilo et al. is individually significant; without it the pooled risk ratio is 1.29 (0.88–1.88), I² 0% (editors' re-analysis).

key_findings.finding: Death from any cause, described as in-hospital: 22 of 374 given a beta-blocker (5.9%) vs 46 of 698 not (6.6%); pooled risk ratio 0.75 (0.46–1.24), not significant (Z=1.11, P=0.27); tau² 0.00, Chi² 0.09 on 2 df (P=0.96), I² 0%. Schmidt 2015 had no deaths in either group (not estimable).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 505); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 506, foot of the left column to the top of the right column); Figure 2, All-Cause Mortality (p. 507)
key_findings.note: Z, P, tau², Chi² and the Schmidt row are read from the journal's Figure 2 image (300 ppi; identical to the manuscript's); they are not in the PDF's text layer. Ibrahim 2013 has no row in this plot, so the pool covers 4 of the 5 studies and 1,072 of the 1,447 patients (editors' arithmetic); the review does not say why (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The twist in the mortality result: one row, Rangel 2010, 18 of 151 vs 27 of 177 (risk ratio 0.78, 0.45–1.36), carries 80.6% of the weight; the other rows are Dattilo, 1 of 33 vs 13 of 277 (0.65, 0.09–4.78; 6.2%), and Fanari, 3 of 164 vs 6 of 212 (0.65, 0.16–2.55; 13.2%). The review itself describes Rangel's death comparison as coming from a follow-up of 5 years with a median of 972 days.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, All-Cause Mortality, study rows; Discussion, 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Forest-plot values read from the journal's Figure 2 image (300 ppi; identical to the manuscript's); they are not in the PDF's text layer. Rangel's row holds 45 of the 68 pooled deaths (editors' arithmetic). 18 and 27 match Rangel's deaths by emergency-department beta-blocker over a median follow-up of 972 days (18, 12%, vs 27, 16%, among 317 patients with National Death Index data; Rangel et al., 2010, Results › Mortality, 1st paragraph, p. 877, which prints no group denominators; Shin et al., 2019, enter them as 18 of 149 vs 27 of 168, Table 1, p. 42), not its in-hospital deaths (2 of 151 vs 3 of 177; Rangel et al., 2010, Table 3, p. 877). With the in-hospital counts the pool is 6 of 374 vs 22 of 698 deaths, risk ratio 0.68 (0.26–1.77) (editors' re-analysis).

key_findings.finding: Beta-blockers were started in the ED or within the first 24 hours of admission in all five studies; one study excluded patients already taking a beta-blocker and the other four gave no information on prior use.
key_findings.note: The Discussion says 44% of Fanari's 376 patients were on a beta-blocker when they arrived (p. 507); 164 of 376 (44%) is the size of Fanari's beta-blocker group in Figure 2 (editors' arithmetic), and Fanari et al. themselves describe those 164 as given a beta-blocker in the first 24 hours (Fanari et al., 2014, Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1803), so the Discussion most likely misdescribes that study rather than contradicting this finding.

key_findings.finding: Four studies of beta-blockers after cocaine were not pooled: a randomized catheterization-laboratory study of 30 patients (Lange et al.) in which intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine potentiated coronary vasoconstriction; a catheterization study of 15 patients (Boehrer et al.) in which labetalol after intranasal cocaine lowered blood pressure without further narrowing the coronary arteries; a prospective cohort of 90 patients with cocaine-related acute coronary syndrome (Hoskins et al.) in which labetalol and diltiazem lowered blood pressure and heart rate similarly, with no adverse cardiopulmonary effects; none of the three reported MI or mortality; and a retrospective cohort of more than 350 patients (Mohamad et al.) whose data were judged insufficient to derive odds ratios.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 506, right column, to p. 507, left column) and 3rd paragraph (p. 507)

key_findings.finding: The left-out cohort was the only one reporting harm: in Mohamad et al., patients already on a beta-blocker had MI more often than those not on one (14% vs 4.4%, chi-squared 6.9, P=0.01), and so did patients whose beta-blocker was continued or started on admission (23.3% vs 10.7%, chi-squared 5.6, p<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (foot of the left column to the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: A chi-squared of 5.6 on 1 degree of freedom corresponds to p of about 0.018, not below 0.01 (editors' calculation); whether the slip is the review's or the primary paper's cannot be told from this review. Pham et al. (2018) and Shin et al. (2019) both pooled this cohort.

key_findings.finding: From the pooled studies the review also quotes: Dattilo's propensity-matched odds ratio for MI with a beta-blocker, 0.08 (0.01–0.65); Rangel's hazard ratio for cardiovascular death in patients discharged on a beta-blocker, 0.29 (0.09–0.98), after a median of 972 days; no difference in peak troponin by beta-blocker type in Ibrahim et al.; similar outcomes despite higher baseline risk in Fanari's beta-blocker group; and significantly lower blood pressure with beta-blockers in Schmidt et al., described as a retrospective cohort of 378 patients with cocaine-related acute coronary syndrome. Suggested note: Espana Schmidt et al. report no significant blood-pressure or heart-rate difference in any window shown (Table 2, p. 168) and compare 58 of their 378 patients (sc_espana_schmidt_2015).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 507, right column, to p. 508, left column)

key_findings.finding: The review says that, among the included studies, the evidence appears strongest for the safety of labetalol, as it was tested prospectively (the Clinical Significance box says labetalol seems to have the strongest safety evidence), and that metoprolol also appeared to be safe, citing the Table and the five pooled studies (references 6, 9–11 and 15); no analysis by agent was done, and for the agents the Table lists only how often each was used.
key_findings.locator: Clinical Significance box (p. 506); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 508, left column); Table (p. 508)
key_findings.note: In the accepted manuscript the metoprolol sentence cited Table 1 only (PDF p. 9) and the box was headed Bullet points (PDF p. 2); the citations of the five pooled studies were added in the version of record. Of those studies, the review describes only one comparison by agent type: Ibrahim et al. found no difference in peak troponin between beta-selective and combined alpha- and beta-blocking agents (p. 507).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the suggested ill effects of beta-blockers after cocaine use are not borne out by existing evidence and that beta-blockers do not appear to be associated with higher rates of MI or all-cause mortality; as limitations they list mostly retrospective studies, mixed agents, mostly African American male participants, missing information on prior beta-blocker use, and only two studies of high-risk patients.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 508, right column); Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 508, right column, to p. 509, left column)

key_findings.finding: The review calls itself the first meta-analysis of beta-blockers and clinical outcomes in cocaine-related chest pain; its reference list does not include the meta-analysis of the same question by Pham et al. in the Emergency Medicine Journal (sc_pham_2018).

reporting_issues.issue: The mortality outcome is defined and reported as in-hospital (pp. 505, 506), but its largest row, Rangel 2010 with 18 of 151 vs 27 of 177 deaths (80.6% of the weight; p. 507), matches Rangel's deaths over a median follow-up of 972 days, as the review's own Discussion describes that study (p. 507): Rangel et al. report 18 vs 27 deaths by emergency-department beta-blocker over that follow-up (Results › Mortality, 1st paragraph, p. 877; entered by Shin et al. as 18 of 149 vs 27 of 168, Table 1, p. 42) and 2 of 151 vs 3 of 177 deaths in hospital (Table 3, p. 877).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated in-hospital mortality of 5.9% vs 6.6% is mostly long-term mortality; with in-hospital counts the deaths fall from 68 to 28 and the risk ratio is 0.68 (0.26–1.77) (editors' re-analysis). Claims must not cite 5.9% or 6.6% as in-hospital death rates.

reporting_issues.issue: Fanari 2014 enters as 5 of 164 vs 2 of 212 for MI and 3 of 164 vs 6 of 212 for death (p. 507), the same rows that sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019 identify, against the Fanari et al. PDF, as that study's Table 3 percentages (5%, 2%, 3%, 6%) entered as counts; the implied counts are about 8 vs 4 and 5 vs 13.
reporting_issues.consequence: The same extraction error appears in all three meta-analyses, which suggests shared rather than independent data handling; corrected, the pooled estimates change little (MI 1.11, 0.64–1.93; editors' re-analysis).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table gives study sizes of 348, 331, 378, 376 and 378 (p. 508), summing to 1,811, while the forest plots use 310, 328, 375, 376 and 58 (p. 507), summing to the 1,447 in the abstract (editors' arithmetic); Schmidt et al. are described as a cohort of 378 in the Table and the Discussion (p. 508) but contribute 26 vs 32 patients, and sc_shin_2019 records a different estimate for the same study (MI risk ratio 1.01, 0.63–1.64).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which patients from each study were pooled, and why only 58 of Schmidt's 378, cannot be told from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Ibrahim 2013 enters with 213 patients without a beta-blocker (p. 507), while the Table gives the study as n=378 (162 + 216) (p. 508), and Pham et al. and Shin et al. both enter 216 (sc_pham_2018, sc_shin_2019).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; with 216 the pooled MI risk ratio is 1.08 (0.61–1.93) (editors' re-analysis).

reporting_issues.issue: Dattilo 2008's death row (1 of 33 vs 13 of 277; p. 507) is the row that sc_pham_2018 and sc_shin_2019 identify as the full cohort's deaths (1 of 60 vs 13 of 288) placed over the denominators of Dattilo's infarction analysis; the review's Table gives Dattilo's size as 348 (p. 508).
reporting_issues.consequence: The death denominators for this study do not match its numerators; the effect on the pooled estimate is small (weight 6.2%).

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the search covered five databases but name four Ovid databases (p. 506).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a database is unnamed or the count is wrong; the search cannot be reproduced exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that among the studies included in the meta-analysis the evidence appears strongest for the safety of labetalol, as it was tested prospectively (p. 508), and the Limitations that a handful of studies provided prospective data (p. 508); but all five pooled studies are retrospective (Table, p. 508), and the prospective labetalol studies were excluded for lacking MI and mortality data (pp. 506–507).
reporting_issues.consequence: The labetalol statement in the Clinical Significance box and the Discussion has no support in the pooled analysis; it rests on two small studies with haemodynamic outcomes that the review did not pool.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say beta-blockers were started in the ED or within 24 hours of admission in all included studies and that four studies gave no information on prior beta-blocker use (p. 506), but the Discussion says 44% of Fanari's patients were on a beta-blocker when they arrived (p. 507), which matches the share of Fanari's patients in the beta-blocker group (164 of 376, editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Fanari et al. themselves describe these 164 patients (44%) as given a beta-blocker in the first 24 hours (Fanari et al., 2014, Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1803), so the Discussion's description of them as on beta-blockers at presentation is most likely the review's own misdescription, not a sign that Fanari's treated group took beta-blockers before arrival; it shows that the review's summaries of its included studies cannot be relied on alone.

reporting_issues.issue: Mohamad's second comparison is reported as chi-squared 5.6 with p<0.01 (p. 507); a chi-squared of 5.6 on 1 degree of freedom gives p of about 0.018 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the comparison is significant at 0.05, not at 0.01.

reporting_issues.issue: In the accepted manuscript, references 11 and 15 were the same paper (Ibrahim et al., 2013) and the Discussion spelled the first author of reference 10 'Datillo' (manuscript PDF pp. 8, 10–11). The version of record lists Ibrahim et al. once (reference 11), renumbers the later references (Fanari et al. becomes 15, Barbato 16, Hodgson et al. 17) and spells Dattilo correctly (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 507; References, p. 509), but misspells Guidelines as 'Gidelines' in the title of reference 8 (p. 509) and drops the full stop after 'as shown in Figure 1' in the Results (p. 506).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; typographical. The manuscript's references 16–18 are the journal's 15–17 and its reference 15 (the duplicate) is gone, so a citation by reference number must say which version it follows.

reporting_issues.issue: Ibrahim 2013 has no row in the all-cause mortality forest plot, which lists Dattilo, Rangel, Fanari and Schmidt only (Figure 2, p. 507), and the review does not say why; the abstract and Results give the mortality estimate beside the five studies and 1,447 patients (pp. 505, 506).
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality pool covers 4 of the 5 studies (3 estimable) and 1,072 of the 1,447 patients (374 + 698; editors' arithmetic). Ibrahim et al. report 18 in-hospital deaths (5%) only for their whole cohort, with no split by beta-blocker group (Ibrahim et al., 2013, section 3.3, p. 615), which would explain the omission; the review does not say so.

reporting_issues.issue: In the Table, the agent shares listed for Ibrahim et al. are metoprolol 53%, labetalol 27%, carvedilol 27% and atenolol 2% (p. 508), with no note on whether some patients received more than one agent; the accepted manuscript's Table 1 has the same values. By editors' arithmetic they sum to 109%, while the other studies' shares sum to 100% to 102%, within rounding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the shares cannot be read as a breakdown of treated patients by agent, which adds to the doubts about the review's statements on labetalol and metoprolol (reporting issue 6; key finding 10).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table and the Discussion (p. 508) say Espana Schmidt et al. found significantly lower blood pressure with beta-blockers; the primary paper reports no significant blood-pressure or heart-rate difference in any time window (Table 2, p. 168 of that paper; card sc_espana_schmidt_2015). Its pooled 'MI' row for that study (7 of 26 vs 7 of 32, p. 507) is the primary paper's 0–3 h positive-troponin row (Table 3, p. 169), which that paper does not call infarction.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's description of one pooled study, and what its 'infarction' counts mean for that study, do not match the primary paper.

design_detail: Letter to the editor (Annals of Emergency Medicine, Correspondence, 2008;52(1):89) by one author, Peter J. Mariani, MD (Department of Emergency Medicine, SUNY Upstate Medical University, Syracuse, NY), on Dattilo et al. (2008). One paragraph and 4 references (the article; a two-page 1999 item by Leikin in Critical Care Medicine, its type not stated; two labetalol reports from 1987 and 1988, the first co-authored by Mariani); no data: it welcomes the study and asks its authors three questions about acute hypertension, blood pressure after β-blockers and differences between agents. The original authors' reply on the same page (Philip B. Dattilo and Charles Nordin) answers this letter and Fung et al.'s; its answer to this letter, in its 5th and last paragraph, gives presenting systolic pressure counts from the study's records and is recorded here. The file is one page, identical to p. 89 of the Fung et al. file; the reference of that letter at the top of the page is not part of this card.
can_establish: That an emergency physician, co-author of a 1987 report on labetalol for cocaine toxicity, welcomed Dattilo et al. as questioning a ban on β-blockade after cocaine use and asked about acute hypertension and blood-pressure responses to β-blockers; and that the original authors replied that blood pressure after β-blockers was not consistently recorded in their records, reporting presenting systolic pressures instead.
cannot_establish: Anything about blood-pressure responses to β-blockers after cocaine use or about differences between agents: the letter asks questions without data, and the reply reports only presenting blood pressure (no values after β-blockers) and the authors' judgment that no death appeared related to a hypertensive emergency.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The reply's counts come from Dattilo et al.'s records of admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test (p. 89).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; 4 references chosen by the author.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The reply states that blood pressure measured over time, and specifically after β-blocker administration, was not consistently available in the retrospective records (p. 89).
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable as a sample. The letter's evidence of initial clinical successes is two labetalol reports from 1987 and 1988, one co-authored by Mariani; the reply is written by two of the study's five authors.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (letter). The questions concern β-blockers given in hospital in the study's cohort, by agent and class (p. 89).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (no data). The letter asks about patients with normal or mildly raised blood pressure given β-blockers and about comparisons between agents or classes; the reply reports no comparison (p. 89).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The reply notes that 23 of the 34 admissions with a presenting systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or more had a previous diagnosis of hypertension (p. 89).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcomes asked about: hypertensive emergencies or urgencies, blood-pressure responses to β-blockade, hypertensive crisis after β-blockers, and outcome trends by agent or class. The reply reports presenting blood pressure and deaths judged unrelated to hypertensive emergencies (p. 89).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable. Neither the letter nor the reply defines a hypertensive emergency, urgency or crisis.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. The reply's counts: 34 admissions with a presenting systolic blood pressure of 180 mm Hg or more, the highest recorded 254 mm Hg; 23 of the 34 with a previous diagnosis of hypertension; no death judged related to a hypertensive emergency, including the death after β-blocker administration (p. 89). The denominator is not stated; editors' calculation: if it is the full cohort of 348 admissions (sc_dattilo_2008), 34 is 9.8%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a study. The reply answers the first question only in part (presenting pressure, not responses to β-blockade), the second not directly, and the third (outcomes by agent or class) not at all.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The letter itself grants that the study lacked the power to conclude definitively on comparisons between agents (p. 89).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data in the letter. The reply reports that blood pressure after β-blockers was not consistently recorded, gives presenting systolic pressure (34 admissions at 180 mm Hg or more, highest 254, 23 of them with known hypertension) and states that no death appeared related to a hypertensive emergency.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter frames the caution against β-blockade after cocaine as a ban that "might be another unclothed emperor of medicine" and says patients with cocaine-induced acute hypertension were subject to it despite initial clinical successes (p. 89); the successes are two labetalol reports, one his own, neither described or appraised, and the framing is hedged. The reply's confident statement that no death appeared related to hypertensive emergencies cannot show that β-blockers caused no hypertensive reactions, since the records did not consistently hold blood pressure after β-blockers; its own conclusion, that blood-pressure response after β-blockers should be measured in a prospective study, is the accurate one.

timeline.event: Lange et al.: the catheterization study in which propranolol made cocaine-induced coronary constriction worse, as both editorials in the February issue describe it
Boehrer et al.: labetalol, the combined α/β agent of Mariani's own earlier report, essentially without effect on cocaine-induced coronary constriction, as both editorials describe it
Dattilo et al. (February issue): the record study the letter welcomes
Hoffman's editorial in the February issue cites Mariani's 1987 labetalol report (its ref 8) among the case reports supporting labetalol, while arguing against β-blockers in this setting

Freeman and Feldman's editorial in the February issue argues that the caution rests on uncontrolled observations, beginning with a 1985 single-patient report of a blood-pressure rise after propranolol
Letter by Fung, Chan and Lau, answered in the same reply, which concedes an error in the study's flow figure

Rangel et al. recorded blood pressure before and after the first β-blocker in patients admitted with cocaine-associated chest pain: systolic pressure fell after an emergency-department β-blocker (median −8 mm Hg), more than after a first dose on the ward (adjusted difference 8.6 mm Hg, 95% CI 2.5 to 14.7), as recorded on sc_rangel_2010

replication.where_it_stands: The letter's questions were left largely unanswered by the study's records: blood pressure after β-blockers had not been consistently recorded, and outcomes by agent were not reported (nor could they be drawn reliably from the article, whose agent classes sum to 61 for 60 admissions, as recorded on sc_dattilo_2008). A later record study (Rangel et al., 2010) recorded blood pressure around the first β-blocker dose and found a fall, in a non-randomized comparison without a protocol.

funding.funder: None stated (letter).
funding.declared_conflicts: By the journal's policy all authors must disclose any commercial, financial and other relationships related to the subject that might create a potential conflict of interest; the author stated that no such relationships exist (Funding and support, p. 89). The reply carries no disclosure statement on this page.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Emergency Medicine, SUNY Upstate Medical University, Syracuse, NY (p. 89). One of the letter's four references is Mariani's own 1987 report on labetalol for cocaine toxicity (ref 3, Dusenberry, Hicks and Mariani), cited among the initial clinical successes; the Hoffman editorial in the February issue cites the same report (its ref 8) among case reports supporting labetalol. The reply is by two of the study's five authors (Dattilo and Nordin; Jacobi Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount either.

what_would_settle_it: As the reply proposes: a prospective study recording blood pressure and heart rate at fixed times before and after each β-blocker dose in hospital patients with cocaine-associated chest pain or hypertension, by agent class (β1-selective, non-selective, combined α/β), with hypertensive crisis defined in advance and assessed blind to agent; for clinical outcomes, a randomized comparison of agents, or of β-blockade with none.

domains.note: A one-paragraph letter with 4 references; no search.
It welcomes the study's systematic light without appraising its design, and calls the earlier labetalol reports (one his own) initial clinical successes without describing or appraising them.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 1 of 4 references is his own labetalol report, offered as evidence of clinical success.
The ban is called possibly another unclothed emperor (hedged), and its cost to patients with acute hypertension is asserted from case-level reports; the rest of the letter is questions.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on blood-pressure effects of β-blockers after cocaine use
domains.note: The framing favours β-blockade, but the questions seek evidence on both sides, including hypertensive crises after β-blockers. Under-represented side: the evidence behind the caution (catheterization and case-series reports of harm).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used (METHODS §5.3), and the overall judgment follows the absence of search and of appraisal. The letter has no data. The reply's counts on presenting blood pressure come from the same records as Dattilo et al. and inherit that study's appraisal (ROBINS-I, overall critical, sc_dattilo_2008); they are descriptive, with no denominator or comparison, and need no separate rating. Citable for: the original authors' statement that blood pressure after β-blockers was not consistently recorded in their records, the presenting systolic pressures they report (34 admissions at 180 mm Hg or more, highest 254), and the questions an emergency physician put to the study. Not citable for: the safety of β-blockers for blood pressure after cocaine use, or for initial clinical successes of labetalol.

key_findings.finding: A one-paragraph letter to the editor (Correspondence) by Peter J. Mariani, MD (Department of Emergency Medicine, SUNY Upstate Medical University, Syracuse, NY), with 4 references, one of them a 1987 report on labetalol for cocaine toxicity that he co-authored (ref 3). It reports no data; it asks the study's authors questions.

His framing: Dattilo et al. shine some needed systematic light on what "might be another unclothed emperor of medicine": the ban on all β-blockade after cocaine exposure (ref 2: Leikin, Critical Care Medicine, 1999, two pages; the letter does not say what kind of item it is). Patients with cocaine-induced acute hypertension, he writes, have been subject to that ban despite initial clinical successes (refs 3 and 4, labetalol reports from 1987 and 1988).

He notes that the article's Introduction does not list acute hypertension among cocaine's pathophysiological effects and that it is not among the 5 commonest admission diagnoses, and asks three questions: were there hypertensive emergencies or urgencies among the rest of the cohort, and how did their blood pressure respond to β-blockade; was any hypertensive crisis seen after a β-blocker given to a patient with normal or mildly raised blood pressure; and, granting insufficient power to conclude definitively, do outcome trends differ between particular β-blockers or classes?

The original authors' reply (Dattilo and Nordin) on the same page: because the data in the retrospective review were heterogeneous, blood pressure measured over time, and specifically after β-blocker administration, was not consistently available. They had recorded presenting blood pressure: 34 admissions had a systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or more, the highest recorded being 254, and 23 of those 34 had a previous diagnosis of hypertension. They say they can state confidently that none of the deaths appeared related to hypertensive emergencies, including the death after β-blocker administration, and that blood-pressure response after β-blockers would be an important outcome to measure in a prospective study.
key_findings.note: Editors' note: no denominator is given; the full cohort had 348 admissions (sc_dattilo_2008), so 34 would be 9.8% (editors' calculation). The one death after a β-blocker is recorded on sc_dattilo_2008 as pericardial tamponade after thrombolysis for ST-elevation infarction, the β-blocker given after the ST elevation.

key_findings.finding: The reply does not answer the question on outcomes by β-blocker agent or class, and reports no observation of blood pressure after β-blockers, so whether any hypertensive crisis followed a β-blocker given to a patient with normal or mildly raised pressure is left unanswered.
key_findings.note: Editors' note: on sc_dattilo_2008 the article's agent classes sum to 61 for 60 admissions and list propranolol as β-selective, so agent-specific comparisons could not be drawn reliably from it either.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply gives 34 admissions with a presenting systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or more without a denominator or a breakdown by β-blocker group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure describes the cohort's presentation only; it cannot show how blood pressure responded to β-blockers or whether it differed between groups.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply's statement that no death appeared related to a hypertensive emergency comes without a method (who judged it, from which records), in records that, by the reply's own account, did not consistently hold blood pressure after β-blockers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of recorded hypertensive deaths is not evidence that β-blockers caused no hypertensive reactions; cite it as the authors' judgment.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Ann Emerg Med 2008;52(1):89, 1 page, identical when rendered to p. 89 of the Fung et al. file: the letter (left column) and the original authors' reply (foot of the left column and right column), read in full and checked as rendered at 150 dpi; the reference of the preceding letter (Fung et al.) at the top of the page is not part of this card. The erratum the reply announces was not among the files and was not read. Dattilo et al. (2008) was not re-read: its counts are taken from sc_dattilo_2008.
verification.checked_by: AI reader 506 (round-2 check) and AI reader 511 (card adjudication)

disagreements.first_pass: His framing: Dattilo et al. shine some needed systematic light on what "might be another unclothed emperor of medicine": the ban on all β-blockade after cocaine exposure (ref 2, a 1999 editorial). Patients with cocaine-induced acute hypertension, he writes, have been subject to that ban despite initial clinical successes (refs 3 and 4, labetalol reports from 1987 and 1988).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 506 (round-2 check): Finding confirmed. The letter does not say what kind of item ref 2 is (Leikin, Crit Care Med 1999, 2 pages); a 1999 editorial (also in design_detail) is the editors' label, not the source's.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 89 (the letter's reference 2: Leikin JB, Crit Care Med 1999;27:688–689, cited without any description): ref 2 is now described by author, journal, year and length, with its type not stated, in key finding 1 and design_detail.

design_detail: Laboratory analysis of samples, not of people or cells: the schema has no design for an analysis of objects such as banknotes, and 'in-vitro' is the nearest, as for the product analyses sc_vandrey_2015 and sc_mallock_2024. Ten US$1 bills in general circulation from each of five places (Baltimore, Chicago, Denver and Honolulu, and San Juan, Puerto Rico), 50 bills in all, obtained in everyday transactions; each bill was soaked in 5 ml of acetonitrile for 2 hours and the extract analysed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (selected-ion monitoring) for cocaine, heroin, 6-acetylmorphine (6-AM), morphine, codeine, methamphetamine, amphetamine and phencyclidine (PCP) at the Addiction Research Center of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA). Single author from the Cuyahoga County Coroner's Office, Cleveland, Ohio. Received 3 November 2000, accepted 8 January 2001; the dates the bills were collected are not stated.
can_establish: How many of these 50 circulating one-dollar bills carried a detectable amount of each of eight drugs, and how much cocaine each carried, under this extraction and measurement method.
cannot_establish: How common drug contamination is on US or other currency in general or today (50 bills of one denomination, obtained by an undescribed procedure on unstated dates), how the drug got onto the bills (the mechanisms in the Introduction were not studied), whether the amounts are the total on each bill (extraction recovery from paper was not measured), or whether handling such bills could make a person test positive or make a sniffer dog alert: neither was tested, and the paper's statements on both rest on cited studies.

sample.recruitment: Bills, not people. US$1 bills described as collected randomly while in general circulation (p. 190, 2.2); the Discussion says they were obtained in day-to-day transactions in stores, restaurants and admission fees to public sites in each city (p. 192). On collection they were placed in plastic storage bags and kept at room temperature until analysis (p. 190). Who collected them, when, and how long they were stored are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: US$1 denomination only; ten bills per place (p. 190, 2.3).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (banknotes).
sample.attrition: None: all 50 bills appear in Table 1 (p. 191).
sample.selection_effects: A convenience collection called random without any sampling procedure; one denomination; four US cities and San Juan; collection dates unstated (the paper was received in November 2000). Whether bills were bagged singly or together is not stated, so transfer of drug between bills during storage cannot be excluded.

exposure.measurement: Each bill in a 15 ml tube with 5 ml of acetonitrile, vortexed four times for 30 s over 2 h; 1 ml of extract per assay (p. 190, 2.3). Cocaine, PCP and codeine: solid-phase extraction and GC-MS by a modified published method, eight-point calibration in duplicate (cocaine 3.1-1000 ng/ml, codeine 2.5-500, PCP 1.25-250), controls in every run, detection limit about 1.0 ng/ml. Heroin, 6-AM and morphine: published method, six-point calibration 2.5-50 ng/ml, detection and quantitation limit about 1.0 ng/ml. Methamphetamine and amphetamine: solid-phase extraction with chlorphentermine as internal standard, four-point calibration 500-5000 ng/ml, detection and quantitation limit about 100 ng/ml. For the cocaine and heroin assays, samples were diluted when above the calibration range; no dilution is mentioned for the amphetamine assay (p. 190, 2.4). Drugs were identified by retention time against calibrators and characteristic ions (p. 190, Results). Not reported: extraction recovery from paper, ion-ratio acceptance criteria, and how concentrations in the extract were converted to micrograms per bill.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: amounts measured on bills, reported in micrograms (µg) per bill; no one was exposed in this study.
exposure.polysubstance: Eight drugs were measured on every bill; several bills carried more than one (Denver bill 9: heroin and PCP; Denver bill 10: methamphetamine and PCP; Chicago bill 5: heroin, 6-AM and morphine as numbered in the Results). Other substances (for example benzoylecgonine or cannabinoids) were not measured.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (banknotes).

comparison.controls: No blank (new or uncirculated) bills were analysed; acetonitrile alone served as the drug-free control (p. 190, 2.3), with negative and positive controls in the amphetamine runs (p. 190, 2.4). Places are compared descriptively (ten bills each) and with earlier studies as cited (Discussion, pp. 191-192).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to an analysis of bills. Not measured or not described: collection dates, storage time, handling history of each bill, whether bills were stored separately, extraction efficiency, and contamination control while handling bills in a laboratory that works with drug standards.

outcomes.instruments: Hewlett-Packard 5890A gas chromatograph with a 5971A or 5970 mass-selective detector in selected-ion monitoring mode (p. 190, 2.5).
outcomes.validity_norms: Calibration curves and controls with every run; no recovery experiment on paper, no blank bills and no replicate bills are reported.
outcomes.operationalization: A bill was positive for a drug when the drug was identified by retention time and characteristic ions; cocaine amounts are given in µg per bill to two decimal places, 'ND' when not detected (Table 1, p. 191). Amounts of the other drugs are given in the text for most positive bills; 6-AM and morphine on two Denver bills only as nanogram quantities.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive results, no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only, without intervals. Cocaine: 46 of 50 bills (92%); editors' Wilson 95% interval 81.2% to 96.8%. Mean 28.75 µg per bill with an unlabelled spread of 139.07, median 1.37 µg, range 0.01-922.72 µg (abstract, p. 189); the editors' recomputation from Table 1 reproduces these exactly as the mean, sample standard deviation and median of the 46 positive bills (over all 50 bills, with undetected as zero: mean 26.45 µg, median 1.24 µg). Other drugs (counts from the Results; editors' Wilson 95% intervals): heroin 7 of 50 (14%; 7.0% to 26.2%), 6-AM and morphine 3 (6%; 2.1% to 16.2%), methamphetamine 3 (6%; 2.1% to 16.2%), amphetamine 1 (2%; 0.4% to 10.5%), PCP 2 (4%; 1.1% to 13.5%), codeine 0 (0%; 0% to 7.1%).
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only cocaine is tabulated bill by bill; amounts of the other drugs are given in the text, and those of 6-AM and morphine on two Denver bills only as nanogram quantities.
analysis.power: Not addressed; ten bills per place.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 50 circulating US$1 bills from five places, 46 carried detectable cocaine, mostly around a microgram (a millionth of a gram): median 1.37 µg, 18 of the 46 below 1 µg; two bills carried far more (233.55 and 922.72 µg), and the single highest bill held about 70% of all the cocaine measured (editors' calculation). Seven bills carried heroin, three 6-AM and morphine, three methamphetamine, one amphetamine, two PCP, and none codeine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and summary speak of drug contamination of US paper currency in general and say that microgram amounts of drug may be present on bills in general circulation (p. 192), from 50 bills of one denomination obtained by an undescribed procedure on unstated dates. The Discussion concludes that it "appears unlikely" that cocaine or the other drugs found could be transferred to people handling bills in amounts that would produce positive urine tests (p. 192); that rests on one cited experiment in which one person handled two bills dipped in coca paste (ElSohly, as cited), and it is extended to heroin, PCP and methamphetamine, which were not tested. The study itself measured nothing in people and nothing about sniffer dogs. A headline version ('nine in ten dollar bills carry cocaine') would overstate the finding for currency in general and would hide that most amounts were around a microgram.

timeline.event: Hearn, as cited (a news item in Science): cocaine on 131 of 135 bills of US$1 to US$100 obtained from banks in 12 US cities, average 7.3 µg per bill.
Hudson, as cited: Canadian banknotes from the Bank of Canada typically carried under 1 ng of cocaine; notes seized in drug investigations averaged 2.7 to 1069 ng per note.
ElSohly, as cited: one person handled two bills dipped in coca paste; urine benzoylecgonine detectable only at 12.5 to 21 h (72, 36 and 24 ng/ml) and negative at the 300 ng/ml cut-off.

Poupko et al., as cited (conference abstract): police dogs alerted to drug-free uncirculated currency used as negative controls and responded inconsistently to bills contaminated with 1 to 5000 µg of cocaine.

Jourdan and Donnelly, as cited (conference proceedings): bills from financial institutions; upper limit of general background cocaine 13 ng per bill; at least 100 ng regarded as different from background.
Oyler, Darwin and Cone, as cited in the Introduction: 0 to 1327 µg of cocaine per bill on randomly collected bills.
Negrusz, Perry and Moore, as cited: cocaine detected on US$20 bills.
This study: cocaine on 46 of 50 circulating US$1 bills, mostly microgram amounts, plus heroin, 6-AM, morphine, methamphetamine, amphetamine and PCP on a few bills.

replication.where_it_stands: Within the studies this paper cites, the finding that most circulating US bills carry detectable cocaine agrees with Hearn, and the microgram amounts agree with Hearn and with Oyler et al., but not with the nanogram levels reported by Hudson and by Jourdan and Donnelly; for Jourdan and Donnelly the author offers the source of bills (financial institutions versus everyday transactions) as a partial explanation, although Hearn's bills, also from banks, averaged microgram amounts. The detections of other drugs were, to the author's knowledge, the first for US currency. Later studies were not read for this card.

funding.funder: No funding statement. The analyses were performed at the Addiction Research Center, Intramural Research Program, National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health, Baltimore (p. 190, 2.2), and the Acknowledgements thank a member of NIDA's Drug Chemistry and Metabolism Section for help with the drug analysis (p. 192).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Amanda J. Jenkins, Office of the Cuyahoga County Coroner, Cleveland, Ohio (p. 189).

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a probability sample of circulating notes of several denominations, collected on known dates with documented handling and stored singly, with new notes carried through collection, storage and analysis as blanks, extraction recovery measured on spiked notes, and repeat measurements; and, separately, a controlled study of people handling contaminated notes with urine testing at standard workplace cut-offs.

domains.note: Ten US$1 bills per place obtained in everyday transactions and called random without a procedure; collectors, dates and storage time not reported. Describes these 50 bills, not US currency.

Bills kept in plastic bags (singly or together not stated) at room temperature; no blank bills, only a solvent blank. Low-level positives (18 of the 46 positive bills below 1 µg) are the results most exposed to contamination, although four Chicago bills with no cocaine show the method could return negatives. A second reader judged this domain borderline high: if bills from one place shared a bag, cocaine could have passed from Honolulu bill 9 (922.72 µg) or Denver bill 5 (233.55 µg) to others. Kept at some concerns because the paper gives no sign of shared bagging, so this is a possibility rather than a shown bias.

Established GC-MS methods with calibration and controls in every run; but no recovery from paper, no ion-ratio criteria, no stated conversion to µg per bill, and methamphetamine and amphetamine amounts that appear to lie below the lowest calibrator (see reporting issues).

Complete per-bill cocaine table that reproduces the abstract's statistics; but no intervals, the abstract does not say its mean and median are over positive bills only, and the Results and Discussion disagree on whether a Chicago bill carried heroin together with 6-AM and morphine.
The urine-test conclusion is hedged and attributed to a cited study, but it rests on one person and is extended to drugs that were not tested; the title generalizes to US paper currency.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of samples such as banknotes (METHODS 5.3 lists none, and scripts/rob_vocab.py assigns none to in-vitro), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to the design, as for sc_vandrey_2015; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The measurements are standard and the cocaine table is complete and internally consistent; the concerns are a small convenience sample without dates, no blank bills, no recovery data, and a conclusion about urine tests that is borrowed from a cited single-person experiment. A second reader may judge sampling or contamination control more severely. Citable for: the share of these 50 bills carrying each drug and the cocaine amounts in Table 1, with the denominator. Not citable for: contamination of currency in general or today; the claim that handling money cannot cause a positive drug test (not tested here); or the methamphetamine and amphetamine amounts as precise values.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine was detected on 46 of the 50 bills (92%): on all 10 bills from Baltimore, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan, and on 6 of the 10 (60%) from Chicago, where bills 7 to 10 had none detected. Editors' calculation: Wilson 95% interval 81.2% to 96.8%.

Cocaine amounts: mean 28.75 µg per bill with a spread of 139.07 (labelled only as ±), median 1.37 µg, range 0.01 to 922.72 µg. Editors' recomputation from Table 1: these are the mean, sample standard deviation and median of the 46 positive bills (over all 50 bills with undetected as zero, mean 26.45 and median 1.24); 18 of the 46 positive bills carried less than 1 µg, 6 carried 10 µg or more and 2 more than 100 µg (Denver bill 5, 233.55 µg; Honolulu bill 9, 922.72 µg); Honolulu bill 9 alone held about 70% of all the cocaine measured on the 50 bills.
key_findings.note: Amounts are in micrograms (µg); the PDF text layer renders the micro sign as 'm' and prints the abstract's 28.75 and 139.07 as 28:75 and 139:07, so units and decimals were read on the rendered pages.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine by place: Baltimore 0.01 to 13.05 µg per bill; Chicago 0.02 to 1.27 µg on the six positive bills; Denver 0.41 to 233.55 µg, nine of the ten below 10 µg and three below 1 µg; Honolulu 0.54 to 922.72 µg; San Juan 0.06 to 26.72 µg, half the bills below 1 µg.

Heroin was detected on 7 of the 50 bills, from 0.03 to 168.50 µg per bill: Baltimore 2 (bill 3, 76.5 µg; bill 9, 168.5 µg), Chicago 3 (0.03, 0.14 and 8.90 µg, bills 3 to 5), Denver 1 (bill 9, 0.03 µg) and San Juan 1 (bill 2, 0.09 µg); none in Honolulu. Editors' calculation: 14% (Wilson 95% interval 7.0% to 26.2%).
6-Acetylmorphine and morphine were detected on 3 bills: Chicago bill 5 (6-AM 9.22 µg, morphine 5.51 µg) and Denver bills 4 and 5 (given only as nanogram quantities).

Methamphetamine was detected on 3 bills (Denver bills 8 and 10, 0.55 and 0.60 µg; Honolulu bill 3, under 1 µg), which the Discussion calls 6% of the samples; amphetamine on 1 bill (Chicago bill 2, 0.85 µg); PCP on 2 bills (4%), both from Denver (bill 9, 0.78 µg; bill 10, 1.87 µg); codeine on none. Denver bill 9 also carried heroin and Denver bill 10 also carried methamphetamine.

Method: each bill soaked in 5 ml of acetonitrile for 2 h with vortexing (4 x 30 s); 1 ml extract per assay; GC-MS in selected-ion mode, identification by retention time and characteristic ions. Calibration: cocaine 3.1-1000 ng/ml, codeine 2.5-500, PCP 1.25-250 (detection limit about 1.0 ng/ml); heroin, 6-AM and morphine 2.5-50 ng/ml (limit about 1.0 ng/ml); methamphetamine and amphetamine 500-5000 ng/ml (limit about 100 ng/ml). The only drug-free control was the solvent; no blank bills and no extraction recovery from paper are reported.
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Collection of dollar bills; 2.3 Extraction; 2.4 Analysis; 3. Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Earlier studies as the author cites them: Hearn found cocaine on 131 of 135 bills of US$1 to US$100 from banks in 12 cities, average 7.3 µg; Hudson found typically under 1 ng per Canadian banknote and 2.7 to 1069 ng per note on notes seized in drug investigations; Jourdan and Donnelly put the upper limit of general background at 13 ng per bill (over 95% of bills below it), found over 65% of 40 case submissions below 30 ng, and regarded at least 100 ng as different from background. The author says the microgram amounts found here disagree with Hudson and with Jourdan and Donnelly and, for the latter, suggests that the different sources of the bills (financial institutions there, everyday transactions in stores, restaurants and admission fees here) may partly explain the difference.
key_findings.note: Editors' observation: Hearn's bills also came from banks (p. 191) yet averaged 7.3 µg, which the source-of-bills explanation does not address.

key_findings.finding: Sniffer dogs, as cited (Poupko et al.): in tests at a police department in Fayetteville, Arkansas, with uncirculated currency contaminated with 1 to 5000 µg of cocaine, dogs alerted to the drug-free uncirculated negative controls and responded inconsistently to contaminated bills, from alerting at 1 µg to not alerting until 500 µg; with clean bond paper as the negative control none alerted, and two dogs failed to alert to any contaminated paper. The author also cites a 1994 Ninth Circuit decision that a drug dog's alert on money is not sufficient probable cause to seize it.

Urine tests, as cited (ElSohly): one person handled two US$1 bills that had been immersed in powdered coca paste, several times through a day without washing the hands; urine benzoylecgonine by immunoassay was negative up to 8.5 h, detectable at 12.5, 18 and 21 h (72, 36 and 24 ng/ml) and negative afterwards, and negative at a 300 ng/ml cut-off. On this basis the author judges it unlikely that drugs found on currency could reach people in amounts that produce positive urine tests. This study tested no people.

Author's conclusions: several drugs were present on US currency from five places; microgram amounts of drug may be present on bills in general circulation; to the author's knowledge this is the first report of heroin, PCP or methamphetamine on US currency; contamination of currency other than US and Canadian dollars had not been reported.

Background given in the Introduction (not studied here): cocaine had been reported on US$1 and US$20 bills, in amounts from 0 to 1327 µg per bill on randomly collected bills; the main source of contamination is thought to be bills rolled up to snort cocaine, with drug deals contributing and bank counting machines spreading small amounts to other bills.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results place heroin on Chicago bills 3 to 5 and 6-AM and morphine on bill 5 of the same city, whereas the Discussion says the three bills with 6-AM and morphine were not the bills on which heroin was measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the bill numbering or the Discussion statement is wrong; whether 6-AM and morphine were found together with heroin on any bill, which bears on their likely source, cannot be settled from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives cocaine as a mean of 28.75 ± 139.07 µg per bill and a median of 1.37 µg without saying that these are computed over the 46 positive bills only, or what the ± value is.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' recomputation from Table 1 shows they are the mean, sample standard deviation and median of the 46 positive bills; claims should say so. The mean is dominated by one bill and the median is the better summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say how concentrations in the extract were converted to amounts per bill. The methamphetamine and amphetamine calibration ran from 500 to 5000 ng/ml with a limit of about 100 ng/ml, and the amounts reported were 0.55, 0.60 and 0.85 µg per bill and under 1 µg. Editors' calculation, assuming amounts were computed from the 5 ml extract: these correspond to about 110 to 170 ng/ml, below the lowest calibrator and close to the limit.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the assumption holds, the methamphetamine and amphetamine detections are near the method's limit and their amounts are extrapolated; they should not be cited as precise values.

reporting_issues.issue: No blank bills (new or uncirculated notes carried through collection, bagging, storage and extraction) were analysed; the only drug-free control was the solvent, and whether bills were stored singly is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Contamination during collection, storage or laboratory handling cannot be excluded for the low-level results, which make up much of the 92% figure.

reporting_issues.issue: In describing the cited dog work (Poupko et al., which the paper calls a series of studies), the paper says all three dogs in the study alerted to the negative controls, and, for the test with clean bond paper, that two dogs failed to alert to any contaminated paper and the other two gave varying results; it does not say whether these tests used different dogs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of dogs is unclear from this second-hand account, not necessarily inconsistent; cite the primary study, not this summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the material as 10 randomly collected US$1 bills from five cities (readable as ten in total), the Methods as 10 bills from each city, and the Discussion as bills obtained in everyday transactions; no random sampling procedure, collection dates or storage times are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is 50 bills (10 per place); 'random' should not be repeated in claims, which should describe the bills as a convenience collection of unknown date.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says several hundred micrograms of cocaine were measured in several of the bills, but Table 1 has only two bills above 100 µg (233.55 µg, Denver bill 5; 922.72 µg, Honolulu bill 9) and only one above 300 µg.
reporting_issues.consequence: High loads were rare (2 of 50 bills) and the wording should not be repeated. The disagreement with nanogram background levels does not depend on it: the median bill with cocaine carried 1.37 µg.

Every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, where units read µg; the text layer renders the micro sign as 'm'. Cocaine summary statistics recomputed from Table 1. No supplement.
