design_detail: Single-centre retrospective review of medical records at Metropolitan Hospital Center, New York (New York Medical College), June 2006 to June 2009. Of 378 patients admitted to a medical unit to rule out acute coronary syndrome, all with a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain and a positive urine test for cocaine metabolites, 26 had been given one dose of a beta-blocker in the emergency department while having chest pain. They were compared with 32 patients described as paired by age, sex, race and history of hypertension who did not receive a beta-blocker while having chest pain; how these 32 were chosen is not described. Outcomes: blood pressure and heart rate in three time windows up to 6 h, troponin I positivity in three windows up to 12 h, length of stay, in-hospital cardiac complications and death. The rest of the 378 are not described. The paper calls the treated patients the case group, but selection was by treatment, not by outcome, so this is a matched retrospective cohort comparison of 58 patients.
can_establish: That in this hospital's records, 26 patients given a beta-blocker in the emergency department while having cocaine-associated chest pain had no recorded deaths or cardiac complications, and no higher group-mean blood pressure, heart rate or troponin positivity in the following hours, than 32 selected patients who were not given one at that time.
cannot_establish: That early beta-blockers are safe or that an unopposed alpha effect does not occur (26 treated patients, no events, treatment chosen by physicians, unadjusted comparison with selected controls); anything about rates of myocardial infarction (troponin positivity is not defined and is not called infarction); or anything about the other patients of the 378, who were not analysed.

sample.recruitment: Hospital records: all patients admitted to a medical unit of Metropolitan Hospital Center, New York, for cocaine-induced chest pain to rule out acute coronary syndrome, June 2006 to June 2009 (p. 167, Methods, 1st paragraph); 378 found (p. 168, Results, 1st paragraph). The 320 patients outside the two compared groups (editors' arithmetic, 378 minus 58) are not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain and a positive urine test for cocaine metabolites (p. 167). No exclusion criteria are stated. Treated group: a beta-blocker given in the emergency department while the patient had chest pain (p. 168, Results, 1st paragraph). Comparison group: patients paired by age, sex, race and history of hypertension who did not receive a beta-blocker while having chest pain (abstract, p. 167); the Methods say only that they did not receive beta-blockers (p. 168). How the 32 were chosen from the untreated patients (editors' arithmetic: 352), and why 32 rather than 26, are not reported.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 168), beta-blocker vs comparison group: age 50 vs 48.3 years (P=0.4216; mean or median not stated, no dispersion); men 23 (88.5%) vs 30 (93.8%) (P=0.8078); Black 14 (53.8%) vs 15 (46.9%), Hispanic 10 (38.5%) vs 16 (50.0%), White 2 (7.7%) vs 1 (3.1%) (P=0.6181); history of hypertension 18 (69.2%) vs 18 (56.3%) (P=0.4163). No characteristics are given for the rest of the cohort.
sample.attrition: Not reported. Whether every patient had blood pressure, heart rate and troponin recorded in each time window is not stated; the troponin denominators are 26 and 32 in every window (Table 3, p. 169).
sample.selection_effects: Only patients admitted to a medical unit with a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain, a diagnosis assigned after treatment and the hospital course: patients discharged from the emergency department, admitted elsewhere or given another final diagnosis are outside the cohort, and the paper does not say whether patients later diagnosed with infarction were kept. Beta-blockers were given at the emergency physicians' discretion, and the authors say patients with higher blood pressure and heart rate were more likely to receive one (p. 168). The comparison group was selected from the untreated patients by an undescribed procedure. Small single-centre sample (58 patients compared).

exposure.measurement: Medical records: a beta-blocker given in the emergency department while the patient had chest pain, with agent and route (p. 168). Cocaine exposure by a qualitative urine test for cocaine metabolites; the authors note the amount of cocaine taken cannot be estimated (p. 169).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Hospital treatment as recorded (study condition, not advice): one dose in the emergency department; oral metoprolol 13 patients (50%), intravenous metoprolol 5 (19%), intravenous labetalol 2 (8%), oral carvedilol 2 (8%), oral atenolol 2 (8%), oral propranolol 2 (8%) (p. 168, Results, 1st paragraph). Doses not reported. The authors state the beta-blockers were discontinued once cocaine metabolites were found in the urine (p. 169). Time since cocaine use and route of cocaine use not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: alcohol and other drug use were neither recorded nor analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; time from cocaine use to presentation not reported.

comparison.controls: 32 patients from the same cohort, also with cocaine-induced chest pain, who did not receive a beta-blocker while having chest pain (p. 167; p. 168). Whether any of them were given a beta-blocker later in the admission is not reported.
comparison.matching: Described as paired by age, sex, race and history of hypertension, but the groups differ in size (26 vs 32) and all comparisons use unpaired tests (Mann–Whitney test for blood pressure and heart rate, Fisher's exact test for troponin; p. 168), so at most the groups were similar in distribution (frequency matching).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported for either group: prior coronary disease or infarction, smoking, diabetes, lipids, kidney function, electrocardiogram findings at presentation, amount and route of cocaine, time since use, other drugs, and co-treatments given in the emergency department.

outcomes.instruments: From the records: systolic, diastolic and mean arterial blood pressure and heart rate in windows 0 to 1 h, 1–3 h and 3 to 6 h (Table 2, p. 168); number of patients with a positive troponin I, and a mean value, in windows 0–3 h, 3–6 h and 6–12 h (Table 3, p. 169); length of stay; in-hospital cardiac complications and in-hospital death (p. 168). The Methods give the blood-pressure times as baseline, 1 to 3 h after the beta-blocker and 3 to 6 h later, and the troponin times as admission, 6 h after admission and 12 h later (p. 168).
outcomes.validity_norms: No threshold or units for a positive troponin, no definition of a cardiac complication, and no reference time (time zero) for the comparison group's windows; units of blood pressure and heart rate are not printed.
outcomes.operationalization: An unopposed alpha effect was looked for as higher blood pressure or heart rate after a beta-blocker than in the comparison group; harm as in-hospital cardiac complications (undefined) and death; troponin and length of stay were secondary endpoints (p. 167, Introduction, last paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 12 blood-pressure and heart-rate comparisons, 3 troponin comparisons and length of stay, each judged at P<0.05; complications and deaths had no events.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the record review is not described as blinded to treatment.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (p. 168), beta-blocker vs comparison group, mean (95% CI): at 0 to 1 h systolic 147.8 (136.5 to 159.1) vs 135.5 (127.9 to 143.1), P=0.0647; diastolic 88.5 (80.9 to 96.0) vs 82.5 (77.7 to 87.3), P=0.1730; mean arterial 108.2 (99.9 to 116.4) vs 100.17 (94.8 to 105.6), P=0.0966; heart rate 86.4 (80.7 to 92.1) vs 87.6 (81.8 to 93.4), P=0.7786. At 1–3 h systolic 135.1 vs 133.3 (P=0.8053), heart rate 79.63 vs 79.1 (P=0.8911). At 3 to 6 h systolic 126.7 (118.3 to 135.2) vs 130.1 (123.9 to 136.4), P=0.5177; diastolic 75.57 vs 76.9, P=0.7150; mean arterial 92.62 vs 94.7, P=0.5893; heart rate 73.11 (68.7 to 77.6) vs 75.8 (71.1 to 80.5), P=0.4222. Troponin positive (Table 3, p. 169): 7/26 vs 7/32 at 0–3 h, 4/26 vs 5/32 at 3–6 h, 3/26 vs 5/32 at 6–12 h, none significant. Length of stay 4.6 vs 2.65 days, P=0.04 (test and dispersion not given). No deaths and no cardiac complications in either group (p. 168). Editors' calculations: risk ratios for a positive troponin 1.23 (0.49 to 3.06) at 0–3 h, 0.98 (0.29 to 3.30) at 3–6 h and 0.74 (0.19 to 2.80) at 6–12 h; systolic pressure fell from the first to the last window by 21.1 in the beta-blocker group and by 5.4 in the comparison group (difference of group means, not a within-patient analysis).
analysis.covariates: None: unadjusted comparisons; no adjustment for the blood pressure and heart rate that guided treatment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported; approved by the IRB of New York Medical College and the hospital health corporation (p. 169).
analysis.selective_reporting: The text says blood pressure and heart rate were lower in the beta-blocker group at 6 and 12 h (pp. 168–169), but Table 2 ends at the 3 to 6 h window; the troponin times in the Methods (admission, 6 h and 12 h later) differ from the windows of Table 3; nothing is reported for the patients outside the two compared groups; cardiac complications are reported only as absent, without a definition.
analysis.power: Not reported. Editors' calculation: with no events among 26 treated patients, the exact 95% upper limit for the risk of an in-hospital complication or death is 13.2% (Clopper–Pearson), so the data are compatible with a risk of up to about 1 in 8.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 58 of 378 patients (26 given a beta-blocker in the emergency department while having chest pain and 32 selected comparison patients), mean blood pressure and heart rate did not differ significantly in any window up to 6 h (the treated group started with higher blood pressure and was slightly lower by 3 to 6 h), troponin positivity was similar (7/26 vs 7/32 at 0–3 h), no patient died or had a recorded cardiac complication, and the treated group stayed longer (4.6 vs 2.65 days, P=0.04).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the study does not support an unopposed alpha effect and that "BB appeared safe when given early on admission to patients with CICP" (p. 167). Gaps: safety is inferred from zero events in 26 treated patients (editors' calculation: 95% upper limit 13.2%); the Results and Discussion say blood pressure and heart rate were lower at 6 and 12 h (pp. 168–169), times for which no data are shown; the Discussion calls the treated group more tachycardic on admission (p. 169), although Table 2 shows a slightly lower heart rate (86.4 vs 87.6, p. 168); the authors suggest, without data, that the longer stay might be due to unrelated comorbidities and social problems (p. 168); and a fall in blood pressure in the group whose pressure was higher and that was more likely to be treated is expected from the natural course and regression to the mean, so it does not show the beta-blocker's effect. The comparison is with 32 selected patients, not with the 378 named in the abstract.

timeline.event: Lange et al.: coronary vasoconstriction with cocaine during intracoronary propranolol infusion, cited here as the experimental basis of the concern (p. 167)
American Heart Association statement (McCord et al.), cited here for beta-blockers being considered contraindicated in cocaine-associated chest pain (pp. 167–168)
Mohamad et al., cited here for raised cardiac biomarkers in patients given beta-blockers while having cocaine-induced chest pain (p. 167)
Dattilo et al., cited here among studies that found no harm from beta-blockers (p. 168)
Rangel et al., cited here for lower long-term mortality with beta-blockers (p. 168)
Canning et al., cited here for the view that patients with acute cocaine toxicity are at greater risk of adverse effects from beta-blockers (p. 169)
Ibrahim et al., cited here among studies showing beta-blockers can be used safely (p. 167)
Fanari et al., cited here among studies that found no harm (p. 168)
Pham et al. meta-analysis of five cohorts published 2008–2014; this study is not among them (as recorded on sc_pham_2018)

Lo et al. meta-analysis pooled this study as myocardial infarction 7 of 26 vs 7 of 32 (risk ratio 1.23, 0.49–3.06) and death 0 vs 0, while describing it as a cohort of 378 (as recorded on sc_lo_2019). Editors' check: these counts are the 0–3 h troponin-positive row of Table 3 (p. 169), which the paper does not call infarction

Shin et al. meta-analysis pooled this study for in-hospital infarction or necrosis with risk ratio 1.01 (0.63–1.64) (as recorded on sc_shin_2019). Editors' calculation: this estimate and interval are reproduced exactly by 14 of 26 vs 17 of 32, the sums of the three troponin windows of Table 3, which count a patient positive in more than one window more than once

replication.where_it_stands: The in-hospital safety of beta-blockers in cocaine-associated chest pain rests on small retrospective cohorts whose results the paper cites in both directions (raised biomarkers in Mohamad et al., 2008; no harm in Dattilo et al., 2008, and Fanari et al., 2014; lower long-term mortality in Rangel et al., 2010) and on meta-analyses that pool them. This study adds only 58 compared patients with no events, and the counts that meta-analyses took from it are troponin results, not infarctions. Of the three meta-analyses on the editors' list, two pooled it (Lo et al., 2019, and Shin et al., 2019), each with a different row of its Table 3; Pham et al. (2018) did not. The paper cites no randomized trial with clinical outcomes.

funding.funder: No funding was received (p. 169, Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Medicine and its Unit of Cardiology, Metropolitan Hospital Center/New York Medical College, New York; the corresponding author's address is the hospitalist service of The Reading Hospital (p. 167). IRB approval by New York Medical College and the hospital health corporation (p. 169).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of an early beta-blocker against no beta-blocker or another treatment in patients in hospital with cocaine-associated chest pain, with prespecified clinical outcomes (infarction by a stated troponin threshold, arrhythmia, death); failing that, a prospective cohort that analyses every eligible patient from a common time zero and adjusts for the blood pressure, heart rate and electrocardiogram findings that guide treatment, either of them large enough to bound serious complications below a few per cent.

domains.note: Treatment at the emergency physicians' discretion, more often given to patients with higher blood pressure and heart rate (p. 168); groups similar only in age, sex, race and hypertension history; no adjustment for presenting blood pressure, electrocardiogram or troponin, cocaine amount or time since use, co-treatments or other drugs. For the blood-pressure outcome the confounder is the outcome's own starting value (systolic 147.8 vs 135.5 at 0 to 1 h), so later falls also reflect regression to the mean.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Cohort defined by admission to a medical unit and a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain, both settled after treatment and the hospital course; whether patients later diagnosed with infarction were kept is not stated. The 32 comparison patients were chosen from the untreated patients by an undescribed procedure. Follow-up starts at the beta-blocker dose for treated patients and at an unstated time for the comparison group.

Beta-blocker, agent and route taken from records, but whether chest pain was ongoing at the time was judged retrospectively; the comparison group is defined differently in the abstract (no beta-blocker while having chest pain, p. 167) and the Methods (no beta-blockers, p. 168), and later beta-blocker use is not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-treatments in the emergency department are not reported for either group; the beta-blockers were stopped once urine metabolites were found (p. 169).

The numbers with blood pressure, heart rate and troponin in each window are not reported; the troponin denominators are the full 26 and 32 in every window, and the paper does not say whether every patient was tested in every window.

Outcomes taken from records by investigators who knew the treatment; no threshold for a positive troponin and no definition of a cardiac complication; the treated group's windows are anchored to the beta-blocker dose and the comparison group's to an unstated time.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; the text reports lower blood pressure and heart rate at 6 and 12 h without data, the troponin times in the Methods differ from the windows of Table 3, and the printed P values in Table 3 cannot be reproduced with the stated test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Serious risk of bias from confounding by indication, a comparison group selected by an undescribed procedure from a cohort defined by final diagnosis, and outcomes without definitions or a common time zero; with no events among 26 treated patients, imprecision dominates any safety inference (editors' calculation: 95% upper limit 13.2%). It may be cited for what this hospital's records showed: 26 patients given a beta-blocker (18 of them metoprolol) in the emergency department while having cocaine-associated chest pain had no recorded deaths, cardiac complications or rise in group-mean blood pressure or heart rate compared with 32 selected patients. It should not be cited as a cohort of 378, for infarction rates (its troponin counts are not defined as infarctions and the authors report no cardiac complications), as showing that beta-blockers are safe, or for individual agents (2 patients each received propranolol, labetalol, carvedilol and atenolol; no analysis by agent).

key_findings.finding: Of 378 patients admitted with cocaine-induced chest pain between June 2006 and June 2009, 26 were given a beta-blocker in the emergency department while having chest pain and were compared with 32 patients who were not. All outcome data in the paper concern these 58 patients; the rest of the cohort is not described.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods) and Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 167); Results, 1st paragraph, and Table 1 (p. 168)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 320 of the 378 patients have no data in the paper. This is why meta-analyses could pool only 26 vs 32 patients from this study (editors' comparison with sc_lo_2019 and sc_shin_2019); describing it as a cohort of 378 overstates its contribution about 6.5-fold.

key_findings.finding: The comparison patients are described as paired by age, sex, race and history of hypertension, but how they were selected is not reported, the groups differ in size (26 vs 32) and the analyses are unpaired (Mann–Whitney test for blood pressure and heart rate, Fisher's exact test for troponin). Beta-blockers were given at the discretion of the emergency physicians.
The authors state that patients with higher blood pressure and heart rate were more likely to receive a beta-blocker.

Agents and routes among the 26: oral metoprolol 13 (50%), intravenous metoprolol 5 (19%), intravenous labetalol 2 (8%), oral carvedilol 2 (8%), oral atenolol 2 (8%) and oral propranolol 2 (8%); doses not reported and no analysis by agent.
The groups were similar in age (50 vs 48.3 years, P=0.4216), sex (men 88.5% vs 93.8%), race (Black 53.8% vs 46.9%, Hispanic 38.5% vs 50.0%) and history of hypertension (69.2% vs 56.3%, P=0.4163).

In the first window (0 to 1 h) the beta-blocker group had higher blood pressure than the comparison group (systolic 147.8, 95% CI 136.5 to 159.1, vs 135.5, 127.9 to 143.1, P=0.0647; mean arterial 108.2 vs 100.17, P=0.0966) but not a higher heart rate (86.4 vs 87.6, P=0.7786).

No blood-pressure or heart-rate difference was significant at 1–3 h or 3 to 6 h (P from 0.4222 to 0.8911). Group means in the beta-blocker group fell across the windows (systolic 147.8, 135.1, 126.7) and at 3 to 6 h were slightly below the comparison group (systolic 126.7 vs 130.1, P=0.5177; heart rate 73.11 vs 75.8, P=0.4222).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 1–3 h and 3 to 6 h

key_findings.finding: Troponin I was positive in 7/26 vs 7/32 patients at 0–3 h, 4/26 vs 5/32 at 3–6 h and 3/26 vs 5/32 at 6–12 h (printed P 0.8900, 0.7612 and 1.000). The mean values printed beside them (0.1631 vs 0.5406, 0.0923 vs 0.0372, 0.0130 vs 0.0597) carry no units, and the threshold for a positive result is not given.
key_findings.note: The paper does not call these results myocardial infarctions and reports no cardiac complications (p. 168). Editors' calculation of risk ratios for a positive troponin: 1.23 (0.49 to 3.06) at 0–3 h, 0.98 (0.29 to 3.30) at 3–6 h, 0.74 (0.19 to 2.80) at 6–12 h.

key_findings.finding: No cardiac complications were found and no patient died in hospital in either group (0 of 26 and 0 of 32).
key_findings.note: Cardiac complications are not defined. Editors' calculation: the exact 95% upper limit for 0 events in 26 patients is 13.2% (Clopper–Pearson).

key_findings.finding: Length of stay was longer in the beta-blocker group (4.6 vs 2.65 days, P=0.04); the authors suggest, without data, that this might be due to patients who stayed for unrelated reasons (unrelated comorbidities and social problems that prevented discharge).

The authors list as limitations: no standardized follow-up protocol after the beta-blocker, different beta-blockers given intravenously and orally, beta-blockers stopped once urine cocaine metabolites were found, and a qualitative urine test that cannot estimate the amount of cocaine taken.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Discussion say blood pressure and heart rate were lower in the beta-blocker group at 6 and 12 h, but Table 2 has only the windows 0 to 1 h, 1–3 h and 3 to 6 h.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower values claimed at 6 and 12 h cannot be checked; in the last window shown (3 to 6 h) the differences were small and not significant (P 0.4222 to 0.7150).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the treated patients were more hypertensive and tachycardic on admission (p. 169), but in Table 2 their heart rate in the first window was slightly lower than the comparison group's (86.4 vs 87.6, P=0.7786; p. 168).
reporting_issues.consequence: Only blood pressure (systolic 147.8 vs 135.5, P=0.0647) was higher at the start, and not significantly.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give troponin times as admission, 6 h after admission and 12 h later, and blood-pressure times only for treated patients (baseline, 1 to 3 h after the beta-blocker, 3 to 6 h later); Table 3 uses windows 0–3 h, 3–6 h and 6–12 h, and no reference time is given for the comparison group.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which measurement falls in which window, or whether the windows mean the same in both groups. Meta-analysts had to choose: Lo et al. took the 0–3 h row, and Shin et al.'s estimate matches the sum of all three rows (editors' calculations; see replication timeline).

reporting_issues.issue: None of the three P values in Table 3 equals Fisher's exact test, the test the Methods name, on its own row's counts (editors' calculation: 0.7612 at 0–3 h, 1.000 at 3–6 h and 0.7195 at 6–12 h, against printed 0.8900, 0.7612 and 1.000); 0.8900 equals a Yates-corrected chi-squared test of the 0–3 h counts. In Table 1 the P value for sex (0.8078) also matches a Yates-corrected chi-squared test rather than Fisher's exact test (0.6482), while the P values for race and hypertension match exact tests.
reporting_issues.consequence: The P column of Table 3 appears shifted by one row or computed with other tests; no conclusion changes, because every comparison is non-significant either way, but the counts and tests cannot be fully reconciled.

reporting_issues.issue: Troponin positivity has no threshold or units and cardiac complications are not defined; 7 of 26 and 7 of 32 patients had a positive troponin at 0–3 h (Table 3, p. 169), yet the Results report no cardiac complications (p. 168).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any troponin-positive patient had a myocardial infarction cannot be told; meta-analyses that entered these counts as infarctions used a measure the paper does not define as infarction.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group is defined in the abstract as patients who did not receive a beta-blocker while having chest pain (p. 167) and in the Methods as patients who did not receive beta-blockers (p. 168); later beta-blocker use is not reported for either group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast may be early against later or no beta-blocker. The classification of this study's exposure as given during admission while having chest pain or at discharge (as recorded on sc_shin_2019) is not supported by this paper, which describes one dose in the emergency department (p. 168), stopped once urine metabolites were found (p. 169).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the diastolic mean at 1–3 h in the beta-blocker group (80.01) does not match the midpoint of its own interval (72.9 to 87.3) or the printed mean arterial pressure (98.42), both of which imply, by the editors' calculation, about 80.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a transposed digit; no consequence for the conclusions.

Gaps: safety is inferred from zero events in 26 treated patients (editors' calculation: 95% upper limit 13.2%); the Results and Discussion say blood pressure and heart rate were lower at 6 and 12 h (pp. 168–169), times for which no data are shown; the Discussion calls the treated group more tachycardic on admission (p. 169), although Table 2 shows a slightly lower heart rate (86.4 vs 87.6, p. 168); the longer stay is put down to unrelated comorbidities and social problems (p. 168) without data; and a fall in blood pressure in a group treated because its pressure was higher is expected from the natural course and regression to the mean, so it does not show the beta-blocker's effect.
